source_metadata.title: Limited Cutaneous Leishmaniasis as Ulcerated Verrucous Plaque on Leg, Tucson, Arizona, USA
source_metadata.notes: Case report of a 34-year-old man with limited cutaneous leishmaniasis in Arizona, USA.

evidence_events.source_span: The patient had no major medical history and no history of skin cancer or immunosuppression. He came to the dermatology clinic in Tucson, Arizona, because of a new onset of a painless lesion on the right lateral lower leg. The lesion was present for 6 weeks before the visit.
Physical examination demonstrated a 2.1 × 1.1 cm solitary, nonhealing, verrucous plaque with central ulceration on the right proximal lateral pretibial region.

The patient reported considerable time outdoors and recreational activities, such as mountain biking and hiking in Arizona; he specifically denied a history of recent travel outside of the United States and denied any trauma to the site of infection.

Shave biopsy and subsequent staining with hematoxylin and eosin showed focal ulceration with mixed acute, chronic, and granulomatous inflammatory infiltrate and minute organisms in the cytoplasm of histiocytes favoring parasitized histiocytic infection.
The organisms were negative by staining with periodic acid–Schiff.
Microscopic examination by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention observed small intracellular organisms compatible with protozoal amastigotes within macrophages.
Immunohistochemical analysis subsequently confirmed a diagnosis of leishmaniasis.

The patient was referred to an infectious disease department, where observation was recommended because he had a solitary cutaneous lesion that was removed in entirety by biopsy and had no mucosal involvement.

source_metadata.title: Case of elderly onset possible neuro-Behçet’s disease with HLA-B51 homozygosity

evidence_events.source_span: A man in his 70s was referred to our hospital on suspicion of a brain tumour on MRI. The patient first presented to a local doctor due to a 3-day history of gait disturbance, left hemiparaesthesia, dysarthria and dysphagia.

He had a history of uveitis and retinitis pigmentosa in his 30s and was blind. He also had a medical history of hypertension and bronchial asthma and was being treated with esaxerenone, azilsartan, amlodipine and tulobuterol patch.

On physical examination, he had a mild fever of 37.2°C, without headache or consciousness disturbance. He showed no skin rash on the extremities or body trunk. No vulvar ulcers or stomatitis were noted. The pathergy test was negative.

On neurological examination, he showed dysarthria and dysphagia. He displayed mild paraesthesia and hypoesthesia on the left half of the body, including the face. The deep tendon reflexes in the extremities showed hyper-reflexia, and his gait was spastic. Areflexia was detected for the plantar reflexes.

Blood examination revealed no elevation of white cell count, liver enzymes, normal kidney function and no increased levels of cancer markers (carcinoembryonic antigen, carbohydrate antigen 19-9 and soluble interleukin (IL)-2 receptor). Autoimmune antibodies (rheumatoid factor, antinuclear antibody, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, antiaquaporin-4 antibody and antimyelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody) were negative.
Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed normal results without elevation of IL-6 (11.0 pg/mL; normal <17 pg/mL); CSF oligoclonal IgG bands and CSF cytopathology were negative.
HLA analysis revealed homozygosity for the B51 alleles.

MRI of the brain showed hyperintense lesions in the brainstem and left caudate nucleus. These lesions were hyperintense in diffusion-weighted and apparent diffusion coefficient images. Gadolinium enhancement was absent, and MR spectroscopy showed an elevation of the choline peak and preserved N-acetyl aspartate (NAA) peak, suggesting neuroinflammation.
We started oral corticosteroid and colchicine therapy after intravenous methylprednisolone administration (1000 mg/day for 3 days) on suspicion of neuro-Behçet’s disease.

After administration, his symptoms gradually ameliorated, and 2 months later, he returned home with minor sequelae of mild left hemiparesis and gait disturbance. Follow-up MRI showed a reduction of the brain lesions.

source_metadata.title: Dermatomyositis: a debilitating paraneoplastic phenomenon following a diagnosis of localised squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case presentation, investigations, treatment, and outcome sections.

evidence_events.source_span: A female in her 70s presented with postmenopausal paravaginal bleeding alongside slowly progressing weakness in her shoulders.
She was diagnosed with stage IIIC SCC cervix with a 5 cm cervical tumour and 3 cm internal iliac lymph node.

Three weeks following this diagnosis, the patient presented acutely with poor oral intake secondary to dysphagia, plus, difficulty living independently as a result of significant proximal muscle myopathy.

Examination revealed a macular rash of purple/red discolouration over the metacarpophalangeal joints, outer thighs and knees bilaterally, muscle wasting of shoulder girdles and marked proximal muscle weakness; MRC power grade 2/5 in shoulder abduction and hip flexion bilaterally.

Routine blood panel on admission highlighted multiple raised inflammatory markers including CRP 100 mg/L, CK 288 U/L, LDH 415 U/L, AST 102 U/L, WCC 18.2 ×10⁹/L, neutrophils 11.03 ×10⁹/L, sodium 122 mmol/L, urea 10.8 mmol/L, creatinine 116 umol/L.
Serum immunology showed positive anti-NXP2 antibody; anti-TIF1-γ antibody was not tested.
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: Anti-NXP2 positivity supports diagnosis of dermatomyositis and paraneoplastic association.

evidence_events.source_span: MRI of thighs bilaterally showed diffuse heterogeneous, predominantly high T2 signal throughout the pelvic girdle and thigh muscles with marked subcutaneous fat stranding and oedema.

Biopsy of macular rash from lateral aspect left thigh showed basal spongiosis, vacuolar degeneration, mild perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate, no dysplasia or malignancy, and mildly increased dermal mucin on ABPAS staining.
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: Histopathology consistent with dermatomyositis.

evidence_events.source_section: Investigations - Speech and language therapy review
evidence_events.source_span: Double swallow was noted on liquid and solid consistencies with throat clearing, suggesting protective reflex and possible penetration/aspiration.
Baseline lung function showed mild reduction in vital capacity with no significant airflow limitation.

Patient received radical chemoradiotherapy with 28 fractions of radiotherapy and five cycles of weekly Carboplatin, plus 5 days of intravenous immunoglobulins and a 4-week course of prednisolone 40 mg daily.

By day 27, all cutaneous lesions had resolved and the patient was independent of personal care; at 1 month post-discharge, good arm movement and no swallowing difficulty; at 3 months post-discharge, steroids discontinued and symptoms continued to improve with complete oncological response on MRI and CT-PET.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: By day 27; 1 month post-discharge; 3 months post-discharge

source_metadata.title: Case of primary low-grade neuroendocrine carcinoma of the skin
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case presentation, investigations, outcome, and discussion sections.

evidence_events.source_span: A man in his late 30s presented to his general practitioner with a small skin tumour of 4 mm underneath his left nipple that caused pain when he was wearing clothes. The tumour had been present for 5–6 years.

On the H&E-stained slides, a 4 mm tumour was found in the dermis with a solid pattern in the centre and a more organoid pattern without any necrosis or mucin in the border of the tumour, deeper in the dermis.
The tumour cells were fairly uniform with oval to round nuclei with dispersed chromatin, inconspicuous nucleoli and eosinophilic and fine granular cytoplasm. The mitotic counts were 8 per 2 mm².

The immunohistochemical staining was positive in the peripheral part of the tumour for synaptophysin, CD56, S-100, SOX-10, SATB2, ISLET-1 and dot-like positive stain for pan cytokeratin (AE1/AE3). The centre of the tumour stained negative for synaptophysin but was partly positive for CD56, S-100 and SOX-10. Staining was negative for CK7, CK20, TTF-1, Melan A, chromogranin A, CDX-2, serotonin, MSA, MITF, CD45, CD3, CD20 and Merkel Cell Polyomavirus (MCPyV). The KI-67 index varied but was up to 10%.

After removal of the tumour, a whole-body fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography (FDG-PET) scan was negative, while a Gallium-PET scan highlighted two cutaneous lesions above the umbilicus, equivalent to the position of two birthmarks. The birthmarks were not malignant.
The patient has been followed every 6 months with CT/MRI scans for 30 months now, and there is no sign of recurrence or of any other primary neuroendocrine tumour (NET).

source_metadata.title: A Rare Coexistence: Cutaneous Lobular Carcinoma with Pyoderma Gangrenosum

evidence_events.source_span: An 84-year-old woman presented to the dermatology clinic with concern of a “rash” on her anterior chest wall and ulcerations on her lower extremities present for the past 6 years.

Her past medical history included rheumatoid arthritis, ulcerative colitis, acid reflux, venous insufficiency, hypertension, stage III chronic kidney disease, and lobular breast carcinoma in remission.
She received acetaminophen and tramadol for her arthritis, furosemide for her kidney disease, and hydralazine for her hypertension.
The remission of the patient’s lobular carcinoma and subsequent development of ulcers occurred 6 years prior to her presentation at our clinic.
She reported the development of ulcerative lesions on her bilateral lower extremities 1 year after remission of her lobular carcinoma.
The lower-extremity lesions first appeared on her left leg and were attributed to venous insufficiency.
Healing of these ulcerations was slowed due to multiple secondary infections caused by Corynebacterium striatum, which required treatment with intravenous vancomycin and ceftriaxone.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: treatment with intravenous vancomycin and ceftriaxone

evidence_events.source_span: Following initial surgical debridement and weekly dressing changes, the lesions progressively worsened, with increased pain and edema in and around the ulcerated areas and increased size of the lesions.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: surgical debridement and weekly dressing changes

evidence_events.source_span: She was evaluated by vascular surgery for her venous insufficiency due to the slow healing time, but no additional treatment was recommended.
The ulcerations then appeared on her right leg. More lesions developed and worsened concurrently with the development of a rash on her anterior chest wall.
Upon presentation to our dermatology clinic, physical examination revealed a 20×13 cm erythematous, hardened plaque covering most of the patient’s anterior chest wall.
Multiple ulcerations were found on the medial and lateral aspects of both ankles. The lesions on her extremities presented as erythematous, friable, bleeding ulcers with a well-defined border.

A histopathological review of the chest wall biopsy was consistent with the diagnosis of recurrent cutaneous metastatic lobular carcinoma with lymphovascular invasion. The carcinoma was positive for polyclonal keratin and negative for E-cadherin.
The histopathological report of the lower extremities showed reactive epidermal changes and undermining of the adjacent epidermis consistent with well-developed lesions of pyoderma gangrenosum.
After a dermatological evaluation, standardized wound care and oral prednisone treatment were initiated for PG, resulting in 50% improvement based on decreased lesion size, depth, and erythema.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: standardized wound care and oral prednisone treatment

evidence_events.source_span: Radiation therapy for her metastatic lobular carcinoma was discussed but not initiated due to the coronavirus pandemic; the patient died soon after.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: not initiated due to pandemic; patient died soon after

source_metadata.title: Case report: A case of Paget disease outside the axillary breast

evidence_events.source_span: A 57 year old female patient presented with a left axillary mass for over 2 years. Two years ago, the patient had no obvious cause of a lump about the size of peanuts in the left armpit. The surface was red and swollen, without pain or tenderness, and there was no nipple discharge. Recently, the patient realized that the lump had increased and the surface skin was ulcerated.

Physical examination: Bilateral breasts are symmetrical, with average breast development. Bilateral nipples were normal and there was no nipple discharge. A red and swollen area of 3 cm × 2 cm in size could be seen in the left armpit, accompanied by ulceration and a small amount of secretions. A mass of approximately 3.0 cm × 2.0 cm in size could be palpated in the left armpit, which was hard and had a clear boundary, with moderate activity. No obvious abnormal mass could be palpated in the right breast, and no obvious enlarged lymph nodes could be palpated in the right armpit.

Laboratory and auxiliary examinations: Blood routine, coagulation, and bowel and bowel routine tests were all normal. No abnormalities were found in liver and kidney function, electrolytes, blood sugar, and blood lipids. The myocardial enzyme spectrum and tumor 7 items were all within the normal range. Hepatitis A, B, C, human immunodeficiency virus, and syphilis showed no significant abnormalities. Among the 5 items of thyroid function, anti thyroglobulin antibodies were 188.50 IU/mL, and anti thyroid microsomal antibodies were > 1000.0 IU/mL.
The electrocardiogram indicated sinus rhythm and changes in some lead T waves.

Chest and abdominal computed tomography plain scan showed several miliary lesions in both lungs and hepatic steatosis. No obvious abnormalities were found in the gallbladder, pancreas, spleen, kidneys, and bladder.
No obvious abnormalities were found on plain and enhanced dual breast magnetic resonance imaging scans.

Breast ultrasound indicates hypoechoic areas in both breasts, considering the possibility of breast adenosis, the United States of America breast imaging reporting and data system Class 2, bilateral lipoma, and left axillary lymph node enlargement.
The postoperative pathology of Jiangxi Provincial Dermatology Hospital is consistent with Paget disease outside the armpit breast.

Under general anesthesia, left subaxillary mass resection, freezing and left breast cancer breast conserving surgery was performed. The size of the tissue, including the lesion, was approximately 7 cm × 5 cm and frozen during the surgery. The results showed that fibrous adipose tissue can be seen in the left armpit, and a large number of inflammatory cells infiltrate. The diagnosis was to be confirmed by paraffin section.

The postoperative pathology of the left axillary mass combined with morphological and immunohistochemical results was consistent with Paget disease. The pathological examination of the skin lesions showed an abundance of keratinization in the epidermis, a large number of atypical cells in the epithelial layer, infiltration of interstitial lymphocytes, and infiltration of Paget cells in the superficial dermis.
Postoperative immunohistochemistry showed estrogen receptor (+, 20%), progesterone receptor (−), human epidermal growth factor receptor-2 (3+), Ki-67 (30%), cytokine7 (+), and p63 (−).

The patient incision healed well after surgery and did not undergo chemotherapy or radiotherapy. Regular follow-up and endocrine therapy were recommended for at least 5 years. Following up for 16 months, there has been no local recurrence, no swelling of the right axillary lymph node, no distant metastasis found on follow-up, and no complications such as upper limb lymphedema, upper limb sensory abnormalities, or motor disorders have been observed.

source_metadata.title: Infection may play an important role in the pathogenesis of alveolar osteonecrosis following facial herpes zoster: a case report and literature review

evidence_events.source_span: A 67-year-old man presented to the dermatology clinic with a 5-week history of erythema and clustered blisters accompanied by great pain in the right face

He had a severe toothache in the upper right jaw, was diagnosed with acute periodontitis and HZ, and was treated with intravenous ceftizoxime and metronidazole and oral acetaminophen for 2 weeks, but facial rashes worsened

A 10-day regimen of oral valacyclovir 1 g twice a day was initiated, but intense pain was not relieved and four teeth of his upper right jaw exfoliated in succession 10 days before he visited our clinic

The patient had a 30-year on-and-off history of toothache, poor oral hygiene with decayed teeth, residual roots, and periapical cysts, and a history of hypertension and hepatitis B virus infection; no history of tumors, radiotherapy, or antiangiogenic/antiresorptive drugs

Extraoral exam showed pigmentation and scars on the right face; intraoral exam revealed complete loss of crowns from teeth 11 to 17 and 35, gingival recession, and exposure of alveolar process in the right maxillary arch

Laboratory tests showed normal coagulation, blood glucose, urine and stool tests, ECG, chest radiography; HIV antibody negative; HBV DNA 4.18 × 10^5 IU/mL; elevated WBC 10.84 × 10^9/L; CRP 20.8 mg/L; slightly elevated ALT 54 U/L and serum creatinine 138 μmol/L; ultrasonography showed multiple hepatic and renal cysts

Panoramic radiography revealed decreased bone density and poor alveolar socket healing in the right maxilla with decayed teeth, residual roots, and periapical cysts; CT showed empty tooth sockets on the right maxilla

Biopsy of alveolar process and adjacent mucous membrane showed hyperplasia of squamous epithelium with no atypia, fibrinoid necrosis of vascular walls, lumen occlusion, infiltration of histiocytes and neutrophils, fragments of nonvital lamellar bone devoid of osteoblasts and osteocytes, surrounded by neutrophils and bacterial aggregates

During debridement, extensive malodorous osteonecrosis was observed in the right maxilla; postoperative pathology showed similar findings to biopsy with osteonecrosis, neutrophils, and bacterial aggregates inside marrow cavity

Bacterial culture of necrotic bone tissue identified Prevotella denticola, Streptococcus intermedius, Actinomycetes oris, and Actinomyces viscosus; next-generation sequencing detected Prevotella, Streptococcus, Lactobacillus, Veillonella, Actinomyces, Candida, varicella-zoster virus (VZV), hepatitis B virus (HBV), human gammaherpesvirus 4, and Torque teno virus

During the perioperative period, the patient received a 7-day regimen of oral valacyclovir and antibiotic therapy with intravenous cefathiamidine and oral cefuroxime; granulation tissue formation was observed three weeks after debridement; at 9-month follow-up, no further tooth exfoliation was found

source_metadata.title: Successful Treatment of Angiolymphoid Hyperplasia with Eosinophilia Associated with Scalp Demodicosis Using Cryotherapy and Topical Metronidazole

evidence_events.source_span: A 25-year-old female patient presented to a dermatology clinic in Rustaq, Oman, in 2021 with multiple, itchy, pearly papules on her scalp of approximately 6 months duration
She reported ulcerations and discrete bleeding after scratching due to pruritus and denied any history of systemic symptoms or local trauma
Clinical examination of the scalp showed multiple, grouped, erythematous papules and nodules, with an average diameter of 1 cm, located on the left temporo-occipital region
The systemic examination was unremarkable and there was no evidence of regional or systemic lymphadenopathy
A complete blood count (including eosinophils), renal function test, serum immunoglobulin E levels, HIV screening and urine analysis were all normal

Following a biopsy of one of the lesions, the histopathological examination revealed the proliferation of variable-sized blood vessels lined by plump histiocytoid endothelial cells, as well as inflammatory infiltrates comprising lymphocytes and eosinophils in the dermis
The biopsy also revealed evidence of Demodex mite infestation in the sebaceous ducts
Based on these histopathological and clinical features, a diagnosis of ALHE and scalp demodicosis was made
The patient was treated with 10 sessions of cryotherapy (each session consisted of 2 freeze-thaw cycles per week for each lesion) and twice-daily application of a topical metronidazole gel
The patient showed remarkable clinical improvement within 7 weeks
She was subsequently followed-up for the next year with no signs of recurrence or new lesions appearing

source_metadata.title: Epithelioid Hemangioendothelioma as a Dangerous, Easy to Miss, and Nearly Impossible to Clinically Diagnose Condition: Case Report
source_metadata.notes: Extraction based on Case Report section and associated figures/tables.

evidence_events.source_span: A 24-year-old woman presented to our dermatology clinic with a left posterior auricular papule and left preauricular papule present for 8 and 4 months, respectively.
The patient had no significant medical or social history, including no tobacco or heavy alcohol use. Both lesions were painful and progressively enlarging. The patient denied any other symptoms.
Shave biopsy was taken of both lesions.
The histology of both lesions demonstrated cellular dermal proliferations of epithelioid cells with the eosinophilic cytoplasm arranged in cords within a myxohyaline stroma.
Subtle vacuoles containing red blood cells were present within some of the cells.
Histological and immunohistochemical findings were consistent with the diagnosis of EHE.
Computed tomography (CT) scans of the head, neck, chest, abdomen, and pelvis were performed.
Innumerable bilateral pulmonary nodules, a 1.8-cm hypoattenuated hepatic lesion, and prominent bilateral axillary lymph nodes were noted, all consistent with metastatic disease.
After seeking multiple opinions from oncology, our patient elected the watchful waiting approach. Serial CT scans every 3 months were recommended to monitor disease progression.

source_metadata.title: Aquagenic urticaria: presentation, diagnosis and management

evidence_events.source_span: A girl in her early adolescence with no significant medical history other than known allergies to dust, rabbits and cats was referred to our clinic, presenting with an urticarial rash.
She presented with a 2-year history, starting around menarche, of multiple pinpoint sized wheals with surrounding 1–3 cm erythematous flares which developed immediately after contact with water.
The lesions occurred immediately after water exposure, irrespective of temperature or source including showering/bathing, swimming pools, seawater and getting rain soaked.
Each episode typically lasted approximately 30–60 min and would spontaneously resolve without the use of medication.

The patient did not experience any symptoms due to exposure to sweat, or tears, however, she reported abdominal discomfort while drinking water and symptomatic episodes when in contact with animal saliva.
She had no systemic reactions, such as headache, shortness of breath, wheezing, dizziness or fainting and no family history of urticaria.
The individual did not show any other forms of inducible urticaria.
On physical examination, skin appeared clear with a distinct absence of dermographism.

A routine laboratory evaluation was performed, encompassing a complete blood count, liver and renal function tests, urine analysis, panels for immunoglobulins, thyroid function tests, all yielding results within normal limits, ruling out any underlying abnormalities.
After discontinuing antihistamines for 1 week, a water provocation test was administered involving regional contact using a damp cloth on the patient’s trunk, maintained at 35°C.
After 20 min, there was a development of urticarial eruption on the trunk, consistent with the patient’s natural exposure to water.
Cetirizine, a second-generation H1 antihistamine, was prescribed at 10 mg daily, leading to further symptom relief.
At the 8-month follow-up, she did not report any further episodes of symptoms, unless a dosage of cetirizine was missed.
At the 14-month follow-up, the patient continued to report further improvement in her condition, enabling participation in daily activities without restrictions.

source_metadata.title: Diagnostic Challenges of Multiple Sporotrichoid Skin Lesions Caused by Mycobacterium marinum

evidence_events.source_span: A 23-year-old man working in aquarium management presented with a chronic progression of multiple skin nodules on his right forearm and thumb.
The patient was referred from the Dermatology Department to the Outpatient Clinic due to suspected skin tuberculosis, as indicated by a positive T-SPOT.TB test.

Physical examination revealed a 3-cm nodule on the radial side of the right forearm with a crusted surface, mild surrounding erythema, no spontaneous pain, and tenderness upon palpation; a similar 1-cm nodule was noted near the proximal phalanx of the right thumb.

Laboratory test results revealed a white blood cell count of 6000/μL, hemoglobin of 14.8 g/dL, platelet count of 254×10³/μL, creatinine of 0.81 mg/dL, liver enzymes within normal limits, and C-reactive protein less than 0.04 mg/dL.

Whole-trunk computed tomography with contrast revealed no findings in the chest or lymphadenopathy; magnetic resonance imaging of the right forearm showed increased fat tissue density but no evidence of subcutaneous abscess or osteomyelitis.

The initial excisional biopsy performed at 37°C was negative for acid-fast bacilli culture and PCR for tuberculosis; the second excisional biopsy performed and stored at around 30°C was positive for Mycobacterium marinum by PCR sequencing.
Histopathology of the second biopsy revealed moderate infiltration of inflammatory cells without epithelioid granulomas, multinucleated giant cells, or necrosis.
Cultures incubated at 32°C on Ogawa medium detected colonies by day 11, and PCR sequencing confirmed Mycobacterium marinum.
Susceptibility testing showed low minimum inhibitory concentrations for clarithromycin, rifabutin, moxifloxacin, and linezolid among others.
Initial treatment with rifabutin and clarithromycin was started; due to liver dysfunction, regimen was changed to moxifloxacin and rifabutin, then to linezolid and clarithromycin due to nausea.
The patient's skin nodular lesions showed a trend toward resolution with flattening and fading of pigmentation over 7 months of treatment.

source_metadata.title: Hyperpigmented mycosis fungoides with histological spongiosis in a 61-year-old Syrian male: a case report
source_metadata.notes: Extraction based on case presentation and discussion sections with source order preserved.

evidence_events.source_span: A 61-year-old Syrian male with a history of alcoholism and heavy smoking presented to the dermatology department with complaints of itchy pigmented lesions without telangiectasias, scaling, or atrophy on the right side of his trunk and his right thigh.

These lesions were persistent for 3 years, and the patient was previously prescribed a topical 0.1% hydrocortisone cream by a local dermatologist to relieve the itching; the patient used the cream intermittently and only when the itching was severe.
The patient denied prior history of exposure to chemicals or solvents, and there was no family history of skin cancers, skin diseases, or relevant systemic conditions.
Upon clinical examination, hyperpigmented patches on the right side of his trunk and the lateral surface of his right thigh were evident, with no other clinical features.
Blood tests of the patient were all within normal ranges except a slight increase in the white blood cell count.

A skin biopsy was performed for further evaluation, and histopathological examination of the biopsy revealed parakeratosic hyperkeratosic epidermis with slight spongiosis. Papillary dermis was infiltrated moderately by atypical lymphocytes with mild deposition of melanophages. Lymphocytic infiltrate was situated in clusters and in linear basilar distribution along the dermoepidermal junction.
Immunochemistry of the atypical lymphocytes were CD3+, CD8+, CD4−, CD20−.
A chest and abdomen computed tomography (CT) scan was conducted, but yielded only normal findings with no lymphadenopathy or organomegaly.

The patient was diagnosed with early stage hyperpigmented mycosis fungoides and was subsequently treated with psoralen and ultraviolet A light (PUVA) therapy, with oral 8-methoxypsoralen two times a week, and was prescribed a topical 0.1% betamethasone dipropionate.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: PUVA therapy and topical betamethasone prescribed

evidence_events.source_span: After 12 weeks of treatment, the itching was relieved, and the hyperpigmentation regressed, but did not disappear.

source_metadata.title: Primary cutaneous adenoid cystic carcinoma arising in the scalp: a diagnostic challenge

evidence_events.source_span: A woman in her 20s presented to the plastic surgery clinic with chief complaints of a persistent swelling localised to the right posterior scalp associated with pruritus first observed approximately 4 months prior to consultation.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: first observed approximately 4 months prior to consultation

evidence_events.source_span: Dermatological examination revealed the presence of two right parieto-occipital scalp lesions: a subcutaneous, mobile, tender cystic structure measuring 12 mm in diameter with intact overlying skin, and a second lesion, 11 mm in diameter, erythematous with irregular borders, soft consistency and brown discolouration; both lesions had a thickness of 3 mm.
The most likely differentials were lipoma or epidermoid cyst; however, it was essential to rule out adenoid basal carcinoma of the skin and primary cutaneous mucinous carcinoma.
Sonographic evaluation of the scalp revealed two adjacent hypoechoic lesions located in the parietal region, with the largest measuring 10×8 mm, resembling epidermoid cysts.

An initial excisional biopsy of the second lesion was performed under local anaesthesia and submitted for histopathological analysis revealing a basaloid cutaneous lesion consistent with adenoid cystic carcinoma.

Immunohistochemistry showed patchy infiltrates positively staining for epithelial membrane antigen at the apical aspect of the pseudo glandular cyst and diffuse positive staining for pan-cytokeratin (AE1/AE3).

A multidisciplinary team meeting led to performing a PET-CT scan which revealed absence of fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) uptake or hypermetabolic activity, with normal physiological FDG distribution in lymph nodes, organs and bone marrow.
Wide local excision of the two scalp lesions was performed with 2 cm peripheral margins extending to the skull's periosteum, followed by reconstruction using a rotational local flap.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: wide local excision and rotational flap reconstruction

evidence_events.source_span: Histopathological examination of the excised tissue confirmed the diagnosis of PCACC and demonstrated clear surgical margins.

The postoperative phase was uneventful with appropriate wound healing and no evidence of infection; the patient was enrolled in a long-term follow-up protocol with clinical examinations every 3–6 months for 2 years, then annually.

source_metadata.title: An Atypical Presentation of VEXAS Syndrome: A Diagnostic Conundrum

evidence_events.source_span: A 76-year-old man presented with a 5 year history of an intermittent rash characterised by erythematous, granulomatous , discoid plaques on his trunk, arms, and back
The rash flared intermittently with new areas persistently developing throughout the 5 year period. He had no joint swelling, no night sweats, and no weight loss.

The first biopsy demonstrated a superficial dermal inflammatory infiltrate of histiocyte-like cells and scattered neutrophils. The original reporting pathologist suggested several possible differential diagnoses including sweet’s syndrome and interstitial granulomatous dermatitis.
He was commenced on a 3 monthly trial of Colchicine 500 micrograms BD with no improvement in his rash.

He had a background history of normocytic anaemia, left lower para-aortic lymph node, inguinal hernia, prostatism, hyperlipidaemia and hip osteoarthritis. Laboratory tests showed normocytic anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and elevated inflammatory markers

As his condition evolved, the rash reappeared with a new-onset inflammatory arthritis affecting his shoulder, wrist and 1st metacarpal phalangeal joint. This was associated with fatigue, joint pain and stiffness in hands
He was administered I.M. Depomedrone which gave him relief for few days but his joint pain recurred again.

A further skin biopsy of the rash was performed which demonstrated similar features to the original. This contained more prominent papillary dermal edema. Both neutrophils and histiocyte-like cells stain with myeloid cell nuclear differentiation antigen and myeloperoxidase. This indicates that the histiocyte-like cells are in fact immature myeloid precursors and confirms the diagnosis of histiocytoid sweet’s syndrome.

The reporting haematopathologist considered the possibility of VEXAS syndrome based on thrombocytopenia, arthritis, blood investigations and clinical record review. Dermatopathology agreed and recommended genetic testing.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: clinical record review and multidisciplinary consultation

evidence_events.source_span: Subsequent genetic testing identified a pathogenic variant in the UBA1 gene with a variant allele frequency of 27.7%, confirming the diagnosis of VEXAS.
He was placed on long-term steroid therapy of Prednisolone. He responded very well to steroids with complete clearance of rash and resolution of shoulder pain.

source_metadata.title: Epidermophyton floccosum, an etiological agent of tinea pedis and tinea unguium: about two cases
source_metadata.notes: Case report of two elderly patients with dermatophytosis due to Epidermophyton floccosum, including clinical, mycological, and molecular evidence.

evidence_events.source_span: a 70-year-old patient with history of diabetes type 2 on oral antidiabetics and rheumatoid arthritis on tocilizumab, presented with fever and painful swelling of the right leg
clinical examination showed erythematous, well-demarcated, warm and tender to the touch plaque of the leg, scaly plantar keratoderma and intertrigo of all toe web spaces
a mycological sampling on the Toe web spaces and soles of feet was carried out. Direct examination objectified mycelial filaments
The culture after 5 days showed radiated powdery colonies of khaki yellow color
Direct examination of the colony showed terminal and intercalary chlamydospores
a real-time PCR was performed using the DermaGenius® 2.0 kit ... This allowed the identification of Epidermophyton floccosum
the patient was put on amoxicillin and clavulanic acid and terbinafine ointment twice daily
a 70-year-old patient with no medical history consulted for damage to the nails of the two big toes that had been evolving for one year
clinical examination showed bilateral subungual hyperkeratosis, longitudinal melanonychia on the right, xanthonychia and distal onycholysis on the left
a mycological sample was taken with visualization at direct examination of mycelial filaments
The culture showed beige glabrous colonies on the front and smooth brown on the back
Microscopy examination showed intercalary and terminal chlamydospores with club-shaped macroconidia clustered in a banana bunch
Epidermophyton floccosum was identified on these microscopic criteria as well as confirmation by real-time PCR
the patient was put on terbinafine 250 mg daily for 6 months (patient ongoing treatment)

evidence_events.source_span: Physical examination identified verruca vulgaris on the limbs and face.
Laboratory examinations demonstrated CD4+ T lymphocytopenia, low levels of C3 complement, and positive antinuclear antibodies.
Renal function tests indicated nephrotic syndrome.

Laboratory tests showed CD4+ T cell counts persistently below 150 cells/μL despite treatment and near quiescent lupus activity.

source_metadata.title: Necrolytic migratory erythema as the first manifestation of pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor

evidence_events.source_span: A 44-year-old woman presented with a 3-month history of pruritic rash of the extremities and oral cavity. The rash progressed to involve the groin, abdomen, axillae, and gluteal region. She was found to have well demarcated, erythematous plaques in these regions. Tiny fragile vesicles were observed at the margins of several plaques.
The patient underwent allergen patch testing, which was negative, and was treated with topical steroids without clinical improvement.

Skin biopsy revealed psoriasiform acanthosis and abrupt necrosis of the upper layers of stratum; whereas the lower half of epidermis appears viable, the detached necrolytic portion appears pale with pyknotic nuclei. Perivascular lymphocytic infiltration and scattered extravasated red blood cells were present in the upper dermis.

A glucagon level was obtained and a contrast-enhanced CT scan was conducted. Her level of serum glucagon was elevated at 720 ng/L (normal values 40 to 130 ng/L) and the scan revealed a 3-cm enhancing pancreatic head mass.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: serum glucagon measurement, contrast-enhanced CT scan

evidence_events.source_span: Admission laboratory measurements demonstrated hyperglycemia (132 mg/dL, normal values 60 to 99 mg/dL) and anemia (hemoglobin 11.4, normal values 12 to 16 g/dL). Serum levels of chromogranin A were elevated (243 ng/mL, normal value <96 ng/mL), as were levels of glycosylated hemoglobin (6.3%, normal value <5.7%) and the patient was diagnosed with diabetes mellitus.
On hospital day 7, she underwent pancreaticoduodenectomy.
Pathology confirmed a pancreatic neuroendocrine carcinoma with evidence of vascular and perineural invasion, consistent with a diagnosis of a glucagonoma.

In the days following her operation, the patient was admitted to the ICU, where she faced pancreatic fistula that resolved with non-operative care. Her glucagon and glucose blood levels dropped dramatically post-operatively. One week after the surgery, the patient's cutaneous lesions almost disappeared.
Currently, more than 1 year post-operatively, there was no sign of cutaneous or systemic disease.

evidence_events.source_span: During clinical examination, besides the presence of secretion, granulation tissue (detected only in the first consultation), erythema and pain, we observed an increase in the nail plate transverse curvature, causing the ingrowth
In the external corner of the same nail we noted the presence of xanthonychia, thickening of the nail plate, and heightened transverse curvature
Dermoscopy of the free edge of the nail plate showed the presence of small perforations, limited to the site of the thickening
MRI was requested and revealed the presence of filament-like digitations protruding from the matrix
The patient underwent surgery with the diagnosis later confirmed by anatomopathological examination
After a year of follow-up there was no sign of relapse or ungual dystrophy

The patient reported general weakness, loss of appetite, weight loss, and dark urine for several weeks. presenting_symptoms: dark gray skin coloration on face, neck, and upper torso
known_prior_history: 2 surgeries due to malignant melanoma (MM): in 1981 lesion on left thigh removed, in 2011 dark ulcerated tumor 2 cm diameter removed from left scapular region, histological diagnosis nodular type MM, Clark IV, Breslow >3 mm, sentinel node metastasis identified

source_metadata.title: Diffuse melanosis cutis related to dermal micrometastases as the first clinical symptom of distant metastatic malignant melanoma
source_metadata.notes: Case report of a 72-year-old man with diffuse melanosis cutis as first clinical sign of metastatic melanoma progression.

evidence_events.source_span: A 72-year-old caucasian man suffering from angina pectoris, hypertension, type 2 diabetes, with a history of coronary angioplasty was admitted to the Department of Dermatology for diagnosis of a dark gray skin coloration which had been present for 4 months.
The pigmentation intensity was most pronounced on the face, neck, and upper torso.
The patient reported general weakness, loss of appetite, weight loss, and dark urine for several weeks.
Two weeks before admission, other causes for the skin discoloration, that is, Addison's disease, and porphyria were excluded.

The patient had a history of 2 surgeries due to MM: in 1981 on the left thigh and in 2011 a nodular type MM, Clark IV, Breslow more than 3 mm, was removed from the left scapular region; the sentinel node showed subcapsular MM metastasis.
Nine months after the second surgery, a generalized blue–gray discoloration of the skin appeared.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: Nine months after the second surgery

evidence_events.source_span: Four months later, a diagnostic skin biopsy was taken from his right shoulder area and revealed intracellular and extracellular melanin deposition in the dermis.

Intracellular melanin was detected in CD68(+) macrophages and melanoma metastatic cells with immunohistochemical profile: Melan-A (+), HMB45 (+), S100(+), CD68 (−), distributed in deep layers of the dermis.
Laboratory tests indicated slightly increased CA 15-3 antigen, beta-2-microglobulin, AST, ALT, and triglycerides levels; serum S100 protein was elevated at 19.320 μg/L (normal < 0.105 μg/L).
Urine analysis showed brown-amber color but no other abnormalities.
Imaging tests including abdominal, thyroid and cardiac ultrasonography, chest x-ray and CT, colonoscopy, PET-CT revealed a 2 cm tumor in the right kidney.
The patient refused treatment and died eight months after DMC appeared.

hidden_reference.final_diagnosis_verbatim: Diffuse melanosis cutis related to dermal micrometastases as the first clinical symptom of distant metastatic malignant melanoma.
diagnostic_reasoning_verbatim_spans: Histological and immunohistochemical examinations of DMC biopsy indicated melanoma metastatic cells as well as free deposits of melanin and melanophage presence in the dermis.
The patient had a history of two melanomas treated surgically 30 years and 9 months before present hospitalization.
Nine months after the second surgery, a generalized blue–gray discoloration of the skin appeared.
No anticancer treatment was administered before DMC developed.
The pathomechanisms of the discoloration of the skin are not fully explained.
The role of micrometastases, as well as melanin precursors, released during lysis of MM metastases, and growth factors may play a role in the development of the symptom.
diagnostic_reasoning_items: Diffuse melanosis cutis (DMC) is a rare sign of malignant melanoma progression.
DMC usually develops after about one year from melanoma diagnosis in patients with metastatic tumors and after cytostatic treatment, but in this case appeared without prior chemotherapy.
Skin biopsy confirmed melanoma micrometastases and melanin deposits in the dermis.
Elevated serum S100 protein supports melanoma activity.
Imaging revealed a renal tumor, but the main cause of DMC was dermal micrometastases.
Patient outcome was poor, dying eight months after DMC onset.
hidden_reference.final_diagnosis: Diffuse melanosis cutis due to dermal micrometastases from metastatic malignant melanoma.
hidden_reference.diagnostic_reasoning: The diagnosis was confirmed by skin biopsy showing melanoma micrometastases and melanin deposits. The patient's history of melanoma with sentinel node metastasis and the timing of skin discoloration support the diagnosis. Elevated serum S100 protein and imaging findings further support disease progression. The absence of chemotherapy and presence of micrometastases suggest DMC was caused by dermal melanoma micrometastases rather than tumor lysis syndrome.
hidden_reference.article_derived_evidence_summary: Patient with history of melanoma developed diffuse melanosis cutis nine months after surgery. Skin biopsy confirmed melanoma micrometastases and melanin deposits. Laboratory and imaging studies supported disease progression. Patient died eight months after DMC onset.

source_metadata.title: Langerhans' cell histiocytosis with neurological injuries diagnosed from a single cutaneous lesion

evidence_events.source_span: A 45-year-old, white, male patient had exhibited, for the past two years, a partially ulcerated, circular, erythematous infiltrate plaque, measuring 2cm in diameter, on the right scapular region

For the past six years, he had been under neurological investigation for imbalance, diplopia, and slurred speech, and the case had evolved to an inability to walk, dysphagia, and dysarthria a short time before the last appointment

Nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) imaging of the encephalon showed diffuse encephalic volumetric reduction and multiple hyperintense lesions in T2 and Flair, with no expansive nature, the majority of which impaired the cerebellar bridge and peduncles - findings considered to be unspecific
Muscular biopsy on the left biceps and biopsy of the cerebellar peduncle were inconclusive

Histopathology of the skin lesion revealed the proliferation of histiocytic cells with increased volume and hyperchromatic nuclei, abundant cytoplasm and multinucleate areas exhibiting atypical mitosis figures, associated with eosinophils, attacking the entire reticular dermis
The immunohistochemistry was positive for CD1A, protein S100 and langerin markers
The patient received pulse therapy with methylprednisolone, with was no response; later on, the patient developed diabetes insipidus

Two months later, a new NMR of the encephalon revealed an expansive lesion with an extra-axial, right parietal calcification, involving the meninges and the internal bone plate, and compressing the encephalon, suggesting a bone lesion by histiocytosis
The patient was subjected to decompressive neurosurgery; chemotherapy was also indicated

The histopathological examination of the calvarium and the dura mater (surgical piece) also revealed alterations that were compatible with LCH, in addition to hemorrhage and necrosis areas, confirming they had been impaired by the disease
The condition evolved with pneumonia, a worsened general medical condition, and death

source_metadata.title: An illusion of septic shock: acute generalised exanthematous pustulosis with multiorgan dysfunction
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case presentation, investigations, treatment, and outcome sections with source-grounded evidence events and milestones.

evidence_events.source_span: A 61-year-old man with morbid obesity, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease, hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus was admitted to the hospital for a 1-week history of acute onset rapidly progressive diffusely erythematous rash within the deep folds of his pannus and in the intertriginous areas.
The rash was refractory to over-the-counter topical nystatin therapy which the patient had used at home for 5 days prior to admission.

On initial presentation, the rash was suspicious for candidal intertrigo based on the appearance of the rash and presence of risk factors (obesity, DM). Erythrasma was also high on the differential diagnosis based on coral red florescence noted with woods lamp, appearance of the rash and presence of risk factors (obesity and DM).
The patient was started empirically on oral erythromycin and oral fluconazole for possible erythrasma and candidal intertrigo since the rash was extensive.
Within 3 days, the patient's rash spread diffusely across his trunk and extremities to form erythematous morbilliform papules which coalesced to form plaques.

Within 12 hours of noticeably worsening rash, the patient acutely decompensated, became short of breath and developed metabolic and respiratory acidosis, requiring transfer to the intensive care unit.
He was initially started on BiPAP, however, due to increasing somnolence he was intubated.
He was noted to be hypotensive, not responsive to intravenous fluid resuscitation. Patient was started on vasopressor support with norepinephrine.
He also developed shock liver and acute kidney failure requiring CVVHD.
Complete Blood Count revealed neutrophilic leucocytosis (white blood cell 31.10 × 10^9/L).
Basic Metabolic Profile and Arterial Blood Gas Analysis showed acute kidney failure (creatinine 3.06 mg/dL, hyperkalaemia 6.3 mmol/L, phosphorus 7.0 mg/dL), metabolic and respiratory acidosis.
Liver Function Tests were consistent with shock liver (AST 4902 units/mL and ALT 3073 units/mL).
Infectious workup was negative including normal chest X-ray, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis without focal infection, and negative blood and urine cultures.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: CXR, CT, blood and urine cultures

evidence_events.source_span: Superficial wound culture grew polymicrobial skin flora including Streptococcus agalactiae, rare Proteus mirabilis, rare Klebsiella and coagulase-negative Staphylococcus.

Skin biopsy showed diffuse spongiosis and numerous subcorneal pustules filled with a mixed inflammatory infiltrate predominately consisting of neutrophils with some lymphocytes, establishing a diagnosis of AGEP.
Erythromycin and fluconazole were immediately discontinued on acute decompensation.
Broad spectrum antibiotics (vancomycin, meropenem, micafungin) were started initially but discontinued after negative infectious workup.
Patient was treated with methylprednisolone 80 mg every 8 hours for 3 days with eventual slow taper on oral steroids.

The patient had marked improvement in haemodynamics and rash once started on steroids, no longer required vasopressors, was extubated on day 3 of methylprednisolone, required 4 days of CVVHD and had complete recovery of kidney and liver function.

evidence_events.source_span: At the age of 9 months, she was referred to the paediatric nephrology due to bilateral polycystic kidneys found on ultrasound, performed for evaluation of a left flank palpable mass.
Screening of family members for kidney and hepatic cysts was negative.
Kidney function, blood pressure and microalbuminuria remained within normal range.
At the age of 10, she was referred to the paediatric dermatology due to the appearance of a cutaneous eruption on the face.
She presented with facial erythema and angiofibromas with malar distribution and various hypopigmented maculas in the upper body, arms and legs, meeting the criteria for TS.
Repeat ultrasound (at 10 years old) identified two nodules, suggestive of angiomyolipomas, in the left kidney.
Diagnostic hypothesis of TSC2/PKD1 Contiguous Gene Syndrome was placed, which was confirmed by the genetic testing.
Laboratory investigations, including routine haematological and biochemical workup, were normal.
At the age of 13, microalbuminuria (52.00 µg/mL) was detected, with normal blood pressure.

Brain MRI showed multiple corticosubcortical lesions involving both cerebral hemispheres, hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted images, with morphological characteristics compatible with cortical tubers, as well as multiple calcified subependymal nodules.
Echocardiogram was normal, and ophthalmologic evaluation showed no hamartomas or other alterations.
The genetic testing revealed a heterozygous deletion which included the TSC2 genes (exon 37) and the terminal portion of the PKD1 gene.
At 13 years of age, patient continued to be seizure free; she had normal cognitive functions and an unremarkable neurological examination.
She had persistent hypopigmented maculas in the upper body, arms and legs, without Shagreen patch or Koenen tumours.
Facial lesions significantly improved with topical sirolimus.
During follow-up, her renal function and blood pressure remained within normal limits.
Patient was started on enalapril 10 mg once daily for microalbuminuria, with subsequent improvement.

source_metadata.title: Cutaneous lymphangitis carcinomatosa made cervicofacial oedema intractable in a patient with superior vena cava syndrome
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from BMJ Case Reports 2018 article, preserving source order and granularity.

evidence_events.source_span: A 64-year-old woman with a 20-pack-year smoking history presented with a persistent cough for 3 months.
Chest CT showed a 10 mm-diameter nodule in the right upper lobe of her lung and swelling of the supraclavicular, mediastinal and right hilar lymph nodes.
Tissue samples obtained via mediastinoscopy indicated adenocarcinoma harbouring EGFR mutations: G719S (exon 18) and T790M (exon 20).
Enhanced brain MRI showed frontal and occipital brain metastases.
The patient was diagnosed with stage IV lung adenocarcinoma (cT1aN3M1b).
She achieved partial response after four cycles of carboplatin, pemetrexed and bevacizumab triplet therapy, which was discontinued due to drug-induced interstitial pneumonia.
Two weeks after the onset of drug-induced interstitial pneumonia, the patient developed prominent oedema and erythema in her neck and face, followed by dyspnoea.
Contrast-enhanced CT revealed severe SVC stenosis, which suggested that the symptoms primarily resulted from SVC syndrome.
The patient underwent angiography and balloon dilation, after which SVC blood flow remained despite prominent stenosis.
Although the SVC was dilated by the procedure, cervicofacial oedema and dyspnoea improvement was observed for only a few hours.
Chest CT performed the following day revealed that the SVC remained constricted, suggesting the existence of other causes that made the patient’s symptoms more intractable.
Concomitantly, the patient developed painless erythema and induration of the chest and abdomen.
Before angiography, a skin biopsy was performed at the erythematic site.
Skin biopsy revealed neoplastic cells within the lumina of dermal lymphatic vessels and infiltration into the dermis and hypodermis.
Immunohistochemistry staining revealed that the cells were positive for cytokeratin, thyroid transcription factor-1 and napsin A.
From these results, we diagnosed the cause of oedema and dyspnoea of the patient as CLC and SVC syndrome.
The patient died of respiratory failure 1 week after CLC diagnosis.

source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case presentation and discussion sections with source-ordered evidence events and milestones.

evidence_events.source_span: A 15-month-old white Caucasian girl with a negative personal medical clinical history was seen by her family pediatrician for the appearance of petechiae on the soft palate during the last 24 h.
She had been vaccinated with the measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine 12 days before and had presented a mild episode of febrile diarrhea 8 days beforehand.
A platelet count was immediately performed and excluded immune thrombocytopenic purpura (171,000 platelets/mmc3).

The patient was moderately febrile during the following two days, with a maximum ear temperature of 38.3 °C. The fever disappeared on the third day, whereas the hemorrhagic rash progressively increased and extended to the skin in different parts of the body.

At admission, the patient’s general condition was good, but a rash characterized by petechial-hemorrhagic lesions with sharp merges of varying sizes localized to the limbs, face and auricles associated with a strong oedematous component was evidenced.

On the second day of hospitalization, bilateral oedema of the metacarpophalangeal joints with joint pain appeared. The articular manifestations were responsive to analgesic therapy with paracetamol and resolved spontaneously in a week.

Blood counts, hepatic and renal function, C-reactive protein, coagulation, antineutrophil cytoplasmic autoantibodies, serology for Epstein Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, Rubella, Herpesvirus, parvovirus B19, fractions C3 and C4 of the complement, pharyngeal swab, blood culture, urinalysis, factor V leiden, D-dimer, erythrocyte sedimentation rate and peripheral blood smear were collected.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: multiple blood and serological tests collected

evidence_events.source_span: The blood and serological tests showed an increase in C-reactive protein concentration (3.58 mg/dL) in the absence of leukocytosis and with a normal platelet count (180,000/mm3). The examination of the peripheral smear showed the presence of some large mononuclear elements with hyperbasophile cytoplasm. No alterations in platelet morphology were evidenced.
Ultrasound examination of the abdomen and the urinary tract excluded visceral involvement.
To avoid an invasive procedure in a child with an already well-defined diagnosis, cutaneous biopsy was avoided, given the good general condition of the patient.
The skin manifestations progressively diminished and disappeared spontaneously within 3 weeks, leaving no sequelae.

hidden_reference.final_diagnosis_verbatim: The aetiology of this case is likely suggestive of idiopathic form but is not conclusive. Psoriatic arthritis is a likely diagnosis given the destructive DIP joint change, but the patient does not meet CASPAR criteria due to lack of psoriasis history, nail changes, or dactylitis. Long-term follow-up is required to make the definitive diagnosis.
diagnostic_reasoning_verbatim_spans: The aetiologies of acro-osteolysis can be classified as idiopathic disease, occupational disease (caused by exposure to polyvinyl chloride, frostbite, or trauma), immunological disease (systemic sclerosis and psoriasis), infections (leprosy), endocrinological disease (hyperparathyroidism and diabetes mellitus), genetic condition (Hajdu-Cheney syndrome with or without syringomyelia) and lysosomal storage disorder (Gaucher’s disease).
The familial form of acro-osteolysis is often well established by the late teens, whereas the idiopathic form may not present until the third decade of life or later.
Acro-osteolysis is often a prominent feature of psoriatic arthritis.
A destructive change of DIP joint of the right middle finger makes psoriatic arthritis a likely diagnosis.

However, the patient does not meet the CASPAR criteria enough to diagnose psoriatic arthritis since there is no personal or family history of psoriasis, no typical psoriatic nail change and no current or past dactylitis.
On the other hand, acro-osteolysis can also develop in patients with psoriasis without arthritis.
Long-term follow-up is required to make the definitive diagnosis.
diagnostic_reasoning_items: Consider idiopathic, occupational, immunological, infectious, endocrinological, genetic, and lysosomal storage causes of acro-osteolysis.
Lack of exposure history and negative labs reduce likelihood of occupational and endocrinological causes.
Imaging shows band acro-osteolysis and destructive DIP joint change, raising suspicion for psoriatic arthritis.
Absence of psoriasis history, nail changes, and dactylitis limits fulfillment of CASPAR criteria for psoriatic arthritis.
Definitive diagnosis requires long-term clinical follow-up.

hidden_reference.diagnostic_reasoning: The case presents band acro-osteolysis with destructive DIP joint changes but lacks clinical criteria for psoriatic arthritis. source_metadata.title: Scleredema associated with immunoglobulin A-κ smoldering myeloma: a case report and review of the literature
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case presentation and clinical course sections with image figure references.

evidence_events.source_span: A 66-year-old Sri Lankan woman who had been followed in a dermatology unit for 34 years for diffuse systemic sclerosis presented with an acute exacerbation of the skin disease.
She was treated with corticosteroids and cyclophosphamide pulses and subsequently with mycophenolate mofetil for the skin condition.
On examination, she had widespread thickening of the skin predominantly involving the trunk and proximal extremities.
She did not have sclerodactyly but had deformities in keeping with osteoarthritis.
She denied cold-induced episodic acral bluish discoloration suggestive of Raynaud’s phenomenon.

Repeated echocardiography did not reveal any evidence of pulmonary hypertension; upper gastroduodenoscopy did not show reflux disease; radiographically, there was no evidence of interstitial lung disease.

The patient’s autoimmune antibody profile (antinuclear antibody, anti-double-stranded DNA, perinuclear and cytoplasmic antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, anti-Smith antibody, anti RO and anti-LA, antitopoisomerase antibody, anticentromere antibody, and complements) was persistently negative.
Full blood count, urine full report, and renal and liver function were normal.

Skin biopsies from four body sites showed normal epidermis and thickened reticular dermis with swollen collagen bundles separated from one another by clear spaces, resulting in fenestration; skin appendages were not atrophied or bound down; Alcian blue staining showed interstitial mucin deposition.
Serum protein electrophoresis demonstrated an abnormal monoclonal band in the gamma region with a paraprotein level of 8.9 g/dl.
Immunofixation showed an abnormal band in the gamma region consisting of immunoglobulin A and κ.
Bone marrow biopsy revealed abnormal monoclonal plasma cells (15%) with multinuclearity.
There was no evidence of end organ damage with normal calcium, renal function, and full blood count.
Whole-body magnetic resonance imaging did not reveal any evidence of bone involvement.
The patient’s diagnosis was revised as scleredema type 2 associated with IgA-κ smoldering myeloma.
She was commenced on intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) monthly and intravenous bortezomib cycles, with significant improvement of the skin condition.

source_metadata.title: A Cheek Nodule in a Child: Be Aware of Idiopathic Facial Aseptic Granuloma and Its Differential Diagnosis

evidence_events.source_span: A three-year-old girl with a previous negative clinical history was referred to our hospital for the evaluation of some asymptomatic nodules on the convexity of the left cheek.
The nodules had appeared two months before, and had gradually increased in size. Her mother denied any association with trauma or insect bites.

Initially considered skin abscesses, they had been treated at home by the primary-care pediatrician with systemic amoxicillin-clavulanate by mouth (50 mg/kg/die as amoxicillin for 10 days) without benefit.
At admission, the examination of the cheek revealed two nodules one centimeter in diameter, and another two centimeters in diameter with overlying erythematous skin and negative thermotouch.
The nodules had a hard-elastic consistency, were moderately firm, and were not fluctuant. No associated lymphadenopathy was observed. The girl was afebrile and in a good general condition.
An ultrasound examination performed using a 12 Hz linear probe showed that the lesions were homogenous, hypoechoic, and solid.

A histologic evaluation of a biopsy specimen of the largest nodule revealed an inflammatory, granulomatous-diffuse infiltrate in the superficial and deep dermis consisting of giant cells, histiocytes, lymphocytes, neutrophils, eosinophils, and plasma cells.

The Ziehl–Neelsen and Gram stains were both negative. The cultures for the anaerobic and aerobic bacteria, fungi, and acid-fast bacilli were negative, as they were the antibody tests for Bartonella henselae and Afipia felis.
Suspecting an IFAG, treatment with topical fusidic acid and oral clarithromycin for 14 days was started, and a monthly follow-up was scheduled.
After two months from the first evaluation, the lesion resolved and did not recur after one additional month.

There was sparing of the palms, soles, rectum, oral labia, and mucosa. There were tender, vesicular, dry varicella-appearing lesions on the right upper back. source_metadata.title: Disabling Pruritus in a Patient With Cervical Stenosis

evidence_events.source_span: A 56-year-old male nurse practitioner presented to our office with disabling pruritus affecting his bilateral upper extremities.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: The pruritus developed over the past 6 years and was concurrent with increasing neck pain.

evidence_events.source_span: The patient underwent extensive evaluation including dermatology, rheumatology, neurology, and psychiatry. He had no evidence of either dermatologic disease or peripheral neuropathy, and his regular medications did not cause the pruritus.
He had extensive multimodal conservative therapies including numerous epidural steroid injections that offered only transient relief.

The patient reported constant bilateral neck pain and intermittent bilateral upper extremity pain, burning, and pruritus, which extended into the bicep in a C6 dermatomal distribution. The symptoms worsened with reaching and lateral rotation of the neck, and decreased with ice application.

On physical examination, the area of itching skin was grossly normal. Neurologic examination was notable for a positive Spurling sign bilaterally. He had 5/5 strength in the major myotomes of the upper extremities and a 2+ bicep and triceps reflex response on a symmetric fashion. He denied decreased sensation in the distal dermatomes.
Spinal radiographs revealed multilevel cervical spondylosis.
MRI showed notable spinal stenosis with early cord flattening at C3-4 and C4-5. In addition, multilevel foraminal stenosis from C3 to C7 was present.

The patient's chronic axial mechanical neck pain and bilateral upper extremity radiculopathy correlated with the degenerative and stenotic segments from C3 through C7. The pruritus was possibly caused by compression of the nerve roots and/or spinal cord at the affected levels.

Given his multiyear history of multimodal conservative therapies and correlation between imaging and physical examination, it was thought that surgical intervention in the form of an ACDF from C3 to C7 would provide the patient permanent relief of his pain and pruritus.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: The planned procedure was done without complication.

evidence_events.source_span: After surgery, the patient's symptoms improved instantly. At his most recent visit four months postoperatively, the patient related 95% improvement in his preoperative symptoms without any notable pain and only occasional sensation of pruritus.

evidence_milestones.dialogue_visible_evidence: Multidisciplinary workup was negative for dermatologic or neuropathic disease. Physical exam showed positive Spurling sign bilaterally with normal strength and reflexes.
evidence_milestones.test_visible_evidence: Negative dermatologic and neuropathic evaluations; positive Spurling sign on exam.
evidence_milestones.source_span: The patient underwent extensive evaluation including dermatology, rheumatology, neurology, and psychiatry. He had no evidence of either dermatologic disease or peripheral neuropathy, and his regular medications did not cause the pruritus. On physical examination, the area of itching skin was grossly normal. Neurologic examination was notable for a positive Spurling sign bilaterally. He had 5/5 strength in the major myotomes of the upper extremities and a 2+ bicep and triceps reflex response on a symmetric fashion. He denied decreased sensation in the distal dermatomes.
evidence_milestones.question: How do the negative multidisciplinary evaluations and positive Spurling sign influence the differential diagnosis, and what imaging studies should be pursued next?

hidden_reference.final_diagnosis_verbatim: Disabling bilateral brachioradial pruritus caused by cervical nerve root and spinal cord compression due to multilevel cervical spondylosis and stenosis, confirmed by symptom resolution after multilevel anterior cervical decompression and fusion.
diagnostic_reasoning_verbatim_spans: The pruritus developed over the past 6 years and was concurrent with increasing neck pain.
He had no evidence of either dermatologic disease or peripheral neuropathy.
Spinal radiographs revealed multilevel cervical spondylosis.
MRI showed notable spinal stenosis with early cord flattening at C3-4 and C4-5 and multilevel foraminal stenosis from C3 to C7.
The patient's chronic axial mechanical neck pain and bilateral upper extremity radiculopathy correlated with the degenerative and stenotic segments from C3 through C7.
After surgery, the patient's symptoms improved instantly with 95% improvement at 4 months.
diagnostic_reasoning_items: Chronic disabling bilateral upper extremity pruritus with neck pain suggests neuropathic etiology.
Negative dermatologic and peripheral neuropathy workup excludes common alternative causes.
Imaging confirms multilevel cervical spondylosis and stenosis causing nerve root and cord compression.

hidden_reference.final_diagnosis: Brachioradial pruritus secondary to cervical nerve root and spinal cord compression from multilevel cervical spondylosis and stenosis.
hidden_reference.diagnostic_reasoning: The patient's disabling bilateral upper extremity pruritus and neck pain, negative dermatologic and neuropathy evaluations, and imaging showing multilevel cervical spondylosis and stenosis with cord compression support a diagnosis of brachioradial pruritus caused by cervical nerve root and spinal cord compression. The rapid symptom resolution after multilevel anterior cervical decompression and fusion confirms the diagnosis.
hidden_reference.article_derived_evidence_summary: A 56-year-old man with 6 years of disabling bilateral upper extremity pruritus and neck pain underwent extensive negative dermatologic and neurologic workup. source_metadata.title: Disseminated tuberculosis associated with reactive arthritis of Poncet in an immunocompetent patient
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case report section and figures; evidence events and milestones constructed per instructions.

evidence_events.source_span: A 23-year-old male patient, previously healthy, started with watery diarrhea, abdominal pain and weight loss of 6 kg, associated with nocturnal episodes of fever, 9 months before admission.

The patient evolved with multiple ulcers with necrotic crust, some with granular floor and raised borders, associated with soft erythematous painful nodules on the lower limbs and ulcers of the fibrinous floor in the glans.
He complained of arthralgia in the phalanges, with signs of oligoarthritis of small joints on physical examination.
He showed normal exam of the joint fluid and laboratory tests, except for the presence of leukocytes in the feces, and had no previous history of any kind of immunosuppression.
At colonoscopy, multiple shallow ulcers covered by thick fibrin associated with enanthem, mainly in the sigmoid, and aftoid ulcers in the proximal rectum were evidenced.
The tuberculin sensitivity test (PPD) was negative and the chest X-ray had no alterations.
Anatomopathological examination of one of the ulcers was performed on the lower limb, which revealed an epithelioid granulomatous process with palisade granulomas and central caseous necrosis.
The study of acid-fast bacilli (AFB) by Ziehl-Neelsen staining showed intact bacilli.
Culture was positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, confirming the diagnostic hypothesis of cutaneous TB.
The histopathological analysis of the intestinal biopsy revealed a mild inflammatory infiltrate without the presence of bacilli.
After the beginning of the RIPE treatment regimen, the patient evolved with complete healing of the ulcers and gradual resolution of the diarrhea and oligoarthritis.

source_metadata.title: An adult co-presented with varicella and herpes zoster caused by varicella zoster virus genotype J, China: a case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 44-year-old Chinese man suffered papules and vesicles with pain on the left ear
Physical examination revealed that small vesicles surrounded by erythema had developed on his trunk, back and neck, and unilateral papules and vesicles in ribbons had also developed on the left ear
This patient was excluded from human immunodeficiency virus and Treponema pallidum infections by ELISA antibody tests
Laboratory tests revealed that the ratio of eosinophils (0.1%) and eosinophil count (0.0 × 10⁹/L) were significantly downregulated
Treatment with valacyclovir, ebastine, mecobalamine, pregabalin and calamine lotion for 5 days was effective therapy for varicella and herpes zoster
Polymerase chain reaction for vesicular fluids from varicella and herpes zoster was positive for VZV
The viral load of VZV in the head (mean of Ct = 17.35) was higher than that in the trunk (mean of Ct = 18.64)
6 ORFs (ORFs 1, 21, 22, 50, 54 and 68) of the VZV genome were amplified and phylogenetic analysis indicated that the genotypes of VZV in the trunk and head were genotype J (clade 2)

A total of 13 SNP variations were found in 5 ORFs, confirming that VZV in the trunk and head were genotype J; a synonymous G → A mutation in codon 150 of ORF68 did not occur, confirming that VZV was not a VZV-MSP mutant virus

evidence_events.source_span: A 46-year-old staff nurse presented with a 24-hour history of a widespread red-raised blanching and itchy rash.
She had no fever or continuous cough but did have some nasal congestion.
The general practitioner described a classical urticarial rash affecting her upper and lower limbs in addition to her trunk.
The following day the rash worsened and was now associated with swelling of her lips and hands; she now felt feverish and had developed a dry cough.
She had a slight wheeze but no tongue or throat swelling. Temperature was 36°C, pulse 98 beats/min, oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
She had a widespread urticarial eruption affecting her face, arms, torso, legs and loins.
Reverse transcriptase PCR test on combined nasopharyngeal/oropharyngeal swabs was positive for SARS-CoV-2, 2 days after first presenting to the emergency doctor.

She was prescribed fexofenadine hydrochloride 180 mg two to four times per day, commenced on prednisolone 40 mg once daily for 3 days, and later chlorphenamine maleate 4 mg four times per day was added.

evidence_events.source_span: Prednisolone helped her lip and hand swelling, but her rash was still itchy.
The rash resolved completely over the next few days and the patient made a full clinical recovery.

source_metadata.title: Degos disease: a case report and review of the literature

evidence_events.source_span: A 35-year-old Hindu woman presented to our dermatology outpatient department with complaints of painful depigmented lesions of 1½ years’ duration.
On examination, the lesions were porcelain white atrophic papules with surrounding erythema present over the trunk, upper limbs, thighs, and chest.
She had a history of joint pain for the last 7–8 years and a history of headache, giddiness, and ocular pain for the last 3 months.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: for the last 7–8 years; for the last 3 months

evidence_events.source_span: Results of her laboratory tests for antinuclear antibody, lupus anticoagulant, cardiolipin antibody, and β2-glycoprotein were all negative.
Ultrasonography of the abdomen was unremarkable.
Ophthalmological examination of bilateral eyes showed myopic astigmatism.
The result of stool occult testing of the patient’s blood was negative.
A skin punch biopsy was taken from the porcelain white lesion over the trunk.

Histopathological examination showed atrophic epidermis with mild hyperkeratosis and flattened rete ridges focally; papillary dermis with band-like mucin deposit and focal sclerosis; middle and deep dermis with patchy mucin and focal fibrosis; mild to moderate lymphomononuclear infiltrate cuffing around perivascular areas; few blood vessels showing endothelial cell proliferation.
Alcian blue staining for dermal mucin was positive.
Owing to the absence of systemic complications, the patient was diagnosed with benign cutaneous Degos disease.
She was prescribed antiplatelet agents (aspirin 75 mg and clopidogrel 75 mg once daily).
New lesions stopped appearing within 1 month of starting this therapy.
At 3 months follow-up, the lesions had started flattening, the erythema had decreased, and her pain was completely subsided.

source_metadata.title: Mucosal-dominant pemphigus vulgaris in a 90-year-old woman

evidence_events.source_span: A 90-year-old Japanese woman was referred to our department with a 3-month history of painful gingivae that first appeared at age 90 years.
She reported difficulty in eating because of multiple painful erosions following easily ruptured vesicles in the buccal mucosa and tongue during the last 3 weeks.
Her medical history included hyperlipidaemia and reflux esophagitis, for which she regularly consumed atorvastatin calcium hydrate and esomeprazole.
A general examination revealed a few erythematous erosions on the back.
An intraoral examination revealed multiple erosions and desquamation with erythematous areas on the right and left buccal mucosa, palate, lateral border of the tongue and gingiva.
She was positive for Nikolsky’s sign.
A gingival biopsy for histopathology revealed intraepithelial cleavage with acantholysis in the suprabasal region and retaining of basal keratinocytes along the basement membrane zone.
Direct immunofluorescence study showed the deposition of IgG and C3 between the epithelial cells.
The indirect immunofluorescence ELISA for desmoglein-3 and desmoglein-1 antibodies revealed their elevated levels (126 U/mL and 21 U/mL, respectively, reference range for both is <20).
Based on all clinical, histopathological and serological findings, we confirmed mucosal-dominant PV with minimal skin lesions.
The patient received oral prednisolone at an initial dosage of 35 mg/day (1 mg/kg/day). This helped in rapid epithelialisation of the erosions on the back.
The intraoral erosions diminished significantly in 2 weeks, and the dose was tapered to 30 mg/day.
A marked improvement in the lesions was observed on subsequent follow-up. The patient is currently on prednisolone treatment (15 mg/day), and to date, no other lesions have been reported.

source_metadata.notes: Case report from BMJ Case Reports 2020 describing atypical chilblain-like lesions with bullae in COVID-19.

evidence_events.source_span: A 27-year-old woman requested a teledermatology consult concerning a 2-day history of bilateral, progressively oedematous and pruritic toes that were painful when confined by shoes.
The patient had no underlying medical conditions, including any history of collagen vascular disease, Raynaud’s phenomenon, chilblains and cold exposure, and was not taking any medications.
6 weeks prior to her toe manifestation, she experienced 10 days of ageusia and anosmia with no other symptoms.

On examination, multiple bilateral non-haemorrhagic bullae of various sizes up to approximately 1.5 cm in diameter were present on the dorsa of her toes. Her toes were oedematous with widespread erythema. Acrocyanosis and livedo reticularis were not present.
Two days following her initial presentation, the bullae appeared haemorrhagic. No other clinical changes were noted and there were no petechiae or signs of bruising or bleeding elsewhere.
