source_metadata.title: A large verrucous plaque on the buttocks: a case report of an atypical presentation of tuberculosis verrucosa cutis
source_metadata.notes: Extraction based on case narrative Patient and observation section and supported by Introduction and Discussion.

evidence_events.source_span: A 35-year-old male was referred to our outpatient clinic with a large verrucous plaque and malodorous purulent discharge on the buttocks, thigh and scrotum.

The lesion started two years ago as small, mildly pruritic and multiple plaques that were limited to the buttocks. Some painful and itchy nodules then developed over the lesions in the last five months. The nodules ulcerated and extended with foul-smelling seropurulent discharge. The lesions thickened and expanded rapidly covering the left buttock, thigh and scrotum, forming an annular hyperkeratotic plaque with central healing.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: two years ago onset; last five months progression

evidence_events.source_span: The patient had been treated in a local hospital with antifungal and antibiotic therapy without significant improvement.
The patient worked in an oil palm plantation and often wore shorts and sat on the ground when working.
The patient had a history of untreated cough and night sweats without fever in the past two years.

Dermatological examination showed extensive verrucous plaque covered in dark dense crust over the buttocks, thigh and scrotum with an irregular border. Fissures and multiple ulcers were seen over the dense crust with foul-smelling seropurulent discharge.

Routine blood workups were performed, with liver function, renal function and blood sugar levels were within normal limits. His leucocyte was slightly raised to 14.580/μl. Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) for HIV was nonreactive.
Mantoux test was positive and chest radiograph revealed extensive pulmonary TB.
Acid Fast Bacilli (AFB) were not found in the sputum specimen, but The GeneXpert was able to detect M. tuberculosis that was sensitive to rifampicin.
Pus culture was performed and revealed Escherichia coli colonization.

Skin biopsy of the lesion was performed and histopathology analysis showed marked pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia of epidermis, epithelioid granulomatous inflammation surrounding the caseous necrosis along with several Langerhans cells in the dermis and many lymphocytic infiltrates.
AFB staining using Ziehl-Neelsen and culture on Lowenstein-Jensen medium were negative.
Fungal infection was ruled out by negative potassium hydroxide (KOH) examination from the lesion skin scraping and negative Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS) stain from the skin biopsy specimen.
Anti-tuberculosis treatment (ATT) regimen 1 was given consisting of two-month intensive phase followed by four-month continuation phase.
At two-month follow-up, the skin lesions showed significant improvement and the lesions were completely resolved after four months of therapy leaving atrophic scars.

source_metadata.title: Concurrent development of HIV-negative Kaposi’s sarcoma and mycosis fungoides in an elderly Inuit from Canada
source_metadata.notes: Case report from BMJ Case Reports 2021; includes clinical, lab, pathology, imaging, flow cytometry, treatment and outcome data.

evidence_events.source_span: An 88-year-old Inuit man from a village in Northern Quebec, Canada was transferred on 8 November 2019, to the McGill University Health Centre in Montreal, Quebec for violaceous subcutaneous nodules on his palms and lower extremities, preceded a few months before by a rapid onset of total body erythematous, pruritic and scaly skin lesions. He also had problem of a 6 kg weight loss, night sweats, and fever for the last 4 months.

Physical examination revealed generalised scaly erythematous plaques, accompanied with about 60 violaceous nodules affecting the trunk and upper and lower limbs. Physical examination revealed a small left cervical lymph node (<1 cm) in the absence of hepatosplenomegaly.

Laboratory results showed normocytic anaemia with haemoglobin 104 g/L, platelets 175 ×10^9/L, neutrophils 4.4 ×10^9/L, lymphocytes 1.5 ×10^9/L, moderate eosinophilia of 0.98 ×10^9/L, normal creatinine, transaminases and mild elevation of lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) 321 U/L. Serologies were negative for viral hepatitis, syphilis, HIV, and human T-lymphotropic virus (HTLV)-I/II and positive for Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). PCR testing on peripheral blood was positive for HHV8 (non-quantitative) and EBV (4786 copies/mL), while PCR for HIV and cytomegalovirus (CMV) was negative. CD4 cell count was 665 cells/mm3 with CD8 at 374 cells/mm3, with a normal CD4/CD8 ratio of 1.7. Stool analysis and culture were negative for ova and parasites.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: at the time of initial presentation

evidence_events.source_span: Histological examination of a skin biopsy from a violaceous nodule on his left palm revealed a malignant vascular proliferation and spindle cells that were positive for HHV8 by immunohistochemistry, consistent with KS.

A biopsy of a scaly erythematous skin lesion on his right arm revealed an atypical infiltrate of predominantly CD4-positive T-cells with mild epidermotropism and partial loss of CD7 expression assessed by immunohistochemistry. Molecular studies showed clonal TCR gene rearrangement, indicating the presence of a T-cell clonal population, most consistent with CTCL.

Flow cytometry on peripheral blood showed no clonal B-cell population but T-cells comprised 94% of lymphocytes with a CD4/CD8 ratio of 2.7. CD4+CD26 cells were increased up to 72% (normal <30%) with an immunophenotype consistent with circulating Sézary/MF cells.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: at the time of initial presentation

evidence_events.source_span: MRI showed normal-sized liver and spleen, symmetrical and mildly enlarged (1.0–1.5 cm) axillary, mediastinal and hilar lymph nodes. PET scan demonstrated mildly hypermetabolic lymph nodes in the right submandibular area (SUV up to 4.5), and right and left axillary and inguinal lymph nodes (SUVs up to 3). No hypermetabolic activity was noted in upper or lower limbs. Such symmetrical and mildly enlarged lymph nodes with low metabolic activity were considered reactive.

The patient’s MF was classified as T4, N0, M0 and B1 according to the American Joint Committee on Cancer. Skin lesions involved at least 80% of total skin surface area (T4). No cancer spread to nearby lymph nodes (N0), no metastasis detected (M0), and circulating Sézary cell count below 1000 cells/mm3 (B1). Prognosis classification was IIIB.

The patient was prescribed oral acitretin 10 mg daily for 4 weeks then increased to 30 mg daily for 8 weeks for KS lesions. MF skin lesions were treated with 1% hydrocortisone topical cream twice daily and UVB phototherapy. Oral clindamycin was prescribed for infected excoriated skin lesions.

After treatment, blood tests showed decreased LDH, beta2 microglobulin, and IgG levels, partial improvement of anaemia, and normalization of eosinophil count. Flow cytometry showed decreased CD4 cells, slight increase in CD8 cells, and increased B cell population with higher kappa and lambda light chain expression. Skin lesions resolved and patient was discharged home.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: follow-up blood tests and flow cytometry

source_metadata.title: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) panniculitis in a patient undergoing stem cell mobilisation

evidence_events.source_span: A female in her 20s with relapsed Hodgkin lymphoma (HL) was referred to our centre for autologous stem cell transplantation.

She underwent salvage chemotherapy with bendamustine and brentuximab (BB), which was uneventful except for a grade 1 cutaneous adverse drug reaction (CADR) to BB affecting 5% of her body surface area that resolved with topical steroids and antihistamines.
The patient went on to receive mobilisation chemotherapy with ifosfamide, carboplatin and etoposide. Pegfilgrastim was administered on days 5 and 11.

On day 11, she was admitted with a fever of 38.3°C and pain in her legs. Examination revealed bilateral scattered tender, indurated subcutaneous nodules over her shins with mild overlying erythema, approximately 3–5 cm in diameter.

Investigations on admission showed a white cell count of 0.79×10⁹/L, with neutrophils 0.56×10⁹/L. C-reactive protein (CRP) was elevated at 74, and procalcitonin was 0.18. Blood cultures and a blood fungal culture were negative.
An ultrasound scan of the leg nodule showed vague increased echogenicity and increased vascularity in the subcutaneous tissue with no evidence of abscess formation.

A punch biopsy of the nodule confirmed lobular panniculitis with an inflammatory cell infiltrate composed of numerous neutrophils, mixed with lymphocytes, eosinophils, histiocytes and occasional multinucleated giant cells. Gram-positive cocci were present in the dermis and subcutis. No fungal organisms or acid-fast bacilli were seen on Grocott’s methenamine silver or Ziehl-Neelsen stains.
Culture from the punch biopsy grew MRSA. Her antinuclear antibody titre was negative at <1:80. A tuberculosis quantiferon test was negative, and a chest radiograph was normal.
A diagnosis of infective panniculitis secondary to MRSA was made. She was started on doxycycline with resolution of her fever and nodules.
Her lower limb subcutaneous nodules resolved completely without scarring nor atrophy following treatment with doxycycline.

evidence_events.source_span: A three-year-old, otherwise healthy girl suffering from mild atopic dermatitis (AD) (SCORAD index of <25) presented in our Pediatric Dermatology Outpatient Clinic in reduced general condition with high-grade fever and a new skin rash.

Her skin exhibited generalized blisters of 2–5 cm in diameter, partly translucent, partly with pus accumulation in the dependent part of the flaccid bullae forming a transverse fluid level (hypopyon sign). Erosions were visible at sites of ruptured blisters.

Further inspection revealed pinhead-sized papules, vesicles, pustules, erosions, and crusts surrounded by erythematous skin disseminated between the large blisters. Palms, soles, scalp as well as genital and oral mucosa were disease free.
Rapid diagnosis was made by Tzanck smear from a small intact vesicle revealing multinucleated giant cells and acantholytic keratinocytes.
Herpes polymerase chain reaction (PCR) from both serum and blisters were positive for varicella-zoster virus (VZV).
VZV serology demonstrated a recent infection (IgM antibodies positive, IgG antibodies negative).
Bacterial culture from the skin smear revealed superinfection with Staphylococcus aureus without methicillin resistance.
The patient was isolated in the pediatric ward and received acyclovir and amoxicillin/clavulanic acid intravenously for 5 days, followed by oral therapy for an additional 5 days.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: intravenous then oral antiviral and antibiotic therapy

evidence_events.source_span: Topical treatment consisted of neomycin sulfate powder on intact blisters and methylprednisolone aceponate 0.1% cream plus sterile paraffin gauze dressing of the erosive skin.
She recovered completely, only some eczema plaques persisted from the known AD.

source_metadata.title: Spontaneous pneumothorax as a clinical manifestation of neurofibromatosis type 1
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from BMJ Case Reports 2021 article, case report section prioritized.

evidence_events.source_span: A 56-year-old man diagnosed with NF1 was referred to our clinic with a suspicion of Birt-Hogg-Dubé syndrome (BHD) due to a history of recurrent spontaneous pneumothorax.

The physical examination of the patient showed multiple café-au-lait macules, freckling of axillae and groins, multiple neurofibromas and plexiform neurofibromas on his face, trunk and extremities, and fibromas of the tongue. The patient was also known to have an optic pathway glioma in his right eye. He had a mother and a sister with known NF1.

He was a former smoker with a smoking history of 10 pack years. During the years, he had seven neurofibromas and one malignant schwannoma removed. He had Barrett’s oesophagus, irritable bowel syndrome, bilateral sensorineural hearing loss and conductive hearing loss on his right ear.
He had a remarkable history of at least four incidents of pneumothorax. Both lungs had been involved, and each pneumothorax was treated by tube thoracostomy.

The most recent incident was in 2006. The patient experienced shortness of breath and pain located to the left side of the chest. An X-ray showed an apical pneumothorax of the left lung. The pneumothorax was treated by tube thoracostomy for two days, until the lung was fully inflated.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: The most recent incident was in 2006
evidence_events.procedural_cue: An X-ray showed an apical pneumothorax; treated by tube thoracostomy

evidence_events.source_span: Several bilateral lung bullae and apical cysts were demonstrated on a high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT). However, the cysts were not removed surgically due to the diffuse localisation.
A chest scan in 2017 revealed several cysts, bilateral paraseptal and centrilobular emphysema, pleural thickening, and fibrosis causing interstitial lung disease.
The patient was genetically tested for NF1 and BHD, and was found to have a pathogenic variant only in the gene encoding NF1 (c.6709C>T; p.Arg2237).
The patient has not had any worsening in his pulmonary aspects, although he does suffer from shortness of breath.

source_metadata.title: Severe urticarial rash as the initial symptom of COVID-19 infection
source_metadata.notes: Case report of a 54-year-old woman presenting with urticarial rash preceding other COVID-19 symptoms.

evidence_events.source_span: A 54-year-old woman presented with shortness of breath for 1-day duration along with generalised weakness and diffuse rash associated with itching and burning sensation that progressively got worse for 3 days prior to presentation to emergency department.
She denied any fever, chills, cough, nausea, loose stools, abdominal pain, joint pains or sore throat. She had no known exposure to COVID-19 positive people.
On arrival in the emergency department, a COVID-19 test was performed given hypoxia (oxygen saturation 84% on room air) with new requirement of 2 L of nasal cannula oxygen.
COVID-19 test returned positive.

A widespread rash that was erythematous, raised and pruritic and consistent with urticarial rash was noted on her bilateral upper extremities and lower extremities. The urticarial rash was also present on the trunk but did not involve the palmar and plantar surfaces or any mucosal surfaces. No vesicular rash or acral lesions were noted.

White cell count 8.4 ×10⁹ cells/L with a normal differential count including no lymphopaenia or eosinophilia. C reactive protein elevated at 60.9 mg/L. D-dimer elevated at 725 ng/mL. Chest X-ray revealed left basal atelectasis and no other major abnormality. Serum creatinine is 2.6 mg/dL, with baseline creatinine ranging from 2.3 to 2.6 mg/dL.

Differential included hypersensitivity reaction to environmental toxin, drug reaction, viral infectious process and autoimmune vasculitis. No new medication or environmental exposure identified. Autoimmune vasculitis considered less likely given urticarial appearance. Skin biopsy considered but deferred initially.
Treatment included oral antihistamines with loratadine 10 mg daily and topical triamcinolone 0.1% cream. Antiviral therapy with remdesivir was initiated given hypoxia.
Within 48 hours of initiation of treatment, she had complete resolution of the rash.
Patient had complete resolution of rash, rash-associated itching and burning sensation, and hypoxia within 48 hours of initiation of therapy. She discharged safely on day 5 of hospitalisation.

source_metadata.title: Pityriasis rosea Gibert triggered by SARS-CoV-2 infection
source_metadata.notes: Case report of a 54-year-old female with pityriasis rosea and confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection.

evidence_events.source_span: 54-year-old Caucasian female presented for a 3-week duration of an extremely pruritic erythematous-squamous lesion, initially on the trunk and upper limbs, extending to lower limbs, sparing cephalic extremity, palms, and soles

One week before the rash, patient had respiratory tract infection symptoms (nasal obstruction, dysphagia, dry cough, retrosternal pain) treated with antitussives and paracetamol with rapid improvement
During 3 weeks before dermatology exam, patient used systemic antihistamines and topical dermatocorticosteroids at home with unfavorable evolution, spread of lesions and increased pruritus
RT-PCR assay from nasal and pharyngeal swabs for COVID-19 was performed and was positive, confirming SARS-CoV-2 infection

Physical exam on admission: temperature 36.5°C, oxygen saturation 98%, normal pulmonary auscultation, respiratory rate 16/min, heart rate 84 bpm, blood pressure 134/79 mm Hg; dermatological exam showed right supraclavicular oval erythematous squamous plaque (herald patch) 2.5x1.5 cm with white adherent scales and disseminated oval erythematous-papulosquamous lesions 0.5-1 cm with linear pattern and centrifugal extension sparing palms, soles, and face

Laboratory tests: complete blood count, C-reactive protein, fibrinogen, syphilis serology, procalcitonin, ferritin, D Dimers normal except ESR 23 mm/h (normal 0-20) and LDH 247 U/L (normal 125-220); pulmonary radiography showed no pathological changes
Serological tests for secondary syphilis and HIV antibodies were negative; serologies for IgM parvovirus B19, HHV-6, HHV-7, and Epstein Barr virus were negative

Clinical features consistent with pityriasis rosea: oval erythematous-squamous lesions with scaly aspect, centrifugal progressive extension, supraclavicular herald patch, linear pattern, lesions on thorax, abdomen, upper and lower limbs, sparing palms, soles, and face; negative syphilis serology and no drug exposure
Treatment initiated with systemic corticosteroids (hydrocortisone hemisuccinate 200 mg/day for 7 days), loratadine 10 mg twice daily, topical dermatocorticosteroids and emollients
Partial remission of skin lesions after 7 days of treatment
Two weeks after admission, patient discharged with partial resolution of skin lesions, no respiratory symptoms, and negative SARS-CoV-2 RT-PCR from nasal and pharyngeal swabs

source_metadata.title: Pityriasis rubra pilaris post-infection due COVID-19: case report

evidence_events.source_span: 32-month-old male patient presented with pruritus and skin lesions; four days before admission, skin rashes with redness and itching on hands and feet that spread to the whole body including the face
Initial primary care diagnoses included urticaria due to intoxication of unknown origin treated with antihistamines, and later scalded skin syndrome by Staphylococcus aureus

On hospital admission, physical exam showed generalized erythema, follicular papules, progressive non-painful desquamative exanthem on hands, feet, genitalia, and periorificial areas with pruritus; patient was afebrile, alert, no toxic appearance

Laboratory tests showed leukocytosis (15,140/mm3) with differential: segmented 41%, cay 1%, eosinophils 5%, lymphocytes 53%; platelets normal (378,000/mm3); hemoglobin 12.8 g/dL; C-reactive protein 12 mg/L; urea 29.9 mg/dL; creatinine 0.7 mg/dL; TGP 73.5 u/L; TGO 75.2 u/L; triglycerides 71.7 mg/dL; prothrombin time 12 sec; parvovirus B19 IgM negative; two rapid SARS-CoV-2 tests IgM negative and IgG positive; no nasal swab performed

Epidemiological history: patient from Motupe, Lambayeque-Peru; no significant medical history; fully vaccinated; parents had acute respiratory infection two months prior but patient asymptomatic and family not tested for COVID-19

Patient defined as post-infected with COVID-19 based on positive IgG and family epidemiological history; hospitalized for suspected Staphylococcus aureus scalded skin syndrome and started on intravenous oxacillin 100 mg/kg/day every 6 hours

During hospitalization, clinical evolution was favorable with slight improvement, stable vital signs, good oral tolerance, afebrile; antibiotic treatment continued; dermatologist consultation requested

source_metadata.title: Reactive non-sexually related acute genital ulcers associated with COVID-19

evidence_events.source_span: A 13-year-old Caucasian girl presented with severe ulceration and oedema of the vulva. Her vulvar symptoms began with stinging and burning of the external genitalia, with vulvar oedema starting 1 day later, followed by increased swelling, ulceration and severe vulvar pain. She also noted pain with urination. Her symptom began 3 days following systemic symptoms of fevers, chills, sore throat and decreased taste due to COVID-19, for which she and her sister both tested positive.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: Her symptom began 3 days following systemic symptoms of fevers, chills, sore throat and decreased taste due to COVID-19

evidence_events.source_span: She is not sexually active. Menarche was age 13 and she was not menstruating at that time of symptoms. Her medical history is significant for a minor deletion of the SHOX gene and she takes human growth hormone. She has a history of recurrent oral aphthae. Her sister has a history of Lipschütz ulcers from EBV.

Physical examination revealed multiple, shallow ulcers with raised and sharply demarcated borders located on the medial aspects of the labia minora. Grey exudate and eschar are noted. The surrounding vulvar tissue was erythematous and markedly oedematous.

Herpes simplex virus (HSV) type 1 and 2 were negative, as well as rapid plasma reagin screening for syphilis and HIV testing. Evaluation for Behcet’s syndrome was also performed, revealing negative C reactive protein (CRP), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and human leucocyte antigen-B51 (HLA-B51). Testing for EBV was negative. A nasopharyngeal swab for SARS-CoV-2 using reverse transcription PCR (RT-PCR) was positive.

She was initially prescribed a steroid cream and topical lidocaine; however, she was unable to use the steroid cream due to extreme pain and was started on an oral corticosteroid regimen of prednisone tapering over 14 days. Six days after initial vulvar symptoms, she began to have severe dysuria for which she started Pyridium. She was hospitalised for pain control for 5 days, completing the oral steroid course. The genital oedema had decreased, but ulcers and vulvar pain were still present.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: Six days after initial vulvar symptoms
evidence_events.procedural_cue: hospitalised for pain control for 5 days

evidence_events.source_span: She was started on colchicine 1.2 mg daily and was noted to have further improvement of oedema and pain within 1 week. Subsequent evaluation by Rheumatology was not consistent with Behcet’s syndrome, revealing negative CRP, ESR and HLA-B51.

Ulceration and oedema resolved within 6 weeks; however, she was noted to have agglutination of the labia minora. Adhesions were refractory to a trial of topical clobetasol propionate 0.05% ointment and she underwent lysis of labial adhesions under sedation. Postoperative evaluation revealed normal anatomy, no evidence of scarring and resolution of pain.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: underwent lysis of labial adhesions under sedation

evidence_events.source_span: 47-year-old female patient, liver transplant one year before due to cirrhosis of alcoholic etiology associated with hepatitis B, on tacrolimus and mycophenolate mofetil
Multiple skin lesions with 15-day exacerbation, high fever, malaise, weakness; weight loss, lack of appetite, dry cough, and dyspnea for approximately three months
evidence_events.temporal_cue: 15-day exacerbation; symptoms for approximately three months

evidence_events.source_span: Physical examination showed numerous acneiform and solid erythematous-normochromic papules with ulcerated center or crusts spread throughout the skin including the face
Diagnostic hypotheses included histoplasmosis, cryptococcosis, and paracoccidioidomycosis
Histopathological analysis of skin lesion biopsy showed epidermal hyperplasia and granulomatous and dermal suppurative inflammatory infiltrate with fungal elements inside giant cells
Grocott-Gomori staining showed multi-budding fungal cells characteristic of the Paracoccidioides genus
Biopsy fragment culture, general biochemical analyses, blood cultures, and serology including anti-HIV and anti-Paracoccidioides were normal or negative
Chest CT showed coalescent pulmonary consolidations, septal thickening, excavated lesions in lower lung portions, and lymph node enlargement compatible with paracoccidioidomycosis

Treatment with liposomal amphotericin B for 4 weeks required ICU transfer due to hemodynamic instability; patient discharged after clinical recovery and remission of paracoccidioidomycosis, maintained on itraconazole

source_metadata.title: Leg ulceration due to cutaneous melioidosis in a returning traveller
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case presentation, investigations, treatment, and outcome sections with source order preserved.

evidence_events.source_span: A 26-year-old man who returned to the UK having travelled extensively in Asia was referred with a 3-month history of distal left leg ulceration following an insect bite while in Thailand.

The lesion was erythematous, enlarged and subsequently ulcerated; it was debrided in Nepal and India with no improvement, and despite multiple courses of oral antibiotics, he developed two more ulcers adjacent to the original ulcer.
The edges of the ulcers were undermined which raised the clinical suspicion of pyoderma gangrenosum; the patient was systemically well with no fever, lymphadenopathy or organ dysfunction.

Full blood count, urea and electrolytes, ESR and CRP were normal; serology tests for HIV, Schistosoma, Strongyloides, Mycoplasma and Leishmania were negative; weakly positive antinuclear antibody (1:80 nucleolar) and negative double-stranded DNA.
MRI scan of the left leg did not demonstrate evidence of tendinopathy or osteomyelitis.

Incisional skin biopsy showed ulceration and acanthotic epithelium with deep dermal inflammatory infiltrate of neutrophils, lymphocytes, histiocytes and plasma cells; no granulomas, vasculitis, malignancy or viral inclusions; special stains (Gram, DPAS, Grocott, Giemsa, Ziehl-Neelson, Wade-Fite) were negative; histology was non-specific.
Tissue bacterial and fungal cultures produced no significant growth; Leishmania PCR was negative.
A wound swab taken at the referring hospital grew an organism identified as Burkholderia thailandensis.

The bacterial identification methodology identified Burkholderia thailandensis, a closely related but non-pathogenic relative; however, the organism's unusual antibiotic susceptibility profile made Burkholderia pseudomallei a more likely culprit; the isolate was discarded so further analysis was not possible.
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: Isolate discarded, no confirmatory testing possible

evidence_events.source_span: Initial multiple courses of oral antibiotics including amoxicillin, flucloxacillin, clindamycin and co-amoxiclav with no improvement; intravenous ceftazidime three times a day with oral co-trimoxazole started; topical corticosteroid and wound dressings used with no significant effect.

evidence_events.source_span: After diagnosis of cutaneous melioidosis, co-trimoxazole dose increased to high dose for 3 months with folic acid supplementation; topical corticosteroid stopped; wound debrided and dressed with negative pressure dressing weekly; patient taught to manage dressing.
Within 3 weeks of starting higher dose co-trimoxazole and negative pressure dressings, ulcers re-epithelialised with scarring; no recurrence 20 months after stopping oral co-trimoxazole.

evidence_milestones.source_span: The patient had an initial course of antibiotics, followed by debridement at a hospital in India. On his return to the UK, he received multiple courses of antibiotics including amoxicillin, flucloxacillin, clindamycin and co-amoxiclav with no improvement. Intravenous ceftazidime three times a day with oral co-trimoxazole (160 mg/800 mg) one tablet two times a day was started. Fucibet cream (a combined topical potent corticosteroid and fusidic acid), along with various wound dressings were used with no significant effect. The topical corticosteroid was stopped. Our specialist dermatology nurse debrided and dressed the wound with a negative pressure dressing on a weekly basis for several weeks. The patient was then taught how to manage the negative pressure dressing.

source_metadata.title: Non-occlusive Mesenteric Ischemia with Significant Hyperphosphatemia

evidence_events.source_span: An 86-year-old Japanese woman was admitted to the hospital with a 12-hour history of sudden-onset abdominal pain.
Her medical history was significant for diabetes mellitus, hypertension, angina pectoris, and chronic kidney disease.
Upon admission, her O2 saturation was 98% with the administration of 4 L of oxygen, and her limbs were cold with mottled skin.
Arterial blood gas testing showed metabolic lactic acidosis (pH 7.110, pCO2 32 mmHg, HCO3 9.5 mmol/L, lactate 9.1 mmol/L).
Further laboratory investigations revealed leukocytosis, marked inflammatory signs, and renal dysfunction.
A remarkable elevation in serum phosphate level (14.4 mg/dL), disproportionate to the renal dysfunction, was noted.
One hour after admission, her systolic blood pressure decreased from 139 to 60 mmHg and she went into shock.

Abdominal contrast-enhanced CT revealed a dilated colon and small intestine, containing fluids, but no free air, ascites, complete or closed-loop obstruction, absence of bowel wall enhancement, pneumatosis intestinalis, hepatic portal venous gas, or bowel wall thickening.
The patient underwent emergency laparotomy after six hours of intensive resuscitation.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: after six hours of intensive resuscitation

evidence_events.source_span: The ileum and whole colon, except for the sigmoid, were discontinuously necrotic despite pulsation of the superior mesenteric artery.
The patient was diagnosed with NOMI and underwent ileal resection, subtotal colectomy, and jejunostomy; after surgery, her serum phosphate level immediately returned to normal.

source_metadata.title: Acute Aortic Dissection Presenting as Rectal Tenesmus

evidence_events.source_span: A 69-year-old woman with a past medical history of anxiety, depression, fibromyalgia, irritable bowel syndrome, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and COPD presented to the ED with a chief concern of abdominal pain and back pain.
Prior to arrival, she had rectal tenesmus, an abrupt onset of “gas pains” along with abdominal distention, which were symptoms she would typically experience while constipated.

Given her history of irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), she initially thought that she was experiencing symptoms related to her IBS and self-administered an enema, but she had no output and experienced poor relief of her symptoms. Her gastrointestinal symptoms persisted for 12 h.
When the symptoms evolved and she began experiencing abdominal pain radiating to her back, she came the Emergency Department.
In the Emergency Department, her blood pressure was 170/68, but other vital signs were within normal limits.
Pertinent risk factors included hypertension, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and first-degree relatives with aortic and brain aneurysms.
She also noted that her pain began wrapping around her abdomen to her back and radiating up into her chest.
Physical exam revealed only diffuse abdominal tenderness with no pulse discrepancies.
Using the ADD-RS (Aortic Dissection Detection Risk Score), the patient was considered high risk and underwent computed tomography (CT) of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis with intravenous contrast.
The imaging study revealed a Stanford Type A aortic dissection extending from the aortic root to the aortic bifurcation.
She was started on a nicardipine infusion with a systolic pressure goal of less than 120 and an esmolol infusion with a heart rate goal of less than 60.
Cardiothoracic Surgery was consulted and she was taken to the operating room for emergent intervention.
She spent 8 days in the hospital, during which she made a complete recovery and then was discharged.

source_metadata.title: Rapid-onset methemoglobinemia from traditional-medicine-induced potassium nitrate poisoning: successful treatment with methylene blue—a case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 14-year-old Pakistani boy presented to the emergency department with sudden onset of severe generalized headache, shortness of breath, and bluish discoloration of the nose, lips, cheeks, skin of back of trunk, limbs, and nail beds.
Patient's family reported increasing agitation, drowsiness, and reduced ability to respond to commands effectively.
Family reported use of traditional medication (kalmi shora) in powder form, one tablespoon for renal lithiasis 2 hours before presentation.

Physical examination showed pulse rate 113 bpm, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute, hypothermia (34.5 °C), oxygen saturation 58%, and pronounced cyanosis on trunk, chin, lips, oral mucosa, and nail beds.

Patient was delirious with altered consciousness, Glasgow Coma Scale score 12, normal pupillary responses, cardiovascular auscultation without murmurs, respiratory exam with increased rate but no adventitious sounds.
Routine baseline investigations including EEG, cardiac enzyme test, and chest X-ray were unremarkable.
Dark-brown blood color noticed while obtaining arterial blood sample.

Arterial blood gas analysis showed acidemia (pH 7.02), normal partial pressure of oxygen (pO2 90 mmHg), decreased oxygen saturation (SpO2 85%), reduced pCO2 (23 mmHg), base excess −24.0 mmol/L, and elevated lactate (20 mmol/L).
Urine toxicology was unremarkable for any toxin.
Discrepancy between oxygen saturation and pO2, chocolate-colored blood, and sudden-onset cyanosis suggested nitrate methemoglobinemia.
Search of traditional medication confirmed potassium nitrate content, leading to diagnosis of potassium nitrate-induced methemoglobinemia.
Serum methemoglobin level was not assessed due to cost constraints and limited availability.
Initial treatment included 15 l oxygen via non-rebreather mask, hydrocortisone 100 mg IV, calcium gluconate infusion, methylene blue bolus (1 mg/kg over 10 minutes), and colloid infusion.
Within 10 minutes of methylene blue administration, oxygen saturation reached 100% on room air, consciousness restored, and cyanosis significantly reduced.
Bluish discoloration completely resolved within 30 minutes; patient remained stable during 2-day hospitalization and was discharged with multivitamins and co-enzyme Q.

source_metadata.title: Delayed traumatic subcutaneous emphysema: a case report

evidence_events.source_span: A white British female in her 70s attended the emergency department 24 h after a fall at home with the complaint of right sided chest pain and shortness of breath.
On arrival, the patient appeared well, with no sign of compromise.
The ambulance crew reported a global pleural rub and wheeze.

The patient rapidly deteriorated over the course of the next 30 min with massive crepitus swelling identified of her upper and lower limbs, head (including palpebral closure), neck, chest, and abdomen.
Vocal changes and early airway obstruction features were identified.
Arterial blood gas (ABG) results postintubation indicated a mixed respiratory and metabolic acidosis (pH 7.17, pO2 25 kPa, pCO2 8.4 kPa, and HCO3 19.9 mmol/L).
Full blood count indicated a raised white cell count (14.4 10^9/L) and neutrophil count (11.36 10^9/L) but normal red blood cell studies.
Renal function tests identified hyponatremia (130 mmol/L).
Coagulation studies (including Clauss fibrinogen) were normal.

An anteroposterior portable chest X-ray taken in the resuscitation room post-intubation, demonstrating severe subcutaneous emphysema. Pneumothoraces are not appreciable in this image, due to overlying emphysema.

CT imaging identified extensive thoracic injuries including fractures of ribs 7, 8, and 9 in two places on the right side, bilateral moderate-volume pneumothoraces, right-sided lower-lobe pulmonary hemorrhage, and left-sided lower-lobe laceration and collapse.
Bilateral 28Fr chest drains were inserted in the emergency department, initially draining air, with a commiserate reduction in ventilatory pressures noted following the insertion.
The patient was intubated with a C-mac video laryngoscope after rapid-sequence induction; airway anatomy was noted as highly edematous.
The patient was ventilated and sedated for 3 days in intensive care, then extubated successfully; chest drains were removed without complications.
At 1 month post-discharge, the patient had good recovery with return to usual activities but reported tiredness and generalized weakness.

hidden_reference.final_diagnosis_verbatim: Delayed traumatic subcutaneous emphysema resulting in airway compromise, with bilateral pneumothoraces and rib fractures, without cardiorespiratory compromise from tension pneumothoraces.
diagnostic_reasoning_verbatim_spans: A white British female in her 70s attended the emergency department 24 h after a fall at home with the complaint of right sided chest pain and shortness of breath.

The patient rapidly deteriorated over the course of the next 30 min with massive crepitus swelling identified of her upper and lower limbs, head (including palpebral closure), neck, chest, and abdomen.
Vocal changes and early airway obstruction features were identified.

CT imaging identified extensive thoracic injuries including fractures of ribs 7, 8, and 9 in two places on the right side, bilateral moderate-volume pneumothoraces, right-sided lower-lobe pulmonary hemorrhage, and left-sided lower-lobe laceration and collapse.
Bilateral 28Fr chest drains were inserted, initially draining air, with a commiserate reduction in ventilatory pressures noted following the insertion.
The patient was intubated with a C-mac video laryngoscope; airway anatomy was noted as highly edematous.
The patient was ventilated and sedated for 3 days in intensive care, then extubated successfully; chest drains were removed without complications.
diagnostic_reasoning_items: Initial presentation with chest pain and shortness of breath after fall.
Rapid progression of subcutaneous emphysema causing airway obstruction.
Imaging confirmed bilateral pneumothoraces and rib fractures.
Airway edema required intubation; chest drains relieved pneumothoraces.
Patient stabilized and recovered with supportive ICU care.
hidden_reference.final_diagnosis: Delayed traumatic subcutaneous emphysema with airway compromise and bilateral pneumothoraces secondary to rib fractures.
hidden_reference.diagnostic_reasoning: The patient presented with delayed symptoms after blunt chest trauma, rapidly developing massive subcutaneous emphysema and airway obstruction. Imaging confirmed bilateral pneumothoraces and rib fractures. Airway protection via intubation and chest drain insertion were critical. The absence of tension pneumothorax-related cardiorespiratory compromise was noted. The clinical course and imaging findings support the diagnosis of delayed traumatic subcutaneous emphysema causing airway compromise.
hidden_reference.article_derived_evidence_summary: A woman in her 70s presented 24 hours after a fall with chest pain and shortness of breath, initially stable but rapidly deteriorated with massive subcutaneous emphysema and airway obstruction. Laboratory tests showed acidosis and leukocytosis. Chest X-ray showed severe subcutaneous emphysema but no pneumothoraces. CT revealed bilateral pneumothoraces, rib fractures, and lung injuries. She was intubated and had bilateral chest drains placed. ICU care included ventilation and sedation. She recovered and was discharged with good outcome.
diagnosis_synonyms_or_variants: Bilateral pneumothoraces secondary to rib fractures
evidence_limitations: Chest X-ray limited by overlying emphysema obscuring pneumothoraces.

source_metadata.title: Don’t Forget What You Can’t See: A Case of Ocular Syphilis
source_metadata.notes: Case report from West J Emerg Med 2016; 24-year-old male with bilateral painless vision loss, diagnosed with ocular syphilis and HIV.

evidence_events.source_span: A 24-year-old male presented to the emergency department (ED) with five days of acute painless progressive bilateral loss of vision without photophobia, discharge, trauma, or contact lens use.
Review of systems was negative except for recent alopecia.
The patient was a sexually active homosexual male with a negative HIV test three months prior. Social history included marijuana, cocaine and methamphetamine use.

ED vital signs reported a temperature of 98.7 degrees F, respiratory rate of 16 breaths per minute, heart rate of 90 beats per minute, blood pressure of 113/70 mmHg, 98% O2 saturation on room air, visual acuity of 20/600 bilaterally and intraocular pressures of 8 mmHg in the left eye and 10 mmHg in the right eye.

Pupils were equal, round, reactive to light and accommodation and extra ocular movement intact, without Argyll Robertson (AR) pupils. Anterior chamber was clear, without conjunctival injection, foreign body, abrasion or ulceration. No afferent pupillary defect was appreciated.

Ophthalmology was urgently consulted to evaluate the patient and perform a dilated fundus exam. Fundoscopy revealed bilateral vitritis with scattered white tufts and globular white opacities inferiorly suggestive of posterior uveitis.
ED rapid plasmin reagin (RPR) and HIV tests were positive.

Inpatient cerebral spinal fluid (CSF) results were a white blood cell (WBC) count of 33 cells/μL, red blood cell (RBC) count of 26 cells/μL, a protein level of 44 mg/dL, glucose 53 mg/dL, and a Venereal Disease Research Laboratory (VDRL) titer of 1:2.
CSF ink stain, quantiferon gold, Lyme Ig, Bartonella Henselae, HBsAg, HCVAb were negative, as were bacterial and fungal cultures.
The patient had an absolute CD4 count of 1347 cells/μL and a viral load of 52,900 c/mL HIV RNA.

evidence_events.source_span: An 8-year-old girl presented to the emergency department (ED) with reported ventricular tachycardia. The patient stated that when she stood up to walk out of the classroom she began to experience lightheadedness and had two presyncopal episodes.
On scene, rhythm strip showed a wide rapid rhythm consistent with ventricular tachycardia so she was brought to the ED for further evaluation.

Her Corrected QT Interval (QTc) on the first ECG obtained was 423. In the ED, she denied chest pain, shortness of breath or palpitations and remained haemodynamically stable. She was noted to have multiple runs of stable non-sustained ventricular tachycardia with the longest run lasting approximately 10 s.
Her laboratory tests including complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, troponin I and chest radiograph were unremarkable.
Echocardiogram was obtained and was unremarkable.
On hospital day 2, her chest MRI showed a right ventricular cardiac contusion, subacute precordial haematoma and a small pericardial effusion with possible pericardial haematoma.
She remained in the hospital for 3 days for continued monitoring due to recurrent runs of premature ventricular contractions.
She was started on verapamil 40 mg every 8 hours on arrival; on hospital day 3 her dose was increased to 60 mg every 8 hours due to sustained frequent ectopic beats.

One month after discharge, the patient presented to the ED with non-specific leg weakness, spasms, fatigue and complaints of 'feeling hot all over'. Cardiac monitoring revealed continuing PVCs. Basic metabolic panel, complete blood count, magnesium, phosphorus, venous blood gas and chest radiography were unremarkable.
Her last two Holter recordings demonstrated 26%–27% PVCs. Her ECGs have continued to demonstrate sinus rhythm with monomorphic PVCs and occasional couplets.
Follow-up exercise treadmill after her most recent cardiology appointment demonstrated appropriate suppression of PVCs during exercise.

She remained on verapamil 120 mg total daily therapy for 1 year following the inciting event; however, due to her continuing frequent PVCs her verapamil was discontinued and metoprolol 25 mg extended release tablets taken at bedtime were started.

source_metadata.title: Neisseria meningitidis sepsis in a patient with acute epiglottitis and respiratory failure
source_metadata.notes: Case report from BMJ Case Reports 2018 describing acute epiglottitis with Neisseria meningitidis sepsis and respiratory failure.

evidence_events.source_span: A 78-year-old woman with a known history of hypertensive cardiomyopathy and paroxysmal benign positional vertigo presented to the emergency department with a 5-day history of throat pain and hoarseness, as well as a progressive and dolorous swelling in the submandibular area.
She further suffered from progressive coughing and dysphagia for 2 days and ultimately breathing difficulties.

The body temperature measured at the emergency department was 37.7 °C (100 °F). Haemodynamically, the patient was stable with a slightly hypertensive blood pressure (150/80 mm Hg) and tachycardia (118/min) as well as a room-air oxygen saturation of above 90%.
Blood analysis showed leucocytosis of 17.2 g/L and elevated C-reactive Protein (CRP) of 125 mg/L.

The initial clinical examination confirmed the submandibular swelling; the enoral examination was severely limited by a restricted mouth opening. Otoscopic examination was impossible due to ceruminal occlusion. Meningism was ruled out.
A neck CT scan performed with intravenous contrast showed the thumbprint sign typical for acute epiglottitis as well as extensive supraglottic and subglottic swelling resulting in stenosis.

After returning from the CT scan, the patient’s condition deteriorated within minutes. The oxygen saturation dropped to about 70% and did not recover even with 10 L of O2 administered via reservoir mask. Respiratory exhaustion was imminent.

While intravenous Solu-Medrol and Co-Amoxicillin were administered, intubation was initiated, which proved to be extremely difficult due to swelling of the supraglottic soft tissue, although video-guided GlideScope was used.

Consequently, the patient went into hypoxaemia and eventually into cardiac arrest. Reanimation protocol was immediately initiated. After even direct tracheal airway access failed, another attempt was made to orally intubate the patient, this time with success. After around 5 min of mechanical reanimation and a total of 2 mg intravenous adrenalin, ROSC was achieved.
During the course of hospitalisation, the initially sampled blood cultures revealed Neisseria meningitidis bacteraemia.
The antibiotic regimen was changed from Co-Amoxicillin 2.2 g every 8 hours to ceftriaxone 2 g every 12 hours. Intravenous steroid application was continued.

The patient remained intubated for a week when a follow-up CT scan showed decreased swelling of the epiglottis while swelling of the larynx and subglottic area remained grossly unchanged. The swelling was furthermore monitored by regular direct laryngoscopy.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: follow-up CT scan and direct laryngoscopy

evidence_events.source_span: In time, the decision was made to perform a surgical tracheotomy for adequate long-term ventilation.
After 11 days, the respiratory situation had improved enough to cease mechanical ventilation and eventually tracheostomy was reversed.

About 6 months after discharge, the patient was interviewed via telephone. All temporary neurological impairments were completely regressive over time. The patient though reported that delayed, she started suffering from panic attacks and states of anxiety regarding the incident.

source_metadata.title: 25-year-old man with sudden onset paraplegia
source_metadata.notes: Case report from BMJ Case Reports 2019; includes clinical presentation, imaging, treatment, and outcome.

evidence_events.source_span: A 25-year-old man presented to the emergency department with sudden onset paraplegia and pain in the lower extremities. His medical history included Crohn’s disease, managed with sulfasalazine. He was otherwise healthy, worked as a tradesman, and was competing in fitness championships.

Earlier in the morning, while lifting a 10 kg object at work, he experienced sudden onset of bilateral leg pain and felt the urge to defecate. While in the bathroom, he lost power in his lower extremities and was found on the floor by his coworkers.
On arrival, the patient presented with abdominal and bilateral leg pain in addition to numbness and paralysis of the legs. He had faecal incontinence and had soiled his clothes and the floor.

His legs were pale, cold and numb with flaccid paralysis. Femoral and distal peripheral pulses were impalpable. Sensory loss extended distally from the umbilical level, whereas examination above the umbilical level was normal. Rectal examination revealed total loss of sphincter tone and sensation in the perianal area.
Bedside arterial blood gas showed metabolic acidosis with pH 7.2, base excess −13 mmol/L, lactate 6.2 mmol/L, an elevated creatinine at 155 µmol/L and otherwise unremarkable.
CT angiography of the whole aorta revealed aortic thrombosis, extending from the level of the diaphragm to the aortic bifurcation. No signs of atherosclerosis were visible.

Emergency hybrid surgery was performed including thrombectomy and stenting of the right renal artery, superior mesenteric artery and distal aorta. Open exploration revealed extensive visceral ischaemia. No macroscopic anomaly of the aorta was identified.

On reperfusion, there was massive swelling of both legs requiring several fasciotomies. The patient was transferred to ICU and remained intubated for 2 days. Second-look surgery revealed viable abdominal organs except for the gallbladder, which was removed.
The patient was investigated by the coagulation department, but no coagulation disorder was identified and the underlying reason for developing this massive aortic thrombosis remains a mystery.
After rehabilitation, the patient regained some sensory function of the lower extremities but remained wheelchair-dependent.

On arrival, the patient presented with abdominal and bilateral leg pain in addition to numbness and paralysis of the legs. He had faecal incontinence and had soiled his clothes and the floor.

evidence_events.source_span: He denied a history of cancer or current cigarette use. He denied fevers, nasal congestion, sore throat, chest pain, or shortness of breath that was different from baseline. He denied recent travel or sick contacts.
On arrival to the ED, vital signs were temperature 37.3 °C, heart rate 96 beats per minute, blood pressure 137/70, 20 respirations per minute, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air.
Lung examination was notable for non-labored respirations with clear breath sounds bilaterally. The remainder of his physical examination was unremarkable.

evidence_events.source_span: On arrival to the medical unit he was febrile to 38.4 °C and mildly tachycardic with a heart rate of 104 beats per minute.
He was started on hydroxychloroquine 400 mg BID for one day, followed by 200 mg BID for 5 days for suspected COVID-19 infection.
The following day the patient was found to be COVID positive.
Symptomatic care was continued and the patient was discharged three days after admission in stable condition.

source_metadata.title: Tension pneumothorax in a patient with COVID-19
source_metadata.notes: Case report from BMJ Case Reports 2020 describing a 36-year-old man with suspected COVID-19 complicated by tension pneumothorax.

evidence_events.source_span: A 36-year-old man was brought to the emergency department with suspected SARS-CoV2 infection, presenting with a 3-week history of a dry cough, fevers and shortness of breath, worsening in the previous 4 hours with left-sided pleuritic chest pain.

On presentation, the patient was hypoxaemic with an SpO2 of 88% on 15 L/min oxygen, tachycardic at 150 beats/min, respiratory rate 50 breaths per minute using accessory muscles, trachea central, jugular venous pressure 3 cm above sternal angle, blood pressure 110/65 mm Hg, and absent breath sounds throughout the left hemithorax with reduced vocal fremitus and asymmetrical chest expansion.

Portable anteroposterior chest radiograph demonstrated a large left-sided pneumothorax with mediastinal shift and radiological signs of tension; the right lung showed widespread patchy consolidative changes consistent with severe COVID-19.

Full blood count showed raised white cell count (13.64 ×10⁹/L) with neutrophilia (8.91 ×10⁹/L), lymphocyte count 3.81 ×10⁹/L, haemoglobin 146 g/L, platelets 1051 ×10⁹/L; biochemical markers showed raised C-reactive protein (28.7 mg/L) and alanine aminotransferase (107 IU/L); ECG showed sinus tachycardia at 155 beats/min.
Lung ultrasound following definitive treatment demonstrated multiple confluence B-lines with pleural thickening bilaterally, consistent with COVID-19.
Repeat chest radiograph confirmed lung re-expansion with extensive bilateral consolidation consistent with severe COVID-19.
Thoracic CT demonstrated widespread areas of patchy consolidation consistent with severe COVID-19 infection, with associated bullae.

Emergency needle decompression of the pneumothorax was performed with a 14-gauge cannula inserted in the second rib space mid-clavicular line, followed by insertion of a 12-French Seldinger chest drain into the left axilla.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: needle decompression and chest drain insertion

evidence_events.source_span: Treatment resulted in immediate improvement in respiratory and cardiovascular physiology with clinical and radiological evidence of lung re-expansion; oxygen requirement reduced from 15 L/min to 4 L/min within an hour, with normalization of respiratory and heart rate.
Initial COVID-19 swab returned negative; infectious diseases team felt patient very likely had COVID-19 based on history and imaging despite negative swab.

source_metadata.title: Addressing a rare cause of paediatric stridor: subglottic cyst

evidence_events.source_span: An 18-month-old girl child was brought by her parents to emergency service with noisy breathing and increased breathing effort progressive over several months, but significantly worsened for 1 week following fever and diarrhoea.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: progressive over several months, worsened for 1 week

evidence_events.source_span: She had a weak cry with no difficulty in feeding and coughing or choking episodes.
She was hospitalised and received treatment for croup multiple times in the past without complete symptomatic relief.
The child was born preterm and kept intubated for a month after birth.

At presentation, child was irritable with tachypnoea and tachycardia without cyanosis. Her biphasic stridor with suprasternal and intercostal retraction worsened on crying and was not relieved on postural changes.
Due to her symptomatology during the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic, the COVID-19 test was sent and endoscopy was avoided.
Significant subglottic airway compromise was noted in the lateral neck radiograph.
The contrast-enhanced CT of neck revealed a hypodense, non-enhancing lesion measuring 9×8 mm in the subglottis.
With a presumptive diagnosis of subglottic cyst and a negative COVID-19 test, the child was taken to operating room and tracheotomy was performed with mask ventilation.
Direct laryngoscopy revealed a submucosal cystic lesion immediately beneath the mobile vocal cords without any significant patent airway around the cyst.
Using a 22-gauge microlaryngeal needle, 1 mL of thick yellowish clear fluid was aspirated from the cyst.
The cyst arising from the right posterolateral wall of subglottis was marsupialised using coblator.
Through the adequately patent airway tracheoscopy was performed which was unremarkable.
Postoperatively, child recovered well and was discharged with a corked tracheostomy tube and nasal breathing.
Follow-up endoscopic evaluation at 2 months did not suggest cyst recurrence.

source_metadata.title: Acute transverse myelitis in COVID-19 infection

evidence_events.source_span: A 60-year-old man presented to hospital with progressive bilateral lower limb weakness, urinary retention and constipation.

He had been diagnosed with COVID-19 10 days prior after positive SARS-CoV-2 PCR on day 7 of illness; respiratory symptoms resolved after 13 days; neurological symptoms started on day 16 with acute urinary retention, progressing to lower limb stiffness, difficulty walking and constipation.
On examination, increased tone, hyperreflexia, reduced proprioception, patchy paresthesia bilaterally to umbilicus level, decreased anal tone; consistent with upper motor neuron lesion.
Preliminary blood tests showed mildly elevated C reactive protein (21 mg/L), elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (44 mm/hour), elevated D-dimer (0.79 g/L), and lymphopaenia (0.8 ×10⁹/L).

CT lumbosacral spine showed diffuse disc bulge at L5/S1 with mild thecal sac indentation but no significant central canal stenosis; CT brain was normal; CT chest showed scattered peripheral ground-glass opacities and consolidation in both lungs.
MRI whole spine demonstrated long segment of T2 signal elevation centrally in spinal cord from T7 to T10 without significant enhancement or mass; MRI brain and orbits showed no inflammatory changes.
Lumbar puncture showed elevated protein (0.79 g/L), normal glucose (3.2 mmol/L), normal white blood cell count; CSF and blood cultures negative; SARS-CoV-2 PCR negative in CSF.

Serology for SARS-CoV-2 showed recent infection (IgG 640, IgA 160, IgM 20); serology for other viruses (mycoplasma, Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, HIV, hepatitis B and C) negative; autoimmune panel negative; antibodies for anti-myelin-associated glycoprotein IgM, myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein, and neuromyelitis optica IgG negative.
Serum ferritin elevated (711 μg/L) and interleukin-6 normal (7.8 pg/mL) measured on day 10 of admission (28 days after symptom onset).
evidence_events.temporal_cue: day 10 of admission (28 days after symptom onset)
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: IL-6 measured post-steroid therapy

evidence_events.source_span: Patient treated with intravenous methylprednisone 1 g per day for 3 days; no antivirals, antibiotics or other immune-modulatory drugs given.

Neurological symptoms improved shortly after corticosteroid therapy; repeat MRI on day 10 showed almost complete resolution of spinal cord changes; full lower limb motor strength regained; paresthesias resolved; urinary catheter removed; discharged on day 11 of admission.

evidence_events.source_span: A 57-year-old man with a medical history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus presented in the emergency department with worsening swelling of the tongue, difficulty in speaking and shortness of breath since the morning.
He was given multiple doses of intramuscular epinephrine in the prehospital setting with no change in symptoms.
He had no associated pain, itchiness or rash, and he denied fever, nausea, vomiting, chest pain or cough.
The patient stated he began taking a new blood pressure medication, benazepril, approximately 4 months ago.

On examination, the patient was afebrile and normotensive, with an oxygen saturation of 96% on room air. There was pronounced oedema involving the lingual mucosa and subcutaneous tissues of the perioral area without pain or pruritus. Cardiac auscultation revealed tachycardia without any pathological murmurs. Auscultation of the lungs revealed decreased breath sounds bilaterally with inspiratory effort, but no wheezing or crepitations. No jugular venous distention or lower limb swelling was appreciated. No urticarial eruption was noted throughout.

Laboratory tests revealed mild leucocytosis (10.8×10⁹/L) with lymphopenia (800×10⁹/L) and elevated high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (7.80 mg/dL), ferritin (866 ng/mL) and lactate dehydrogenase (1295 IU/L).
Chest X-ray showed bilateral infiltrates in lung bases.
CT imaging of the neck showed oedema along the prevertebral and submucosal tissues of the oropharynx and hypopharynx, as well as in the submandibular area surrounding the submandibular glands.
A nasopharyngeal swab was taken for COVID-19 assay by real-time PCR.

Anaphylaxis was our initial diagnosis of exclusion. Without positive clinical response following epinephrine administration, delay in considering alternative diagnoses may have lead to a fatal outcome.
Other differential diagnoses chiefly included deep space abscess and hereditary or acquired angioedema.

In the absence of family history or repeated occurrence of angioedema, hereditary angioedema was less likely. ACE inhibitor-associated angioedema was our primary diagnosis due to the recent use of ACE inhibitors in the last few months.
Other workup showed bilateral pulmonary infiltrates and elevated inflammatory markers with lymphopenia consistent with COVID-19 infection.
The patient’s clinical presentation improved over 3 hours once tranexamic acid was given. Intravenous diphenhydramine and famotidine were given, and benazepril was withheld.

source_metadata.title: Respiratory dysfunction as first presentation of myasthenia gravis misdiagnosed as COVID-19

evidence_events.source_span: A 46-year-old man, with hypertension and past history of cigarette smoking, presented to the emergency department (ED) on March 26 for symptoms consistent with upper respiratory infection (cough, sore throat, and fever).
Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assay on nasal-pharyngeal swab sample was negative for SARS-CoV-2, while a chest X-ray was reported as suggestive for mild interstitial pneumonia.

The patient was hospitalized in a COVID-19 ward and eventually discharged 3 days after, afebrile and without signs of respiratory dysfunction. The diagnosis at discharge was “mild SARS-CoV-2-related pneumonia.”

A few days after discharge, the patient suffered from shortness of breath, generalized weakness, and marked effort intolerance. He occasionally found low values of arterial oxygen saturation on self-measurement at home (O2 saturation swinging from 91–97% over the day).
On April 4, another nasal-pharyngeal swab PCR for SARS-CoV-2 was negative. The chest CT scan showed modest bibasilar infiltrates, and the arterial blood gases were within normal values.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: PCR assay, chest CT scan, arterial blood gases

evidence_events.source_span: On April 24, the patient returned to the ED for persistence of asthenia and blood oxygen desaturation. PCR assay and rapid Ig test for SARS-CoV-2 were both negative. Arterial gas analysis showed SO2 97%, pO2 74 mmHg, pCO2 44 mmHg, lactate 1.6 mmol/L, HCO3- 26 mmol/L. Echocardiography was normal. Chest CT scan showed mild basilar infiltrates. Six-minute walking test showed arterial oxygen desaturation down to 84%.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: PCR assay, Ig test, arterial gas analysis, echocardiography, chest CT scan, six-minute walking test

evidence_events.source_span: Neurological evaluation revealed slight hypophonia after sustained speech, slight diplopia, ptosis in one eye during sustained upward gaze, and slight weakness in proximal lower limb muscles (Medical Research Council scale 4/5), with normal deep tendon reflexes.
Repetitive nerve stimulation showed 15% decrement in the amplitude of compound muscle action potential registered in right nasalis muscle while stimulating at low frequency (5 Hz) the facial nerve.
Serological testing for antibodies against acetylcholine receptor (AChR), muscle-specific kinase (MUSK), and ryanodin receptor (RyR) was negative.
Chest CT scan was reviewed and no thymic residual tissue was identified.
After introduction of anticholinesterase therapy and oral steroid, dyspnea and fatigue significantly improved. The 6-minute walking test did not show arterial blood desaturation.

source_metadata.title: A Patient with speechlessness and rhabdomyolysis: a rare presentation of severe hypocalcaemia
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from BMJ Case Reports 2020 article, case report sections prioritized.

evidence_events.source_span: A 29-year-old man presented to the emergency room with episodes of sudden speechlessness, hoarseness, vomiting after drinking cold water and spasms of his hands.
General physical and neurological examination showed no abnormalities except for a positive Chvostek’s and Trousseau’s sign.

Blood tests showed severe hypocalcaemia (1.03 mmol/L), raised phosphate (2.21 mmol/L), raised creatine kinase (2962 IU/L), low magnesium (0.58 mmol/L), normal albumin, and normal kidney and liver function tests.
Later blood tests showed hypoparathyroidism (0.7 pmol/L) and low 25-hydroxy(OH)-vitamin D3 concentrations (11 nmol).
ECG showed a prolonged QTc interval of 501 ms.
Further investigations showed no mutations of the calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) and no parathyroid antibodies.

Differential diagnosis included malnutrition, chronic kidney failure, magnesium depletion, vitamin D deficiency, rhabdomyolysis and hypoparathyroidism; malnutrition and kidney failure were excluded by history and labs; magnesium depletion was mild; rhabdomyolysis was present but not severe enough to explain hypocalcaemia; hyperphosphataemia and low PTH supported hypoparathyroidism.
Immediate treatment with intravenous calcium gluconate and magnesium sulphate was given, resulting in quick improvement of voice and normalization of creatine kinase.

Patient was diagnosed with idiopathic primary hypoparathyroidism with vitamin D deficiency requiring lifelong calcium supplements and alphacalcidol; follow-up showed normalization of calcium and CK with treatment adherence.

source_metadata.title: Ruptured functioning adrenal tumour, atypical presentation with renal colic and hypertension

evidence_events.source_span: A 30-year-old Tunisian man has presented to Hamad General Hospital with severe left flank pain associated with headache, sweating, anxiety, excruciating pain, diffuse left-sided chest pain and shortness of breath; blood pressure was 162/102 mm Hg, heart rate 116 bpm, respiratory rate 21 per minute, oxygen saturation 98%, afebrile

Bedside point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) showed no hydronephrosis bilaterally, no free fluids, normal diameter of the aorta, normal heart contractility, no right-sided strain, and no pericardial effusion

Complete blood count showed leucocytosis (20x10^9/L) and mild anaemia (haemoglobin 12.4 g/L, haematocrit 37.5%), mild renal impairment with creatinine 170 µmol/L, electrolytes and liver function within normal limits, cardiac markers normal, urine analysis normal, ECG showed no acute ischaemic changes, chest X-ray normal

CT of the abdomen and urinary tract showed a large soft tissue like lesion at the left adrenal region with hyperdensities, pushing the left kidney downward and laterally with severe surrounding fat stranding and perinephric fluid; no significant hydronephrosis or stones noted
CT angiography showed posteromedial active extravasation of contrast in the left adrenal lesion measuring 9.7×12.3×12.6 cm, consistent with active bleeding

Patient received intravenous phentolamine (alpha-blocker) to control blood pressure; left adrenal artery angioembolisation was performed 12 hours after presentation with embolisation of superior and inferior adrenal arteries but failure of middle artery embolisation; no immediate complications and no extravasation postembolisation

Post-embolisation, patient admitted to ICU with persistent tachycardia and hypertension; oral prazosin 1 mg (alpha-blocker) started; serial blood pressure monitoring showed fluctuating but elevated readings

Serial CBC showed a drop in haemoglobin to 7.1 g/L and haematocrit to 23.3%; patient deteriorated clinically and required transfusion of three units of packed red cells; emergency laparotomy was performed

Surgical pathology showed pheochromocytoma with mitotic figures >4/10 HPF, high cellularity, large nests or diffuse growth, focal or confluent tumour necrosis; total Pheochromocytoma of the Adrenal Gland Scaled Score was 8/20 indicating aggressive potential

Follow-up CT abdomen with contrast showed no recurrence of the mass; whole-body FDG-PET showed no evidence of metastatic or recurrent disease; blood pressure controlled without medications; patient asymptomatic

source_metadata.title: Renal angiomyolipoma rupture in a young female with COVID-19

evidence_events.source_span: A 22-year-old female presented to the emergency department with acute-onset left flank pain that began while at rest, reached maximum intensity within minutes, radiated to her left shoulder, and was described as having been “kicked in the back.”
Two weeks prior, the patient had presented to the ED with five days of cough, shortness of breath, myalgias, and fevers, and was subsequently diagnosed with COVID-19 via nasopharyngeal PCR assay.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: diagnosed with COVID-19 via nasopharyngeal PCR assay

evidence_events.source_span: Her initial vital signs included: heart rate 109, blood pressure 135/84, oxygen saturation 99%, respiratory rate 18, and temperature 36.9C. An abdominal exam revealed a soft, nondistended abdomen with focal left upper quadrant tenderness. There was no palpable mass, rebound, or guarding. The patient also had severe tenderness upon percussion of the left costovertebral angle.
Laboratory studies revealed: white blood cell count 13.8 cells/mm3, hemoglobin 13.4 g/dl, PT 14 s, APTT 35.4 s, INR 1.1. Urine studies showed microhematuria and a negative pregnancy test.
A chest x-ray was unremarkable.

Non-contrast computed tomography of her abdomen and pelvis demonstrated left peri-renal moderate volume hemorrhage with a fat dense lesion in the left kidney measuring 2.5 × 2.3 × 2.1 cm, consistent with ruptured renal AML.
Interventional radiology performed embolization 12 h after admission. The intraprocedural evaluation of the renal artery system found no aneurysmal dilatation.
The patient's post-procedural course was complicated by continued hemorrhage and retroperitoneal hematoma, with a hemoglobin nadir of 6.8 g/dl requiring transfusion of 2 units packed red blood cells.
On hospital day 6 she developed respiratory COVID-19 symptoms and again tested positive by PCR assay for COVID-19.
She was discharged on hospital day 8 with oral analgesics.

source_metadata.title: Case Report: An Unusual First Manifestation of a Pheochromocytoma

evidence_events.source_span: A 30-year old male presented to the emergency department complained of hemoptysis as a first manifestation a year ago without obvious predisposing cause.
The hemoptysis was manifested as bloody sputum, with a total volume of 50–100 ml. The accompanying symptoms included paroxysmal chest distress, shortness of breath, and palpitation.
During his stay in the emergency department, the physical examination was unremarkable.
The pulmonary CT (taken in another hospital) showed mild infection. The abdominal ultrasound and echocardiography were both normal. The reexamination of pulmonary CT showed normal.
His symptoms were relieved quickly after hemostatic therapy and antibiotic treatment. The patient was discharged without further evaluation.
After a year’s duration, those paroxysmal symptoms sometimes start with nausea and emesis. This time, he visited the emergency department complaining of a recent attack.
Physical examination was unremarkable. He was conscious, afebrile, and oriented, with a blood pressure of 107/85 mmHg, a heart rate of 79/min, and a respiratory rate of 18 breaths/min.

A complete blood count revealed the following: white blood cell 23,720/mm3, hemoglobin 18.1 g/dl, hematocrit 52%, and platelets 275,000/mm3. Liver function test results were ALT 62 IU/L, AST 58 IU/L, and LDH 326 IU/L. His blood glucose was 297 mg/dl, and serum creatinine was 114 ummol/L. Prothrombin time and activated partial thromboplastin time were 10.7 and 29.2 s, respectively. The examination of the urine showed proteinuria and glucosuria.

At admission, the pulmonary CT scan showed patchy high-density shadow and ground-glass opacity, compatible with diffuse alveolar hemorrhage (DAH). The bronchoscopy confirmed the diagnosis. The bronchoalveolar lavage reported macrophage (86%), lymphocyte (1.5%), neutrophil (12.5%).
evidence_events.procedural_cue: pulmonary CT scan and bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage

evidence_events.source_span: Autoimmune diseases were suspected at first. Further laboratory tests showed anti-DNA, c-ANCA, anti-MPO, ANA, and anti-GBM antibodies were negative. Blood and sputum cultures were negative as well.

The cortisol levels were 2.5 μg/dl (0 AM), 12.3 μg/dl (8 AM, reference value 5–25 μg/dl), 11.6 μg/dl (4 PM, reference value 2.5–12.5 μg/dl). Moreover, CT reexamination showed the diffuse alveolar hemorrhage resolved completely 5 days after the initial CT without any targeted treatment.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: at second admission and 5 days later

evidence_events.source_span: Acute coronary syndrome and stress-induced cardiomyopathy were both suspected. However, the patient did not show any signs of pulmonary edema. Biomarkers of myocardial injury were normal at admission. The echocardiography was normal with favorable systolic and diastolic functions. The electrocardiogram revealed normal sinus rhythm. The blood pressure remained normal under close monitoring.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: cardiac biomarkers, echocardiography, electrocardiogram, blood pressure monitoring

evidence_events.source_span: The paroxysmal symptoms indicated high levels of catecholamine. The abdominal CT scan discovered left adrenal mass with intravenous contrast (69 * 61 * 62 mm).
evidence_events.procedural_cue: abdominal CT scan with intravenous contrast

evidence_events.source_span: The diagnosis of pheochromocytoma was confirmed biochemically by the elevated catecholamine and metanephrine levels in the blood [metanephrine 2,506.2 pmol/L (<605.9 pmol/L), normetanephrine 16,279.2 pmol/L (413.9–4434.2 pmol/L)], and urine (VMA 40.3 μg/24 h, reference value 1.9–13.6 μg/24 h).
evidence_events.procedural_cue: blood and urine catecholamine and metanephrine measurement

evidence_events.source_span: The patient received treatment of phenoxybenzamine, doxazosin mesylate, and moxifloxacin. During the hospital stay, the patient’s condition was getting better without any symptoms.
Two months after discharge from the respiratory intensive care unit, the patient revisited the urology surgery department. The left adrenalectomy was performed by laparoscopy.
Pathology examination revealed pheochromocytoma with moderate atypia histological features, immunohistochemical staining [Syn (+), SDHB (+), CD56(+), Ki-67(≤1%)].
We followed the patient for 6 months. His symptoms gradually improved, and he was discharged.

evidence_events.source_span: Baseline workup showed normal creatinine, hypokalaemia (K=2.5), elevated total lymphocyte count (14) with neutrophils of 87.4 and elevated C reactive protein of 153. Urine detail report was positive for mild proteinuria, glucosuria with ketones 3+ and haematuria. He had a glycated haemoglobin of 11.9 with positive galactomannan and negative beta D-glucan. Blood and urine cultures did not grow any microorganisms.
Nasal and throat fungus smear/potassium hydroxide preparation revealed few broad coenocytic (A-septate) hyphae, moderate budding yeast cells with pseudohyphae and culture-grown Rhizopus spp.
CT of the chest with COVID-19 screening protocol revealed multifocal patchy areas of ground-glass haziness involving right lung field and left lower lobe suggestive of COVID-19 infection.

CT of the facial region with contrast showed abnormal soft tissue thickening in the region of the right side of the face with thickening and enhancement of right lacrimal gland, mild pre-septal swelling, thickening and enhancement of temporalis, lateral pterygoid and muscles of mastication on the right side. There was pansinusitis with air fluid levels in bilateral maxillary sinuses and sphenoid sinuses. Pneumatised petrous temporal bone apex was visualised with fluid within it. There were ill-defined hypodensities in bilateral cerebellar hemispheres and right temporal lobe indicating possibility of an infarction.

MRI of the head revealed abnormal T2 hyperintense signals in the right infratemporal region involving the pterygoid muscles and extending into the right side of the face and the pre-septal region. Superiorly they were extending intracranially and infiltrating into the right temporal lobe. There were abnormal T2 hyperintense signals showing diffusion restriction in the right cerebellum and the pons representing an acute infarct. Subtle acute lacunar infarcts at the posterior aspect of the bilateral lateral ventricles were also visualised.
Emergency right face debridement, right eye exenteration and bilateral functional endoscopic sinus surgery were performed, and the patient was shifted to intensive care unit (ICU).

Histopathology examination of the biopsy specimen showed right cheek skin and right eyeball invaded by numerous aseptate fungal hyphae and multiple nasal tissue pieces exhibiting numerous aseptate fungal hyphae which further supported our working diagnosis.

Postoperatively, head CT scan showed interval removal of the right orbital structures with soft tissue removal of the right cheek with interval packing of the defects. Interval maturation in the infarcts in the right cerebellum, right hemipons and right temporal lobe was visualised. There was redemonstration of the high-density material in the bilateral sphenoid and left maxillary and bilateral ethmoid sinuses.

evidence_events.source_span: 2-year-old Emirati boy presented with fever, diarrhea, vomiting, and fluctuating levels of consciousness; partially immunized with no immunizations after 4 months

On examination, drowsy but arousable with GCS fluctuating between 10 and 11, low-grade fever (38°C), tachycardia (137 bpm), hypotension (80/50 mmHg), capillary refill time 4 seconds, pupils 3 mm with slow reaction, no neck stiffness, erythematous mildly enlarged tonsils
Diagnosed with septic shock secondary to meningitis and encephalitis; treated immediately with oxygen, intravenous ceftriaxone, acyclovir, dexamethasone, and fluids; admitted to PICU
CT head performed immediately after antibiotics showed mild diffuse cerebral edema with no raised intracranial pressure
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: CT head showed mild diffuse cerebral edema

evidence_events.source_span: Initial blood tests: low WBC (2.73), high neutrophil % (80.20), high CRP (72.91 mg/L), very high procalcitonin (95.72 ng/ml), prolonged PT (19.4 s), prolonged PTT (41.2 s), high INR (1.65), high lactate (3 mmol/L)

First blood culture (on admission) isolated beta-lactamase-negative ampicillin-resistant (BLNAR) Haemophilus influenzae type b, sensitive to ceftriaxone, meropenem, cefotaxime; resistant to ampicillin/clavulanic acid

evidence_events.source_span: Antibiotic changed to meropenem on day 7 due to ceftriaxone resistance; patient became afebrile and improved
