initial_presentation.chief_complaint: painful, acute worsening of chronic left thigh swelling
initial_presentation.first_contact_summary: She denied additional symptoms, trauma, personal and family history of thrombosis or coagulopathy, and tobacco or illicit substance use. A routine workout 2 days prior was unchanged from her usual described intensity. The pain was described as ‘tightness’, which was relieved by rest and aggravated by movement. The patient reported that her chronic asymmetry was never investigated by previous physicians because it was only slightly wider in girth and non-painful since childhood. Her only prescribed medication was a levonorgestrel intrauterine device, and family history was significant for ulcerative colitis and coronary artery disease. The physical examination revealed her to be in no acute distress with normal vital signs. Relevant findings included a left thigh, which was roughly double the circumference, but the same length, as the right. Otherwise, both thighs had soft compartments without erythema, crepitus, warmth or tenderness to palpation (figure 1). Her neurovascular function was normal bilaterally, there was no pitting oedema or calf swelling, and no discomfort was noted behind the knee on forced dorsiflexion. Finally, no urine colour changes were noted. All other findings were either normal or not clinically relevant. Notably, capillary malformations in the patient’s left thigh had been present since birth but were not noted on the treating physician’s examination.

source_metadata.title: Parkes-Weber syndrome in the emergency department

evidence_events.source_span: A 20-year-old woman with no relevant previous medical history presented to the emergency department (ED) with 1 day of painful, acute worsening of her chronic left thigh swelling without an identifiable trigger.

Physical examination revealed left thigh roughly double the circumference but same length as right, soft compartments without erythema, crepitus, warmth or tenderness; neurovascular function normal bilaterally; no pitting oedema or calf swelling; capillary malformations in left thigh present since birth but not noted on exam.

Initial labs showed normal complete blood count, normal basic metabolic panel, negative pregnancy test, elevated d-dimer at 3.25 µg/mL (normal <0.49), and elevated creatine kinase at 7697 U/L (normal <200).
Venous Doppler ultrasound of lower extremities revealed patent, compressible, bilaterally symmetric femoral and popliteal veins and soft tissue oedema in the medial left thigh.
Left femur radiograph showed no acute fracture with normal femur morphology.

MRI of left thigh showed subcutaneous and fascial oedema with biceps femoris and semitendinosus muscle hyperintensity; no fluid collections or mass lesions; neurovascular bundle intact; no evidence of arteriovenous malformation on radiologist's read.

Patient received 30 mL/kg bolus normal saline, 1000 mg IV acetaminophen, and 4 mg IV morphine for pain control.
Patient discharged with diagnosis of rhabdomyolysis after stable presentation >11 hours, improvement in swelling and pain, and creatine kinase downtrend from 7697 U/L to 1800 U/L.

Over 6 months, patient had three ED visits with similar symptoms; rheumatology ruled out autoimmune diseases including myositis; dermatology noted large 'birthmarks' on left leg and referred to interventional radiology for suspected vascular malformations.

source_metadata.title: Ruptured angiomyolipoma, a novel entity for emergency physicians in the differential diagnosis of haemorrhagic shock in a female patient of reproductive age

evidence_events.source_span: A woman in her 30s with a medical history of hypertension, chronic kidney disease (CKD) not yet on dialysis prior to transplantation, status post living unrelated kidney transplant one decade prior and IgA nephropathy, presented to the emergency department via ambulance with abdominal pain approximately 1 year ago.
She reported progressively worsening left lower quadrant abdominal pain radiating to her left flank that began abruptly after exercise 1 day prior.
She also complained of numbness to her left lower extremity, as well as feeling a 'bulge' in the left lower quadrant of her abdomen.

On arrival to the emergency department, the patient had an initial blood pressure of 90/66 mm Hg, heart rate 84 bpm, respiratory rate 24, oxygen saturation 100% on room air, and oral temperature 34.4°C. She appeared diaphoretic and pale, with cool skin and diminished capillary refill. Her abdomen was distended and exquisitely tender to palpation of the left lower quadrant with involuntary guarding.
A point-of-care ultrasound performed by the emergency physicians revealed free intraperitoneal fluid and a large complex-appearing left-sided intra-abdominal mass.

Initial labs were significant for venous blood gas (VBG) showing pH 7.31, pCO2 41 and bicarbonate 20.6 mmol/L; haemoglobin 82 g/L, decreased from baseline of 123 g/L; lactate elevated to 2.6; blood urea nitrogen (BUN) 30 mg/dL and serum creatinine 2.59 mg/dL, increased from baseline 21 mg/dL and 2.01 mg/dL respectively 6 months prior.
Obtaining a urine pregnancy initially was difficult due to minimal urine output; however, once obtained, this test was negative.

A CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast demonstrated large volume hemoperitoneum and left retroperitoneal haematoma with contrast extravasation from the left renal artery. A ruptured AML in the region of the patient’s atrophic native left kidney was the suspected cause of haemorrhage.

Resuscitation began with placement of two large bore peripheral intravenous lines, supplemental oxygen via nasal cannula, crystalloid infusion with 1 L of lactated ringers, and two units of uncrossmatched O+ packed red blood cells due to presumed intra-abdominal bleeding causing haemorrhagic shock.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: placement of IV lines, oxygen, fluids, blood transfusion

evidence_events.source_span: A left renal angiogram demonstrated an actively haemorrhaging left renal artery. The left renal artery was embolised successfully with 5 cm3 of ethanol and 6 coils. The patient’s haemodynamics stabilised while in the IR suite.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: Ultimately, the patient was taken to the IR suite

evidence_events.source_span: While in the surgical ICU, the patient developed worsening acute allograft dysfunction with hyperkalaemia and oliguria. Haemodialysis was initiated due to potassium of 7.7 mmol/L. Creatinine peaked at 4.18 mg/dL with estimated GFR of 13 mL/min. Kidney function and urine output improved and no further dialysis was needed.

The patient was discharged home in stable condition 10 days following presentation. One month later, outpatient follow-up showed stable renal function and diminishing haematoma size on non-contrast CT and renal ultrasound.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: 10 days following presentation; one month later
evidence_events.procedural_cue: follow-up imaging with non-contrast CT and renal ultrasound

source_metadata.title: Destructive osteomyelitis involving Parvimonas micra and Campylobacter rectus
source_metadata.notes: Case report of primary sternal osteomyelitis caused by oral flora bacteria Parvimonas micra and Campylobacter rectus.

evidence_events.source_span: A female patient in her mid-40s presented to the emergency department due to a spontaneous rupture of an abscess located on the mid-frontal chest wall.
The patient had noticed a progressive swelling of the chest wall over the past 4 weeks with general discomfort and loss of appetite but no fever.
Physical examination revealed a significant swelling of 20×10 cm on the chest wall with an abscess perforating the skin under the left clavicle, discharging bad-smelling purulent fluid and blood.

Laboratory testing showed elevated C reactive protein (402 mg/L), elevated white cell count (15.4 G/L), elevated thrombocyte count (429 G/L), slightly elevated serum creatinine (102 µmol/L), and significantly elevated procalcitonin (44 µg/L).

CT imaging revealed osteomyelitic erosion of the sternum with abscess formation measuring 20×13.5 cm extending from the processus xyphoideus to the left side of the glandula thyreoidea, compromising the sternocleidomastoid muscle.
Blood and deep tissue cultures from sternal bone and abscess revealed infection with Parvimonas micra and Campylobacter rectus; mycobacterial cultures were negative.
Dental examination confirmed chronic periodontitis with poor dental hygiene, a non-vital tooth 47, and loss of cavity occlusion in tooth 36.

Serological testing excluded HIV infection; HbA1c was normal excluding diabetes mellitus; mycobacterial cultures and PCR were repeatedly negative excluding tuberculosis; no malignancy was detected on CT or biopsy samples.

Emergent surgical debridement was performed with empiric antibiotic treatment initiated and later adjusted to co-amoxicillin after culture results; sequential surgical debridement with vacuum-assisted closure therapy and split-skin grafting was done.

The patient made a quick recovery with normalization of blood parameters and well-healing wound; antibiotic therapy was continued for 8 weeks; dental treatment for periodontitis was recommended to prevent recurrence.

Physical examination revealed a significant swelling of 20×10 cm on the chest wall with an abscess perforating the skin under the left clavicle, discharging bad-smelling purulent fluid and blood.

source_metadata.notes: Extraction based on case presentation and clinical course narrative.

evidence_events.source_span: A 70-year-old male White patient was hospitalized in the intensive care unit following an intrahospital cardiac arrest. History started a year before with repeated deep vein thrombosis and episodes of skin eruption compatible with Sweet’s syndrome.
Skin biopsy confirmed Sweet’s syndrome.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: By the end of the year

evidence_events.source_span: Chest and abdomen computed tomography (CT) scan was interpreted as neoplasia-free. Other investigations showed an inflammatory syndrome with C-reactive protein (CRP) at 187 mg/L and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia at 20.9 g/L. Screening for JAK-2 mutation was negative. Screening for viral and bacterial infection was also negative.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: By the end of the year

evidence_events.source_span: Steroids tapering resulted in multiple skin eruption recurrences in January and April 2020, hindering complete drug withdrawal until November 2020.

Admission tests revealed an inflammatory biological syndrome with a CRP at 257 mg/L. Polychondritis was suspected on the basis of laryngeal pain, helix pain of the left ear, and sudden unilateral hearing loss. Right eye episcleritis along with chemosis and left eyelid edema were diagnosed. Swallowing disorders and dysphagia developed progressively.

Cerebral and cervical spinal cord magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) were normal and lumbar puncture found no abnormalities: absence of cells, proteinorachia of 0.58 g/L, normoglycorachia, no microorganisms, no malignant cells, and negative serologic testing for Lyme disease. Autoimmune encephalitis antibodies testing in the cerebrospinal fluid was negative.

Positron emission tomography (PET) scan showed diffuse and heterogeneous muscular metabolic hypersignal and MRI confirmed a diffuse muscular short tau inversion recovery (STIR) hypersignal. Autoimmune myositis was suspected but ruled out based on non-elevated creatine phosphokinase (CPK) enzymes and negative antiextractable nuclear antigen (anti-ENA) autoantibodies. Myasthenia gravis specific autoantibodies were also negative.
New deep vein thrombosis (DVT) appeared on the right humeral vein with extension to the right axillary and subclavian veins, despite appropriate use of rivaroxaban since June 2020.

Tests for thrombophilia found a mild antithrombin III deficiency (66%) and positivity of one antiphospholipid antibody out of three, with negative controls 3 weeks later. Switch from rivaroxaban to subcutaneous tinzaparin sodium was followed by new DVT of the right leg. Tinzaparin was stopped and intravenous heparin was started.

While lying on the CT scan table on 10 January 2021, the patient developed non-shockable cardiac arrest. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) was performed for 12 minutes with intravenous epinephrine. Orotracheal intubation and transfer to ICU followed.

During the ICU stay, skin lesions on both feet consisting of livedo associated with distal necrosis progressed. Arterial Doppler of lower limbs showed no macrovascular lesion. Skin biopsy found one focus of microvascular thrombosis but no vasculitis or inflammatory infiltrate. Serum cryoglobulinemia was positive with oligoclonal immunoglobulins G, A, and polyclonal M (type IIb). Hepatitis B and C screening was negative.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: skin biopsy, arterial Doppler, cryoglobulinemia screening

evidence_events.source_span: During the ICU stay, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and leukopenia developed over 2 weeks. Hemoglobin declined from 7.6 to 6.5 g/dL, platelets from 207 to 17 × 10^9/L, and leukocytes from 4.2 to 1.6 × 10^9/L. Ferritin was 3836 µg/L. Bone marrow aspirate showed moderate dysplastic features and vacuoles in myeloid and erythroid precursors, no blast excess, and no argument for hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. Myeloid next generation sequencing (NGS) panel did not find any classic myelodysplastic syndrome mutation.

New deep vein thrombosis on the left leg appeared under heparin therapy, along with thrombocytopenia. Diagnosis of heparin-induced thrombocytopenia was confirmed with positive platelet aggregation test and positive PF4-heparin ELISA test (4T score of 5). Switch to danaparoid sodium prevented recurrence of vein thrombosis.

Neurological complications such as delirium and swallowing disorders persisted. New brain MRI was normal. Lumbar puncture found no abnormality: absence of cells, proteinorachia of 0.45 g/L, normoglycorachia, no microorganism, negative Cryptococcus antigen test, and negative antineurone antibodies testing. Residual neurological symptoms were interpreted as cardiac arrest sequelae.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: brain MRI, lumbar puncture, serologic testing

evidence_events.source_span: Testing for a genetic UBA1 mutation in the patient’s blood came back positive (amino acid substitution p.Met41Val), establishing the diagnosis of VEXAS syndrome.

High-dose corticosteroids (2 mg/kg/day methylprednisolone) were started, resulting in stabilization of all symptoms and allowing ICU discharge. Interleukin 1 receptor-1 inhibitor (Anakinra) was proposed to reduce corticosteroid dose.

evidence_events.source_span: In June 2021 a 71-year Caucasian old female presented in the 2nd Department of Internal Medicine Cluj-Napoca without any complaints, in order to reevaluate a subcapsular hypoechoic nodule located in the VI/VIIth hepatic segment detected during an abdominal ultrasound in October 2020.

evidence_events.source_section: Case report - History of past illness
evidence_events.source_span: The disease was diagnosed in 2014 when the patient was admitted for high values of arterial blood pressure, severe fatigue and pallor was found at the physical exam. Laboratory findings showed severe microcytic anemia (hemoglobin of 7 g/dl), increased transaminases (AST = 122U/L, ALT = 74 U/L), and increased GGT (126 U/L). Abdominal ultrasound revealed enlarged and slightly inhomogeneous liver and enlarged spleen. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed some antral vascular ectasia, while lower GI endoscopy was normal. During the diagnostic workup for chronic liver diseases, HBs antigen and HCV antibodies were negative, ferritin was low, ANA, SMA and AMA antibodies were positive with titers of 1/640, 1/320 and 1/320 respectively. The diagnosis of overlap syndrome (AIH type 1 and PBC) was established. To confirm the diagnosis, a liver biopsy was performed at the time. The result of the histological exam, which included 11 portal spaces, confirmed the overlap syndrome, showed severe interface hepatitis, proliferation of the bile ducts, fibrotic changes with rare regenerative nodules, suggestive for cirrhosis. Given the severe interface hepatitis, increased transaminases and increased values for IgG (35.8 g/L, 2.2 × ULN), and IgM (4.62 g/L, 2 × ULN), the induction of remission with prednisone (40 mg/day) was started. Azathioprine (1.5 mg/kg/day) and UDCA (15 mg/kg/day) were also initiated. The prednisone was tapered in 3 months to 15 mg/day. There were several attempts to reduce further the dose of Prednisone, but transaminases had increased every time. In 2017, while transaminases were within normal range, the corticosteroid was stopped, and the patient continued only on UDCA and azathioprine. The patient had regular follow up visits in our department, every 6 months, laboratory tests, including alpha fetoprotein and abdominal ultrasound were performed on every visit. The Fibroscan performed in 2019 showed a hepatic stiffness of 5.2 kPa, corresponding to F1 fibrosis.

evidence_events.source_section: Case report - Personal and family history
evidence_events.source_span: The patient was also diagnosed in the past with systemic sclerosis sine scleroderma, Hashimoto's thyroiditis, antiphospholipid syndrome, gastric antral vascular ectasia (GAVE) (with 2 previous sessions of argon plasma coagulation), arterial hypertension and nephro-angiosclerosis. Surgical history: cholecystectomy (1998).

The patient's blood pressure was 125/80 mmHg at admission, a heart rate of 82 bpm, the temperature was normal (36.4 °C) and a SpO2 of 97%. The physical examination was normal, without any pathological element.

Blood analysis revealed a increased value of total bilirubin 2.05 mg/dL, direct bilirubin of 0.40 mg/dL, creatinine 1.01 mg/dL and urea 51.43 mg/dL. The AFP level was slightly increased 10.8 ng/ml (ULN = 9 ng/ml).

At the moment of diagnosis (October 2020) the nodule had a diameter of 9/10 mm and was localized in the VI/VIIth hepatic segment. In June 2021 the abdominal ultrasound revealed the growth of the nodule to a diameter of 29 mm.

Contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) showed fast and intense enhancement from the periphery to the center of the nodule. In the portal phase, the nodule remained slightly hypo-enhanced. In the venous phase (1 min 20 s) the washout started, without a complete washout. This perfusion pattern was considered specific for hepatocellular carcinoma (LI-RADS 5). Shear-Wave Elastography showed a liver stiffness of 8.8 kPa, compatible with F3 fibrosis.
Liver MRI using gadoxetate disodium showed the nodule was hypovascular, non-specific, being classified as LI-RADS 3.

evidence_events.source_section: Case report - Treatment and histological findings
evidence_events.source_span: In July 2021 an atypical resection of the VIIth hepatic segment was performed.

Histological examination revealed a moderately differentiated hepatocellular carcinoma (G2), pT2 Nx Mx L0 V1 R0, with predominant solid architecture of the tumor, without tumoral necrosis. Immunohistochemistry staining was performed (Hep Par-a positive, Glypican3 positive, CD34 positive). The liver capsule was intact. A lymph node was resected but no malignant cells were found. The histological exam of the liver parenchyma revealed porto-portal bridging fibrosis, interpreted as Ishak 3 (F2 Metavir), and inflammation and injury of the bile ducts suggestive for PBC.

Final diagnosis: Hepatocellular carcinoma (G2), pT2 N0 M0 L0 V1 R0, BCLC Stage A. The tumor was under 5 cm, classified as T2; N0 shows no regional lymph node metastasis; M0 shows no distant metastasis; L0 no lymphatic invasion; V1 venous invasion; R0 complete tumor resection with microscopically negative margins.

Five months after surgery (December 2021), abdominal ultrasound showed a surgical triangular scar in the VIIth hepatic segment, liver inhomogeneous typical for cirrhosis, no hepatic nodules. Blood analysis revealed nitrogen retention, slightly increased bilirubin, normal platelet count, normal hemoglobin, and normal AFP level. CT scan in January 2022 showed no sign of tumor recurrence.

source_metadata.title: Doege-Potter Syndrome; A Case of Solitary Fibrous Pleura Tumor Associated with Severe Hypoglycemia: A Case Report in Internal Medicine
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case presentation and results sections with source order preserved.

evidence_events.source_span: A 59-year-old male was referred with a complaint of recurrent and documented fasting hypoglycemia for the past two months, experiencing excessive sweating, tremors, and weakness during episodes.
Finger stick tests confirmed hypoglycemia with blood glucose levels ranging from 20 to 50 mg/dL; symptoms resolved after breakfast with postprandial glucose about 70 mg/dL.
Physical exam revealed severely diminished breath sounds and dullness on percussion in all areas of the right lung; cardiovascular and abdominal exams were unremarkable.

Biochemical work-up showed non-insulin-mediated hypoglycemia with blood glucose 25 mg/dL, low serum insulin (1 microIU/mL), low serum C-peptide (<0.5 microg/L), and low serum IGF-1 (60 mcg/L, below 1st percentile); pituitary function normal; cortisol deficiency ruled out; insulin antibodies negative; renal and hepatic functions normal.
Chest X-ray showed a sub-total white right hemithorax with loss of lung volume, lung consolidation, and pleural mass.
Microbiological tests including Legionella and Streptococcus pneumonia urine antigens, multiplex PCR for respiratory viruses, and blood cultures were all negative.

Chest/abdomen CT scan revealed a large heterogeneous enhancing mass measuring 22.5×16.5×22.5 cm in the right lower hemithorax compressing adjacent lung and cardiomediastinal structures; no rib involvement, adenopathy, other masses, or bone metastasis.
IGF-2 bioassay was unavailable, so IGF-2:IGF-1 ratio could not be calculated.
Transthoracic echocardiography showed a large mass compressing the right atrial cavity.

Bronchoscopic evaluation revealed a friable mass; cytology was negative for cancer cells; initial biopsy was inconclusive; CT-guided biopsy performed; microbiological stains and cultures were negative.

Histological evaluation showed spindle-shaped cells without nuclear pleomorphism or necrosis; immunohistochemistry was positive for Bcl-2, STAT6, CD34 and negative for S100, CK7, WT1, D2-40, calretinin, and MDM2.
Continuous infusion of 10% glucose and frequent meals were administered but hypoglycemia episodes persisted.

Patient underwent right posterolateral open thoracotomy with resection of a 25.3×19×17 cm encapsulated mass weighing 3720 g originating from the anterior mediastinum and involving the right lung lower lobe.
Histological examination of surgical sample confirmed solitary fibrous tumor with high risk features: age >55 years, tumor size >15 cm, Ki-67 index 10-12%, mitotic activity >4/10 HPF, necrosis <10%.

Post-operative serum glucose levels normalized; patient discharged without further hypoglycemic episodes; dyspnea resolved; chest radiograph two weeks post-discharge showed pulmonary re-expansion in right hemithorax.

Laboratory testing results showed haemoglobin 113 g/L, MCV 60.6 fL, MCH 20.2 pg, RBC 5.74 x10^12/L, fasting blood glucose (FBG) 10.8 mmol/L, 2-hour plasma glucose (2h-PG) 18.4 mmol/L, HbA1c by HPLC showed 'no result', glycated albumin 3.1 mmol/L, fasting insulin 10.61 mIU/L, C-peptide 2.72 nmol/L, serum iron 5.04 µmol/L, total iron-binding capacity (TIBC) 23.17 µmol/L, eGFR 71 mL/min/1.73 m2, and urinalysis with protein +2 and albumin creatinine ratio ≥ 300 mg/gCr.

The Mentzer Index was < 13, indicating the possibility of thalassemia, haemoglobinopathy, and iron deficiency anaemia. A peripheral blood smear showed hypochromic microcytic anisopoikilocytosis (normocytic, many ovalocytes, and target cells).
Haemoglobin electrophoresis identified homozygote haemoglobinopathy E (HbE) with HbA 2.9%, HbF 3.8%, HbE 89.4%, and HbA2 3.9%.
The HbA1c examination by HPLC method (D-10, Biorad) showed 'no result' and no peak on the chromatogram.

Previous HbA1c measured by immunoturbidimetric method averaged 51 mmol/mol (reference < 48 mmol/mol), fasting blood glucose averaged 7.7 mmol/L, and 2-hour plasma glucose averaged 13 mmol/L, showing discrepancy between HbA1c and glucose levels.
The patient was advised to exercise, oral diabetes medication was changed to insulin, and referral to haematologic-oncologic division was made for HbE management.
Recommendations included monthly monitoring of blood glucose, glycated albumin, and 6-monthly albumin to creatinine or protein to creatinine ratio to monitor diabetic kidney disease complications.

source_metadata.title: Giant Ovarian Tumor

evidence_events.source_span: 23-year-old woman hospitalized due to enlargement of the abdominal circumference, periodic pains on the left side of the abdomen, scanty and irregular menses (up to 37 days), and infertility

Physical examination: afebrile, moderately good general condition, HR 110/min, RR 25/min, BP 180/96 mmHg, abdomen markedly distended above chest level with dilated superficial veins, significant edema of lower extremities and sacral region, slightly weakened peripheral pulse in legs, no signs of deep vein thrombosis

Laboratory tests: hemoglobin, electrolytes, and GFR within normal range; urea and creatinine at lower end of range; coagulation test and gasometry showed no abnormalities; tumor markers CA-125, HE4, ROMA algorithm, CA-19.9, CA-15.3, AFP, and CEA within normal range
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: Malignant nature of tumor could not be excluded at that point

evidence_events.source_span: Chest X-ray: lung fields with normal aeration without focal changes, sharp costophrenic angles, elevation of the domes of the diaphragm with markedly reduced lung volume without effusion, large tumor under diaphragm compressing abdominal organs; cardiac silhouette not assessed

Abdominal and pelvic ultrasound: massive fluid-filled tumor mass with segmentally visible solid components; origin of neoplasm could not be reliably identified due to size of abdomen; ultrasound transducer visualized tumor maximally up to 24–25 cm
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: CT and MRI ruled out due to technical limitations

evidence_events.source_span: Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging were ruled out due to technical limitations of positioning the patient; apparatus can only accommodate abdominal circumference below 180 cm, patient measured 195 cm
Laparotomy performed under general anesthesia by multiperson team; patient positioned on left side initially for hemodynamic stability, then Trendelenburg position due to airway ventilation problems

During surgery, tumor wall incised and 100 L of clear, colorless fluid aspirated; tumor originated from left ovary; right ovary, right fallopian tube, uterus, and other abdominal organs normal; tumor wall removed along with part of left ovary; specimen sent for frozen section

Frozen section gross description: empty, glistening, multiloculated cyst 80 × 50 × 50 cm with smooth inner and outer surfaces; cyst wall thickness 3 to 10 mm; fallopian tube stretched on cyst surface; no macroscopic signs of malignancy
Histopathological report from intraoperative examination confirmed serous cystadenoma; fragment of left ovary not bound to cyst preserved to maintain fertility

Definitive histopathological diagnosis on formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded sections: serous cystadenofibroma of the ovary (ICD-O 9014/0); multiple samples showed more prominent stromal component; no pathological findings in fallopian tube sections
Fluid from cyst and peritoneal washing examined; no malignant cells found; peritoneal washing showed mesothelial cells, inflammatory cells, and numerous erythrocytes

Postoperative course: patient tolerated surgery well, no intraoperative complications or blood loss, uneventful recovery; started walking day after surgery with physiotherapy; Foley catheter removed on second day; discharged in good condition on seventh postoperative day; symptoms subsided

source_metadata.title: Hyperglycemia with hypogonadism and growth hormone deficiency in a 17-year-old male with H syndrome: the first case report from Syria

evidence_events.source_span: A 17-year-old male was admitted to the internal medicine department complaining of polyurea, polydipsia, general weakness, and pallor for the past month.
The patient had a history of bilateral progressive hearing loss that had started in childhood and a history of not gaining weight for the last three years.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: started in childhood; last three years

evidence_events.source_span: Physical examination revealed a scrotal mass, a small penis (less than 0.5 cm) with enclosed testicles, no pubic or axillary hair, hand and foot joint abnormalities, short stature, hallux valgus, dilated lateral scleral vessels, a percussible but not palpable spleen, a fibrous protrusion near the navel, Boutonniere deformity in the toes and hands, and hyperpigmented non-itchy painful skin plaques.
Urologic evaluation showed an underdeveloped penis with a small protuberance at the base and testicular volume of 3 centimeters for each testis measured by orchidometer.
Ophthalmologic examination showed visual acuity of 6/10 and audiological examination revealed profound bilateral sensorineural hearing loss.

Laboratory tests showed hemoglobin 11 g/dL, red blood cells 4.8 mcL, MCH 23 pg, MCV 69 fL, white blood cells 5100, neutrophil to lymphocyte ratio 3.5, ESR 72 mm/hour, fasting blood glucose 130 mg/dL, alpha-fetoprotein 1.7 ng/mL, rheumatoid factor 32 IU/mL, negative antinuclear antibody, immunoglobulin M 96 mg/dL, immunoglobulin G 1006 mg/dL, and immunoglobulin A 3.1 mg/dL.
Random blood glucose was 407 mg/dL, fasting blood glucose 132 mg/dL, and HbA1c was 8.5%, indicating diabetes.

Fasting growth hormone induction test with arginine showed peak values below normal (0.6 ng/mL initially, 0.7 ng/mL after 30 minutes, 4 ng/mL after 1 hour, normal peak at least 10 ng/mL), demonstrating growth hormone deficiency.
Chromosomal analysis showed a normal male karyotype (46XY).
Hormonal tests showed low testosterone level (181 ng/dL) with high follicle-stimulating hormone (37.4 mIU/mL) and luteinizing hormone (17.4 mIU/mL), consistent with primary hypogonadism.
Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) showed Z score −2.4 and T score −2.3, indicating osteopenia.
Duodenal biopsies showed non-specific inflammation, excluding celiac disease.
Perineal MRI showed testicular atrophy and a heterogeneous mass in the perineum; excisional biopsy of the mass revealed inflammatory granulomatous tissue with no evidence of malignancy.
Chest CT showed heterogeneous density in the lower part of the left lung.
Abdominal and pelvic ultrasound revealed numerous inguinal lymphadenopathies measuring 2–4 cm and clear edema in the pubic area with microcalcifications in both testicles.
Mutation analysis of SLC29A3 was done to confirm the diagnosis of H syndrome.

source_metadata.title: Unmasking an unusual presentation of Hodgkin’s lymphoma masquerading as ocular inflammation: a case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 17-year-old Caucasian female presented to our ophthalmic emergency department reporting right eye redness, pain, and blurred vision along with intermittent temporal photopsia with onset 5 days before consultation.
General symptoms were vague encompassing nausea, headaches, left shoulder pain and long-standing night sweats.
The patient’s history was significant for right eye conjunctivitis, conjunctival hyperhemia and papillary edema since 2017 but best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) remained 1.0 in both eyes.

On presentation, the patient’s BCVA was 1.0 in both eyes. Initial slit lamp examination revealed right eye non-necrotizing scleritis, endothelial haze and 1+ cells in the anterior chamber. Upon fundus examination, right eye vitreous turbidity, inferior vitreous condensations and vitreous snowballs in the inferior periphery were visualized. Papillary edema was also present as well as peripheral white/yellowish lesions in the superior and inferior retinal peripheries.

Fluoroangiography (FA) and indocyanine green angiography (ICGA) showed early arterial filling of central choriocapillaris, peripheral vasculitis, a hot disc papillitis appearance and peripheral hypofluorescent spots.
Spectral Domain OCT (SD-OCT) did not show any alterations in retinal layers, retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) or the vitreoretinal interface.
The left eye slit lamp examination, fundus examination, FA, ICGA and SD-OCT were strictly normal.

evidence_events.source_span: A complete workup ruling out infectious causes such as Toxoplasmosis, Whipple's disease, Syphilis, Lyme disease, Cat scratch disease, Herpes simplex virus, Varicella-zoster virus, Cytomegalovirus as well as systemic disease: sarcoidosis, Behçet’s disease and systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) came back negative. IGRA testing for tuberculosis came back positive but with negative Quantiferon.

evidence_events.source_span: A positron emission tomography-computed tomography (PET-CT) scan revealed hypermetabolic left supra-clavicular and mediastinal bilateral lymph nodes.
A bronchioalveolar lavage was carried out with subsequent negative results.
A left supra-clavicular lymph node biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of nodular sclerosing Hodgkin’s lymphoma stage IIB.
Chemotherapy led to remission of the disease and the ocular lesions became quiescent with persistent pigmented chorioretinal scars.

source_metadata.title: Total atrioventricular block as a cardiac manifestation in Weil’s disease: a case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 43-year-old Asian woman reported worsening chest pain that began 3 days prior and had intensified significantly over the past day. She reported experiencing lethargy, anorexia, nausea, fever, and intermittent headaches.

Upon admission, the patient was alert and conscious but appeared weak, with blood pressure of 81/43 mmHg, heart rate of 41 bpm, respiratory rate of 20 times/minute, and temperature of 38.2 °C. Physical examination revealed anemic conjunctiva, icteric sclera, and jaundice. Lung auscultation detected crackles, and abdominal examination showed hepatosplenomegaly and tenderness, particularly in the right upper quadrant.
The electrocardiogram showed a total atrioventricular block with a junctional escape rhythm of 45 bpm and no signs of myocardial infarction or other pathological conditions.
Chest X-ray revealed cardiomegaly (cardiothoracic ratio 0.52) with increased bronchovascular markings.

Laboratory tests revealed leukocytosis, anemia, thrombocytopenia (98,000/μL), increased blood urea nitrogen (92 mg/dL), creatinine (4.1 mg/dL), elevated liver enzymes (AST 102 IU/L, ALT 65 IU/L), increased C-reactive protein (9 mg/dL), elevated troponin I (361 ng/dL), and hyperbilirubinemia (total bilirubin 6.1 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 5.3 mg/dL).
Serology tests showed positive immunoglobulin G and M anti-Leptospira and positive microscopic agglutination test (MAT). Dengue serology was negative.
The patient was diagnosed with Weil’s disease (Faine’s score 32) complicated by total atrioventricular block and unstable hemodynamics, likely due to cardiogenic or septic shock.

Initial management included transcutaneous pacing at 40 mA with a rhythm maintenance rate of 70 bpm, dopamine infusion starting at 5 mcg/kgBW/minute titrated to 10 mcg/kgBW/minute, ceftriaxone 2 g, doxycycline 100 mg twice daily, and supportive treatments.
Transthoracic echocardiography revealed reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) of 44% and global hypokinesia.
The patient experienced cardiac arrest and died within 48 hours after admission despite cardiopulmonary resuscitation; cardiogenic shock was suspected as the cause of death.

source_metadata.notes: Extraction based on case narrative and clinical course sections.

evidence_events.source_span: A 71-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus and remote history of Roux-en-Y bypass surgery 35 years ago and cholecystectomy 50 years ago presented with an 8-month history of steatorrhea and 41-kg weight loss despite increased caloric intake.
He reported a sudden onset of 10–15 oily, greasy stools per day and excessive foul-smelling gas approximately 8 months prior to presentation.
Physical examination was notable for weight of 84 kg (body mass index 26.8 kg/m2), mild bilateral triceps and iliopsoas weakness, and bilateral peripheral edema up to the knees.

Laboratory findings revealed multiple vitamin deficiencies: 25-hydroxy D total 9.4 ng/mL, vitamin A 15.8 mcg/dL, vitamin E 4.7 mcg/dL, total serum calcium 7.9 mg/dL, and albumin 2.8 g/dL. B12 and B1 were unremarkable at 254 ng/L and 221 nmol/L, respectively.
A comprehensive malignancy workup, including skull-to-thigh PET-CT scan, colonoscopy with random colon biopsies, and celiac disease testing were unremarkable.
EMG was performed and showed length-dependent peripheral neuropathy (consistent with known diabetic neuropathy) and myopathy, with no evidence of neuromuscular transmission defects.
Biopsy of the right triceps muscle demonstrated type 2 fiber atrophy with rimmed vacuoles, consistent with nutritional myopathy.
CT enterography demonstrated marked pancreatic atrophy without any sign of pancreatic tumor.
A 48-hour fecal fat study demonstrated massive steatorrhea (total fat in 24 hours of 277 g) and fecal elastase less than 40 µg/g.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: fecal fat study and fecal elastase testing

evidence_events.source_span: He was started on pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (PERT) with 2 tablets of lipase-protease-amylase by mouth 3 times a day with meals. His diarrhea improved 2 months after initiation of PERT, allowing him to regain weight to his previous baseline while reducing his caloric intake.

source_metadata.title: Polyarteritis nodosa and Sjögren’s syndrome: overlap syndrome

evidence_events.source_span: Since 2003, a woman aged 53 has been hospitalized several times at surgery, internal medicine, and rheumatologic wards due to her ailments. She had been complaining of power diminution, abdominal pains, pains in joints and muscles, headaches, loss of weight, dysaesthesia in lower limbs, xerostomia, and xeromycteria of both eyes.
Hypertension and sensomotor polyneuropathy had been found out during her stays in hospital.

Laboratory checks had shown the presence of following antibodies: antinuclear (ANA) and anti-Ro/SSA as well as the positive result of Schirmer’s test; however, primary Sjögren’s syndrome had not been diagnosed.
No aneurysms or vessel’s malformations had been discovered during angio-computer tomography of brain arteries.

The pains in abdomen, the loss of weight, increased blood sedimentation rate (ESR > 45 mm/h), high concentration of C-reactive protein (CRP) 20 mg/dl, alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 114 U/l, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 109 U/l, gammaglutamyltransferase (GGTP) 322 U/l, and alkaline phosphatase (Ap) 320 U/l were the cause of admittance to PAM gastroenterology clinic; in the course of which, the reasons of patients complaints were not discovered.
Normalization of aminotransferaces and decrease in Ap and GGTP concentrations were observed.
Due to lasting abdominal pains and acroparaesthesia the patient was transferred in July 2006, after consultation, to rheumatology department with presumptive diagnosis of connective tissue illness.

During subjective examination the following symptoms were found: underweight, livedo reticulates on the lower limbs’ skin, painful palpation of epigastrium and intra-abdomen, manual impairment of both hands and the lack of strength in the right hand.
Neurological examination showed the lack of both Achilles tendon reflexes and left knee reflex, strength reduction in right hand around elbow nerves and expansion symptoms in lower limbs.

Additional checks revealed: Hb 9.7 g/dl, lymphopenia (800/mm3), increased ESR (60 mm/h), and high concentration of CRP (10.9 mg/dl). Concentrations of complement fraction (60.5 mg/dl) and C4 (below 1.5 mg/dl) were below normal values. Gammaglutamyltransferase exceeded the normal level twice. Total protein lower concentrations (5.1 g/dl) as well as albumins (49.19%) were noticed.

There were no antigens (HBs), antibodies (HCV), antismooth muscles bodies (ASMA), and antimitochondrial antibodies (M2). Coagulation system checkup (INR- 0,96; APTT- 23.6 s; fibrinogen- 298 mg/dl), cholesterol balance checkup (HDL- 47 mg/dl; LDL- 79 mg/dl; TG- 109 mg/dl), carbohydrate metabolism (glycemia- 83 mg %) and kidney competence (creatinine- 0.5 mg %) proved to be normal.

Antinuclear antibodies ANA (titer 1: 320 staining pattern type) were found as well as antibodies anti-Ro (SSA–4.3) anti-La (SSB–1.6) and rheumatoid factor of IgM class (RF–193 U/ml); however, cryoglobulins and immune complexes were absent.
EMG showed sensomotor polyneuropathy of primary axonal type and features of fresh and massive lesion of right elbow nerve.

The results of computer tomography (CT) of abdominal cavity with vessel option revealed 40% stenosis of right renal artery, 50% stenosis of superior mesenteric artery and 30% stenosis of left common iliac artery.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: CT of abdominal cavity with vessel option

evidence_events.source_span: In histopathological examination of gastrocnemius muscle’s segment as well as in echocardiographical examination (ECHO), no valid changes from the norm were found.
There were not noticed any activities of submandibular glands and only imparimental action of parotid glands in salivary glands’ scintigraphy.
In histopathological examination of lower lip salivary gland there was discovered focal lymphoid infiltration and focal periductal fibroma—according to Greenspan IV.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: histopathological examination of lower lip salivary gland

evidence_events.source_span: The diagnosis was primary Sjögren’s syndrome and PAN.

The treatment started with intravenous methylprednisolon in dose of 500 mg for 3 days and intravenous cyclophosphamid in dose of 0.6 g/1 m² of body surface 6 times in 4-week intervals with low molecular weight heparin, enalapril, amlodypine, spironolacton, venlafaxine and carbamazepine administered too.

After 8-month treatment the condition of the patient is good. There is still hypertension but the symptoms of polyneuropathy are less visible though there has been muscular atrophy in both hands observed. Control EMG examination has shown slow regeneration process and beginning of reinnervation changes in checked muscles. Abdominal pains have disappeared and there is the gain of weight. In laboratory test there are still anemia (Hb 11.6 g/dl) and lymphopenia (700/mm³).

evidence_milestones.source_span: Due to lasting abdominal pains and acroparaesthesia the patient was transferred in July 2006, after consultation, to rheumatology department with presumptive diagnosis of connective tissue illness. During subjective examination the following symptoms were found: underweight, livedo reticulates on the lower limbs’ skin, painful palpation of epigastrium and intra-abdomen, manual impairment of both hands and the lack of strength in the right hand. Neurological examination showed the lack of both Achilles tendon reflexes and left knee reflex, strength reduction in right hand around elbow nerves and expansion symptoms in lower limbs.
evidence_milestones.question: How do these clinical findings refine the differential diagnosis, and what laboratory or imaging studies should be prioritized next?

evidence_milestones.grouping_reason: Laboratory and electrophysiological studies showing inflammation, immunologic markers, and neuropathy.
evidence_milestones.visible_evidence: Labs showed anemia (Hb 9.7 g/dl), lymphopenia (800/mm3), elevated ESR (60 mm/h), high CRP (10.9 mg/dl), low complement C4 (<1.5 mg/dl), elevated GGTP, low total protein and albumin. Viral and autoimmune hepatitis markers were negative. ANA titer 1:320, anti-Ro (4.3), anti-La (1.6), and RF IgM (193 U/ml) were positive; cryoglobulins and immune complexes were absent. EMG showed primary axonal sensomotor polyneuropathy and fresh lesion of right elbow nerve.
evidence_milestones.dialogue_visible_evidence: Laboratory tests reveal systemic inflammation, immunologic autoantibodies consistent with Sjögren’s syndrome, and electrophysiology confirms polyneuropathy.
evidence_milestones.test_visible_evidence: Inflammatory markers, autoantibodies, and EMG consistent with systemic autoimmune disease and neuropathy.
evidence_milestones.source_span: Additional checks revealed: Hb 9.7 g/dl, lymphopenia (800/mm3), increased ESR (60 mm/h), and high concentration of CRP (10.9 mg/dl). Concentrations of complement fraction (60.5 mg/dl) and C4 (below 1.5 mg/dl) were below normal values. Gammaglutamyltransferase exceeded the normal level twice. Total protein lower concentrations (5.1 g/dl) as well as albumins (49.19%) were noticed. There were no antigens (HBs), antibodies (HCV), antismooth muscles bodies (ASMA), and antimitochondrial antibodies (M2). Coagulation system checkup (INR- 0,96; APTT- 23.6 s; fibrinogen- 298 mg/dl), cholesterol balance checkup (HDL- 47 mg/dl; LDL- 79 mg/dl; TG- 109 mg/dl), carbohydrate metabolism (glycemia- 83 mg %) and kidney competence (creatinine- 0.5 mg %) proved to be normal. Antinuclear antibodies ANA (titer 1: 320 staining pattern type) were found as well as antibodies anti-Ro (SSA–4.3) anti-La (SSB–1.6) and rheumatoid factor of IgM class (RF–193 U/ml); however, cryoglobulins and immune complexes were absent. EMG showed sensomotor polyneuropathy of primary axonal type and features of fresh and massive lesion of right elbow nerve.
evidence_milestones.question: How do these laboratory and EMG findings influence the diagnostic considerations, and what imaging or biopsy studies should be pursued next?

evidence_milestones.grouping_reason: Treatment initiation and clinical outcome after 8 months.
evidence_milestones.visible_evidence: Treatment with intravenous methylprednisolone and cyclophosphamide was started along with other supportive medications. After 8 months, the patient’s condition improved with reduced polyneuropathy symptoms, disappearance of abdominal pain, weight gain, but persistent hypertension and mild anemia.

evidence_milestones.test_visible_evidence: Treatment response and clinical outcome.
evidence_milestones.source_span: The treatment started with intravenous methylprednisolon in dose of 500 mg for 3 days and intravenous cyclophosphamid in dose of 0.6 g/1 m² of body surface 6 times in 4-week intervals with low molecular weight heparin, enalapril, amlodypine, spironolacton, venlafaxine and carbamazepine administered too. After 8-month treatment the condition of the patient is good. There is still hypertension but the symptoms of polyneuropathy are less visible though there has been muscular atrophy in both hands observed. Control EMG examination has shown slow regeneration process and beginning of reinnervation changes in checked muscles. Abdominal pains have disappeared and there is the gain of weight. In laboratory test there are still anemia (Hb 11.6 g/dl) and lymphopenia (700/mm³).

source_metadata.title: Esophageal schwannoma: a case report
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case presentation and clinical course sections with figure references.

evidence_events.source_span: A 55-year-old woman visited our hospital with complaints of palpitations and discomfort during swallowing.

A frontal chest radiograph showed a smooth round mass, and a lateral radiograph showed a smooth mass slightly larger than 7 cm in diameter in the middle mediastinum between the trachea and the vertebral bodies.
A chest computed tomography (CT) scan showed a lobulated tumor (75 × 57 × 80 mm) in the upper to middle mediastinum, with a homogenous inner component, compressing the esophagus.
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the chest revealed no invasion of surrounding organs.
Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy showed a smooth elevated lesion, 22 cm from the incisor teeth, with a mucous membrane accompanied by venous dilation.
A schwannoma was diagnosed based on the biopsy result for the lesion.
Surgery was performed due to the large size of the tumor, dysphagia, palpitations caused by tumor compressing the heart, and suspicion of malignant potential.

A mass slightly larger than 8 cm in diameter was found adjacent to the mid-thoracic esophagus and excised; the defect in the adventitia and muscular layer was extensive, so subtotal esophagectomy and esophagogastrostomy in the right thorax were performed.
The resected specimen showed normal esophageal mucosa; the tumor was well demarcated, elastic hard, globular, measuring 75 × 57 × 80 mm, with an almost uniformly milky white cut surface.
Histopathological examination revealed spindle-shaped cells in a fasciculated and disarrayed architecture and nuclei in a palisading pattern.
Immunohistochemical studies revealed S100 protein positivity and absence of staining for α smooth muscle actin (αSMA), CD34 and CD117, establishing the diagnosis of benign schwannoma.
Her postoperative course was uneventful and there has been no evidence of recurrence to date.

source_metadata.title: Importance of multidisciplinary approach in diagnosis of histoplasmosis

evidence_events.source_span: The patient was referred by the infectologist for evaluation of subcutaneous nodules that appeared one year before.
He had undergone kidney transplantation 15 years ago and was using prednisone (20 mg/day) and sodium mycophenolate (5.760 mg/day), besides propranolol and nifedipine for hypertension.

The dermatological examination revealed two subcutaneous nodules measuring around 2 cm each, painful when pressed, with a firm consistency, barely delimited and adherent, covered by slightly swollen and erythematous, cyanotic skin on the right arm and near the elbow on the left forearm.
He also described history of fever, cough and weight loss, beginning simultaneously with the onset of the subcutaneous nodules.
Although sputum cultures were negative for AFB, he was treated for tuberculosis because he continued to be febrile and with a TB-suggestive clinical condition and pulmonary image.
The treatment for tuberculosis was suspended 40 days later, as there was no improvement and the patient remained febrile.

A biopsy of the nodule on the right arm was carried out and revealed cellular tissue with proliferation of macrophages and rare multinucleated giant cells, in addition to lymphoplasma neutrophilic infiltrate.
Methenamine silver staining showed a great quantity of intracytoplasmatic microorganisms characteristic of Histoplasma capsulatum, sometimes forming hyphae and spores.
Finally, one year after the onset of symptoms, he received the diagnosis and treatment for disseminated histoplasmosis.

source_metadata.title: Inflammatory bowel disease mimicking granulomatosis with polyangiitis: a case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 54-year-old African-American man presented with several months of systemic inflammatory features: anterior uveitis, auricular chondritis, monoarthritis, fever, and weight loss.
He had been well until 7 months earlier when he developed unilateral pain and redness of his right eye; ophthalmologic evaluation revealed anterior uveitis which resolved with topical steroids.
Five months later he sought care for right ear pain; CT imaging revealed inflammation of his pinna consistent with auricular chondritis, which resolved spontaneously without treatment.
Two months later, he returned with pain and redness of his right wrist; diagnosed with cellulitis and treated with oral clindamycin for 7 days with minimal improvement.
Three days later, admitted for sudden onset of fever and diarrhea; viral etiology suspected and symptoms resolved quickly with conservative therapy.

At outpatient visit, persistent right wrist swelling with limited motion due to pain; 27 kg unintentional weight loss over 6 months; denied epistaxis, cough, hemoptysis, chest pain, dyspnea, recurrent ocular symptoms, rash, low back pain, abdominal pain, frequent stools, melena, or hematochezia.

Physical exam: well-developed, well-nourished, comfortable, alert, oriented; vital signs normal; no rash, oral ulcers, cutaneous nodules, or lymphadenopathy; mild synovitis of right wrist without erythema but limited range of motion due to pain; cardiac, pulmonary, abdominal, neurologic exams unremarkable.

Laboratory evaluation during admission showed iron deficiency anemia (hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL), WBC 12,100 cells/mm3 with normal differential, low albumin (2.9 g/dL), elevated alkaline phosphatase (182 U/L), mild transaminitis, microscopic hematuria (RBC 55/hpf), normal creatinine, no proteinuria, elevated inflammatory markers (CRP 11.1 mg/dL, ESR 124 mm/hr), positive fecal lactoferrin.
Chest radiograph showed a small ill-defined patchy infiltrate in the upper lobe of the right lung.
Infectious workup negative: bacterial stool and blood cultures, HIV viral load, CMV serum PCR, gonorrhea and chlamydia urine PCR, stool Clostridium difficile toxin, stool ova and parasites.

Autoimmune serologies negative: ANA, anti-mitochondrial antibody, anti-smooth muscle antibody, rheumatoid factor, anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide; complements normal; c-ANCA positive at titer 1:40 with elevated proteinase 3 by ELISA (102.6 units); p-ANCA and myeloperoxidase by ELISA negative.

With infection ruled out, clinical picture seemed most consistent with granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA); started on prednisone 60 mg daily with marked improvement in symptoms and laboratory abnormalities.
Eight weeks later, developed hematochezia, left lower quadrant pain, and a perirectal abscess and fistula.
Colonoscopy performed with multiple biopsies taken.

Histologic examination of descending colon biopsy showed cryptitis and crypt abscesses; rectal biopsy showed early crypt distortion and basal plasmacytosis; no granulomas, vasculitis, or dysplasia; findings suggestive of chronic colitis and/or inflammatory bowel disease (IBD).

Treatment for IBD initiated with azathioprine and infliximab resulting in healing of fistula and continued clinical improvement; therapy well tolerated; patient doing well for 1.5 years with no further GI or extraintestinal manifestations.

source_metadata.title: Inflammatory Myofibroblastic Tumors in a Case with Hypogastric Discomfort

evidence_events.source_span: A 68-year-old man referred to the Internal Medicine Department of Razi Hospital in Rasht with a hypogastric region discomfort, especially in the right lower quadrant for one month

The pain was a colicky form which had a few episodes each day, each episode lasting for 4–5 minutes; the pain radiated to the back and was alleviated by resting to one side; no association between the pain, defecation, and eating were reported
The patient complained of a 2–3 kg weight loss over the last one month followed by anorexia; no symptoms of nausea, vomiting, fever, or shaking chills were demonstrated
No history of HIV, diabetes, smoking, or alcohol consumption was recorded
His vital signs were normal at the time of admission
On physical examination, the abdomen was soft, there was no distention, and bowel sounds were normoactive; tenderness in the right lower quadrant of the abdomen with no rebound state was noted

Peripheral blood analysis showed WBC 8.7×103/μl, CRP 45 mg/l, Hb 12.1 g/dl, ESR 68 mm/hr, HCT 38.3%, platelet 332×103/μl, neutrophil 60%, lymphocyte 30%, monocyte 4%, eosinophil 6%, ferritin 70 ng/ml, Fe 59 mg/dl, TIBC 400 mg/dl, and normal liver function tests
Stool examination, urine analysis, and evaluation of electrolytes were all normal
An abdominal CT scan showed a well-demarcated and homogenous solitary mass in the cecum with no distention in the ileum; the ileum wall was thickened

source_metadata.title: Melanoma Masquerading as a Zosteriform Rash

evidence_events.source_span: A forty-nine-year-old man with an initially unknown past medical history (except recent treatment for herpes zoster) was brought to the emergency department for a right thoracic rash and skin lesions.

Physical examination revealed a middle-aged man, not in apparent distress but who appeared confused and could not provide his own history. Scars from previous staples were seen near the right scapular region. Skin examination was significant for a dark red papular skin rash in the right thoracic area roughly at the fourth and fifth intercostal areas (dermatomal T2 and T3 distribution) extending to posterior axilla where multiple hard lumps were palpated in groups. Lesions were tender with purulent discharge.
Given the recent history of possible herpes zoster and immunocompromised status he was started empirically on acyclovir 1 g intravenously every eight hours.
The firmness of the skin lesions and the prominent axillary lymph nodes prompted our team to proceed with skin biopsy to rule out an underlying malignancy.

The patient had cutaneous melanoma two years ago in the right scapular area, which had been resected, and he had one cycle of chemotherapy but was not willing to continue treatment. He had a recent admission for another skin lesion in the same area (also resected).
Skin biopsy of the lesions demonstrated cells strongly positive for S-100 and Melan-A immunostain. The biopsy was negative for CK AE1/AE3 immunostain.
Computed tomography (CT) of the chest showed evidence of subcutaneous invasion, lung metastasis, and metastatic bony lesions.

Given the patient’s poor functional status and minimal benefit of pursuing further treatment palliative care was consulted and the patient elected for discharge with hospice care. No further treatment was administered.

source_metadata.title: Giant Splenic Aneurysm with Arteriovenous (A-V) Shunt, Portal Hypertension, and Ascites

evidence_events.source_span: A 43-year-old man presented at the Internal Medicine Department of Ahepa University Hospital with symptoms of fever and ascites.
He was an ex-medical student with an anamnesis of sickle cell anemia, who underwent splenectomy and cholecystectomy on urgent basis 26 years ago and had a transit ischemic attack at the age of 21.
Diagnostic imaging control with CT scan revealed a large amount of free ascites and a giant mass in the left upper-abdominal quadrant, paraaortic and underneath the pancreas.

A following CT-angio with i.v. contrast infusion in arterial and venous phases revealed a giant splenic aneurysm 9.8 cm in diameter and 5 cm in length, located in the previous common ligation of the splenic vessels.
The most interesting finding was the concomitant contrast infusion into the enlarged splenic vein (an AV-shunt, due to common ligation of the vessels after splenectomy and long stump presence).
A diagnostic centesis was performed by internists to exclude malignancy.

Twenty-four hours later, he underwent open surgery via supra-infraumbilical incision; the lesion was included into a giant omentum sac, extremely fragile and hemorrhagic due to chronic inflammation, with a covered rupture revealed.
A cross clamp to the orifice of the splenic artery including the splenic vein was performed and the vessels were ligated using 4-0 Prolene sutures and Teflon implants.
Post-operatively, the patient remained in the ICU for 48 h and then was transferred to the General Surgery Department.
Three days after the operation, he suffered a portal vein thrombosis and his antithrombotic treatment was modified from prophylactic Tinzaparin to therapeutic Fondaparinux.
Six days later, he developed fever with high levels of laboratory inflammation markers, paralytic ileus, and low hematocrit.

Diagnostic imaging control with CT and digital subtraction angiography (DSA) showed no signs of major bleeding and only minor signs of bleeding in the area of the stomach atrium, with concomitant hemorrhagic pancreatitis.
General surgeons performed an investigative laparotomy, intraperitoneal lavage, and vacuum-assisted closure (VAC) of the abdominal cave.
After sepsis was successfully treated, the patient was discharged in good clinical condition after closure of the abdominal cave without further complications.

diagnostic_reasoning_verbatim_spans: Diagnostic imaging control revealed a giant splenic aneurysm 9.8 cm in diameter and 5 cm in length, with a concomitant A-V shunt due to common ligation of the vessels after splenectomy and long stump presence.
The giant splenic aneurysm resulted from the commonly ligated long stump of the splenic artery and vein after urgent splenectomy.
Degenerative erosion of the aneurysm wall due to turbulence and inflammation led to AV-shunt and hyperdynamic portal circulation conditions.
Immediate surgical repair was mandatory because of the high risk of rupture.
Endovascular repair was excluded due to the high risk of systemic embolization in the portal circulation.
Open surgical ligation of the splenic artery and vein was performed.
Postoperative complications included portal vein thrombosis and hemorrhagic pancreatitis, managed surgically and medically.
The patient survived and was discharged in good clinical condition.

Postoperative complications are recognized but managed successfully.
Final diagnosis is confirmed clinically and surgically.

evidence_events.source_span: 34-year-old man hospitalized on 18 January 2018 with bloody and febrile diarrhea
Symptom onset on 10 January 2018 with diarrhea of soft, yellowish, sometimes mucusy, blood-ribbed stools three to four times a day and constant unquantified fever
Initial outpatient treatment from 12 January 2018 with paracetamol, quinine, metronidazole, ciprofloxacin, diazepam, albendazole without paraclinical investigations
Symptom relapse on 16 January 2018 with bilious vomiting, odynophagia, intense headaches, and generalized aches

Admission clinical exam on 18 January 2018: temperature 39°C, tachycardia 86 bpm, polypnea 30/min, BP 130/100 mmHg, palatal tonsil inflammation with whitish coating, right iliac fossa pain, heart sounds muffled

Admission labs: negative thick drop for plasmodium trophozoites, RBC 4.53x10^6/mm3, Hb 15.33 g/dL, Hct 41.6%, platelets 123x10^9/L, leukocytes 6.6x10^9/L (neutrophils 70%, lymphocytes 27%), azotemia 0.65 g/L, creatinine 14.13 mg/L, Na 135.7 meq/L, K 4.08 meq/L, Cl 115.4 meq/L, ALT 82 IU/L, AST 62 IU/L, HIV negative
Initial diagnosis of severe sepsis and treatment with ceftriaxone, metronidazole IV, gentamycin, tramadol, glucose serum, saline, and oxygen therapy
Persistent fever ranging 36.3°C to 40.1°C during hospitalization; on third day, melena, facial puffiness, and conjunctival hemorrhage appeared, raising suspicion of viral hemorrhagic fever

Patient isolated and blood sample sent to national viral hemorrhagic fever laboratory on 22 January 2018; ribavirin treatment started with loading dose 30 mg/kg IV then 15 mg/kg IV every 6 h for 4 days, vitamin K1, blood transfusion, and oxygen therapy
Patient died on 23 January 2018 after repeated convulsions, bradypnea, and cardio-circulatory arrest
Lassa fever confirmed post-mortem by RT-PCR assay on blood sample received on 24 January 2018

initial_presentation.encounter_context: The patient was referred to the Emergency Department by a nephrologist with a diagnosis of acute kidney injury associated with a three-month history of symptoms.
initial_presentation.chief_complaint: Progressive dyspnea on exertion, fatigue, rash, and weight loss.
initial_presentation.first_contact_summary: He initially presented to his primary care physician with a cough. Chest X-ray was unremarkable and proton pump inhibitor prescribed with partial symptom improvement; gradually developed dyspnea on exertion, fatigue, and weight loss. Mild anemia, elevated CRP and rheumatoid factor were noted. History included resected malignant melanoma of the left foot. Cardiology referral found a systolic murmur and mild to moderate mitral regurgitation with leaflet prolapse. Rheumatology referral noted elevated ESR, increasing CRP and RF, and a new petechial rash; a skin biopsy showed suppurative folliculitis; prednisone prescribed with partial improvement but tapering was not tolerated. Pulmonary function testing showed mild restriction. Nephrology evaluation showed worsening proteinuria, microscopic hematuria, and elevated creatinine. On arrival to ED, the patient had hypertension, crackles at lung bases, grade III/VI apical systolic murmur radiating to left axilla, non-blanching petechiae on lower extremities and torso, acute kidney injury, microscopic hematuria, low C3 level. Initial diagnosis was rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis secondary to vasculitis; intravenous methylprednisolone treatment was begun and echocardiogram was planned for the following Monday.

source_metadata.title: Cardiac Point-of-Care Ultrasound for the Diagnosis of Infective Endocarditis in a Patient with Non-Specific Rheumatologic Symptoms and Glomerulonephritis

evidence_events.source_span: A 57-year-old man was referred to the Emergency Department by a nephrologist with a diagnosis of acute kidney injury associated with a three-month history of symptoms that included progressive dyspnea on exertion, fatigue, rash, and weight loss.
Laboratory investigations showed mild anemia and elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) and rheumatoid factor (RF).

Seven weeks before hospital admission, a cardiology referral was made; a grade III/VI systolic murmur was noted. Transthoracic echocardiography showed mild to moderate mitral valve regurgitation with moderate prolapse of the anterior mitral valve leaflet but was otherwise normal.

Three weeks before hospital admission, the patient reported worsening symptoms and a new lower extremity petechial rash. Laboratory investigations showed an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) and increasing CRP and RF. A skin biopsy demonstrated perivascular and interstitial neutrophilic infiltrates compatible with suppurative folliculitis.

Three days prior to hospital admission, pulmonary function tests showed mild restriction. Repeat laboratory investigations showed worsening proteinuria and microscopic hematuria, and a newly elevated creatinine level of 3.20 mg/dL from a baseline of 0.89–1.02 mg/dL.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: Three days prior to hospital admission

evidence_events.source_span: On arrival in the Emergency Department, cardiopulmonary examination was notable for crackles at both lung bases and a grade III/VI apical systolic murmur that radiated to the left axilla. Non-blanching petechiae were present over the bilateral lower extremities and torso. Laboratory investigations showed hypertension, acute kidney injury, microscopic hematuria, and a low C3 level.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: on arrival in the Emergency Department

evidence_events.source_span: Given the findings, the patient was diagnosed with rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis secondary to vasculitis and treatment was begun with intravenous methylprednisolone 1000 mg daily. A renal biopsy and transthoracic echocardiogram were planned for the following Monday.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: on admission and planned next steps

evidence_events.source_span: The following morning, cardiac point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) showed left ventricular systolic function appeared normal, but the mitral valve had markedly thickened leaflets, prolapse, and moderate to severe mitral valve regurgitation. The left atrium was enlarged and the inferior vena cava was dilated with reduced respiratory variation.

An urgent cardiology consultation and transthoracic echocardiogram performed the same day showed thickening of both mitral valve leaflets and a vegetation on the posterior leaflet. Blood cultures were positive for Streptococcus mutans.

Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed two subacute strokes with petechial hemorrhage and a small subarachnoid hemorrhage. Transesophageal echocardiography demonstrated mitral valve vegetations with rupture of the chordae tendinae, 4+ mitral regurgitation, 1–2+ aortic regurgitation, and a Lambl’s excrescence on the aortic valve.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: after antibiotic treatment and transient altered mental status

evidence_events.source_span: On hospital day 14, the patient underwent bioprosthetic mitral valve replacement and debridement of a 5 mm excrescence on the aortic valve. Histopathology of the mitral valve demonstrated fibrosis, extensive acute and chronic inflammation, necrosis, and Gram-positive cocci in pairs and short chains. The aortic valve lesion also demonstrated necrosis, inflammation, and Gram-positive cocci.

source_metadata.title: Differential diagnosis of memory impairment in areas affected by a natural disaster: a case report

evidence_events.source_span: On March 11, 2011, the patient witnessed his wife being swept away in front of him by the tsunami resulting from the Great East Japan Earthquake.

After returning to his hometown 1 year later, he lived with his father and son’s family, then began to frequently lose valuable items and suspect his son of theft, leading to family separation and worsening memory impairment.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: 1 year later; after living with son’s family for more than 1 year

evidence_events.source_span: At first hospital visit, patient scored 16 on the Revised Hasegawa Dementia Scale (HDS-R), CT showed suspected dilatation of the lower horn of the right lateral ventricle, and he was diagnosed with Alzheimer’s disease and prescribed donepezil.
Four months later, patient reported details of an emotional fight with his son accurately, and memory for recent events improved clinically.
Blood tests showed no anemia, hypoproteinemia, thyroid dysfunction, liver or renal dysfunction, or abnormal glucose metabolism; MMSE was 23 with delayed recall 0 points.

During hospitalization, MRI showed no cortical atrophy, slight left-right hippocampal asymmetry without abnormality, and no high-intensity regions in hippocampus; DaT scan showed slight reduction in nigrostriatal pathway binding ratios but no significant abnormality; EEG showed normal alpha activity without slow waves or epileptic findings.
Neuropsychological tests showed full-scale IQ of 81, verbal IQ 80, performance IQ 87 (normal range), but many errors on Benton Visual Retention Test indicating cognitive decline.

Patient’s daily activity remained normal, no depressive mood, no evidence of epilepsy, delirium, or internal medicine diseases causing cognitive decline; psychological trauma and family separation considered as cause of dissociation resulting in memory impairment.

Treatment strategy changed from dementia drug therapy to emotional support and creating a supportive living environment; sertraline started at 25 mg daily, increased to 100 mg, then stopped due to suspected drug-induced hypomania.
After sertraline discontinuation, patient’s memory impairment improved gradually; MMSE improved to 26 points with delayed recall 2 points approximately 9 months after discharge.

diagnostic_reasoning_verbatim_spans: Initially, he was diagnosed with dementia. However, after several tests, neither could a definitive diagnosis of dementia be reached, nor was there any apparent evidence for depression, epilepsy, delirium, or internal medicine diseases.

Because of this traumatic experience, we suspected that dissociative disorder was involved in the development of the memory impairment and thus, we switched to treatments focusing on emotional support.

No obvious abnormalities were observed in the imaging studies, we could not positively diagnose him with dementia.
EEG and blood analyses revealed no abnormalities, the possibility of cognitive decline due to epilepsy, delirium, or other physical diseases was considered low.
As his daily activity remained normal and he felt no depressive mood, the possibility of memory impairment due to depression was low.
The patient’s symptoms are not explained by a dissociative disorder alone.
The patient’s memory disorder improved—although not completely—after he began to receive emotional support also suggests that psychological stress was involved in the memory disorder in this case.

source_metadata.title: Secondary hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis: a case report

evidence_events.source_span: The patient was an 83-years old Caucasian man with a personal history of aortic valve stenosis treated about 20 years ago with mechanical valve prosthesis and evidence of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (40%) since the last 5 years. Left atrium was markedly dilated (4.5 cm) and patient manifested with permanent atrial fibrillation under warfarin therapy. The patient also suffered from a previous stroke and presented chronic vascular encephalopathy with mild cognitive impairment.

He was admitted to our Division of Internal Medicine and Nephrology due to marked asthenia associated with fever, mental confusion, drowsiness and hyporexia. At the admission, patient also presented hypotension (90/60 mmHg), tachycardia (115 bpm) and dehydration. Body temperature was constantly about 38°C.

Blood tests showed increased blood urea nitrogen (159 mg/dl) and serum creatinine levels (1.99 mg/dl) with hyperkalemia (5.9 mEq/L), increased LDH (2494 IU/L) and CRP concentrations (5.96 mg/dl), normochromic macrocytic anemia (Hb = 11.2 g/dl, MCV = 99 fl, MCHC = 34 g/dl), severe thrombocytopenia (platelet count of 30,000 per microliter) and mild hypertransaminasemia (AST = 141 UI/l, ALT= 40 UI/L).

A brain CT scan without contrast confirmed previous stroke without any other relevant abnormalities while an electroencephalogram presented not relevant electrical alterations. Chest X-ray showed diffuse hypodiafania of both lungs and left pleural effusion. The whole abdomen ultrasound imaging revealed splenomegaly (bipolar diameter = 15.5 cm) and no other significant abnormalities.

During the hospitalization period the peripheral blood smear was not suggestive of noteworthy alterations and showed rare myeloid precursors and 3% metamielocytes. Blood tests showed: hyperferritinemia (2656 ng /ml), vitamin B12 (127 pg/ml) and folic acid deficiencies (3.3 ng/ml), mild hypothyroidism (TSH = 5.07 mU/ml, fT3 = 1.00 pg/ml, fT4 = 0.7 ng/dl), slight positivity of anti-platelet antibodies, hypertriglyceridemia (343 mg/dl), normal haptoglobin levels (100 mg/dl), and positive urine culture for Escherichia Coli. Procalcitonin, blood cultures and viral antibodies were all negative.

An urine culture-guided antibiotic therapy with meropenem was started, together with the administration of cyanocobalamin, folates, levothyroxine and corticosteroids (methylprednisolone 1 mg/kg/day, given the presence of anti-platelet autoantibodies and laboratory findings possibily consistent with an autoinflammatory disorder). Absence of leukocytosis, negativity of procalcitonin and blood cultures as well of lacked response to meropenem made our initial tentative diagnosis of sepsis increasingly unlikely.

Progressive increment in serum ferritin concentration (from 2656 ng/ml on day 1 to 4500 on day 7) focused attention to hyperferritinemic syndromes such as Still's disease, catastrophic syndromes due to antiphospholipid antibodies, septic shock, and macrophage activation syndrome. Based on the available clinical data and laboratory elements the first three hypotheses were excluded, and a secondary form of HLH was considered.
Bone marrow examination showed no significant alterations.
Despite corticosteroids, platelet count tended to decrease and infusions of platelet pools were performed.

Histological examination of the bone marrow clot sections showed a non-Hodgkin lymphoma of large B cells, derived from the activated B cell. Atypical lymphoid cells were CD20 +, MUM +, bcl-2 +, bcl-6 +, CD10-, with very-high proliferative index (Ki67 + in 100% of neoplastic cells) and coexistent aspects of hemophagocytosis.
Despite immediate target therapy instauration, the patient died immediately after diagnosis due to acute pulmonary edema and cardiogenic shock.

source_metadata.title: Remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting edema: a case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 82-year-old Asian male was admitted to the Department of General Internal Medicine with 2-month history of symmetrical swelling in both hands.
The swelling was localized to the dorsum of hands and did not extend to the face and lower extremities.
Despite treatment with loop diuretics furosemide 40 mg daily, his condition did not respond to the medication and his quality of life deteriorated.
On physical examination, his vitals were stable with blood pressure of 147/85 mmHg and heart rate of 98 beats per minute.
He had swelling restricted to the dorsum of both hands with pitting edema.
Examination of the joints showed tenderness suggestive of synovitis with restricted movements in bilateral proximal interphalangeal joint.

Laboratory findings revealed hyperglycemia, elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) of 118 mm/hour, and elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) of 6.58 mg/dL, and slight anemia with hemoglobin of 12.1 g/dL.
Plain radiographs of both hands showed soft tissue swelling with neither narrowing of the joint spaces nor bone erosion.
The diagnosis of bilateral RS3PE was made.
Treatment with prednisolone 15 mg daily was instituted.
At follow-up after hospitalization, dramatic improvement of all his symptoms was noted. The swelling on the dorsum of his hands had drastically resolved.
At 1 week follow-up after hospitalization, ESR and CRP had returned to normal.
