source_metadata.title: Leukemic retinopathy presenting as concurrent bilateral subhyaloid hemorrhage and subarachnoid hemorrhage in a patient with acute monocytic leukemia: a case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 36-year-old Persian male was first referred to our hospital because of increasing fatigue, pallor, scattered petechiae, and abnormal gum bleeding.

Anemia and thrombocytopenia in initial lab results prompted the hematologist–oncologist to obtain peripheral blood smear (PBS). Upon spotting blasts in the PBS, the hematologist–oncologist requested flow cytometry and bone marrow biopsy analysis, which subsequently confirmed the diagnosis of acute monocytic leukemia (AML-M5).
evidence_events.procedural_cue: peripheral blood smear, flow cytometry, bone marrow biopsy

evidence_events.source_span: The patient was then started on four sessions of induction chemotherapy, using cytosine arabinoside in combination with daunorubicin in the first session and cytosine arabinoside in combination with idarubicin for the following sessions. The last induction chemotherapy session took place 3 months after the initial diagnosis, after which it was concluded that the patient’s disease had entered remission phase.
Ten days following the last chemotherapy session, the patient presented to the emergency room with complaints of fever, headache, and blurred vision.

Initial lab results revealed pancytopenia including severe neutropenia (total white blood cell count 300 × 10⁹/L), anemia (hemoglobin 4.1 g/dL), and thrombocytopenia (platelets 7000 × 10⁹/L). C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate were significantly elevated (176 mg/L and 130 mm/hour, respectively). Coagulation parameters prothrombin time, partial thromboplastin time, and international normalized ratio were normal.
Spinal brain computed tomography (CT) scan was carried out, which indicated subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) in the left frontal and parietal lobes of the brain.

Ophthalmic examination revealed visual acuity of light perception in the right eye and 3-m finger count in the left eye. Fundus examination revealed bilateral peripapillary subhyaloid and intraretinal hemorrhages, confirming leukemic retinopathy.

The patient’s thrombocytopenia and anemia were improved by multiple transfusions of platelets and packed cells. He was also started on antibacterial, antifungal, and antiviral medications for neutropenic fever. The patient’s vision did not improve during the course of admission; however, he did not develop any neurologic deficit and his retinal hemorrhage appeared to be limited. Therefore, conservative treatment and regular follow-ups were continued.
Follow-up after 3 months showed significant improvement in visual acuity and shrinkage of retinal hemorrhages in both eyes. Bilateral macular edema was detected on OCT.

source_metadata.title: A case of IgG4-related interstitial nephritis with ureteral obstruction: case report and literature review

evidence_events.source_span: An 87-year-old male presented with anorexia and nausea for half a month and acute kidney injury with serum creatinine 428 µmol/L and urea nitrogen 20.9 mmol/L
Urinary CT examination revealed a right lower ureter mass with right renal and ureter hydronephrosis
Ultrasonography showed generalized superficial lymph node enlargement throughout the body
Three urine examinations for abnormal cells were all negative

Cystoscopy and right ureteroscopy showed local bulging and stenosis of the right ureteral orifice; biopsy revealed extruded and deformed fibrous tissue with small IgG-positive and IgG4-positive plasma cells
Serum IgG4 was significantly elevated at 1890 mg/dL

Renal biopsy showed mesangial cell proliferation, basement membrane thickening, diffuse fusion of foot processes, abundant IgG4-positive plasma cells in renal interstitium with IgG4+/IgG ratio 35%, and storiform pattern fibrosis
Double-J tube implantation in the right ureter led to serum creatinine decrease from 428 to 279 µmol/L
Treatment with methylprednisolone starting at 32 mg/day, tapered to 16 mg/day after five weeks, led to serum creatinine decrease to 196 µmol/L and IgG4 decrease to 171 mg/dL after two months

After one year of low-dose methylprednisolone maintenance, serum creatinine stabilized around 200 µmol/L, IgG4 normalized to 59 mg/dL, systemic superficial lymphadenopathy and right ureteral mass and hydronephrosis disappeared
2019 ACR/EULAR classification criteria score was 28 (>20), confirming diagnosis of IgG4-RD

source_metadata.title: Systemic lupus erythematosus presenting as lupus erythematosus tumidus and lupus nephritis: a case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 38-year-old North African female patient was referred to Nephrology department with lower extremity edema for 1 month. She had a history of Primary hypothyroidism and secondary infertility with amenorrhea for a year. She reported asthenia and a weight loss of 3 kg in 1 month. She was apyretic. She had no arthralgias or myalgias. She did not suffer from oral or ocular dryness. She reported the appearance of skin patches, which were photosensitive and showed fine scaling and associated pruritus.

On examination, her blood pressure was 110/70 mmHg, pulse was 99/min, temperature was 36.3 °C, and respiratory rate was 18/min. Urinalysis showed 2+ proteinuria and 1+ hematuria. The skin examination revealed firm curved erythematous patches on the neck, face, and chest and moderate edema of both lower limbs. There was no atrophy, scarring or dyspigmentation over the skin lesion.

Initial laboratory investigations showed a decreased serum albumin level of 33.5 g/L then 28.2 g/L (normal range: 35–50 g/L) and proteinuria of 4.5 g/day (urinary total volume 1000 mL). Microscopic examination of the urine showed microscopic hematuria (80–100 cells/HPF) and leukocyturia (50,000/mL). Electrophoresis of serum proteins showed a polyclonal peak in gamma globulins at 33.6 g/L. Serum creatinine was 58 µmol/L. The patient's blood test results showed a leukocyte count of 4900/mm3, with 1100/mm3 being lymphocytes, hemoglobin level of 12 g/dL, and a platelet count of 178,000/mm3.

The patient's antibody test showed a positive result with a titer of 1:1800 and homogenous pattern. Additionally, the patient tested positive for anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies with a titer of 1:40, and for anti-Sm (+ +), anti-RNP (+ +), and anti-SSA antibodies (+). The complement C3 and C4 levels were reduced to 42 mg/L (normal range: 81–157 mg/dL) and 7 mg/dL (normal range: 13–39 mg/dL), respectively, while CH50 was 9.5 U/mL (normal range: 31.7–95 U/mL). The results for Anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody, anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, Coombs' test, antiphospholipid antibody, serum cryoglobulins, serum and urine immunofixation electrophoresis, and anti-PLA2R antibody were all negative.

The skin biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of LET, with the presence of inflammatory lymphohistiocytic infiltrates and dermal mucin on and below the skin surface, with little or no involvement of the epidermis or dermo-epidermal layer. Direct immunofluorescence of skin biopsy confirmed LET by the presence of CD3/CD4 lymphocytes.

Ultrasound examination of the kidneys showed normal-sized kidneys (left 11.8 cm; right 11.7 cm). A renal biopsy was performed. Light microscopy showed that 8/34 glomeruli were sclerotic and the rest showed segmental mesangial deposits and infiltration of neutrophils, but no mesangial cell or stromal proliferation. The glomerular basement membrane was diffusely thickened with segmental spikes. The renal interstitium contained some inflammatory infiltrates, and the tubules showed small focal atrophy and scattered proteinaceous and red blood cell casts. There was intimal fibrous proliferation and sclerosis of small arteries. Congo red stain for amyloid was negative. Direct immunofluorescence showed full-house staining along the mesangium and the capillary loops with subepithelial immune deposits of IgG (3+), IgA (+), IgM (1+), C3 (2+), C1q (1+), fibrinogen (2+), albumin (−), kappa (2+), lambda (3+).

The patient met six of the EULAR/ACR 2019 classification criteria for systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), with a total score of 31 including glomerular proteinuria, and a Class V renal biopsy. Positive ANA results, positive anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm antibodies and reduced complement C3 and C4 proteins.

Symptomatic treatment was based on anti-proteinuric treatment with ACE inhibitors (Captopril 25 mg 1 tablet × 2/day) and substantive treatment combined oral corticotherapy at 1 mg/kg/day (prednisone 12 tablets/day) for 1 month followed by tapering 5 mg/15 days and hydroxychloroquine 200 mg twice a day. No DMARD therapy for SLE has been initiated. After 1 month, the skin lesions regressed. At 6 and 12 months follow up, proteinuria improved to respectively 0.8 g/24 hour and 0.5 g/24 hour.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: After 1 month; At 6 and 12 months follow up

evidence_events.source_span: At the latest check-up, 22 months after the initial presentation, the patient's proteinuria was 684 mg/24 hour, serum creatinine was 51 µmol/l, and there was complete resolution of the lesions.

source_metadata.title: Discordance of light chain isotypes between serum and glomerular deposits in proliferative glomerulonephritis with monoclonal IgG deposits: a case report and review of the literature

evidence_events.source_span: The patient was a 50-year-old man who had been followed up at a local clinic due to hypertension, type 2 diabetes, hyperlipidemia, hyperuricemia, fatty liver, and obesity.
Proteinuria was noted at an annual health checkup five years previously, and hyperproteinemia, high gamma globulin, and κ Bence-Jones protein (BJP) positivity were noted one year previously.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: five years previously; one year previously

evidence_events.source_span: Bone marrow aspiration showed 5% plasma cells, which did not lead to a diagnosis of multiple myeloma.

He was hypertensive, and his estimated glomerular filtration rate was 54.2 ml/min/1.73 m2. His urinary protein level was 0.84 g/g·Cr. Urine and serum immunofixation showed BJP-κ type and IgG-κ type, respectively. The blood immunoglobulin free light chain κ/λ ratio was elevated.

Kidney biopsy showed an increase in mesangial cells and matrix without nodular lesions under light microscopy. Immunofluorescence microscopy showed granular deposits of IgG and C3 on the capillary wall and weak positivity for C1q. IgG3 was predominant among the IgG subclasses, and intraglomerular κ and λ staining was negative for κ and positive for λ. Direct fast scarlet staining was negative. Electron microscopy showed lumpy deposits without a fibrillar structure in the subepithelial area.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: kidney biopsy, immunofluorescence microscopy, electron microscopy
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: Fig1: Light microscopy showed increased mesangial cells and matrix without nodular lesions; Fig2: Immunofluorescence showed granular IgG and C3 deposits, IgG3 predominance, κ negative and λ positive staining; Fig3: Electron microscopy showed granular nonorganized electron-dense deposits in subepithelial area.

evidence_events.source_span: Based on the above findings, a diagnosis of membranous nephropathy-type PGNMID was made.

Computed tomography showed mildly enlarged cervical, supraclavicular, axillary, mediastinal, para-aorta, hepatic portal, and bilateral inguinal lymph nodes, splenomegaly, and fatty liver. Positron emission tomography (PET)-CT showed mild accumulation of fluorodeoxyglucose in the cervical, supraclavicular, axillary, and inguinal lymph nodes.

His anti-nuclear antibody (ANA) and anti-SS-A antibody levels were high (2560 times and 240 times, respectively). C4 was low, but there were no other systemic symptoms or findings to diagnose systemic lupus erythematosus or Sjögren’s syndrome.

Proteinuria increased gradually over three years of treatment with valsartan, and oral prednisolone was initiated, which led to decreased proteinuria. The dose of oral prednisolone was gradually tapered to 10 mg per day, and proteinuria was 0.88 g/g·Cr at that time.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: over three years; after treatment initiation
evidence_events.procedural_cue: treatment with valsartan and oral prednisolone
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: Fig4: Clinical course showing eGFR and proteinuria changes with treatment.

source_metadata.title: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease with ectopic unilateral multicystic kidney: a case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 46-year-old Ghanaian male presented to our outpatient department (OPD) with a history of hematuria and left flank pain. The hematuria was painless and total. The pain was dull in nature; constant, non-radiating with no aggravating or relieving factors. There were no lower urinary tract symptoms and no associated fever or vomiting. There was no childhood history of hematuria. His blood pressure was 154/112 mmhg. There was no abdominal tenderness or mass on examination. Other physical examinations were unremarkable.
The full blood count had hemoglobin of 13.2 g/dl. His renal function was deranged. [sodium 140 mmol/l, potassium 4.9 mmol/l, urea 13.6 µmol/l, creatinine 518 µmol/l, eGFR 13 ml/min].
Abdominal ultrasonography showed both kidneys to be larger than normal and had multiple cysts of varying sizes with the right kidney located in the right iliac fossa.

Abdominopelvic computer tomographic scan (CT-Scan) without contrast showed enlarged kidneys with the renal parenchyma replaced by innumerable cyst of varying sizes. The right kidney was ectopically located in the right aspect of the pelvis. The right and left kidneys measure 18.8 cm × 8.0 cm and 21 cm × 9.8 cm respectively. The cysts were hypodense with thin walls with some of the walls calcified. The other intra-abdominal organs did not have cysts.

A urine cytology was negative for malignancy and urethrocystoscopy showed normal findings with no lateralizing signs. Renal scintigraphy was not done but will be considered, if necessary, in subsequent follow ups.
The symptoms were hence attributed to the polycystic disease.
He was put on antihypertensives, analgesia for the left flank pain and to have follow up at the urology and nephrology departments.

source_metadata.title: Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis due to IgA nephropathy accompanied by collagenofibrotic glomerulopathy. A nephrology picture

evidence_events.source_span: A 69-year-old Japanese woman was admitted with an approximately one-month history of fatigue and generalized pitting edema.
The patient had been diagnosed with renal dysfunction with serum creatinine (SCr) levels of approximately 1.5 mg/dL and proteinuria, but her disease was not progressive and had not been investigated.
At referral she exhibited gross hematuria, elevated SCr levels (5.8 mg/dL), nephrotic syndrome, and a weight gain of 10 kg above her usual body weight.
There was no marked decrease in complement levels, and test results for antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, and anti-GBM antibodies were negative.
Renal biopsy showed a membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis (MPGN)-like pattern of all glomeruli with cellular crescent formation in one glomerulus.
Immunofluorescence study showed IgA deposition dominated the capillary walls and was positive for the KM55 monoclonal antibody specific to Gd-IgA1.
Electron microscopy revealed mesangial area alterations and electron-dense deposits in the subendothelial areas.
Congo red staining was negative, while immunohistochemical analysis for type III collagen was positive.
Serum procollagen III N-terminal propeptide and hyaluronic acid levels were elevated to 602 ng/mL and 138,000 ng/mL, respectively.

Temporary hemodialysis was necessary; however, steroid pulse therapy and cyclophosphamide improved the SCr to 2.66 mg/dL and resolved the patient's hematuria, though proteinuria remained at a nephrotic level.

source_metadata.title: Fibronectin glomerulopathy in an elderly patient with FN1 gene mutation: a case report and literature review
source_metadata.notes: Extraction based on case presentation and clinical course sections with image figure 1 assigned to pathology milestone.

evidence_events.source_span: A 75-year-old Korean female visited the nephrology clinic for evaluation of azotemia and proteinuria, after experiencing generalized edema for 2 months.

Her blood pressure was 135/78 mmHg. Laboratory testing revealed elevated BUN (25.9 mg/dL) and serum creatinine (1.36 mg/dL). Her estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) was 38 mL/min/1.73 m2. Urinalysis revealed proteinuria 3+ in dipstick and microscopic hematuria (urine RBC 10-20/HPF). The spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio (PCR) was 3.99 g/g, and 24-hour urine collection showed urine total protein of 3629 mg/day.

Results were negative in tests for anti-nuclear antibodies (ANA), anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (ANCA), anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) antibodies, anti-streptolysin O (ASO) antibodies, and rheumatoid factor (RF). Serologic test results were within normal limits including IgA, IgG, IgM, C3, and C4. Negative results were obtained from serologic tests for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and human immunodeficiency viruses. Serum M protein was not detected and serum protein electrophoresis was unremarkable.
Renal ultrasound showed that the kidneys were of normal size and increased parenchymal echogenicity.

Renal biopsy was performed. The glomerulus exhibited mesangial expansion and lobular accentuation without mesangial hypercellularity upon PAS staining. The mesangial expansion is negative staining in Periodic Acid Methenamine Silver (PAM) staining. Congo-red staining was negative for amyloid. Immunohistochemistry for fibronectin showed strong positive staining in the glomerulus. Immunofluorescence results for IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, C1q, and fibrinogen were all negative in glomeruli and vessels. Electron microscopy revealed massive mesangial and subendothelial electron dense deposits, along with diffuse foot process effacement. These deposits exhibited a granular and fibrillary substructure, with fibril diameters ranging from 11 to 16 nm.
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: Fig1 shows histologic, immunohistochemistry, and electron microscopy findings supporting fibronectin glomerulopathy.

evidence_events.source_span: The patient’s mother had clinical features of wax and wane generalized edema and suffered from kidney disease, although no specific disease name was known. The patient has two younger brothers and two younger sisters, of whom one brother and one sister are being treated for proteinuria. These two siblings had not undergone renal biopsy; therefore, their specific diagnoses were also unknown.

Genetic testing of whole-blood samples revealed an FN1 gene mutation with an adenine changed to guanine at nucleotide 2,918 of the complementary DNA (c.2918 A > G) causing a substitution in which the tyrosine at amino acid 973 is replaced by cysteine (Y973C).

The patient’s anti-hypertensive medication was changed to angiotensin II receptor blocker (Azilsartan 20 mg/day), and torsemide (10 mg/day) was added for edema control. At 6 months after kidney biopsy, serum creatinine was 1.41 mg/dL (eGFR 36 mL/min/1.73 m2) and spot urine PCR was 2.35 g/g. At 1 year after biopsy, serum creatinine was 1.43 mg/dL (eGFR 35 mL/min/1.73 m2) and spot urine PCR was 0.48 g/g. At 2 years after renal biopsy, the patient’s renal function maintained stable (serum Cr 1.56 mg/dL, eGFR 32 mL/min/1.73 m2) and proteinuria was reduced (spot urine PCR 0.14 g/g).

source_metadata.title: Fabry disease in female monozygotic twins with complex intronic haplotype variants: a case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 61-year-old woman was referred to our nephrology department for the management of chronic kidney disease. She had a history of stroke, a right internal carotid artery occlusion, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, chronic kidney disease, and chronic hepatitis B.

Two years previously, a kidney biopsy had been performed to evaluate the cause of proteinuria. Light microscopy revealed basement membrane thickening, mesangial matrix widening with focal mesangial cell proliferation, and moderate interstitial fibrosis and tubular atrophy diagnosed as chronic glomerulonephritis. Initially, no abnormal findings were described in the EM of the biopsy.

At the time of her visit, she complained of intermittent lower abdominal cramping, but did not exhibit acroparesthesia, hypohidrosis, or angiokeratoma. She denied use of cationic amphiphilic drugs such as chlorpromazine, amiodarone or chloroquine.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: At the time of her visit

evidence_events.source_span: Initial laboratory tests indicated a serum creatinine level of 2.86 mg/dL, an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of 17.18 mL/min/1.73 m2, and a urinary albumin-to-creatinine ratio of 2790.6 mg/g creatinine.

evidence_events.source_span: Echocardiography showed hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with a left ventricular mass index of 163.5 g/m2 (normal range < 115 g/m2).
evidence_events.temporal_cue: At the time of her visit

evidence_events.source_span: Her monozygotic twin sister had histories of atrial flutter, carotid stenosis, proteinuria, left ventricular hypertrophy, and syncope.
The α-galactosidase enzyme activity and plasma lyso-Gb3 level were measured, but they were within normal ranges (3.02 μmol/h/L and < 1.00 ng/mL, respectively).
evidence_events.procedural_cue: enzyme activity and plasma lyso-Gb3 measurement

evidence_events.source_span: Genetic test for the GLA gene, including intronic regions, revealed 5 variants of complex intronic haplotype (CIH): c.-10 C > T, c.369+990 C > A, c.370-81_370-77delCAGCC, c.640-16 A > G, and c.1000-22 C > T.
Electron microscopy of previous kidney biopsy showed lamellated lipid inclusions in podocytes, compatible with Fabry disease.
Genetic testing of her family confirmed that her monozygotic twin sister and son had the same CIH variants in their GLA genes.

The α-galactosidase enzyme activity of the twin sister and son were within normal range (5.58 μmol/h/L and 4.92 μmol/h/L, respectively) and plasma lyso-Gb3 levels were also normal (< 1.00 ng/mL in both).
evidence_events.procedural_cue: enzyme activity and plasma lyso-Gb3 measurement

evidence_events.source_span: Enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) with 1 mg/kg agalsidase-β every 2 weeks was started. Within the early period of ERT, abdominal pain was substantially reduced.

During 2 years of follow-up with ERT, eGFR decreased to 9.87 mL/min/1.73 m2. Echocardiography showed no progression of left ventricular hypertrophy and a slight decrease in left ventricular mass index to 152.8 g/m2.
The level of lyso-Gb3 did not change and stayed below 1.00 ng/mL during follow-up after starting ERT.
Her monozygotic twin sister refused ERT treatment. Follow-up echocardiography after 3 years showed little change in left ventricular hypertrophy and eGFR was maintained at 51 mL/min/1.73 m2.

hidden_reference.article_derived_evidence_summary: The case report describes a 61-year-old woman with chronic kidney disease, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and cerebrovascular disease, whose genetic testing revealed complex intronic haplotype variants in the GLA gene. Electron microscopy of kidney biopsy showed lamellated lipid inclusions characteristic of Fabry disease. Family testing confirmed the same variants in her monozygotic twin sister and son. source_metadata.title: Severe pregnancy-associated atypical hemolytic uremia syndrome in the context of the COVID-19 pandemic: a novel survival case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 26-year-old patient with a history of four pregnancies and one delivery (P4G1) presented at 30 weeks and 2 days of gestation with vaginal fluid leakage and fetal growth restriction detected by ultrasound at a different hospital.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: presented at 30 weeks and 2 days of gestation

evidence_events.source_span: During labor induction, the patient developed a high fever and coagulopathy, followed by heart failure, acute kidney injury, anemia, and severe thrombocytopenia.
The patient remained alert and coherent, with no evidence of neurological dysfunction.
She was transferred to our department and was given invasive respiratory support, blood transfusion, continuous renal replacement therapy, capacity management, and other comprehensive treatments.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: invasive respiratory support, blood transfusion, continuous renal replacement therapy

evidence_events.source_span: Due to the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic, ADAMTS13 testing and complement inhibitor therapy were unavailable.
A diagnosis of pregnancy-associated aHUS was made based on the patient's history, clinical presentation, and standard laboratory results.
The patient was prescribed 13 sessions of hemodialysis.
Post-treatment evaluation showed normalized complement C3 and C4 levels, stabilized platelet and hemoglobin levels, and gradual normalization of liver function.
Renal function improved gradually, and a bone marrow biopsy revealed no fragmented red blood cells.
The patient was transferred to the Department of Nephrology on day 40 and back to the local hospital on day 42.
The patient was followed up for 3 years, during which her renal function returned to normal, with no recurrence of thrombocytopenia or microangiopathic hemolytic anemia.
On day 4, the results of stool and blood cultures, autoantibody tests, the Coombs test, hepatitis B DNA, and cervical secretion culture were all negative.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: stool and blood cultures, autoantibody tests, Coombs test, hepatitis B DNA, cervical secretion culture

evidence_events.source_span: Her peripheral blood smear showed the presence of fragmented red blood cells and decreased levels of complement C3 and C4.
The pelvic computed tomography (CT) scan showed no intrauterine infection.
aHUS was confirmed as the final diagnosis, and the patient underwent plasmapheresis without anti-complement therapy.
Following treatment, her vital signs improved. The antibiotic therapy was discontinued, and the patient underwent three consecutive plasma exchanges based on her clinical needs.
On day 8 after admission, the patient's blood pressure and hemoglobin level decreased, and her abdominal tension increased.
Abdominal ultrasound revealed a large hematoma above the bladder.
Computed tomography angiography (CTA) and digital subtraction angiography (DSA) confirmed the presence of a pelvic hematoma and multiple ruptures in the left femoral artery.
A stent was implanted in the left femoral artery, and the abdominal hematoma was removed.
The patient subsequently underwent nine sessions of plasma exchange, along with intermittent hemofiltration, blood transfusions, and additional treatments.

source_metadata.title: A case of rapidly progressive IgA nephropathy in a patient with exacerbation of Crohn’s disease
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case presentation and clinical course sections with source-ordered evidence events and milestones.

evidence_events.source_span: An 18-year-old male was referred to our nephrology clinic for evaluation of azotemia and proteinuria in March 2011.

He had previously undergone an operation to repair an anal fistula in December 2008 and an appendectomy in January 2009; he was diagnosed with Crohn’s disease in June 2009 after colonoscopy revealed linear, geographic ulcers with non-caseating granulomas in the distal ileum.
In July 2009, he was diagnosed with an ascending colon perforation and underwent an emergency right hemicolectomy.

In December 2010, the patient experienced exacerbation of Crohn’s disease symptoms with non-bloody diarrhea three to four times daily; colonoscopy revealed geographic ulcers consistent with Crohn’s disease.
In December 2010, urinalysis revealed mild proteinuria (1+ dipstick) and microscopic hematuria; blood urea nitrogen and serum creatinine were normal.

In March 2011, the patient developed dark loose stools, pale conjunctiva, facial puffiness, edema in lower extremities, blood pressure 137/96 mmHg, proteinuria (2+ dipstick), microscopic hematuria, and deteriorated renal function with BUN 30.3 mg/dL and creatinine 3.42 mg/dL.

24-hour urine study revealed proteinuria of 3,967 mg/day; serologic tests showed mildly increased IgA (492 mg/dL), normal IgG, IgM, C3, C4; ANA, ANCA, anti-GBM, ASO, RF, cryoglobulin, hepatitis B, C, and HIV tests were negative; renal ultrasound showed normal-sized kidneys with increased cortical echogenicity.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: urine study, serologic tests, renal ultrasound

evidence_events.source_span: Renal biopsy revealed nine crescent formations and eight scleroses in 17 glomeruli, endocapillary hypercellularity, interstitial inflammatory cell infiltration, mild tubular atrophy with interstitial fibrosis; immunofluorescence showed 2+ diffuse fine granular IgA staining, 1+ IgM and C3; electron microscopy revealed dense mesangial deposits.
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: Figure 1 shows histological and immunofluorescence findings.

evidence_events.source_span: Immunostaining for interleukin-17 (IL-17) was positive in renal tissue and in previously exacerbated colonic ulcers from December 2010; IL-17 staining was negative in renal tissue from a primary IgAN control patient.
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: Figure 1C, D, E show IL-17 staining.

evidence_events.source_span: Two days after renal biopsy, serum creatinine increased from 3.9 mg/dL to 4.8 mg/dL; patient was treated with prednisolone pulse therapy (250 mg twice daily for 3 days) followed by tapering to 1 mg/kg/day.
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: Figure 2 shows clinical course and treatment.

evidence_events.source_span: On the fifth day of steroid treatment, patient developed watery diarrhea 10 times daily with metabolic acidosis (pH 7.24, HCO3 9.7), serum chloride 121 mmol/L, BUN 89 mg/dL, creatinine 3.88 mg/dL; treated with 5-ASA, loperamide, and intravenous fluids; diarrhea subsided in 2 weeks.

After discharge, patient was treated with oral deflazacort (48 mg/day) and cyclophosphamide (100 mg/day), tapered over 3 months; 5-ASA maintained at 2 g/day; renal function improved with BUN 61.2 mg/dL, creatinine 2.5 mg/dL; proteinuria 2+ dipstick, urine protein-creatinine ratio 1.8 mg/g.

In September 2011, cyclophosphamide was replaced with azathioprine (100 mg/day), then switched to mycophenolate sodium (360 mg/day) due to bone marrow suppression; intestinal symptoms stable and renal function maintained (BUN 33.8 mg/dL, creatinine 2.32 mg/dL) in December 2011.

source_metadata.title: Acute Interstitial Nephritis Following Multiple Asian Giant Hornet Stings

evidence_events.source_span: A 42-year-old man arrived at the Emergency Department about 5 hours after he was attacked by swarms of Asian giant hornets. On admission, he had difficulty breathing, headache, and numbness in both limbs (arm and leg).
On physical examination, he was found to have approximately 66 sting marks in exposed areas of the face, head, neck, upper limb, and upper thorax.

His blood pressure was 136/90 mmHg, and heart rate was 46/min. An initial blood laboratory test revealed white blood cells 32.94×10^9/L, hemoglobin 141 g/L, and platelets 199×10^9/L. Urine examination revealed a specific gravity of 1.01 and absence of proteinuria and red blood cells. Chest X-ray was normal, and electrocardiography showed sinus bradycardia of 45/min. Urine output was 200 ml/24 h on the first day.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: initial blood laboratory test, urine examination, chest X-ray, electrocardiography

evidence_events.source_span: The patient was given methylprednisolone, plasma exchange, and continuous veno-venous hemofiltration (CVVH).

On day 3, laboratory investigation revealed direct bilirubin 13.69 umol/L, alanine transaminase 163.9 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 1124.00 U/L, creatine kinase 5342.3 U/L, creatine kinase-MB 577.0 U/L, troponin I 1.092 ng/ml, and serum creatinine 185.00 umol/L.
Ten days later, creatine kinase-MB and troponin I became normal. However, the patient had progressively worsening oliguria (200 ml/24 h) and the serum creatinine increased to 534 umol/L.

On day 17, he remained oliguric (250 ml/24 h) and serum creatinine increased to 1130.5 umol/L. His renal function further deteriorated, color Doppler sonographic signal of the size of the kidneys increased, and renal parenchyma was 2.5 cm thick.

A kidney biopsy was performed. Under a light microscope, 19 glomeruli appeared normal. Tubular epithelial cells were distended by abundant, large, cytoplasmic vacuoles, while the blood vessels were normal. The interstitial inflammation was accompanied by interstitial edema and focal interstitial infiltration with eosinophils and lymphocytes.
The patient was continually given methylprednisolone orally 32 mg/day. On day 31, his urine output gradually increased to more than 2.8 liter/day and serum creatinine decreased to 159.3 umol/L.

source_metadata.title: A case report of a giant rectal adenoma causing secretory diarrhea and acute renal failure: McKittrick-Wheelock syndrome

evidence_events.source_span: A 75-year-old woman was admitted to the emergency department with vomit, diarrhea, confusion and epigastric pain.

She had a diagnosis of chronic renal insufficiency for several months, and she recently suffered several episodes of urinary tract infection and acute renal failure due to severe dehydration consequent to diarrhea.
She reported consistent weight loss in the last period.
She had hypertension, cardiac insufficiency, chronic pulmonary obstructive disease, hiatal hernia and an history of cardiac arrhythmias.
On admission, blood pressure was 140/85 mmHg and pulse rate was 95. On physical examination, abdomen was nontender. Abdominal ultrasound was negative. An electrocardiograph was normal.

Laboratory analysis were significant for hyponatriemia (124 mmol/L), hypokalemia (3.1 mmol/L), high creatininemia (318.24 μmol/L), hyperazotemia (188 mg/dl), leukocytosis (10.810 x 10^9/L), and proteinuria (2.5 g/day).

After adequate rehydration and PPI infusion epigastric pain subsided. She was treated with intravenous 0.9 % saline and potassium infusion. A complete normalization of her biochemistry, followed by normalization of her creatinine values, occurred only after 10 days of intravenous therapy.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: rehydration, PPI infusion, intravenous saline and potassium infusion

evidence_events.source_span: In light of her persistent, mucous diarrhea a digital examination was performed, documenting a circumferential lesion of the rectum, with mucosal involvement of the anal canal up to 1 cm from the anal verge, and a colonoscopy was ordered.
The colonoscopy showed sigmoid diverticula and a giant polyp of the rectum, occupying three quarters of the luminal circumference, with a cranial-caudal extension of 8-9 cm.
Considering the typical clinical presentation, McKittrick-Wheelock syndrome was diagnosed.
A biopsy was performed on the polyp, and pathology showed a villous adenoma with focal high-grade dysplasia.

Subsequently, the patient underwent a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the thorax and abdomen for staging of the disease. The CT scan did not show any signs of mural involvement, nor sphincterial or mesorectal involvement or signs of distant metastases.

Given the dimension and the extension of the polyp transanal surgery was excluded, and considering the good general conditions and continence status of the patient a low anterior rectal resection with mucosectomy of the anal canal had initially been planned.

An intra-operative frozen section pathological examination showed involvement of the distal margin by intramucosal adenocarcinoma, and a conventional abdomino-perineal resection with end-colostomy was performed.
Pathological examination on the whole specimen showed a villous adenoma with areas of intramucosal adenocarcinoma and high grade dysplasia (TisN0).

After surgery, the patient showed persistent normalization of physical and serological parameters and full recovery of her renal function. She did not have any medical or surgical postoperative complication. At 10 months follow-up, she was in good general conditions, without signs of local recurrence, with a regular GI function and no signs of renal insufficiency or electrolyte disturbance.

source_metadata.notes: Case report from Pan African Medical Journal 2016

evidence_events.source_span: A 52 year's old men with no medical history was admitted in the department of nephrology for 2 months of fatigue, dizziness and acute renal failure: creatinine 330 µmol/l and clearance of creat 14 ml /min.
No abnormalities were observed in physical examination except conjunctival jaundice, liver and spleen were not palpable.

Laboratory investigation showed: hemoglobin 86g/L, red blood cell (RBC) 3.67*10^12/L, reticulocytes count of 5.2%, white blood cells (WBC) 12.3*10^9/L, platelet count 36*10^9/L, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) was 451UI/L, indirect bilirubin 49 mmol/L and total bilirubin 96 mmol/L.
Direct Coomb's test (DCT) was positive for auto-antibody. The autoantibody eluted was warm IgG antibody.
Total serum protein 113 g/L and a spike in gamma globulin estimated to 69 g/l. Serum immune electrophoresis showed that the M protein was the IgG kappa chain. Urinary M protein was 2g/day.
Bone marrow aspirates showed infiltration by 78% of plasma cells.
Cytogenetics by conventional karyotyping showed no chromosomal abnormalities.
A whole body CT-Scan showed osteolytic lesions of vertebral body of C5, D4, L3, L4 and the left iliac wing.
After a diagnosis of multiple myeloma and Evan's syndrome was made, chemotherapy was rapidly initiated by BTD (bortezomib-thalidomide-dexamethasone) and continuous corticosteroid therapy.
Evolution was marked by deterioration of the hematological and renal state along with the occurrence of hemorrhagic symptoms such as echymosis and haematemesis.
The patient died secondary of a lactic acidosis.

source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case presentation section of PMC5334399

evidence_events.source_span: A 14-year-old Caucasian girl with a history of primary hypoparathyroidism and unstable calcium and phosphorus levels and on ongoing treatment was admitted to the Department of Pediatric Nephrology because of the onset of nephrocalcinosis and difficulties achieving normocalcemia.
The first symptoms of the disease appeared at the age of 9 years and consisted of several episodes of syncope and seizures.
At presentation, apart from a white-coated tongue, dental caries, and enamel hypoplasia, the clinical, neurological, cardiovascular, and ophthalmic examinations were normal.
Laboratory tests revealed hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and low serum parathyroid hormone (sPTH).
Computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance (MR) imaging revealed bilateral calcifications in the basal ganglia and the frontal lobes (Fig. 1).
The thyroid gland was slightly heterogeneous on ultrasound, and antithyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) antibodies were present, without any other clinical or biochemical features of hypothyreosis.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: thyroid ultrasound and anti-TPO antibody testing

evidence_events.source_span: A treatment of primary hypoparathyroidism based on calcium supplementation and 1-alpha-hydroxycholecalciferol administration was prescribed.

During a period of 3 years (2011–2014), the dosage had to be progressively increased due to persisting hypocalcemia, to a maximum of 4.0 g of calcium carbonate and 1.75 μg of 1-alpha-hydroxycholecalciferol daily.

In January 2015, the patient was hospitalized because of dyspnea, generalized weakness, polydipsia, nausea, and tachycardia. She was severely hypercalcemic at that moment but recovered rapidly after intensive fluid therapy, loop diuretics, and temporary withdrawal of the vitamin D and calcium.
In September 2015, features of mild nephrocalcinosis appeared, with increased echogenicity of the borders of the renal pyramids, which led to her referral to the nephrology department.
On admission, the girl was in good general condition. Physical examination showed the same oral findings as described above, with the confirmation of candidiasis in swab culture.

Laboratory tests showed biochemical findings similar to the aforementioned: low level of sPTH, 25-OH-vitamin D, and alkaline phosphatase; hyperphosphatemia; and clearly decreased levels of total and ionized calcium.
Persistent hypercalciuria was observed, with an elevated calcium-to-creatinine ratio in a morning urine sample of 0.24 mg/mg, and a decreased magnesium-to-calcium ratio of 0.25 mg/mg.

The other results were within the normal range, including an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) by Schwartz formula of 92 ml/min/1.73 m2. A bone densitometry (total body and lumbar region) was appropriate for age.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: renal function and bone densitometry testing

evidence_events.source_span: During hospitalization, the girl reported transient acute pain in her right knee. X-ray imaging showed no pathological changes.

Ultrasound examination revealed, besides mild nonprogressive bilateral nephrocalcinosis, a duplex left kidney with a mild dilatation of the upper-pole collecting system of 10 mm in sagittal dimension.

hidden_reference.final_diagnosis_verbatim: Coexistence of hypoparathyroidism, oral candidiasis, dental enamel hypoplasia, and subclinical Hashimoto’s disease was strongly suggestive for autoimmune polyglandular syndrome (APS) type I.
diagnostic_reasoning_verbatim_spans: A 14-year-old Caucasian girl with a history of primary hypoparathyroidism and unstable calcium and phosphorus levels and on ongoing treatment was admitted to the Department of Pediatric Nephrology because of the onset of nephrocalcinosis and difficulties achieving normocalcemia.
The first symptoms of the disease appeared at the age of 9 years and consisted of several episodes of syncope and seizures.
At presentation, apart from a white-coated tongue, dental caries, and enamel hypoplasia, the clinical, neurological, cardiovascular, and ophthalmic examinations were normal.
Laboratory tests revealed hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, and low serum parathyroid hormone (sPTH).
Computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance (MR) imaging revealed bilateral calcifications in the basal ganglia and the frontal lobes.
The thyroid gland was slightly heterogeneous on ultrasound, and antithyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) antibodies were present, without any other clinical or biochemical features of hypothyreosis.
On admission, the girl was in good general condition. Physical examination showed the same oral findings as described above, with the confirmation of candidiasis in swab culture.

Laboratory tests showed biochemical findings similar to the aforementioned: low level of s PTH, 25-OH-vitamin D, and alkaline phosphatase; hyperphosphatemia; and clearly decreased levels of total and ionized calcium.
Persistent hypercalciuria was observed, with an elevated calcium-to-creatinine ratio in a morning urine sample of 0.24 mg/mg, and a decreased magnesium-to-calcium ratio of 0.25 mg/mg.
diagnostic_reasoning_items: Primary hypoparathyroidism with biochemical abnormalities and brain calcifications.
Presence of oral candidiasis and dental enamel hypoplasia.
Subclinical autoimmune thyroid involvement (anti-TPO antibodies).
Development of nephrocalcinosis despite treatment.
Combination of these features suggests autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type I.
hidden_reference.final_diagnosis: Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type I (APS I) presenting with primary hypoparathyroidism, oral candidiasis, dental enamel hypoplasia, subclinical Hashimoto’s disease, and nephrocalcinosis.
hidden_reference.diagnostic_reasoning: The constellation of primary hypoparathyroidism with persistent hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia, brain calcifications, oral candidiasis, dental enamel hypoplasia, and positive anti-TPO antibodies without overt hypothyroidism strongly supports the diagnosis of autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type I. The onset of nephrocalcinosis despite treatment and the presence of multiple endocrine and immune abnormalities further corroborate this diagnosis.

Laboratory and imaging findings, along with clinical features, support the diagnosis of APS type I.

evidence_events.source_span: A 24-year-old female patient presented to the renal outpatient in September 2014 on account of body swelling and frothy urine while being managed for periodontal gingival cellulitis.
She had facial puffiness, jaw swelling, and massive lower limb edema and ascites. The blood pressure was 120/80 mmHg.
In the 3rd week of admission, she was observed to develop hyperpigmented malar rash, gum hypertrophy, and bleeding with oliguria and rising serum creatinine levels.

At admission, her serum creatinine was 167.3 umol/l with an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of 42 ml/min/1.73m2. Her hemogram showed leukopenia and anemia of 1.7 × 10^9/L and 18%, respectively; the erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 133 mm in the 1st h (Westergren).

She had reduced level of high-density lipoprotein cholesterol of 0.8 mmol/L and elevated triglyceride of 5.8 mmol/L, severe hypoalbuminemia (17.2 g/L), and heavy proteinuria (2.7 g/day). Spun urine sample showed 15-20 pus cells/hpf, numerous dysmorphic red blood cells, granular casts, and epithelial cell casts. The urine culture was sterile.
Renal scan showed enlarged kidneys with multiple cysts of varying sizes (2.7-31.4 mm). Other intra-abdominal organs were normal.
Serology showed a strong positive homogenous pattern for the antinuclear factor while the anti-double stranded DNA titer was elevated to 30 IU/ml (normal < 4 IU/ml) by ELISA.

Renal tissue histology on light microscopy showed marked mesangial cell increase, some containing apoptotic debris; acute tubular necrosis with simplification of tubular epithelial cells, some cystically dilated containing amorphous eosinophilic material; interstitial fibrosis with tubular atrophy in about 10-20% of the section examined; no increase in mesangial matrix or thickening/duplication of glomerular basement membrane. Features were in keeping with lupus glomerulonephritis (ISN/RPS Class II).

She underwent a series of dialysis sessions when she became oliguric and uremic during admission and received intravenous methyl prednisolone followed by tapered oral prednisolone and mycophenolate mofetil.
After 6 months of treatment, proteinuria, serum creatinine, and ESR reduced to 0.2 g/day, 94 umol/l and 44 mm/h, respectively. Her eGFR rose to 82 ml/min/1.73 m2.
At 10 months, she remains stable on medications with proteinuria of 0.07 mg/day, ESR of 16 mm in 1st h, and hemoglobin concentration of 12 g/dl.

source_metadata.title: The complex treatment including rituximab in the Management of Catastrophic Antiphospholid Syndrome with renal involvement

evidence_events.source_span: A 35-year-old woman who displayed dyspnoea and peripheral edema was admitted to the Nephrology Clinic because of rapidly progressive renal insufficiency.
Her history included autoimmune hemolytic anemia, two miscarriages and the diagnosis of APS with the treatment of heparin and acetylosalicylic acid during her next pregnancy.
Despite this treatment, she gave birth to a dead fetus in 22 Hbd.
She then developed CAPS with involvement of the kidneys, brain, skin, peripheral veins and central retinal artery.
Lupus anticoagulant and β2-glicoprotein-I antibodies were positive.

Ultrasounds with power Doppler of the lower limbs revealed deep vein thrombosis; ophthalmic examination revealed right central retinal artery thrombosis; CT scan of the head showed ischemic stroke in the right temporal lobe; abdominal ultrasound revealed enlargement of both kidneys with interstitial edema and left renal vein thrombosis; chest X-ray demonstrated a high amount of fluid in both pleural cavities.

Laboratory abnormalities included anemia (Hgb 7 g/dl), thrombocytopenia 134 G/l, leucocytosis 14.36 G/l, elongated activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) 69.7 s, elevated D-dimer (4.33 μg/ml), elevated serum creatinine (4.8 mg/dl) and urea (79 mg/dl), elevated lactate dehydrogenase (548 U/L), elevated C-reactive protein (4.7 mg/dl), elevated ferritin (308 ng/ml), reduced complement components C3 (77 mg/dl) and C4 (10 mg/dl), positive lupus anticoagulant and elevated anti-β2-glicoprotein I antibodies (14 U/ml).
Histopathological examination showed thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) secondary to APS.

Anticoagulation with high molecular weight heparin infusion, glucocorticoids (methylprednisolone 1 g i.v. for 3 days followed by prednisone 1 mg/kg/day), therapeutic plasma exchanges (5 sessions), and daily hemodialysis were initiated.

Under this treatment, general state improved with disappearance of dyspnoea and respiratory failure, increase in hemoglobin, normalization of platelets, but persistent oliguria requiring hemodialysis.
Because of persistent renal failure, intravenous immunoglobulin (5 doses of IgG 0.4 g/kg/day) was added.
After intravenous immunoglobulin therapy, kidney function recovered and renal replacement therapy was stopped; antiphospholipid antibodies became negative.
Four weeks later, lupus anticoagulant began to increase again.
Rituximab therapy was introduced with 2 g administered in three separate doses over two months intervals after infection screening was negative.
During rituximab therapy, no new thrombotic events occurred, renal function further improved, and antiphospholipid antibodies remained negative.

source_metadata.title: Young patient with hantavirus-induced myocarditis detected by comprehensive cardiac magnetic resonance assessment

evidence_events.source_span: A 36-year-old white male patient suffering from headache and abdominal pain presented at our emergency department.
Initial ECG showed a sinus rhythm (40/min.) with a single T-wave inversion in lead V2, and an incomplete right bundle branch block.
Thrombocytes were decreased with 71,000/µl, creatinine was elevated (2.0 mg/dl) with a maximum increase to 3.0 mg/dl and massive proteinuria. C-reactive protein was also elevated: 8.6 mg/dl.
Puumala virus IgG ELISA turned out to be positive, and specific antibodies (IgG and IgM) could be detected in the serum, and confirmed by immunoassay.
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: Serologic confirmation of Puumala virus infection

evidence_events.source_span: Six days later, the patient reported chest pain and dyspnea. High sensitivity troponin I rose up to 0.32 µg/l (normal below 0.04 µg/l) with an increase of the creatinkinase to 319 U/l (normal max. 190 U/l), no dynamic ECG changes could be observed.
Echocardiography revealed a normal left ventricular function (65%) without regional wall motion abnormalities, no pericardial effusion or valve abnormalities.
Coronary artery disease was ruled out by coronary CT angiography after creatinine normalized.
A multiparametric cardiac magnetic resonance protocol including recent mapping techniques was performed for work-up of suspected myocarditis.
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: CMR performed with mapping techniques and LGE

evidence_events.source_span: Native T1-mapping demonstrated markedly elevated T1 values with preponderance in the inferoseptal wall (1068 ± 73 ms in the entire slice vs. 1122 ± 31 ms in the inferoseptal wall). T2-mapping revealed increased values (entire slice 52 ± 6 ms, inferoseptal wall 55 ± 6 ms), suggesting myocardial edema representing active myocardial inflammation by hantavirus infection. Late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) image was negative.
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: CMR mapping shows myocardial inflammation without irreversible damage

evidence_events.source_span: In the next few weeks, the patient’s state of health rapidly improved and symptoms of chest pain and dyspnea disappeared.

Five months later, follow up multiparametric CMR exam showed substantial decrease of native T1 values (957 ± 58 ms entire slice vs. 971 ± 36 ms inferoseptal wall) and T2 values (entire slice 44 ± 5 ms, inferoseptal wall 45 ± 3 ms), again LGE-negative, suggesting myocardial healing.

source_metadata.title: Hypophosphatemic Osteomalacia Associated with Adefovir-induced Fanconi Syndrome Initially Diagnosed as Diabetic Kidney Disease and Vitamin D Deficiency

evidence_events.source_span: A 68-year-old Japanese man with a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus and chronic HBV infection was referred for evaluation of a newly detected liver tumor and management of chronic kidney disease (creatinine 1.84 mg/dL; eGFR 29.7 mL/min/1.73 m2).

He had type 2 diabetes mellitus diagnosed in 1986, treated with insulin, HbA1c controlled around 7.0%, and chronic HBV infection treated with interferon since 1993, lamivudine since 2002, and low-dose adefovir dipivoxil (ADV) 10 mg daily added in 2005 after lamivudine resistance.
Kidney dysfunction was first noted in 2008 (creatinine 1.79 mg/dL; eGFR 31.7 mL/min/1.73 m2) and attributed to diabetic kidney disease (DKD).
At nephrology presentation, physical exam was unremarkable except mild bilateral lower limb pain; abdominal CT showed slightly atrophic kidneys without stones, tumors, or obstruction.

Laboratory tests revealed hyperphosphatasemia (1,148 IU/L), hypophosphatemia (1.6 mg/dL), hypouricemia (1.6 mg/dL), increased fractional excretion of phosphate (79.3%) and uric acid (69.3%), normal anion gap metabolic acidosis (HCO3- 14.6 mmol/L; anion gap 13.3), highly elevated urinary β2-microglobulin (66,919 μg/L), and glycosuria (4+) with casual blood glucose 184 mg/dL.
Pan-aminoaciduria was later confirmed, leading to diagnosis of Fanconi syndrome.

Patient had muscle weakness and bilateral knee joint pain since January 2014, with non-traumatic fracture of left first metatarsal bone; treated initially with weekly oral alendronate and later switched to daily teriparatide injections in March 2015 without pain relief.

In September 2015, multiple pathological fractures in bilateral metatarsal bones were discovered; blood tests showed hyperphosphatasemia (684 IU/L), hypophosphatemia (1.4 mg/dL), and decreased serum 25-hydroxy vitamin D (18 ng/mL).

X-ray of metatarsal bones and proximal tibias showed multiple radiolucent zones (Looser zones); diagnosed as hypophosphatemic osteomalacia due to vitamin D deficiency from chronic liver disease; oral phosphate and vitamin D supplementation promptly relieved pain.

Whole-body bone scintigraphy with 99mTc hydroxymethylene showed multiple lesions with increased uptake in bilateral ribs, lumbar spine, knee joints, ankle joints, and metatarsal bones indicating insidious pathological fractures caused by hypophosphatemic osteomalacia.

Other possible causes were unlikely and interferon, insulin, and lamivudine monotherapy have not been reported to cause Fanconi syndrome; thus, 11-year history of ADV treatment was considered the main cause of Fanconi syndrome and hypophosphatemic osteomalacia.
After partial hepatic resection for HCC, ADV was switched to entecavir; oral phosphate and vitamin D supplementation continued; oral sodium bicarbonate added for normal anion gap metabolic acidosis.

Hyperphosphatasemia, hypophosphatemia, and metabolic acidosis gradually improved; lower limb pain did not recur; kidney function remained almost unchanged; urinary β2-microglobulin remained high over two years; pan-aminoaciduria, glycosuria, and hypouricemia were not completely ameliorated.

source_metadata.title: Refractory hypercalcemia due to an ectopic mediastinal parathyroid gland in a hemodialysis patient: a case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 70-year-old Chinese man was presented in the study. The patient had the past medical history of diabetes, hypertension and cerebral infarction, and had received hemodialysis three times a week due to renal failure for 2 years.

SHPT was confirmed in December 2016 since the serum PTH had elevated 100.3 pmol/l (normal range 1.6–6.9 pmol/l). Cinacalcet (25 mg per day) was prescribed based on the concurrent hypercalcemia and hyperphosphatemia.

In April 2017, the PTH level was stable at 94.44 pmol/l with normal calcium level (2.06 mmol/l). Subsequently, calcitriol pulse therapy combined with low calcium dialysate (Ca2+, 1.25 mmol/l) was given. The PTH level then increased dramatically to 197.3 pmol/l.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: Calcitriol pulse therapy and low calcium dialysate

evidence_events.source_span: Since August 2017, the patient had leg discomfort with restless legs syndrome, loss of appetite, nausea, constipation, refractory hypertension, generalized weakness and sleep deprivation. Physical examination was normal. Serum albumin corrected calcium was 3.96 mmol/l and alkaline phosphatase (ALP) was 160 u/l (normal 45-125 u/l), supporting hypercalcemic crisis and tertiary HPT.
Bone X-ray imaging showed no abnormalities; M protein and tumor markers were negative; parathyroid ultrasound around neck was normal.

Continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) with low calcium dialysate was applied; calcitriol pulse therapy was ceased; cinacalcet dose increased to 50 mg per day; calcitonin 50u subcutaneously daily was given but serum calcium remained elevated at 3.77 mmol/l. Hormone therapy with methylprednisolone and prednisone was considered.

Bone turnover markers osteocalcin and I-type collagen prolongation peptide were elevated above normal limits (300 ng/ml and 1200 ng/ml respectively), β-crosslaps was 5.96 ng/ml. High bone turnover and refractory HPT suggested presence of ectopic parathyroid gland.

Contrast-enhanced neck CT scan revealed a 2.5 × 1.9 cm mass with nodular mixed density in the upper anterior mediastinum (Fig. 1a, b). Tc-99m dual-phase parathyroid scan detected a hyperfunctioning parathyroid gland in the same region (Fig. 1c).
Video-assisted thoracoscopic parathyroidectomy was performed despite high anesthesia risk. The mass was completely excised (Fig. 1d).
Histopathological examination revealed a 2 cm well-encapsulated mass with solid and cystic components composed of parathyroid gland chief cells.

Calcium and PTH levels dropped stably within 10 days after surgery (2.12 mmol/l and 21.41 pmol/l respectively) and were maintained for 3 months. Phosphorus level dropped to 1.77 mmol/l; ALP increased to 347 u/l. Patient symptoms resolved and no complications observed during 16 months follow-up.

On February 14, 2019, calcium, phosphorus, ALP and PTH were 2.42 mmol/l, 1.83 mmol/l, 70 u/l and 13.77 pmol/l respectively. Bone turnover markers normalized (osteocalcin 121.3 ng/ml, I-type collagen prolongation peptide 213.5 ng/ml, β-crosslaps 0.707 ng/ml).

hidden_reference.article_derived_evidence_summary: The case report describes a hemodialysis patient with refractory tertiary hyperparathyroidism and hypercalcemic crisis. Postoperative labs and clinical status improved and remained stable over 16 months.

evidence_events.source_section: Case presentation / Case: a 36-year-old woman / Primary complaint: intense epigastric pain
evidence_events.source_span: A 36-year-old woman was diagnosed with idiopathic membranous nephropathy (Stage II) and treated with immunosuppressive therapy consisting of prednisolone, mizoribine, and cyclosporine; nephrosis improved and prednisolone dose was reduced

evidence_events.source_section: Case presentation / Physical findings on Day 79
evidence_events.source_span: On Day 79, the patient developed sudden intense epigastric abdominal pain with strong spontaneous pain and tenderness but no muscular guarding or rebound tenderness; vital signs stable; no cutaneous findings or joint pain; bilateral edema present

evidence_events.source_section: Case presentation / Laboratory tests on Day 79
evidence_events.source_span: Laboratory tests on Day 79 showed neutrophil-dominant elevated white blood cell count, slightly reduced platelet count, reduced total protein and albumin, elevated transaminase and lactate dehydrogenase, slightly increased C-reactive protein, hypogammaglobulinemia, and enhanced coagulability; negative autoantibodies and no hypocomplementemia
Abdominal CT on Day 79 revealed mildly increased fat tissue density around the celiac artery and root of the superior mesenteric artery with no perforation, intestinal obstruction, or thrombosis

Despite intense abdominal pain, vital signs were stable and no peritoneal irritation signs were present; prophylactic cefmetazole and opioid analgesics were administered; cause of pain was unknown and patient was monitored

On Day 80, a large number of small blisters appeared on the face and trunk, diagnosed as varicella; skin lesion biopsy showed blisters in the epidermis with cells having ground-glass nuclei; PCR of skin biopsy was positive for VZV
Blood VZV-DNA concentration was markedly increased (200,000 copies); initial VZV IgG positive and IgM negative on Day 80; paired sera on Day 86 showed positive VZV IgM
evidence_events.procedural_cue: Blood VZV-DNA quantification and antibody testing

evidence_events.source_span: Treatment with intravenous acyclovir (1500 mg/day) and immunoglobulin (5 g/day) was started immediately; immunosuppressive therapy doses were reduced; liver function worsened temporarily and disseminated intravascular coagulation was treated; abdominal pain resolved rapidly and platelet count and liver function improved within 1 week
evidence_events.procedural_cue: Acyclovir and immunoglobulin administration; immunosuppressant dose reduction

evidence_events.source_span: Repeat abdominal CT on Day 104 showed normalization of previously increased fat tissue density around the celiac artery and root of the superior mesenteric artery

source_metadata.title: Tumor Lysis Syndrome in Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia: A Rare Case Report from Nephrology

evidence_events.source_span: 89-year-old female with stable chronic lymphocytic leukemia for more than 40 years, without any related treatment for the last 15 years

Admitted because of worsening dyspnea and dry cough; vital signs normal except sinus tachycardia; physical exam showed distress, dyspnea, sweaty but afebrile, anxious, alert and oriented; lung exam revealed reduced air entry with bibasilar crackles; no peripheral edema or DVT signs

WBC 67×10³/uL, neutrophils 5%, lymphocytes 78%, hemoglobin 11.2 g%, platelets 72×10³/uL, serum creatinine 0.76 mg/dL, potassium 4.9 mEq/L, blood sugar 122 mg/dL, BUN 24 mg/dL, calcium 8.9 mg/dL, phosphorus 4 mg/dL, albumin 4.6 g/dL, total protein 6.5 g/dL, CRP 0.9 mg/L; liver enzymes and lipid profile normal; uric acid and LDH not available
Chest x-ray revealed enlarged cardiac silhouette, pulmonary congestion, and infiltration in the left lower lobe consistent with pneumonia or congestion

Started IV furosemide, IV ceftriaxone, oral azithromycin, and IV methylprednisolone 62.5 mg for upper respiratory infection; steroids lasted 1 day, then switched to oral prednisone 20 mg/day for 1 day

Day 1 labs: WBC increased to 157×10³/uL, lymphocytes 69%, neutrophils 4%, Hb 12.1 g%, platelets 129×10³/uL, serum creatinine 0.69 mg/dL, potassium 5.1 mEq/L, blood sugar 146 mg/dL, BUN 27 mg/dL; IgG slightly low at 640; troponin elevated from 60 to 2600 ng/L indicating silent NSTEMI; no ischemic ECG changes; conservative cardiology treatment started

Day 2 labs: oliguric acute renal failure with urine output 100 mL/24h; serum creatinine 1.63 mg/dL, BUN 55 mg/dL, phosphorus 7.8 mg/dL, magnesium 2.9 mg/dL, uric acid 20.4 mg/dL, calcium 8.3 mg/dL, WBC 135×10³/uL, platelets 129×10³/uL, Hb 12.1 g/dL, LDH 966 U/L, pH 7.30, bicarbonate 17 mEq/L; diagnosis of tumor lysis syndrome raised as differential
Conservative treatment started with intravenous fluids, bicarbonate for metabolic acidosis, febuxostat 80 mg/day, and sevelamer 2.4 g/day

Day 3 labs: anuric with worsening labs: phosphorus 26.3 mg/dL, uric acid 42.5 mg/dL, calcium 7.2 mg/dL, magnesium 3.55 mg/dL, LDH 1135 U/L, BUN 107 mg/dL, creatinine 2.2 mg/dL, potassium 6.94 mmol/L, pH 7.30, bicarbonate 16 mmol/L, WBC 190×10³/uL, lymphocytes 64%, neutrophils 5%, Hb 9.6 g/dL, platelets 166×10³/uL; diagnosis of TLS confirmed
Urgent hemodialysis and hemodiafiltration initiated with 3 consecutive sessions leading to full recovery of kidney function and electrolyte balance
At discharge, serum creatinine 0.78 mg/dL, BUN 39 mg/dL, calcium 7.5 mg/dL, phosphorus 2.6 mg/dL, LDH 694 U/L, uric acid 9.7 mg/dL, pH 7.43, bicarbonate 25.5, pCO2 39

One month after discharge, patient stable with WBC 12×10³/uL, lymphocytes 69%, platelets 103×10³/uL, serum creatinine 0.44 mg/dL, BUN 21 mg/dL, potassium 4.6 mEq/L, phosphorus 3.8 mg/dL, calcium 8.2 mg/dL, uric acid 5.6 mg/dL, LDH 645 U/L

Treatment with hemodialysis resulted in recovery, supporting TLS diagnosis.
Spontaneous TLS is rare in CLL but should be considered in acute renal failure with malignancy.

source_metadata.title: Cobalamin c deficiency associated with antifactor h antibody-associated hemolytic uremic syndrome in a young adult

evidence_events.source_span: A 19-year-old woman was admitted to the medical intensive care unit for acute kidney failure associated with severe neurologic impairment. She had no relevant past medical history and her familial history was unremarkable. She presented with asthenia and dyspnea of several weeks duration. Clinical examination showed high blood pressure of 170/90 mmHg and lower limb edema.

Initial laboratory test results: serum creatinine 246 µmol/L, hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL, platelets 151 G/L, lactate deshydrogenase 700 U/L (normal < 246), haptoglobin < 0.08 g/L, with schistocytes on peripheral blood smear, proteinuria 7.6 g/g of creatinine, and hematuria 348.10³/mL. Direct antiglobulin and pregnancy tests were negative.
Transthoracic echocardiography showed preserved left ventricular function and renal ultrasonography excluded an obstructive cause of acute kidney injury.

Diagnosis of thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA) was considered and plasma exchanges were started in emergency. On day 2, after thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura was excluded based on normal serum ADAMTS13 values (101%), plasma exchanges were stopped and eculizumab (900 mg per week) was initiated.

Diagnosis of STEC-HUS was ruled out on the basis of negative Shiga toxin tests. Antibody testing for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV, antinuclear antibody, lupus anticoagulant, antiphospholipid, anti-DNA and neutrophil cytoplasmic antigen antibodies was negative. Complement pathway exploration including CH50, C3, C4, Factor H (CFH) and factor I was normal. No mutations in C3, MCP, factors B, H, and I genes were identified. Antibody testing for CFH was positive: 7450 UA/ml (reference < 100 AU/mL). Serum homocysteine was increased: 285 µmol/L (normal 3.2-10.7). Serum vitamin B12 and folate were normal.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: complement and antibody testing, genetic sequencing

evidence_events.source_span: Kidney biopsy performed on day 2 showed mesangial sclerosis, noticeable thickening of the capillary wall with a duplication aspect of the glomerular basement membrane and presence of intraglomerular and intravascular thrombi. Immunofluorescence showed mild glomerular capillary wall IgM and C3 deposits and was negative for IgG and IgA.

Plasma and urinary amino acid chromatography indicated low plasma and urine methionine: 12 µmol/L (ref 21-35), <1 µmol/mmol creatinine (ref 2-16). Gas chromatography-mass spectrometry of urinary organic acid showed high methylmalonic aciduria: 247 mmol/mol creatinine (normal < 4 µmol/l).
evidence_events.procedural_cue: amino acid chromatography, gas chromatography-mass spectrometry

evidence_events.source_span: Continuous vitamin supplementation with hydroxycobalamin 1 mg/d intramuscularly, folinic acid 10 mg/d, betaine 12 g/d and levocarnitine 3 g/d was started. Kidney function dramatically improved and hemolysis resolved. Normal serum homocysteine and plasma methylmalonic acid were achieved within one month.
Rituximab infusion at 375 mg/m2 was administered once a week for 4 weeks, resulting in a dramatic decrease in serum anti-factor H antibody (< 1000 UA/ml) and allowed weaning from eculizumab.

Methylmalonic aciduria and homocystinuria type C (MMACHC) gene sequencing showed two heterozygous pathogenic variants: c.556G > A (p.Arg189His) and c.271dupA (p.Arg91Lysfs*4), confirming cblC deficiency associated with anti-factor H antibody-associated hemolytic uremic syndrome.

source_metadata.title: Transient hyponatremia of prematurity caused by mild Bartter syndrome type II: a case report

evidence_events.source_span: female patient was born at 33 weeks and 6 days to non-consanguineous, Caucasian parents by spontaneous vaginal delivery with antenatal polyhydramnios and possible duplex collecting system without hydronephrosis
On day of life 7 she was clinically dehydrated with 22% weight loss since birth, blood pressures normal at 74/41 mmHg

Initial blood gas at 15 h of life showed respiratory acidosis with pH 7.26, pCO2 59 mmHg, bicarbonate 28.3 mmol/L; repeated capillary blood gases over 7 days showed hyponatremia 121-137 mmol/L, hyperkalemia 5.5-8.0 mmol/L, chloride 86-100 mmol/L
evidence_events.temporal_cue: 15 h of life and next 7 days

evidence_events.source_span: At day 7, arterial blood gas showed sodium 121 mmol/L, potassium 2.8 mmol/L, chloride 82 mmol/L, urea 19 mmol/L, creatinine 52 μmol/L; cystatin C eGFR at 7 weeks was 58 mL/min; postnatal renal ultrasound showed no medullary nephrocalcinosis

Magnesium normal at 0.95 mmol/L; aldosterone elevated >27,000 pmol/L; renin elevated >3000 ng/L; cortisol 629 nmol/L; ACTH 6.6 pmol/L; 17-OHP mildly elevated at 14.8 nmol/L, ruling out congenital adrenal hyperplasia

Urine on day 7 showed osmolality 369 mOsm/kg, high sodium 118 mmol/L, low potassium 7 mmol/L, chloride 94 mmol/L, low creatinine 0.3 mmol/L; fractional sodium excretion 16.9% in hypovolemic patient suggesting tubular dysfunction

Initial differential included Bartter syndrome and pseudohypoaldosteronism; adrenogenital syndromes unlikely due to normal female genitalia and newborn screening; Bartter type II more likely given initial absence of hypokalemia or hypochloremia; pseudohypoaldosteronism types I and II unlikely due to normal blood pressure and lack of metabolic acidosis

Sodium chloride supplementation started day 7 up to 7.9 mmol/kg/day; trial of fludrocortisone on day 9 with no clinical response; electrolytes normalized by 4 weeks and supplementation weaned off by 7 weeks; mild metabolic alkalosis peaked at 2 months but normalized
Gene panel showed two pathogenic KCNJ1 variants: paternally inherited frameshift deletion p.Glu334Glyfs*35 and maternally inherited missense variant p.Pro110Leu

At 6 months, electrolytes normal (Na 138, K 4.5, Cl 101 mmol/L), calcium slightly elevated at 2.92 mmol/L, phosphate and magnesium normal; Schwartz eGFR 56 mL/min/1.73m2; persistent hypercalciuria with urine calcium/creatinine ratio >8; renal ultrasound showed no nephrocalcinosis; venous blood gas normal; ongoing polyuria and polydipsia; at 15 months renin and aldosterone normalized

source_metadata.title: Peritonitis after exposure to biocontrol-agent fumes containing Talaromyces flavus: a case report in peritoneal dialysis patient

evidence_events.source_span: A 77-year-old Thai female with kidney failure on continuous ambulatory PD presented with acute abdominal pain and catheter malfunction on 17 June 2019
Numerous white colonization was observed inside the PD catheter lumen; catheter malfunction was confirmed with delayed inflow and outflow rates
Dialysate cell counts disclosed numerous erythrocytes and leukocytes of 230/mm3 (35% neutrophils, 35% eosinophils, and 30% mononuclear cells)
Clumping of filamentous hyaline and septate hyphae was detected by bedside wet smear; fungal peritonitis was initially diagnosed
The PD catheter was removed due to fungal biofilm occlusion and temporary hemodialysis was initiated
Liposomal amphotericin B 5 mg/kg daily was started on day +3 and continued for 14 days, followed by oral itraconazole 400 mg daily starting day +17

Microbiological exams of PD effluent and catheter showed colonies on Sabouraud dextrose agar initially white, turning white to orange and brown after 14 days; microscopic examination demonstrated classic Penicillium genus features
The pathogen was confirmed as Talaromyces flavus by molecular phylogeny using ribosomal DNA (ITS and 28s rDNA) sequences

Fungal susceptibility testing was inconclusive on day +21 due to lack of MIC breakpoints for Talaromyces; using Aspergillus spp. as reference, organism was resistant to amphotericin B, fluconazole, itraconazole, caspofungin but susceptible to voriconazole
Root-cause analysis revealed patient exposed to homemade biocontrol-agent fumes containing T. flavus before performing PD bag exchange without changing clothes
evidence_events.temporal_cue: day -17 and 8 days before peritonitis onset

evidence_events.source_span: Cultures from patient's environment and hands were negative except the biocontrol agent, which was positive for T. flavus, confirming a potential source of infection
Patient used non-antiseptic soap for handwashing, which has limited activity against fungi and mycobacterium; antiseptic agent and hand hygiene were emphasized
Patient discharged on day +21 with partial response to antifungal medications; symptom score decreased from 20 to 7; afebrile with mild hypertension, moderate anorexia, and constipation
Patient died at home on day +23 from unknown etiology; death classified as peritonitis-associated death according to 2022 ISPD guidelines

source_metadata.title: Correct approach in urticarial vasculitis made early diagnosis of lupus nephritis possible: a case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 61-year-old Caucasian woman was referred to our dermatology department in July 2019 because of a skin eruption that had initiated 3 months earlier. In April there was an acute onset of erythematous macules and papules on both thighs, which later spread to the back, arms, and the back of the hands.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: in July 2019; initiated 3 months earlier; in April acute onset

evidence_events.source_span: Individual lesions tended to last for approximately 2 days before regression, but were asymptomatic. There were no bullae or erosions, nor mucosal lesions. Exposure to the sun aggravated the skin eruption.
The patient did not experience musculoskeletal, gastrointestinal, pulmonary, or any other symptoms. There was no family history of autoimmune or other relevant diseases.

On clinical examination, we found multiple sharply demarcated erythematous plaques on the back, chest, abdomen, and legs, and somewhat less on the arms and hands. There were no lesions on the groin, palmoplantar, or on the scalp.

A 4-mm punch biopsy had already been taken by the referring dermatologist and showed no epidermal abnormalities. In the superficial dermis, however, there was a perivascular inflammatory infiltrate consisting of neutrophils, some histiocytes, lymphocytes, and eosinophils. There was remarkable leukocytoclasis. The vascular endothelium was mildly swollen but without any fibrinoid necrosis of the vascular walls.

Complete blood count showed white blood cells of 10.80 × 10⁹/L with an increase in neutrophils (8.7 × 10⁹/L), but a normal red blood cell and platelet count. The erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) was 31 mm and C-reactive protein 7.6 mg/L. The alanine aminotransferase (ALAT) and gamma glutamyl transferase (gammaGT) were mildly increased (ALT 33 U/L, gammaGT 41 U/L).

Antinuclear factor (ANF) was positive (1:320) with dsDNA Farr titer of 38.9 IU/mL (normal range < 7.0 IU/mL). Lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipine immunoglobulin M (IgM), anti-Streptolysine O antibodies, and hepatitis B and C serology were negative. Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (c-ANCA) was negative, perinuclear antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (p-ANCA) was 1/160 but with negative identification of proteinase 3 and myeloperoxidase. Cryoglobulins were present but without monoclonal fractions.

Complement analysis showed hypocomplementemia with low component C3 fraction (0.58 g/dL), low component C4 fraction (0.06 g/dL), low C1q (0.09 g/dL), and anti-C1q antibodies > 400 U/mL (normal < 15 U/mL).
Urinalysis showed proteinuria 2+ and massive hematuria, and a white blood cell count of 32/μL (normal ≤ 10).
On the basis of the clinical image, histopathology, and lab results, a diagnosis of hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis was made. Additional chest radiography and spirometry were normal.
Because of the positive ANF with high dsDNA Farr titer, and proteinuria with massive hematuria on urinalysis, an underlying systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) was suspected.

More comprehensive laboratory investigations showed a serum creatinine of 0.82 mg/dL and calculated glomerular filtration rate of 77 mL/min/1.73 m² (CKD-EPI), corresponding with chronic renal disease GFR category G2 (KDIGO guidelines). Twenty-four-hour urinalysis showed proteinuria of 0.33 g. Ultrasound showed normal kidney size.
Because of the pathological proteinuria, massive hematuria, increased white blood cell count, hypocomplementemia, and positive ANF (U1RNP positive), a kidney biopsy was performed.

Histopathological evaluation showed focal crescentic and focal mesangial type of glomerular damage. Immunohistochemically there was a full-blown positivity of immunoglobulin A (IgA), immunoglobulin G (IgG), and C1q. These features fit the diagnosis of lupus nephritis class III-A (ISN/RPS 2003 classification).
