source_metadata.title: A case of emphysematous cystitis complicated by unilateral hydronephrosis and septicemia: nephrology picture

evidence_events.source_span: A 65-year-old woman with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes was admitted to the hospital due to mild COVID-19 pneumonia.
On the 11th day of admission she developed high-grade fever and gross hematuria.
Physical examination revealed mild tenderness in the suprapubic area.
Laboratory investigations revealed severe acute kidney injury (AKI).
Urinalysis showed a high number of leukocytes with positive nitrites, in a context of macroscopic hematuria.
An ultrasound of Kidneys-Ureters-Bladder was performed, showing mild right hydronephrosis.
Urgent computed tomography (CT) scan with intravenous contrast was subsequently carried out due to clinical septicemia.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: CT scan with intravenous contrast performed

evidence_events.source_span: Air content in the urinary bladder, which was compatible with emphysematous cystitis, and a moderate degree of right hydronephrosis were observed.

She was started on empirical antibiotic therapy with piperacillin/tazobactam injection, and de-escalated to ceftriaxone injection after blood and urine cultures showed growth of Klebsiella pneumoniae sensitive to ceftriaxone.
Despite a 1-week course of the appropriate antimicrobial agent, she continued having high-grade fever and persistent bacteriuria.
Blood and urine cultures were evaluated again. About 72 h later, a second micro-organism (Enterococcus faecium) was isolated in both cultures.
Fosfomycin and amikacin were prescribed according to the culture and sensitivity report.
Cystoscopy and cystogram were performed 3 weeks after the initial presentation, revealing severe necrotizing mucosal inflammation of the bladder wall with evidence of submucosal emphysema.
Neither vagino-vesical nor enterovesical fistulas were detected.
The cause of right hydronephrosis was suspected from severe mucosal inflammation of the right ureter due to severe ascending infection.
After completing a 21-day course of intravenous antibiotics, a follow-up CT scan showed resolution of emphysematous cystitis and right hydronephrosis.
Renal function recovered despite exposure to nephrotoxic agents.

source_metadata.title: An Unusual Presentation of Neurosarcoidosis

evidence_events.source_span: A 63-year-old White man with a past medical history of hyperlipidemia presented to an ophthalmologist in September 2019 with concerns of increasingly blurry vision and glare for 1 month.

On presentation, visual acuity in his right eye was 20/50 and 20/100 in his left eye; both could be corrected to 20/20. Intraocular pressures were 33 mm Hg and 38 mm Hg by applanation in each eye, respectively, and external examination was normal except for decreased confrontational fields in the left eye. The slit lamp examination was normal, including a clear anterior chamber and vitreous with open angles by gonioscopy in both eyes. The fundus examination demonstrated mild edema of the optic nerves and scattered cotton-wool spots with congestion of retinal vessels bilaterally. In addition, dot-blot hemorrhages were seen in the right retinal periphery.
A preliminary diagnosis of bilateral hypertensive retinopathy with optic nerve swelling was made, and magnetic resonance imaging was ordered to rule out intracranial pathology.
The magnetic resonance imaging results were normal, with no evidence of any intracranial abnormality or mass.
Improvement in disc edema was noted during the retinal consultation, and fluorescein angiography identified delayed transit of dye in the vessels, without leakage in both eyes.
Two months later, the patient developed vertical diplopia worsening on downgaze and was referred to an ophthalmologist specializing in strabismus.
A motility examination identified an 8-diopter right hypertropia, suggesting a fourth cranial nerve palsy. Retinal examination demonstrated persistent cotton-wool spots in both eyes.
A blood pressure reading taken in the office read 129/80 mm Hg. The 24-h blood pressure monitor revealed an average blood pressure of 126/80 mm Hg.

The urinalysis results were remarkable for mild hematuria and proteinuria. The urine protein-creatinine ratio was 0.69 (reference range, less than 0.2), and the albumin-creatinine ratio was 22.4 mg/g (reference range, less than 30.0). A urine sediment analysis showed increased urinary B2-microglobulin of 359 mcg/L (reference range, less than 300 mcg/L). The serum creatinine had increased to 2.73 mg/dL from a baseline reading of 1.51 mg/dL, which was obtained 6 months prior.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: urinalysis, urine sediment analysis, serum creatinine

evidence_events.source_span: A serologic workup for secondary causes of acute glomerulonephritis was performed. The results were inconclusive, however, with a positive ANA titer of 1:640 and low complement 3 of 72.4 mg/dL. The calcium level was in the reference range at 8.6 mg/dL. Serum and urine protein electrophoresis demonstrated a normal pattern. C-reactive protein (CRP) levels were normal at 0.2.
A renal biopsy demonstrated non-caseating granulomatous interstitial nephritis, staining negative for acid fast bacilli and fungi.
The vitamin D levels showed a 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3 to 25-hydroxyvitamin D3 ratio greater than 2 (50 ng/mL: 12.5 ng/mL), indicating extrarenal vitamin D3 production.
The angiotensin-converting enzyme level was elevated at 73 U/L (reference range, less than 52 U/L).
A chest computed tomography scan disclosed a 4-mm partially calcified nodule in the left lower lobe, a 2.3-cm nodule in the right lung base, and non-specific mediastinal lymphadenopathy.
A diagnosis of sarcoidosis was made based upon the renal biopsy findings and the above serological test results.
The patient was then immediately started on treatment with oral prednisone 10 mg 4 times a day.

Five months later, the patient returned for a follow-up with the nephrologist. His serum creatinine level had improved to 1.72 mg/dL, and the calculated glomerular filtration rate (GFR) had improved from 24 mL/min to 40 mL/min. On ophthalmic assessment, all neurologic symptoms had resolved, although he continued to receive treatment for glaucoma, with normal intraocular pressures of 15 mm Hg and 18 mm Hg, respectively.

source_metadata.title: Combined crystal-storing histiocytosis, light chain proximal tubulopathy, and light chain crystalline podocytopathy in a patient with multiple myeloma: a case report and literature review
source_metadata.notes: Extraction based on case presentation, investigations, pathology, and treatment sections.

evidence_events.source_span: A 69-year-old Chinese woman had intermittent lower back and leg pain for 6 months without obvious causes, and no significant improvement was observed after 1 month of treatment with traditional Chinese medicine.

Laboratory studies revealed hemoglobin levels of 112 g/L, platelet of 90 × 10^9/L, serum creatinine of 11.10 mg/dL, potassium of 3.05 mmol/L, and bicarbonate 10.4 mmol/L. Levels of blood glucose, uric acid, and phosphorus were normal.

After hemodialysis, the patient was referred to our hospital. Her serum creatinine level pre-dialysis fell to 5.63 mg/dL without any specific treatment. Serum calcium was 2.21 mmol/L. Morning urinalysis revealed 2+ protein, 2+ glucose, urine specific gravity of 1.006, and normal blood glucose.

Renal glycosuria, with normal serum phosphorus, normal serum uric acid, low serum bicarbonate levels, and continuous hypokalemia under severe renal insufficiency raised clinical suspicion of Fanconi syndrome.
The protein level in a 24-h urine sample was elevated to 2.66 g/day. Urine protein electrophoresis revealed mixed overflow proteinuria, tubular proteinuria, and glomerular proteinuria.

Serum protein electrophoresis revealed monoclonal gamma paraprotein (8.4 g/L). Both serum and urine immunofixation electrophoresis revealed restricted immunoglobulin G kappa (IgGkappa) and kappa light chain. Serum free light chain results were kappa > 4850 mg/L, lambda 61.8 mg/L, and kappa/lambda ratio > 78.48.
Ultrasound showed bilateral renal atrophy (right kidney, 8.7 cm; left kidney, 8.8 cm). X-ray of the lumbar spine revealed a pathological fracture of L1.
Bone marrow aspirate showed plasma cells accounting for approximately 15% of total marrow cellularity, with cytoplasmic granular inclusions and needle-shaped crystals.

Flow cytometry analysis identified a monotypic, cytoplasmic kappa light chain-restricted CD38+, CD138+ plasma cell population. Cytogenetic analysis revealed 46, XX. IGH/CCND1 translocation was confirmed by fluorescence in situ hybridization analysis.

Renal biopsy revealed 31 glomeruli, nine globally sclerosed. Proximal tubular lesions with focal atrophy and brush border disappearance were seen. Eosinophilic needle-shaped crystals were observed in proximal tubular epithelial cells and podocytes, as well as in tubular lumens, interstitial histiocytes, and mesangial cells.

Proximal tubular lumen was engorged by abundant small periodic acid–Schiff (PAS)-positive granular casts, different from the homogeneous casts seen in cast nephropathy. Renal interstitium showed interstitial fibrosis and diffuse lymphocytes, mononuclear cells, and histiocytes without eosinophils. Congo red staining for amyloid was negative.
Immunohistochemistry showed histiocytes positive for CD68 and kappa light chain, and negative for lambda light chain.
Direct immunofluorescence on frozen tissue was initially negative for kappa light chain, but kappa positivity was confirmed with pronase digestion on formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded tissue.

Electron microscopy showed irregular effacement of podocyte foot processes, increased lysosomes in proximal tubular epithelial cells, and rods and needlelike crystalline materials arranged in parallel and longitudinally in proximal tubular cells, podocytes, mesangial cells, and histiocytes.
Immunoelectron microscopy showed particulate kappa staining of the crystals and no staining for lambda light chain.
The patient was treated with two cycles of induction chemotherapy with dexamethasone and bortezomib. Serum creatinine decreased to 3.39 mg/dL, urine output normalized, and dialysis was withdrawn.
The patient refused further chemotherapy and remained clinically and biologically stable during a 2.5-year follow-up, with serum creatinine 3.39–3.85 mg/dL and persistent anemia and thrombocytopenia.

source_metadata.title: Radiographic evolution of myelitis in a case of glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) astrocytopathy

evidence_events.source_span: A man in his 50s with a history of paroxysmal atrial fibrillation presented with 1 week of fever, nausea, vomiting and generalised weakness. Two days prior to presentation, he developed confusion, back pain, urinary hesitancy, and lower extremity numbness and weakness.

At presentation, the patient was febrile to 38.9°C, disoriented to situation and had impaired concentration. He had 4+/5 strength in the hip and knee flexors, ankle clonus and upgoing toes bilaterally. Upper extremity strength, cranial nerves and coordination were intact.

MRI of the thoracic and lumbar spine showed normal signal throughout the spinal cord parenchyma and was read as normal. On retrospective review, subtle contrast enhancement of the leptomeninges surrounding the conus was noted.
MRI brain showed diffuse leptomeningitis. On retrospective review, linear radial perivascular enhancement surrounding the lateral ventricles was noted.

Lumbar puncture demonstrated a normal opening pressure, elevated white blood cells (85 to 501/mm3) with a lymphocytic predominance (87%), elevated red blood cells (8 to 123/mm3), elevated protein (306 mg/dL), normal glucose and normal lactate dehydrogenase.

Metabolic, neoplastic and preliminary autoimmune workup were negative, including oligoclonal bands, ACE, AQP4 and myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG). Extensive infectious workup was negative (CSF and serum), including MTB-QuantiFERON, MTB PCR, AFB, HIV, syphilis, coccidioides, histoplasma, cryptococcus, brucella, West Nile, Lyme disease and a meningitis/encephalitis panel (including HSV, cytomegalovirus and enterovirus).
Due to the rapidly progressive disease course despite broad antimicrobial coverage, he underwent biopsy of the meninges and brain, which showed no evidence of infectious organisms.

Repeat spine imaging (eleven days after initiation of RIPE and dexamethasone) showed longitudinally extensive patchy T2 hyperintense signal throughout the central grey and lateral columns of the cervical and thoracic spine.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: Eleven days after initiation of RIPE and dexamethasone

evidence_events.source_span: Several days later, the Mayo Clinic CSF autoimmune encephalitis panel returned positive for GFAP 1:128 (ref <1:2) confirming a diagnosis of meningomyeloencephalitis due to GFAP astrocytopathy.
He underwent five sessions of plasmapheresis. Two weeks after the second MRI, he had clinical and radiologic improvement.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: Two weeks after the second MRI

evidence_events.source_span: Given the association between GFAP astrocytopathy and malignancy, he was screened with CT chest-abdomen-pelvis and testicular ultrasound, which found no evidence of occult malignancy.

source_metadata.title: Case of Amaurosis Fugax in the Setting of a Persistent Primitive Hypoglossal Artery Requiring Carotid Endarterectomy with Regional Anesthesia

evidence_events.source_span: An 83-year-old male presented with 2 weeks of intermittent self-resolving episodes of visual disturbance, which he described as white lines curving on the road and “furniture tilting” lasting for approximately 30 s, followed by an episode of left eye amaurosis fugax.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: 2 weeks of intermittent symptoms followed by amaurosis fugax

evidence_events.source_span: Ophthalmologic examination revealed reduced left eye visual acuity (6/9 pin hole) and otherwise was unremarkable.

Carotid Doppler ultrasound demonstrated an ICA peak systolic velocity of 480 cm/s and a peak systolic velocity ratio (ICA: common carotid artery) of 7.5, consistent with carotid stenosis diagnostic criteria of >90% but less than near occlusion.

Computed tomography carotid and circle of Willis angiography confirmed a mixed, ulcerated plaque and revealed a persistent left hypoglossal artery originating from the left ICA 3.7 cm from its origin, ascending posterior to the ICA, which was the dominant supply to the posterior circulation with hypoplastic vertebral arteries bilaterally.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: CT carotid and circle of Willis angiography

evidence_events.source_span: Stroke protocol MRI of the brain confirmed aberrant anatomy with both old and subacute infarcts within the left frontal, parietal-occipital, and cerebellar regions.

The patient proceeded to undergo left carotid endarterectomy with a Braun polyurethane patch under conscious sedation and regional anesthesia using ultrasound-guided intermediate cervical plexus and subplatysmal blocks.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: left carotid endarterectomy under regional anesthesia

evidence_events.source_span: Metaraminol infusion was titrated to maintain systolic blood pressure of 190 to 200 mmHg during carotid clamping with continuous neurological monitoring; no neurological deterioration was observed.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: blood pressure management and neurological monitoring

evidence_events.source_span: Operative findings revealed a near-occlusive soft hemorrhagic plaque at the origin of the left ICA.
The patient recovered well and was discharged 2 days after surgery with no residual neurological deficits.

source_metadata.title: Paravertebral paraganglioma with spinal extension: a case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 23-year-old female of African descent, recently diagnosed with hypertension, was referred to the endocrine clinic for investigation. She had a background history of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection with a recent absolute cluster of differentiation 4 (CD4) count of 390 cells. She was virally suppressed on a first-line fixed-dose combination treatment of tenofovir-lamivudine-dolutegravir. On further history, the patient reported paroxysmal episodes of headaches, palpitations, and sweating. She did not have any focal neurological symptoms. On physical examination, she had a tachycardia of 110 beats per minute and a sustained elevated blood pressure with an average of 160/90 mmHg.

On biochemical investigation, she had significantly elevated urine catecholamine metabolites with normetanephrine levels of 50,060 nmol/24 h (562–2129 nmol/24 h). Chromogranin A was extremely high with a value of 554.9 ng/mL (< 101.9 ng/mL). Plasma metanephrines testing was not available in South Africa at the time.

Initial contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen was normal. Subsequent CT chest imaging showed a large avidly enhancing left posterior mediastinal T1–T3 paraspinal soft tissue mass abutting the apical-posterior segment of the left upper lobe of the lung. Medial extension into the second thoracic vertebral body, and further extension into the intervertebral neural foramen, resulted in spinal cord abutment.
A 68Ga DOTATATE scan showed DOTA receptor avid uptake in the left posterior mediastinal mass supporting the clinical diagnosis of a paraganglioma.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated extension into the epidural space via the left neural foramina of T1/T2 and T2/T3 with resultant displacement and compression of the spinal cord at the T2 level; however, no spinal cord edema was noted. There was additional infiltration of the posterior left parietal pleura with encasement of the left subclavian artery and abutment of the left common carotid artery, brachiocephalic trunk, and aortic arch posterior walls.

The patient was medically optimized with an alpha blocker (doxazosin) and a beta blocker (atenolol) prior to surgery. After 14 days of alpha blockade and 72 h of beta blockade, she underwent emergency surgery with a T2–T4 laminectomy and posterior resection of the paraganglioma lesion. The surgery was uncomplicated and postoperative assessment showed preserved neurology.

Histology confirmed the typical nested (zellballen) growth pattern of the tumor with invasion into the surrounding capsule and a focus of lymphovascular space invasion. Immunohistochemistry stains were diffusely positive for chromogranin. Histology and immunohistochemistry were in keeping with a well-differentiated paraganglioma. The grading system for adrenal pheochromocytoma and paraganglioma (GAPP) was 1.
Genetic testing for pheochromocytoma-paraganglioma syndromes was performed at an internationally accredited commercial laboratory and yielded no key pathogenic DNA mutation.

At 6 weeks postoperation, urine normetanephrine level remained elevated at 66,124 nmol/24 h. A postoperative meta-iodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) scan revealed avid disease in the left upper thoracic region, representing residual disease.
Medical therapy with alpha and beta blockade was continued, and the patient was referred for radiation therapy. The patient defaulted follow-up and unexpectedly demised.

source_metadata.title: Autoimmune gastritis as an unexpected cause of diarrhea in a young adult with type I diabetes: a case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 20-year-old African American female with T1DM was referred by her endocrinologist to pediatric gastroenterology for 2 months of nocturnal, non-bloody diarrhea, left lower quadrant pain, and nausea; she was also being followed by neurology for complaints of lower extremity paresthesias and pain.

Physical exam during her pediatric gastroenterology appointment was benign, including abdominal exam. Neurological exam was remarkable for slightly diminished sensation to vibration and pinprick in bilateral toes, but otherwise normal motor and strength testing, reflexes, and cranial nerve function.
Initial lab-workup was remarkable for a low total Immunoglobulin A (IgA) level of < 6.7 mg/dL.
The patient underwent upper and lower endoscopy which was grossly unremarkable; however histology revealed a pattern consistent with autoimmune gastritis.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: upper and lower endoscopy with biopsy

evidence_events.source_span: Biopsies were negative for Helicobacter pylori.
Subsequent serum evaluation was remarkable for an elevated fasting gastrin level and an elevated parietal cell antibody level without macrocytic anemia, iron deficiency, or vitamin B12 depletion.
Celiac disease was excluded based on upper endoscopy with small bowel biopsies, which did not demonstrate the typical pathologic pattern of celiac disease.
The patient was diagnosed with autoimmune gastritis and subsequently initiated on parenteral B12 supplementation therapy with improvement in her neurologic and gastrointestinal symptoms.

source_metadata.title: Painless nondiabetic lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy with complete recovery: a case report
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case presentation and clinical course sections with source order preserved.

evidence_events.source_span: A 35-year-old Chinese woman with no significant past medical history, family history, or medication history was admitted via our emergency department with a 1-week history of gradually worsening left lower limb weakness and numbness. She was without pain.

On examination, her left-sided ankle deep-tendon reflex was absent, and there was diffuse weakness (modified medical research council scale grade 4) of hip extension, hip adduction, knee extension, knee flexion, ankle plantar flexion, and ankle dorsiflexion in the left lower limb. Sensory testing demonstrated diminished proprioception and pain perception in the left lower limb, distal to the mid-calf.

A nerve conduction study (NCS) and electromyography (EMG) performed eight days from symptom onset suggested a plexopathy. Specifically, there was an asymmetrically absent left-sided tibial H-reflex, diminished left saphenous sensory response of 1.93 μV compared with a right saphenous sensory response of 4.2 μV, and reduced recruitment on EMG of the left-sided vastus lateralis, gastrocnemius, and tibialis anterior muscles.

Gadolinium-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the lumbosacral plexuses and lumbar spine demonstrated enhancement of the cauda equina nerve roots bilaterally, sparing the lumbosacral plexuses.

A lumbar puncture was performed 12 days from symptom onset, showing a normal opening pressure of 12 cm H2O. Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination revealed cytoalbuminologic dissociation (CSF protein 1.03 g/L, with a CSF white blood cell count of 1/μL) but was otherwise negative for oligoclonal bands.
Microbiological and autoimmune assays performed on blood and CSF samples were unyielding.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: blood and CSF microbiological and autoimmune assays performed

evidence_events.source_span: Computed tomography (CT) of her neck, thorax, abdomen, and pelvis showed no suspicious masses.
The patient was diagnosed with nondiabetic LRPN and was treated with IVIg at 2 g/kg divided over 5 days (13–17 days from symptom onset).
A subsequent MRI scan of her lumbar spine performed 18 weeks after symptom onset showed resolution of the cauda equina nerve root enhancement.
She remained asymptomatic when reviewed 20 weeks after symptom onset, and examination was normal, demonstrating a return of her left ankle tendon reflex and full power in all limbs.
One year after the episode, the patient reported by phone interview that she had no recurrence of symptoms.

source_metadata.title: Baló’s concentric sclerosis presenting asymptomatically in a child: clinico-radiological-pathological correlation

evidence_events.source_span: A school-aged, asymptomatic, healthy boy attended a routine optician appointment, which raised concerns about papilloedema (subsequently diagnosed as drusen).
A non-enhanced head CT demonstrated a well-demarcated hyperdense lesion in the left posterior frontal lobe with surrounding hypodensity suggesting oedema.
On MRI brain, the lesion had features in keeping with Baló’s concentric sclerosis with alternating circular layers of high and low density giving the appearance of an onion bulb.
Advanced neuroimaging supported the probable benign nature of the lesion.
Repeat imaging, 3 months later, demonstrated an increase in the size and change in signal characteristics of the lesion leading to the decision to biopsy and exclude a tumour.
Histopathological examination confirmed a demyelinating inflammatory lesion.
Further MRI, 6 months after the original imaging, revealed the lesion had substantially reduced in size, with just a rim of enhancement.
Four years following his original imaging findings, the child remains entirely free of any signs or symptoms.

Dynamic susceptibility contrast (DSC) perfusion imaging demonstrated that the relative cerebral blood flow within the demyelinating lesion is equal to that of the contralateral normal brain parenchyma.
Magnetic resonance spectroscopy demonstrated minimal elevation of choline (choline:creatinine ratio: 1.3) and lipid/lactate peak. The N-acetylaspartate:creatinine ratio was normal (2.1).

White matter tractography from diffusion tensor imaging shows the lesion to lie close to the descending corticospinal tracts. Tracts are seen passing through the area of abnormality around the enhancement; the lesion does not appear to significantly disrupt tracts.

H&E staining, supplemented by Luxol fast blue staining, confirmed the presence of an inflammatory demyelinating lesion with an obvious transition between preserved white matter and demyelinated white matter.

Affected white matter showed reactive gliosis and prominent lymphocytic activity with striking perivascular cuffs of lymphocytes and dispersed parenchymal inflammation accompanying phagocytosing macrophage activity.

The lymphocytes were predominantly T lymphocytes (mainly CD8 positive, but with a CD4 contribution), with some cuffs of perivascular inflammation contributed by an outer cuff of B lymphocytes. Both B and T cell populations lacked cytological atypia.
Neurofilament protein immunostaining showed that axons were generally preserved with little axonal loss; beta-APP immunostaining highlighted some axonal injury seen as axonal bulbs and threads.
Routine blood tests were unremarkable. Examination of the CSF was normal including PCR for viral pathogens; oligoclonal bands were not present.

A serum autoantibody screen including antinuclear antibodies, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein, anticardiolipin, and aquaporin-4 antibodies were all negative; serum complement levels were normal.
Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was mildly elevated (13 mm in 1 hour), but the child had tonsillitis at the time.

The lymphocytes were predominantly T lymphocytes (mainly CD8 positive, but with a CD4 contribution), with some cuffs of perivascular inflammation contributed by an outer cuff of B lymphocytes. Both B and T cell populations lacked cytological atypia.
Neurofilament protein immunostaining showed that axons were generally preserved with little axonal loss; beta-APP immunostaining highlighted some axonal injury seen as axonal bulbs and threads.

source_metadata.title: Subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord in a patient with nitrous oxide use and autoimmune atrophic gastritis

evidence_events.source_span: A man in his 30s presented with lower extremity sensory changes and falls. Three weeks before presentation, he noticed patchy, symmetric numbness and paresthesias in his legs and abdomen, just below the umbilicus.
In the week preceding his presentation, he began experiencing weakness in his lower extremities and difficulty walking, with two falls causing ankle injury.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: In the week preceding his presentation

evidence_events.source_span: He denied sensory changes in the perineum or loss of bowel or bladder control. He reported normal diet without food restrictions and no gastrointestinal symptoms. He denied recent fevers or illnesses.

Past medical history notable for Generalised Anxiety Disorder and Major Depressive Disorder, treated with fluoxetine, quetiapine, and aripiprazole. Previous labs showed intermittently borderline B12 levels (275-300 pg/mL) over 8 years without formal diagnosis.
He reported using 450 canisters of nitrous oxide daily for the past 4–5 months. He drank three glasses of wine per week and smoked marijuana, with no other illicit substances.

Physical examination revealed absent vibratory sense in the lower extremities, impaired proprioception distally to proximally, diminished two-point discrimination in both lower and upper extremities, patchy impairment in light touch sensation up to the umbilicus, decreased pinprick sensation bilaterally to mid-shins, preserved temperature sensation, wide-based stance, positive Romberg sign, absent lower extremity reflexes, and normal upper extremity reflexes.

MRI of the spinal cord revealed patchy hyperintense T2 signal abnormality without enhancement in the dorsal aspect of the cervical and thoracic cord from C3 to T9-T10 disc level. MRI brain was normal.

Laboratory testing showed normal hemoglobin (140 g/L) with macrocytosis (MCV 94 fL), normal vitamin B12 level (672 pg/mL), elevated methylmalonic acid (5.86 μmol/L) and homocysteine (32 μmol/L), and presence of intrinsic factor blocking antibodies.

Gastric biopsy showed chronic inflammation and reactive changes in antral and oxyntic mucosa; duodenal biopsy showed peptic duodenitis and reactive epithelial cells. Biopsies were negative for giardia, coeliac disease, and Helicobacter pylori immunostain.
The patient was diagnosed with subacute combined degeneration of the spinal cord and polyneuropathy secondary to concomitant nitrous oxide abuse and autoimmune atrophic gastritis.

source_metadata.title: Varicella-zoster virus vasculopathy in a patient with multiple sclerosis receiving natalizumab

evidence_events.source_span: A woman in her 30s with natalizumab-treated MS contacted our neurological outpatient clinic due to a new onset headache that started 2 months after a right-sided ophthalmic zoster infection.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: 2 months after a right-sided ophthalmic zoster infection

evidence_events.source_span: She had no vascular risk factors, migraine or any other neurological or inflammatory condition and was not taking any other medication apart from natalizumab.
During treatment with natalizumab, the patient remained stable both clinically and radiologically. Annual JC virus testing (quantitation of virus DNA by real-time PCR) remained negative.

In 2021, 6 years after initiation of treatment with natalizumab, the patient developed symptoms compatible with right-sided ophthalmic zoster, with blisters over her right forehead and right upper eyelid.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: In 2021, 6 years after initiation of treatment

evidence_events.source_span: She was treated with orally administered valacyclovir 1 g three times per day for 7 days starting immediately. She showed remission at follow-up 10 days later.

Two months later, she experienced daily, pounding and pressing bilateral headache which, after 4 weeks, changed to a right-sided occipital and retroorbital pain and after another month ended spontaneously.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: Two months later; after 4 weeks; after another month

evidence_events.source_span: She had no fever but was sensitive to light and sounds. She also reported isolated recurrent twitches in her right cheek while experiencing the right sided headache; there was no postictal state.
The physical examination was normal except hyper-reflexia in her left arm.

Brain MRI including angiographic and gadolinium enhanced sequences, performed 4 months after the ophthalmic zoster infection, demonstrated the presence of subacute ischaemic changes in the right basal ganglia and the right cerebral peduncle. Narrowing of the supraclinoid segment of the right internal carotid artery (ICA) and the A1 segment of the anterior cerebral artery (ACA) and gadolinium enhancement in the vessel wall of the right ICA and ACA were noted.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: 4 months after the ophthalmic zoster infection
evidence_events.procedural_cue: Brain MRI including angiographic and gadolinium enhanced sequences

evidence_events.source_span: No parenchymal lesions or vascular changes were detected in the left hemisphere, to explain the short episodes of right facial twitches reported by the patient.

A lumbar puncture was performed including analyses of cell count, protein, lactate and glucose as well as a broad microbiological assay. White and red cell count, glucose, lactate and albumin were normal. CSF was positive for VZV-DNA. In serum, VZV IgG was positive, and IgM was at the threshold limit value. All other virological and microbiological CSF and serum PCR investigations were negative.
Additional neuroradiological examinations with CT angiography and MRI including black blood sequences supported the diagnosis.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: CT angiography and MRI including black blood sequences

evidence_events.source_span: Genetical investigations did not show any pathogenic variation in the POLR3F gene, associated with increased risk for CNS vasculopathy caused by reactivation of VZV.
On admission, the patient was started on methylprednisolone intravenously 1 g once a day, acyclovir intravenously 750 mg three times per day and acetylsalicylic acid 75 mg once a day.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: treatment with methylprednisolone, acyclovir, acetylsalicylic acid

evidence_events.source_span: A follow-up lumbar puncture 17 days after admission showed VZV-PCR DNA was negative. Virological and microbiological analyses were still negative.
Treatment with natalizumab was paused and later terminated; she was started on rituximab instead.

A follow-up MRI scan 6 weeks after the MRI preceding hospitalisation demonstrated persisting vasculitic vessel wall changes in the right ICA and the right ACA with gadolinium enhancement still present.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: 6 weeks after the MRI preceding hospitalisation

evidence_events.source_span: The next follow-up MRI scan 9 months later demonstrated regression of the gadolinium enhancement in the vessel walls but persisting vessel wall thickening in the affected vessel segments. No new lesions were found.
The patient remained clinically stable to date, 2 years and 2 months later.

source_metadata.title: Ramsay Hunt Syndrome Associated with Varicella-Zoster Virus Encephalitis in a Child
source_metadata.notes: Case report of an 8-year-old boy with RHS complicated by VZV encephalitis, including clinical, lab, imaging, and treatment evidence.

evidence_events.source_span: An 8-year-old previously healthy boy presented with a 3-day history of fever, progressive left ear pain and swelling and vesicular rash around the left ear pinna.

On examination, left ear was swollen with redness extended to pre-auricular and postauricular area, vesicular lesions with red base on outer ear canal extending to left maxillary dermatome, yellowish discharge, and tender enlarged left cervical node (2 × 3 cm).
Laboratory investigations showed normal full blood count, C-reactive protein, serum electrolytes and random blood sugar.
VZV polymerase chain reaction (PCR) from the ear swab was positive while bacterial culture and Herpes simplex PCR were negative.
The patient developed lower motor neuron facial nerve palsy on day 2 of admission and later dizziness and increased sleepiness.
On day 3, he developed vomiting, dysarthria and unsteady gait without seizures, meningeal signs or motor/sensory deficits.
Brain MRI and MRV were performed urgently and both were reported normal.
Cerebrospinal fluid showed 10 leukocytes (8 mononuclear, 2 polymorphonuclear), 2 red cells, normal protein and glucose; bacterial culture negative; VZV PCR positive from CSF.
Acyclovir was switched to intravenous formulation and prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily was added.
In the following days, ear pain, swelling, vomiting and unsteady gait improved significantly; patient was asymptomatic at discharge.
At 6 months follow-up, patient remained asymptomatic with normal neurological examination and normal MRI with no evidence of cerebral arteritis or vasculopathies.

source_metadata.title: Antithrombin deficiency caused by SERPINC1 gene mutation in white matter lesions: A case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 25-year-old male presented to the neurology department with recurrent headaches for more than 4 years. His headache was characterized by bilateral paroxysmal cephalalgia, mostly occurring in the afternoon, lasting 1 to 2 hours, which can be relieved spontaneously after rest. Limb numbness sometimes occurs when the patient gets emotional. The patient was healthy previously with no smoking or alcohol habits, and the neurological examination was negative.

Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed multiple white matter hyperintensity lesions on T2-weighted and T2 fluid-attenuated inversion recovery images. The lesions were distributed in the periventricular deep white matter as well as frontal and parietal lobes, some lesions were confluent and perpendicular to the lateral ventricles. T1-weighted contrast images showed lesions were not enhanced.
Serum and cerebrospinal fluid examination did not demonstrate oligoclonal bands, and the cerebrospinal fluid IgG index was normal.

Whole exon sequencing on the patient detected a novel heterozygous missense mutation in SERPINC1 gene (1q25.1). Sanger sequencing of his parents revealed the same mutation in the father. The mutation was predicted to be likely pathogenic by Mutpred2 software.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: whole exon sequencing and Sanger sequencing performed

evidence_events.source_span: Antithrombin III (AT III) activity in the patient was slightly decreased (72.2%, reference range: 80%–120%), while AT III antigen level was normal (235 mg/L). The father had similarly decreased AT III activity (75.1%) and normal antigen level (263.3 mg/L).

Transcranial doppler and transthoracic echocardiography diagnosed the patient with patent foramen ovale, which was considered the most likely cause of his migraine. The father had no neurological symptoms and negative transthoracic echocardiography.

The patient received percutaneous patent foramen ovale closure surgery and oral antiplatelet therapy. Follow-up at 1 and 6 months showed unchanged MRI lesions but significant improvement in headache frequency, duration, and severity.

Cranial nerve examination was normal, and motor strength was intact. Intermittent involuntary, non-rhythmic, flailing movements of the right arm and leg were observed. The patient was unable to execute any voluntary movements in his right arm because of hyperkinetic dyskinesia. He was alert but frustrated by these involuntary movements.

Laboratory tests were remarkable for acute on chronic kidney injury (serum creatinine 3.63 mg/dL, baseline 2.93 mg/dL) and hyperglycaemia 597 mg/dL. Thyroid stimulating hormone was 2.6. Venous blood gas showed pH 7.34, serum bicarbonate was 21 mmol/L. Urinalysis showed no ketosis. Calculated serum osmolarity was 308 mosm/kg making hyperosmolar hyperglycaemia state unlikely. Hb A1c level returned elevated at 17.0%.

Non-contrast CT scan of his head demonstrated a faint hyperdensity involving the left lentiform nucleus and caudate nucleus. Brain MRI showed an increased T1 signal intensity in the putamen on the left. MRI did not demonstrate evidence of acute ischaemic or haemorrhagic stroke.

History and laboratory findings helped exclude hereditary, metabolic and toxic disorders such as Huntington’s disease, thyroid dysfunction, Wilson disease, manganese toxicity, carbon monoxide poisoning and cocaine toxicity which may also present with chorea. Imaging helped exclude bilateral striatal lesions and haemorrhage.

The patient was admitted to the hospital for further management. Intravenous hydration and subcutaneous basal and prandial insulin were administered. Serum blood glucose levels normalised over the next 24–48 hours. Severe hemichorea-hemiballismus persisted, impairing ambulation and sleep.

Due to severe insomnia and overnight agitation, the patient was initially treated with escalating doses of olanzapine. Low-dose clonazepam was added on day 3 with minimal improvement. On day 4 olanzapine was stopped and risperidone 2 mg nightly was started with improvement in sleep and right arm and leg chorea-hemiballismus.

He was discharged to an acute rehabilitation facility with subcutaneous insulin, sitagliptin and risperidone. Two months post-hospitalisation the intensity and frequency of hemichorea had decreased and he had returned to all usual activities. At 6-month follow-up, mild chorea in his right arm persisted.

source_metadata.title: A 48-year-old man with fever, nauseous, vomiting, and dizzy: A CARE case report
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from full case presentation and discussion sections with source order preserved.

evidence_events.source_span: A 48-year-old man was admitted to the neurology department due to dizziness, nausea, and vomiting.

Twenty days ago, the patient suddenly experienced nausea, vomiting, and dizziness after lunch; initial treatment with intravenous acyclovir and dexamethasone at another hospital did not improve symptoms.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: initial treatment with acyclovir and dexamethasone

evidence_events.source_span: Fifteen days later, he developed fever up to 39 °C; blood routine showed WBC 19.52 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 18.01 × 10^9/L; blood culture showed Listeria infection.
Lumbar puncture showed CSF cells 210 × 10^6/L, protein 1371.5 mg/dL, glucose 1.1 mmol/L; cranial MRI showed lesions in right pontine and brachium pontis.

On admission to our hospital, physical exam showed sluggish light reflex and stiff neck; lumbar puncture CSF pathology showed severe CNS inflammation with lymphocyte predominance; NGS of CSF indicated Listeria infection with high sequence number and relative abundance.

On third day of admission, patient had swelling and pain in left leg; deep vein ultrasound and D-dimer were normal; muscle ultrasound showed occupying lesions in left gastrocnemius muscle with low echo area approximately 12.6 × 0.5 cm and thickening/swelling of left plantar tendon.

Follow-up CSF after 10 days showed slight improvement in cell counts but low pressure; cranial MRI showed persistent large lesion around pons, new abnormal high signal in posterior horn of left lateral ventricle on DWI, and meningeal enhancement.

After 35 days of antibiotic treatment, CSF pressure normalized to 125 cm H2O with only protein elevation; cranial MRI showed shrinkage of brainstem lesion but brain edema in lateral ventricle; head CT at 45 days showed hydrocephalus concentrated in lateral ventricle.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: lumbar puncture, cranial MRI, head CT

evidence_events.source_span: On second admission after relapse, neurological exam showed increased muscle tone and neck stiffness; lumbar puncture showed high protein and slightly elevated cells; muscle MRI showed increased high signal in gastrocnemius muscle; brainstem lesion smaller; hydrocephalus improved.
Half a year later, reexamination showed only protein elevation in CSF and hydrocephalus on MRI; symptoms did not recur and patient recovered well after discharge.

source_metadata.title: Isolated primary CNS lymphoma after liver transplantation for autoimmune hepatitis: a case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 64-year-old woman, who had a liver transplant 18 months earlier for autoimmune hepatitis and was on mycophenolate and tacrolimus, experienced a week of generalized weakness, headaches, confusion, and disorientation.

The patient was confused. Fundoscopic examination revealed papilledema. The neurological evaluation showed left-sided hemiparesis, left-sided sensory changes, and left-sided pyramidal signs. Additionally, the patient demonstrated visuospatial deficits and loss of sensation on the right side of the body.

Laboratory tests, including C-reactive protein, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, showed normal results. However, gamma-glutamyl transferase levels and platelet counts were elevated. Tests for CMV IgM, Hepatitis B & C, HIV, and Toxoplasma gondii returned nonreactive results, with the CMV IgG test also being negative.
An initial brain CT without contrast was performed before transferring the patient to our institution, showing the absence of hemorrhage.

An MRI scan was ordered, revealing multiple ring-enhancing lesions, primarily located in the right frontal lobe, temporoparietal regions, and left parietal lobe, with the largest measuring 2.7 cm in maximal diameter. These lesions were associated with moderate vasogenic edema.

Given the suspicion of toxoplasmosis, the patient was started on sulfadiazine and pyrimethamine, and blood cultures were collected. As the patient’s clinical condition deteriorated, an urgent craniotomy and brain biopsy were carried out to determine whether the lesions were due to toxoplasmosis, lymphoma, brain abscess, or other pathologies.

The brain biopsy revealed diffuse infiltrates of closely packed intermediate to large mononuclear cells with scant cytoplasm. Additionally, a perivascular infiltrate composed of atypical lymphoid cells and a widespread infiltrate of neoplastic intermediate to large lymphocytes tested positive for the B-cell marker CD20.

The patient was diagnosed with CNS PTLD, specifically high-grade diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) of the activated B-cell phenotype. Treatment was initiated with a regimen of systemic rituximab and methotrexate.
Following the completion of eight cycles of high-dose rituximab-methotrexate, the patient’s clinical status improved. A follow-up brain MRI 14 months later showed improved imaging findings.

source_metadata.title: Gerstmann Syndrome in an Elderly Patient: A Case Report Presented with a Complete Tetrad of Symptoms
source_metadata.notes: Extraction based on case presentation and discussion sections with source-order preservation.

evidence_events.source_span: An 86-year-old female patient, known with type 2 diabetes mellitus, was admitted to our clinic for hemiparesis on the right side and suggestive signs of Gerstmann syndrome in the last 3 weeks.

Neurological examination presented right-sided hemiparesis MRC 3/5 and cognitive impairments. Specifically, the patient presented finger agnosia, agraphia, acalculia, and right–left disorientation, suggestive manifestations of Gerstmann syndrome.

The intracranial chronic subdural hematoma in this patient is attributed to several factors commonly associated with elderly patients. Age-related cerebral atrophy, which was also observed in the patient’s brain imaging, can lead to an increased vulnerability of the bridging veins, making them more prone to rupture, even with minor trauma.

A non-contrast brain CT scan revealed a chronic subdural hematoma, Markwalder grade 2, located on the left hemisphere, at the level of frontal and parietal lobes, depicting a hypodense aspect measuring about 1.5 cm, without mass effect or subfalcine herniation. Moderate age-related cerebral abiotrophy was also observed.
Computer tomography examination on the next day revealed signs of resorption and a decrease in the hematoma’s thickness.

Considering the patient’s age, the significant reduction of the hematoma, and especially the signs representative of vascular resorption, surgical intervention was not mandatory. At discharge, the patient showed slightly remitted right hemiparesis MRC 4/5; regarding Gerstmann syndrome presentation, no improvements or worsening of the symptoms was observed, and she was prescribed Fludrocortisone for the intracranial hematoma.
Gerstmann syndrome involves a combination of four neurological deficits, commonly referred to as a tetrad of symptoms: agraphia, acalculia, right–left disorientation, and finger agnosia.
The literature contains few cases of Gerstmann syndrome in elderly patients, making it challenging to determine age-related differences in individuals with this condition.
Table 1 indicates that Gerstmann syndrome in elderly patients typically presents as a complete tetrad of symptoms, manifesting irrespective of the individual’s gender.
Unconventional manifestations of chronic subdural hematomas encompass extrapyramidal symptoms and other infrequent neurological conditions, such as Gerstmann syndrome.

The inaugural documentation of chronic subdural hematoma associated with Gerstmann syndrome was provided by Maeshima et al. in 1998, involving a 71-year-old female with left fronto-parietal hematoma and clinical improvement after surgical evacuation.

source_metadata.title: Atypical presentation of arachnoid web causing paraparesis with absence of sensory symptoms

evidence_events.source_span: A man in his 60s with a history of atrial fibrillation status postablation and transurethral resection of the prostate procedure (TURP) was referred to the neurosurgery clinic for approximately 2 years of spastic paraparesis.

He initially presented to his local neurologist with gradually worsening gait imbalance with frequent falls, severe thoracic and lumbar back pain, back and leg spasms and decreased functional endurance.

On the physical examination, he had hyperreflexia in all four extremities with positive Babinski reflexes in his lower limbs bilaterally, positive left-sided Hoffman reflex, intact cranial nerves, no clonus or saddle anaesthesia, and muscle strength graded at 5/5 bilaterally in both upper and lower extremities.
The patient described weakness that began in his left leg, quickly followed by right leg involvement with a complete absence of sensory symptoms.
He received an initial diagnosis of Parkinson's disease and was prescribed levodopa/carbidopa with equivocal results.

Electromyography testing demonstrated acute and chronic denervation changes in L3–S1 myotomes, although these findings were relatively mild and out of proportion to the severity of his clinical picture.
Repeat spinal imaging, including a CT myelogram and a non-contrasted MRI of the thoracic spine, demonstrated a possible arachnoid cyst in the midthoracic spine (T7).
The arachnoid web was identified on MRI at vertebral levels 7 and 8 of the thoracic spine, indicated by a minimal dorsal indentation along the spinal cord, most suggestive of a positive scalpel sign.
The patient underwent laminectomy and intradural exploration with fenestration of the arachnoid adhesions at T6–T8.

Intraoperatively, thickened arachnoid webbing from T7 and T8 was found, causing increased localized pressure and ventral displacement of the spinal cord; microdissection fenestration was performed with visible increase in cerebrospinal fluid flow after fenestration.

At 5 months postsurgery, the patient had improved muscle strength and gait, was able to walk with a walker, and was diagnosed with cervical myelopathy from previous spinal cord compression by the arachnoid web.

source_metadata.notes: Extraction based on case presentation, test results, and discussion sections.

evidence_events.source_span: A 37-year-old Hispanic male patient, native to southern Honduras, presented with dizziness and tinnitus. These symptoms progressed to include left-sided sensorineural hearing loss.
Neurological examination, including cranial nerves and cerebellar function, was normal. Hallpike maneuver caused dizziness without nystagmus. Physical exam normal except left nasal septal deviation.
Provisional diagnosis of left-sided Meniere’s disease; referred for electrocochleography (ECOG) and vestibulonystagmogram (VNG).
Detailed history revealed prior tapeworm infection at age 14 in Honduras; details unknown.
MRI of the brain revealed postinflammatory calcifications in the right parietal lobe and generalized volume loss greater than expected for age.

Laboratory testing showed normal CBC, CMP, CRP (1 mg/L), sedimentation rate (8 mm/hr), negative anticardiolipin antibodies, negative beta-2 glycoprotein antibodies, negative Lyme IgG/IgM, negative ANA and rheumatoid factor, and normal TSH (2.020 uIU/mL).

The C-reactive protein (CRP) level was 1 mg/L, which fell within the normal range of 0–10 mg/L. The sedimentation rate was 8 mm/hour, which was within the normal range of 0–15 mm/hour. Anticardiolipin antibody levels for immunoglobulin (Ig)A, IgG, and IgM were all less than 9 units, each within their respective normal ranges. Similarly, beta-2 glycoprotein antibody levels for IgA, IgG, and IgM were all less than 9 units, well within their normal ranges. Additionally, the Lyme IgG/IgM antibodies test was negative, as were the tests for antinuclear antibodies (ANA) and rheumatoid arthritis factor. The thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) level was 2.020 uIU/mL, within the normal range.

source_metadata.title: Tabes dorsalis: a rare presentation of neurosyphilis in Western Europe

evidence_events.source_span: A married carpenter in his 60s presented to an ophthalmological department of a hospital in Switzerland with diplopia for 3 months.

Orthoptic diagnostics demonstrated a presumed congenital paresis of the left IVth cranial nerve with exophoria, hyperopia and astigmatism on both sides and presbyopia with good visual acuity. Strabismus surgery was successfully performed with initial resolution of diplopia.

8 months later, the patient presented at a private neurological practice due to recurrent diplopia accompanied by pain in his pelvis radiating to his right leg, urge incontinence and symptoms of a sensory polyneuropathy on his lower limbs. Furthermore, a left VIth cranial nerve palsy, decreased deep tendon reflexes, reduced sense of vibration and an unsteady gait were documented.
Electrophysiological examination and laboratory results including screening for Lyme disease and vasculitis were unremarkable, an MRI showed cervical spinal cord stenosis.

During the subsequent 9 months, visual acuity deteriorated considerably to a Snellen fraction of less than 20/200 on the right side and 25/100 on the left side. Concomitant bilateral cataracts and significant atrophy of the optic nerve (right > left) were documented. Bilateral cataract surgery was performed without any amelioration of visual acuity. A tumour or inflammatory alterations of the optic nerve were ruled out by a brain MRI. A genetic panel for >100 genes related to hereditary optic atrophy including Leber’s hereditary optic neuropathy was unrevealing.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: Bilateral cataract surgery performed; brain MRI performed; genetic panel performed

evidence_events.source_span: One year later, the patient presented again due to further progression of his ataxia. A prominent relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) was found. A repeated MRI scan showed regression of the formerly described herniated disc without any signs of myelopathy.

Laboratory rheumatological screening (antineuronal antibodies) and tumour markers were unremarkable again. Electrophysiological testing did not show any clear evidence for the presence of a polyneuropathy.

4 years after his first symptoms with extensive but unsuccessful diagnostics and treatments, including several MRIs, broad genetic analysis and multiple eye surgeries, he was referred to our neurological department. On referral, the patient suffered from severe gait ataxia due to diminished proprioception and absent deep tendon reflexes. Furthermore, diminished pupillary reflex to light with preserved constriction during convergence, described as an Argyll-Robertson pupil as well as an almost complete loss of vision were found. Syphilis screening test was positive, which was confirmed by serological confirmation tests and positive CSF studies. The patient disclosed a previous syphilis infection 30 years ago, likely treated insufficiently with an unknown oral antibiotic.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: Syphilis screening and CSF studies performed

evidence_events.source_span: Laboratory screening revealed positive titres for a syphilis screening test, positive Treponema pallidum haemagglutination assay, and serological activity with a rapid plasma reagin (RPR) of 1:8. CSF study revealed pleocytosis with 93 cells/µL, predominantly mononuclear, elevated protein, albumin and lactate, as well as intrathecal synthesis of IgG directed against Treponema pallidum.

After diagnosis confirmation, the patient received penicillin G intravenously six times per day for 14 days, followed by outpatient parenteral antibiotic therapy with penicillin G 24 million IU per day. One shot of long-acting Benzathine-Penicillin 2.4 million IU intramuscularly was added after intravenous therapy.

6 months after treatment, the patient did not notice any significant clinical amelioration. Visual acuity remained poor and ataxia unchanged. Laboratory markers improved: CSF mononuclear pleocytosis decreased from 93 to 12 cells/µL, protein from 1.65 to 0.79 g/L, albumin from 0.89 to 0.43 g/L, and serological activity decreased to Treponema RPR of 1:2 after 9 months.

hidden_reference.final_diagnosis_verbatim: Tabes dorsalis
diagnostic_reasoning_verbatim_spans: Syphilis screening test was positive, which was confirmed by serological confirmation tests and positive CSF studies.
The patient disclosed a previous syphilis infection 30 years ago, which was likely treated insufficiently with an unknown oral antibiotic.

The constellation of an insidiously progressive afferent ataxia with diminished deep tendon reflexes along with normal nerve conduction studies and urinary incontinence points towards an involvement of the spinal cord, particularly of the dorsal column or the dorsal roots.
Laboratory screening revealed positive titres for a syphilis screening test, positive Treponema pallidum haemagglutination assay, and serological activity with a rapid plasma reagin (RPR) of 1:8.
CSF study revealed pleocytosis with 93 cells/µL, predominantly mononuclear, elevated protein, albumin and lactate, as well as intrathecal synthesis of IgG directed against Treponema pallidum.
diagnostic_reasoning_items: Initial neurological and ophthalmological symptoms suggested cranial nerve and sensory pathway involvement.
Negative imaging and genetic tests ruled out common structural and hereditary causes.
Progressive neurological signs with negative autoimmune and tumour markers narrowed differential diagnosis.
Positive syphilis serology and CSF inflammatory markers confirmed neurosyphilis.
Clinical presentation and history consistent with tabes dorsalis, a late manifestation of neurosyphilis.
hidden_reference.final_diagnosis: Tabes dorsalis
hidden_reference.diagnostic_reasoning: The diagnosis of tabes dorsalis was established based on the clinical presentation of progressive sensory ataxia, cranial nerve palsies, and optic neuropathy, combined with positive syphilis serology and confirmatory CSF findings indicating active neurosyphilis. The patient's history of prior inadequately treated syphilis infection supports the diagnosis of late neurosyphilis manifesting as tabes dorsalis.
hidden_reference.article_derived_evidence_summary: The patient initially presented with diplopia and cranial nerve palsies, followed by progressive sensory and motor neurological symptoms. Extensive negative workup for other causes was performed. Positive syphilis serology and CSF studies confirmed neurosyphilis. Treatment with penicillin was initiated, resulting in laboratory improvement but no clinical recovery, consistent with irreversible neurological damage from late-stage disease.

source_metadata.title: Varicella-zoster virus meningitis with hypoglycorrhachia, presenting with painless occipital herpes zoster mimicking atopic dermatitis

evidence_events.source_span: The patient was a young man in his 20s who presented with fever and back pain as his chief complaints. He had developed chills 4 days prior to visiting our clinic. The next day, he experienced a headache and a fever of 38.7°, prompting a visit to a local clinic, where he was prescribed antipyretic analgesics. Despite this treatment, his fever persisted, and he began experiencing vomiting.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: 4 days prior to visiting clinic; next day

evidence_events.source_span: The patient’s atopic dermatitis and pre-existing back pain worsened, making it difficult for him to sleep while lying down. His mother reported a significant worsening of his atopic dermatitis, with a severe occipital rash—the worst she had ever seen.

On arrival, his vital signs were: Blood pressure 117/83 mm Hg, heart rate 88 beats per min, respiratory rate <20 breaths per min, body temperature 37.5°, SpO2 97% on ambient air. Although his general appearance was sickly, he had a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 15/15, and his cognition was clear.

The patient had a painless rash on the right side of the occipital region. Atopic dermatitis was also present on his back and lower legs. He exhibited no nuchal rigidity or jolt accentuation of the neck. Spontaneous back pain consistent with lumbar herniation was noted, but there was no spinal tapping pain. He was oriented to date, location and memory, and no unusual neurological abnormalities were observed.

White cell count 9.2 ×10^9/L (70.5% neutrophils, 15.5% lymphocytes, 12.0% monocytes), C reactive protein 2.1 mg/dL, serum glucose 151 mg/dL. CSF was clear and colourless with initial pressure 25 cm H2O, white cell count 173 cells/μL (98% lymphocytes), protein concentration 168 mg/dL, glucose concentration 28 mg/dL, CSF/serum glucose ratio 0.18. Gram staining of centrifuged CSF revealed primarily mononuclear leucocytes but no bacteria were detected.
evidence_events.evidence_type: routine_lab | routine_lab | routine_lab | routine_lab | routine_lab | routine_lab | microbiology

evidence_events.source_span: MRI revealed no abnormal intracranial signals. PCR testing for herpes simplex virus (HSV) was performed and was negative. Serum HIV antigen and antibody tests were negative. Bacterial and mycobacterial cultures from CSF and blood cultures were negative.

The finding of lymphocyte predominance led to a diagnosis of aseptic meningitis; however, the 28 mg/dL glucose level was too low for a diagnosis of viral meningitis. Antibodies against Epstein-Barr virus and cytomegalovirus in serum were negative. Mycoplasma pneumoniae IgM in serum was negative. Bacterial meningitis with lymphocyte predominance was considered due to prior oral cephalosporin use, including Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Listeria monocytogenes.

The patient was admitted and treated with intravenous acyclovir (10 mg/kg every 8 hours) and ampicillin (2 g every 6 hours). Ampicillin was discontinued after blood and CSF cultures tested negative. After hospitalisation, the exudate from a painless skin rash on the right occipital area worsened. A dermatologist diagnosed herpes zoster based on the nature, distribution and associated pain of the rash.

The patient’s fever resolved and symptoms improved after 5 days of intravenous acyclovir, followed by 5 days of oral valacyclovir. At 10-day follow-up, the right occipital rash persisted but was crusted. CSF PCR test for HSV was negative. Residual refrigerated CSF was tested by PCR for VZV DNA, which was positive at 11 × 10^6 copies/mL. Serum VZV antibodies were positive for both IgM and IgG, confirming reactivation of VZV infection.

source_metadata.title: POLG epilepsy presenting as new-onset refractory status epilepticus (NORSE) in pregnancy

evidence_events.source_span: A 21-year-old woman presented to a district general hospital with focal impaired awareness seizures when 18 weeks pregnant.
Seizure semiology comprised right upper limb extension followed by twitching and impaired awareness, progressing to bilateral tonic-clonic seizures.

Her focal seizures progressed to prolonged, refractory status epilepticus, requiring intensive care unit (ICU) admission. Seizure control was established with multiple anti-seizure medications. Intravenous corticosteroids were also given to cover for potential immune-mediated seizure pathology.
She was transferred to the tertiary centre hospital, under the obstetric team, for a late surgical termination of pregnancy at 23 weeks of gestation, in line with the patient’s choice.

The day before the procedure, she again developed status epilepticus. There were two seizure semiologies: one involved right arm myoclonic jerks with preserved awareness; the second involved extensor posturing of the right arm, and flexor posturing of the left arm, progressing to generalised tonic-clonic activity.
An electroencephalogram (EEG) confirmed electroclinical status epilepticus.
MR brain scan showed new abnormal cortical signal involving the left parietal, posterolateral temporal and occipital lobes.

Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed a normal white cell count and protein concentration, with no oligoclonal bands. CSF was negative for viral PCR RNA and immune-mediated antibodies (anti-CASP2, NMDA, LGI1, GABA B, AMPA 1 and 2, GAD and glycine).
Repeat EEG showed continuous repetitive discharges over the left posterior region, consistent with epilepsia partialis continua.
Valproate was withdrawn given the possibility of POLG and thus concern about potential valproate hepatotoxicity.
Repeat MR scan of the brain with contrast showed persisting left thalamic changes, likely gliotic scarring.
Subsequent POLG genetic testing on blood detected a biallelic compound heterozygous pathogenic variants in POLG c.2243G>C p.Trp748Ser and c.3720G>C p.

One year later there have been no further generalised seizures, but she reported occasional myoclonus, predominantly right sided, which worsens after exercise. Her jerks increased after reducing levetiracetam, which was reinstated. She has developed bilateral ptosis without ophthalmoplegia, with a right hemiparesis and a high-stepping gait.

source_metadata.notes: Extraction based on case presentation and clinical course sections with source-order evidence events and milestones.

evidence_events.source_span: A 49-year-old woman with a history of migraine presented on October 4, 2022, with 20 days of difficulty finding words and unresponsiveness; no classical cerebrovascular risk factors; examination showed apathetic expression, decreased memory and orientation, no limb weakness or facial asymmetry; vital signs normal; cerebral MRI showed chronic cortical infarct in the left frontal lobe; MRA and carotid ultrasound showed no stenosis or occlusion.
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: Initial presentation with left frontal lobe infarct and no vascular stenosis.

evidence_events.source_span: Hospitalized on July 21, 2023, with sudden right limb weakness and dysarthria for 4 hours; exam showed somnolence, global aphasia, right facial palsy, right hemiparesis (MRC 3/5), NIHSS 11; treated with intravenous alteplase thrombolysis; partial neurological improvement (NIHSS 7); MRI showed left temporal insular lobe infarcts with small hemorrhagic transformation in basal ganglia; MRV showed no venous thrombosis; ECG, lower-extremity Doppler, chest and abdominal CT normal; TEE showed patent foramen ovale (PFO) approx. 3 mm; TTE normal cardiac function; PFO closure performed after hemorrhage absorption.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: MRI, CT, MRV, TEE, TTE, intravenous thrombolysis, PFO closure
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: Second ischemic stroke with PFO identified and treated by closure.

evidence_events.source_span: Nine months later, on April 23, 2024, re-admitted with recurrent right hemiplegia and slurred speech; neurological exam showed alert mental status, right hemiplegia (MRC 2/5), NIHSS 9; MRI revealed acute infarct in left corona radiata; thrombolysis not performed due to time window and prior hemorrhage; routine labs unremarkable; follow-up TEE showed no shunt; livedo reticularis noted on inner side of feet.
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: Recurrent stroke with new infarct and vascular skin manifestation (livedo reticularis).

evidence_events.source_span: Thromboembolic laboratory tests including anticardiolipin antibodies (aCL), anti-beta 2 glycoprotein-I (aβ2GPI), lupus anticoagulant (LAC), protein C, protein S, antithrombin III, antinuclear antibody, and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies were negative or within normal limits except for positive aβ2GPI IgA; immunological tests for non-criteria antiphospholipid antibodies showed positive antibodies to vimentin/cardiolipin complex and anti-annexin A5 antibody.
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: Positive non-criteria antiphospholipid antibodies indicating seronegative APS.

evidence_events.source_span: Patient was treated with long-term low-dose aspirin and warfarin with INR target 2-3; at manuscript submission, no stroke recurrence was reported.
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: Treatment and outcome context without new diagnostic narrowing.

evidence_events.source_section: Case presentation - History of present illness
evidence_events.source_span: During a routine ophthalmology follow-up for previously diagnosed amblyopia, bilateral pupil dilation (7 mm diameter) with complete loss of light and accommodation reflexes was noted; patient denied ocular pain, visual disturbances, diplopia, ptosis, or systemic symptoms.

Bilateral fixed mydriasis (right: 7.0 mm, left: 7.5 mm) unresponsive to light or accommodation; preserved convergence reflex; extraocular movements full; no ptosis or diplopia; visual acuity 1.0 bilaterally; funduscopy and intraocular pressure normal.

Neurological examination: cranial nerves intact; normal muscle tone and strength; normal gait and coordination; physiological and deep tendon reflexes normoactive; no meningeal signs or pathological reflexes.
Routine labs including complete blood count, electrolytes, renal/hepatic function, thyroid studies, inflammatory markers (CRP), and autoimmune serology (ANA) were within normal limits.
Provocative testing: Neostigmine challenge negative; 1% pilocarpine failed to induce pupillary constriction.
Neurophysiology studies including nerve conduction and EEG were normal.
Cranial and orbital MRI, chest CT, and ocular ultrasound were unremarkable; ophthalmologic exam confirmed bilateral pupil dilation and loss of light reflex.
Empirical therapies (mannitol, acyclovir, dexamethasone, B vitamins) yielded partial improvement with pupil diameter reducing to 6 mm and diminished light reflexes; etiology remained unclear.
CSF analysis showed no albuminocytological dissociation and was antibody-negative.
Serum anti-GQ1b (IgM/IgG) and anti-GT1a (IgG) antibodies were positive by western blotting.
Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) 400 mg/kg/day for 5 days was administered.
Post-treatment, pupil diameter normalized to 3–4 mm with restored light reflexes within 5 days.
At 6-month follow-up, sustained resolution without recurrence or development of classic MFS features was observed.

source_metadata.title: Adult-onset acute disseminated encephalomyelitis mimicking complex migraine: A CARE-compliant case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 35-year-old male was presented with a 12-hour history of decreased consciousness following a complex progression of symptoms over the preceding week.
One week prior to admission, he began experiencing severe headaches, generalized joint pain (arthralgias), and muscle aches (myalgias).
He was initially diagnosed with an upper respiratory tract infection and treated with intravenous fluids, resulting in temporary symptomatic relief.
He presented with a severe, throbbing headache, visual disturbances, and sensitivity to light and sound-symptoms that were highly suggestive of a complex migraine.
Neurological examination was unremarkable, and a brain MRI was performed, revealing nonspecific findings typically associated with migraine.

Despite initial improvement, the patient developed further concerning symptoms, such as difficulty sleeping, worsening headaches, tongue heaviness, hypoactivity, numbness in the right hand, and bluish discoloration of the lips.
His condition worsened with new symptoms, including speech difficulties, numbness in his right hand, episodes of disorientation, hypotension, and hypoactivity.

On admission, he had a temperature of 38.2°C, heart rate of 104 beats/min, blood pressure of 133/80 mm Hg, oxygen saturation of 95%, was confused with Glasgow Coma Scale score of 10/15, swelling in the right eye, tachycardia, decreased breath sounds, and meningeal irritation signs.
Initial brain CT and limited MRI did not reveal acute ischemic changes or intracranial hemorrhage.

Follow-up brain MRI revealed newly developed areas of high T2-weighted fluid attenuated inversion recovery signal intensities in the left hemisphere, right parietal, and temporal lobes, as well as mild leptomeningeal enhancement.
Extensive laboratory investigations including hematological workup, basic metabolic and liver panel, CSF analysis, and drug toxicology screen were performed.
CSF analysis revealed elevated protein levels (145 mg/dL) and lymphocytic pleocytosis (70% lymphocytes), supporting the diagnosis of ADEM.
PCR testing for viral pathogens, including HSV, was negative; CSF cultures showed no bacterial growth.
Empiric antiviral and antibiotic therapies were discontinued after 5 days due to negative infectious workup.
The patient was promptly started on high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone as pulse steroid therapy, with significant improvement in consciousness and orientation over 3 days.
Benzodiazepines, haloperidol, and anticonvulsants were administered to manage agitation and seizure prophylaxis.

At discharge, the patient had returned to full orientation, with resolution of confusion and marked improvement in cognitive and motor functions; he was able to walk unassisted and perform activities of daily living independently.
At 2-week follow-up, the patient remained clinically stable without recurrence of neurological symptoms.
