source_metadata.title: TWO ACUTE STEMIS AND TWO ACUTE ISCHEMIC STROKES IN THE SAME PATIENT WITHIN FIVE DAYS – WHAT WENT WRONG?
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case report section and discussion; images assigned per milestone.

evidence_events.source_span: A 68-year-old patient with no previous medical history was hospitalized for chest pain. Upon admission, the patient was in extremely poor health: cachectic, weight 60 kg, height 170 cm, with severe microcytic iron-deficiency anaemia (Hb 68, MCV 61, Fe 3) and reactive thrombocytosis (trc 518). The first electrocardiogram (ECG) showed lateral STEMI (slight ST elevation in D1, aVL, slight ST depression in inferior leads, hyperacute T-waves in the anterior wall).

Approximately three hours after admission, the pain subsided completely, and ECG returned to normal. Due to severe anaemia, complete regression of pain and ECG changes, emergency coronary angiography was not performed. Anaemia was corrected with erythrocyte concentrate with control level of Hb up to 95, patient received pantoprazol 40 mg IV, ASA 100 mg orally and no low molecular weight heparin.

On the third day after admission, the patient developed respiratory arrest with bradycardia. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (only chest compression) was immediately initiated. After a short time, the patient restored a sinus rhythm up to 88/min, systemic blood pressure up to 110/60 mmHg and spontaneous breathing. Then we noticed short runs of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, one paroxysm of atrial fibrillation on telemetry, apicolateral hypokinesia on echocardiography, total left ventricular ejection fraction preserved and no significant valvular pathology, so we decided to perform coronary angiography.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: on the third day after admission

evidence_events.source_span: Coronary angiography was performed via right transfemoral access without periprocedural heparin. We found the first diagonal branch (D1) occlusion, left anterior descending (LAD) and trifurcation branch (RI) irregularities, normal circumflex (ACx) and normal right coronary artery (RCA).

Based on the findings (smaller blood vessel and small supply area), stabilized clinical condition of the patient and due to anaemia of unknown aetiology and the fact that the continuation of dual antiplatelet therapy if we perform PCI would be required, we opted for a conservative treatment. Only ASA was continued, without heparin.
Forty-eight hours after the first coronary angiography, the patient experienced severe chest pain. ECG showed lateral STEMI with diffuse ST depression in most other leads.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: forty-eight hours after first coronary angiography

evidence_events.source_span: Emergency coronary angiography was re-initiated through the right transfemoral access. In addition to the previously known D1 occlusion, thrombotic occlusion of the RI and thrombotic lesion in the left main coronary artery (LMCA) ostium were found.
PCI of the RI and afterwards LMCA were performed with periprocedural heparin (7000 units intra-arterial). One drug eluting stent (DES) was implanted in the RI and one DES in the LMCA ostium.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: PCI with stent implantation and heparin administration

evidence_events.source_span: Towards the end of the procedure, the patient became restless, showed signs of motor dysphasia and developed left hemiplegia. Emergency MSCT of the head excluded haemorrhage. Computed tomography angiography revealed occlusion of the right internal carotid artery (ICA) above the bifurcation.

An attempt of mechanical thrombectomy was indicated in consultation with a neurologist and an interventional neuroradiologist. Within three hours from the onset of neurological deficits, cerebral angiography was performed and an occlusion of the terminal part of the right ICA was found.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: within three hours from neurological deficit onset
evidence_events.procedural_cue: cerebral angiography and mechanical thrombectomy performed

evidence_events.source_span: After multiple manipulations, a solid embolus was aspirated using a wide aspiration catheter. A follow-up angiogram showed TICI 2c flow and stenosis of the M1 segment of the right middle cerebral artery (MCA), which persisted even after balloon angioplasty. Atlas stent was implanted into the lesion. A follow-up angiogram showed TICI 2c flow distal to the implanted stent.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: aspiration of embolus, balloon angioplasty, stent implantation

evidence_events.source_span: CT of the brain parenchyma did not show marked ischemic lesions immediately after the stenting of the MCA.

Immediately after the stenting of the MCA, the patient periprocedurally received IV 400 mg ASA and IA bolus 20 mL of eptifibatide. Treatment was continued in the neurological intensive care unit with ASA 100 mg daily orally and ticagrelor 180 mg daily orally added after admission. Eptifibatide infusion was then discontinued. The initial neurological deficit started to recover. The patient was cardiologically completely stable.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: immediately after MCA stenting and during ICU stay

evidence_events.source_span: Sixteen hours after the stenting of the MCA, the patient became somnolent, unable to verbally communicate, with deterioration of motor function of left extremities leading to hemiplegia again. Follow-up CT of the brain showed acute ischemia in the supply area of the right MCA with indirect signs of thrombotic stent occlusion in the MCA.

Then we noticed short runs of nonsustained ventricular tachycardia, one paroxysm of atrial fibrillation on telemetry, apicolateral hypokinesia on echocardiography, total left ventricular ejection fraction preserved and no significant valvular pathology, so we decided to perform coronary angiography. It was performed via right transfemoral access without periprocedural heparin. We found the first diagonal branch (D1) occlusion, left anterior descending (LAD) and trifurcation branch (RI) irregularities, normal circumflex (ACx) and normal right coronary artery (RCA).

source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case report and clinical narrative sections only.

evidence_events.source_span: A 79-year-old female complained with right limb involuntary activities for 1 day. The activity was aggravated during the day and decreased to disappear during sleep.
She had a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus for more than 18 years with poor blood glucose control. Her mother and brother also had a history of diabetes.

Physical examination: vital signs were temperature 36.5°C, blood pressure 165/95 mm Hg, respiratory rate 18/min, pulse 85 beats/min, oxygen saturation 99% on ambient air. Neurological exam: somnolent with fluent speech, pupils equal and reactive, extra ocular movements normal, face symmetrical, tongue midline, left muscle tension and strength normal, right upper and lower limb muscle tension decreased with dance-like movements, left coordination stable, other physical exam normal.

Laboratory tests showed random blood glucose was 33.3 mmol/L, glycosylated hemoglobin was 17.85%, urinary sugar 4+, urinary ketone negative. Further studies including EEG, cerebrospinal fluid analysis, serum and urine copper, ceruloplasmin, iron, ferritin, and antinuclear antibodies were unremarkable. Ophthalmologic consultation did not find Kayser-Fleischer ring.
Computed tomography of her head was negative for cerebral infarction, cerebral hemorrhage, or brain tumor in the basal ganglia.

Brain MRI on the second day of symptoms: T1, T2, and diffusion weighted imaging were normal; ADC showed low signals in the left basal ganglia and high signals in E-ADC in the same part. The ADC value of left basal ganglia was 413×10⁻⁶ mm²/s, while contralateral side was normal at 857×10⁻⁶ mm²/s.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: on the second day of symptom

evidence_events.source_span: After admission, the patient was diagnosed with non-ketotic hyperglycemic chorea; intravenous infusion of insulin was given to reduce blood glucose, and intramuscular injection of 5 mg haloperidol per day for 3 days.

After 3 days, the dance-like movement gradually decreased, and movement range was reduced compared to before. After oral haloperidol 2 mg twice a day, the right limb chorea gradually disappeared after 4 days.
After a week, head MRI was reviewed: the low signals of ADC and E-ADC were improved compared to before. The ADC value of left basal ganglia was 625×10⁻⁶ mm²/s, contralateral side 842×10⁻⁶ mm²/s.

source_metadata.title: A case of acute embolic stroke resulting from endocarditis and aortic aneurysm concurrent with aortic dissection in a healthy young patient: a case report
source_metadata.notes: Extraction based on case report narrative sections only, preserving source order and granularity.

evidence_events.source_span: A 31-year-old Gilaks male was admitted owing to fever and chills; he was a nonsmoker and nondiabetic with no history of hypertension, connective tissue disorders, congenital diseases, or cardiovascular diseases.
Vital signs on admission: blood pressure 100/60 mmHg; heart rate 100 bpm; temperature 38 °C; respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute.

Initial lab tests showed elevated ESR (107 mm/hour), leukocytosis (WBC 11.1 × 10^3/UL), anemia (Hb 10 mg/dL), elevated LDH (789 U/L), elevated CK-MB (30 IU/L), mild hyponatremia (Na 133 mEq/L), and other biochemistry and hematology abnormalities.
During hospitalization, the patient developed neurological symptoms including facial nerve palsy, diplopia, dysarthria, and seizures; NIHSS score was 8.
Brain MRI revealed multiple cortical infarcts in bilateral corona radiata, superior branch of middle cerebral artery, left thalamus, and centrum semiovale.
Cardiac echocardiography revealed an aortic aneurysm measuring 7.7 cm in diameter.

Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) showed EF 40–45%, very severe aortic aneurysm (6.9 cm), mild mitral regurgitation, minimal tricuspid regurgitation, mild pulmonary insufficiency, pulmonary artery pressure 50 mmHg, severe left ventricle enlargement with mild systolic dysfunction, a large (1.1 cm) semi-mobile mass on the arterial side of the noncoronary cusp resembling vegetation, very severe aortic regurgitation, aneurysmal aortic root with effacement of sinotubular junction, aneurysmal dilation of ascending aorta, visible linear flap of aortic dissection originating 1.3 cm after the aortic valve, thickened and infected dissecting flap, and mild circumferential pericardial effusion.
Based on TEE findings indicating endocarditis, aortic aneurysm, and aortic dissection, the patient was transferred for emergent Bentall surgery.
Bentall procedure was performed replacing the aortic valve, ascending aorta, and root with a mechanical composite graft; postoperative ICU admission and initiation of warfarin therapy.
Postoperative antibiotic therapy continued with ciprofloxacin, ampicillin/sulbactam, and vancomycin in the infectious ward.

At discharge, lab tests showed WBC 4000 × 10^3/UL, platelets 327,000 × 10^3/UL, INR 2.6, sodium 145 mEq/L, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, hemoglobin 9.10 mg/dL, and potassium 3.7 mEq/L; patient was discharged on warfarin, bisoprolol, acetylsalicylic acid, captopril, spironolactone, and pantoprazole.

Follow-up neurology clinic visits showed stable neurological and cardiac condition; NIHSS score improved to 3 with partial resolution of visual field defect and facial palsy, speech disturbance remained, and ataxia resolved.

evidence_events.source_span: 15-year-old girl from a consanguineous family of south Tunisian origin admitted with a 4-month history of increasing chronic holocranial headache, nocturnal and continuous for 45 days, aggravated by visual blurring

Previous medical history of paroxysmal hallucinations treated with haloperidol and venlafaxine; no oral contraceptives, no severe illnesses, no family history of cancer, bleeding, or thrombotic disease

On admission, conscious, normal blood pressure and temperature, alert with bilateral papilledema, reduced visual acuity unable to count fingers, intact cranial nerves and gag reflex, unremarkable sensory testing, no abnormalities in lungs, heart, abdomen

Blood count and coagulation tests: hematocrit 32.2%, hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL, WBC 6500/mm3, platelet count 544,000/mm3, prothrombin time 14.7 s, aPTT 38 s, fibrinogen 260 mg/dL, random blood sugar 57 mg/dL; liver function, serum calcium, electrolytes, and urea unremarkable; not pregnant
Lumbar puncture with normal opening pressure; cerebrospinal fluid analysis excluded infectious CNS disease and subarachnoid hemorrhage
Cranial CT scan unremarkable brain parenchyma; MRI with gadolinium revealed linear filling defect in superior sagittal sinus confirming venous thrombosis

Tests for acquired and inherited thrombophilia: anticardiolipin and antiphospholipid antibodies negative; plasma homocysteine normal; protein C 97%, protein S 84%, antithrombin 82%; activated protein C resistance negative; D-dimers elevated at 1227 ng/mL (normal <500)
evidence_events.procedural_cue: enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay and coagulation assays

evidence_events.source_span: Genetic testing for factor V Leiden (FVL), prothrombin G20210A, and MTHFR C677T mutations: negative for prothrombin and MTHFR mutations; homozygous for FVL mutation
Treatment with intravenous heparin followed by 6-month coumarin course led to complete resolution of CVT; 3-year follow-up showed no complaints, normal neurological exam, and intact visual acuity

source_metadata.title: An unexpected case of Ramsay hunt syndrome: case report and literature review

evidence_events.source_span: A 54-year-old Caucasian female, with no past medical history, developed right-sided neck pain on day 1.
On day 4, an erythematous, vesicular rash erupted at the site of pain.
She was diagnosed with contact dermatitis at a walk-in clinic.
Over days 4–9, she developed a right earache and headache and the rash spread to her upper right chest-wall.

On day 9, exam showed an erythematous, vesicular eruption on the right anterior chest, neck and shoulder (C2, C3 and C4 dermatomes). The rash halted at the midline (Figure 1). It was tender, warm and blanched when palpated.
The patient was diagnosed with herpes zoster (HZ) and secondary cellulitis. Valacyclovir, cephalexin and acetaminophen were started.
On day 12, she returned with right ear discomfort and difficulty hearing. Exam showed a similar rash along the auricle but the external auditory canal was normal.
Nortryptyline was started for neuralgia.
On day 14, she woke up with partial right-sided facial paralysis.
In the Emergency Room, RHS was diagnosed. Valacyclovir was extended to 10 days and prednisone started. A neuro-ophthalmology referral was made.
On day 46, the patient returned showing significant improvement. She could smile symmetrically and close her right eye completely.

source_metadata.title: Multifocal subdural hematomas as the presenting sign of acquired hemophilia A: a case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 25-year old Asian woman with a history of lupus presented to the emergency room with headaches not responding to over the counter analgesics.

She described the headaches as a gradual onset of intermittent 10/10 sharp right-sided head pain which lasted for several seconds only, and occurred multiple times per day. The pain occasionally spread to the right neck with a pulsating quality but without tinnitus. There was no postural component, no associated migrainous features, and no trigeminal autonomic symptoms. She occasionally had brief lower back spasmic-type pain with no radiation.
She did not have any symptoms of coagulopathy including easy bleeding, GI bleeds, epistaxis, or hemoptysis.

She was taking prednisone 15 mg daily and mycophenylate 500 mg BID (she had self-discontinued the mycophenylate 1 week prior to admission), and a family history significant for a sister who died of anemia of an unknown etiology at the age of 24.
Neurologic examination was unremarkable.
Brain MRI revealed bilateral infracerebellar and right pre-pontine extra-axial collections most consistent with hematomas.
Basic laboratory studies were significant for an isolated elevation of PTT at 74 with a normal CBC, chemistry panel, liver panel, INR, and urine toxicology screen.
Brain MR venogram showed no venous thrombosis, CT angiogram showed no vasculitis or aneurysms, and spinal MRI showed additional subdural hematomas in her cervical and lumbar regions.

evidence_events.source_span: Lupus anticoagulant testing was negative including anti-cardiolipin IgG and IgM, anti-beta-2-glycoprotein IgG and IgM, Russell Viper Venom Test, and confirmation testing.
Urine pregnancy testing was negative and she was not post-partum.

Infectious labs revealed a positive beta-D-glucan and negative galactomannan; bronchoalveolar lavage was positive only for candida and rare gram-positive cocci and negative for acid fast bacilli, other fungi, and viral cultures. Other infectious testing was negative including nasopharyngeal swab for influenza A and B, urine cultures, blood cultures, histoplasma antigen, and hepatitis panel.

source_metadata.title: Lymphomatosis cerebri: a treatable cause of rapidly progressive dementia
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case report section and figure 1 imaging data.

evidence_events.source_span: A 50-year-old previously fit and well lady with no vascular risk factors presented to her general practitioner with personality change and emotional lability, against a background of subacutely progressive amnestic syndrome over 3 weeks.
She next developed severe anxiety and insomnia and was commenced on citalopram and temazepam.

Neurological examination demonstrated universally brisk reflexes with no clonus and downgoing plantar responses. There was marked language difficulty with both expressive and receptive components and ideational and ideomotor apraxia.

Formal neuropsychometric testing showed marked impairment in memory, naming, literacy skills and information processing speed (all <5th centile) with relative preservation of executive functioning (phonemic fluency 25th–50th centile). Testing was consistent with marked and pervasive cognitive dysfunction affecting mainly posterior, cortical and subcortical regions.
Full blood count, C-reactive protein, ESR, renal and liver function tests were normal.
EEG showed left temporal irregular slowing with occasional low-voltage sharp waves suggestive of epileptiform activity.

MRI examination demonstrated extensive confluent areas of T2-weighted hyperintensity diffusely throughout the cerebrum and brainstem. There was no perceptible mass effect, abnormal post-gadolinum contrast enhancement nor restriction of diffusion of the diffusion weighted imaging sequences.

The following were normal or negative: JCV, HIV 1 and 2 and syphilis serology; plasma amino acids, white cell enzymes and very long chain fatty acids levels. Copper studies, coeliac screen, vitamin E levels, autoimmune antibody tests, serum lactate, pyruvate, phytanic and glutaric acid levels were also normal.

Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination showed a protein level of 0.74 g/L with a glucose of 3.2 mmol/L (serum 5.5 mmol/L), <1 white blood cell per millilitre and negative oligoclonal bands. CSF PCR for viruses including JC and HIV were also negative. CSF cytology showed a moderately cellular fluid with increased numbers of lymphocytes and macrophages with no atypical cells, consistent with a mild chronic inflammatory/reactive process.
Opthalmological screening revealed no evidence of vitreoretinal disease.
Her cognitive symptoms deteriorated over months to the point where she required 24 h nursing care due to significant confusion and anxiety.

A repeat MRI showed more extensive signal changes in the frontal, parietal, occipital and temporal lobes. This also involved the right corticospinal tract, resulting in symmetrical T2-weighted hyperintensity along the paired tracts through the capsular, mesencephalic, pontine and medullary regions. A further focus of T2-weighted hyperintensity was seen in the left cerebellar hemisphere. There was now patchy enhancement in the peritrigonal white matter bilaterally.
Given the rapid clinicoradiological progression and lack of diagnosis, a brain biopsy of an enhancing region in the left parietal lobe was performed.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: after rapid progression and lack of diagnosis

evidence_events.source_span: Histological examination showed diffuse and nodular infiltration of cerebrum by large atypical lymphoid cells. The cells showed nuclear pleomorphism and showed clusters around blood vessels and diffuse spread into the surrounding cortex. Further tests confirmed a diffuse large B cell lymphoma.
Following a bone marrow biopsy and PET/CT scan, no evidence of lymphoma outside the central nervous system was found.

Treatment commenced, including high-dose methotrexate, cytarabine and rituximab, followed by radiotherapy (40 Gy total). Repeat MRI showed significant improvement in the central nervous system disease and she also improved functionally, being discharged home without a package of care after previously needing 24 h nursing care.

Ten months later, functional status had not deteriorated and neuropsychometric testing was equivalent to that done several months prior to commencement of treatment, however remaining below premorbid estimates. Her gait and mobility also improved dramatically.

source_metadata.title: From arterial hypertension complications to von Hippel-Lindau syndrome diagnosis

evidence_events.source_span: The patient - a boy aged 14 with uncomplicated perinatal history underwent ophthalmic examination due to bilateral scotoma

Eye examination showed increased intraocular pressure and regions with retinal detachment, which in combination with elevated values of arterial hypertension (180/98 mmHg) indicated hypertensive retinopathy

Contrast computed tomography scan of the head showed a fluid-dense, non-contrast enhanced 3.5 × 2.5 × 4.0 cm area in the anterior part of the temporal lobe with thinned lamellae of adjacent bones corresponding to an arachnoid cyst; additional foci in right temporal lobe and cerebellar hemispheres

Increased arterial hypertension of approx. 180/135 mmHg and tachycardia ca.120/min; echocardiography showed hypertensive cardiomyopathy with grade II mitral regurgitation and left ventricular hypertrophy
Patient developed severe headaches with vomiting, tongue numbness, and paresthesia of upper and lower left limbs; head CT showed cerebral oedema

Abdominal ultrasound showed a 41 × 35 mm hypoechoic tissue lesion in the right adrenal gland without visible vascularization; left adrenal gland normal; Doppler ultrasound of aorta and renal arteries normal
Patient history revealed periodic bouts of anxiety accompanied by skin pallor and excessive sweating, typical symptoms of phaeochromocytoma

Laboratory tests showed elevated glucose (143 mg/dl), hypokalemia (3.19 mmol/l), hypocalcaemia (8.2 mg/dl); 4-fold assays of catecholamines in serum showed very high noradrenaline with normal adrenaline; 24-hour urine catecholamines and methoxycatecholamines substantially elevated
Neuron-specific enolase and calcitonin levels normal; thyroid ultrasound normal to exclude neuroblastoma and MEN 2
Abdominal CT scan confirmed a 50 × 40 × 52 mm nodular lesion in the right adrenal gland and a smaller 24 mm lesion in the left adrenal gland
131 I-MIBG isotopic scintigraphy showed increased tracer accumulation in both adrenal glands, larger in the right adrenal gland

Bilateral adrenalectomy performed; right adrenal gland showed a 5-cm solid-cystic tumour and a 1.5-cm solid tumour; microscopic image consistent with phaeochromocytoma; immunohistochemistry chromogranin A (+), synaptophysin (+), Ki67 3-4%, PASS score 1 (capsule invasion); left adrenal gland had a 2.7-cm encapsulated tumour consistent with phaeochromocytoma, Ki67 <2%, PASS score 0
Genetic test showed a mutation in the VHL ex.1 p.Y112 C gene responsible for hereditary phaeochromocytoma confirming von Hippel-Lindau syndrome

20 months after surgery, patient is asymptomatic with normal arterial tension and heart rate; follow-up abdominal and thyroid ultrasonography normal; 131 I-MIBG scintigraphy 8 months post-surgery showed no abnormal tracer accumulation; catecholamines and methoxycatecholamines in 24-h urine normal; ophthalmic exams showed regression of previous changes and improved vision; CNS MRI showed no abnormalities except arachnoid cyst; slight left ventricular hypertrophy persists

source_metadata.title: A Case of Tuberous Sclerosis Without Multiorgan Involvement
source_metadata.notes: Case report of a 15-year-old female with intellectual disability, seizures, dermatologic findings, and brain MRI findings consistent with tuberous sclerosis complex without multiorgan involvement.

evidence_events.source_span: A 15-year-old female with intellectual disability, who was referred to the Tabriz Dentistry Hospital with chief complaint of dental caries and tooth pain. She is followed up at neurology clinic for history of seizure and takes Carbamazepine and Phenobarbital.
She had wart like lesions distributed in form of butterfly over the face especially involving nose.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: She started to develop these wart like lesions on her face at the age 7

evidence_events.source_span: Multiple fibromatous lesions characterized with popular, sessile, flat, firm consistency, sized 1×1×1cm dimension are also found in inner folds of hair.
She had 2×2 cm hypomelanotic lesions (ash leaf spot) on her back.

She did not have any sign and symptom of heart, kidney, lung, bone and eye involvement such as retinal hamartomas, micronodular multifocal pneumocyte hyperplasia, cardiac rhabdomyomas, lymphangioleiomyomatosis, angiomyolipomas, uterine leiomyomas and sclerotic bone lesions.
Her laboratory tests were normal.
The panoramic radiography showed that teeth had old filling or need endodontic treatment, because of hypoplastic enamel or intellectual disability and epilepsy with poor oral hygiene.

Despite the physical examination showed absolutely intact neurologic examination, brain MRI and CT scan revealed several cortical and subcortical tubers, and subependymal glial nodules; no evidence of giant cell astrocytomas and aneurysm.

source_metadata.title: Case report: subacute tetraplegia in an immunocompromised patient

evidence_events.source_span: Six weeks after stem cell transplant for myelodysplastic syndrome, a 51 year old caucasian patient developed a high-grade pure motor flaccid tetraparesis within a few days.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: Six weeks after stem cell transplant

evidence_events.source_span: While cognitive and brainstem functions – including the function of facial muscles – were preserved, the patient was tetraplegic except for minimal finger movements of the left hand. The deep tendon reflexes were absent, and Babinski testing revealed mute soles on both sides. There was considerable generalized muscle atrophy which had already been noticed at first neurological assessment five days before transplant.

Development of tetraparesis within several days along with absent deep tendon reflexes might be indicative of GBS. However, the simultaneous and generalized rather than ascending development of tetraparesis is uncommon in GBS. In addition, ongoing strong immunosuppression by cyclosporine A and mycophenolate mofetil made the new occurrence of an autoimmune disorder unlikely. Therefore, taking into account that the patient had been treated in ICU for pneumonia with respiratory failure before, critical illness polyneuromyopathy was suspected.

A few days later, however, an acute confusional state prompted brain MRI. Fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) imaging revealed symmetrical hyperintensities strictly limited to the subcortical precentral gyrus. Correspondingly, diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) showed signal hyperintensity, along with normal ADC and without any contrast enhancement. Six days before transplant, the patient had received cranial MRI without any pathological finding.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: A few days later; Six days before transplant

evidence_events.source_span: Stroke, for example due to cardiac embolism, was not supported by normal ADC. “Stroke mimics” with positive DWI, but without lesion hypointensity on the ADC map, include active MS plaques, cerebral abscess, and viral encephalitis. The spatial pattern of the MRI lesions appeared virtually incompatible with MS, and the absence of a mass effect or rim enhancement rendered bacterial cerebritis or cerebral abscesses very unlikely.

Subacute development of tetraparesis along with new subcortical lesions in an immunocompromised patient were highly suggestive of infection by or reactivation of neurotropic viruses. Sole motor affection may make poliovirus highly suspicious, particularly in the light of recent reports of polio cases in Germany. However, given the patient’s vaccination against polio virus, this differential diagnosis was considered rather unlikely.

Spinal tap revealed a normal cell count (1 leucocyte/mm3, normal range 0–4) along with slightly elevated protein (56.2 mg/dl, normal ≤50) and albumine (50.9 mg/dl, normal ≤35). CSF PCR was negative for herpes simplex virus type 1/2, varizella zoster virus, Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, human herpes virus six, JC virus, adenovirus, enterovirus, poliovirus, and bacterial DNA (universal primer). However, repeat serum PCR for CMV showed a progressively increasing number of up to 8,600 copies/ml, starting shortly prior to the development of tetraparesis.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: shortly prior to the development of tetraparesis

evidence_events.source_span: Sensitivity of CSF PCR for CMV encephalitis is generally believed to be high, yet unequal to 100%. Moreover, CSF virus PCR might initially be false-negative, with increasing probability of a positive PCR when there is a time frame of 3 – 14 days between symptom onset and lumbar puncture. Therefore, while the laboratory findings were unable to prove CMV encephalitis, they were compatible with this suspected diagnosis.

Intravenous ganciclovir treatment (5 mg per kg per day over two weeks) was initiated. Over the following three weeks, serum PCR for CMV turned negative. Tetraparesis slowly improved, with still moderate pareses of the upper (between MRC 3 and 4), but severe pareses of the lower (between MRC 1 and 2) extremities at neurological reassessment four weeks after symptom onset.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: Over the following three weeks; four weeks after symptom onset

evidence_events.source_span: In the further course the patient developed a septic syndrome, most likely owing to a pulmonary focus, and exspired due to septic multiple organ failure. Autopsy was prohibited.

source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case narrative sections Patient and observation, Introduction, Discussion.

evidence_events.source_span: 20 years old patient resident in Senegal with no known medical history
abrupt onset of left body side weakness five days before admission preceded by acute headaches and rotatory vertigo without nausea or vomiting
Physical examination found paralysis of right oculomotor movements, right facial palsy, and left hemiparesis sparing the face
brain CT scan shown spontaneous hemorrhage in the right pontine’s posterolateral part compressing the fourth ventricle
Etiological investigations done to determine the cause of this hemorrhagic stroke remain non contributives

Our patient presented hemorrhagic stroke of the right posterolateral part of the pons corresponding to the right lower tegmentum

source_metadata.title: Pituitary abscess

evidence_events.source_span: A 20-year-old Bahraini man presented to accident and emergency department in Salmaniya Medical Complex in March 2016 complaining of headache which he described as severe, continuous and exacerbated with exposure to bright light. In addition, he complained of photosensitivity, nausea, left eye blurred vision and generalised body fatigue.
These symptoms were worsening over a month period of time. He denied history of limb weakness, abnormal movements or seizure, loss of consciousness or sensory manifestations.

MRI brain showed presence of heterogeneously hyperintense lesion on T2-weighted images with peripheral hypointensity and not suppressed on fluid-attenuated inversion recovery images. The optic chiasm was compressed and displaced superiorly by the lesion. Both cavernous sinuses were mildly compressed with sparing of internal carotid artery blood flow. T1 images with no contrast showed fluid level.
MRI findings suggested macroadenoma of pituitary gland (size 1.8×1.5×1.3 cm) with haemorrhage and a mass effect on optic chiasm.
Pituitary hormonal assessment showed central hypogonadism, central hypoadrenalism, normal thyroid function and mildly elevated level of prolactin.
Patient gave history of loss of libido, failure of erection, polyuria and polydipsia but denied any gynaecomastia or change in body part size.
On examination, patient did not show any cranial nerve, limb or gait abnormalities. There was no thyromegaly or signs of acromegaly. A chest X-ray done was normal.

Intraoperatively, thick capsule of abscess incised with yellowish pus was drained. The cavity was cleaned and irrigated with antibiotics and saline. The pus was sent for Gram stain, culture, acid-fast bacilli (AFB) stain and histopathological evaluation. The pituitary was not removed.

Histopathology showed features suggestive of inflammatory lesion possibly an abscess. There is no evidence of pituitary adenoma in this small and partly compressed biopsy. The Gram stain showed few WBC and a sterile culture. AFB stain did not show any acid fast bacilli.
Postoperatively, patient was commenced on metronidazole, ceftriaxone and vancomycin for 6 weeks. He was doing well with improvement in symptoms and normal functional status.

Patient continued to have pituitary insufficiency on follow-up and was treated with oral hydrocortisone. Follow-up MRI showed no more enhancing residual abscess pockets within the pituitary fossa suggesting complete resolution.

evidence_milestones.source_span: Intraoperatively, thick capsule of abscess incised with yellowish pus was drained. The cavity was cleaned and irrigated with antibiotics and saline. The pus was sent for Gram stain, culture, acid-fast bacilli (AFB) stain and histopathological evaluation. The pituitary was not removed. Histopathology showed features suggestive of inflammatory lesion possibly an abscess. There is no evidence of pituitary adenoma in this small and partly compressed biopsy. The Gram stain showed few WBC and a sterile culture. AFB stain did not show any acid fast bacilli.

The patient had a lumbar punction; the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) showed moderate pleocytosis (140 leucocytes/μL with a mononuclear cell dominance).

Several days later, intrathecal IgM and IgG antibodies came back positive.

source_metadata.title: An adult case with shigellosis-associated encephalopathy

evidence_events.source_span: A 45-year-old man was presented at the emergency department with altered neurological status and a 1-day history of diarrhoea and fever

Physical examination showed a lethargic patient with a temperature of 39.5°C, blood pressure of 100/50 mm Hg and a pulse of 104/min; he was confused and disorientated, unable to speak nor to perform any assignments; abdomen was soft and non-tender with normal bowel sounds; other physical examination revealed no abnormalities
Bacterial meningitis or viral encephalitis were suspected and antibiotic and antiviral therapy was started accordingly; ceftriaxone, amoxicillin and acyclovir intravenously
CT brain scan showed no sign of cerebral bleeding or hydrocephalus

Cerebrospinal fluid revealed mild pleiocytosis of 8×10⁶ cells/L with normal glucose and protein levels; bacterial culture and PCR for enterovirus, herpes simplex virus type 1 and 2 and varicella zoster virus were negative
C reactive protein in serum was 210 mg/L with decreased leucocyte count of 2.4×10⁹ cells/L; serum creatinine levels were elevated with 136 µmol/L
Stool culture showed Shigella flexneri, sensitive to ceftriaxone, resistant to ciprofloxacin and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole
The patient tested negative for HIV

Further blood investigation revealed normal calcium, thyroid-stimulating hormone and slight hyponatraemia (130 mmol/L) and hypokalaemia (3.4 mmol/L), all of which could not explain his neurological status
Sepsis was considered unlikely since blood cultures remained negative, blood pressure was within normal limits and serum lactate levels were normal

After negative PCR results of the CSF, acyclovir was stopped; fluid resuscitation and potassium supplementation were given; neurological status recovered within 36 hours after start of ceftriaxone intravenously
Normalisation of sodium levels occurred within 24 hours and potassium levels normalised within 48 hours, after which fluid resuscitation was stopped
Three days after admission and start of intravenous antibiotic treatment, the patient was discharged with recovery except for some memory problems at follow-up several weeks later

source_metadata.title: Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection presenting as stroke and meningoencephalitis with aortic and subclavian aneurysms without pulmonary involvement
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from BMJ Case Reports 2018 article, case report sections used for evidence ordering.

evidence_events.source_span: A 39-year-old Philipino man presented with acute-onset, moderate-grade, intermittent fever, bifrontal dull aching headache, neck pain, vomiting, lethargy, and neck stiffness with positive Kernig's sign; no respiratory symptoms.
Neurological examination was normal except for neck stiffness and positive Kernig's sign; no cranial nerve, motor, sensory, or cerebellar deficits initially.
A week after hospitalisation, he developed acute right-sided weakness with mild upper motor neuron facial weakness and mild dysarthria without aphasia.
Complete blood count showed hemoglobin 13.9 mg/dL, platelet count 450,000/μL, WBC 10,700/μL with 86% neutrophils, ESR 35 mm/hour.

CSF analysis showed mild protein increase (52 mg/dL), normal sugar (80 mg/dL), 58 WBCs with 92% lymphocytes, negative gram stain and culture, negative PCR for herpes simplex and varicella zoster virus.
Chest X-ray was normal.
MRI showed acute infarct in the left centrum semiovale (figure 1A, B).
Conventional angiogram showed aneurysms in the left subclavian artery and aortic arch (figure 2).

Mycoplasma pneumoniae IgM antibody was positive with a titre of 1:100 (positive ≥1:80), IgG titre was 1:120; IgG titre increased to 1:320 after 2 weeks and decreased to 1:80 after 3 months; rest of the workup was negative.

He was initially treated with ceftriaxone and acyclovir, which were stopped after negative CSF PCR; aspirin was started after stroke; azithromycin was started after positive mycoplasma antibody and continued for 5 days.
He became afebrile, headache subsided, sensorium improved, and neurological deficits completely resolved; asymptomatic at 1-month and 3-month follow-up.

source_metadata.title: Dyke-Davidoff-Masson syndrome: a case report
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from BMC Neurology 2018 case report, PMCID 5972440

evidence_events.source_span: A 13-year-old girl presented to us for further management of episodic complex-partial seizures and right hemiparesis.
She initially had episodes of headaches starting at the age of 7. Mother noticed that she had accompanying right sided weakness; which prompted medical attention.
Initial evaluation revealed power of 4/5 on the right side, with reduced sensation and brisk reflexes. Minimal facial asymmetry was evident.
A head CT was done, which revealed left parieto-temporal infarct, with cerebral atrophy.
Complementary MRI was of no significant additional value.
Workup for young stroke, which included protein S, protein C, anti-thrombin III, anti-phospholipid antibody, anti-cardiolipin antibody, and lupus anticoagulant were negative.

One year after the initial presentation, her mother noticed new onset of brief moments of the child mumbling followed by blank stare and drowsiness, prior regaining consciousness. She was diagnosed as having complex-partial seizures, and initiated on syrup sodium valproate 200 mg bd.

Upon further evaluation of the previous imaging studies, in addition to the left sided infarct, we noticed that the left cerebral hemisphere was universally atrophic with ventricular enlargement. There was also evidence of calvarial thickening on the ipsilateral side, and hyperpneumatization of the left frontal sinus.
A final diagnosis of DDMS was made.
Patient has been on regular Neurology follow up since.

source_metadata.title: Hypothalamic relapse of a cardiac large B-cell lymphoma presenting with memory loss, confabulation, alexia–agraphia, apathy, hypersomnia, appetite disturbances and diabetes insipidus

evidence_events.source_span: In 2007, a 37-year-old Hispanic man presented with symptoms of haemodynamic cardiac compromise and was found to have a cardiac mass invading the right atrium and mediastinum.

MRI of the chest showed a large right heart mass (8.4×7.4×7.6 cm) centred at the lateral aspect of the right heart near the atrioventricular plane extending inside the cardiac lumen and outside into the pericardial and epicardial fat. The tricuspid valve was deformed by the mass.

Initial FDG-PET scan showed normal tracer uptake in the brain, nasopharynx, oropharynx, larynx and adjacent structures, including the sternocleidomastoid muscles, without the presence of pathological lymph nodes in the neck.

The patient underwent median sternotomy, atrial tumour debulking and tricuspid valve replacement. DLBCL was diagnosed and he completed eight cycles of chemotherapy (R-CHOP) followed by involved field radiotherapy.

About 1 month after completing his radiation therapy, tumour recurrence in the mediastinum was found and he was reinduced with chemotherapy (R-ESHAP) receiving two cycles followed by consolidative high-dose chemotherapy (BEAM) and autologous stem cell support.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: About 1 month after completing radiation therapy

evidence_events.source_span: The patient was followed for 4 years with several total-body FDG-PET, CT and MRI scans that showed no extracardiac location of the lymphoma and no evidence of disease recurrence after his bone marrow transplant.

In 2012, 5 years after initial presentation of the lymphoma, the patient’s family reported that for the past 3 months, he had exhibited marked memory deficits for recent events, severe daytime sleepiness and behavioural changes such as apathy, loss of interest, lack of energy and hyperphagia.

On examination, the patient was a 42-year-old obese man with normal vital signs. His level of arousal fluctuated with brief periods of alertness followed by intermittent sleep attacks. He knew his name but was disoriented to time and space. He spoke slowly, showed poor recall and confabulated. No focal neurological findings were present.

CT scan demonstrated a mass in the third ventricle. Brain MRI confirmed a 21×26×25 mm uniform enhancing mass involving the anterior–inferior portion of the third ventricle and adjacent structures, including the hypothalamus, with suprasellar extension. There was no hydrocephalus.

The lymphoma in the heart and mediastinal lymph nodes resected in 2007 was a DLBCL. By flow cytometry, the lymphoma expressed CD10, CD19, CD20 and CD79b with kappa light chain restriction and was EBV negative. In 2012, the brain biopsy pathology showed that the tumour was recurrent DLBCL with similar immunophenotype confirming cerebral relapse of the PCL.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: flow cytometry and brain biopsy pathology

evidence_events.source_span: The patient was successfully reinduced with high-dose methotrexate resulting in disappearance of the brain mass.

On several occasions, he was admitted for treatment of electrolyte disturbances with hypernatraemia from diabetes insipidus. Desmopressin treatment optimised sodium levels and hydration, but despite successful lymphoma treatment, his altered mental status persisted.

In 2013, neuropsychological evaluation showed persistent memory loss, confabulation, sleepiness, abulia, apathy and crying spells. EEG showed sleep attacks with fluctuating attention. Patient was disoriented to time, space and person. Neuropsychological performance indicated global cognitive loss and executive dysfunction consistent with moderate to severe dementia.
MRI in 2014 showed no evidence of the hypothalamic mass; the previous hypothalamic mass had disappeared and no definite enhancing lesions were appreciated.

He presented apathy, depression and pseudobulbar crying spells; he received treatment with dextromethorphan–quinidine and sertraline with improvement of these symptoms. Obstructive sleep apnoea was demonstrated and treated with nasal continuous positive airway pressure resulting in control of excessive daytime sleepiness.

He was last seen in 2017, 10 years after onset of cardiac symptoms and 5 years after CNS relapse; there was no evidence of tumour recurrence. He had returned to gainful manual work despite persistence of amnesia and inability to read and write.

source_metadata.title: Limbic encephalitis associated with leucine-rich glioma-inactivated 1 antibodies
source_metadata.notes: Case report of a 59-year-old man with limbic encephalitis and LGI1 antibodies, including clinical, lab, imaging, immunologic, and treatment evidence.

evidence_events.source_span: A 59-year-old man was received in the Department of Neurology with a 5-month history of gradually worsening behavior disturbances, insomnia, short-term memory impairment, disorientation, visual hallucinations, myoclonus, and faciobrachial dystonic seizures (FBDS) that frequently cause the dropping of objects.

His medical history was significant for vitiligo that had appeared 2 years ago on his hands, neck, and back. He also suffered from verruca seborrhoica on his back and gastroesophageal reflux disease. Diabetes was diagnosed 2 months prior to admission and rapidly required insulin therapy. The patient was a user of neither illicit drugs nor alcohol.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: 2 years ago, 2 months prior to admission

evidence_events.source_span: During the last 3 months, he had been treated with antiepileptic drugs (AEDs) (sodium valproate, lamotrigine, and diazepam), but the treatments were ineffective and the seizures continued.

On admission, he appeared to be confused, drowsy, disoriented in time and place, and had a marked impairment of short-term memory. He scored 15/30 on the Folstein mini-mental state examination (MMSE). During his examination, a notable number of FBDS occurred. They were brief (5 seconds) but very frequent, occurring 30 to 50 times per day. FBDS involved the arm, the ipsilateral face, and occasionally the ipsilateral leg. These seizures were often triggered by severe emotional stress. A neurological exam also revealed asymmetric akinetic-rigid syndrome and bilateral palmomental reflexes.
A brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed no hippocampal lesions.
The electroencephalogram (EEG) showed disorganization and slowing of background activity without periodic synchronous discharges.

Initially, the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) findings were normal. A second lumbar puncture showed an elevation of total protein (0.91 g/L) but a normal white cell count (0/μL). The CSF concentration of protein 14-3-3 was normal.

Serologies for human immunodeficiency virus, herpes simplex virus, Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, varicella zoster virus, hepatitis B and C viruses, syphilis, brucellosis, Lyme, as well as mycobacteria in blood and CSF were all negative. Polymerase chain reaction detection for the polyomavirus BK was also negative.
Other studies including a cholesterol panel and blood tests to determine homocysteine, folate, and B12 levels as well as thyroid function were all normal.

Hyponatremia (116 mmol/L [normal range 135–145 mmol/L]), hypochloremia (84 mEq/L), hyperglycemia, and elevated glycated hemoglobin were noted. The diagnosis of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (ADH) release was first suggested. Other causes of hyponatremia were excluded.

Immunologic tests (antinuclear antibody, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, antithyroglobulin antibody, antimicrosomal [antiperoxidase] antibody, anti-endomysial antibody, anticardiolipin antibodies, antiphospholipid antibodies) were all negative. His antineuronal paraneoplastic antibodies (anti-Hu, anti-Yo, anti-Ri, anti-PNMA2, anti-amphiphysin), antibodies to N-methyl-D-aspartate receptors, and antiglutamic acid decarboxylase were also negative.

High titers of serum anti-voltage-gated potassium channel (VGKC)-complex antibodies were found (678.3 pmol/L [positive > 85 pmol/L]), leading to the definitive diagnosis of VGKC-complex antibody LE. LGI1 antibodies were identified as the specific antigenic target within the VGKC-complex. Anti-contactin-associated protein-like 2 (CASPR2) antibodies were negative.
Computed tomography (CT) of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis revealed intraductal papillary mucinous neoplasia of the pancreas (IPMN) with no signs of malignancy which was confirmed by MRI.

Serum carbohydrate antigen 19-9, carcinoembryonic antigen, alpha-fetoprotein, and prostate specific antigen were all normal. Markedly elevated neuron-specific enolase (NSE) was detected (NSE=125.3 μg/L [normal <16.3]). The bronchial fibroscopy was normal.

The initial treatment consisted of slow correction of the hyponatremia via fluid restriction followed by administration of isotonic saline. It led to a slight cognitive improvement. Other AEDs were utilized. Phenytoin, piracetam, and levetiracetam proved ineffective. Carbamazepine led to significant side effects of a localized rash appearing on his face and neck and was then interrupted. Methylprednisolone was contraindicated since his diabetes was not equilibrated.

He was started on immunotherapy with intravenous immunoglobulin (0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days). After 1 month, the patient responded to this treatment becoming seizure free and showing significant improvement in his cognitive state. He achieved an MMSE score of 27/30.

initial_presentation.chief_complaint: recurrent aseptic meningitis first presenting 18 years ago
initial_presentation.first_contact_summary: The patient had 121 episodes of recurrent aseptic meningitis starting 18 years prior, with prior history of recurrent urticaria and arthralgia since age 30; episodes started occurring several times a year from age 53 with preceding low-grade fever, general fatigue, arthralgia and urticaria then high fever and headache; white blood cell count and C reactive protein levels were normal or mildly elevated during meningitis; cerebrospinal fluid showed >1000 polymorphonuclear leucocytes/mm3; no bacteria, fungi, or mycobacteria cultured; PCR negative for herpesviruses and enteroviruses; urticarial biopsy showed neutrophil infiltration; corticosteroids shortened attack duration but did not prevent recurrence; colchicine trial without evidence of familial Mediterranean fever; genetic analysis showed no mutations in MEFV, MVK, TNFRSF1A, NLRP3 or NLRP12

source_metadata.title: Recurrent aseptic meningitis with PIGT mutations: a novel pathogenesis of recurrent meningitis successfully treated by eculizumab

evidence_events.source_span: A 71-year-old man had experienced a total of 121 episodes of recurrent aseptic meningitis that first presented 18 years ago
Prior to the episodes of meningitis, he had a history of recurrent urticaria and arthralgia since he was 30 years old
Low-grade fever, general fatigue, arthralgia and urticaria preceded the episodes, and high fever and headache ensued the next day
White blood cell count and C reactive protein levels were normal or mildly elevated during the meningitis period

Examination of the lumbar cerebrospinal fluid demonstrated >1000 polymorphonuclear leucocytes/mm3; no bacteria, fungi or mycobacteria were cultured; PCR tests were negative for herpesviruses and enteroviruses
A biopsy from urticarial lesion showed neutrophil infiltration
Symptoms of meningitis recovered spontaneously 7–10 days after its onset; corticosteroid administration shortened the duration but was not effective in preventing the attacks
Genetic analysis revealed no mutations in MEFV, MVK, TNFRSF1A, NLRP3 and NLRP12

At the age of 68, the patient developed severe haemolysis with haemoglobin declined to 8.2 g/dL and lactate dehydrogenase elevated up to 3004 IU/L; he also developed acute renal failure requiring temporary haemodialysis
A bone marrow study revealed no sign of aplasia or hypoplasia
Flow cytometric analysis of erythrocytes and granulocytes revealed deficiency of CD59 and CD55, glycophosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored proteins, and he was diagnosed with PNH
Genetic analysis showed no mutations in PIGA but revealed a nonsense germ-line mutation (c.250G>T, p.E84X) and a somatic 18 Mbp deletion in chromosome 20q including PIGT
The patient was administered eculizumab, an anti-C5 antibody, immediately after the diagnosis
All the symptoms, such as urticaria, arthralgia, headache and haemolysis, completely disappeared due to regulated administration of eculizumab; remission has lasted for 3 years

source_metadata.title: Combination of exome sequencing and immune testing confirms Aicardi–Goutières syndrome type 5 in a challenging pediatric neurology case

evidence_events.source_span: The female proband was born at 40-week gestational age via vaginal delivery to an unrelated couple with no prior children. Her parents first noticed strabismus at 4 months and motor delay persisted despite surgical correction. She had significant central hypotonia and peripheral hypertonia and could not sit unsupported until 26 months. At around age 2.5 years, she developed epilepsy controlled by benzodiazepine and spasticity requiring baclofen. At age 4 years, she had no ambulatory skills, required orthoses and wheelchair, delayed speech, and persistent erythema on toes that swelled and worsened in winter.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: At 4 months, at 2.5 years, at age 4 years

evidence_events.source_span: Brain MRIs at ages 6, 18, and 30 months showed diffuse and confluent abnormal T2/FLAIR hyperintensity within bilateral cerebral white matter with frontal and parietal predominance, involving periventricular white matter and subcortical U fibers, sparing the cerebellum. Small foci of magnetic susceptibility artifact consistent with calcification were noted throughout cerebral white matter.

Urine organic acids, plasma amino acids, plasma lactate, plasma acylcarnitine profile, lysosomal enzyme panel, 7-dehydrocholesterol, very long chain fatty acids, and N-glycan testing were all normal, ruling out multiple metabolic and lysosomal disorders.

Routine karyotype was normal. SNP chromosomal microarray showed multiple regions of homozygosity totaling 3.8% of the genome but no regions of imbalance. WES identified two variants in SAMHD1: c.602T>A p.I201N (previously reported pathogenic) maternally inherited, and c.1293A>T p.L431F (variant of uncertain significance). No other variants were reported.

Follow-up testing on the proband's mother showed the p.I201N variant was maternally inherited but the p.L431F variant was not, suggesting the two variants are in trans, although the possibility of a de novo event on the maternally inherited allele remains. The father was not available for testing.
Peripheral blood testing showed significantly increased levels of six interferon-stimulated genes consistent with a SAMHD1-mediated process and diagnosis of AGS5.

Retrospective review showed features consistent with AGS5 including seizures, developmental delay, leukodystrophy with possible basal ganglia calcifications, and chilblains on toes that flare in cold weather. The proband's mother does not have chilblains, indicating incomplete penetrance of the p.I201N variant.

source_metadata.title: Disseminated nocardiosis with infective endocarditis of a transplanted heart
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case presentation, investigations, treatment, and outcome sections.

evidence_events.source_span: A 64-year-old man with a history of chronic kidney disease and heart transplantation 3 months prior, treated with tacrolimus, prednisone and mycophenolate mofetil, was admitted with fever and chills. He had dull aching pain in the right thigh starting 3 weeks prior. On examination, temperature was 38°C, heart rate 130 beats/min, new grade 2/6 holosystolic murmur over left lower sternal border, dullness and decreased breath sounds at right lung base, and right thigh tenderness.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: 3 weeks prior to presentation; on admission

evidence_events.source_span: Peripheral white blood cell count was 3 × 10⁹/L, stable from prior. Chest CT showed multiple peripheral lung nodules with right-sided pleural effusion. MRI of right proximal leg showed 2 × 1.5 × 3 cm fluid collection consistent with abscess in right vastus lateralis muscle.

Gram stain of blood demonstrated Gram-positive bacilli. Transthoracic echocardiogram showed new moderate tricuspid regurgitation without clear vegetation. Transoesophageal echocardiogram revealed a small mobile mass on the tricuspid valve.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: blood Gram stain, transthoracic and transoesophageal echocardiogram

evidence_events.source_span: Blood cultures returned positive for Nocardia asteroides. Brain MRI revealed a 9 mm ring-enhancing lesion in the right temporal lobe.

Oral trimethoprim–sulfamethoxazole (TMP/SMX) was initiated after Gram stain results. Imipenem–cilastatin was added after CNS involvement confirmed. Imipenem–cilastatin was replaced with ceftriaxone based on sensitivity. TMP/SMX was switched to linezolid due to nephrotoxicity. Ceftriaxone continued for 12 weeks then switched to oral minocycline, which was discontinued due to side effects. Linezolid monotherapy continued for 4 more months, total antibiotic therapy approximately 7 months.
Patient improved clinically with treatment. Follow-up brain MRI showed resolution of abscess. Echocardiogram demonstrated stable tricuspid regurgitation with no residual infection.

source_metadata.title: Spontaneous spinal subdural haematoma in a patient on apixaban

evidence_events.source_span: A 68-year-old man normally fully independent with a history of atrial fibrillation, controlled with apixaban, presented to the ED with sudden onset mid-back pain following a long-haul flight.
He was investigated for suspected pulmonary embolus (PE) given the history of recent air travel, however D-Dimer was not raised and observations were stable.
He was discharged with analgesia and a diagnosis of mechanical back pain.

He represented 2 days later with a more severe recurrence of the pain through his shoulder blades, described as a 'burning' pain. Due to new nature of the pain, new onset hypoxia seen on arterial blood gas and stiff calves, a CT aortogram was performed to rule out an aortic dissection or PE.
There was no evidence of dissection on the imaging, he was discharged with antibiotics for a presumed infection as some reactive lymph nodes were found.

He presented for the third time the next day as a primary care referral due to urinary retention. 1300 mL of urine was seen on bladder scan and he was successfully catheterised. Normal power and sensation in his lower limbs were noted and there was normal anal tone on rectal examination.

After an assessment by urology it was thought the retention was secondary to constipation, having started codeine recently. Bowels had last opened 3 days previously and an enema was administered in the ED with satisfactory results.

He presented for the fourth and final time, with headache, neck stiffness, vomiting and dramatically reduced coordination in his lower limbs. On examination he was alert with no photophobia or confusion, normal power and sensation in his upper limbs, but reduced power and coordination bilaterally in his lower limbs and difficult to elicit reflexes. A broad-based, ataxic gait was observed.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: fourth presentation, next day after third discharge

evidence_events.source_span: Apixaban was stopped due to a clinical suspicion of haemorrhagic spinal pathology.
Urgent CT of his head showed a small possible subarachnoid haemorrhage.
MRI of his spine was initially reported as showing a thoracic syringomyelia in T1–T5 with extension in L4–S1, but was later determined to be a spinal subdural haematoma.
After transfer to a tertiary neurosurgical centre, the spinal multidisciplinary team decided on conservative management due to bleeding risk and subacute presentation.
Further imaging with CT angiogram and MR angiogram showed no vascular abnormality; spinal angiogram was abandoned due to intraoperative complications.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: CT angiogram and MR angiogram performed; spinal angiogram abandoned

evidence_events.source_span: He remained neurologically stable and was discharged to a spinal injury rehabilitation centre.
Repeat MRI 1 month following the initial imaging demonstrated near complete resolution of the haematoma.

source_metadata.title: “I am not delusional!” Sensory dysaesthesia secondary to degenerative cervical myelopathy

evidence_events.source_span: A 62-year-old woman was referred to our neurosurgical outpatient service with abnormal sensation in her trunk, arms and legs.

Since her symptoms commenced 3 years previously, the patient had presented to emergency department (ED) on 11 occasions with dysaesthetic sensory symptoms including a feeling of water retention and a gel infiltrating the skin of her face, trunk, arms and legs.
In the weeks before the onset of her symptoms, the patient started using an olive oil moisturising cream, to which she attributed her symptoms.
While dermatological examination was conducted, comprehensive neurological examinations were not documented during the first presentations to the ED.
Over time her symptoms progressed to back pain, multiple falls, episodes of right leg giving way, severely compromised walking and coordination, and episodes of urinary and faecal incontinence.
A lumbar MRI ruled out cauda equina syndrome.
In her final presentation before referral, she complained of stiff legs, difficulty walking, difficulty passing urine, reduced manual dexterity and neck pain.

On examination in the neurosurgical clinic, the patient had hyperaesthesia from the neck down, reduced grip strength and other upper and lower limb weakness, very brisk reflexes with pathological spreading, bilateral ankle clonus, positive Hoffmann’s and Babinski reflexes, severe loss of coordination and balance, and impaired gait requiring a frame.
The severity of the patient’s cervical myelopathy was scored as 6 (severe) on the modified Japanese Orthopaedic Association scale (mJOA).

MRI imaging showed multilevel degenerative changes of the cervical spine with broad-based disc osteophyte protrusions at C3/4 and C5/6 causing spinal cord compression and T2 hyperintense signal changes within the cord.
The patient underwent anterior cervical discectomy at C3/4 for severe cervical myelopathy.
Three months post-surgery, the patient showed improved grip strength, wrist flexion and extension, elbow and shoulder power, and lower limb power, with reduced sensory problems and paraesthesia.
At 9 months, the patient had improved mJOA score of 10 and reported improved manual dexterity, walking, bladder function and resolution of incontinence, though dysaesthesia persisted but was reduced.

initial_presentation.first_contact_summary: Six days before the hospital visit, the patient experienced numbness in the right upper limb and instability while holding without obvious incentive but did not seek immediate medical intervention. Three days before admission, the patient experienced convulsive seizure in the right upper limb while remaining conscious, which was relieved after 1 min. Similar attacks occurred intermittently on six further occasions. The patient had a 3-year history of hypertension with the highest blood pressure being 180/110 mmHg. He also had a history of smoking and drinking lasting more than 30 years. He was born and has always lived in Beijing, with no history of contact with infested water, infectious zone, other radioactive substances or toxins. Upon admission, the patient was examined to be obese with no subcutaneous nodules. Neurological examinations showed full level muscle strength in the right upper limb, accompanied with diminished needling response. Emergency head CT scan (2016-1-1) showed lower density in the left parietal lobe. As the patient manifested as an acute onset of right limb weakness and hemiparesis, with low density lesions in the left occipital lobe on CT and a history of hypertension, the patient was hospitalised with a preliminary diagnosis of acute stroke and secondary epilepsy.

source_metadata.title: Nociceptive pain unmasking a serious pathology – paraneoplastic hypertrophic osteoarthropathy: A case report
source_metadata.notes: Extracted from case report narrative and figures in Medicine (Baltimore) 2019

evidence_events.source_span: A 41-year-old man presented to our Neurology Department with pain at the level of the right shoulder and right interscapular–vertebral region, with onset for about 6 months. In the last 30 days, the pain exacerbated and radiated in the anteromedial part of the arm and clavicular area. The patient also reported pain in the joints of the distal part of upper and lower limbs, especially in the small joints, which afterward became swollen.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: with onset for about 6 months; in the last 30 days

evidence_events.source_span: The neurologic examination was normal, except for slightly diminished deep tendon reflexes of the lower limbs. The patient reported pain that did not correspond to any radicular or nerve territory, which was exacerbated by pressure on the distal third of radius and ulna, but was not related to active or passive movements of the cervical spine.

The general examination showed clubbing of the fingers and toes with an increase of the shoe size of more than 1.5 sizes, enlargement of the large joints, swollen extremities with a tubular appearance, a right lateral cervical mobile, painless adenopathy of 1 cm diameter, and pachydermia with thickening of the skin of the scalp, forehead, and fingers, with cranial skin folds.

Cervical magnetic resonance imaging performed in another clinic before the admission showed the presence of disc protrusions from C2 to C7, with concomitant C2, C4, and C5 root compressions. The electrophysiological study revealed an active denervation in the territory of the right C5, C6, and C7 roots.

The radiographic examinations of the upper and lower limbs depicted symmetric osseous abnormalities, typical for periostosis, and linear halving of the diaphysis with an increase in the bone circumference. There were no fractures or cortical destruction.

The computed tomography (CT) of the thorax revealed the presence of a 23/19 mm and 20 mm mass lesion with speculated margins, contrast enhancement, and areas of necrosis at the level of the dorsal segment of the right upper pulmonary lobe. The mass presented several extensions to the pleura and determined pleural invasion. Multiple mediastinal adenopathy were noticed, some with central necrosis.

Laboratory findings were normal, except for the presence of inflammatory syndrome, slight anemia, and high values of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) (1291 pg/mL, with normal values less than 100 pg/mL).

The patient was admitted to the Pneumology Clinic, where biopsy from the lateral cervical adenopathy was performed. The anatomopathological examination of multiple fragments from the lymph node revealed multiple neoplastic infiltrates, suggestive of adenocarcinoma metastasis.
Positron emission tomography with 2-deoxy-2-[fluorine-18]fluoro-D-glucose confirmed the presence of the pulmonary malignant tumor with multiple active adenopathy.

Based on the clinical examination, radiological and histologic findings, the diagnosis of pulmonary adenocarcinoma with lymph nodes metastases and paraneoplastic hypertrophic osteoarthropathy was established.
The patient received treatment with nonsteroidal antiinflammatory drugs and opiate analgesics, which relieved the pain without any adverse event.

The patient was treated with different types of chemotherapeutics, immunotherapy, and gamma-knife radiotherapy for cerebral metastases. Despite all therapeutic measures, the disease progressed and the patient died 9 months later.

source_metadata.title: Thymoma associated paraneoplastic encephalitis (TAPE), a potential cause of limbic encephalitis

evidence_events.source_span: A 59-year-old man with no significant medical history was in his usual state of health until 5 days prior to a visit to his primary care physician with a chief complaint of a 'strong bitter taste in his mouth'. This was associated with expressive aphasia, short-term memory deficits and confusion, all primarily noticed by his wife.
He also started having occasional staring spells, and intermittent right hand spasms, preliminarily thought to be simple partial seizures.

On presentation, his temperature was 99.0°F (37.2°C), blood pressure was 115/81 mm Hg, heart rate of 95 beats/min, respirations were 20 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation was 99% on room air. Physical exam findings were significant for expressive aphasia, mild cognitive deficits most notably with short-term memory loss (unable to recall three simple items after 5 min). Remainder of neurological exam was unremarkable.
Outpatient MRI brain without contrast revealed a large confluent area of signal intensity involving the left medial temporal lobe and hippocampus.
Repeat MRI brain with and without contrast demonstrated T2/FLAIR hyperintensities of the left frontal and medial temporal lobe and right cingulate gyrus with minimal enhancement.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: MRI brain with and without contrast

evidence_events.source_span: Continuous EEG showed abnormal left frontotemporal periodic lateralised epileptiform discharges (PLEDs) with probable electrographic seizures from the left temporal regions.
Lumbar puncture with cerebrospinal fluid testing was negative for HSV 1&2 DNA amplification and showed elevated protein with no pleocytosis.
Serum and CSF autoimmune encephalitis panel revealed positive serum muscle acetylcholine receptor (AChR) binding antibody; all other usual autoimmune encephalitis antibodies were negative.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: Serum and CSF autoimmune encephalitis panel
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: Muscle AChR antibody is associated with myasthenia gravis and is not pathogenic to CNS.

evidence_events.source_span: CT chest/abdomen/pelvis with contrast and whole body PET-CT scan revealed bilateral subsegmental pulmonary emboli and a partially calcified 4.0×2.3×1.5 cm anterior mediastinal mass, most likely a thymoma.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: CT chest/abdomen/pelvis with contrast and PET-CT

evidence_events.source_span: The patient was started on intravenous immunoglobulin G and high dose intravenous steroids, with subsequent clinical improvement.
The patient underwent video assisted thoracoscopic surgery for tumour resection; pathology revealed a type B2–B3 thymoma.
One month post-hospitalisation MRI brain showed significant interval resolution of previously described lesions.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: MRI brain with and without contrast

evidence_events.source_span: Three months after discharge, the patient experienced a generalised tonic–clonic seizure requiring re-hospitalisation; repeat MRI showed recurrence of multifocal bilateral T2/FLAIR hyperintensities in new areas.
The patient was treated with high dose intravenous steroids and plasma exchange therapy, with clinical improvement and subsequent discharge on steroid taper and levetiracetam for seizure prophylaxis.
Repeat MRI brain imaging 3 and 6 months after second admission showed interval resolution of new brain lesions and neurological status returned to baseline with no further recurrences.

source_metadata.title: Familial glucocorticoid deficiency presenting with hyperpigmentation, gigantism, and motor development delay: a case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 10-month-old Sri Lankan Sinhalese baby boy presented with generalized hyperpigmentation and overgrowth since birth
He was born at term following an uncomplicated antenatal period and had a normal perinatal period without episodes of hypoglycemia or circulatory collapse
His growth chart demonstrated accelerated growth in weight, length, and head circumference
His parents observed hyperpigmentation at birth which worsened gradually over time

His developmental history revealed marginal gross motor developmental delay; at 10 months of age, he was able to sit without support but unable to come to seated position on his own, stand with support, or crawl

On examination, his length was 84 cm (above +3 SD), weight was 12.6 kg (at +3 SD), and head circumference was 48 cm (at +2 SD); he had generalized hyperpigmentation involving oral mucosa, palms, and soles

Basic hematological and biochemical investigations including full blood count, C-reactive protein, renal and liver function tests, and serum electrolytes were normal; random blood glucose was 76 mg/dl
Investigations revealed very low serum cortisol (< 22 nmol/l; normal 55–304 nmol/l) and very high ACTH (> 1734 pg/ml; normal 10–50 pg/ml) suggesting glucocorticoid deficiency
Serum aldosterone level was normal
ACTH stimulation test demonstrated markedly reduced basal cortisol levels (< 4.39 nmol/L) with no cortisol response following administration of synthetic ACTH at 30 and 60 minutes
MRI of the brain showed normal pituitary gland with marginal dilatation of the trigone and the body of the lateral ventricles; no hydrocephalus or structural brain abnormalities
Diagnosis of familial glucocorticoid deficiency was made based on isolated glucocorticoid deficiency, hyperpigmentation, and tall stature
Molecular testing was not done due to unavailability
The baby was started on orally administered hydrocortisone 10 mg/m2 per day
Review 5 months after treatment revealed less pigmentation and slowing of growth in weight, length, and head circumference

source_metadata.title: Diagnostic challenge of rapidly progressing sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease

evidence_events.source_span: 76-year-old man referred to emergency department for investigation of suspected stroke after a 2-week history of sudden-onset motor, functional and cognitive decline characterised by confusion, memory loss, visual deficit and gait unsteadiness

On initial assessment at ED, he appeared confused with loss of ability to speak or read English, severe slurring of speech, dysgraphia, ataxic gait, left-sided visual neglect, grossly normal tone, power, sensation and reflexes, and no myoclonic jerks

By day 7 since admission, episodes of severe agitation, akinetic mutism, aphasia, echolalia, echopraxia, stiffness of limbs with upper limb myoclonic jerks, rapid functional decline to bedbound and incontinent state, and loss of swallowing function requiring nasogastric feeding
Initial CT brain did not show any intracranial pathology

Basic full blood count, blood sugar level, liver and renal panels, electrolytes and vitamin B12 level were normal; thyroid function test including anti-thyroid peroxidase was normal; inflammatory markers and autoimmune screen were normal; HIV, serum VDRL, serum cryptococcal antigen, paraneoplastic panel and heavy metal screening were negative
MRI brain with gadolinium on day after admission revealed no stroke but bilateral cortical ribboning on diffusion-weighted images and FLAIR, suggestive of sCJD
Lumbar puncture performed for 14-3-3 CSF assay at reference laboratory

Video EEG on day 6 postadmission revealed abnormal EEG pattern suggestive of diffuse encephalopathy with posterior dominant rhythm 5-7 Hz, runs of delta activity 1-2 Hz, and diffuse sharply contoured theta activity; no triphasic, periodic wave complexes or epileptiform discharges recorded
Repeat MRI on day 10 showed no significant interval change in cortical ribboning despite clinical deterioration

CSF assay for 14-3-3 protein was positive; CSF showed no cells, normal glucose and protein, no oligoclonal bands; other CSF tests for bacterial, fungal, tuberculosis, cryptococcal antigen, antimeasle antibody, viral encephalitis, syphilis and heavy metal screening were negative
Empirical treatment with intravenous acyclovir for viral encephalitis and 5 days of intravenous methylprednisolone for autoimmune encephalitis showed no clinical improvement
