source_metadata.title: An Anti-PM/Scl-75 Antibody-positive Japanese Woman Who Developed Inflammatory Myopathy

evidence_events.source_span: A 69-year-old Japanese woman was referred and admitted to our department with suspected myositis. She had histories of unexplained weight loss over three years and mild muscle weakness from several months before this presentation.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: over three years; several months before presentation

evidence_events.source_span: Physical examination revealed mild muscle weakness confined to the neck and symmetrical, proximal parts of the upper and lower limbs. The muscles in those areas showed mild atrophy. No skin lesions, such as sclerosis, Gottron's lesion, heliotrope rash, or mechanic's hands, were evident.

Laboratory tests showed aldolase 12.7 IU/L; erythrocyte sedimentation rate 50.9 mm/h; C-reactive protein 4.76 mg/dL; creatine kinase 1,081 IU/L; and Krebs von den Lungen (KL)-6 589 IU/mL (normal <499 IU/mL). Anti-aminoacyl tRNA synthetase, anti-DNA, anti-Jo-1, anti-Scl 70, anti-Sjögren's syndrome-A/B, anti-Sm, and anti-U1-ribonucleoprotein were all negative. Antibodies for immune-mediated necrotizing myopathy (anti-signal recognition particle/anti-HMG-CoA reductase) were negative. Anti-centromere antibody was positive. Anti-PM/Scl-75 antibody was qualitatively detected; anti-PM/Scl-100 antibody was negative. HLA typing showed DRB1*01 and DRB1*15.
Magnetic resonance imaging of the upper and lower limbs showed no abnormalities.

Needle electromyography of the right upper and lower limbs showed normal spontaneous activity and an abnormal myogenic pattern (early recruitment in voluntary contraction and motor unit potential with small amplitude).

Muscle biopsy from the left rectus femoris revealed active muscle fiber necrosis and regenerative changes. Reactive mononuclear cell infiltration surrounded necrotic and regenerating fibers. Immunostaining showed expression of HLA-ABC and deposition of membrane attack complex on muscle fiber membranes. Perifascicular atrophy, fibers with internal nuclei, endomysial fibrosis, and perivascular inflammatory cell collections were absent.

Whole-body search including upper and lower gastrointestinal endoscopy showed no malignant tumors. Chest computed tomography showed mild interstitial changes at the base of the lower lung fields bilaterally.
Oral prednisolone was initiated at 40 mg/day, and muscle weakness gradually improved. Serum CK level before discharge was 211 U/L. No recurrence was noted six months after discharge.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: after treatment and six months follow-up

evidence_events.source_span: A 56-year-old man was referred due to right inguinal lymphadenopathy. He developed weakness in the lower extremities at age 32, worsening gradually, and was diagnosed with HAM/TSP at age 42 by anti-HTLV-1 antibody detection and cerebrospinal fluid examination.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: diagnosed with HAM/TSP by anti-HTLV-1 antibody detection and cerebrospinal fluid examination

evidence_events.source_span: At initial visit, no B symptoms; right inguinal lymph node swelling was elastic to hard, 3.0 cm, no tenderness, poor mobility; both lower limbs showed slight atrophy, spastic paralysis with muscle weakness (0/5), hyperreflexia, and positive Babinski sign.

Blood examination showed high soluble interleukin-2 receptor level of 1000 U/L and positivity of anti-HTLV-1 antibody (ELISA and western blotting assay); serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) was normal; no atypical lymphoid cells initially in peripheral blood film.

Lymph node biopsy revealed diffuse infiltration of small to medium-sized lymphocytes with rare nuclear irregularities distorting nodal architecture; scattered giant cells with irregularly lobulated nuclei resembling Reed-Sternberg cells; macrophages and angiogenesis also observed.

Immunohistochemical analysis showed giant cells positive for CD30 and CD15, negative for CD3, CD20, PAX5, and EBER-ISH; background lymphocytes positive for CD3, CD4, CD5, and partially CD25; findings consistent with lymphocyte-rich classic Hodgkin lymphoma.

Fluorodeoxyglucose-positron emission tomography and bone marrow core biopsy staged disease as IIA (Ann Arbor); Southern blot analysis detected di-clonal proviral HTLV-1 DNA bands in lymph node and peripheral blood samples, confirming Hodgkin-like ATLL (lymphoma type).
evidence_events.procedural_cue: PET, bone marrow biopsy, Southern blot analysis

evidence_events.source_span: C-C chemokine receptor 4 (CCR4) expression detected in tumor cells by immunohistochemical staining.

Initial treatment with ABVD regimen was given due to initial diagnosis of cHL; after diagnosis changed to Hodgkin-like ATLL, treatment changed to THP-COP; patient developed drug-induced eruptions and grade 3 febrile neutropenia during first cycle of THP-COP and refused further cycles.

Patient received low-dose oral chemotherapy (sobuzoxane, etoposide, prednisolone) outpatient; temporary increase in soluble IL-2 receptor level (max 2018 U/L) and appearance of atypical lymphoid cells (max 160/μl) in peripheral blood; computed tomography suggested stable disease for approximately 2 years.

source_metadata.title: Complete horizontal gaze palsy due to bilateral paramedian pontine reticular formation involvement as a presentation of multiple sclerosis: a case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 16-year-old Iranian girl was referred to the neurology department because of having bilateral horizontal gaze palsy. The gaze palsy was sudden in onset, developing overnight. The patient also reported a history of paresthesia in both of her feet since 2 months ago, which had progressed in the course duration of 2 weeks reaching her trunk at the level of the umbilicus. She experienced similar symptoms in both of her hands approximately 1 year ago.

Physical examination showed complete bilateral horizontal gaze palsy in the horizontal plane while vertical gaze was normal, aside from slightly decreased velocity of saccadic movements. Pupils were midsize and reactive, and nystagmus, diplopia or blurry vision were not found. Mild bilateral peripheral facial nerve palsy was also presented. Hyperreflexia in all four limbs was detectable without clonus, plantar reflexes were down going, and muscle forces were not reduced. There were no apparent signs of spasticity and ataxia.

Magnetic resonance imaging indicated multiple hyperintense subcortical, and periventricular lesions visible on the fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) and T2-weighted images, in addition to bilaterally involving PPRF at the level of the pons, anterior to the cerebral aqueduct. Two hyperintense lesions were also presented in the sagittal sections of the spinal MRI, one at the level of C7 and the other adjacent to T4. After gadolinium injection, the PPRF lesions were not enhanced, however, T4 thoracic spine lesion was enhanced.

Visual evoked potential (VEP) undertaken indicated no abnormality. Anti-aquaporin 4 (AQP4) and anti-myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (MOG) antibodies were accomplished in order to rule out neuromyelitis optica (NMO) and both tests were negative. All other diagnostic tests and routine lab works were normal.

With respect to the clinical findings and the history of a previous attack, the patient has had two clinical attacks at two different sites in the CNS, which were confirmed using MRI, and an enhancing lesion at the level of T4, diagnosis of MS was made in terms of the 2017 revised McDonald’s criteria.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: diagnosis made per 2017 revised McDonald’s criteria

evidence_events.source_span: The patient was treated with 1000 mg of intravenous methylprednisolone for three consecutive days, along with other supportive measures. Eye motion indicated significant improvement by passing 1 week from therapy and complete ocular movements were retrieved on the one-month follow up visit of the patient.

source_metadata.title: Acute visual impairment as a main presenting symptom of non-convulsive status epilepticus: a case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 62-year-old man was admitted to the neurology department complaining of an inability to see in the right eye for 2 days along with acute headache.

He had a history of atrial fibrillation in rheumatic heart disease and suffered an ischaemic stroke in the left frontotemporal parietal lobe 4 years ago, with mild right limb paralysis and mild vascular dementia; he also had symptomatic epilepsy due to ischaemic stroke 2 years ago treated with levetiracetam and valproic acid.

Physical examination revealed arterial pressure 170/100 mmHg, arterial blood lactic acid 3.3 mmol/L, normal liver and renal function, electrolytes, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, procalcitonin, cerebrospinal fluid examination, syphilis antibody and HIV testing.

Neurological examination revealed cognitive decline with inability to answer questions accurately or reply with full sentences; ophthalmological exam showed inability to read visual chart in either eye but ability to grasp a pen shaken in front of both eyes, suggesting macular avoidance or partial visual field avoidance.

MRI showed marked diffuse cortical hyperintensities in the left temporoparietal and occipital lobes on T2 and diffusion-weighted images; apparent diffusion coefficient map demonstrated decreased signal intensity in the same area.
CT angiography did not find corresponding vascular occlusion, and the lesion was not consistent with vascular distribution, excluding arterial cerebral infarction.

Liver function, kidney function and plasma glucose were normal; metabolism or toxic encephalopathy was considered less likely; reversible posterior leukoencephalopathy syndrome (RPLS) was less likely due to unilateral cortical lesion and cytotoxic brain oedema rather than vasogenic oedema.
Lactic acid level was initially elevated but later found normal; MELAS was considered but less likely due to absence of exercise intolerance and older age.
One day after hospitalization, the patient suffered limb twitches of the right lower limb lasting approximately 1 minute; wife reported patient was more taciturn in the past week.
Continuous EEG monitoring found continuous sharp wave discharges especially in the regions of the left temporal, parietal and occipital lobes.
Continuous intravenous administration of diazepam and oral addition of topiramate (50 mg bid) were prescribed.
After treatment, the patient recovered quickly, and follow-up EEG monitoring was normal.
A follow-up MRI performed 11 days later showed that the abnormal signals of the left temporoparietal and occipital lobes were markedly attenuated.

EEG demonstrated continuous epileptiform discharges consistent with NCSE.
Rapid clinical and EEG improvement after antiepileptic treatment supports diagnosis.
Resolution of MRI abnormalities on follow-up imaging consistent with transient peri-ictal MRI abnormalities.
hidden_reference.final_diagnosis: Nonconvulsive status epilepticus (NCSE) presenting with acute visual impairment and transient peri-ictal MRI abnormalities (TPMA).

source_metadata.title: Chemical meningitis in children as a risk factor following craniopharyngioma resection – a case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 7-year-old girl was admitted to the Neurology Department with severe headache, vomiting, muscle weakness and balance disorders.
Preoperative computed tomography (CT) revealed the existence of a large cystic tumour with peripheral calcifications expanding from the sella to the third ventricle area and acute hydrocephalus.
Magnetic resonance imaging identified a large solid pathological area with fluid accumulation in the sellar and suprasellar region.
The patient was diagnosed with a tumour expanding from the sella to the third ventricle, most likely an adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma with concomitant acute occlusive hydrocephalus.

A right-sided pterional craniotomy was performed with extensive resection of the tumour. Pathomorphological examination of the surgical specimen revealed a craniopharyngioma G1-WHO testing positively for AE1/AE2, GFAP, MIB-1 and CD 68.
The first 6 days after the surgery were without complications. Substitution therapy was introduced for multi-hormonal pituitary insufficiency with L-thyroxine, hydrocortisone and desmopressin.

On the seventh day after surgery, the patient presented with seizures, fever, severe headache, weakness, irritability, stiffening of the neck, positive Kernig's and Babinski signs, convergent strabismus, and gradual degradation of consciousness.

Lumbar puncture showed transparent CSF with 18 cells/μl (60% neutrophils, 38% lymphocytes), positive Pandy's reaction, negative Nonne-Apelt reaction, protein 154 mg/dl, normal glucose 79 mg%, lactic acid 2.7 mmol/l. CSF cultures and latex test were negative. Blood and urine cultures were negative. Serology for anti-CMV, anti-EBV, anti-HSV, anti-poxvirus and anti-Borrelia burgdorferi IgM antibodies were negative.

Because of lack of an etiological factor for bacterial or viral meningitis, the patient was diagnosed with aseptic (chemical) meningitis and treated with vancomycin, ceftriaxone, fluconazole, acyclovir, nystatin, and valproic acid for seizures.
Increasing intracranial pressure required placement of external drainage on day 11 after tumour resection. CT scan on day 14 showed no hydrocephalus and the drain was removed.
Follow-up MRI scan on day 152 after surgery showed status after surgical resection of the craniopharyngioma with possible small remnant of solid part of the tumour in sella.

Six months after the procedure, the patient was in good neurological condition without focal damage to the central nervous system but still required hormone substitution, anti-epileptic treatment, and ophthalmic and psychological counselling.

source_metadata.title: Kinking of Bilateral Internal Carotid Arteries as Cause of Cognitive Dysfunction

evidence_events.source_span: The 55-year-old male patient was admitted to the Department of Neurology due to dizziness and instability while walking, forgetfulness, memory loss and low mood.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: symptoms lasted for a year; symptoms more pronounced for two months

evidence_events.source_span: He has previously been reported to be hypertensive and with diagnosis of diabetes mellitus and dyslipidemia.

At the age of 54, he had a stroke with discrete hemiparesis on the right extremities (brain CT showed micro-ischemic lesions with different time of occurrence and a stroke of lacunar size perimesencephalic left).
6 months ago he had a transitory ischemic attack with short-term speech impairment and transient weakness of his right arm.

Neurological status: conscious, oriented, communicative, without deficit on cranial nerves, with reduced cognitive function. The Mini-Mental State Exam (MMSE) was 21. No motoric weakness on extremities, motor tendon reflexes without deficit, Romberg negative. Low mood observed without psychotic symptoms.
Electroencephalogram (EEG), otoscopy and vestibulogram were within physiological limits.
Echocardiography examination was within physiological parameters.

Initial dilation of both carotid joint arteries with mutually low hemodynamic parameters in the right internal carotid artery was verified by Doppler sonography. Doppler sonography also suspects on distal subocclusion of the internal carotid artery (low flow rates were observed).

Diagnostic transcranial Doppler (TCD) of vertebrobasilar artery showed decreased blood flow velocities in both vertebral and basilar artery and indicated atherosclerotic altered blood vessels of the brain.
CTA findings indicate bilateral kinking of internal carotid artery with right duplex Kinking.
SPECT with 15 mCi 99mTc-hexamethylpropyleneamineoxime (99mTc-HMPAO) verified global cortex hypoperfusion, indicating chronic vascular failure.
The patient was treated with acetylsalic acid, clopidogrel, atorvastatin, donepezil, memantine, escitalopram, bromazepam, along with antihypertensive and antidiabetic therapy (per os).

source_metadata.title: Kayser–Fleischer ring with keratoconus: a coincidence? A case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 19-year-old male visited the Ophthalmology Department in November 2013 due to a rapid decline in visual acuity within a short period of time.
Ocular examination with slit-lamp biomicroscopy showed that the corneas of both eyes were transparent, but the inferior corneal quadrant thinned and bulged slightly, and Vogt’s striae were visible.

There was a dense copper-brown depositional ring (KF ring) in the Descemet membrane around the periphery with a mean width of approximately 1.5 mm, widest at the 12 o’clock position at approximately 2 mm.

The sclera did not stain yellow, the anterior chamber was clear, the pupils exhibited equal size and shape and were sensitive to light, the lens was transparent, and there was no obvious abnormality on fundus examination.

Corneal topography showed that the Sim K value of the right eye was 52.5D@99/49.9D@9, with the thinnest point 0.8 mm below the center and thickness of 361 μm; the left eye had Sim K value 55.9D@80/51.2D@170, thinnest point 0.7 mm below the center, thickness 336 μm.
The patient was referred to the Neurology Department for further consultation because of the existence of KF ring.
Serological examination showed low serum ceruloplasmin (18 mg/L; normal 204–407 mg/L) and high urinary copper (363 μg/24 h; normal <150 μg/24 h).
Abdominal ultrasound showed fine granular changes in the liver parenchyma.
Brain MRI showed abnormal signals indicative of cerebral peduncle and globus pallidus on both sides.
All physical examinations were negative.
Based on these findings, the patient was diagnosed with asymptomatic Wilson’s disease.

Over 5 years, the patient wore RGP lenses, consumed a low-copper diet, and took penicillamine, zinc gluconate, and occasionally dimercaptopropane sulfonate to promote copper excretion and inhibit absorption.

evidence_milestones.source_span: A 19-year-old male visited the Ophthalmology Department in November 2013 due to a rapid decline in visual acuity within a short period of time. Ocular examination with slit-lamp biomicroscopy showed that the corneas of both eyes were transparent, but the inferior corneal quadrant thinned and bulged slightly, and Vogt’s striae were visible. There was a dense copper-brown depositional ring (KF ring) in the Descemet membrane around the periphery with a mean width of approximately 1.5 mm, widest at the 12 o’clock position at approximately 2 mm. Corneal topography showed that the Sim K value of the right eye was 52.5D@99/49.9D@9, with the thinnest point 0.8 mm below the center and thickness of 361 μm; the left eye had Sim K value 55.9D@80/51.2D@170, thinnest point 0.7 mm below the center, thickness 336 μm.

source_metadata.title: Fat embolism syndrome with cerebral fat embolism through a patent foramen ovale

evidence_events.source_span: A 46-year-old woman was urgently presented to a nearby hospital because of a femur fracture caused by an accident.
She began to experience sleepiness approximately 5 hours later.
A follow-up helical computed tomography (CT) of the brain revealed the absence of any additional severe lesions or skull fractures.
Chest CT confirmed an exudative lesion, and a pulmonary vascular computed tomography angiography (CTA) revealed no obvious abnormalities.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: Chest CT and pulmonary vascular CTA

evidence_events.source_span: Based on the clinical and imaging findings, the patient was suspected to have cerebral fat embolism (CFE).
After 2 days, the patient was moved to our neurology department to receive the appropriate care.
Immediate physical examination on arrival revealed a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 4, a positive bilateral Babinski sign, a positive Kernig sign, and neck stiffness.
The patient's left thigh presented bruising and swelling and had been fixed with external fixation with restrained movement in the previous hospital.
She presented an arterial pressure of 148/80 mm Hg, heart rate of 124 bpm, and partial pressure of oxygen (PO2) of 64 mm Hg. Her blood gas analysis revealed a pH value of 7.4.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: blood gas analysis and vital signs

evidence_events.source_span: Total body CT revealed a left femoral comminuted fracture with dislocation.
Her bilateral lung presented an exudative lesion as well as pleural effusion.
Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed diffuse abnormal signals in the bilateral cerebral hemisphere, brainstem, and cerebellum, which were suggestive of embolization.

Combined with the patient's trauma history and imaging findings of the lung and brain, the patient was initially diagnosed with fat embolism syndrome (FES), whose corresponding treatment is mainly supportive.
Subsequent cardiovascular screening, including echocardiography, cervical artery ultrasound and bilateral lower extremity vascular ultrasound, was performed, and all the findings were negative.

Four days after the femur fracture, the patient presented with moderate dyspnea, and her arterial blood gas analysis retrieved a pH value of 7.4, PO2 was 35 mm Hg, partial pressure of carbon dioxide was 126 mm Hg, and arterial oxygen saturation was 97.5% under nasal oxygen.
Fourteen days after the fracture, both the lung symptoms and lung CT findings were considerably improved.
Transthoracic echocardiography ultrasound was performed again, and shunts through a patent foramen ovale (PFO) were observed.
On the following day, there was a gradual improvement in consciousness. However, the patient's speech indicated dysphasia.

diagnostic_reasoning_verbatim_spans: Based on patients history of trauma and supportive imaging data, she was diagnosed with fat embolism syndrome obviously.
Severe brain damage confused our understanding of the pathogenesis.
The subsequent diagnosis of fat embolism syndrome with patent foramen ovale provided a reasonable explanation.
Transthoracic echocardiography ultrasound was performed again, and shunts through a PFO were observed.
The patient was more likely to have paradox embolism than FES because fat emboli are mostly associated with the pathological pathway.
Patent foramen ovale as the embolization pathway, particularly in young and middle-aged patients with cerebral embolism, is often mistaken for a rare situation.

Laboratory investigation showed slightly elevated white blood cell count (11.6 × 10^9 /L), C-reactive protein level (10 mg/L), and positive antinuclear antibodies (1:1000); serum sodium, anti-dsDNA, ENA antibodies, ANCA, RF, tumor markers, chest CT and abdominal ultrasound were unremarkable

Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination showed normal intracranial pressure, 2 leukocytes/uL, glucose 6.11 mmol/L, protein 0.63 g/L, elevated IgG index 4.13, and oligoclonal bands (Type III); CSF antibodies for cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus, herpes simplex virus were negative; no infectious pathogens identified in blood or CSF
Anti-Hu, anti-Yo, anti-Ri, anti-Amfi, anti-CV2, anti-Ma2, anti-NMDAR, anti-VGKC, anti-AMPAR, anti-GABA_B, anti-AQP4 and anti-MOG antibodies in blood and CSF were all negative

Brain MRI on the night of hospitalization demonstrated focal symmetrical bilateral thalamic lesions with hyperintense T2 and FLAIR signals; after 17 days, MRI showed enlargement of bilateral thalamic lesions with low density changes on CT and slightly high intensity on DWI; progressive multiple lesions in subcortical white matter, brain stem and a hyperintense long segment of T2 in thoracic spinal cord; cranio-cervical CTA was unremarkable

hidden_reference.final_diagnosis_verbatim: Probable acute disseminating encephalomyelitis (ADEM) with symmetrical bilateral thalamic lesions
diagnostic_reasoning_verbatim_spans: Our patient had a polyfocal clinical CNS event following an influenza vaccination.
No other etiology has been found to explain these events in this patient.
CSF test showed normal intracranial pressure, leukocyte count and negative results for some common virus antibodies.
Other autoimmune antibody-mediated diseases were excluded by the negative results of the antibody tests including anti-AQP4, anti-MOG and many other antibodies related to paraneoplastic syndrome.
Chest CT, abdominal ultrasound, tumor markers and paraneoplastic antibodies were all negative.
DWI images showed a slightly high intensity which can be seen in the acute phase of ADEM.
Rapid progress over a few days and the longitudinally extensive lesions in the thoracic spinal cord did not support a diagnosis of lymphoma or vasculitis.
No evidence of signal changes in the deep cerebral veins or the straight sinus was found.
The diagnosis for our patient is probable ADEM with bilateral thalamic lesions.

Negative tumor screening and imaging

Rapid clinical progression and spinal cord involvement inconsistent with lymphoma or vasculitis
No vascular abnormalities on CTA
Diagnosis of probable ADEM based on clinical, laboratory, and imaging findings

hidden_reference.diagnostic_reasoning: The diagnosis of probable ADEM was made based on the patient's rapid neurological deterioration, multifocal CNS involvement including bilateral thalamic and spinal cord lesions, exclusion of infectious, autoimmune, neoplastic, and vascular causes by laboratory and imaging studies, and the clinical context of recent influenza vaccination. Imaging findings and CSF analysis supported demyelination. Other diagnoses such as CNS lymphoma, vasculitis, infection, and neuro-Behçet disease were excluded or considered unlikely.

source_metadata.title: Common variable immunodeficiency with granulomatous-lymphocytic interstitial lung disease and preceding neurological involvement: a case-report

evidence_events.source_span: A 50-year-old Caucasian female presented to the neurology clinic with marked cerebellar ataxia. Her medical history included Evans syndrome – a combination of idiopathic thrombocytopaenic purpura (ITP) and autoimmune haemolytic anaemia (AIHA) diagnosed in her 30s, hypogammaglobulinaemia with recurrent chest infections, and hypertension.

MRI Brain showed an abnormal, wedge-shaped, bright signal intensity lesion in the right cerebellar hemisphere, with slight mass effect on the fourth ventricle. The area of abnormality extended through the grey and white matter.

A cerebellar biopsy was subsequently performed to exclude malignancy. This showed focal infiltration of both the cerebellum and meninges with macrophages and lymphocytes consistent with meningo-cerebellitis. No granulomata were seen, and the infiltrating lymphocytes were predominantly T-cells. Immunohistochemistry demonstrated no evidence of lymphoma.
A chest x-ray (CXR) showed linear shadowing in the left midzone and nodular opacification in the right upper and lower zones.
The patient was treated with corticosteroids and methotrexate, and her symptoms and MRI brain abnormalities resolved within 3 months.
Approximately 7 years after her original presentation, she was noted to have pulmonary nodules on a CT thorax performed as she was experiencing symptoms suggestive of recurrent chest infections.
A CT-guided lung biopsy of one nodule showed chronic inflammation (lymphocyte predominant) with no evidence of granulomatous disease.

She was admitted to hospital with pneumococcal pneumonia and sepsis and was found to be profoundly hypogammaglobulinaemic. Following assessment by the immunology service, she was commenced on immunoglobulin replacement therapy.
A year later (aged 59) the patient developed parotid gland swelling and underwent sub-mandibular gland biopsy. The biopsy revealed smeared lymphocytes but no evidence of granulomata or malignancy.

Approximately 10 years after her initial presentation (aged 60), the patient was referred to the specialist Interstitial Lung Disease clinic for management of her sarcoidosis. At the time of clinic, she was relatively asymptomatic with respect to her chest, with no cough or exertional dyspnoea.
On examination, pulmonary examination revealed some crackles in the right lower zone with no squawks or wheezes. Abdominal examination revealed an enlarged spleen 4 cm below the costal margin.

Blood tests demonstrated a mild anaemia (115 g/L) and thrombocytopenia (110 × 10^9/L). Serum IgA (0.09 g/L) was low and serum IgG (6.4 g/L) was at the lower end of the normal range (patient was noted to be on immunoglobulin therapy at that time). There was no evidence of infection, while serum ACE (13 U/L), corrected calcium (2.19 mmol/L), liver enzymes, renal profile and autoimmune screen were all unremarkable.
Spirometric lung volumes measured in the ILD clinic were within normal range and stable over 6 months. Gas transfer and KCO were notably reduced at 48 and 64% predicted respectively.

Review of her CT thorax imaging (over a 3-year period) showed fluctuating bilateral parenchymal nodular changes (including fissural nodularity), areas of ground glass opacification and reticular change. Stable sub-centimetre mediastinal adenopathy and massive splenomegaly (18 cm) were also noted. A PET CT showed a right lower lobe pulmonary nodule with low/moderate FDG avidity.

Microscopy of fine needle aspirates, taken 3 years previously from a lung nodule, demonstrated a non-specific infiltrate, predominantly lymphoid in nature, with features consistent with a diagnosis of GLILD.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: fine needle aspirate of lung nodule

evidence_events.source_span: A diagnosis of CVID with associated GLILD was made following multidisciplinary team review of the clinical, radiological and histological features of this case. Re-review of her brain biopsy histology showed focal infiltration of lymphocytes and excluded other pathologies (lymphoma, mycobacterial disease), supporting a retrospective diagnosis of CVID-associated neurological involvement.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: re-review of brain biopsy and multidisciplinary team review

source_metadata.title: Guillain-Barré syndrome associated with COVID-19 disease

evidence_events.source_span: Two weeks prior to this hospital admission, she developed a fever, cough and back pain amidst the COVID-19 pandemic. The patient tested positive for COVID-19 and was treated with azithromycin for 5 days at home.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: Two weeks prior to this hospital admission

evidence_events.source_span: Over the next 2 weeks, her fever and cough resolved, but the lower back pain persisted, characterised by a throbbing, 7/10 intensity, radiating to both lower extremities. She then had new onset of numbness, pins and needles sensation in the left lower extremity associated with mild weakness, progressing to the contralateral lower extremity over 24 hours with unstable gait.

Physical examination showed stable vital signs, motor strength 5/5 in all extremities, normal deep tendon reflexes, negative Babinski sign bilaterally, no defined spine sensory level, and no upper motor neuron weakness findings.

On admission, white cell count was 13.5×10⁹/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, vitamin B12, and thyroid stimulating hormone were normal. CT head showed no mass, hemorrhage, or hydrocephalus. Lumbar spine radiograph showed multilevel degenerative changes.
MRI lumbar spine without contrast showed moderate bilateral and moderate left-sided neural foraminal narrowing at L2–L3 and L3–L4, respectively, with unremarkable conus medullaris.
MRI brain was performed due to persistent headaches and showed normal findings.

Repeat COVID-19 test was positive. The patient developed worsening weakness with muscle strength 3/5 in both lower extremities and 4/5 in left upper extremity, with numbness, tingling, paresthesias, and diminished deep tendon reflexes compared to previous day.
Lumbar puncture revealed cerebrospinal fluid with white cell count of 2/cu mm and protein count of 117 mg/dL, suggestive of albumin-cytologic dissociation.
Nerve conduction study was not performed as it was not available in the inpatient setting.

source_metadata.title: When polyuria does not stop: a case report on an unusual complication of hantavirus infection

evidence_events.source_span: A 49-year old male patient self-reported to the hospital with strong piercing headaches, which were initially located at the front, but spread occipitally later, and were accompanied by photophobia. For the three previous days, the patient had suffered from severe nausea, vomiting, diarrhea and general sickness.

Computed tomography scan showed a mass in the sellar region. Subsequently, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a haemorrhagic sellar mass, thus, the diagnosis of subacute pituitary apoplexy was made.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: Computed tomography scan; magnetic resonance imaging

evidence_events.source_span: Laboratory workup on day five after admission showed that pituitary apoplexy was associated with insufficiency of the corticotropic, thyrotropic and gonadotrophic axis.
Laboratory follow-up revealed severe acute kidney injury with a creatinine of 11.6 mg / dl and an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) < 20 ml/min on day 5 after admission.

The combination of kidney failure, thrombocytopenia and neurological symptoms prompted us to consider hantavirus-infection. The patient reported on digging out a bamboo hedge prior to hospitalization.

Testing on day three after admission revealed hantavirus infection by detection of IgM and IgG antibodies against Puumala hantavirus using immunofluorescence assays and line immunoassays. Polymerase chain reaction for hantavirus was also positive. Specific amplification and sequencing of the partial L-Segment revealed an infection with a puumalavirus circulating in the Middle Rhine region in Germany.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: Immunofluorescence assays, line immunoassays, PCR, sequencing

evidence_events.source_span: Infection by hepatitis B virus, hepatitis C virus and HIV was ruled out by serological testing. Because testing for hantavirus yielded positive results, leptospirosis was not tested.

evidence_events.source_span: Despite improvement and withholding diuretic medication from day 5, there was no decline in urine excretion (urinary volume 6.25 ml/kg/h).

At 6-month follow-up, the patient was in good general condition. Laboratory parameters were unremarkable except for a reduced serum level of LH (0.4 U/l; normal range: 1.7–8.6). Dosage of desmopressin and hydrocortisone were reduced; thyroid and testosterone replacement continued unchanged.

source_metadata.notes: Extraction from BMJ Case Reports 2020 article, preserving source order and granularity.

evidence_events.source_span: A 57-year-old right-handed woman presented with shortness of breath and fever in mid April 2020. The patient was lethargic and too breathless to provide a history of the events leading up to admission.
Collateral history was taken from her sister who explained that she had become non-verbal in the week prior to admission and had been increasingly breathless.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: in the week prior to admission

evidence_events.source_span: For the previous 18 months she had resided in a mental health hospital being treated for schizoaffective disorder. Her medical history includes depression, pancreatectomy, splenectomy (for which she is on long-term antibiotics), and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. She has a long smoking history (40 pack/years). She had a pulmonary embolism in October 2019, which was provoked after a traumatic fall sustaining multiple fractures. She had type 2 diabetes mellitus, which was managed with metformin and insulin. She had also reported episodes of mutism and unresponsiveness (lasting several days at a time).

On examination at presentation, she was saturating at 91% on 40% oxygen and was unable to speak due to breathlessness. Her respiratory rate was 22 breaths per minute and she was hypotensive. An arterial blood gas indicated a type 1 respiratory failure (PaO2 7.2 kPa and PaCO2 4.0 kPa). Her Glasgow Coma Score (GCS) was seven (withdrawing and opening eyes to pain, without a verbal response).

She was transferred to intensive care for intubation and ventilation the day after admission. She was treated with antibiotics to cover a community-acquired pneumonia and treated for an Epstein-Barr viraemia. She was nursed prone for acute respiratory distress syndrome. She developed an acute kidney injury for which she required haemofiltration. She was intubated and ventilated for one month.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: the day after admission; one month

evidence_events.source_span: Her sedation was gradually lightened as she was weaned off the ventilator. Her GCS was 15 by the 25th of May and she was self-ventilating. She was weak in all four limbs.

Two days later she was less engaged, she was unable to speak or obey commands and opened her eyes only to pain. Some new onset intermittent right-sided facial jerks were noted. She was diagnosed with NCSE on electroencephalogram (EEG). She was commenced on Levetiracetam.

During the next 12 hours, her GCS improved to 14, she was opening her eyes spontaneously, and obeyed motor commands; however, was not completely oriented to time or place and a repeat EEG confirmed a resolution of the status epilepticus.
Nasopharyngeal and oropharyngeal swab specimens were obtained and real-time PCR (RT-PCR) assay was performed, which tested positive for SARS-CoV-2.
She had a CT brain scan without contrast which demonstrated bilateral calcification of the globus pallidus in keeping with mild age-related changes. An MRI brain scan was normal.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: when patient was noted not to be waking following extubation

evidence_events.source_span: At day ten postextubation, she underwent an EEG. Frequent (2.5–4 Hz), florid bilateral, non-synchronous epileptiform discharges were seen over both hemispheres throughout most of the recording. The patient was unresponsive during this period of recording. 2mg of intravenous lorazepam was given, after which the epileptiform discharges subsided and a 6–7 Hz background predominated. The patient became slightly more alert, in that she could obey some motor commands and vocalise to a small extent. The EEG findings were in keeping with NCSE with clear electroclinical improvement after lorazepam administration.

One day later, she had another EEG study to investigate whether there were residual subclinical seizures. The EEG showed a background rhythm reaching 7–8 Hz, which was reactive to external stimulation. Frequent multifocal epileptiform discharges were seen as well as intermittent frontotemporal theta/delta waves. There was a significant improvement compared with the first EEG study. There was no evidence to suggest NCSE; however, frequent epileptiform discharges were seen over both hemispheres, without a clear focus.

After being diagnosed with NCSE, the patient was initially loaded on Levetiracetam and then continued on 500 mg twice daily. During her admission, her regular Clozapine dose of 150 mg in the morning and 300 mg at night was held. This was gradually reintroduced by psychiatry in increments during the first six weeks of her stay.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: during admission and first six weeks
evidence_events.procedural_cue: Levetiracetam started; Clozapine held then reintroduced

evidence_events.source_span: At the time of onset of her facial jerks and lower GCS, she was taking 100 mg in the morning and 175 mg at night. This was then reduced abruptly the following day to 125 mg at night only, and the following day, when the EEG confirmed NCSE, she was prescribed clozapine 50 mg two times per day.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: at time of facial jerks and NCSE diagnosis

evidence_events.source_span: The patient gradually improved in that she was able to verbalise and obey motor commands. She still however had episodes of fluctuating confusion three weeks after being discharged to the neurology ward; however, she did have a concomitant urinary tract infection at that time.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: three weeks after discharge to neurology ward

hidden_reference.final_diagnosis_verbatim: Non-convulsive status epilepticus (NCSE) in a 57-year-old woman with schizoaffective disorder, with two possible aetiologies including SARS-CoV-2 infection and clozapine uptitration.
diagnostic_reasoning_verbatim_spans: She was diagnosed with NCSE on electroencephalogram (EEG).
Nasopharyngeal and oropharyngeal swab specimens were obtained and real-time PCR (RT-PCR) assay was performed, which tested positive for SARS-CoV-2.
The EEG findings were in keeping with NCSE with clear electroclinical improvement after lorazepam administration.
Clozapine can induce seizures and EEG changes, especially during rapid titration.
The two most likely aetiologies for her NCSE include either SARS-CoV-2 infection and/or the reintroduction and relatively rapid uptitration of Clozapine.
diagnostic_reasoning_items: Clinical presentation and EEG confirmed NCSE.
SARS-CoV-2 infection confirmed by RT-PCR supports possible viral etiology.
Brain imaging excluded acute structural causes.
EEG responsiveness to lorazepam supports seizure diagnosis.
Clozapine dose changes temporally related to NCSE onset suggest drug-induced seizure risk.
Lumbar puncture was not performed, limiting direct evidence of CNS infection.
Final diagnosis remains with two possible etiologies: COVID-19 related or clozapine-induced NCSE.
hidden_reference.final_diagnosis: Non-convulsive status epilepticus likely precipitated by SARS-CoV-2 infection and/or clozapine uptitration.
hidden_reference.diagnostic_reasoning: The diagnosis of NCSE was confirmed by EEG with characteristic epileptiform discharges and clinical improvement after lorazepam. The patient tested positive for SARS-CoV-2, which has been associated with neurological manifestations including seizures. Brain imaging was unremarkable for acute lesions. Clozapine, known to induce seizures especially during rapid titration, was being reintroduced and adjusted around the time of NCSE onset. Lumbar puncture was not performed, so direct CNS infection evidence is lacking. Thus, the NCSE is attributed to either SARS-CoV-2 infection or clozapine effects.

evidence_events.source_span: Ambulance staff recorded an oxygen saturation of 85% on room air. On admission he had a respiratory rate of 60 and arterial blood gas (ABG) showed hypoxia with partial pressure of oxygen (PO2) of 8.87, partial pressure of carbon dioxide of 3.5 and pH of 7.5 on 1 L of oxygen confirming type I respiratory failure
His admission chest X-ray showed peripheral opacities in right middle and left upper and mid zones
His COVID-19 swab came back positive on day 3 though due to pandemic he was treated as probable COVID-19 since admission

He required supplementary oxygen through venture mask for 5–6 days before requiring continuous positive airway pressure for 24 hours due to increasing oxygen demand evident on ABGs with PO2 of 7.4 with normocapnea
He developed focal neurology, with reduced Glasgow Coma Scale score, right-sided weakness with hemisensory loss and diplopia. An initial CT of the head was negative for haemorrhage
Blood cultures on admission were negative. He had D-dimer 0.59 (normal level <0.5) on admission which significantly elevated through illness to 2.4 on day 10

MRI of the brain with gadolinium was reported as showing multiple acute ischaemic infarctions in the territories of the left posterior inferior cerebellar artery and bilateral posterior cerebral arteries (PCAs), implicating the left cerebellar hemisphere, cerebellar vermis, left thalami and bilateral occipital lobes
A possible cardiogenic septic source was ruled out. Transthoracic, transoesophageal echocardiogram and bubble echocardiogram were all normal

Cerebral CT angiogram ruled out vascular malformation or intra-arterial thrombus. Magnetic resonance angiography of the neck showed multifocal areas of narrowing and occlusions in both PCA, especially in the left PCA suggestive of CNS vasculitis probably due to the known COVID-19 viral infection
CT pulmonary angiogram was in keeping with the proved COVID-19 infection without evidence of acute pulmonary embolism. CT venogram showed no filling defect in the major dural venous sinuses
evidence_events.procedural_cue: CT pulmonary angiogram and CT venogram

evidence_events.source_span: Lumbar puncture was unremarkable with the exception of mildly raised protein. It was negative for herpes simplex virus (HSV) I and II PCR, enterovirus RNA and varicella zoster. Cerebrospinal fluid could not be tested for SARS-CoV-2 virus at that time in the pandemic
evidence_events.procedural_cue: lumbar puncture and CSF viral PCR

evidence_events.source_span: On day 12 he was referred to liaison psychiatry due to poor engagement in rehabilitation. He was diagnosed with adjustment disorder, started on the antidepressant citalopram and discharged back to the stroke team

He was re-referred to liaison psychiatry 10 days later, when he presented with irritability, aggression and sexual disinhibition. A small dose of olanzapine was started. The contemporary hospital records describe disorientation, distractibility, confabulation, paranoid affect, and verbal and physical aggression
On a Montreal Cognitive Assessment the patient initially scored 12/30, improved to 21/30 after a couple of weeks
evidence_events.temporal_cue: initial and after a couple of weeks

evidence_events.source_span: Initial cognitive screening indicated significant impairments in attention, processing speed, visuospatial skills, visuospatial construction, verbal fluency, immediate memory, and delayed memory for verbal and visual information
A battery of standardised neuropsychological tests was administered and the patient’s performance was compared with an estimate of his premorbid ability and published UK normative data

Within 2 weeks from admission to the neurorehabilitation unit, the patient showed rapid improvements in attention, processing speed and memory, with residual mild to moderate cognitive impairments in executive and visuospatial functions and verbal fluency, and impulsivity
evidence_events.temporal_cue: within 2 weeks from admission to neurorehabilitation

evidence_events.source_span: Psychotropic medications were gradually withdrawn and stopped. Functional outcome was evaluated using the UK Functional Independence Measure (FIM) and Functional Assessment Measure (FAM). On admission, the patient scored 104/126 on the FIM and 157/210 on the FAM. At discharge he scored 123/126 on the FIM and 195/210 on the FAM, showing greater improvement in cognitive and psychosocial functions

source_metadata.title: Stroke masquerading as cardiac arrest: the artery of Percheron
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case presentation, investigations, outcome, and discussion sections with source-order evidence events and milestones.

evidence_events.source_span: A 79-year-old woman with a medical history of hypertension and mild Alzheimer’s dementia presented with acute onset loss of consciousness in the community.

She was a passenger in a car and found to be unresponsive, with a family member reporting absence of a palpable pulse. She was presumed to have had a cardiac arrest and received 2 min of cardiopulmonary resuscitation in the community before the return of spontaneous circulation was noted.

On arrival, she was unresponsive with a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) of 3 and intubated. She was in sinus rhythm with a heart rate of 84 beats/min, blood pressure 140/110 mm Hg, and blood glucose 6.7 mmol/L. There was no obvious focal neurology.

She was transferred to a tertiary hospital on the same day for further work-up in light of her ongoing reduced level of consciousness. The patient was extubated 24 hours later, with her GCS improving to 13–14 over the next day.
CT of the brain and CT angiogram (CTA) performed 3 hours after symptom onset showed no evidence of ischaemic damage or vascular occlusion.

Blood tests including complete blood examination, renal function, electrolytes, C reactive protein and creatine kinase were normal. Telemetry showed normal sinus rhythm. Electroencephalogram showed no evidence of seizure activity.
MRI of the brain completed 72 hours after symptom onset revealed symmetrical, bilateral thalamic diffusion restriction consistent with an artery of Percheron infarction.
Echocardiogram showed concentric increase in left ventricular wall thickness suggestive of cardiac amyloidosis.

Haematological work-up showed raised lambda light chains (442.50 mg/L) and Bence-Jones proteinuria (456 mg/L) suggestive of a plasma cell disorder. Bone marrow biopsy was not performed. Skeletal survey was normal.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: haematological tests performed; bone marrow biopsy not performed

evidence_events.source_span: CT scans of chest, abdomen and pelvis prior to current presentation showed no significant pathology.

Patient’s GCS remained 13–14 with persistent cognitive impairment, disorientation, and vertical gaze palsy noted later. She was discharged to stroke rehabilitation with NIH Stroke Scale score of 5 and modified Rankin Scale score of 4.
Discharged from stroke rehabilitation to residential care 5 weeks after infarction with residual cognitive deficits, mild global weakness, and expressive and receptive aphasia.

Normal CT and CTA initially delayed diagnosis. Additional cardiac and haematological findings suggest possible embolic source but are not definitive. Persistent neurological deficits are consistent with the infarction.
hidden_reference.article_derived_evidence_summary: A 79-year-old woman presented with acute unresponsiveness initially treated as cardiac arrest. Early CT and CTA were normal. MRI at 72 hours showed bilateral thalamic infarcts consistent with artery of Percheron infarction. Echocardiogram and haematological tests suggested cardiac amyloidosis and plasma cell disorder. The patient had persistent cognitive impairment and vertical gaze palsy.

source_metadata.notes: Case report from BMJ Case Reports 2021 describing an elderly patient with COVID-19 presenting with encephalopathy and evolving imaging consistent with PRES.

evidence_events.source_span: An 85-year-old man was brought to hospital for odd behaviour; oriented to self, place and time but using a remote controller as a phone; blood pressure 184/96 mm Hg; oxygen saturation 97% on room air; history of atrial fibrillation on apixaban, well-controlled diabetes, chronic kidney disease stage 3, and hypertension on losartan and furosemide; no alcohol or illicit drug use reported.

At emergency room, Glasgow Coma Scale was 14; awake, tracking examiner, following simple commands; clear speech; aware of hospital but unable to name the president; decreased attention and impulsive behaviour; no gaze or facial palsy; intact motor strength; chest X-ray showed bilateral lower lobe opacities; SARS-CoV-2 molecular assay positive.

Patient admitted for encephalopathy possibly due to COVID-19 with hypertensive encephalopathy pattern; blood pressure gradually lowered; impulsive behaviour limited continuous intravenous blood pressure medication; on second night became drowsy, not following commands, decreased verbal output, requiring tactile stimulation to open eyes.

Initial labs: normal white cell count, low platelets (93 x10^9/L), elevated serum creatinine (1.81 mg/dL), normal total bilirubin, elevated serum lactate (2.4 mmol/L), normal procalcitonin, normal ammonia, elevated troponin (0.250 ng/mL) stable on follow-up; negative alcohol level; normal blood glucose and electrolytes.
CT head on arrival negative for encephalomalacia, midline shift, hydrocephalus or acute findings.

Brain MRI obtained approximately 8 hours prior to mental status change showed negative diffusion weighted imaging (DWI) and apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) sequences; full MRI limited due to lack of cooperation; FLAIR sequence not obtained.

evidence_events.source_span: A 67-year-old man with a history of multivessel coronary disease, hypertension, peripheral arterial disease, diabetes mellitus type 2, dyslipidaemia and alcohol dependence presented with viral prodromal symptoms, diarrhoea and abdominal cramping for 5 days.

On arrival, his vitals read 38.9°C, 116 beats per min, blood pressure of 144/111 mm Hg and respiratory rate of 30 breaths per minute with an oxygen saturation of 98% on room air. Physical exam was unremarkable apart from an ill-appearing man.
Initial investigations revealed acute kidney injury and lymphopenia.
A chest radiograph revealed patchy infiltrates consistent with pneumonia.

He was started on empiric azithromycin, ceftriaxone, hydroxychloroquine with prophylactic enoxaparin. Hydroxychloroquine was discontinued shortly after as his glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase levels were low.
He continued to remain febrile with increasing oxygen requirements necessitating a high-flow nasal cannula. Repeat chest radiography revealed multilobar progression.
A complete COVID-19 inflammatory panel workup revealed elevated interleukin-6 levels.
Lopinavir, ritonavir and tocilizumab were sequentially added to the regimen. His fevers defervesced, and tachycardia improved.
Around the early morning of day 7, he was found newly disoriented with rambling and incomprehensible speech, right-sided facial droop with upper and lower extremity flaccidity.
CT of the head was negative for an acute intracranial bleed, but he was ineligible for tissue plasminogen activator as his last known well time was beyond 4.5 hours.
Aspirin, clopidogrel and atorvastatin were initiated.

CTA delineated multiple filling defects along the distal portion of the left common carotid artery with complete occlusion at the origin of the left internal carotid artery and proximal right vertebral artery. Additionally, 70%–80% stenosis of the proximal right internal carotid artery was noted.
Electroencephalography revealed focal slowing in the parietal, left and posterior areas of the brain.
Ultrasound with Doppler of the lower extremity demonstrated progression of the previously seen right lower extremity deep vein thrombosis.

Two days later, repeat CT revealed hypodensities within the left frontal and parietal lobes affecting the surrounding insular cortex, suggesting an acute multilobar infarct over distributions of the left anterior and middle cerebral arteries.

His clinical trajectory worsened with higher ventilator requirements, worsening agitation levels and eventual multiorgan failure. The family decided to transition to hospice care, where he passed away on 6 May 2020.

Patient was intubated for respiratory failure within 24 hours; received 5 days of hydroxychloroquine and two doses of a study drug (sarilumab vs placebo); course complicated by transient renal failure, Enterobacter pneumonia and Pseudomonas cystitis treated with piperacillin/tazobactam; hypercoagulable state with elevated D-dimers; treated with high-dose prophylactic enoxaparin

evidence_events.source_span: On day 24, a livedoid, retiform, purpuric rash was noted on the left hand and forearm; dermatology deemed rash characteristic of COVID-19-induced thrombotic microvascular injury; biopsy not performed

evidence_events.source_span: A 37-year-old British Caucasian man, with no medical or travel history, received a first dose of the COVID-19 ChAdOx1 vaccine.

The patient developed persistent back pain, new onset of distal paraesthesia within the hands and feet alongside a symmetrical, progressive ascending muscle weakness, presenting to accident and emergency a week later.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: presenting to accident and emergency a week later

evidence_events.source_span: Neurological examination findings demonstrated reduced motor strength in all four limbs, decreased light touch sensation and proprioception in the lower limbs from the groin distally, ataxic gait on heel-to-toe walking, and areflexia bilaterally in the lower limbs.

Vital signs were temperature 36.9°C, pulse rate 118 beats/min, blood pressure 148/89 mm Hg, respiratory rate 21 breaths/min and oxygen saturation 96%. Normal forced vital capacity (FVC) on admission measured 3.13 L.

Laboratory findings on admission were within normal range including haemoglobin, white cell count, platelet count, neutrophil count, lymphocyte count, monocyte count, sodium, potassium, urea, creatinine, estimated glomerular filtration rate, bilirubin, liver enzymes, albumin, C reactive protein, vitamin B12, folate, free T4, and thyroid stimulating hormone.

Blood-borne viral screen was negative, including hepatitis, Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) and cytomegalovirus (CMV). Antinuclear and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody serology tests were also negative. COVID-19 PCR swab was negative on admission.
Chest radiograph during admission demonstrated clear lungs and pleural spaces, with no radiological features to indicate COVID-19 pneumonitis.

Lumbar puncture revealed elevated protein level of 1.77 g/L with normal glucose and no white or red blood cells. Microbiology and culture of CSF yielded no growth. Oligoclonal band studies showed passive transfer of IgG, not indicative of intrathecal synthesis.

Nerve conduction study showed patchy attenuation of the upper limb motor responses on direct stimulation with no definitive features of demyelination; study was performed early in the suspected clinical course of GBS.
MRI head demonstrated normal brain parenchyma, ventricles and subarachnoid spaces with no abnormal parenchymal, pachymeningeal or leptomeningeal enhancement.

MRI whole spine with gadolinium contrast showed globally thickened cauda equina nerve rootlets bilaterally, particularly at S1, with prominent ventral cauda equina nerve root enhancement and pial enhancement of the conus medullaris.
The clinical picture, CSF analyses, nerve conduction study and MRI features all supported a diagnosis of Guillain-Barre syndrome.

The patient was admitted for FVC monitoring every 4 hours and commenced on intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) 2 g/kg daily for 5 days. Amitriptyline 25 mg once daily was prescribed for neuropathic pain.
On day 3 of IVIg treatment, FVC deteriorated to 2.6 L and the patient was admitted to intensive care for monitoring in case mechanical ventilation was required.
The patient completed 5-day IVIg course and did not require mechanical ventilation. Neurological symptoms were slow to recover and he remained under specialist neurology and physiotherapy care.

evidence_events.source_span: A 35-year-old male presented with sudden-onset expressive and receptive dysphasia, mild confusion and right arm incoordination (National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale: 5).
Initial CT brain showed no significant intracranial abnormalities and the patient received thrombolysis for a suspected ischaemic stroke.
Symptoms resolved over 2 hours and post-thrombolysis CT (day 2) was reported as normal.
Respiratory symptoms were absent, and admission nasopharyngeal swab was negative for SARS-CoV-2.

On day 3, the patient had right arm weakness and later developed expressive and receptive dysphasia, amnesia, headache and vomiting, followed by pyrexia 39.7°C. GCS remained 15/15 without evidence of meningism.
MRI brain (day 3) was normal.

source_metadata.title: Syphilitic meningitis presenting with multiple cranial neuropathies

evidence_events.source_span: A 37-year-old woman presented with a 2-week history of progressive neurological complaints including disequilibrium, unsteadiness, difficulty closing both eyes, right lip numbness, sequential bilateral hearing impairment, and slurred speech

On examination, bilateral cranial neuropathies involving trigeminal (V), abducens (VI), facial (VII), vestibulocochlear (VIII) and hypoglossal (XII) nerves were found with restricted lateral gaze bilaterally, bilateral facial weakness, decreased sensation in right V2 distribution, and weak tongue

Initial labs showed mild inflammation with elevated CRP 12 mg/L, ESR 21 mm/hour, thrombocytosis 447 x10^9/L; other blood tests including renal, electrolytes, liver function were unremarkable; HbA1c was 8.7%
CSF examination showed normal opening pressure 13.5 cm H2O, elevated protein 1.28 g/L, normoglycaemia, and lymphocyte predominant leucocytosis (76%) of 0.441 x10^9/L
MRI brain with gadolinium demonstrated enhancement of the trigeminal nerve at the pons, and facial and vestibulocochlear nerves at the geniculate ganglion
CT scans of neck, chest, abdomen and pelvis were negative for malignancy or lymphadenopathy

Serum T. pallidum particle agglutination assay (TPPA) and chemiluminescent microparticle immunoassay (CMIA) IgG and IgM were positive, with rapid plasma reagin (RPR) titre of 1:32, consistent with active syphilis infection
CSF analysis showed positive TPPA, positive VDRL titre 1:8, and negative T. pallidum PCR
Workup for other infectious, autoimmune and neoplastic disorders was negative including cryptococcal antigen and PCR, acid-fast bacilli stain, viral PCRs, autoimmune serologies, and CSF cytology

Patient was diagnosed with early syphilitic meningitis with multiple cranial neuropathies and commenced on intravenous benzylpenicillin for 15 days; no Jarisch Herxheimer reaction developed; cranial neuropathies improved dramatically by day 8

source_metadata.title: Schizophrenia syndrome due to C9ORF72 mutation case report: a cautionary tale and role of hybrid brain imaging!

evidence_events.source_span: The patient first presented to psychiatry at age 50 with both visual and auditory hallucinations, including command hallucinations to kill her family, which were very distressing to her.
Detailed history revealed the onset of paranoid delusions in her 20s, following an episode of post-partum psychotic depression.

She was diagnosed with schizophrenia, paranoid type, at her first presentation to psychiatry at age 50, with subsequent diagnosis of schizoaffective disorder due to episodes of depression, and episodes of psychosis independent of mood.

She has a family history of schizophrenia in two of her siblings including a recent history of schizophrenia-like illness with rapid cognitive and functional decline in her sister who was placed in a nursing facility and subsequently passed away with a diagnosis of “dementia” not otherwise specified.

Since her diagnosis she required both inpatient and outpatient psychiatric care and case management. She received psychotherapeutic supportive care in addition to pharmacological interventions, specifically atypical antipsychotic medications including olanzapine (up to 40 mg daily) with clonazepam, and then clozapine (up to 400 mg daily) with improvement in the psychotic symptoms.

At age 59 her illness became more resistant to treatment with prominent catatonic features (limited activity level, low oral intake, staying in bed all day and not being able to function in almost all areas).
Clinical computed tomography (CT)-Scan and 1.5 T MRI did not show any focal abnormalities and no general or focal atrophy.

With 15 sessions of bilateral lead placement ECT treatment she became more impaired with increased confusion, further impairment in functioning and memory, inappropriate binge eating and newly emergent disinhibition.
No focal or lateralizing neurological signs where identified.
Clinical CT-Scan and MRI were again read “within normal” by the cognitive neurologist (EF).
Further work-up with genetic testing was ordered to rule out genetic variants of frontotemporal dementia. The latter came back positive for C9ORF72 repeat expansion.
The patient was offered a state-of-the-art FD-Glucose Positron Emission Tomography/Magnetic Resonance Imaging scan available at our centre.
No significant atrophy was observed on T1-weighted images both qualitatively and quantitatively, confirming prior clinical reports of normal brain morphology in some patients with bvFTD with C9orf72.
FDG-PET revealed hypometabolism in medial superior frontal, insula, inferior temporal, thalamus, and anterior cingulate cortex.

source_metadata.title: Acute longitudinal extensive transverse myelitis secondary to asymptomatic SARS-CoV-2 infection

evidence_events.source_span: A 35-year-old woman presented to Accident and Emergency with a 1-day history of gradual onset sharp right-sided back pain, lateral to the thoracic spine at T8, progressive leg numbness and paresthesia bilaterally impairing her ability to walk, urinary retention and constipation.
During pregnancy, she developed ulcerative colitis confirmed on flexible sigmoidoscopy and is well controlled on mesalazine enemas.

Five days prior to admission, she had tested positive asymptomatically on a SARS-CoV-2 reverse-transcriptase PCR nasopharyngeal swab; on admission, a confirmatory positive RT-PCR nasopharyngeal swab was obtained with a low cycle threshold value of 13.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: Five days prior to admission; on admission

evidence_events.source_span: On examination, she had bilaterally exaggerated knee reflexes, positive Babinski's sign, decreased power to grade 2 on ankle dorsiflexion, great toe extension and ankle plantar flexion, impaired sensation at L4 and L5 dermatomes and absent sensation at S1 and S2 dermatomes.

General lab results including haemogram, inflammatory markers, thyroid, liver and renal function tests were normal; urine dipstick was negative; blood tests for syphilis, HIV, anti-neuronal antibodies, vasculitic screen, voltage-gated potassium channel antibodies, NMDA receptor antibodies and GAD antibodies were negative; chest X-ray was normal.

Lumbar puncture CSF analysis for aquaporin-4 antibodies, anti-MOG antibodies, protein, glucose, oligoclonal bands, microscopy, cultures and sensitivities, and viral PCR (including human T-cell leukaemia virus type 1 and SARS-CoV-2) all returned negative; CSF protein was 0.4 g, white cell count <0.001 ×10⁹/L, red cell count 0.0002 ×10¹²/L with no organisms.

MRI of the spine with gadolinium enhancement showed T2-weighted lesions with multiple regions of patchy hyperintensity in the thoracic spinal cord both centrally and peripherally; subarachnoid space and lumbosacral region were normal; MRI of the brain was largely unremarkable with a few tiny frontal parietal high signals.

Cauda equina was ruled out by normal lumbosacral MRI; vascular event was unlikely given young age, lack of risk factors and head imaging; trauma denied; systemic infections including syphilis and HIV were negative; anti-neuronal antibodies negative for paraneoplastic syndrome; vasculitis screen and CSF analysis normal; antibodies for voltage-gated potassium channels, NMDA receptor and GAD were negative and less consistent with presentation.

Given recent positive COVID-19 test, post-viral acute longitudinal extensive transverse myelitis (LETM) was considered most likely; acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy less likely due to upper motor neuron signs; imaging ruled out epidural space-occupying lesion; multiple sclerosis and neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD) considered but aquaporin-4 and anti-MOG antibodies negative and clinical presentation lacked eye involvement.

Patient was catheterised and started on laxatives; methylprednisolone 1 g intravenously once daily for 3 days was started, then stepped down to oral prednisolone 60 mg daily with omeprazole for gastroprotection.

During steroids, she improved clinically with regained full sensation in L4, L5, S1 and S2 dermatomes, regained motor function to walk short distances independently and climb stairs with crutches, and fully regained bladder function.

Repeat MRI on discharge showed interval reduction in conspicuity of previously seen long-segment myelopathy in mid-thoracic cord with no gadolinium enhancement, suggesting resolving transverse myelitis.

source_metadata.title: Neurological Complications of COVID-19: A Rare Case of Bilateral Blindness

evidence_events.source_span: A 49-year-old man was referred to our hospital with abrupt complete vision loss in his right eye and visual impairment in the left eye. Three weeks earlier, he was admitted to the hospital based on his respiratory symptoms and was diagnosed with COVID-19 infection (confirmed with polymerase chain reaction [PCR] test). Four days after he was discharged, he noticed a sudden vision loss in his right eye and a mild visual impairment in his left eye. In addition, he reported moderate headache.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: Three weeks earlier; Four days after discharge

evidence_events.source_span: In the physical and neurological examination, he was afebrile, awake, oriented, and speech was normal. Both pupils were symmetric and mid-sized on the first day of admission. The right pupil was nonreactive and the left pupil was reactive. Visual acuity on the first day was measured as 0/10 for the right eye (no light perception) and 5/10 for the left one. The fundoscopy of the both eyes were normal. All cranial nerves, sensory, motor, deep tendon, plantar reflex and cerebellar examinations, and mental status examination were normal.

Spiral chest computed tomography (CT) scan indicated ground-glass, patchy infiltrations in sub-pleural area, which were attributed to the former COVID-19 infection. Both abdominopelvic ultrasound and CT scan were normal, and no abnormalities were detected in temporal artery biopsy and ultrasound. Also, no evidence of mucormycosis infection was observed in paranasal sinus CT scan.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: Spiral chest CT, abdominopelvic ultrasound and CT, temporal artery biopsy and ultrasound, paranasal sinus CT

evidence_events.source_span: Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) indicated diffuse restricted bilateral foci in both parietal and occipital lobes in favor of acute infarction. Diffuse weighted imaging demonstrated restricted bilateral hyperintense signals in parietal and occipital region.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: Brain MRI with diffusion weighted imaging

evidence_events.source_span: Laboratory tests revealed normal complete blood count and biochemical tests. Moreover, interferon-gamma release assay, anti-MOG and anti-NMDA receptor antibodies, vasculitis tests, viral infection tests, and current SARS-CoV-2 PCR were reported as negative. Lumbar puncture was performed and the results showed negative anti-herpes simplex virus 1 and 2, varicella zoster IgM antibodies, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF).
evidence_events.procedural_cue: Laboratory blood tests and lumbar puncture

evidence_events.source_span: Two days after admission, visual acuity of the left eye deteriorated into complete vision loss, similar to the right eye (no light perception).

Cerebral angiography was done to rule out reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome and other cerebral vessels involvements. Despite normal cerebral angiography findings, nimodipine was administered. Bridging anti-anticoagulant therapy (heparin and then warfarin) was initiated because of a moderate to large patent foramen oval.

Occipital cortex biopsy showed brain tissue with focal infiltration of foamy macrophages mixed with reactive astrocytes and no plasma cell infiltration. No evidence of vasculitis or granuloma were detected. The immunohistochemistry study demonstrated positivity of CD68 and scattered CD3+ cells.
Brain MRI after deterioration revealed extension of infarct lesions to the left cerebellar hemisphere, bilateral frontoparietal lobes, splenium of corpus callosum, and anterior aspect of the pons.

Considering all of the evidence, post-COVID-19 encephalitis diagnosis was considered for the patient. Methyl prednisolone pulse therapy and intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) were initiated, resulting in improvement of mental state and clinical symptoms, but both eyes remained blind (no light perception).
evidence_events.procedural_cue: Methyl prednisolone pulse therapy and IVIg administration

evidence_events.source_span: After 3 months of clinical follow-up, the patient was still blind (no light perception) without pupillary light reflex. Muscle forces returned to normal; MRI showed no new lesions. Prednisolone was tapered and warfarin continued.

source_metadata.title: COVID-19 complicated by immune thrombocytopaenic purpura and internal jugular vein thrombosis
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case presentation, investigations, differential diagnosis, treatment, and outcome sections.

evidence_events.source_span: A 61-year-old woman with a background of hypertension, fibromyalgia and previous lumbar spinal fusion surgery due to prolapsed disc presented with a sudden onset of severe occipital headache associated with nausea and mild photophobia. She was also noted to have a mild breathlessness and productive cough with white sputum for 3 days. She had a positive nasopharyngeal PCR swab for COVID-19 in the community 5 days prior.

On admission, she was afebrile, with normal oxygen saturations. Her full blood count was normal with haemoglobin 134 g/L, white cell count 3.4 ×10⁹/L, neutrophils 2 ×10⁹/L, lymphocytes 0.7 ×10⁹/L, platelets 153 ×10⁹/L, C reactive protein <5 mg/L.

A CT scan of the brain was performed, this showed no abnormality. Her chest X-ray was also unremarkable. X-ray lumbar spine showed four-level posterior transpedicular screw fixation from L3 to S1, with anterior lumbar interbody fusion at L3-L4.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: CT brain, chest X-ray, lumbar spine X-ray

evidence_events.source_span: While the patient was awaiting the MRI scan, she did not have blood tests for 3 days as she was otherwise clinically stable with mild COVID-19 symptoms. The repeated blood test showed an acute marked thrombocytopenia; platelets were 5 ×10⁹/L. The rest of the blood results were unremarkable.
A blood film was requested, which showed true thrombocytopenia with no red blood cell fragments or schistocytes present.

An urgent repeated CT head was performed to rule out acute intracranial bleeding following a significant drop in platelets, this was reported as normal. Further investigations including rheumatological markers, viral panel (hepatitis B, hepatitis C, HIV, cytomegalovirus, Epstein-Barr virus), haematinics, thyroid function, coagulation screen and helicobacter pylori faecal antigen were all unremarkable.
Due to nonresolving headache, she underwent an MRV, which showed bilateral internal jugular vein occlusion with no evidence of infarct or haemorrhage.

The haematology team agreed that the acute reduction in patient’s platelet counts was most likely due to ITP secondary to COVID-19 infection. Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) was excluded based on low 4Ts score and timing. Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura was excluded due to absence of microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, red cell schistocytes or low ADAMTS13 activity. Drug-induced thrombocytopenia and autoimmune disorders were excluded based on history and negative rheumatologic markers. Malignancy was excluded clinically and by investigations.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: Clinical assessment and exclusion of differential diagnoses

evidence_events.source_span: For ITP, she was treated with intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) 1 g/Kg for 2 days. After 1 day of IVIG, blood showed an improvement in platelets to 10 ×10⁹/L. She did not require platelet transfusion as she had no bleeding and normal CT brain.

The patient was followed up in haematology clinic the day after discharge; platelets had increased to 41 ×10⁹/L. A further haematology appointment 5 days later showed platelets back to normal range, 213 ×10⁹/L.
She was commenced on anticoagulation low molecular weight heparin (enoxaparin) for jugular venous thrombosis, later switched to apixaban. Anticoagulation to be continued for at least 6 months.

evidence_events.source_span: General examination was unremarkable. Speech showed nasal intonation. Cranial nerve examination showed normal visual acuity, ocular motility, pupillary size and reactivity, mild bifacial weakness, decreased bilateral palatal movements and poor pharyngeal reflex. Motor and sensory examination, deep tendon reflexes, cerebellar and gait examination were normal.
MRI of the brain and spinal cord was normal.
NCS showed reduced sensory nerve action potential and sensory conduction velocity of ulnar and sural nerves with normal motor nerve conduction parameters suggestive of mild sensory neuropathy.
Slow repetitive nerve stimulation (RNS) of nasalis (41%) and trapezius (18.1%) showed a significant decremental response.
Intravenous neostigmine showed marked improvement in swallowing.
Serum antiacetylcholine receptor antibody (AchR) titres were 4.5 nmol/L (<0.40: negative). Serum antimuscle-specific kinase (MuSK) antibody titres were less than 0.18 U/L (<0.40: negative).
The SARS-CoV-2 IgG ECLIA antibody titres (Roche diagnostics, USA) were 129 (<1.0: non-reactive).
Thyroid function tests were normal.
High-resolution CT of the thorax did not reveal thymic hyperplasia or thymoma.
The absence of arm and neck weakness at presentation, preserved deep tendon reflexes, absence of demyelination on NCS and decremental response on RNS ruled out Guillain-Barré syndrome.
The absence of history suggestive of canned or stored food ingestion and further clinical course negated botulism.
The absence of pyramidal and/or cerebellar signs, preserved sensorium and normal brain imaging ruled out central causes like stroke or brain stem demyelination.
He was started on oral prednisolone (30 mg/day) and oral pyridostigmine (60 mg every 6 hours).

On day 8 of admission, he developed neck and respiratory muscle weakness with a single breath count of eight (MGC 17). Arterial blood gas analysis showed type II respiratory failure (PCo2 52 mm Hg). Because of a myasthenic crisis, he was intubated and connected to a ventilator.
He was treated with intravenous immunoglobulin (0.4 mg/kg/day) for five consecutive days. Prednisolone was increased to 40 mg/day and pyridostigmine was stopped.
On day 10, he developed upper limb proximal weakness (MGC 33). Tracheostomy was done on day 14.

He showed improvement in neck and limb weakness from day 16 (MGC 31). He was later started on azathioprine (50 mg every 12 hours), pyridostigmine (60 mg every 6 hours) and prednisolone (40 mg every 24 hours) were continued.

He was decannulated on day 21, oral soft diet trial was given with a nasogastric tube in situ (MGC 19). He was discharged 2 days later with a nasogastric tube. Bulbar function improved in the subsequent 2 weeks and oral feeds were resumed (MGC 0). Prednisolone was tapered after 2 months of stable course after discharge.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: day 21 and subsequent 2 weeks; 2 months after discharge
