source_metadata.title: SARS-CoV-2 Infection and Emery-Dreifuss Syndrome in a Young Patient with a Family History of Dilated Cardiomyopathy

evidence_events.source_span: 16-year-old female patient with unknown personal pathological history, with a cardiac hereditary history; sister diagnosed with dilated cardiomyopathy requiring ICD and heart transplant; hospitalized for SARS-CoV-2 virus infection with mild COVID-19 symptoms including rhinorrhea and dry cough

At hospitalization, clinical examination revealed good general condition, temperature 37.4 °C, SaO2 99% at room air, rhythmic heart sounds, no retrosternal pain, tachycardia, or tachypnea; stage 2 hypertension (blood pressure 150/90 mmHg), heart rate 80 bpm, normal ECG, Glasgow Coma Scale 15/15

Laboratory tests at admission showed elevated high-sensitive cardiac troponin I (hs-cTnI 40.8 ng/L, normal < 6 ng/L), creatine kinase (CK 590 U/L, normal < 192 U/L), N-terminal probrain natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP 154 pg/mL, normal < 125 pg/mL), D-dimers (580 ng/mL, normal < 500 ng/mL), C-reactive protein (CRP 2 mg/dL, normal 0.5 mg/dL), AST 35 U/L (normal < 25 U/L), ALT 50 U/L (normal < 25 U/L), lactate dehydrogenase (LDH 248 U/L, normal < 220 U/L); normal leukocytes, lymphocytes, neutrophils, platelets, creatinine, sodium, potassium
Dynamic ECGs on day 4 of hospitalization revealed ventricular extrasystoles without clinical manifestations

Heart ultrasound showed slightly dilated left ventricle with dimensions 53/35 mm, left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) 55-60%, hypokinesia in the lower wall, suspicion of viral subacute myocarditis and cardiomyopathy

Heart MRI performed immediately after discharge refuted suspicion of viral subacute myocarditis and confirmed diagnosis of dilated cardiomyopathy; MRI showed slight left ventricular dilation, preserved biventricular systolic function (LVEF 58%), small area of focal mid-myocardial fibrosis at basal interventricular septum, and non-specific focal fibrosis at lower insertion point of right ventricle on left ventricle

One month after discharge, patient developed musculoskeletal disorders including gait disorders with impossible heel strike, Achilles tendon retractions, limitation of extension of arms and ankles, but symmetrical deep tendon reflexes present
Genetic testing identified heterozygous mutation c.448A > C (p.Thr150Pro) in exon 2 of LMNA gene, confirming diagnosis of Emery-Dreifuss Muscular Dystrophy

Patient transferred to Cardiology Department due to rhythm disorders; Holter monitoring showed first-degree AV block, non-sustained ventricular tachycardia (NSVT), isolated and systematized monomorphic extrasystolic ventricular arrhythmia in episodes of ventricular bigeminy; ventricular events represented less than 1% of total events

Cardiac ultrasound showed situs solitus, levocardia, normal atrioventricular connections, normal pulmonary venous return, intact interatrial and interventricular septa; mild left ventricular contractile dysfunction with LVEF 53%, 0-I scale mitral regurgitation
Antiarrhythmic treatment with amiodarone was initiated; PR interval prolonged; patient scheduled for bicameral ICD implantation
evidence_events.temporal_cue: after Holter monitoring and cardiac ultrasound
evidence_events.procedural_cue: Treatment initiated and ICD implantation planned

source_metadata.title: Multiorgan thrombosis as a complication of COVID-19 pneumonia
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case presentation, investigations, outcome and follow-up sections with source order preserved.

evidence_events.source_span: A 47-year-old man, positive for SARS-CoV-2, presented with sudden-onset central compressive chest pain radiating to his left shoulder, pleuritic in nature, associated with shortness of breath at rest, lethargy, myalgias and a non-productive dry cough over 7 days.

On initial examination, blood pressure 120/89 mm Hg, sinus tachycardia 113 beats/min, afebrile, oxygen saturation 92% on room air correcting to 96% on 5 L/min face mask, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, sparse fine-end inspiratory crepitations at both lung bases, normal heart sounds, soft non-tender abdomen, no lower limb oedema or signs of deep vein thrombosis.

Initial blood tests showed elevated white cell count 13.06×10^9/L, neutrophils 10.31×10^9/L, slightly low lymphocytes 1.22×10^9/L, normal eosinophils, haemoglobin 149 g/L, slightly raised creatinine 123 µmol/L, mildly raised procalcitonin 0.192 ng/mL, random blood glucose 25 mmol/L, raised CRP 115 mg/L.

Admission chest X-ray showed diffuse patchy airspace shadowing throughout both lungs consistent with COVID-19 pneumonia; ECG showed right heart strain with new-onset right bundle branch block; D-dimer grossly elevated at 5483 ng/mL; initial troponins highly raised at 504 ng/L, uptrending to 1645 ng/L.

CT pulmonary angiogram showed no pulmonary embolism but bilateral consolidations and widespread ground-glass changes consistent with COVID-19 pneumonia; bedside transthoracic echocardiogram revealed globular dilated left ventricle with ejection fraction 35%, akinetic apical, anteroseptal and anterior walls, borderline dilated right ventricle with normal contractility, no significant valvular abnormality.

Initial diagnosis was acute coronary syndrome complicated by myocarditis on background of COVID-19 pneumonia; patient started on remdesivir, dexamethasone, co-amoxiclav, aspirin, clopidogrel, enoxaparin, enalapril, and atorvastatin; decision to treat medically without percutaneous coronary intervention.

Three days post-admission, patient became drowsy, tachypnoeic, Glasgow Coma Score 12, slurred speech, urinary incontinence; arterial blood gases showed type 1 respiratory failure with metabolic compensation; repeat blood tests showed downtrending CRP, downtrending troponins, normal white cell count.

Urgent CT brain showed small low density area in right occipital lobe likely ischaemic infarct; MRI brain showed established infarcts in large part of left temporal lobe and right occipital lobe with minor micro-haemorrhagic transformation in left temporal lobe and slight sulcal oedema.
Repeat transthoracic echocardiogram showed apical akinesia consistent with myocardial infarct and a large apical mural thrombus; no pericardial effusion or valvular abnormalities.

Thrombophilia screen, erythrocyte sedimentation rate and auto-antibody screen were performed; total extractable nuclear antigen, anti-nuclear antibody, anti-double stranded DNA, complements and immunoglobulins were normal; ESR was raised at 78 mm; thrombophilia screen negative for mutations.

Two days after starting unfractionated heparin, patient developed acute abdominal pain; CT abdomen and pelvis showed infarctions in spleen and kidneys, thrombi in superior mesenteric artery and left femoral artery; no bowel ischaemic changes.
Patient tested negative for SARS-CoV-2 on two consecutive days, 14 days after initial positive swab; contrast echocardiogram showed large pedunculated left ventricular thrombus.

Surgical removal of left ventricular thrombus via midline sternotomy was performed successfully after warfarin reversal; thrombus removed as a whole under direct vision; patient admitted to cardiac ICU postoperatively with no complications.

source_metadata.title: Transient acetylcholine receptor-related myasthenia gravis, post multisystem inflammatory syndrome in children (MIS-C) temporally associated with COVID-19 infection

evidence_events.source_span: A previously well 7-year-old girl presented with a 4-day history of fever, sore throat, cough, diarrhoea and headaches.

Clinical examination revealed a prostrated and dehydrated child in shock (hypotensive—blood pressure 65/53 mm Hg, tachycardic 135 beats/min, cold extremities and a capillary refill time >3 s), temperature 39.5°C, bilateral non-suppurative conjunctivitis, erythematous desquamating rash on the abdomen, back and neck, and swelling of the hands and feet.
In the PICU, the multiorgan failure (respiratory, cardiac and renal) necessitated ventilatory support, inotropes (epinephrine and norepinephrine) and close monitoring of fluid balance.
Based on the clinical presentation, the multiorgan failure, raised inflammatory markers and a positive SARS-CoV-2 antibody test, MIS-C was diagnosed.

Following discharge from the PICU, myalgia and marked proximal muscle weakness were noted, more pronounced in the lower limbs (proximal 2/5, distal 3/5) compared with the upper limbs (proximal 3/5, distal 4/5), with positive Gower sign, waddling gait and compensatory lumbar lordosis; deep tendon reflexes were preserved.

Subsequently, 72 hours later, fluctuating and fatigable bilateral ptosis emerged with impairment of upward gaze, mild diplopia, positive curtain and Cogan eyelid twitch test, preserved pupillary reflexes, and positive ocular cold compression test.

SARS-CoV-2 PCR was negative; SARS-CoV-2 IgG antibodies to N protein were positive; full blood count showed leucocytosis with neutrophilia and lymphopenia; raised inflammatory markers (C reactive protein 292 mg/L, ferritin 1022 µg/L, D-dimer 11.65 mg/L, lactate dehydrogenase 517 u/L); renal function showed urea 22.1 mmol/L, creatinine 259 µmol/L, sodium 126 mmol/L, potassium 3.2 mmol/L; cardiac enzymes elevated (troponin T 477 ng/L, pro-BNP 98,900 ng/L); echocardiogram showed reduced left ventricular function with mildly dilated left ventricle and ejection fraction 38%, no coronary aneurysms.

Creatine kinase was elevated at 6617 u/L; acetylcholine receptor antibody tested positive with a titre of 0.51 nmol/L (normal 0.39); muscle-specific tyrosine kinase antibody test was not done due to lack of availability.
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: muscle-specific tyrosine kinase antibody test unavailable

evidence_events.source_span: Intravenous methylprednisolone and intravenous immunoglobulin were given for MIS-C, followed by oral prednisone tapered over 4 weeks; pyridostigmine was initiated for myasthenia gravis with suboptimal response, then low-dose oral corticosteroids and methotrexate were added.

One month post-discharge, ejection fraction returned to normal, no coronary aneurysms noted, complete recovery of renal, liver and haematological function; repeat SARS-CoV-2 antibody and acetylcholine receptor antibody testing were negative; ptosis and proximal muscle weakness completely resolved; pyridostigmine and corticosteroids were discontinued.

source_metadata.title: Varicella zoster virus meningitis with rashes masked by a mask as a precaution for COVID-19

evidence_events.source_span: A 41-year-old man without prior vaccination of COVID-19 presented with a worsening headache accompanied by nausea and photophobia for 3 days.

On physical examination, he was alert, with a temperature of 36.7°C, blood pressure of 105/60 mm Hg, pulse rate of 70/min, respiration rate of 16/min and oxygen saturation at 97% in ambient air. No signs of meningeal irritation or neurological symptoms were observed.
His blood tests and head CT were unremarkable.
On removing the mask, rashes with blisters were observed on the left side of his nose and hard palate in the area of the second branch of the trigeminal nerve
The rapid test was positive for varicella zoster virus (VZV) (DermaQuick, Maruho, Osaka, Japan), and VZV infection was diagnosed.

Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis revealed an initial pressure of 16 cm H2O, leucocyte count of 217/μL (lymphocytes 92%), protein level of 129 mg/dL and glucose level of 55 mg/dL (blood glucose level of 138 mg/dL).
A week later, his CSF tested positive for VZV DNA via PCR.
He received intravenous acyclovir for 14 days resulting in improvement of symptoms.

source_metadata.title: Fungal brain abscess in a post COVID-19 patient

evidence_events.source_span: A 62-year-old man presented with chief complaints of altered behaviour, slurring of speech and left-side weakness for 6 days. The neurological examination also revealed left-sided weakness.

He had a history of hospitalisation for COVID-19 pneumonia with moderate severity of disease (CT severity score of 15/25). He stayed in the hospital for 30 days with an initial 10 days of intensive care unit admission. He was kept on supplemental oxygen and received methylprednisolone 20 mg intravenous twice a day (BD) for 6 days. He recovered from the disease and was discharged from the hospital only 10 days ago with SpO2 of 92% on room air.
The patient had controlled diabetes for which he was on oral hypoglycaemic drugs.
His routine blood tests were normal except for mildly raised alkaline phosphatase and D-dimer levels.

MRI of the brain was done, which revealed a thick-walled peripherally enhancing lesion of size ~45×43×37 mm in the right parietal lobe in the peritrigonal location. The lesion wall had crenulated margins with intracavitary projections, which showed blooming on susceptibility-weighted imaging (SWI) and diffusion restriction on diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI). The core of the lesion was hyperintense, which was suppressed on a fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) sequence. Marked perilesional oedema was also seen on T2-weighted/FLAIR imaging with surrounding mass effect. On magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS), raised lipid lactates and trehalose were seen.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: MRI brain including SWI, DWI, FLAIR, MRS

evidence_events.source_span: Contrast-enhanced CT of the thorax showed few peripheral pulmonary cavities, segmental right pulmonary artery thrombus and diffuse parenchymal fibrosis.
Biopsy from cavitary lung lesion was positive for Aspergillus infection.

He was started on intravenous antibiotics, vancomycin, voriconazole and subcutaneous enoxaparin 60 mg BD. His neurological symptoms deteriorated despite antifungal treatment; therefore, craniotomy with excision of the brain abscess was done.
The culture of the pus had grown Aspergillus organism.

source_metadata.title: Bilateral basal ganglia ischemia associated with COVID-19: a case report and review of the literature

evidence_events.source_span: A 64-year-old Asian (Pakistani) diabetic and hypertensive gentleman initially presented with fever, cough, and progressive shortness of breath for 3 days.

On presentation to the hospital, his blood pressure was 110/70 mmHg, pulse rate was 100 bpm, respiratory rate was 23/min, and oxygen saturation was 89% on room air. On examination, the patient had coarse crackles in bilateral lower lung fields, which did not change character with cough. Neurological examination was negative for meningeal signs and the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) was 15/15.
A chest X-ray (CXR) demonstrated bilateral diffuse heterogeneous infiltrates, more pronounced on the right side.
A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for SARS-CoV-2 Reverse transcription Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT PCR), which was positive, confirming COVID-19.

A high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT) of the chest showed multifocal, multilobar ground-glass opacities in central and peripheral locations, more pronounced in middle and lower lobes, with septal thickening, giving a classical crazy paving appearance. Radiological Society of North America (RSNA) guidelines were used to calculate disease burden based on HRCT, and the score was 21/40 (severe disease burden).

During the hospital stay, the patient was admitted to the COVID-19 isolation unit, where he received moxifloxacin, piperacillin/tazobactam, enoxaparin, and dexamethasone, based on the local COVID-19 treatment protocol at that time.

On day three of his hospital stay, the patient developed bilateral lower limb pain without any erythema, change in color, or change in the size of his lower limbs. An arterial and venous Doppler ultrasound was negative for occlusion or deep venous thrombosis.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: On day three of his hospital stay

evidence_events.source_span: On day four, the patient was noted to have developed confusion and decreased level of consciousness. The GCS dropped from 15/15 to 10/15. The patient was emergently sedated, intubated, and mechanically ventilated to protect the airway.

An urgent non-contrast computed tomography (NCCT) of the brain revealed accentuated hypodensities in the left basal ganglia (involving caudate nucleus, lentiform nucleus, and anterior limb of internal capsule), with mass effect on the ipsilateral frontal horn. Another smaller hypodensity in the right caudate nucleus was also seen.

With a diagnosis of ischemic stroke, the patient received aspirin and continued to receive statin and antihypertensives. However, thrombolysis was not considered as the exact time of onset of symptoms was not documented, and the patient had well-developed ischemic changes on the NCCT, signifying being past the thrombolytic period.
Over the next few days, the patient received care in the intensive care unit, but his general condition deteriorated, with increasing oxygen requirements.
On day 27 of the hospital stay, the patient developed cardiac arrest. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation was unsuccessful, and he passed away.

diagnostic_reasoning_verbatim_spans: A nasopharyngeal swab was collected for SARS-CoV-2 Reverse transcription Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT PCR), which was positive, confirming COVID-19.

An urgent non-contrast computed tomography (NCCT) of the brain revealed accentuated hypodensities in the left basal ganglia (involving caudate nucleus, lentiform nucleus, and anterior limb of internal capsule), with mass effect on the ipsilateral frontal horn. Another smaller hypodensity in the right caudate nucleus was also seen.
Due to clinical circumstances, we were unable to obtain the magnetic resonance imaging for the patient.
With a diagnosis of ischemic stroke, the patient received aspirin and continued to receive statin and antihypertensives.
The case demonstrates the importance of neuroimaging in the effective management of patients with neurological signs associated with coronavirus disease 2019.

MRI brain was not obtained, limiting further lesion characterization.

Neurological deterioration and imaging findings support COVID-19-associated prothrombotic state causing bilateral basal ganglia ischemia.

evidence_events.source_span: A 63-year-old man presented 14 days following his first dose of Oxford-AstraZeneca vaccination with new-onset lower back pain 9 days postvaccination, then severe bilateral facial weakness, unsteadiness, lower limb weakness and paraesthesia over a 48-hour period.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: 14 days following vaccination; 9 days postvaccination onset of back pain; 5 days later onset of neurological symptoms over 48 hours

evidence_events.source_span: Neurological examination revealed profound sensory ataxia, facial diplegia involving the forehead, proximal lower limb weakness, bilateral lower limb areflexia and impaired distal lower limb proprioception. He was unable to walk without assistance and had incomplete eye closure bilaterally.

On his second day of admission, he reported diplopia on lateral gaze bilaterally. Examination revealed impaired adduction, restricted upward gaze and intorsion with down gaze bilaterally, consistent with partial cranial nerve III palsies. Direct and consensual pupillary responses were normal. His bedside forced vital capacity was 2.2 L. His GBS disability rating score was 3.

Testing for acquired causes of neuropathy was normal, including urea and electrolytes, liver function tests, glycated haemoglobin, B12/folate levels, thyroid function tests, serum protein electrophoresis and serum-free light chains, hepatitis B/C, HIV and syphilis serology, erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C reactive protein, antinuclear antibodies and antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies.

Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) examination revealed albumin cytological dissociation with a markedly elevated protein of 2.99 g/L (normal range 0.15–0.45 g/L), 0/µL erythrocytes, 4/µL lymphocytes and 1/µL polymorphonuclear leukocytes. Serum anti-GQ1b antibody was negative. Other potential causes for an elevated CSF protein were unrevealing with a negative CSF culture, normal CSF cytology and flow cytometry.

MRI of the brain with contrast demonstrated enhancement of the facial and oculomotor nerves bilaterally, consistent with the clinical examination findings of facial diplegia and partial bilateral cranial nerve III palsies.

Nerve conduction studies (NCS) and needle electromyography (EMG) showed evidence of a long-standing axonal neuropathy with reduced motor and sensory amplitudes and length-dependent chronic neurogenic changes on EMG, but no acute abnormalities.

The patient was treated with a 5-day course of intravenous immunoglobulin (2 g/kg) and supportive care including topical lubricating eye drops, eye patches and an indwelling catheter after developing urinary retention.

At 6 weeks after onset of symptoms, the patient’s ophthalmoplegia and ataxia have resolved and he has minimal residual bilateral facial weakness. He has persistent bilateral proximal lower limb weakness (Medical Research Council grade 4). The patient has returned home, is living independently and is ambulating with a four-wheel frame.

source_metadata.title: Isolated Memory Loss in Anti-NMDAR Encephalitis

evidence_events.source_span: A 29-year-old woman started to experience a decrease in job performance with marked impairment in remembering new information and progressive memory disorder worsening with emotional distress; she was unaware of her amnesia and had no anxiety, depression, or psychotic symptoms.
Neurologic examination revealed only an episodic memory deficit without other signs or symptoms; Mini-Mental State Examination showed impaired delayed recall (27/30).
evidence_events.temporal_cue: One month after onset, on admission

evidence_events.source_span: Laboratory investigations on admission were normal.
EEG revealed epileptiform discharges in the temporal lobes but no seizures were experienced; 24-hour EEG showed no seizure activity.
Neuropsychological examination showed a severe isolated deficit of verbal and visual episodic memory.
Brain MRI revealed bilateral hyperintense lesions on fluid-attenuated inversion recovery and T2-weighted images involving both temporal lobes.
CSF analysis showed mild pleocytosis and presence of oligoclonal bands.
NMDAR-IgG was detected in the patient's serum and CSF by cell-based assay and confirmed by indirect immunofluorescence assays.
Ultrasound and MRI of the pelvis were normal.
Total body PET showed slight hypometabolism in the right temporal cortex and cerebellar hemispheres.
The patient was treated with IV immunoglobulins 0.4 g/kg/d for 5 days and oral prednisone 25 mg/d; a second IVIG course was given after 3 months.
Brain MRI performed 4 months after admission showed persistence of T2 hyperintense lesions in the temporal lobes.
At 7 months after onset, the patient showed marked improvement of memory deficit (MMSE 30/30), awareness of improvement, regained social life but had not returned to work.

evidence_events.source_span: A 9-year-old boy presented due to worsening back pain and unsteadiness with lower limb weakness and absent lower limb reflexes

Neurological examination showed intact cranial nerves, normal upper limb tone, power and reflexes, lower limbs power 4/5 with absent left leg reflexes and just elicitable right leg reflexes, bilateral equivocal plantar reflexes, wide based ataxic gait

Blood tests showed haemoglobin 126 g/L, WBC 5.9x10^9/L, slightly decreased neutrophils 1.2x10^9/L, platelets 414x10^9/L, CRP 2.4 mg/L, ESR 10 mm/hour slightly elevated, normal renal, liver, folate, B12, thyroid, CK, immunoglobulin profile, negative infectious and autoimmune screens
Routine admission nasopharyngeal swab for COVID-19 was positive

CSF showed 874/cu mm red blood cells, <1/cu mm polymorphs, 2/cu mm lymphocytes, glucose 3.6 mmol/L, lactate 1.71 mmol/L, protein 0.78 g/L (slightly elevated) suggestive of albuminocytologic dissociation, negative viral PCR and culture
Brain and spine MRI with contrast showed symmetrical enhancement of the proximal mastoid segments of the facial nerves and the cauda equina
Nerve conduction velocity study was requested but not performed due to patient intolerance and clinical improvement
Clinical presentation of back pain, lower limb weakness, areflexia, albuminocytological dissociation in CSF, and MRI enhancement of nerve roots were suggestive of Guillain-Barre syndrome
Patient was managed conservatively without intravenous immunoglobulin; received analgesics, gabapentin, and physiotherapy with gradual clinical improvement
Patient recovered gradually without immunotherapy, regained normal power and reflexes, able to walk independently with mild residual fatigue and back pain at follow-up

source_metadata.title: Severe tick-borne encephalitis in a patient recovered from COVID 19

evidence_events.source_span: A 24-year-old female patient with no medical history of chronic diseases was admitted to the Department of Neurology at Medical University of Bialystok in early December of 2020 with fever, dizziness, and progressive left-sided hemiparesis for the last three days.
She lived in north-eastern Poland, close to the forest, owned a dog, and had recreationally been picking mushrooms. She did not report a recent tick bite and was not vaccinated against TBE.

The patient had a SARS-CoV2 infection three weeks prior to admission to the hospital (as shown by positive IgG against SARS-CoV-2 at admission). During the COVID-19 infection she had fever, myalgia, and mild dyspnoea (without indications for oxygen therapy) and recovered after one week.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: positive IgG against SARS-CoV-2 at admission

evidence_events.source_span: In the Department of Neurology, the patient presented neck stiffness, signs of the lower motor neuron weakness in the upper limb, and upper motor neuron weakness in the lower limb more dominant on the left side (left limbs grade 2 and right limbs grade 3 in the Medical Research Council Scale for Muscle Strength), dysarthria, and right six cranial nerve palsy.

Her clinical condition deteriorated rapidly during the first week of hospitalization, weakness increased to left limbs grade 1 and right limb grade 2 on the MRC scale and head droop appeared due to weakness of the neck muscles.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: during the first week of hospitalization

evidence_events.source_span: The magnetic resonance image (MRI) of the head revealed numerous unspecific lesions, mainly in the thalamus, hyperintense on T2-weighted (T2) and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) images, and similar lesions were presented in both cerebellar hemispheres.
The MRI of the head in axial contrast-enhanced T1-weighted subtraction maps revealed moderate bilateral, mixed pachymeningeal and leptomeningeal contrast enhancement in selected regions.
On the MRI of cervical spinal cord, a longitudinal lesion was found with hyperintense on T2 and short tau inversion recovery (STIR) sequences.
Blood inflammatory parameters were slightly elevated.
The cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed lymphocytic pleocytosis.
High levels of IgM and IgG TBE antibodies in serum and in CSF were found.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: TBE IgG/IgM ELISA for serum and CSF

evidence_events.source_span: The cerebrospinal fluid was tested with polymerase chain reaction (PCR) with a negative result for Escherichia coli, Haemophilus influenzae, Listeria monocytogenes, Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus agalactiae, Streptoccocus pneumoniae, Cytomegalovirus, Enterovirus, Herpes simplex viruses 1 and 2, Human herpesvirus 6, Human parechovirus, Varicella zoster virus, and Cryptococcus neoformans/gattii.
Testing for the presence of Borrelia burgdorferi in serum and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) showed negative results.
Microbiological testing on bacterial cultures from blood and CSF were negative.

Diagnostic tests for autoimmune diseases were performed, including tests for anti-aquaporin-4 antibody (AQP4-Ab), antibodies to myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein (anti-MOG), and myelin basic protein antibodies (anti-MBP), all negative.

Further research excluded connective tissue diseases and paraneoplastic syndromes; serum was negative for rheumatoid factor, anti-prothrombin, antiphospholipid, anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies and multiple other autoantibodies.
Two electroneurographic examinations did not show any pathological changes of motor and sensory nerves compatible with demyelinating and axonal dysfunction.

Based on the initial symptoms, the patient was empirically treated with antibiotic (ceftriaxone) and antiviral agents (acyclovir). Due to severe clinical condition, extensive brain and spinal cord changes, and rapid progression, the patient was treated with an IgG infusion.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: empirical antibiotic, antiviral, and IgG infusion treatment

evidence_events.source_span: During hospitalization, the patient's clinical condition stabilized and began to gradually improve.
After several months of rehabilitation, a significant neurological deficit remained, including limb weakness and muscle atrophy, especially in the shoulder girdle.
On the control MRI performed after 6 months, a complete resolution of the previously seen signal alteration within the cerebrum, cerebellum and spinal cord lesions was seen.

source_metadata.title: Pancoast tumor presenting with multiple joint pains: a case report

evidence_events.source_span: 58-year-old nonsmoking African American male who presented to the neurology clinic with a history of multiple chronic joint pains
The patient complained of shoulder pain that traveled into his right arm and right finger and had worsened over the past 9 months
The patient also reported decreased right proximal strength and swelling of his right hand

Neurological examination revealed joint stiffness, neck pain, arm numbness, arm weakness, and hand weakness; restricted shoulder movements; extensive distal and proximal muscle wasting; right arm adducted and forearm externally rotated; muscle strength of right upper extremity was 2/5 with impaired abduction and 0/5 wrist and finger flexion and extension; decreased sensation in right upper extremity with complete loss at C8–T1 distribution; gross atrophy of thenar, hypothenar, lumbrical, and interossei muscles; right-sided miosis

MRI of the cervical spine demonstrated a right apical mass and mild cervical spondylosis; MRI of the right shoulder showed glenohumeral joint effusion and fullness in the axillary region consistent with lymphadenopathy
Chest x-ray showed extensive bullous changes in the right upper lung
CT of the chest showed a right apical mass that extended to the right supraclavicular region

CT-guided biopsy of the apical mass showed non-small cell lung carcinoma; immunohistochemistry showed tumor cells expressed CK5, p63, and p40 but were immunonegative for TTF1, synaptophysin, and chromogranin; mucicarmine and CK7 immunostaining were diffusely positive; neuroendocrine differentiation was excluded
The patient developed superior vena cava syndrome while waiting for oncology recommendation
Radiation therapy was initiated; the patient’s pain improved significantly following radiation; arm swelling and weakness remained the same
Given the tumor size, chemotherapy was recommended by the oncology team; the patient decided against chemotherapy

source_metadata.title: Mind the gap: IgG4-related disease mimicking infectious cerebral mass lesions

evidence_events.source_span: An 82-year-old male was transferred to our institution from another hospital following the sudden onset of seizures, in absence of fever or other systemic symptoms.

His past medical history comprised pulmonary tuberculosis treated for 9 months about 20 years before, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and surgical removal of a localized cutaneous melanoma on the right shoulder 1 year before.
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan on admission showed multiple CNS lesions in the white matter, with peripheral contrast enhancement, coherent with pyogenic or neoplastic nature.
Blood tests showed signs of systemic inflammation with leukocytosis, moderate neutrophilia, negative HIV serology, and normal immunoglobulin plasma levels.
Echocardiographic findings were negative for vegetations or endocarditis. Serial blood cultures were negative.
A positive serology for Entamoeba histolytica was obtained, with negative serologies for Taenia solium and Echinococcus spp. Toxoplasma gondii serology was positive for IgG, negative for IgM.
Serum β-D-glucan and galactomannan were undetectable.
A total-body CT scan showed bilateral bronchiectasis and a lung cavitation.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: after failing improvement of cerebral abscesses

evidence_events.source_span: Broncho-alveolar lavage fluid was negative for Mycobacterium tuberculosis by PCR and culture, no bacterial or fungal growth was detected, and molecular analysis by PCR was negative for Pneumocystis jirovecii and cytomegalovirus.
Tumor markers, autoimmunity tests, and immunological profile (IgA, IgM, IgG count and flow cytometric lymphocyte subset analysis) were unremarkable.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: tumor markers, autoimmunity tests, immunological profile

evidence_events.source_span: Cerebral spinal fluid (CSF) examination demonstrated a normal cell count, normal glycorrhachia, and an increase in proteins (1103 mg/L) and lactate (2.7 mmol/L). CSF culture and PCR for common bacterial and viral pathogens, T. gondii, Cryptococcus and E. histolytica were negative.
The right frontal lesion was surgically excised en bloc. It presented macroscopically as a firm, elastic, round, well-capsulated mass with a necrotic-like core.

Histology demonstrated the presence of histiocytic granulomatous tissue with a conspicuous plasmacellular component, subsequently defined as an IgG subtype 4 producer (ratio IgG4/IgG 45% on the histological specimen, IgG4 > 10/HPF).
The tissue culture did not provide growth for bacteria, mycobacteria, or fungi.

The patient was started on steroid treatment (1 mg/Kg of prednisone twice daily) and antibiotic treatment was stopped. Clinical improvement became evident after 10 days of treatment, with this otherwise bedridden patient walking successfully with minimal aid by the second week of treatment.

evidence_events.source_span: A 35-year-old female patient, married, has 2 children with no past history of psychiatric or medical diseases.

One and a half month prior to presentation, she had severe on and off headache accompanied by blurred vision and numbness of the left hand, severe night sweating, fatigue, and muscular pain especially in the neck and back.

evidence_events.source_span: One month prior to neurology clinic presentation, she developed acute agitation and behavioral changes including shouting, roaming, confusion, disorientation, and inappropriate speech.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: one month prior to neurology clinic presentation

evidence_events.source_span: Patient presented to ER with psychiatric symptoms and was admitted under psychiatry department for 3 days; investigations including CT, brain MRI, ECG, and CBC were all within normal limits.

After discharge, symptoms persisted; patient admitted again for 3 days as acute confusional state; CBC, brain MRI, MR venography, MR angiography, and brain CT were unremarkable; treated with Quetiapine, Citalopram, and Mirtazapine with symptom improvement.
Physical examination was within normal limits: afebrile, conscious, oriented, normal cognition, normal cranial nerve exam, normal motor and sensory exam, normal coordination and gait.

Routine labs: WBC 6.4, lymphocytes 16.1%, neutrophils 78.1%, hemoglobin 11.1 gm/dl (microcytic hypochromic anemia), platelets 281, CRP 4.69 mg/L; autoimmune screening ANA, lupus anticoagulants, anticardiolipin all negative.
Brain CT, MRI, and MR venography were reported as unremarkable.

CSF analysis showed leukocytosis 27/microliter with 100% lymphocytes, protein 24.28 mg/dl (normal), glucose 95.2 mg/dl (normal), gram stain negative, culture negative, cytology negative for malignant cells.
Brucella antibody test in blood was positive for abortus 1:640 and melitensis 1:160 (positive ratio ≥1:160); Brucella antibody in CSF was not performed due to insufficient sample.
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: Diagnosis-revealing serology for neurobrucellosis

evidence_events.source_span: Patient was started on Rifampicin 600 mg once daily, Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily, and Moxifloxacin 400 mg once daily; Moxifloxacin was given for 6 weeks then stopped; Rifampicin and Doxycycline continued for total 12 weeks with frequent follow-up.
Follow-up spinal tap after one month reported normal cell count; patient completed antibiotic course with significant improvement in symptoms.

source_metadata.title: Spontaneous Bilateral Basal Ganglia Hemorrhage Due to Severe Hypertension

evidence_events.source_span: A 37-year-old man with a past medical history of poorly controlled hypertension was brought to the emergency department due to severe headache, worsening confusion, and right-side weakness for 2 days.

On examination, the patient was in a stuporous condition with a Glasgow coma scale of 8/15 (eye-opening 2, verbal response 2, motor response 4). He had right-side weakness and mixed aphasia (global aphasia with preserved repetition), muscle strength was 0/5 in the right. Pupils were symmetrically equal to normal size and reactive to light.
A non-contrast brain CT was obtained, which demonstrated bilateral basal ganglia hemorrhage (BBGH). Hematoma measured 5x3cm in the left basal ganglia and 3x1cm in the right basal ganglia.

A subsequent brain MRI later revealed a bilateral basal ganglia hematoma with minimal edema (3.5 cm in the left and 2 cm in the right basal ganglia). MR angiography (MRA) was negative for aneurysmal rupture.
On admission, blood pressure was 220/120. Other vital signs were normal.

The patient’s complete blood count, comprehensive biochemistry profile, and coagulation markers were all within normal limits. An ECG showed a normal sinus rhythm. A chest x-ray and CT scan did not reveal any acute cardiopulmonary disease.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: CBC, biochemistry, coagulation markers, ECG, chest x-ray and CT

evidence_events.source_span: The patient was admitted to the ICU and conservatively managed with blood pressure-lowering drugs, mannitol (5 days) and other supportive medications.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: On admission and during ICU stay

evidence_events.source_span: After 2 days, Glasgow coma scale of the patient improved from 8 to 11 (eye-opening 4, verbal response 3, motor response 4), blood pressure was controlled with multiple antihypertensive medications; and he was transferred to the neurology ward on the fifth day.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: After 2 days and on fifth day

evidence_events.source_span: After another 5 days of neurology inpatient unit, the patient clinically improved (GCS 14/15) and was referred to the rehabilitation department.

diagnostic_reasoning_verbatim_spans: A 37-year-old man with a past medical history of poorly controlled hypertension was brought to the emergency department due to severe headache, worsening confusion, and right-side weakness for 2 days.
Non-contrast brain CT was obtained, which demonstrated bilateral basal ganglia hemorrhage (BBGH).
MR angiography (MRA) was negative for aneurysmal rupture.
On admission, blood pressure was 220/120.
The patient’s complete blood count, comprehensive biochemistry profile, and coagulation markers were all within normal limits.
The patient was admitted to the ICU and conservatively managed with blood pressure-lowering drugs, mannitol, and other supportive medications.
After clinical improvement, he was transferred to the neurology ward and later to rehabilitation.
Hypertension was considered to be the underlying etiology since there was no other identified etiology or risk factor.
diagnostic_reasoning_items: Presentation with neurological deficits and stupor in a patient with poorly controlled hypertension suggests hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage.
Imaging confirmed bilateral basal ganglia hemorrhages without aneurysmal cause.
Severe hypertension on admission supports hypertensive etiology.
Normal labs and cardiopulmonary imaging exclude other systemic causes.

source_metadata.title: Extensive actinomycosis with intracranial and mediastinal involvement: a therapeutic challenge

evidence_events.source_span: A male teenager presented with slowly progressive asymptomatic swelling over nape of the neck for last 7 years, increasing in size to cover whole neck and adjacent scalp area, with intermittent discharge of reddish-yellow fluid from elevated lesions

Physical exam showed pallor, reduced mouth opening to two finger width, poor dental hygiene, large diffuse non-tender firm to hard swelling over nape of neck extending bilaterally with multiple papules and plaques with brown crusts and atrophic scars, swelling fixed to underlying structures and overlying skin

Routine labs showed haemoglobin 8.9 g/dL, total leucocyte count 8.36 ×10³/μL with neutrophils 66%, lymphocytes 23%, monocytes 8%, eosinophils 2%; peripheral blood film showed mild anisocytosis, microcytic hypochromic to normocytic normochromic red blood cells with polychromatophils and tear drop cells; liver and kidney function tests, blood sugar, HbA1c, urine routine/microscopy were normal; HIV ELISA, hepatitis B surface antigen and anti-hepatitis C antibody were negative

CSF examination showed colourless, clear fluid with protein 64 mg/dL, chloride 124 Meq/L, glucose 75 mg/dL, WBC 5 cells/mm³, RBC 32 cells/mm³, pauci-cellular cyto-spin smear with few lympho-mononuclear cells and occasional neutrophils, no malignant cells; fungal and aerobic bacterial cultures of CSF showed no growth
Tissue fungal, aerobic, anaerobic and mycobacterial cultures were all negative; Mantoux test was negative

Ultrasonography of neck showed ill-defined heterogeneous soft tissue mass with multiple hypoechoic areas and echogenic foci involving subcutaneous and intermuscular regions; multiple enlarged cervical lymph nodes bilaterally

Non-contrast CT scan showed ill-defined hyperdense mass in left temporal region with perilesional oedema, ipsilateral ventricular compression, dilated right lateral ventricle, mild midline shift, marked hyperostosis and periosteal thickening of left parietal, temporal, occipital bones

Contrast-enhanced MRI showed large infiltrative dural-based T1 isointense, T2 hypointense enhancing mass along left temporal lobe with predominantly extraparenchymal and minimal intraparenchymal component, extensive pachymeningeal thickening along left cerebral hemisphere and cervical spinal canal, perilesional oedema, invasion of left transverse and sigmoid sinus, retropharyngeal spread to superior mediastinum, cervical and upper dorsal vertebral body involvement; 'dot-in-circle' sign seen in cervical soft tissues

Cutaneous punch biopsy showed colonies of filamentous bacteria with surrounding Splendore–Hoeppli reaction and suppurative granulation tissue on H&E staining; Gram stain showed filamentous gram-positive bacilli; Gomori-methanamine silver, Periodic acid Schiff and Ziehl-Neelsen stains were negative

Tuberculosis was ruled out based on absence of clinical symptoms, negative Mantoux test, normal chest X-ray, cerebrospinal fluid examination and negative sputum examination; neoplasms ruled out after CE-MRI and CSF reports; eumycetoma ruled out after histopathological demonstration of filamentous bacterial colonies
Initial treatment with ceftriaxone and oral penicillin G for 3 months led to 20% improvement; swelling remained stable for 3 months then increased beyond baseline over next 6 months

Repeat CE-MRI showed increase in pachymeningeal thickening, dural-based mass, retropharyngeal soft tissue component, vertebral body involvement, new pachymeningeal thickening along inferior orbital fissure and left masticator space; midline shift slightly decreased; repeat tissue bacterial and fungal cultures negative

Treatment with intravenous amikacin, oral rifampicin and cotrimoxazole for 20 days showed decrease in calvarial disease bulk and enhancement, decreased pachymeningeal and cervical spinal canal involvement, intraorbital extension; but extensive increase in retropharyngeal and left masticator space involvement
Patient started on intravenous linezolid and ceftriaxone for 6 weeks with steroids; swelling decreased drastically within 7 days of dexamethasone addition; steroids tapered gradually

Patient developed sudden vomiting, headache, disorientation with decreased mouth opening; urgent NCCT showed increased vasogenic oedema, new hydrocephalus and cerebral oedema; MRI brain with angiography showed increased white matter oedema and midline shift without frank abscess; treated with intravenous mannitol, furosemide, spironolactone and dexamethasone leading to recovery
After 1 month of discharge, swelling decreased by 60%; after 4 months of oral therapy with penicillin G, doxycycline, metronidazole and prednisolone, marked reduction in swelling observed

source_metadata.title: MRI-negative myelitis associated with cerebral venous thrombosis after COVID-19 infection

evidence_events.source_span: A woman in her early 30s presented to our clinic complaining of headache and disturbed sensation on the left side of the body. The symptoms started about 1 week before presentation with a new-onset severe headache, bilateral tinnitus and blurry vision. The headache was also associated with nausea and anorexia. After nearly 48 hours, the patient noticed disturbed sensation on the left side of the lower body. Since then, she also complained of constipation and voiding difficulties.
The patient described symptoms consistent with COVID-19 infection 2 weeks before the onset of the current complaints, including nasal congestion, fever with chills, dry cough, anosmia and ageusia.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: 2 weeks before the onset of the current complaints

evidence_events.source_span: On neurological examination, the patient showed normal muscular strength in the upper and lower extremities with diffusely brisk reflexes. A sensory deficit level was noted at T5–T6 with diminished pinprick and temperature sensation, loss of vibratory sensation and impaired proprioception on the left side of the body. Plantar responses were in extension bilaterally. The patient had a wide-based cautious gait with a positive Romberg sign.

MRI of the brain, cervical and thoracic spine with and without contrast revealed partial thrombosis in the left transverse sinus, along with small atypical bilateral frontal foci, most likely vascular in origin. There was no evidence of compressive myelopathy or signal abnormalities in the spinal cord.

Laboratory study showed normal thrombocytes, coagulation study and D-dimer level. Both IgM and IgG for COVID-19 were positive. Myeloneuropathy laboratory results such as copper and vitamin B12 were within the reference range. Autoimmune tests and hepatic viral study were negative. Homocysteine and antiphospholipid antibodies were within normal range. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis via lumbar puncture did not show abnormalities. Nerve conduction studies and electromyography of the upper and lower limbs were within normal limits. CT of the chest showed no abnormalities related to COVID-19 infection.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: lumbar puncture, nerve conduction studies, electromyography, CT chest

evidence_events.source_span: Postinfectious myelitis constitutes the most probable diagnosis in this case based on the presentation and investigation results.
Treatment included subcutaneous enoxaparin for 10 days followed by oral rivaroxaban for cerebral venous thrombosis, and intravenous dexamethasone for 5 days for myelitis.
Repeat MRI of the brain, cervical and thoracic spine 1 week after initiation of therapy showed the same radiological findings in the brain and a normal spinal cord.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: repeat MRI with and without contrast

evidence_events.source_span: At 3 months follow-up, the patient showed significant improvement in symptoms with very mild residual numbness on the left lower extremity. Therapy with steroids and oral anticoagulants was concluded.

source_metadata.title: SARS-CoV-2-Related Acute Necrotizing Encephalopathy of Childhood With Good Response to Tocilizumab in an Adolescent
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case narrative and clinical course sections only.

evidence_events.source_span: A previously well 11-year-old boy presented to the general practitioner with two days of fever, nausea, and vomiting without respiratory symptoms. SARS-CoV-2 antigen rapid test was positive.

One day later, he re-presented to the children's emergency with acute dizziness, slurred speech, left gaze deviation, progressively unsteady gait, and subjective weakness. SARS-CoV-2 infection was confirmed on nasopharyngeal polymerase chain reaction (PCR) swab (cycle threshold value: 20.49).

Neurological examination revealed reduced consciousness (Glasgow Coma Scale score of 12: E4V2M6), expressive aphasia, bilateral partial ptosis with ophthalmoplegia, bilateral cerebellar signs including dysdiadochokinesia, and past-pointing with mild truncal ataxia. He had normal tone and hyperreflexia in both knee and ankle jerks. Power was 5 in both upper and lower limbs. His right eye was held in an adducted, downward gaze, whereas his left eye held a central, downward gaze, suggesting cranial nerves III and IV palsy, respectively.

Brain magnetic resonance imaging showed swelling and signal changes involving bilateral thalami, midbrain, pons, cerebellar hemispheres, and periventricular white matter, correlating with a diagnosis of ANEC.

Lumbar puncture revealed elevated CSF red cell count (25 cells/uL), elevated protein level (1.02 g/L), normal opening pressure, and no pleocytosis with normal glucose and lactate levels. Oligoclonal bands were absent. CSF meningoencephalitis infectious panel returned negative, including SARS-CoV-2 PCR.
Extensive serum and CSF autoimmune tests were negative, including anti-N-methyl-D-aspartate, anti-myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein, anti-glutamic-acid-decarboxylase, and anti-GQ1b-ganglioside IgG.
Inflammatory markers were elevated: erythrocyte sedimentation rate 65 mm/hr, C-reactive-protein 36 mg/L, and procalcitonin 12.1 μg/L. Ferritin levels and liver function tests were normal.
His ANEC Severity Score was 5 of 9, conferring high-risk for poor neurological outcome.

The patient was promptly initiated on immunotherapy with intravenous methylprednisolone 1000 mg daily for 5 days, intravenous immunoglobulin 2 g/kg over two days, and one dose of intravenous tocilizumab 8 mg/kg 12 hours from hospital presentation.

He received a five-day course of intravenous remdesivir to treat SARS-CoV-2. Other concurrent antimicrobials included empirical intravenous ceftriaxone, azithromycin, acyclovir, and oseltamivir, until respective viral and bacterial studies returned negative.
After eight days, he demonstrated good response to treatment; Glasgow Coma Scale improved to 15, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia improved, and modified Rankin Scale score reduced to 2.

He was discharged home after 16 days with residual deficits including mild ophthalmoplegia, upper limb dysmetria with intention tremor, mild aphasia, and dysarthria. At discharge, modified Rankin Scale score was 1. Two weeks later, modified Rankin Scale score improved to 0, indicating neurological function recovery.

source_metadata.title: Optic neuromyelitis after vaccination against SARS-CoV-2

evidence_events.source_span: A previously healthy woman in her 40s received a dose of the non-replicating vector vaccine AZD1222 against SARS-CoV-2 a day before the onset of symptoms.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: a day before the onset of symptoms

evidence_events.source_span: She developed an intense occipital headache which improved with paracetamol, as well as progressive weakness of the lower limbs until she was incapable of walking 10 metres without support, but without sensory level, bladder or bowel involvement.

First MRI of the brain, not including the spinal cord, found lesions in the juxtacortical and deep subcortical white matter and corpus callosum on axial T2 Fluid Attenuated Inversion Recovery (FLAIR) sequence.
Lesions in both the cerebral peduncles on axial T2 FLAIR sequence with fat suppression and hyperintense lesions in the splenius of the corpus callosum.
Treatment was started with oral prednisone 20 mg daily for 20 days, showing complete remission of symptoms.

Two months later, after discontinuation of oral prednisone, she presented with progressive quadriplegia and loss of sensitivity in all modalities, with a sensory level at C4 and bladder and bowel involvement.

New MRI showed an increase in the number and size of white matter lesions in both cerebral hemispheres and a decrease in the number of lesions in both cerebral peduncles on FLAIR T2 sequence without fat suppression.
Significant longitudinally extensive signal alterations were observed in the cervical and dorsal spinal cord with increased thickness on sagittal Fast spin echo (FSE) imaging T2 sequence.
Routine blood tests were within standard limits, lumbar puncture showed no alterations and oligoclonal bands were negative.
Antinuclear antibodies, c-ANCA, p-ANCA, anti-Ro and anti-LA antibodies were negative.
AQP4-IgG antibody was positive by cell-based assay (CBA).
Acute treatment with methylprednisolone 1000 mg/day for 5 days, followed by intravenous immunoglobulin 400 mg/kg/day for 5 days.
Maintenance therapy with the IL-6 inhibitor tocilizumab was started.

At 3-month follow-up, the patient showed improvement in motor and sensory functions, with sensory level at T10 and recovery of upper extremity strength against gravity and trace muscle activation in the distal right lower extremity.

source_metadata.title: A case report of early diagnosis of asymptomatic hairy cell leukemia using flow cytometry

evidence_events.source_span: The patient is a 41 year old male with low platelets for Hematology consult referred for thrombocytopenia. CBC report revealed WBC 4.2 K/μL, RBC 5.12 M/μL, Hgb 15.4 g/dL, Hct 45.7%, MCV 89 fl, MCH 30.1 pg, MCHC 33.7 g/dL, RDW 13.6%, platelets 120K/μL with differential count of granulocytes 59.4%, Lymphocytes 36.8%, monocytes 3.8%.
Flow cytometry was performed for CD5, CD10, CD19, CD20, CD22, CD25, HLA-DR, FMC7, CD45, CD103, Kappa and Lambda.

Peripheral blood analysis showed a lymphocyte population of about 38.6% with no apparent abnormal antigen expression. The B-cells were approximately 10% of the lymphocytes and appeared polyclonal. There was a small population (about 2.4% of all the lymphocytes) with a slightly higher side scatter that showed brighter CD19 and CD20. This small population showed monoclonal kappa light chain, while the remainder of the B cells were polyclonal.

A bone marrow aspirate was submitted after about 3 weeks of the initial study on the peripheral blood and revealed a lymphocyte population of 34% of the total with B-cells approximately 41% of the lymphocytes and the entire population was positive for CD19, CD20, CD22, HLA-DR, FMC7, and kappa monoclonal. The population also appeared to be partially positive for CD25 and CD103.

Review of the bone marrow morphology demonstrated normocellular marrow with B-cell infiltrate representing 30-40% of the marrow cellularity that were predominantly medium sized mature forms with oval-shaped nuclei and appreciable cytoplasm with cytoplasmic projections. The B cells were positive for CD20, Annexin A1, DBA44, BCL1, BCL2, TRAP and BRAF V600E, but negative for CD5, CD10, LEF1 or BCL6.
On follow-up, the patient showed splenomegaly by ultrasound and started to complain of fatigue.

source_metadata.title: Ovarian Manson's Schistosomiasis: Rare Diagnosis or Underestimated Prevalence?

evidence_events.source_span: A 45-year-old female patient reported that in the middle of 2014 she began to feel a strong pain in her left iliac region.
Endovaginal pelvic ultrasonography (in September 2014) showed enlargement of the left ovary (image of the cyst: 2.84 cm; total volume of the ovary: 16.82 cm3; normal range: 3.0–9.0 cm3).
Tumor marker tests in October 2014 showed normal results (cancer antigen [CA] 125: 11.1 IU/mL; CA 19-9: 13.6 IU/mL).
Magnetic resonance imaging showed that the left ovary was enlarged, and that ovarian neoplasia could not be ruled out.
New blood tests in early 2015 for cancer markers (carcinoembryonic antigen: 3.0 ng/mL; CA 125: 8.7 IU/mL) were also within the normal range.
The patient was referred to the oncological service and underwent a left ovariectomy.

Histopathological examination identified ovarian schistosomiasis caused by granulomatous inflammatory processes surrounding both viable and calcified eggs of Schistosoma mansoni; no evidence of neoplastic tissue was found (April 2015).
Physical examination showed the patient in good general condition with normal vital signs and no abnormalities on abdominal ultrasound.
Three parasitological feces examinations using the Kato-Katz method revealed residual Schistosoma mansoni infection with parasite loads of 60, 192 and 156 eggs per gram of feces respectively.

source_metadata.title: Myeloproliferative Neoplasm Driven by ETV6-ABL1 in an Adolescent with Recent History of Burkitt Leukemia

evidence_events.source_span: The patient presented with a diffuse petechial rash, bilateral subconjunctival haemorrhages, and haemoptysis, on a background of a history of several months of fatigue, bone pain, and night sweats.
Complete blood count (CBC) showed a white blood cell (WBC) count of 101 × 10^9/L, haemoglobin at 106 g/L, and a platelet count of 12 × 10^9/L. A peripheral smear showed 75% leukemic blasts.

Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) analysis with a MYC breakapart FISH probe was consistent with the presence of a MYC gene rearrangement in 170/200 (85%) cells, and G-band analysis showed an abnormal male karyotype of 46,XY,dup(1)(q12q43~44),t(8;14)(q24.1;q32)[18]/46,XY[2].
A diagnosis of Burkitt leukaemia was made, and treatment was started according to the institutional standard of care.

A CBC 7 months after the completion of therapy showed WBC 29.2 × 10^9/L, with a significant left shift, eosinophilia (2.92 × 10^9/L), monocytosis (4.38 × 10^9/L), thrombocytopenia (100 × 10^9/L), and no peripheral blasts. The patient was asymptomatic. Viral workup was negative, and EBV serology was consistent with past infection.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: 7 months after the completion of therapy

evidence_events.source_span: Bone marrow aspirate (BMA) revealed marked hypercellularity with significant eosinophilia and an absence of elevated blasts consistent with a myeloproliferative disorder. Immunophenotyping showed no abnormal cell population. FISH analyses were negative for MYC, PDGFRA, and PDGFRB gene rearrangements, and the karyotype was normal. Molecular analysis was negative for the BCR-ABL1, FLT3-ITD, JAK2 V617F, and CALR variants.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: 7 months after the completion of therapy

evidence_events.source_span: The leucocytosis increased to 192 × 10^9/L over 3 months, accompanied by persistent thrombocytopenia (range 50–100 × 10^9/L). The patient became progressively symptomatic with fatigue, generalized bone pain, as well as significant spontaneous bruising. He was started empirically on Hydroxyurea 25 mg/kg/dose, which normalized his WBC count and improved his symptoms within one month.

Whole-genome sequencing of his MPN BMA sample was performed on an Illumina HiSeqX platform with a depth of 22X, and RNAseq was performed on Illumina HiSeq 2500, with a depth of 294X. Structural variant analysis from whole-genome sequencing showed a dispersed duplication event of approximately 600 kb from ABL1 to PRRC2B (9q34), inserted into the ETV6 locus (12p13). RNAseq analysis confirmed the presence of a corresponding ETV6-ABL1 fusion transcript, with an intact, in-frame ABL tyrosine-kinase domain.

Cytogenetic re-evaluation of the MPN BMA sample using sequential FISH analysis with a BCR-ABL1 probe was suggestive of a cryptic insertion of a portion of the ABL1 locus into one chromosome 12 at 12p13. ABL1 gene rearrangement was present in 193/200 (96.5%) interphase cells. Interphase FISH analysis with a dual colour breakapart probe for the ETV6 locus did not show ETV6 gene rearrangement, and metaphase FISH with subtelomeric probes for 9q and 12p yielded normal results, suggestive of the insertion of ABL1 into ETV6 rather than rearrangement by translocation. FISH analysis with a dual colour breakapart probe for ABL1 demonstrated that the 3′ portion of ABL1 was inserted into 12p13 on the derivative chromosome 12, with the 5′ portion of ABL1 remaining on the derivative chromosome 9. The karyotype was updated to 46,XY[20].

The WGS performed on the diagnostic Burkitt leukemia blood sample did not show evidence of the ETV6-ABL1 fusion. The RNA was not available for analysis. The results of the BCR-ABL1 FISH analysis of 200 stored fixed cells from the Burkitt leukemia sample were also negative for the ABL1 gene rearrangement. The germline analysis by the WGS of the skin’s biopsy-derived fibroblasts did not reveal any pathogenic variants.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: Whole-genome sequencing and FISH analysis performed on archived samples

evidence_events.source_span: The patient was started on a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI; imatinib) and, subsequently, underwent a 10/10 matched unrelated haematopoietic stem cell transplant. He is disease-free five years post-transplant.

source_metadata.title: Multimodal evaluation of osteosarcoma choroidal metastasis

evidence_events.source_span: A 20-year-old man with a history of right tibial osteosarcoma diagnosed at age 17, treated with supracondylar amputation, and recent brain and lung metastases, presented with decreased vision in his right eye (OD).
evidence_events.temporal_cue: presented with decreased vision; history diagnosed at age 17

evidence_events.source_span: Ophthalmic examination revealed a best-corrected visual acuity of hand movements OD and 20/20 on the left eye; anterior segment was unremarkable bilaterally; posterior segment of OD had a large, posterior pole, pink, nodular, subretinal mass with associated fluid.

A and B-scan ultrasonography confirmed the mass was subretinal, heterogeneous, with medium/high reflectivity, areas of localized increased and decreased reflectivity, and a height-to-base ratio (HBR) of 1-1.2 approximately.

Computerized tomography (CT) revealed a heterogeneous, well-defined mass within the uveal layer, hyperdense with areas of decreased density, significant intraocular involvement, and contrast-enhancement.
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed a well-defined, irregular choroidal mass, T1-isointense and T2-hypointense.
The history of widespread disease and the characteristics of the lesion were compatible with choroidal osteosarcoma metastasis.
At one-month follow-up, the right eye was painful, had a fully detached retina, anterior segment neovascularization, and intraocular pressure of 38 mmHg.
The ocular lesion responded to systemic treatment and decreased in volume according to CT and MRI scans, while lung and brain metastases were less responsive.
The patient died one year after the first ophthalmologic assessment due to systemic complications.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: one year after first ophthalmologic assessment

source_metadata.title: Severe hypercalcemia due to metastatic pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor: a case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 51-year-old Iranian man presented with nausea, vomiting, and significant weight loss for 1 month.
Physical exam showed fullness in the right upper quadrant of the abdomen; vital signs were normal.

Laboratory data revealed severe hypercalcemia of more than 15 mg/dl, low PTH level of 4.37 pg/ml, low 25 (OH) vitamin D level of 14 nmol/l, elevated blood urea nitrogen 47 mg/dl, creatinine 4.12 mg/dl, and elevated alkaline phosphatase 545 U/L.
Initial treatment with hydration, calcitonin, and hemodialysis sessions decreased calcium levels from 26-27 mg/dl to 11.9 mg/dl after denosumab injection.

Abdominal sonography revealed multiple mostly hypoechoic structures with calcification in the liver, largest 72 × 62 mm, suggestive of liver metastasis; kidneys showed increased echogenicity indicating parenchymal damage.
Bone scan showed diffuse metastatic calcification in both lungs and stomach, diffuse heterogeneous uptake in the liver, and mild degenerative changes in the right hip.
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: Bone scan showed diffuse metastatic calcification in lungs and stomach, heterogeneous liver uptake, mild right hip degeneration.

evidence_events.source_span: Percutaneous biopsy of the liver mass demonstrated a well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor (low grade) confirmed by immunohistochemistry with strongly positive chromogranin and synaptophysin stains, negative CK20, CK7, LCA, and Ki-67 index <3%.
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: Liver biopsy confirmed well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor with positive chromogranin and synaptophysin.

evidence_events.source_span: After initial discharge, patient developed symptomatic hypocalcemia with corrected calcium 6.5 mg/dl, phosphate 2.5 mg/dl, 25 hydroxy vitamin D 22.8 ng/ml, and PTH 107 pg/ml, treated with intravenous and oral calcium and ergocalciferol.

CT scan of chest, abdomen, and pelvis without contrast showed a heterogeneous solid mass lesion measuring 51 × 47 mm in the body of the pancreas with calcification and multiple hypodense lesions with calcification in both liver lobes, largest 73 × 67 mm.
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: CT showed pancreatic mass with calcification and multiple liver metastases with calcifications.

evidence_events.source_span: Endoscopic ultrasonography demonstrated a large heterogeneous mass with irregular outline and good demarcation in the body of the pancreas measuring 51 × 37 mm with diffuse calcifications; lesion involved common hepatic artery, proper hepatic artery, and splenic vein; multiple large heterogeneous liver lesions were also seen.
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: EUS showed pancreatic mass with vascular involvement and multiple liver metastases.

evidence_events.source_span: Octreotide scan revealed a large donut-shaped octreotide avid lesion in the epigastric region with multiple foci of increased radiotracer uptake in the epigastric region and both lobes of the liver.
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: Octreotide scan showed octreotide avid pancreatic lesion and multiple liver metastases.

evidence_events.source_span: Measurement of other probable hormone secretions of NET, such as gastrin and vasoactive intestinal peptide, was not performed due to absence of related symptoms.
Patient was treated with long-acting octreotide 30 mg monthly and everolimus 10 mg daily; surgical hemi-pancreatectomy and liver transplantation were recommended but refused by patient and family.

Six months later, patient was readmitted with nausea, vomiting, constipation, severe hypercalcemia (14.4 mg/dl), acute kidney injury, low PTH (5 pg/ml), treated with hydration, medical treatment, and hemodialysis; discharged with normalized calcium and creatinine.

diagnostic_reasoning_verbatim_spans: Laboratory data revealed calcium of 26 mg/dl, accompanied by low level of PTH.

Percutaneous biopsy of the liver mass demonstrated a well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor (low grade) confirmed by immunohistochemistry with strongly positive chromogranin and synaptophysin stain.

CT and EUS demonstrated a large heterogeneous mass lesion with vascular invasion in the body of the pancreas and multiple liver metastases.
PTHrP secretion is the most common cause of paraneoplastic hypercalcemia in pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors, although PTHrP assay was unavailable in this case.
diagnostic_reasoning_items: Severe hypercalcemia with suppressed PTH suggests paraneoplastic hypercalcemia rather than primary hyperparathyroidism.
Imaging localizes a pancreatic mass with liver metastases consistent with neuroendocrine tumor.
Pathology confirms well-differentiated neuroendocrine tumor as source of malignancy.
Octreotide avidity supports neuroendocrine tumor diagnosis and guides somatostatin analog therapy.
Lack of PTHrP assay limits biochemical confirmation but clinical and imaging findings support humoral hypercalcemia of malignancy.

source_metadata.title: Mycosis fungoides with spongiosis: a case report

evidence_events.source_span: 31-year-old male of African origin presented with a four-year history of an itchy rash on the face, trunk, and limbs, initially macules and papules over the trunk, progressing to involve limbs, buttocks, face, and entire trunk, eventually ulcerated, unresponsive to topical steroids

Physical examination showed multiple well to ill-defined hyperpigmented erosive plaques, nodules, and tumors on trunk, limbs, and face, occupying more than 95% of body surface area, including non-sun-exposed areas; ulcers on left knee and left elbow; no significant peripheral lymphadenopathy or splenomegaly; normal systemic and neurological exams
Skin biopsy revealed mycosis fungoides with prominent spongiosis; immunohistochemistry showed CD3 positivity; CD4, CD5, and CD8 IHC not done

Complete blood count: WBC 8.67 x10^9/L; Hb 8.6 g/dL; HCT 26.4%; MCV 58.6 fL; Neutrophils 6.39 x10^3/μL; Platelets 656 x10^3/μL; Liver function tests: ALT 47.5 IU/L; AST 21.8 IU/L; Renal function: Serum creatinine 84.17 μmol/L
Urinalysis and microbiology were not done
HIV1 serology test was negative; peripheral blood smear and bone marrow aspirate were not done; chest x-ray and abdominal ultrasound were normal
evidence_events.procedural_cue: HIV test, chest x-ray, abdominal ultrasound

evidence_events.source_span: Patient scored 6 points on ISCL diagnostic algorithm (Persistent and progressive patches/thin plaques-2; Non-sun-exposed location and Size/shape variation-2; Superficial lymphoid infiltrate-1; Lymphocytic atypia-1; CD3+ -1) and diagnosed with MF; TNMB stage 3 (T3N0M0BX)
Initial treatment with oral Prednisolone 10 mg b.i.d for 30 days and oral Ampiclox 500 mg q.i.d for 10 days
Patient treated with low-dose total skin electron beam therapy (TSEBT) 12 Gy in 3 fractions at daily dose of 4 Gy using 3D conformal radiotherapy with LINAC in October 2021
After three sessions of TSEBT, remarkable improvement in lesions, itching and pain subsided; complete response of all lesions within three months after TSEBT; no acute or late radiotherapy effects
evidence_events.temporal_cue: after three sessions and within three months post-TSEBT

evidence_events.source_span: Maintenance therapy with oral methotrexate 50 mg weekly with 1 week rest after every 4 weeks
Five months later, patient developed recurrent lesion on left leg; treated with localized TSEBT 12 Gy in four fractions with complete response
Patient in remission two years post initial treatment and still on maintenance oral methotrexate 50 mg weekly

source_metadata.title: Hodgkin lymphoma associated vanishing bile duct syndrome treated successfully with a brentuximab based regimen

evidence_events.source_span: A male patient in his 20s presented with 3 days of jaundice, abdominal pain and nausea in the setting of 6 months of intermittent fevers and 10 kg of unintentional weight loss.
Physical examination at the time of admission was most notable for jaundice, scleral icterus and diffuse palpable lymphadenopathy.

Laboratory workup demonstrated a leucocytosis (15.0 x 10⁹/L) and elevated inflammatory markers (erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 101 mm/hr and C-reactive protein (CRP) 3.4 mg/dL). Liver tests were notable for a total bilirubin of 10.9 mg/dL with a direct component of 8.5 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase of 941 U/L, and aspartate and alanine aminotransferase levels of 102 and 132 U/L, respectively.
Initial CT revealed diffuse lymphadenopathy, pulmonary nodules, new hepatomegaly and splenic hypodensities.
No obstruction or gall bladder distention was noted on ultrasonography of the abdomen or on magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography.

A viral hepatitis panel, Cytomegalovirus (CMV), Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), Alpha-1 antitrypsin (A1AT), antinuclear antibody (ANA), antimitochondrial antibody (AMA), anti-smooth muscle antibody (ASMA), uric acid level and a ferritin level were all unremarkable.
A cervical lymph node biopsy and medullary femur biopsy confirmed nodular sclerosing classic Hodgkin lymphoma.

Microscopic findings included sclerotic bands causing lymph node effacement and large, atypical, multinucleated cells with prominent eosinophilic nucleoli. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated positivity to CD15 and CD30 with negative staining for CD45.
Given the diffuse, bulky disease and likely pulmonary, bony and splenic involvement, the patient was classified according to Ann Arbour classification as stage IVb disease.
A liver biopsy showed portal tracts inflammation with focal small bile duct destruction and dropout while sparing medium to large bile ducts consistent with acute cholangitis with marked cholestasis.
Fibrosis stage was F0 on biopsy.
CK7 stain confirmed small bile duct obliteration.
No Reed–Sternberg cells were seen within the liver biopsy.

The patient was started on symptomatic treatment for pruritus with colestipol and diphenhydramine while awaiting biopsy results. Additionally, ursodeoxycholic acid was initiated after imaging was negative for obstructive pathology. A prednisolone dose of 35 mg two times per day was given for 7 days initially in the hospital.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: symptomatic treatment and ursodeoxycholic acid, prednisolone

evidence_events.source_span: Despite pretreatment with ursodeoxycholic acid and prednisolone, the bilirubin rose to 19.6 mg/dL with a direct bilirubin of >10 mg/dL.
Therapy with two cycles of brentuximab vedotin (dose reduced for decreased liver function to 1.2 mg/kg) and cyclophosphamide with prednisone (BV-PC) was initiated.

Total bilirubin peaked at 21.7 a few days after the second dose of BV-PC then down trended to 12 mg/dL, at which point the patient was started on a modified brentuximab vedotin, doxorubicin, vincristine, etoposide, prednisone and cyclophosphamide (Bv-AVE-PC) protocol.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: a few days after second dose

evidence_events.source_span: The patient’s bilirubin slowly down trended over the course of treatment.

The patient’s treatment course was complicated by multiple admissions for neutropenic infections including neutropenic fever and both Streptococcus mitis bacteria and Clostridium difficile colitis during cycle 1 of Bv-AVE-PC.

The most recent follow-up was documented 19 months after original admission and 12 months after completion of chemotherapy which showed a bilirubin that has now down trended to 1.7 mg/dL and a continued complete metabolic response on imaging.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: 19 months after admission, 12 months after chemotherapy

evidence_events.source_section: Case presentation - General information and physical examination findings
evidence_events.source_span: Admitted 20 days after showing signs of pharyngitis and asthenia of increasing intensity associated with paleness and fever
Clinical examination showed an abscess fistulated in the left labia majora
Chest X-ray showed some parenchymal infiltrations with micronodules; echo heart and ultrasound were normal
Initial CBC: hemoglobin 6.00 g/dL, MCV 84.1 fL, MCHC 35.3 g/dL, WBC 8100 cells/mm3, neutrophils 570 x10^3 cells/mm3, platelets 41,000 cells/mm3

Bone marrow aspiration showed rich marrow with 97% blast cells of heterogeneous size, very reduced cytoplasm, nucleus with condensed chromatin, basophil cells without granulations, absence of megakaryocytes, 2% myelocytes, and 2% lymphocytes indicating ALL subtype 2
Flow cytometry on bone marrow showed aberrant expression of CD13 (31.06%), CD19 (94.35%), CD22c (92.61%), CD10 (98.14%), and other markers consistent with B-cell lineage with myeloid marker aberrancy
G-banded karyotype analysis of 20 metaphases revealed a clone with translocation t(1;4)(p21;p15) in 10 mitoses, 46,XX,t(1;4)(p21;p15)[10]/46,XX[10]
FISH on 200 mitotic cells showed absence of rearrangement or deletion of the MLL gene

Patient started standard risk induction chemotherapy in November 2016, followed FRALLE 2000-B2 protocol, completed 2 years of maintenance chemotherapy by September 2019, and is in complete remission at 11 years old after 8 years follow-up

source_metadata.title: Sclerosing epithelioid fibrosarcoma associated with WRN gene variant presenting as chronic dyspnea and pathologic cervical fracture: a case report and review of the literature
source_metadata.notes: Extraction based on case presentation and diagnostic workup narrative.

evidence_events.source_span: A 37-year-old Caucasian female nonsmoker with no known past medical history presented with 4 months of dyspnea and back pain.
Initial chest X-ray and CT showed right upper lobe consolidation; treated as pneumonia without symptom resolution.

Outpatient bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and transbronchial right upper lobe biopsy showed negative fungal and acid-fast bacilli studies; biopsy showed chronic inflammation without malignant cells.
On emergency room admission, chest CT with IV contrast showed near-complete right upper lobe collapse, right upper lobe consolidation, enlarged subcarinal and station 6 lymph nodes.
Spine MRI demonstrated a C7 50% compression fracture and lytic lesions throughout the spinal vertebrae, concerning for metastatic disease.
CT abdomen and pelvis revealed a single 15-mm hypodense liver nodule.
Transthoracic right upper lobe biopsy showed dense fibrous pleural bits, interstitial fibrosis, and patchy dense lymphocytic infiltrate; no malignant cells were seen.

Bronchoscopy with endobronchial ultrasound and transbronchial lymph node sampling, brushing, and BAL of right upper lobe showed BAL cytology positive for poorly differentiated neoplastic cells compatible with poorly differentiated carcinoma; cell block insufficient for immunostains.
Fluoroscopy-guided liver biopsy of the liver nodule demonstrated a malignant undifferentiated neoplasm with epithelioid morphology and weak neuroendocrine differentiation.

Tumor cells formed nests and cords in a hyalinized sclerotic stroma with eosinophilic cytoplasm and round-to-ovoid nuclei; immunohistochemistry showed weak synaptophysin positivity, membranous CD99, subset GATA-3 positivity, weak PAX-8 positivity; negative for ER, SATB2, pankeratin, CK7, CK20, Moc-31, TTF-1, WT-1, HMB45, Melan-A, SOX-10, S100, Inhibin, SMA, MyoD1, CD117, CD45, CD30, and CD34.

Specialized panel of immunohistochemical stains revealed tumor cells reactive to MUC4 expression; BRG1 and INI1 immunostains showed preserved nuclear staining; claudin-4, ERG, CD31, CAMTA1, P40, ETV-4, and NUT stains were negative; diagnosis of sclerosing epithelioid fibrosarcoma was concluded.
Next-generation sequencing (Tempus genetic testing) revealed a variant of unknown significance in the WRN gene; no other cancer risk genes identified.
Patient was started on doxorubicin chemotherapy and tolerated treatment well at 3-month follow-up.
