source_metadata.title: Cutaneous melanocytic tumor with CRTC1::TRIM11 fusion: a case report

evidence_events.source_span: An 18-year-old female patient noticed a dull red mass on her left leg three years ago, which developed without any clear cause. The mass was occasionally tender and exhibited slow growth.

In July 2022, she underwent a B-ultrasound examination at our hospital, revealing a hypoechoic nodule in the subcutaneous soft tissue of the proximal left leg measuring approximately 1.2 × 1 cm, with a distinct boundary, uneven internal echo, and enhanced posterior echo; CDFI shows no clear blood flow signal.
The patient underwent subcutaneous tumor resection, followed by an extended resection due to incomplete initial removal.

diagnostic_reasoning_verbatim_spans: Histological examination under high-power magnification revealed that the neoplasm consisted of epithelioid cells arranged in nests, fascicles, bundles, or sheets with round or ovoid nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and visible mitotic figures, with local nevus cell clusters.
Immunohistochemical analysis confirmed melanocytic differentiation with positivity for S-100, SOX10, MelanA, and focal HMB45.
Tests for EWSR1 rearrangement (FISH) and BRAF V600E mutation (PCR-ARMS) were negative, ruling out clear cell sarcoma and common melanoma mutations.
Next-generation sequencing identified a CRTC1::TRIM11 fusion, and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) for CRTC1 confirmed rearrangement.
These findings established the diagnosis of cutaneous melanocytic tumor with CRTC1::TRIM11 fusion, a rare tumor distinct from melanoma, clear cell sarcoma, or malignant Spitz nevus.

Ultrasound imaging showed a well-defined hypoechoic subcutaneous nodule without blood flow.

Immunohistochemistry confirmed melanocytic differentiation.

Detection of CRTC1::TRIM11 fusion by NGS and FISH confirmed the diagnosis.
Complete surgical resection with negative margins and no recurrence at six months follow-up.

source_metadata.title: Post molar choriocarcinoma with solitary renal metastasis in the absence of primary uterine tumor: a case report and review of the literature
source_metadata.notes: Extraction based on case presentation and clinical course sections.

evidence_events.source_span: A 41-year-old Persian woman with history of complete hydatiform mole presented with severe flank pain, nausea, vomiting, gross hematuria, and vaginal bleeding.
Laboratory tests demonstrated a serum beta human chorionic gonadotropin hormone level of 60,000 mIU/mL.
Imaging studies showed a lesion at the lower pole of the left kidney with active bleeding surrounded by hematoma, as well as an empty uterine cavity.
Bilateral pleural effusion was detected without any lesion within the lungs.
The patient underwent laparotomy, partial nephrectomy, and left para-ovarian cystectomy. Endometrial curettage was also carried out.
The histopathology report revealed choriocarcinoma renal metastasis with high expression of beta human chorionic gonadotropin, cytokeratin 7, and Ki 67.
No malignant cells were observed in the endometrial curettage specimens, and a corpus luteum cyst was found within the para-ovarian cyst.
Pleural effusion was free of malignant cells, and there was no evidence of metastatic lesions in the brain.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: pleural fluid cytology and brain MRI

evidence_events.source_span: The patient received chemotherapy with etoposide, methotrexate, actinomycin D, cyclophosphamide, and vincristine/oncovin over 3 weeks, resulting in beta human chorionic gonadotropin levels dropping to 5 mIU/mL.
Monthly measurements of beta human chorionic gonadotropin levels for 6 months indicated levels have constantly remained within normal ranges, showing no evidence of recurrence or new metastasis.

source_metadata.title: Primary malignant melanoma of the oesophagus

evidence_events.source_span: An 80-year-old woman presented with a history of dysphagia and a 13 kg weight loss in the last 2 months.
The physical examination was unremarkable.
Blood test showed an iron deficiency anaemia.
A gastroscopy was performed and showed a voluminous protruding polypoid purple-black lesion in the lower third of the oesophagus, extending towards the gastric cardia.
Biopsies were performed during initial endoscopy and histology revealed a malignant melanoma with expression of S100 and SOX10 on immunohistochemistry with no mutations detected (BRAF, NRAS, c-KIT).

A complete clinical work-up, including endoscopic ultrasound, total body computed tomography (CT) scan, PET-CT scan, cerebral magnetic resonance imaging, dermatologic and ophthalmologic examination, did not show any other suspect lesions.

source_metadata.title: Pulmonary metastatic gestational choriocarcinoma following an uncomplicated term pregnancy: a case report

evidence_events.source_span: 20-year-old Iranian woman, gravida 2 para 1 live 1 abortion 1, referred with sudden onset dyspnea and pain in the left hemithorax the day after her labor

Patient was agitated, tachycardic (pulse 146), respiratory rate 35, oxygen saturation 88%, left lung sound intensity reduced, no vaginal bleeding but suburethral vaginal lesion about 1 cm found on pelvic exam
Chest x-ray showed left-side hemothorax with bilateral pulmonary nodes; HRCT showed pulmonary nodes up to 41 mm in right upper lobe and 34 mm in left lung suggestive of metastases
Computed tomographic pulmonary angiography ruled out pulmonary embolism
Blood tests showed leukocytosis (WBC 14.4), anemia (Hb 9.8), and markedly elevated beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (β-HCG) level of 1,254,800 mUI/mL
Transvaginal ultrasound showed a large heterogeneous mixed echoic mass in the uterine cavity measuring 31 × 21 mm with low-resistant peripheral vessels
Chest, abdomen, pelvis CT and brain MRI showed no evidence of metastases in brain, spleen, kidney, liver, or gastrointestinal tract
FIGO score calculated as 7 or more (high-risk) based on age, term pregnancy, β-HCG >1,000,000, vaginal metastasis, tumor size 31 × 21 mm, and lung metastases
Diagnosis of pulmonary metastatic choriocarcinoma was made based on elevated β-HCG, clinical vaginal lesion, and radiological pulmonary metastases

Chemotherapy with EMA/CO regimen (etoposide, methotrexate, actinomycin D, cyclophosphamide, vincristine) was started after oncology consult; low-dose induction chemotherapy with etoposide and cisplatin was given prior to EMA/CO
Serum β-HCG level decreased to 125 mUI/mL after three cycles of chemotherapy, indicating good treatment response

source_metadata.title: Isolated conjunctival cavernous hemangioma: a rare case report
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case presentation and pathology sections with figure references.

evidence_events.source_span: A 65-years-old male was referred to our clinic with a nasal interpalpebral bulbar conjunctival mass in the right eye. The patient complained of red-eye for three weeks with no epiphora, pain, or photophobia.

On examination, both eyes had the best-corrected visual acuity of 20/20. We identified a firm, oval, dark brown, vascular, dome-shaped, non-mobile and lobulated subconjunctival mass in the right eye measuring 7 × 6 × 3.2 mm.
Dilated fundoscopy and gonioscopic examinations were normal, without any evidence of intraocular extension. Systemic examinations were also normal.
Ultrasound biomicroscopy (UBM) showed a subconjunctival mass with intact sclera except for the temporal side where a posterior shadowing was seen suspicious for an intraocular extension.
No clear intraocular extension was noted on orbital magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).

Based on these findings a clinical diagnosis of presumed conjunctival malignant melanoma was made and the patient underwent excisional biopsy with no-touch technique and 3 mm margin, partial sclerectomy, and cryotherapy.

Histopathology and microscopic examination with hematoxylin and eosin staining showed large vascular channels lined by endothelial cells and filled with red blood cells separated by fibrous interstitium. No sign of malignancy or necrosis was seen.
Therefore a diagnosis of the conjunctival cavernous hemangioma was made.
The patient showed no sign of recurrence after six months of follow-up.

source_metadata.title: Ileo-Ileal Intussusception Secondary to Neuroendocrine Tumor in Adult Patient
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case narrative sections only, preserving source order and granularity.

evidence_events.source_span: A 60-year-old man with a past medical history of peptic ulcer disease presented to the Emergency Department for evaluation of lower abdominal pain, several dark “maroon” colored bowel movements, and hematemesis for the past 2 days.
He had associated palpitations and shortness of breath, which quickly resolved upon arriving to the hospital.
On presentation, his vital signs were stable. Physical examination was notable for mild tenderness across the lower abdomen.
Initial laboratory test results were significant for a hemoglobin level of 12.3 g/dL and hematocrit of 36%. The remainder of his laboratory work was unremarkable.

Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast showed ileo-ileal intussusception in the right lower quadrant. Just distal to this segment, there was an irregular area of mucosal/submucosal thickening, suspicious for an underlying small bowel mass, with no signs of intestinal obstruction.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: CT abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast

evidence_events.source_span: Exploratory laparotomy revealed a small bowel mass approximately 30 cm from the ileocecal valve, serving as the lead point for his intussusception. There was also a small palpable lymph node in the associated mesentery. Approximately 15 cm of small bowel and 13 lymph nodes, including the palpable lymph node, were resected and sent for pathological analysis. No abnormalities were seen on the liver.

Subsequent histopathological examination confirmed a well-differentiated 1.2-cm NET with spread to 1 lymph node, with surgical margins clear of the tumor. The Ki-67 stain was positive for less than 1% of cells.
The final diagnosis was an ileo-ileal intussusception secondary to a T3N1 NET, grade 1.
His postoperative course was complicated by the development of an ileus, which quickly resolved on its own following conservative management.

source_metadata.title: Acquired Erythropoietic Protoporphyria Secondary to Myelodysplastic Syndrome: From Mythology to Oncology

evidence_events.source_span: A 73-year-old man presented to our dermatology clinic with a history of sun sensitivity and development of crusting skin lesions for the past 2 years.

After 30 min of direct sun exposure, he would start to feel burning and excruciating pain in the skin on the face, hands, and fingertips, with crusting skin lesions appearing on the dorsa of the hands within days.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: after 30 min of direct sun exposure

evidence_events.source_span: His medical history revealed a myelodysplastic syndrome with multilineage dysplasia (MDS-MLD) diagnosed 6 years ago, which did not require any treatment at that time.

Clinical examination revealed thickened, lichenified skin with one fresh blister, numerous crusts, indented scars, and milia formation on the dorsa of the hands and some on the back of the neck and face.

CBC showed anaemia, and reduced thrombocyte and white blood cell count consistent with his MDS; liver and renal function parameters were normal; no detectable autoantibodies associated with connective tissue diseases.
Skin biopsy demonstrated subepidermal blistering with scarce inflammatory reaction, suggesting a porphyria.
A plasma fluorescence scan was positive and revealed a massive increase in total porphyrins at 33.9 umol/L (normal < 1.30) and free protoporphyrin 30 umol/L (normal < 0.20).
A diagnosis of erythropoietic protoporphyria (EPP) secondary to MDS was made.

Two years after the diagnosis of acquired EPP, the patient was able to control his photosensitivity with sun-protective measures and did not require the use of afamelanotide; he has not developed any signs of liver toxicity despite consistently high plasma porphyrins.

source_metadata.title: Tracheal airway obstruction induced by a large glomangioma: discussion of management and literature review

evidence_events.source_span: A man in his early 80s was admitted to the emergency department with respiratory distress and massive haemoptysis.

His patient history showed an arterial hypertension, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease, active smoking and moderate alcohol consumption. There was no history of respiratory pathologies, haemorrhagic manifestations of the upper aero digestive tract, coagulopathies, anticoagulants or antiplatelet aggregation therapy.
Emergency upper airway stabilisation and haemostasis were immediately performed in the operating room.
The initial endoscopic examination showed an active and significant bleed emerging from a large tumour in the trachea.

After securing the airway, an endoscopic examination of the trachea revealed bulging, quite fleshy mass located on the posterior tracheal wall, just below the vocal folds, obstructing approximately 90% of the tracheal lumen and extending 2.5 cm distally. The mass was actively and diffusively bleeding.

Radiological workup by CT showed a 25 mm posterior parietal mass of the posterior sub cricoid portion of the trachea uptaking contrast in the arterial phase as well as infiltration of the intertracheaoesophageal fat with mass effect on the oesophagus. There was neither pulmonary nor abdominal lesions nor any evidence of suspicious lymph nodes.
A full blood workup did not show any abnormalities.

Histological analysis showed proliferation of the chorion in the form of small nests with relatively uniform, medium-sized cells and rounded to polyhedral cells containing homogenous, ovoid nuclei with fine chromatin. It was associated with numerous thin-walled vascular structures, lined by endothelial cells without atypia.

The tumour cells containing a cytoplasmic frame well defined by reticulin were positive for actin and caldesmone with low expression for CD99. There was no expression for pancytokeratins, CD34, chromogranin, synaptophysin, S100 protein, SOX-10, desmin or inhibin. There also was no signs of malignancy.
These histological findings were compatible with glomangioma subtype of glomus tumour.

The patient presented a second episode of massive bleeding from the tracheal tumour urging surgical haemostasis endoscopically and through the tracheotomy using bipolar cauterisation. The bleeding was controlled without compromising the airway.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: surgical haemostasis endoscopically and through tracheotomy

evidence_events.source_span: The patient underwent volumetric intensity by arc therapy radiation at a total dose of 53 Gy over 25 sessions, with a frequency of five sessions per week. The treatment was well tolerated without side effects or complications.

The various endoscopic and radiologic checks carried out at 3, 6, 9, 12, and 18 months after radiation therapy demonstrated a regression of more than 80% of the tracheal tumour with stability of the minor residual lesion.

source_metadata.title: Leukocytosis and thrombocytosis after splenectomy: expected finding, infection, or something else: a case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 53-year-old incarcerated Hispanic male presented from jail with worsening abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, tachycardia, and focal peritonitis 4 days after being struck multiple times in the abdomen.
Initial WBC was 38.4 × 10^9/L, platelet count was 691 × 10^9/L, and lipase was 55 U/L.
Computed tomography (CT) scan of the abdomen demonstrated a hematoma encasing the distal pancreas, abutting the stomach and colon, with a small amount of hemoperitoneum.

Emergent exploratory laparotomy revealed a nearly severed distal pancreas and a devascularized colon, necessitating a distal pancreatectomy, splenectomy, and colonic resection with primary anastomosis.

Postoperatively, he had persistently elevated leukocytosis, thrombocytosis, segmented neutrophils, eosinophilia, and basophilia, with leukocytosis peaking at 69.6 × 10^9/L on POD-9 and thrombocytosis peaking at 2293 × 10^9/L on POD-12.
Despite sepsis workup, including repeat CT with oral and intravenous contrast, no source of infection or contrast leak was identified; procalcitonin was consistently low (0.11–0.13 ng/mL).
Hematology/oncology consultation was obtained; peripheral blood smear demonstrated severe leukocytosis and thrombocytosis but no circulating blasts.
Molecular testing for JAK2, CALR, and MPL mutations was negative.
Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) of BCR-ABL was positive.

Bone marrow biopsy demonstrated slightly hypercellular marrow (70%) with trilineage hematopoiesis, mild myeloid and megakaryocytic hyperplasia, molecular evidence of BCR/ABL+ fusion consistent with chronic phase CML.
FISH analysis detected BCR-ABL1 fusions in 91.5% of nuclei, confirming the presence of the Philadelphia chromosome (t(9;22) translocation).
Flow cytometry showed no increased blasts (<1%) and immunohistochemistry estimated CD34-positive blasts at 1% of all cells; Sokal and ELTS scores placed patient in intermediate risk category.
Initial treatment included hydroxyurea, with transition to imatinib (400 mg daily).
Infectious disease specialists recommended post-splenectomy vaccinations and prophylactic azithromycin until vaccine series completion.
Hospital course complicated by intra-abdominal fluid collections requiring antibiotics and interventional radiology drainage.
At outpatient follow-up 1 year later, patient continued imatinib therapy with good tolerance and no adverse effects.

source_metadata.title: Intramuscular endometriosis of the forearm: a case report
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case report narrative and figures with source grounding.

evidence_events.source_span: A 40-year-old, right-hand-dominant, female (G3P3003) presented to the Orthopedic Department with an 18-month history of an intermittently painful mass in the medial aspect of her right forearm. The mass would become increasingly tender and firm in the days before menses and during menstruation.
Physical examination revealed a small palpable mass in the right flexor pronator musculature and was tender to palpation.
Previous imaging, including radiographs of the right forearm demonstrated no acute osseous or soft tissue abnormality.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) without intravenous contrast showed an oval intramuscular mass in the anterior compartment of the proximal forearm, measuring approximately 2.2 × 2.1 × 3.0 cm. The mass demonstrated heterogenous T2 signal and cystic changes. There was no invasion of deeper musculature or fascia.

Ultrasound-guided core needle biopsy of the lesion was performed. On ultrasound imaging, the mass was circumscribed and hypoechoic with internal doppler flow. The core needle biopsy was nondiagnostic.
Open biopsy with frozen section diagnosis was performed, which was consistent with endometriosis.
Additional history revealed three previous uncomplicated Cesarean sections. Physical examination did not reveal any concern for pelvic endometriosis.

Dienogest, a progestin-based medication, was recommended to suppress endometrial proliferation and decrease symptoms. The patient initially declined medication due to ongoing multiple sclerosis treatment.
Approximately 18 months after initial presentation, symptoms worsened with pain radiating into the elbow, distal forearm, and hand. The patient trialed Dienogest but symptoms did not improve.
The patient underwent surgical excision of the mass. At 6 months postoperatively, the patient reported significant improvement with only very mild soreness at menstruation.

initial_presentation.first_contact_summary: The patient, a 69-year-old Chinese male, was admitted for the primary complaint of intermittent gross hematuria that had been present for 10 days. Before admission, the patient underwent a B ultrasound in our department, which revealed hypoechoic nodules in the right upper wall of the bladder (cystoscopy was recommended), prostate enlargement with calcification, and no abnormal findings in either kidney. No distention of the ureters was observed, and about 91 ml of residual bladder urine was present. There are no special past interventions. The physical examination did not reveal any positive findings.

source_metadata.title: Pleomorphic rhabdomyosarcoma of the adult bladder: a case report
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case presentation and discussion sections with figure references.

evidence_events.source_span: 69-year-old Chinese male patient who presented to the urology outpatient clinic because of intermittent full-course macroscopic hematuria for 10 days

B ultrasound indicated hypoechoic nodules in the right upper wall of the bladder, prostate enlargement with calcification, no abnormal findings in either kidney, no distention of the ureters, and about 91 ml of residual bladder urine

Preoperative cystoscopy revealed a 3.0 × 3.0 cm globular mass in the right anterior wall of the bladder, with a narrow pedicle, and the formation of sheet-like yellow calcification on the surface of the mass
Transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBt) with cystoscopic multipoint random biopsy was performed
Postoperative pathological examination showed pleomorphic rhabdomyosarcoma of the adult bladder; tumor biopsy at TURBt showed no residual tumor in the bladder muscularis
Pre-chemotherapy PET-CT scan did not reveal any metastatic lesions throughout the body

Next-generation sequencing (NGS) of tumor tissue showed TP53 gene variation (exon 7 c.743G > T p.(R248L)) with mutation abundance of 91.77%, MAPK1 amplification with copy number 5.78, and microsatellite stable (MSS) status
Immunohistochemical analysis showed GATA3 (−), P53 (tumor: 90%+), KI67 (tumor: 45%+), CK (−), SMA (−), vimentin (+), MyoD1 (+), myogenin (partial +), and desmin (+)
Chemotherapy regimen administered was intravenous dacarbazine with doxorubicin; patient had good adherence and tolerability with no adverse events
Follow-up enhanced CT scans on 7 December 2023, 5 March 2024, and 4 June 2024 showed no tumor recurrence after chemotherapy

source_metadata.title: Metastatic SMARCA4-deficient undifferentiated tumor in the small mesentery: case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 67-year-old male with a history of smoking was admitted to the hospital with complaints of abdominal distention and pain lasting for more than four days.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: lasting for more than four days

evidence_events.source_span: Physical examination revealed a flat abdomen with mild tenderness in the right abdomen at the umbilical level and a pliable, movable, non-tender mass measuring approximately 3.0 × 2.8 cm.

Abdominal computed tomography (CT) revealed a high-density mass measuring approximately 41 × 37 mm in the right lower abdomen with uneven density and surface enhancement, closely associated with the adjacent small intestine, with signs of mechanical small bowel obstruction.

Chest CT identified a high-density mass measuring 63 × 48 mm in the upper lobe of the right lung with irregular edges, thickened adjacent pleura, bronchial stenosis and occlusion, and enlarged right hilar lymph nodes.

Exploratory laparotomy revealed an irregular mass measuring approximately 5 × 3 cm adjacent to the intestinal mesentery causing incomplete intestinal obstruction and proximal intestine dilation; partial small bowel resection was performed.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: exploratory laparotomy, partial small bowel resection

evidence_events.source_span: Postoperative pathological examination identified an oval mass in the mesentery on the serosal surface of the intestinal midsection measuring 4.5 × 4 × 3.5 cm with gray-red cut surface, hemorrhage, necrosis, and poorly defined boundaries blending into surrounding tissue.

Microscopic examination showed diffusely distributed tumor cells with fusiform, ovoid, epithelioid, and rhabdoid morphology, active mitotic figures, geographic necrosis, and numerous apoptotic bodies.

Immunohistochemical analysis showed tumor cells positive for Vimentin and CD34, partial positivity for CK and CD10, a high Ki-67 proliferation index (80%), and negative for BRG1, CK7, TTF1, P40, and multiple other markers.

Based on histopathological and immunohistochemical findings, the diagnosis of SMARCA4-deficient undifferentiated tumor (SMARCA4-UT) originating in the small mesentery was made; no biopsy was performed on the lung mass, but it was presumed to be the primary tumor with metastasis to the mesentery.

Twenty days after discharge, the patient experienced recurrent abdominal pain and distention; abdominal CT showed thickening of the small bowel wall, nodular high-density shadows near the sacrum, and enlarged bilateral inguinal lymph nodes.
Despite symptomatic treatment, the patient rapidly deteriorated and died from respiratory failure 21 days after diagnosis.

source_metadata.title: Concurrent leiomyosarcoma causing small bowel obstruction in a patient with non-Hodgkin lymphoma

evidence_events.source_span: A man in his 80s was diagnosed with SBO following a presentation to the emergency department with colicky abdominal pain, obstipation, nausea and vomiting. His vital signs were unremarkable, and his abdomen was distended but non-tender.

The patient's background was significant for lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma, a low-grade mature B cell lymphoma, on active surveillance after a recent episode of febrile neutropenia while on zanubrutinib, during which an incidental, non-obstructing SB mass was identified. Further history included rheumatoid arthritis and collagenous colitis managed with oral sulfasalazine 1.5 g two times per day and 6 mg of prednisolone daily. He previously had an open appendicectomy.

Blood tests revealed a normocytic, normochromic anaemia with a haemoglobin level of 101 g/L. Inflammatory markers included a white cell count of 11.9 ×10⁹ cells/L and C reactive protein of 71 mg/L. Electrolytes, renal and liver function test results were unremarkable.

CT of his abdomen-pelvis with portal venous contrast demonstrated a large obstructing distal SB mass, which increased in size compared with a CT performed during his admission for febrile neutropenia 4 months prior.

Initial management involved nasogastric tube decompression and intravenous fluid resuscitation. Gastrografin was administered on the second day of admission with clinical and radiological resolution of the obstruction.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: initial and second day of admission
evidence_events.procedural_cue: nasogastric decompression, IV fluids, gastrografin administration

evidence_events.source_span: Haematology was consulted, and it was advised that lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma less frequently involves the SB and is unlikely to be related to the SB mass. Given this advice and the progression of the now symptomatic SB mass over time, the decision was made to proceed with surgical resection.

Laparoscopy demonstrated an SB mass adherent within the pelvis. Adhesiolysis was performed through a lower midline laparotomy to allow an oncological, stapled, side-to-side, antiperistaltic SB resection. The SB lumen was significantly narrowed by the mass, and multiple enlarged, firm mesenteric lymph nodes were palpable. There was no evidence of metastatic disease.

Histopathology demonstrated a 75 mm grade 2 jejunal leiomyosarcoma with negative margins and one of four lymph nodes demonstrating metastatic disease. The remaining three lymph nodes showed features consistent with known lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma. Epstein-Barr virus (EBV)-encoded RNA was negative, and the possibility of an EBV-associated leiomyosarcoma was excluded. Staging CT chest was negative.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: histopathology, EBV RNA testing, staging CT chest

evidence_events.source_span: The case was discussed in a multidisciplinary meeting that concluded only ongoing surveillance was required.

source_metadata.title: Surgical management of umbilical endometrioma within an umbilical hernia
source_metadata.notes: Case report of umbilical endometrioma in umbilical hernia with failed medical management and surgical excision.

evidence_events.source_span: A nulliparous woman in her 40s presented with umbilical pain and bleeding with menses.
Her medical history was significant for hypertension, body mass index (BMI) of 37 kg/m2, uterine fibroids, abnormal uterine bleeding and dyschezia.
Surgical history was significant for two abdominal myomectomy procedures through a Pfannenstiel incision with breach of the endometrium in both surgeries.
Examination revealed a protuberant abdomen with a 3 cm blood-filled cyst at the umbilicus consistent with umbilical endometriosis.
Bimanual examination showed a small uterus and no adnexal masses or nodularity on the uterosacral ligaments, rectovaginal septum, parametrium or cul-de-sac.
MRI showed an umbilical endometrioma.

Before referral for surgical management, the patient attempted medical therapy with medroxyprogesterone acetate without relief and was not a candidate for combined oral contraceptives due to hypertension and elevated BMI.
The patient underwent umbilectomy, excision of umbilical endometriosis, lysis of adhesions and umbilical hernia repair under general anaesthesia.
The endometrioma was densely adherent to the umbilical skin, hernia sac, omental fat contents of the umbilical hernia sac and the anterior rectus sheath.
The lesion was excised en masse with a wide margin, resulting in a large defect in the anterior abdominal wall.
The defect was closed primarily using synthetic mesh and the skin edges were approximated using staples, leaving a subcutaneous drain.
Surgical pathology revealed cystic endometriosis within subcutaneous tissue, consistent with umbilical endometrioma.
Postoperative course was complicated by a surgical site infection requiring oral antibiotics, intravenous vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam therapy and ultrasound-guided percutaneous drainage.
Deep wound culture grew coagulase-negative Staphylococcus and rare Corynebacterium jeikeium sensitive to vancomycin.
At the time of this writing, the patient has had a 2-year recurrence-free interval.

source_metadata.title: Cutaneous metastases of invasive lobular breast cancer as the first clinical manifestation: a case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 53-year-old woman presented to the dermatology department with a 5-month history of bilateral nodules in the armpits, which had spread to the trunk.
Clinical examination revealed asymptomatic, erythematous, infiltrating skin-colored nodules measuring 2 × 3 cm in the axillae and trunk.
The patient reported associated symptoms of asthenia, anorexia, and weight loss of approximately 10 kg.
A clinical breast examination showed no palpable masses, and the patient had no history of smoking, alcohol use, medical conditions, or relevant family history.
Routine laboratory tests were normal except for an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate (98 mm/hour).

A punch biopsy was performed in collaboration with the surgical department, and histopathological analysis revealed diffuse infiltration of atypical cells with large nuclei, prominent nucleoli, and atypical mitoses, consistent with metastatic undifferentiated carcinoma.

Immunohistochemical staining showed positive nuclear staining for estrogen receptor (ER) in 50% of tumor cells with ++/+++ intensity, negative progesterone receptor (PR) staining, and faint cytoplasmic and negative membranous staining for HER2-neu (c-erbB-2).
Controls confirmed the mammary origin of the metastases, consistent with lobular-type metastatic adenocarcinoma involving the skin.
Additional tests revealed an elevated cancer antigen (CA 15-3) level of >500 U/mL and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) level of 6.37 ng/mL.
The patient was referred to the oncology hospital and began treatment with palbociclib at a dose of 125 mg alongside hormone therapy with aromatase inhibitors.
Although the skin lesions resolved, the CA 15-3 and CEA levels continued to rise, indicating ongoing disease progression.
Four months after initiating treatment, the patient developed symptoms of cough, ascites, and lower extremity edema.
A computed tomography scan revealed a significant accumulation of ascites and pleural effusion, though no lung metastases were identified.
The patient died of her illness 7 months after the diagnosis of CM originating from primary breast carcinoma.

source_metadata.title: Case report: Diagnosis of impaired consciousness in a cancer patient using immune checkpoint inhibitors

evidence_events.source_span: A 64-year-old female patient with a history of predominantly epithelioid pleural mesothelioma, treated with pemetrexed and cisplatin chemotherapy for 6 cycles between 2016-2017. At the 6th year of follow-up, she evolved with locoregional progression. Subsequently, she commenced palliative immunotherapy with Nivolumab at a dose of 180 mg and Ipilimumab at 60 mg.

She was admitted to the hospital due to a 2-month history of progressive episodes of disorientation, inattention, frequent forgetfulness, confusion, sporadic nocturnal visual hallucinations, and occasional difficulties in naming objects, notable for the absence of evident aphasia but exhibiting fluctuating patterns throughout the day. The onset of symptoms coincided with the initiation of immunotherapy with nivolumab and ipilimumab.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: 2-month history; onset coincided with initiation of immunotherapy

evidence_events.source_span: She reported asthenia, adynamia, mild gait instability, heat intolerance, nocturnal sweating, palpitations, tremors, low mood, as well as a deterioration in her quality of life and functionality.

At evaluation, the patient was partially disoriented, inattentive, with mild ataxia and dysarthria upon neurological examination. Her vital signs and the rest of the physical examination were without relevant findings.
A mild urinary tract infection was found and treated with amikacin. Hepatic encephalopathy, renal failure, intoxication, drug or medication withdrawal, and urinary or fecal retention were ruled out.

Contrast-enhanced brain MRI revealed non-confluent supratentorial white matter microangiopathy, without evidence of vascular lesions or mesothelioma dissemination; electroencephalogram was normal; lumbar puncture showed no signs of encephalitis or leptomeningeal spread.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: Contrast-enhanced brain MRI, EEG, lumbar puncture

evidence_events.source_span: Further investigations revealed a suppressed thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), elevated levels of peripheral thyroid hormones (total T4 and T3), absence of anti-thyroid-stimulating hormone receptor antibodies (TRAb) and anti-thyroid peroxidase (TPO), along with the presence of anti-thyroglobulin (Anti-Tg) antibodies. Thyroid iodine uptake studies indicated low uptake.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: thyroid function tests, autoantibodies, iodine uptake studies

evidence_events.source_span: It was concluded that the etiology of the delirium was a thyrotoxicosis episode that developed in the context of autoimmune thyroiditis, secondary to ICI treatment.
Symptomatic treatment with beta-blockers was initiated, leading to a gradual amelioration of neurological manifestations.

MRI of spine showed pathological compression fracture of T10 vertebral body with no canal stenosis, raising high suspicion for vertebral metastasis
Biopsy of lesion confirmed diagnosis of mucoepidermoid carcinoma
Wide local excision of scalp lesion performed under general anesthesia; excised tissue sent for histopathological examination confirming invasive mucoepidermoid carcinoma
Post-surgery, patient referred for radiotherapy; at 8 months post-excision, no clinical signs of recurrence and no CNS symptoms; vertebral fracture stable without surgical intervention

source_metadata.title: An Unusual Case of Metastatic Gastric Cancer Presenting with Right Heart Failure and Cardiac Metastasis

evidence_events.source_span: A 51-year-old male patient presented to our clinic in December 2023 with fatigue, abdominal distension and leg edema, which started three weeks prior.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: in December 2023; started three weeks prior

evidence_events.source_span: On physical examination, dullness in the abdomen upon percussion, suggestive of fluid, was observed. Additionally, there were decreased breath sounds in the basals of the lungs, a tachycardic heart rhythm, and significant pretibial edema.
The electrocardiogram (ECG) was consistent with sinus tachycardia. The patient’s blood pressure was 130/90 mmHg.

Laboratory tests revealed hemoglobin: 13.2 g/dL; fasting blood glucose: 95 mg/dL; serum creatinine 1.2 mg/dL; aspartate aminotransferase (AST) 49 U/L; alanine aminotransferase (ALT): 46 U/L; bilirubin: 0.69 mg/dL; albumin: 3.6 g/dL; carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA): 43 ng/mL; and carbohydrate antigen (CA) 19-9: 361 U/mL. Electrolyte levels were within normal limits. Urinalysis showed proteinuria of 0.4 g/day.
Paracentesis revealed a serum-to-ascites albumin gradient greater than 1.1 g/dL. Cytological examination of the fluid revealed benign cytological findings.

Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) revealed a lesion 6.2 × 3.3 cm in diameter, suggestive of a low-moving hypoechoic thrombus or mass. This lesion almost completely filled the right atrium and stuck to the tricuspid valve. Dilation of the inferior vena cava and severe insufficiency of the tricuspid valve were also observed.
Thorax CT showed multiple nodules in the lung and a suspicious mass in the right atrium.

A PET scan showed segmental wall thickening at the stomach and esophagogastric junction, measuring 7.5 cm in size and showing 18-FDG uptake with an SUV max of 22.4, evaluated in favor of primary malignancy. Multiple metastatic lymphadenopathy in the abdomen, free fluid in the abdominopelvic region, metastatic lesions in the liver and lung and supraclavicular lymphadenopathy were detected. The lesion seen on TTE was evaluated as a tumoral thrombus suspicious lesion with dimensions of 8.8 × 5.5 cm at the level of the right atrium on PET-CT and a maximum standard unit value (SUVmax) of 12.8.
Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMRI) was planned to differentiate the tumor/thrombus, but it could not be performed because the patient could not tolerate lying flat.
An ulcerovegetating mass was detected in the upper-GI endoscopic evaluation. Histopathological evaluation of the biopsy specimen was consistent with gastric adenocarcinoma.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: upper GI endoscopy and biopsy performed

evidence_events.source_span: PD-L1 protein expression was assessed using the CPS and found to be positive, with a value of 15. HER-2 IHC score was +3, and SISH demonstrated HER-2 gene amplification with a HER-2/CEP17 ratio ≥ 2 (positive).

A combination regimen of pembrolizumab, trastuzumab, and FOLFOX chemotherapy was initiated. However, trastuzumab could not be given due to cardiac pathology in the first cycle. Twelve cycles of chemotherapy were administered. Treatment with trastuzumab and pembrolizumab continued every 3 weeks until disease progression.

There was no regression in the cardiac lesion during follow-up under treatment, the patient’s heart failure clinic and the risk of sudden death. A 10 × 7 cm mass, which completely filled the right atrium and extended to the tricuspid valve, adhering to the inferior vena cava, was resected during a surgical procedure performed in January 2024.
Histopathological evaluation of the excision material revealed gastric adenocarcinoma metastasis.

One month after surgery, trastuzumab was added to his treatment. Following six cycles of chemotherapy, an 18F-FDG PET/CT scan demonstrated a partial response, with significant regression in pulmonary nodules, decreased metabolic activity and size of the primary lesion and abdominal lymphadenopathy, near-complete metabolic response of hepatic metastases, and no free fluid in the abdominopelvic region.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: one month after surgery; following six cycles

evidence_events.source_span: The patient’s progression-free survival (PFS) was 10 months. The patient remains under follow-up, and overall survival (OS) has not yet been reached.

source_metadata.title: Atypical clinical presentation of oncocytic adrenocortical carcinoma with decompensated metabolic syndrome and psychotic outbreak

evidence_events.source_span: A woman in her 60s was admitted due to decompensated metabolic syndrome with refractory arterial hypertension, dizziness, headache, asthenia, and 20 kg weight gain over 6 months despite maximal antihypertensive therapy.

On admission, she had type 2 diabetes requiring insulin, mixed hyperlipidaemia, hypokalaemia, hypernatraemia, and abnormal liver tests including elevated gamma-glutamyltranspeptidase, bilirubin, ALAT, and ASAT.

During hospitalization, she developed psychotic breakdown with persecutory delirium, visual hallucinations, anxiety, and mistrust, treated initially with haloperidol and clomethiazole, then transferred to psychogeriatric unit.

Physical exam showed blood pressure 189/105 mm Hg, heart rate 104/min, BMI 46.7 kg/m2, alert and oriented, anxiety, regular tachycardia, distended abdomen with mild epigastric tenderness, and bilateral lower limb oedemas.

Urine analysis revealed proteinuria, ketonuria, urobilinogen and haematuria; viral serologies and autoimmune panel were negative; aldosterone renin ratio was normal with renin 27.8 mUl/L and aldosterone 0.08 nmol/L.

Hormonal panel showed normal estradiol, progesterone, 17-OH-progesterone, androstenedione, DHEAS, and cortisoluria; marginally increased DHEAS (9.17 µmol/L) and urinary catecholamines including metanephrine (1283 nmol/24h), normetanephrine (4218 nmol/24h), and methoxytyramine (2107 nmol/24h).

Ultrasound revealed a large bilobed retropancreatic mass near the left kidney and para-aortic region; abdominal CT confirmed a bilobed left adrenal mass measuring 8×5 cm and 1.8×2.2 cm, vascularised without calcifications, with no locoregional or distant spread.
Liver biopsy confirmed histological evidence of NASH consistent with unbalanced metabolic syndrome; haemochromatosis, viral hepatitis, and autoimmune liver diseases were ruled out.

Secretory adenoma was considered unlikely based on radiology and normal renin, aldosterone and cortisol levels; pheochromocytoma was considered due to radiological features and elevated urinary metanephrines.

Patient was treated medically with haloperidol and clomethiazole for psychiatric symptoms, metformin, linagliptin and insulin for diabetes, and multiple antihypertensives including metoprolol, spironolactone, lisinopril and doxazosin; doxazosin was given due to marginally increased metanephrines and suspicion of pheochromocytoma.

Laparoscopic left adrenalectomy was performed without intraoperative complications; patient required adrenergic support until postoperative day four; antihypertensive therapies were discontinued except beta-blocker.

Histology confirmed oncocytic adrenocortical carcinoma (ACON), staged pT2 pN0 R1 with positive margins; tumour fulfilled Lin-Weiss-Bisceglia criteria for malignancy; tumour cells positive for synaptophysin, inhibin, calretinin, Melan-A and CD56, negative for chromogranin and others; Ki67 index 10%.

CT abdomen 2 months post-resection showed post-resection status with a 2.8×2 cm infiltrative lesion near pancreatic tail, left kidney and coeliac trunk, suspected tumour remnant; nodular peritoneal thickening suggested early dissemination.

Adjuvant chemotherapy with mitotane and radiotherapy were initiated; glucocorticoid replacement therapy started to prevent adrenal insufficiency; psychiatric symptoms and hypertension resolved postoperatively.

source_metadata.title: Salivary gland adenoid cystic carcinoma presenting as a large metastatic hepatic mass: a case report
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case presentation and clinical course sections with source order preserved.

evidence_events.source_span: A 29-year-old African American male individual presented to the emergency department (ED) for right upper quadrant abdominal pain and early satiety.
Physical examination was unrevealing except for abdominal tenderness.
A computed tomography (CT) scan revealed hepatomegaly with a large mass centered in the left lobe measuring 14 cm.
Laboratory values showed mildly elevated transaminases, with an alanine transaminase (ALT) of 51, aspartate aminotransferase (AST) of 74, and an alkaline phosphatase of 93 units/L.

One month later, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a 19 cm enhancing left hepatic mass. Laboratory tests demonstrated a mild elevation in transaminases, a negative hepatitis viral panel, and unremarkable tumor marker levels, including alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), and carbohydrate antigen 19-9 (CA19.9).

Two months after initial visit, abdominal CT angiography with contrast showed a 21 cm hepatic mass centered in the left hepatic lobe, and chest CT revealed innumerable bilateral pulmonary nodules measuring up to 8 mm, favoring metastases.

Laboratory tests revealed alkaline phosphatase elevation (451 IU/L) and mildly elevated transaminases, with an AST level of 93 units/L and an ALT of 45 units/L. Tumor marker laboratory results were within normal ranges (CA 19.9 < 14.0; AFP: 1.97; and CEA: 5.28).

Initial histopathological examination of the liver biopsy specimens revealed a well-differentiated carcinoma characterized by a distinctive myxoid stroma with tubular and cribriform structures, consistent with metastatic adenoid cystic carcinoma.
The patient underwent transcatheter arterial chemoembolization (TACE) and was discharged with a hematology–oncology follow-up.

Two weeks later, a CT scan of the neck soft tissue with contrast revealed a complex bilobed mass in the right parotid gland measuring approximately 6.5 cm, with progression into the parapharyngeal space causing notable deformity of the oropharynx.

Biopsy of the parotid mass with immunohistochemistry findings was suggestive of adenoid cystic carcinoma; however, basal cell adenocarcinoma could not be completely excluded without examination of a completely removed salivary gland tumor.
A presumptive diagnosis of stage IV adenoid cystic carcinoma with metastases to the liver and lung was made. The patient was started on a chemotherapeutic regimen with cisplatin and vinorelbine.

Five months later, the patient presented with neurological symptoms including lightheadedness and left-sided weakness. CT scan revealed new right frontal hyperdensities consistent with brain metastasis.

evidence_events.source_span: During surgery, the mass protruded from the inferior vena cava into the right atrium.
Laboratory assessments, including complete blood count, blood biochemistry, urinalysis, and arterial blood gas analysis, yielded normal results except elevated CRP (75 mg/L) and ESR (117 mm/hour).
Abdominal ultrasonography and contrast-enhanced abdominopelvic CT scan revealed a renal mass involving the inferior vena cava with a tumor thrombus extending into the right atrium.
Echocardiography showed a large, rope-like, hyperechoic mass in the inferior vena cava measuring 14 cm × 2.7 cm, protruding into the right atrium, suggestive of massive vein thrombosis.
Macroscopic examination of the left radical nephrectomy specimen revealed a 7 cm × 6.5 cm × 5 cm mass in the lower pole of the kidney with extension to the renal sinus.

Microscopic examination showed sheet-like diffuse infiltration of small and round neoplastic cells with monomorphic nuclei, fine speckled chromatin, inconspicuous nucleoli, and occasional pseudorosette-like structures.
Immunohistochemical staining was positive for NKX2.2, CD99, synaptophysin, and chromogranin; negative for CK7, CK20, CK, LCA, PAX8, AMACR, P63, C41/A3, and TLE1.
Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) study identified translocation at (11;22), indicating the presence of an EWSR1 gene rearrangement.

source_metadata.title: A pilocytic astrocytoma with novel ATG16L1::NTRK2 fusion responsive to larotrectinib: a case report with genomic and functional analysis

evidence_events.source_span: A 7-year-old boy experienced personality change, visual disturbance, and vomiting, which led to a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain at Lund University Hospital in September 2019
The MRI showed a 5×5×7 cm intraventricular tumor with tumor growth also into the temporal lobe, hypothalamus, and basal ganglia
The boy underwent surgery, resulting in the resection of the intraventricular part of the tumor
Postoperatively, he had a loss of vision in both eyes, which was later regained

Clinical routine pathological investigation of the resected tissue showed relatively small cell nuclei, few Rosenthal fibers, occasional mitosis (1 mitosis per 2 mm2), positivity for GFAP and synaptophysin, and a low Ki-67 proliferation rate (4.5% in hot spot areas), suggesting a LGG
The tumor had normal TP53 expression, preserved expression of ATRX, and was negative for H3K27 mutation (H3 p.K28me3 assay) by immunohistochemistry (IHC), excluding other common brain tumor entities
The tumor was screened for BRAF fusion (Oncomine FOCUS panel) and mutations in the BRAF or IDH1/2 genes, but no genetic alterations could be found

evidence_events.source_span: Methylation array profiling was performed on FFPE tumor tissue, resulting in a calibrated match score of 0.99 with pilocytic astrocytoma (PA), WHO grade 1

Over time, the tumor progressed; chemotherapy with vinblastine was initiated 2 years after diagnosis, followed by bevacizumab 7 months later due to progression, and then vincristine and carboplatin 9 months after chemotherapy start

source_metadata.title: A unique case of pulmonary minimally invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma arising from atypical goblet cell hyperplasia in the bronchial epithelium of a 9-year-old girl
source_metadata.notes: Extraction based on case presentation and clinical course sections with source-ordered evidence events and milestones.

evidence_events.source_span: A 9-year-old girl with persistent cough and sputum production lasting for three weeks was admitted to a local hospital.
Despite antibiotic treatment for the suspected respiratory infection, the symptoms did not improve.
Chest CT revealed a solid nodule measuring 1.9 cm × 1.6 cm in the posterior basal segment of the right lower lobe with irregular margins and slight enhancement.
The patient successfully underwent video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) of the right lower lobe without postoperative complications.

Histopathological examination revealed a predominantly lepidic growth pattern with mucin secretion; tumor cells had abundant apical cytoplasmic mucin and small, basally oriented nuclei; partial tumor exhibited an invasive pattern of infiltrative glands lined by tumor cells containing abundant intracytoplasmic mucin measuring less than 5 mm.
A focal area exhibited atypical goblet cell hyperplasia in the bronchial epithelium.
Immunohistochemical staining showed positive CK7, negative TTF-1, and no evidence of basal cell layer by CK5/6 staining.
Next-generation sequencing (NGS) identified the KRAS G12D mutation; no mutations were detected in EGFR, ALK, ROS-1, or TP53 genes.
The final pathological diagnosis was pulmonary minimally invasive mucinous adenocarcinoma, staged as pT1miN0M0.
The patient remained well 11 months after resection and did not require additional treatment.

source_metadata.title: Extrarenal Wilms tumor in the retroperitoneum of a 6-year-old girl: a case report and review of the literature

evidence_events.source_span: A 6-year-old white Iranian girl presented with acute abdominal pain and swelling in the left upper abdomen that had been noticed for the past 2 days.
Physical examination revealed a distended, firm, nontender, and immobile mass in the upper left abdomen. The mass was well defined and oval-shaped, and had smooth borders.
Routine laboratory tests, including a complete blood count, kidney and liver function tests, serum electrolytes, and urinalysis, were all within reference ranges.

Ultrasonography revealed a well-defined heterogeneous mass in the left upper abdomen, containing significant necrotic and cystic areas. The mass exhibited internal vascularity and measured 150 × 112 × 110 mm3, with no evidence of calcification.

An abdominopelvic computed tomography (CT) scan with intravenous contrast revealed a well-defined, large, heterogeneous enhancing mass on the left side of the abdomen. This mass exerted a mass effect on the adjacent pancreas (body and tail), spleen, and left kidney but was distinct from these organs.

The child underwent laparotomy, during which an encapsulated mass was identified on the left retroperitoneal side, distinct from the left kidney. The mass was removed and sent to the pathology department.

Macroscopic pathological examination revealed a round to oval, encapsulated, well-defined grey-brown rubbery mass covered by fibrofatty tissue, weighing 800 g and measuring 14.5 × 9 × 3.5 cm3, with solid cystic surface, variegated fibrotic bands, turbid yellowish fluid in cystic areas, and heterogeneous tan appearance with necrotic and hemorrhagic foci in solid parts.

Microscopic histopathologic examination revealed features consistent with Wilms tumor, including nests, cords, and tubules of epithelial cells surrounded by stromal spindle cells. No evidence of anaplasia or extension into surrounding fibrofatty tissue was observed. Immunohistochemical study showed negative inhibin and calretinin, but positive nuclear staining for WT1.
According to the National Wilms Tumor Study (NWTS) guidelines, this case was classified as stage II extrarenal Wilms tumor.
The patient underwent 19 weeks of chemotherapy including actinomycin-D and vincristine following surgery.
Post-treatment, the patient fully recovered with no abnormalities on end-of-treatment examinations and no signs of recurrence on monthly sonography follow-ups for 6 months.

evidence_events.source_span: A 47-year-old Brazilian woman with no significant past medical, surgical, or family history presented to the emergency room (ER) for evaluation of a fungating right arm mass.
Two days before the ER visit, the patient experienced profuse bleeding from the arm mass, which stopped when a towel was applied to the area.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: Two days before the ER visit

evidence_events.source_span: The patient’s right arm mass appeared approximately 2 years prior as a small pimple and grew over time, growing more rapidly in the preceding 3 months with intermittent fever and chills.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: 2 years prior; more rapidly in preceding 3 months

evidence_events.source_span: The mass was described as round in shape, friable, and ulcerating, with intermittent bleeding episodes. It was nontender and fixed in position.
The patient also reported losing a significant amount of weight during the same duration, but could not quantify it.

In the ER, physical examination revealed pale conjunctiva and a 10 × 12 cm fungating cauliflower-like mass on the right arm with friable, ulcerated skin and necrotic material, pustular and foul-smelling discharge, but no palpable lymphadenopathy or organomegaly.

Triage blood test results were significant for mild leukocytosis, low hemoglobin (4.2 g/dL), elevated reticulocytes, and elevated inflammatory markers; blood cultures and urinalysis were negative for acute infection.
X-ray of the right humerus showed a large hyperdense soft tissue mass in the distal right upper arm with no acute fractures or dislocation.

A computed tomography (CT) scan of the right upper extremity with contrast revealed a large heterogeneous soft tissue mass in the superficial aspect of the mid-upper arm extending into subcutaneous soft tissues with mild adjacent fat stranding but no muscle or bone involvement.
The patient underwent surgical resection of the mass (10 × 9 cm), and histopathology revealed a malignant melanoma with necrosis (nodular melanoma type).
Immunohistochemical staining of the mass cells was positive for Mart-A and S100.
CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis was negative for metastasis.
The patient was discharged with a follow-up plan involving oncology for ongoing management and surveillance.

source_metadata.title: Incidental floating aortic mass as the initial presentation of primary aortic sarcoma

evidence_events.source_span: A man in his 80s, former smoker with a history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidaemia and peripheral arterial disease in the lower limbs, was evaluated for a 3-month history of constitutional symptoms, including unintentional weight loss of approximately 8 kg and progressively worsening anorexia.
He also reported abdominal discomfort and persistent constipation unresponsive to a high-fibre diet and laxatives.
Blood tests revealed iron-deficiency anaemia with haemoglobin level of 120 g/L, a 20 g/L decrease from previous values.
Faecal occult blood testing was positive in two out of three samples.

CT scan revealed an irregular filling defect in the distal descending thoracic aorta measuring 56×18×2 cm, a 1.5 cm nodular filling defect in the superior mesenteric artery (SMA) with distal recanalisation, and a subcapsular splenic infarction measuring 35×16 mm.
No evidence of thoracic or abdominal aortic aneurysms, intestinal ischaemia, gastrointestinal lesions suggestive of malignancy, abdominal lymphadenopathy or hepatic space-occupying lesions was found.

Physical examination revealed tenderness on palpation in the left flank without signs of peritonitis; laboratory results showed haemoglobin 120 g/L, leucocytes 11×10⁹/L with 70% polymorphonuclear cells, CRP 4 mg/dL, and lactate 1 mmol/L.
Outpatient colonoscopy was postponed due to high procedural risk and low clinical suspicion of colorectal malignancy based on CT findings.

A floating thrombus secondary to plaque rupture was considered most likely; anticoagulation with low molecular weight heparin and high-potency statins was started; follow-up CT angiography 10 days later showed no change.

Atypical radiological features including polylobulated morphology, large size (>5 cm) in a high-flow area, absence of aneurysm, and lack of response to anticoagulation raised suspicion of a potential aortic tumour.
Biopsy was not performed due to lesion location and high embolisation risk; non-invasive imaging tests were conducted.
PET-CT revealed a polylobulated, septated, hypodense lesion in the descending thoracic aorta and SMA with no significant radiotracer uptake and low suspicion for high-grade malignancy.

Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) showed an endoluminal lesion occupying the thoracoabdominal aorta (57 mm) and SMA; dynamic contrast-enhanced sequences showed mild late-phase enhancement suggestive of neoplastic process but ultimately reported as non-enhancing and consistent with thrombus.

Comprehensive laboratory work-up including antinuclear antibodies, rheumatoid factor, serum complement, antiphospholipid antibodies, non-treponemal tests, and serum IgG4 levels were negative; no systemic symptoms of autoimmune or infectious disease were present; transthoracic echocardiogram showed preserved biventricular function and no intracardiac thrombus.

Despite inconclusive PET-CT and MRA results, high suspicion for vascular neoplasm remained; management included anticoagulation and planned elective aortic endoprosthesis placement to reduce embolic risk.

Six days after discharge, patient returned with worsening left abdominal pain; repeat CT angiography showed slight increase in size of aortic filling defect to 6.0 cm with polylobulated contours and septa; SMA filling defect unchanged; reduced perfusion in first jejunal branches and distended intestinal loops suggestive of intestinal ischaemia.

Elective open mesenteric thrombectomy was performed; postoperatively, patient developed acute arterial ischaemia in both lower limbs requiring urgent bilateral transpopliteal thrombectomy; whitish gelatinous embolic material was retrieved and sent for histopathological analysis.
Patient died 12 hours after procedure due to multiorgan failure from massive embolic release, 33 days after diagnostic process initiation.

Histopathological examination of embolic material revealed arterial wall tissue with marked cellularity, necrosis, frequent mitotic figures, and rhabdomyoblastic differentiation within a myxoid stroma, consistent with aortic intimal sarcoma.

At the time of the initial evaluation, blood tests were requested and revealed iron-deficiency anaemia, with a haemoglobin level of 120 g/L, representing a 20 g/L decrease from previous values. evidence_milestones.source_span: The CT scan revealed an irregular filling defect in the distal descending thoracic aorta, measuring 56×18×2 cm. Additionally, a 1.5 cm nodular filling defect was noted in the superior mesenteric artery (SMA), with distal recanalisation and a subcapsular splenic infarction measuring 35×16 mm. Given the presence of extensive and significant aortic atherosclerotic disease, these findings were initially interpreted as atherosclerotic thrombi. Notably, there was no evidence of thoracic or abdominal aortic aneurysms, signs of intestinal ischaemia, gastrointestinal lesions suggestive of malignancy, abdominal lymphadenopathy or hepatic space-occupying lesions. On re-evaluation, the patient reported a 1-week history of postprandial abdominal pain localised to the left flank, suggestive of mesenteric angina. Physical examination revealed tenderness on palpation in the affected area, without signs of peritonitis. Laboratory results showed haemoglobin at 120 g/dL, leucocytes at 11×10⁹/L with 70% polymorphonuclear cells, C-reactive protein at 4 mg/dL and lactate at 1 mmol/L. The outpatient colonoscopy was postponed due to the high procedural risk associated with the aortic lesion and the low clinical suspicion of colorectal malignancy, as the abdominal CT showed no gastrointestinal lesions or abdominopelvic lymphadenopathy. The case was discussed with the on-call vascular surgery team, and a floating thrombus—presumed secondary to plaque rupture—was considered the most likely diagnosis. Anticoagulation with low molecular weight heparin at a dose of 1 mg/kg twice daily, along with high-potency statins and radiological monitoring, was recommended. A follow-up CT angiography performed 10 days later showed no changes from the previous imaging.

evidence_milestones.source_span: The polylobulated morphology, its considerable size (>5 cm) within a high-flow region (descending thoracic aorta), absence of an associated aneurysm and lack of response to anticoagulation raised suspicion of a potential aortic tumour. A biopsy was not performed due to the lesion's location and the high risk of embolisation associated with invasive manipulation. A positron emission tomography (PET) with 18-fluorine-fluorodeoxyglucose (18F-FDG) combined with CT (PET-CT) was initially performed. The PET-CT revealed a polylobulated, septated, hypodense lesion within the descending thoracic aorta and at the origin of the SMA, with no significant radiotracer uptake and low suspicion for high-grade malignancy. Magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) of the aorta with gadolinium was also performed. The MRA revealed an endoluminal lesion occupying the thoracoabdominal aorta (57 mm) and another in the SMA. On dynamic contrast-enhanced sequences (DCE-MRA), mild enhancement was observed during the late phase of the lesion's enhancement curve in comparison with the aortic lumen, a feature that could be suggestive of a neoplastic process. However, due to the minimal degree of enhancement, the lesion was ultimately reported as non-enhancing and considered more consistent with thrombus. Additionally, a comprehensive laboratory work-up was conducted to investigate non-tumorous aetiologies. All tests showed negative results, including antinuclear antibodies, rheumatoid factor, serum complement levels (C3 and C4), antiphospholipid antibody profile, non-treponemal tests (Rapid Plasma Reagin (RPR) and Venereal Disease Research Laboratory (VDRL)) and serum IgG4 levels. The absence of systemic symptoms suggestive of autoimmune disease or features of IgG4-related disease, combined with no signs of infection, no history of high-risk sexual exposure and entirely negative laboratory results, made an autoimmune or infectious aetiology highly unlikely. A transthoracic echocardiogram was also performed, which demonstrated preserved biventricular function and no evidence of intracardiac thrombus, thereby excluding a cardiac source of embolism.

evidence_milestones.source_span: The patient returned to the emergency department 6 days later with worsening pain in the left side of the abdomen. A repeat CT angiography revealed a slight increase in the size of the filling defect in the distal thoracic aorta, now measuring 6.0 cm with polylobulated contours and septa. The known filling defect in the SMA remained unchanged; however, reduced perfusion was observed in the first jejunal branches, along with distended intestinal loops with contrast enhancement, raising concern for intestinal ischaemia. The patient was admitted to vascular surgery, where an elective open mesenteric thrombectomy was performed within 24 hours, alongside intravenous unfractionated heparin infusion. Postoperatively, the patient developed acute arterial ischaemia in both lower limbs requiring urgent bilateral transpopliteal thrombectomy. Embolic material was retrieved and sent for histopathological analysis. The patient died 12 hours after the procedure due to multiorgan failure secondary to massive embolic release.

source_metadata.title: Radiation Retinopathy: Case report and review

evidence_events.source_span: A 55 year old male was referred from the oncology department with epiphora. His medical history included type 2, Insulin treated, Diabetes Mellitus of 10-years duration and controlled hypertension.
One year prior to presentation he had undergone a total rhinectomy with a 4 week course of post-operative radiotherapy for an aggressive sqaumous cell carcinoma of the nose.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: total rhinectomy with a 4 week course of post-operative radiotherapy

evidence_events.source_span: He received a total of 5250 rad (52.5 gray) to the tumour (1312.5 rad/13.12 gray per week, 262.5 rad/2.62 gray per session).
He underwent diabetic eye screening through his optometrist and a diabetic retinal check in April 2005 was recorded as showing no diabetic eye disease.

On examination the visual acuity was noted to be 6/36 left eye and 6/9 right eye. He had bilateral medial lower lid ectropion accounting for the epiphora. Anterior segment examination and intraocular pressures were normal.
Posterior segment examination revealed marked retinal ischaemia present in the posterior pole and macular region of both eyes.
Fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) confirmed an ischaemic retina. There were no signs of neovascularization.

The distribution of the retinal changes with severe ischaemic changes in the posterior retina more than in the anterior retina, the relative lack of microaneurysms compared to the high numbers of cotton wool spots and blot haemorrhages and the rapid nature in which the retinopathy developed made the diagnosis of radiation retinopathy likely.
The temporal onset of the retinopathy in relation to the radiotherapy (1 year post treatment) and the dose delivered further supported this diagnosis.
Over the next four months the vision in both eyes rapidly deteriorated to 3/60 left eye and 1/60 right eye. Clinical examination revealed bilateral vitreous haemorrhage.
FFA confirmed bilateral disc neovascularisation and evidence of a grossly ischaemic retina with little residual viable retina.
Bilateral pan retinal photocoagulation was considered to be appropriate treatment at this stage.
At review in September 2006 the visual acuities were counting fingers in the RE and 6/60 aided in the LE. The retinopathy is stable.

source_metadata.title: Multiple inflammatory nodules: a differential diagnosis of new pulmonary nodules in oncology patients

evidence_events.source_span: A 70-year-old male shipyard worker with exposure to asbestos and lead, and a childhood history of polio, was being followed up for unclassified dermal sarcoma of upper back, which was resected with negative margins.
A baseline staging computed tomography (CT) scan was unremarkable.
A routine follow-up CT scan after 6 months showed multiple (approximately 20 in number) new nodules up to 2 cm in size, scattered in both lungs with a lower lobar predominance.

An enhancing soft tissue nodule measuring 2 cm in size was seen at the right T4–5 intervertebral foramen with erosion of the adjacent lamina and pedicle, protruding into the spinal canal without significant mass effect on the spinal cord.
There was no associated lymphadenopathy in chest or abdomen. The patient remained asymptomatic during this period, and inflammatory markers such as C-reactive protein were normal.
A thoracoscopic wedge excision of two peripheral lung nodules from different lobes was performed.
On microscopy, an admixture of lymphocytes, plasma cells and eosinophils were seen in the affected lung tissue with focal areas of fibrosis in areas of inflamed lung.
Gram, fungal and acid fast stains were negative for microorganisms.

The possibility of inflammatory pseudotumor was considered on the initial pathology report, but a final pathologic diagnosis of chronic pneumonitis was given due to absence of abundant myofibroblasts.

In view of multiple nodules scattered throughout both lungs and the concomitant presence of a mass at the intervertebral foramen, the final clinical and radiological impression was that of an inflammatory process resembling an inflammatory pseudotumor.
No treatment was offered, and follow-up CT performed after 18 months showed resolution of the lung nodules and the intervertebral foramen lesion, leaving behind only a persistent bony defect.

source_metadata.title: Small invasive colon cancer with systemic metastasis: A case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 35-year-old woman presented at the referring hospital with swelling of the left cervical lymph node.
Biopsy of the lymph node revealed metastatic adenocarcinoma; however, CT scan and mammography were unable to identify the site of the primary lesion.

Immunohistochemical reevaluation showed the cervical lymph node biopsy specimen to be positive for CDX2 and CK20 and negative for CK7 expression, leading us to suspect the presence of a primary colorectal cancer.

We performed a total colonoscopy, and detected a small protruding lesion in the transverse colon. The tumour was only 12 mm in diameter, with a central depressed component and a severely thickened stalk, which suggested direct cancer invasion of the deep submucosa.
Diagnostic endoscopic mucosal resection was performed. The lesion was found to have an intramucosal cancer component, demonstrating that this lesion represented primary colon cancer.

The tumour was composed of poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma and signet-ring cell carcinoma, infiltrated deeply into the submucosal layer, with severe lymphatic and venous invasion. IHC showed strong MUC5AC expression, weak MUC2 and CDX2 expression, and positivity for CK20 and slight positivity for CK7.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: pathological and IHC examination of EMR specimen

evidence_events.source_span: The patient underwent systemic chemotherapy with capecitabine plus oxaliplatin and bevacizumab, showing initial tumor volume reduction, but later progression with increased tumor markers and peritoneal metastasis.
Genomic analysis revealed KRAS wild type; second-line chemotherapy with cetuximab plus irinotecan was started, resulting in significant tumor marker decrease.
The patient declined MSI testing despite being 35 years old, prioritizing chemotherapy.

evidence_events.source_span: A 42-year-old patient was admitted for a 1-year history of left scrotal swelling, recently complicated by local hyperemia and pain.
The patient had a history of cryptorchidism for which he had surgery in childhood.
Clinical examination was non-specific except for a 6/15 cm, hard, intensely painful on palpation, left testicular tumor with inflamed adjacent tissues.

Basic blood work showed further signs of inflammation with a white cell count of 16500/dl, a high sedimentation rate (74mm/h) and a fibrinogen level of 1084mg/dl. The patient’s alkaline phosphatase had values of 937UI/l.

Structural modifications of the left testis revealed by ultrasonography along with clinical and paraclinical data were characteristic for testicular malignancy. There were no regional adenopathies present on ultrasound examination.
We decided to perform a left orchiectomy that had no intra or postoperative complications.
Histopathologic examination showed cribriform and pseudoglandular pattern seminoma, with T2N0 stage stadialization.
Postoperatively, the patient evolved uneventfully both locally and generally and was referred to an oncology department for further treatment.

diagnostic_reasoning_verbatim_spans: A 42-year-old patient was admitted for a 1-year history of left scrotal swelling, recently complicated by local hyperemia and pain.
The patient had a history of cryptorchidism for which he had surgery in childhood.
Clinical examination was non-specific except for a 6/15 cm, hard, intensely painful on palpation, left testicular tumor with inflamed adjacent tissues.

Basic blood work showed further signs of inflammation with a white cell count of 16500/dl, a high sedimentation rate (74mm/h) and a fibrinogen level of 1084mg/dl. The patient’s alkaline phosphatase had values of 937UI/l.

Structural modifications of the left testis revealed by ultrasonography along with clinical and paraclinical data were characteristic for testicular malignancy. There were no regional adenopathies present on ultrasound examination.
Histopathologic examination showed cribriform and pseudoglandular pattern seminoma, with T2N0 stage stadialization.
diagnostic_reasoning_items: The patient's prolonged scrotal swelling with recent inflammation and pain raised suspicion for a testicular mass.
History of cryptorchidism is a known risk factor for testicular germ cell tumors.
Physical exam revealed a large, hard, painful testicular mass with local inflammation.
Inflammatory markers and elevated alkaline phosphatase supported an active pathological process.
Ultrasound findings were consistent with a testicular malignancy without nodal spread.
Histopathology confirmed seminoma with local tumor stage T2N0, establishing the diagnosis.
hidden_reference.final_diagnosis: Seminoma of the left testis, stage T2N0
hidden_reference.diagnostic_reasoning: The clinical presentation of prolonged scrotal swelling with recent pain and inflammation, combined with a history of cryptorchidism, physical exam findings of a large painful testicular mass, inflammatory blood markers, and ultrasound evidence of testicular structural abnormalities without lymphadenopathy, led to surgical orchiectomy. Histopathology confirmed the diagnosis of seminoma with T2N0 staging, confirming localized testicular cancer.
hidden_reference.article_derived_evidence_summary: The case describes a 42-year-old man with a 1-year history of left scrotal swelling complicated by pain and redness, a history of cryptorchidism, physical exam showing a large painful testicular mass, inflammatory labs, ultrasound consistent with malignancy, orchiectomy performed, and histopathology confirming seminoma T2N0.

source_metadata.title: Case report: Xanthogranulomutous pyelonephritis presenting as “Wilms’ tumor”

evidence_events.source_span: 3 years old boy presented with history of recurrent fever, episodes of painful urination, increased frequency and haematuria for one year
He had been treated with several courses of antibiotics for urinary tract infections with temporary relief of symptoms before recurrence
On examination; the child was febrile with body temperature of 38.8 °C with tenderness on the left lumbar region and had a palpable mass on the same side

Laboratory investigations performed are summarised in Table 1 including leukocytosis (12700/μl), anemia (hemoglobin 6.17 g/dl), and urine analysis showing leukocytes 20/hpf, nitrites 1+, protein 2++, pH 6.8
Repeat abdominal ultrasound showed a left renal mass 7.4X7.1X5 cm with multiple cystic lesions, destroyed renal pelvis with calcific changes, no extension to neighboring structures

Abdominal CT scan showed enlarged left kidney with thinning cortices, loss of corticomedullary differentiation, foci of calcifications, renal parenchyma replaced with multiple septations, peripheral enhancement surrounding non-enhancing cystic foci, no filling defect in renal vein or IVC
Clinical diagnosis of Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis was made and patient underwent left radical nephrectomy

Intra-operatively an enlarged yellowish grey left kidney with multiple mesenteric and hilar lymph nodes was seen; radical left nephroureterectomy and hilar lymph node resection performed; right kidney normal on inspection
evidence_events.procedural_cue: radical left nephroureterectomy and hilar lymph node resection

evidence_events.source_span: Resected tissues sent for culture and sensitivity but no bacterial growth after 7 days

Histological studies showed renal histology infiltrated with foamy lipid laden macrophages in a mixture of chronic inflammatory cells and fibrosis confirming diagnosis of Xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis
Patient faired well postoperatively and was kept on 7 days intravenous Tazobactam/piperacillin and discharged home 10 days post nephrectomy
