evidence_events.source_span: A 70-year-old male first presented with refractory facial paralysis (House Brackmann VI) on the right side for 2 months with no improvement after intravenous cortisone, ceftriaxone and valacyclovir therapy.
Previous medical history included canal wall down tympanoplasty of the right ear in 1966 due to cholesteatoma; no hearing change, vertigo or tinnitus were reported.
Clinical examination showed normal otoscopic findings; audiogram revealed severe combined hearing loss with a 15 dB conductive component on the right side, left side normal.

Laboratory examination was unremarkable including serology for Lyme's disease and varicella zoster virus; ultrasound of the parotid gland was normal; metabolic disorders such as diabetes were excluded; routine ophthalmologic exam was normal.
Facial nerve electromyogram performed 3 months after symptom onset showed no signs of degeneration or reinnervation.

MRI scan suggested recurrent cholesteatoma on the right side; facial nerve showed contrast enhancement and thickening proximal to the geniculate ganglion up to peripheral nerve endings; neuritis was assumed; no tumors detected.

Surgical exploration of the right mastoid removed a small cholesteatoma; bony facial canal was intact with no contact to the facial nerve; this was not regarded as cause of FNP; facial nerve decompression was not performed.

One year after symptom onset, patient developed new hypesthesia in right trigeminal nerve territory (V2 + V3) and swallowing problems with impaired gag reflex; contrast swallow showed upper esophageal sphincter insufficiency; glossopharyngeal nerve affection suspected; aspiration led to placement of percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy tube.

Main stem of the facial nerve was resected after discussion with the patient.

Histology of the facial nerve showed infiltration by squamous cell carcinoma growing in minute nests and cords reminiscent of microcystic adnexal carcinoma (MAC) but with pure squamoid differentiation.
18-Fluoro-deoxyglucose-PET-CT showed no new focus, signs of metastases or any other primary tumor.
Radiochemotherapy was started with a total dose of 66.6 Gy and chemotherapy with Cisplatin (CDDP).

source_metadata.title: An uncommon cause of gastric outlet obstruction

evidence_events.source_span: A 73-year-old male presents with a 5-week history of nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain.

Past medical history is significant for stage IV transitional cell cancer with angiolymphatic invasion treated with neo-adjuvant chemotherapy and radiation followed by radical cystectomy with ileal conduit formation and bilateral pelvic lymphadenectomy.
He had also undergone a diverting sigmoid colostomy for rectal outlet obstructive symptoms from metastases to the rectum.
Subsequent surveillance imaging and colonoscopies were negative for any recurrence as recent as nine months prior to the current symptoms.

CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed new circumferential thickening and inflammatory stranding involving the ascending colon extending to the hepatic flexure as well as the descending/transverse duodenal junction with adjacent inflammatory stranding.
Diffuse intra- and extra-hepatic biliary ductal and main pancreatic duct dilatation (double duct sign) was noted as well. Transaminases and bilirubin were initially normal.

MRI of the abdomen was pursued to further investigate the double duct sign, which did not reveal choledocholithiasis or pancreaticobiliary malignancy. The dilated biliary tree was suspected to be secondary to thickened descending duodenum. This thickening was abutting the hepatic flexure. Additional findings included hydroureteronephrosis on the right with a focally enhancing soft tissue mass.
Upper endoscopy for evaluation of gastric outlet obstruction demonstrated duodenal stenosis with significant edema and congestion without an obvious ulcer.
The stenosis could be traversed only with an ultrathin endoscope but biopsies were nondiagnostic.
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: biopsies nondiagnostic

evidence_events.source_span: Colonoscopy demonstrated a mass at the hepatic flexure.
Biopsies confirmed invasive transitional cell cancer.
Patient underwent a Wall Flex (22 mm × 120 mm) metal stent to help alleviate the gastric outlet obstruction.
Chemotherapy was planned by oncology.
Patient had progressively deteriorated and expired one month later after establishing an agreement on comfort care only.

evidence_events.source_span: An 83-year-old white woman presented to her general practitioner initially with 1 month of nasal obstruction, intermittent epistaxis, and anosmia.

On examination, her vital signs were within normal range and the rest of the physical and neurological examinations were normal. A nasal speculum examination found a large tissue growth in her left nasal cavity.
A subsequent computed tomography (CT) scan revealed a large soft tissue mass opacifying the left maxillary, ethmoidal, frontal, and sphenoid sinuses with no intracranial extension.
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: CT scan showed large soft tissue mass in left sinonasal sinuses without intracranial extension.

evidence_events.source_span: Laboratory findings including a full blood count, renal function, and liver function were unremarkable.
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: Routine labs normal, no systemic abnormalities.

evidence_events.source_span: She underwent a debulking surgery.
On frozen section the provisional diagnosis was a poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma based on evidence of squamous differentiation among poorly differentiated cells.
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: Initial frozen section suggested poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma.

evidence_events.source_span: After processing and examination of the whole lesion it was appreciated that the tumor had both mature and immature components from more than one germ cell line.
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: Histopathology revealed mature and immature components from multiple germ cell lines, diagnostic of sinonasal teratocarcinosarcoma.

evidence_events.source_span: A postoperative positron emission tomography (PET) scan revealed some ongoing soft tissue thickening in her left nasal cavity and her maxillary, ethmoid, and frontal sinuses with no evidence of distal fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG)-avid disease.
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: Postoperative PET showed residual soft tissue thickening without distant FDG-avid disease.

evidence_events.source_span: She received postoperative intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT) 60 Gy in 30 fractions to her sinuses.
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: Postoperative radiotherapy administered to residual disease.

evidence_events.source_span: A repeat PET scan 6 months post-completion of radiotherapy showed no evidence of FDG-avid disease in her left maxillary sinus or nasal region.
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: Post-radiotherapy PET showed no FDG-avid disease, indicating significant tumor resolution.

evidence_events.source_span: She had no evidence of local recurrence on nasal endoscopic examination at her 2-year follow-up.
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: No local recurrence detected at 2 years post-treatment.

evidence_events.source_span: A 25-year-old primigravida woman presented for her initial prenatal visit at ten weeks and three days gestation with a past medical history of chronic hypertension, hidradenitis suppurativa, and morbid obesity.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: initial prenatal visit at ten weeks and three days gestation

evidence_events.source_span: Previously, she had been treated for a urinary tract infection at six-weeks gestation, following a urinalysis done in the emergency department, which revealed moderate numbers of red blood cells and a positive leukocyte esterase test.

At the 18-week antenatal visit, the patient was again noted to have moderate numbers of red blood cells by urine dipstick analysis and was again treated for a urinary tract infection and urine culture was also obtained.

At her 27-week antenatal visit, a three-hour oral glucose tolerance test supported a diagnosis of gestational diabetes. At this time, she complained of dysuria and her urine dipstick analysis again demonstrated the presence of red blood cells. A urine sample was sent for culture, which resulted in a mixed bacterial flora.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: oral glucose tolerance test, urine dipstick, urine culture

evidence_events.source_span: At her 33-week antenatal visit, the patient continued to demonstrate blood in her urine. A plan was discussed for a urology consultation in the post-partum period, to evaluate the reason for the microscopic hematuria and recurrent urinary tract infections.
A third-trimester ultrasound was notable for an estimated fetal weight (EFW) of 79%, and a fetal abdominal circumference of 90%. No vaginal masses were seen on ultrasound.

At 38-weeks and four days gestation, the patient was noted to have a large semi-solid anterior vaginal wall mass that was felt to be separate from the urethra. A transvaginal ultrasound was performed which documented a solid septated mass distending the anterior vaginal wall and distorting the endocervical canal. The mass was 5×5×4.2 cm, the rim of the mass was vascular, and the mass was septated.

After consultation with the Gynecologic Oncology team and review of the images, delivery via cesarean section with core needle biopsy of the vaginal mass in the operating room immediately after the cesarean delivery was recommended.

Following an uncomplicated cesarean delivery and with the patient still under spinal anesthesia, the anterior vaginal mass was examined and found to contain 200 ml of purulent material. Because a diagnosis of urethral diverticulum was made, a biopsy was not performed. The patient was placed on antibiotic prophylaxis for the remainder of her hospital course.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: vaginal mass examined, purulent fluid drained, biopsy not performed, antibiotic prophylaxis started

evidence_events.source_span: Follow-up CT scan confirmed a large urethral diverticulum.
She was referred to the Female Pelvic Medicine and Reconstructive Surgery and Urogynecology units for definitive treatment, following MRI for further assessment of the urethral diverticular mass.

source_metadata.title: Recurrent chylothorax: a clinical mystery

evidence_events.source_span: A 50-year-old Caucasian woman presented to the emergency department with right-sided pleuritic chest that began 1 day prior. She had noted progressive dyspnoea for the past month.

Her medical history was significant for WM, discovered 3 years ago. She was found to have low-grade B-cell non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma, most consistent with lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma, with 20%–30% bone marrow involvement and elevated serum IgM kappa levels.
Physical examination revealed palpable adenopathy in bilateral anterior cervical as well as the left supraclavicular region. Lung examination revealed absent breath sounds in the right lower lobe.

Initial laboratory studies revealed total white cell count 5.8 x10^9, mild lymphopaenia 1.0 bil/L, anaemia with Hb 10.2 g/dL, normal renal function along with a low anion gap and low albumin. Serum protein electrophoresis revealed IgM kappa monoclonal protein with a total IgM level of 82 mg/dL.

Initial chest X-ray demonstrated a right pleural effusion. A CT chest showed a large right-sided pleural effusion with compressive atelectasis and slight mediastinal shift to the left. Additionally, it demonstrated adenopathy in the lower neck and upper thorax, increased in size compared with CT from 3 years ago. Lymphadenopathy was also noted at the thoracic duct near the confluence of the left subclavian and left internal jugular veins.

Thoracentesis removed 1.4 L of milky fluid. Pleural fluid analysis showed total white cell count 13,140/mcL, red blood cell count 4000/mcL, 75% neutrophils, 22% lymphocytes, and monocytes 3%. Pleural fluid triglycerides were elevated at 319 mg/dL consistent with chylothorax.

Flow cytometry of pleural fluid showed 3% monotypic B cells expressing CD19, CD20, CD45 and kappa light chain but negative for CD5 and CD10. T cells were 36% with a CD4:CD8 ratio of 4.8:1 and normal CD5 expression. Cytology revealed moderately cellular effusion with abundant small lymphocytes mixed with reactive mesothelial cells, consistent with B-cell lymphoma.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: pleural fluid flow cytometry and cytology

evidence_events.source_span: Repeat thoracentesis with pigtail catheter placement was required due to re-accumulation of pleural fluid. Repeat fluid analysis showed decreasing triglycerides to 94 mg/dL and negative cultures.

Repeat bone marrow biopsy 1 month later demonstrated hypercellular marrow with 90% infiltrate of small-to-intermediate lymphocytes and plasma cells. Flow cytometry showed B cells positive for CD19, CD20, CD23 and surface immunoglobulin kappa consistent with extensive infiltration by B-cell lymphoma.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: bone marrow biopsy and flow cytometry

evidence_events.source_span: The patient was started on ibrutinib 420 mg every night. Her pleural effusion resolved within 2 months and she did not need any further thoracentesis.

source_metadata.title: Primary cutaneous anaplastic large-cell lymphoma: A case report
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case report narrative and figures in PMC5794364

evidence_events.source_span: A 73-year-old man was admitted because of a skin tumor in the right parotideomasseteric region; 6 months earlier, well-defined skin redness of 10 × 15 mm was noted in the same area.

Blood tests showed high levels of antimitochondrial and anti-nuclear antibodies; immunofluorescence of tissue revealed IgG and IgM deposits on the cutaneous epidermis, leading to diagnosis of discoid lupus erythematosus and treatment with Arechin.
Four months after treatment onset, significant disease progression and dynamic tumor growth were observed.
On admission, a well-demarcated exophytic skin tumor with irregular surface measuring 50 × 70 mm without ulceration was observed in the right parotideomasseteric region.
Histopathological examination of biopsy indicated pilomatrix carcinoma (trichilemmal carcinoma).

Due to discrepancy between clinical features and histopathology, biopsy material was re-examined at another facility, revealing lymphoma infiltration by anaplastic large cells in dermis and subcutaneous tissue with immunohistochemistry: LCA+, CD30+, ALK-, CD3+ (weak), CD5-, CKAE1/3-, MELAN A-, S100-, Ki67+++ (~90%).
Trepanobiopsy of bone marrow showed no lymphoma infiltration.
Computed tomography (CT) scans of chest, abdominal cavity, neck, and nasopharynx confirmed absence of lymphoma foci in other organs.
Definitive diagnosis of primary cutaneous anaplastic large-cell lymphoma (C-ALCL) was established.
Patient underwent 4 cycles of chemotherapy (vincristine, doxorubicin, endoxan, Dexaven, Zofran) with blood monitoring.
Gradual tumor regression was observed during chemotherapy; complete remission was achieved 1 year after first cycle.
At 5 years after treatment, no recurrence of lymphoma was observed.

source_metadata.title: Lymphnode tuberculosis in a 4-year-old boy with relapsed ganglioneuroblastoma: a case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 4-year-old German boy with stage 4 ganglioneuroblastoma was treated with chemotherapy, metaiodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) therapy, autologous HSCT and irradiation according to the German Pediatric Oncology Group Neuroblastoma High risk 2004 protocol.

18 months after initial diagnosis, relapse with new paravertebral lesions was detected by MRI and MIBG scintigraphy. In addition, new lesions in the left lower lobe of the lung and in the perihilar lymphnodes suspicious of metastases of the ganglioneuroblastoma were detected by MRI but did not present in MIBG scintigraphy.
Biopsy of the paravertebral tumor was performed and the suspicious perihilar lymphnodes were resected.

While relapse in the tumor was confirmed, pathologic examination revealed granulomatous lymphadenitis with epithelioid appearance and Langhans-type multinucleated giant cells suspicious of flourishing lymphnode tuberculosis instead of metastases of the ganglioneuroblastoma. The captured granulomatous lymphadenitis was noncaseating.
An interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) yielded positive, whereas polymerase chain reaction (PCR) and cultures could not detect any mycobacteria.

Diagnosis of peripheral lymphnode tuberculosis was made based on histomorphology and IGRA. Notably, no history of tuberculosis exposure could be identified. The boy did not suffer from fever, weight loss or night sweats. He was not vaccinated with BCG.

The patient underwent 2 months of triple therapy with pyrazinamide, rifampin and isoniazid and 3 months of rifampin and isoniazid treatment. For neuroblastoma relapse, chemotherapeutical treatment according to the RIST-relapsed Neuroblastoma-2011 protocol was administered.

Three months after initiating the antituberculostatic treatment and relapse chemotherapy, MRI showed a partial remission of the paravertebral lesions and a nearly complete remission of the lesions in the lung and lymphnodes.
The patient underwent a second MiBG therapy and haploidentical stem cell transplantation. Actually, he is undergoing anti-gd2 antibody therapy.

source_metadata.title: Infant with a skin lesion and respiratory distress
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from BMJ Case Reports 2018 article, case report section 'Description'.

evidence_events.source_span: A 2-month-old full-term male infant presented with worsening tachypnoea and a rapidly enlarging, smooth-topped, infiltrative, bronze-yellow nodule with overlying telangiectasias on the mid-sternum
CT imaging demonstrated multiple pulmonary nodules, and enhancing extradural masses compressing the L4–L5 vertebral neural foramina

Immunohistochemical staining of biopsies from skin and pulmonary lesions demonstrated a highly proliferative histiocytosis, which was positively immunoreactive for ALK (anaplastic lymphoma kinase), CD33 and factor XIIIa, weakly positive for CD68, and negative for CD1a, Langerin, CD34, CD20, CD3, CD43, SOX10, S100, C-KIT, lysozyme and myeloperoxidase
These findings were consistent with a diagnosis of ALK+ histiocytosis with pathological features of juvenile xanthogranulomatosis (JXG)

Whole body MRI and positron emission tomography (PET)/CT imaging confirmed that the extensive pulmonary and compressing spinal cord lesions were fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG)-avid, and further revealed an additional, metabolically active right meningeal/parietal parenchymal brain tumour and extensive mediastinal/abdominal lymphadenopathy
evidence_events.procedural_cue: Whole body MRI and PET/CT imaging

evidence_events.source_span: Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) and DNA mutation sequencing of the histiocytomas revealed a translocated KIF5B-ALK fusion rearrangement

Given the known aggressive nature of ALK mutations in other neoplastic disorders and the presence of systemic and CNS disease in this patient, chemotherapy was initiated with the purine analogue cladribine (2-CDA)
Follow-up PET imaging after six cycles of 2-CDA therapy demonstrated a near-complete resolution of all FDG-avid lesions

The patient was subsequently started on low-dose daily 6-mercaptupurine and weekly methotrexate maintenance chemotherapy, and currently remains in remission of disease on follow-up radiological imaging

source_metadata.title: Case report: Diffuse hyperplastic perilobar nephroblastomatosis complicated by a unilateral Wilms tumour: diagnosis, treatment and follow-up

evidence_events.source_span: A 9-month-old female presented with a 2-month history of abdominal distension and weight loss.

The patient underwent an uncomplicated birth following an unremarkable pregnancy at 39-weeks gestational age via elective caesarean section. The toddler attained normal developmental milestones aside from the inability to roll prone from supine. Initially at the 70th percentile at birth for weight, she presented at the 30th percentile with stable height and head circumference (50th percentile). The patient did not exhibit any clinical features of Beckwith Wiedemann Syndrome including omphalocele, macroglossia and macrosomia.
There is no consanguinity, no family history of recurrent malignancies, haematological or renal conditions.

Initial limited ultrasonographic study of the abdomen demonstrated massively enlarged kidneys with loss of corticomedullary differentiation. The right kidney measured 13.1 cm and the left measured 15 cm (normal approximately 6 cm). Multiple ill-defined hypoechoic areas were seen randomly interspersed within the renal parenchyma bilaterally suggesting presence of nephrogenic rests and therefore nephroblastomatosis. It was not possible to rule out the presence of Wilms tumour within the nephrogenic rests on ultrasound. No evidence of hydronephrosis, hydroureter or free fluid was seen.

Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis with IV and oral contrast demonstrated homogenous, diffuse, renal enlargement and loss of normal architecture with renal parenchyma replaced by homogenous low attenuating peripheral masses bilaterally. There were two ill-defined hypodense areas in the medial aspect of the left kidney concerning for malignancy. Residual normal renal parenchyma was present as areas of striate enhancement, hyperdense in comparison to the thick rind of peripheral nodules. Based on clinical presentation and CT findings, the patient was diagnosed with bilateral DHPLNB.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV and oral contrast

evidence_events.source_span: Gadolinium enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the abdomen performed after 6 weeks of chemotherapy demonstrated hypointense peripheral masses on T1/T2 images with thick septations suggestive of bilateral DHPLNB. A small heterogeneously enhancing lesion with multiple small linear and round cysts in the medial left kidney was characterized on T1 imaging, suspicious for a superimposed Wilms tumor.
No metastases were seen on CT chest with contrast.
Pathology after left partial nephrectomy confirmed Wilms tumor.
Cytogenetic analysis was conducted revealing a normal female karyotype (46XX). No other tumour markers or genetic testing was performed.

source_metadata.title: A snotty nose: more than just a cold

evidence_events.source_span: A healthy 3-year-old girl presented with a 5-day history of right-sided cheek and eye swelling and pain, associated with right-sided green nasal discharge.
Examination revealed diffuse erythematous swelling around the right cheek, jawline and eye.
Oral antibiotics for suspected periorbital cellulitis were ineffective.
Blood inflammatory markers and ultrasound of her neck and parotid glands were normal.
She was discharged as having viral parotitis.

Antibiotics and nasal drops were later restarted for clinical sinusitis; however, she showed no improvement, now having 3 weeks of right-sided facial swelling with thick green and intermittently bloody nasal discharge.
Further history revealed possible squint, mastication pain and breathing difficulty through the right nostril.

Cranial imaging demonstrated a large central but predominantly right-sided nasopharyngeal tumour, extending into the ethmoid sinuses and orbits (with medial recti distortion), infratemporal fossa and pterygoid muscles and anterior and middle cranial fossae. There was accompanying skull base destruction.
Staging and biopsy confirmed the diagnosis of non-metastatic parameningeal rhabdomyosarcoma (PM-RMS).
Chemoradiotherapy ensued.

source_metadata.title: Paraneoplastic syndrome as the presentation of limited stage small cell carcinoma

evidence_events.source_span: A 64 year-old caucasian male presented with a chief complaint of nausea and vomiting for 3 days. He denied pulmonary symptoms, fevers, night sweats, or weight loss. Physical examination revealed mild right upper lung field end-expiratory wheezing and euvolemia.
Initial blood laboratories showed hyponatremia with sodium 110, low serum osmolality 227, and high urine osmolality 579.
Chest radiography was performed and read as no evidence of acute cardiopulmonary disease.
Treatment with fluid restriction led to normalization of sodium and resolution of nausea and vomiting.

Due to suspicion of SIADH from malignancy, a CT chest was performed which showed a conglomeration of nodules and opacities measuring 3.0 × 1.9 cm in the inferior segment of the right upper lobe with ipsilateral mediastinal lymphadenopathy.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: after initial labs and chest radiograph

evidence_events.source_span: CT-guided percutaneous biopsy was performed; specimen stained positive for CK, CD56, NSE, BcL2, Synaptophysin, PAX-5, and TTF-1, but negative for Chromogranin, CD57, and NFP; consistent with small cell carcinoma.
Further metastatic workup including CT abdomen and pelvis and brain MRI showed no evidence of metastasis.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: CT abdomen and pelvis, brain MRI

evidence_events.source_span: Whole-body PET scan revealed uptake in one ipsilateral mediastinal lymph node as the only site of metastasis, classifying the patient as limited stage small cell lung cancer (LS-SCLC).
Patient received three rounds of chemotherapy, chest and prophylactic cranial radiation, and was deemed in remission by oncology at 4 months follow-up.

source_metadata.title: Exogenous estrogen therapy, testicular cancer, and the male to female transgender population: a case report

evidence_events.source_span: A previously healthy 38-year-old Caucasian male to female transgender patient was placed on hormonal therapy for 15 months with estradiol 2 spironolactone while awaiting gender re-assignment surgery.
In early 2016, she developed progressive right-sided scrotal swelling, abdominal and back pain, fatigue, and weight loss of 7 kg.
A clinical examination revealed a right-sided testicular mass and palpable adenopathy in the left supraclavicular fossa but no palpable axillary or inguinal adenopathy.

A computed tomography scan of her abdomen/pelvis identified a right groin lesion measuring 6.4 × 4.9 × 6.3 cm, a retroperitoneal mass (11.5 × 10.6 × 17.4 cm) causing right-sided hydronephrosis, extensive deep vein thrombosis involving the common iliac and femoral vessels, and pathologically enlarged lymph nodes in the celiac axis, retrocrural space, and external iliac chains.

Laboratory investigations revealed hemoglobin 103 g/l, white blood cells 10.9 × 10⁹/L, platelets 446 × 10⁹/L, sodium 130 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/l, creatinine 127 umol/L, lactate dehydrogenase 5294 U/L, alpha-fetoprotein < 2.5 μg/L, and beta-human chorionic gonadotrophin 2526 IU/L.
Medical oncology advised the discontinuation of hormonal therapy and initiated treatment with four cycles of bleomycin, etoposide, and cisplatin chemotherapy.
Following completion of chemotherapy, tumor markers were AFP 2.7 μg/L, beta-HCG 2.4 IU/L, and LDH 247 U/L.
She underwent a radical right inguinal orchiectomy in October 2016 with pathology revealing scarring related to treatment effect but no evidence of malignancy.
Restaging CT scans revealed a residual retroperitoneal mass measuring 6.1 × 2.4 cm and persistent thrombosis of the inferior vena cava.

Due to the location and surgical morbidity, the residual retroperitoneal mass was followed with serial positron emission tomography-computed tomography scans with no evidence of recurrent disease 2 years since diagnosis.
In August 2017, she underwent orchiectomy of the remaining testicle which showed no evidence of malignancy or other significant pathology.
She continues with indefinite anticoagulation given her ongoing use of exogenous estrogen.

source_metadata.title: Secondary extramedullary plasmacytoma of sigmoid colon in a patient with multiple myeloma: a case report
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case presentation and clinical course sections with source order preserved.

evidence_events.source_span: A 71-year-old Caucasian woman with known diverticular disease of the colon and multiple myeloma diagnosed 3 years previously, with monoclonal bands of immunoglobulin A, lambda light chains, and multiple osteolytic lesions, presented to our hospital with abdominal pain, abdominal discomfort, and pneumoperitoneum.
The clinical examination revealed acute abdomen with free air on an abdominal plain x-ray, and elevated levels of leukocyte cells at 18,000/μl and C-reactive protein at 145 mg/L.

An abdominal CT scan showed a 5-cm-wide, 12-cm-long sigmoid mass with medial extension into the fatty tissue at the same localization, pneumoperitoneum, diverticula, free abdominal fluid collections, and distended loops of the small and large intestines.

Intraoperative findings were purulent peritonitis and an obstructive mass of the sigmoid colon causing massive central colonic distention. The mass was extending toward the mesosigmoid. It was impossible to define if the mass might be originating from the mesocolon.

An extended left colectomy was performed with high ligation of the superior mesenteric artery and retrieval of all regional and apical lymph nodes. Peripheral transection was performed at the level of the upper rectum, and a transverse stoma was established (a modified Hartmann’s procedure).

The histopathologic study of the lesion showed large oval cells consisting of a round nucleus in eccentric position with coarse chromatin, protruding nucleolus, and enough cytoplasm. There were also a few cells with double nuclei as well as giant nuclei. Few cells had the morphology of typical plasmacytes. There were many mitoses and higher cell apoptosis was observed in the largest part of the tumor. The neoplasm densely infiltrated the muscular wall of the intestine and the pericolic fat without reaching the surface of the serum and without infiltrating the mucosa, which had severe ischemic lesions. The surgical margins were free.

In immunohistochemical (IHC) analysis, the tumor cells were CD20−, CD5−, CD79a+, CD138+ (moderate), CD38+ (moderate), CD56+, CD10−, CD30−, CD117+ (a few), keratins AE1/AE3−, and S-100−. IHC analysis for both kappa-light and lambda-light chains gave an unreliable effect owing to a very high substrate material. The Ki-67 cell proliferation index was approximately 40%. In the lymph nodes, infiltration by the neoplastic cell population was not documented.
The patient did well postoperatively.

source_metadata.title: Rare presentation of renal cell cancer as dysphagia: a case report
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case presentation and clinical course narrative with figure references.

evidence_events.source_span: A 56-year-old Caucasian man presented for evaluation of intermittent dysphagia to solids for the past few weeks. He had no significant past medical history. He had the sensation of food getting stuck in substernal area. Otherwise he reported good appetite and no weight loss. A physical examination revealed a well-nourished man with no palpable mass or lymph nodes. An abdominal examination revealed no localized tenderness or organomegaly.
An esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) examination revealed a single 6 mm nodule at gastroesophageal junction (GEJ) and Los Angeles grade A distal esophagitis.

Pathology examination from the GEJ nodule showed squamous mucosa with mucosal ulcer and associated acute and chronic inflammatory infiltrates. Nests of atypical cohesive cells with clear cytoplasm, and mild nuclear pleomorphism were noted in submucosa. Multiple immunostains showed vimentin (+), PAX-8 (+), CD10 (focally and weakly positive), and epithelial membrane antigen (EMA; focally and weakly positive). These cells were negative for RCC, TTF1, S100 protein, CD68, cytokeratin 5/6, pancytokeratin, p63, cytokeratin 7 and 20, p40, and pan melanoma marker. Histological features and staining patterns were consistent with metastatic RCC.

A computed tomography (CT) study of chest, abdomen, and pelvis with oral and intravenous contrast showed unremarkable esophagus and no mediastinal lymphadenopathy. A solid-appearing, partially exophytic mass involving his superior left kidney measuring 5.8 × 5.3 cm was seen, abutting the inferior aspect of his spleen but separated by a thin fat plane. A small 0.6 cm gastrohepatic lymph node appeared benign.

A positron emission tomography (PET) scan with 16 mCi of 18-flurodeoxyglucose showed a left upper pole renal mass measuring 5 cm with standardized uptake value (SUV) of 3, suspicious for renal malignancy. No other abnormal uptake was seen to suggest metastatic disease or lymphadenopathy.

Pathology conference and expert opinion concluded that the GEJ nodule biopsy was consistent with metastatic renal clear cell carcinoma (Fuhrman grade 2) involving esophageal mucosa with erosion. Clear cell morphology showed sharp cell borders and lack of glands or mucin, consistent with RCC.

The patient underwent left radical nephrectomy and pathology showed clear cell RCC, with no sarcomatoid features, Fuhrman nuclear grade 3. Resection margins were negative and no involvement of adrenal gland was noticed.

Endoscopic submucosal dissection of the GEJ nodule area was performed, which showed squamous and gastric-type mucosa with chronic inflammation and underlying adipose tissue in submucosa, negative for malignancy.
The patient has been clinically asymptomatic for 16 months after left nephrectomy. Oncology recommended close surveillance and conservative management.

source_metadata.title: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis in a patient with biopsy-proven IgG4-related pulmonary disease and coincident small cell lung cancer

evidence_events.source_span: A 64-year-old man with a history of IgG4 lung disease presented with 3 weeks of progressive productive cough, haemoptysis, myalgias, arthralgias, weakness, fever and chills for 2–3 days

Diagnosis of IgG4 lung disease was made 16 months prior by wedge biopsy showing plasma-cell rich nodular fibroinflammatory lesion with endothelialitis, marked increase in IgG4+ cells (>30/HPF), heavy chronic inflammatory infiltrates, marked fibrosis, intimal inflammation without necrosis, and increased IgG4/IgG ratio >10%
Laboratory studies at IgG4-RD diagnosis showed elevated IgG4 >135 mg/dL, positive ANCA and anti-proteinase 3 (PR3) antibodies
Serial CT scans showed partial resolution of lung masses over 13 months without treatment

On admission, patient had temperature 38.1°C, pulse 105 bpm, respiratory rate 20/min, BP 100/70 mm Hg, oxygen saturation 90% on room air, moderate respiratory distress, right eye mild injection, diffuse tender cervical lymphadenopathy, grade II/VI systolic murmur, diffuse crackles and decreased breath sounds at lung bases, 1+ lower extremity edema

Admission labs showed WBC 10.9x10^9/L, hemoglobin 97 g/L, hematocrit 29.7%, platelets 348x10^9/L, AST 30 U/L, ALT 32 U/L, BUN 43 mg/dL, creatinine 3.7 mg/dL, CRP 150 mg/dL, ESR >120 mm/hr, IgG4 289 mg/dL, c-ANCA 1:640 (confirmatory PR3 not done), urinalysis with protein 200 mg/dL, RBC 148/hpf, WBC 85/hpf, negative nitrates
Chest CT showed marked interval increase in diffuse lung opacities, some coalesced into irregular marginated nodules and masses
Renal biopsy showed diffuse acute necrotising/crescentic glomerulonephritis, pauci-immune type
Bronchoalveolar lavage revealed copious blood in right main stem bronchus and right middle lobe
Treated with intravenous methylprednisone, monthly cyclophosphamide, plasmapheresis, required haemodialysis, then extubated and improved
Two months later, repeat chest CT showed increased size of left upper lobe mass present since initial IgG4-RD diagnosis; biopsy revealed small cell carcinoma

Patient received one cycle of chemotherapy for small cell lung cancer, declined further treatment, continued cyclophosphamide and azathioprine for GPA, remained on home oxygen, died one year after admission from lung cancer

source_metadata.title: Giant cell tumour of the middle phalanx of the middle finger

evidence_events.source_span: A healthy, active, 49-year-old woman initially presented to our team in January 2017 with a history of pain, tenderness and swelling in the left middle finger following a minor trauma to her right hand 1 year previously. She denied any history of constitutional symptoms. Physical examination showed a swollen and tender mass with firm consistency at the middle phalanx of the middle finger of the left hand. Range of motion of the adjacent joints (distal interphalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints) was preserved and capillary refill time was normal.

Plain radiography showed a geographic osteolytic lesion on the shaft of the middle phalanx of the left middle finger with a well-defined sclerotic border; no periosteal reaction or fracture line were seen.
MRI evaluation showed a hypointense solid intramedullary lesion with hyperintense surrounding soft tissue.

At 6-month follow-up, plain radiograph showed progression of an expansile osteolytic lesion with articular involvement indicating an aggressive tumour with cortical extension and articular involvement. Repeat chest radiographs showed no evidence of pulmonary metastasis.
An incisional biopsy was performed in July 2017, 6 months after the initial visit. Histopathology was compatible with giant cell bone tumour and was classified as Campanacci stage III.

Middle phalanx resection and interphalangeal joint arthrodesis with iliac bone graft were performed following the diagnosis. Since the lesion involved nearly the entire middle phalanx with some local invasion, tumour resection was chosen rather than the standard extended curettage to help insure there was no residual tumour. No immediate complications were observed. Since there was no evidence of metastasis, no systemic treatments were scheduled.

At the 1-year follow-up, the patient’s middle phalanx was pain-free with some functional attenuation due to phalangeal fusion. A plain radiograph revealed a union of the middle phalanx with no sign of GCT recurrence.

source_metadata.title: Primary pulmonary artery sarcoma with deep vein thrombosis: A case report
source_metadata.notes: Case report of a 26-year-old man with PAS initially misdiagnosed as PE and DVT.

evidence_events.source_span: A 26-year-old man with fever and dyspnea was admitted to the department of invasive technology.

Blood tests showed inflammatory activity (white blood cell [WBC] 13400/mL, C-reactive protein [CRP] 95.32 mg/L), a slight increase of D-dimer (2.78 μg/mL) and Fibrin Degradation Product (FDP)-20.81 μg/mL (normal range <5.0 μg/mL).
The chest enhanced computed tomography (CT) scanning revealed multiple filling defects occurred in the main trunk of both pulmonary arteries and branches of the left pulmonary artery.
Echocardiography revealed the dilated right atrium and ventricle, impaired right ventricular systolic function, and abnormal echo in the pulmonary artery and its branches.
Color-Doppler ultrasound showed venous thrombosis of the lower extremity and its blood flow stagnation.

Because of his symptoms, high blood coagulation, the CT scanning and deep venous thrombosis revealed by the angiographic, the patient was treated with the transcatheter thrombolysis therapy and inferior vena cava filter implantation, under the diagnosis of pulmonary embolism (PE) and DVT.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: transcatheter thrombolysis therapy and inferior vena cava filter implantation

evidence_events.source_span: There was no relief of symptoms after transcatheter thrombolysis therapy, and the pulmonary artery computed tomography angiography (CTA) revealed multiple filling defects as same as the last CT scanning.

Under general anesthesia and cardiopulmonary bypass, midline sternotomy was performed, and main pulmonary artery was opened. Grey white tissue mass in thrombosed areas was removed by separating it from the main pulmonary artery, bilateral pulmonary artery branches, and pulmonary valves. The diameter of the mass was 1.5 to 5 cm, and the total length was about 20 cm.

In histopathology, the tumor is composed of spindle to epithelioid cells exhibiting marked pleomorphism with vascular growth pattern. Strange nuclei, giant nuclei, and multiple nuclei can be seen in tumor cells. Interspersed mitotic figures and areas of focal myxoid change and fibrinoid necrosis showed features of high-grade sarcoma.
The immunohistochemistry results of tumor cells were positive for EMA, vimentin, and CD68, focally weakly positive for CR, SMA, ckp and bcl-2, and negative for WT1 and GFAP.
The final diagnosis was primary pulmonary artery high-grade sarcoma.
The enhanced CT scanning of head, chest and belly revealed that no other tumor tissue was found.
The patient underwent 4 cycles of postoperative chemotherapy according to the recommendation of another cancer hospital.
Follow-up visit of the patient for 6 months showed he was still alive.

source_metadata.title: Pure yolk sac tumour, post-pubertal type, arising from cryptorchid testes

evidence_events.source_span: A 46-year-old married man was referred to the oncosurgery department in April 2018 with complaints of gradually progressive, mildly tender, abdominal lump of insidious onset, since the last 1 month. Other significant contributory history included the fact that the patient had delayed bowel movements since 15–20 days, as well as one to two episodes of non-projectile non bilious vomiting—1 week prior to admission—with the fact that the patient has bilateral cryptorchidism and was infertile and not on any treatment for the same. On detailed interrogation, the patient gave history of progressive painless diminution of bilateral visual fields over the course of 10 years.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: since the last 1 month; 15–20 days; 1 week prior to admission; over the course of 10 years

evidence_events.source_span: On examination, the patient presented with a single, ovoid, non-tender, firm, non-ballottable, abdominal lump approximately 25 cm × 15 cm, predominantly occupying infra-umbilical segment of the abdomen, with pelvic extension. Percussion revealed a tympanic note in the supra-umbilical region and a dull note in infra-umbilical region. Auscultation was unremarkable. Per rectal examination was normal. Examination of the scrotum revealed absence of both testes within the scrotal cavity.
Ophthalmological examination revealed that visual acuity had reduced to hand movements with typical findings of optic atrophy on fundoscopic examination.
Apart from neutrophilic leukocytosis on haemogram and presence of calcium oxalate crystals on urine examination, all other routine blood investigations were within normal limits.
Serum α-fetoprotein level was >15 160 ng/mL, which was significantly elevated. Serum β-HCG level was 2 mIU/L and serum LDH was 198 U/L, both of which were within normal limits.

Contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen was suggestive of a large, well-defined, heterogeneous soft tissue density mass in the hypogastric supra vesical region measuring about 7.8 × 9.2 × 11.2 cm. Post contrast study shows moderate heterogeneous enhancement with significant irregular non-enhancing necrotic areas within. Predominant tumorous feeders are seen arising from the left gonadal artery. The lesion displaces the small bowel loops superiorly and extends laterally to the right iliac fossa, anteriorly to the right common iliac and external iliac vessels. Superiorly, there is a small exophytic tumorous extension seen into the mesenteric sleeve. Inferiorly, the lesion indents the dome of the bladder with thin intervening fat planes. There is a well-defined hypodense nodular structure seen in the right iliac fossa measuring about 2.5 × 3.0 × 2.7 cm inferior to the base of caecum. Post-contrast study shows minimal heterogeneous enhancement with arterial supply arising from right gonadal artery. Both scrotal sacs are empty suggestive of undescended testes.
Non-contrast brain CT revealed normal study.
Ultrasound-guided tru-cut biopsy was positive for malignant cells and favoured seminoma.

Intra-operative findings were consistent with large irregular greyish-white to grey yellow to grey brown mass seen arising from pelvic cavity. The mass was extremely friable to touch, with variable tissue consistency, due to which it could not be removed completely. The mass was fixed to bladder dome and base, as well as to two to three segments of jejunum and ileum, without evidence of perforation. The second mass (right cryptorchid testis) could not be separately identified from the mass. Around 1700 g gross weight of tumour was removed, leaving behind fixed areas as mentioned above.

Histopathology examination of cut section showed tumour cells in an alveolar to endodermal sinus to microcystic pattern. Most of the tumour cells had large pleomorphic vesicular nuclei with predominant nucleoli and meagre cytoplasm. Microcystic areas were composed of flattened cells. Schiller–Duval bodies, hyaline globules, areas of necrosis and haemorrhage were noted.

Immunohistochemistry report revealed diffuse strong positive for cytokeratin (CK), patchy strong positive for placental-like alkaline phosphatase (PLAP), moderate positive for Glypican 3, moderate patchy positive for alpha fetoprotein (AFP), ki-67 proliferative index was 30%, negative for epithelial membrane antigen (EMA), Oct3/4 and CD30.

Two weeks after discharge, the patient was readmitted with abdominal pain and discharge through suture line which was serosanguinous and non-foul smelling. Over the course of the next week, the patient turned severely cachexic, discharge increased and patient developed septicaemia, which was refractory to treatment. Ten days after re-hospitalisation, the patient succumbed to septicaemic shock, without even initiating the first chemotherapy cycle.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: Two weeks after discharge; over the course of the next week; ten days after re-hospitalisation

source_metadata.title: Spontaneous intracardiac microcavitations in a patient with a colonic carcinoma
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from BMJ Case Reports 2019;12(9):e229932

evidence_events.source_span: A man in mid-70s was admitted to our emergency department because of an acute weakness in both legs which had led to a fall. He also reported chest pain, combined with a feeling of tachycardia after his fall.

His medical history is remarkable for mitral regurgitation and hypertensive heart disease (HFpEF), chronic renal failure KDIGO II, normochromic normocytic anaemia and AF. Cardiovascular risk factors were arterial hypertension, dyslipidaemia and a former nicotine abuse.

At presentation, the patient had a temperature of 39.8°C with normal blood pressure, heartrate and oxygen saturation. The clinical examination was unremarkable except for a systolic murmur. There was no more weakness in the legs.
The ECG showed AF with T-negativities in III.
Laboratory tests showed a haemoglobin of 88 g/L, leucocytes of 15.9 x10⁹/L, CRP of 60 mg/L (ref.: <10 mg/L), creatinine of 198 µmol/l (ref.: <104 µmol/l). Blood cultures were negative.
The X-Ray of the thorax only showed signs of venous congestion.
Echocardiography revealed continuous spontaneous microcavitations in the right atrium, right ventricle, right ventricular outflow tract and truncus pulmonalis.
No right-to-left shunt could be detected.
A CT scan of the chest confirmed the findings of microcavitations and showed several hypodense hepatic lesions suspicious for metastatic disease.
A colonoscopy was performed, revealing an ulcerated colonic carcinoma at the ileocecal valve.
The patient refused any further examinations or treatment and left the hospital before the workup could be completed. He died 4 months thereafter.

source_metadata.title: Bochdalek hernia with Diamond-Blackfan anemia associated with RPS19 gene mutation

evidence_events.source_span: A 19-month-old male child was brought to our pediatric hematology-oncology outpatient clinic for the management of recurrent anemia of unknown cause.
There was a history of hydrops fetalis being detected on the patient's fetal ultrasound examination.
The patient was anemic at birth, treated with surfactant and underwent 6 packed red blood cell (PRBC) transfusions in the neonatal intensive care unit within the first month of his birth.
He continued to receive PRBC transfusions every 3 to 4 weeks for persistent anemia until 3 months of age, with hemoglobin levels sustained >9.0 g/dL from 4 months of age.

At 19 months, recurrence of anemia with short stature, developmental delay, and strabismus was noted; physical exam showed severe anemia (Hb 5.4 g/dL), normal WBC and platelets, elevated MCV (105.9 fL), elevated HbF (12.1%), and increased erythrocyte adenosine deaminase (60.2 IU/L).
Parvovirus B19 serological test (IgM and IgG) results were negative.
Abdominal computed tomography (CT) scan revealed herniation of stomach and spleen into the thoracic cavity at the posteromedial aspect of the left hemidiaphragm, diagnosed as Bochdalek hernia.
Bone marrow study revealed normocellular marrow with markedly decreased erythropoietic cells and a high myeloid-to-erythroid ratio of 18:1; other cell lines were unaffected.
Echocardiogram showed an atrial septal defect measuring 5.58 × 3.77 mm.
Genetic analysis revealed a heterozygous RPS19 gene mutation, c.380G>A (p.Gly127Glu), confirming the diagnosis of Diamond-Blackfan anemia.

Initial treatment included PRBC transfusion followed by oral prednisone at 2 mg/kg/day for 4 weeks, then tapered to maintenance dose of 0.3 mg/kg on alternate days, resulting in sustained hemoglobin >9.0 g/dL without further transfusions.

source_metadata.title: A case of acute megakaryoblastic leukaemia (FAB M7), a rare type of acute myeloid leukemia (AML), in a teenager
source_metadata.notes: Case report from Malawi Medical Journal 2018 describing clinical, laboratory, imaging, and immunophenotyping evidence for AML M7 in a 19-year-old Nigerian female.

evidence_events.source_span: A 19-year old Nigerian female presented with recurrent headache, fever, easy fatiguability and breathlessness of 2 months duration.
She was severely pale with slight tinge of jaundice. No significant peripheral lymph node enlargement or bleeding from orifices or gums. Chest clinically clear. Liver and spleen not palpable.
Full blood count showed PCV 10.8%, WBC 4.1 × 10^9/L (Neutrophil 18.3%, lymphocyte 78%, mid 3.4%), platelet 50 × 10^9/L.
Peripheral blood film showed normocytic normochromic red blood cells, few nucleated red blood cells and immature mononuclear cells with cytoplasmic blebs. Giant forms of platelets also seen.

Bone marrow aspiration yielded a dry tap; bone marrow biopsy performed. Bone marrow imprint showed increased immature mononuclear cells with abundant basophilic cytoplasm containing vacuoles and hyperchromatic, pleomorphic nuclei; some had cytoplasmic blebs constituting over 90% of nucleated cells.
Immunophenotyping of peripheral blood showed positivity for CD33 (46%), CD41 (24%), and CD61 (20%). CD41 and CD61 are megakaryocyte specific antigens; CD33 is a myeloid marker.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: immunophenotyping performed by Safety Molecular Pathology Laboratory, Enugu

evidence_events.source_span: Biochemical parameters including uric acid, bilirubin, creatinine, and liver enzymes were normal.
X-rays of tibia and fibula showed increased fibrosis.

Repeat full blood count on day 7 of induction chemotherapy showed PCV 17.7%, WBC 0.38 × 10^9/L, platelet 22 × 10^9/L; peripheral blood film revealed leucopenia, thrombocytopenia, and no abnormal mononuclear cells.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: repeat FBC and peripheral blood film

evidence_events.source_span: Repeat bone marrow aspiration showed blasts less than 5%, indicating remission.

source_metadata.title: A case of a 22-month-old boy with necrotizing pneumonia presenting with leukaemoid reaction misdiagnosed as leukaemia: a case report and review of the literature
source_metadata.notes: Extraction based on case presentation and clinical course sections with source order preserved.

evidence_events.source_span: A 22-month-old patient was referred to our unit due to fever, cough and night sweats for a period of 3 weeks.
He was initially administered intravenous antibiotics (ampicillin and gentamycin) for 1 week and was then started on medication for tuberculosis (TB) for 2 weeks after a suspicious chest radiograph.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: initially ... for 1 week ... then started on medication for tuberculosis for 2 weeks

evidence_events.source_span: A complete blood count (CBC) showed an elevated TLC with a suspicion of leukaemia; this was the primary reason for his referral to our unit.

On physical examination, he showed signs of wasting (his weight was 8.4 kg and his weight-for-height Z score was less than −3 standard deviations). The patient was also pale, dyspnoeic with chest indrawing and crackles on the right side of his chest. He was febrile with a temperature of 39.8°C, tachypnoeic, and tachycardic with an oxygen saturation of 89% on room air.

Laboratory investigations including a CBC showed a TLC of 103,000 cells/µl (neutrophils, 84.2%; lymphocytes, 9.925%; monocytes, 7.9%) and a red blood cell (RBC) count of 2.7×10⁶. Other laboratory data included haemoglobin, 5.08 g/dl; mean corpuscular volume (MCV), 76.1 fl; mean corpuscular haemoglobin (MCH), 24.8 pg, MCHC, 32.6 g/dl, red cell distribution width (RDW), 16.4%; and a platelet count of 649×10⁶. A peripheral smear showed hyper-segmented neutrophils, bands, metamyelocytes with microcytic hypochromic RBCs; C-reactive protein (CRP) was 102.5 mg/l.
Flow cytometry of bone marrow aspirate was performed for leukaemia and was negative for CD34, CD10, CD19, CD117, HLA-DR but positive for CD13, indicating the predominance of mature neutrophils.
A chest radiograph showed heterogeneous opacification in the upper part of the right lower lobe, middle lobe and lateral aspect of the right upper lobe.

A subsequent chest computed tomography (CT) scan showed consolidations in the right middle lobe and upper part of the right lower lobe with emphysematous regions which were suggestive of necrotizing pneumonia.
Blood cultures were negative for bacteria.
Based on radiological findings, the patient was empirically started on piperacillin-tazobactam for necrotizing pneumonia.
Three days after the antibiotics were started, the fever and respiratory distress declined, the condition gradually improved, the cough resolved, and the child's weight began to increase.
The child was discharged home after 17 days with a normal TLC of 7670 cells/µl.

source_metadata.title: Signet-ring cell adenocarcinoma of unknown primary presenting with superior vena cava (SVC) syndrome: rare type of cancer

evidence_events.source_span: A 53-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of progressive, non-productive, on-and-off cough followed by upper back pain and occasional swelling of the face and upper extremities, with noted engorgement of neck veins

Physical examination on admission revealed distended neck veins, prominent superficial vessels at the neck, decreased breath sounds with decreased vocal fremiti at the base of the right lung and upper extremity swelling
Chest X-ray revealed a right paratracheal mass with right-sided pleural effusion
Diagnostic thoracentesis revealed findings consistent with metastatic adenocarcinoma

Complete blood count, serum creatinine, lipid profile and coagulation tests were unremarkable; urinalysis showed glucosuria consistent with type 2 diabetes mellitus; haemoglobin A1c was 9.4% and random blood sugar elevated

CT chest with contrast revealed a 3.4×3.5×2.7 cm moderately enhancing mass lesion at the right lower lung compressing the posterior aspect of the right lower bronchus with associated atelectasis, fissural thickening, perilesional ground glass densities, prominent carinal lymph node with calcification, multiple subcentimetre right cervical and axillary lymph nodes, and a 3.7×4.3×4.5 cm heterogenous mildly enhancing right paratracheal mass with mass effect

Repeat CT chest with contrast 2 weeks later showed no significant change in right paratracheal mass size with compression of SVC, increased right pleural effusion, minimal left pleural effusion and elevated right hemidiaphragm

Pleural fluid cytology and cell block revealed rare atypical cells with specific gravity 1.010, WBC 1500/μL, RBC 750/μL, 5% polymorphonuclear cells, 90% lymphocytes, 5% monocytes, glucose 12.69 mg/dL, total protein 41.5 mg/dL, and LDH 140 U/L consistent with an exudative picture

CT abdomen and pelvis with triple contrast revealed multiple hypodense, peripherally enhancing nodular foci in bilateral psoas muscles, gluteal muscles, paravertebral and proximal medial thigh muscles; slight diffuse thickening of gastric fundus and sigmoid colonic walls; hypodense nodules at liver, right adrenal gland and spleen; enlarged lymph nodes with necrotic centers in left iliac and superficial inguinal regions; a 0.7 cm hypodense cystic focus in right kidney cortex; pericardial thickening; subcutaneous fat stranding in chest wall and flanks; multiple lytic areas in sacrum, iliac bones, ischium, proximal femurs, and vertebrae; and a 3.0×3.2 cm right parahilar mass
evidence_events.procedural_cue: CT abdomen and pelvis with triple contrast

evidence_events.source_span: Bronchoscopy revealed a pale and stunted trachea with multiple white nodules in the carina; superior segment of right lower lobe was narrow but without visible mass or irregularities; bronchial alveolar lavage was performed and samples sent for diagnostic studies
Blood, sputum, and bronchial washing specimens for gram staining, cultures and acid-fast bacilli studies were negative; procalcitonin level was 0.05 ng/mL (normal 0-0.25 ng/mL)
Tumour markers: carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) was 28.69 ng/mL (normal <5), CA 19-9 was 198.51 IU/mL (normal <37)

Bronchial alveolar lavage cytology showed atypical cells with high nuclear to cytoplasmic ratio and pleomorphism; some cells showed signet-ring pattern with mucin inclusion pushing nucleus to periphery; biopsy showed similar findings consistent with metastatic adenocarcinoma with signet-ring features
evidence_events.procedural_cue: bronchial alveolar lavage cytology and biopsy

evidence_events.source_span: Immunohistochemistry panel showed tumour cells diffusely positive for cytokeratin-7 (CK-7), negative for cytokeratin-20 (CK-20), thyroid transcription factor-1 (TTF-1), and calretinin, consistent with metastatic disease of gastric or pancreaticobiliary origin
Patient underwent three sessions of radiotherapy with noted improvement of symptoms
Patient was discharged with plans for further work-up on an outpatient basis but was lost to follow-up

source_metadata.title: Paraneoplastic Leukemoid Reaction in Gastroesophageal Junction Adenocarcinoma: A Case Report

evidence_events.source_span: A 72-year-old Caucasian female with a past medical history of chronic kidney disease, gastroesophageal reflux disease, remote history of peptic ulcer disease, and 60+ pack-year smoking history was referred to a hematologist/oncologist for evaluation of leukocytosis with neutrophilia.

The patient complained about mild and intermittent discomfort in the left upper quadrant, similar to her duodenal ulcers, well controlled with omeprazole. She denied melena, hematochezia, or changes in bowel habits. No signs of infection or recent illness.

Initial complete blood count revealed leukocyte count of 25,600/uL with absolute neutrophil count of 21,000/uL, monocyte count of 1,500/uL, hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL, and platelets 282,000/uL. Blood urea nitrogen 34 mg/dL, creatinine 1.8 to 2.0 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase 324 U/L, normal total bilirubin, lactic dehydrogenase 228 U/L, and uric acid 10.3 mg/dL.
Initial hematological workup including peripheral smear, JAK2 V617F mutation, and BCR/ABL revealed no evidence of leukemia or other myeloproliferative neoplasms.

In late July 2018, bone marrow biopsy and aspiration showed left-shifted maturation with segmented neutrophils 18%, band neutrophils 30%, metamyelocytes 18%, myelocytes 11%, eosinophils 2%, monocytes 3%, and lymphocytes 6%.

Over the next few months, leukocytosis worsened to 48,200/uL with neutrophilia (42,400/uL) and severe anemia (6.6 g/dL). The patient developed progressively worsening dysphagia to solid foods, unintentional 20-pound weight loss, and fatigue.
CT chest/abdomen/pelvis showed significant wall thickening at the gastroesophageal junction with nodular abnormality projecting into the proximal stomach and multiple hypodensities of the liver.

On admission in early September 2018, physical exam showed a thin, chronically ill-appearing female with diminished breath sounds throughout; vital signs were stable. Labs showed leukocytosis 50,500/uL with neutrophilia 48,200/uL and immature myelocytes, creatinine 2.2 mg/dL, hyponatremia 131 mmol/L, hypochloremia 90 mmol/L, albumin 3.3 g/dL, alkaline phosphatase 320 U/L, total bilirubin 1.8 mg/dL, and normal lactate.

Sepsis workup including urinalysis, respiratory panel, and blood cultures was negative for infection. Chest x-ray showed mild nodular opacities in mid and lower lung and right base. Procalcitonin was elevated at 2.95 ng/mL (normal <0.09 ng/mL). Peripheral smear showed marked absolute neutrophilia and macrocytic anemia without blasts or dysplastic features.
Esophagogastroduodenoscopy revealed a fungating mass at the gastroesophageal junction without active bleeding.
Histopathology of the biopsy showed adenocarcinoma with HER2 overexpression (immunohistochemical score 3+).

During hospitalization, patient was treated with IV piperacillin/tazobactam for presumed pneumonia with fever up to 39.4°C, then discharged on amoxicillin/clavulanate. Leukocytosis and neutrophilia improved to 30,100/uL and 25,900/uL on discharge.
Systemic therapy with FOLFOX chemotherapy was initiated 1.5 weeks after discharge. Leukocytosis completely resolved after 1 round of FOLFOX.
Trastuzumab was added to chemotherapy after a normal echocardiogram. Patient remained progression-free.
Repeat CT scan 6 months after therapy showed improving gastric cardia mucosal thickening and decrease in hepatic metastasis.
G-CSF level was not obtained as it was not available in the institution.

source_metadata.title: Mediastinal germ cell tumour during the COVID-19 pandemic
source_metadata.notes: Case report of a 23-year-old male with mediastinal germ cell tumor diagnosed during COVID-19 pandemic with imaging, labs, histology, and treatment details.

evidence_events.source_span: A 23-year-old male accountant with no comorbidities developed a cough and dyspnoea while travelling for work in the UK during March 2020.

His symptoms developed over 2 weeks and having contacted a local primary care office, he was referred to a COVID-19 test centre. A swab was not performed as he was considered to be young and in a low-risk category. He was advised to take analgesia, bed rest and self-isolate.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: referred to COVID-19 test centre; no swab performed

evidence_events.source_span: On returning to Ireland, he was required to self-isolate for a further 14 days. Five weeks and three negative swabs later, his symptoms deteriorated with pleuritic chest pain and a severe cough.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: Five weeks and three negative swabs later

evidence_events.source_span: His primary care physician requested a plain chest radiograph, which demonstrated a large mass within the right hemithorax.
On admission to hospital, he did not require oxygen and was haemodynamically stable.

A CT of the thorax, abdomen and pelvis showed a 10×11 cm mass arising in the anterior mediastinum with marked stenosis of the superior vena cava and the pulmonary artery trunk. No distant metastatic disease was identified confirming clinical stage II disease.
Testicular examination and ultrasound were unremarkable.

Histological evaluation of the mediastinal lesion confirmed an extragonadal germ cell tumour, of yolk sac origin, with a serum alpha-fetoprotein level of 17,000 ng/mL (normal 0.9–8.8 ng/mL). Other blood tests included an elevated lactate dehydrogenase of 699 unit/L (220–450 unit/L) and an undetectable beta-human chorionic gonadotropin (<1 unit/L).
According to the International Germ Cell Cancer Consensus Group, this represented poor-risk disease due to the mediastinal origin.

Urgent chemotherapy was commenced as an inpatient with the regimen VIP, a 21-day cycle consisting of etoposide, ifosfamide with mesna, and cisplatin. Pegfilgrastim was administered to reduce the risk of neutropenia.

source_metadata.title: Triphasic waves in electroencephalogram as a possible early marker of carcinomatous meningitis: a case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 76-year-old man reported incremental headache, nausea, emesis, and intermittent fever for 2 months.
Neurological examination showed negative findings but cervical rigidity.
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed unremarkable abnormalities except for some small lacunar infarctions in the basal ganglia region.
Routine scalp EEG showed mild slow background activity (basic rhythm 7–8 Hz), but neither discharge nor focal slow activity nor underlying seizures were found.
Blood tests showed a raised white blood cells (WBC) count of 18 × 10^12 cells/L and a mildly decreased hemoglobin level of 96 g/L; hepatic and renal function tests were all within the normal range.

The CSF pressure was 220 mmH2O, the protein level was slightly increased at 0.76 g/L, the WBC count was 6 × 10^6 cells/L with 80% mononuclear cells and 20% multinuclear cells, and glucose and chlorides were within the normal range. Cytology did not find any atypical cells.

Five days after admission, a long-term EEG was performed because of his fever and mild abnormalities in the routine EEG. The second EEG showed a substantially slowed background activity without a normal rhythm, and asymmetric triphasic complex sharp waves were found in frontal brain regions, but no underlying seizure was detected.

A lung computed tomography scan showed a nodule in the upper lobe of the right lung. Adenocarcinoma cells were found by exfoliative cytologic examination of sputum. Non-small cell lung cancer was diagnosed (stage IVB, T1bN2M1c).

A second cytologic examination of CSF was performed, and abnormal cells were found. These cells had larger cell areas and nucleocytoplasmic ratios than monocytes and enlarged and hyperchromatic nuclei.

The patient received systemic therapy including whole brain radiotherapy and intrathecal injection of methotrexate once a week in the first month then monthly thereafter. The clinical symptoms (headache and vomiting) relieved after the third month.
The patient was lost to follow-up in the sixth month after carcinomatous meningitis was diagnosed.

source_metadata.title: Primary intradural Hodgkin lymphoma of the conus medullaris and cauda equina: case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 48-year-old female presented with a 2-month history of lower back pain and a 4-week history of right L5-S1 radiculopathy with associated perianal paresthesia. For the few days prior to her admission, she developed anal and urinary sphincter dysfunction with incomplete emptying of her bowels and occasional urinary incontinence. She was systemically well with no history of fevers, weight loss, night sweats or fatigue. On physical examination, she had preserved motor function with loss of sensation to S3-5 dermatomes and preserved reflexes. Routine blood workup was normal.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: For the few days prior to her admission

evidence_events.source_span: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the lumbosacral spine revealed a lobulated homogenously enhancing exophytic lesion involving the conus medullaris and filum terminale measuring 13 × 14 × 22 mm, associated with cord edema extending to the level of T11. A further small lesion of 5 mm was noted in the cauda equina at the L5/S1 level. Subsequent imaging of the remainder of the cranio-spinal axis revealed no abnormality, with no leptomeningeal enhancement.

A L1/2 laminectomy was undertaken with midline dural opening. The tumor was identified within the conus and tracking down the filum terminale. Tumor was found encasing the right side of the cauda equina with intraneural tumor in affected nerve roots. No clear tumor–conus interface was seen. The conus component was debulked and biopsies of the cauda equina component were sent for histopathological analysis.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: L1/2 laminectomy with midline dural opening

evidence_events.source_span: Histology demonstrated features of classic Hodgkin lymphoma involving spinal cord parenchyma and peripheral nerve fascicles. The tumor tissue was composed of scattered Hodgkin cells, Reed–Sternberg cells and lacunar cells surrounded by a mix of small lymphocytes, histiocytes, eosinophils and occasional neutrophils. The mixed cellularity subtype was favored. Immunohistochemistry showed membrane staining for CD30, weak-positive staining for CD20 and PAX5, positivity for MUM1 and EBV-encoded RNA (EBER) in-situ hybridization. CD45 negativity excluded other lymphoma differentials.

Whole body positron emission tomography (PET)/CT was negative for further CNS involvement or systemic disease. Bone marrow trephine and serological screening, including for Epstein–Barr virus, was normal. The patient was staged as Stage IE Hodgkin lymphoma of the CNS according to the Ann Arbor system.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: Whole body PET/CT and bone marrow trephine

evidence_events.source_span: The patient completed radiotherapy to the residual tumor with a dose of 36 Gy in 20 fractions to T10-sacrum, delivered with intensity modulated radiation therapy. Chemotherapy was not given as primary treatment but reserved for relapse.

At 10 months postoperatively, the patient was well with no motor deficit and normal bowel and bladder function. MRI showed complete resolution of enhancement at L1/2 and L5/S1 with no further disease on cranio-spinal imaging.

source_metadata.title: Novel presentation of intraocular metastases in a patient with penile squamous cell carcinoma: a case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 43-year-old Asian man with a 3-year history of progressively invasive penile cancer presented with pain in his right eye and had lost his vision more than a month earlier.
He was staged T4N3M1 and diagnosed with metastasis in bilateral inguinal lymph nodes, ipsilateral iliac nodes, and systemic metastasis to liver and lungs.

On presentation, best corrected visual acuity was no light perception in right eye and 20/20 in left eye; right pupil dilated to 5 mm with absent pupillary reaction; mild proptosis and ocular movement in all directions; dilated fundus exam showed post equatorial retinal detachment with black eminence and pale optic disk in right eye.
Ophthalmic B-scan ultrasound showed retinal detachment with hemorrhage in right eye.

Orbital MRI showed thickening and strengthening of right lateral wall, thickened and hardened internal and lateral rectus muscles, thickened 2-cm optic nerve with invasion by metastasis; T1-weighted images showed hyperintensity; T2-weighted images showed hypointensity; contrast-enhanced MRI showed inhomogeneous enhancement of posterior wall.
Right eyeball enucleation was performed due to severe eye pain and irreversible vision loss.

Histopathological examination of enucleated eye showed metastatic moderately differentiated penile squamous cell carcinoma infiltrating sclera, choroid, retina, optic nerve, and external intraocular sites; hematoxylin and eosin staining showed keratin pearls, infiltrative growth of keratinized cells, and intercellular bridges in nests of carcinoma cells.
Patient received chemotherapy and radiotherapy during 6 months of follow-up and died due to brain metastasis.

source_metadata.title: Atypical localisation of pleomorphic adenoma issue from heterotopic salivary tissue in the supraclavicular region: diagnosis and management
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from BMJ Case Reports 2020 article, focusing on case presentation and diagnostic trajectory.

evidence_events.source_span: A 72-year-old Caucasian man was referred to the department of otorhinolaryngology for investigations and management of left-sided supraclavicular mass.

He was in good general health and his medical background showed a history of melanoma type superficial spreading melanoma in the right elbow, initially staged; Clark III, Breslow 0.77, treated surgically 11 years ago; he was followed-up by his dermatologist with no evidence of local recurrence or distant metastasis.
He presented a supraclavicular mass on the left side, appeared since 4 months with a progressive evolution.

An initial evaluation of this mass was made by his dermatologist with a fine needle aspiration biopsy. Thin Prep processed sample did not showed any melanoma cells but a moderately cellular specimen containing slightly atypical epithelial-type cell. Cohesive sheet of cells with increased nucleocytoplasmic ratio were intermixed with plasmocytoid discohesive cells, rare oncocyte cells were also present.

The otorhinolaryngology examination showed a left-sided supraclavicular solid mass, measured approximately 2×3 cm, subcutaneous, mobile and painless on palpation. There was no evidence of other cervical mass. The patient had no symptoms, such as sore throat, dysphagia, dyspnoea or dysphonia.

The clinical examination of the oral cavity showed discreet asymmetry in favour of the right palatine tonsil with no evidence of any exophytic or ulcerated lesion. The rest of the clinical examination of the hypopharynx and larynx did not showed any other pathological signs or suspicion lesion.

A total body radiological evaluation by positron emission tomography (PET)-CT was performed and showed a metabolic hyperactivity of the supraclavicular mass, on the left side (maximum Standardized Uptake Value (SUV) at 3.2). Asymmetric metabolic hyperactivity on both palatine tonsils, on favour the right side (maximum SUV at 5.9).

The decision to perform a surgical resection of the left-sided cervical mass in combination with bilateral tonsillectomy was made after discussion with the patient. The surgery was performed under general anaesthesia without intra- or postoperative complications.
Histological analysis of both tonsils showed a lymphoepithelial proliferation without any anomalies or signs of malignancy.

The macroscopic appearance of the supraclavicular mass consisted of an elastic nodule, measured 3×1.8×1 cm with a shiny myxoid cut surface. The whole-mount slide of the nodule showed a well-circumscribed intranodal lesion consisting of variable sized cystic structure intermixed with basophilic epithelial sheet and acidophilic stromal component.

Microscopic analysis revealed an intranodal proliferation with a biphasic growth pattern of epithelial/myoepithelial cells and chondromyxoid stroma. Compact sheet of epithelial cells focally forming ductal structure were associated with less cohesive ovoid myoepithelial cells interspersed in a chondomyxoid stroma. A more oncocyte type of epithelium layered some of the ductal structure. The mitotic index MIB was at 14%.

Immunostaining study showed positivity for SOX10, P63, GFAP and keratin 5/6 with partial expression for Gata 3 and cytokeratin 7. There was no expression for CEA, Actin, PAX8, chromogranin, synaptophysin, CK20, PSA, HMB45, TTF1 and CDX2.
These microscopic and immunostaining findings were compatible with benign salivary tissue proliferation type pleomorphic adenoma into a lymph node.

Due to the benign nature of the supraclavicular mass, no further investigations or procedures were performed. Cervical ultrasonography of control 3 months after the surgery did not revealed recurrence of the tumour.

source_metadata.title: NUT midline carcinoma in a young pregnant female: a case report
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case presentation and clinical course narrative with source order preserved.

evidence_events.source_span: A 34-year-old woman was referred to our outpatient clinic during her 31st week of pregnancy suffering from shoulder pain of the right side after lifting her 11-month-old first born.
During the first pregnancy, one and a half year ago she started noticing dyspnea which was still present at the time of her presentation in our clinic.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: one and a half year ago, still present at presentation

evidence_events.source_span: She was still reporting of dyspnea especially at physical activity and new symptoms, cough and hemoptysis, had appeared.
A chest X-ray showed a tumor mass in the right lung in close relation to the scapula.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: after persistent symptoms and chest X-ray arranged by GP

evidence_events.source_span: Clinical examination showed a local swelling at the medial border of the right scapula with dull pressure pain; shoulder movement was painless with full range of motion and strength; lung auscultation showed slightly attenuated vesicular breath sounds on the right side.
Ultrasound showed a large for gestational fetus with normal amniotic fluid and normal feto-placental perfusion; no pregnancy-related complications were detected.

MRI scans of the cranium and thorax revealed several highly suspicious lesions in the right lung, mediastinum, inferior angle of the right scapula with soft tissue component, and an osteolytic lesion of the 3rd thoracic vertebral body with affection of dura and spinal nerve.
Fine-needle biopsy of the pulmonary tumor mass was done by bronchoscopy; subsequently, cesarean section was directly followed by an open biopsy of the right scapula tumor lesion.
A NUT midline carcinoma was diagnosed by immunohistochemistry while FISH analysis did not show the typical NUT gene rearrangements due to cryptic translocation.
Examination of the placenta did not show any signs of malignancy.
PET-CT showed multiple metastases in both mammae in addition to the known tumor lesions.

Due to disseminated tumor disease in multiple non-resectable locations, palliative systemic chemotherapy with nab-paclitaxel and carboplatin was started; osteoprotective bisphosphonate therapy and ovary protection were also administered; radiotherapy was planned for bone metastases.
After five courses of systemic chemotherapy, the patient showed a decline of dyspnea and PET-CT demonstrated partial remission of known metastases in the right lung and both mammae.

PET-CT after 5 months showed tumor progression with growth of known metastases and new lesions in spine and pelvis; systemic treatment was changed to pembrolizumab; indication for BET inhibitors was proved.
