initial_presentation.encounter_context: presented at the Orthopaedic Outpatient Clinic of National Taiwan University Hospital, in June 2009
initial_presentation.chief_complaint: 2-week history of limp, fever and difficulty in moving the left leg
initial_presentation.first_contact_summary: At the emergency room, a physical examination showed no gross deformity, swelling, skin lesion, pitting oedema or local tenderness at the left leg. There were no recent body weight loss, jaundice, polyuria or palpable lymph nodes noted. Except for leucocytosis, all laboratory values were within reference range (white blood cell (WBC) count, 14.67 × 10^3/µl; red blood cell (RBC) count, 4.17 × 10^6/µl; haemoglobin (Hb), 11.5 g/dl; haematocrit (HCT), 34.2%; mean corpuscular volume (MCV), 82.0 fl; mean corpuscular haemoglobin (MCH), 27.6 pg; MCH concentration (MCHC), 33.6 g/dl; platelets, 363 × 10^3/µl; aspartate aminotransferase, 28 U/l; alkaline phosphatase, 121 U/l; lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), 220 U/l; and creatinine (CRE), 0.4 mg/dl). Plain radiography revealed a radiolucent lesion at the left proximal tibial meta-diaphysis with periosteal reaction.
presenting_symptoms: difficulty in moving the left leg

source_metadata.title: Solitary tibial lesion as the initial presentation of Langerhans cell histiocytosis: report of two cases and literature review
source_metadata.notes: Extraction based on case narrative sections and figures 1 and 2.

evidence_events.source_span: A 1-year-old male presented with a 2-week history of limp, fever and difficulty in moving the left leg; physical exam showed no gross deformity, swelling, skin lesion, pitting oedema or local tenderness at the left leg; no recent weight loss, jaundice, polyuria or palpable lymph nodes
Laboratory values showed leucocytosis (WBC 14.67 × 10^3/μl) with other labs within normal limits
Plain radiography revealed a radiolucent lesion at the left proximal tibial meta-diaphysis with periosteal reaction
Patient underwent curettage of the lesion and grafting with tobramycin-impregnated OSTEOSET® T Bone Graft Substitute

Pathology showed diffuse mononuclear cell infiltration with positive immunostaining for CD1a, S-100, and CD207, features of histiocytic origin; immunohistochemistry was negative for BRAF-V600E mutation
Skeletal survey and bone scan showed no additional skeletal lesions except the left tibia; brain MRI was negative for multisystem involvement
evidence_events.procedural_cue: skeletal survey, bone scan, brain MRI

evidence_events.source_span: Two months after curettage, a painless mass was observed at the left fronto-temporal area; skull radiographs and MRI revealed an osteolytic bone lesion at the left frontal skull and a mass near the left temporal facial region with temporalis involvement
Diagnosis updated to multifocal osseous LCH; chemotherapy with vincristine and prednisolone was started following the TPOG-LCH2002-LR protocol
Follow-up at 9 years showed no recurrence or new lesion
A 2-year-old female presented with a painful contusion of the right lower leg after a fall 1 week prior; palpable mass without cutaneous lesion at the right middle calf; no other systemic symptoms
Standard laboratory tests were within normal limits

Radiographs showed an osteolytic lesion at the tibial diaphysis with erosion of the medial cortex and laminated periosteal reaction; MRI showed uneven cortical thickening with amorphous bone marrow hyperaemia and oedema in the right anterior proximal tibial shaft
Right tibial shaft debridement was performed
Pathology revealed scattered dendritic Langerhans cells with positive immunohistochemistry for CD1a and CD207, but negative for BRAF-V600E mutation
Follow-up bone survey showed no other definite bone lesion
Patient received prophylactic chemotherapy following the TPOG-LCH2002-LR protocol
At one-year follow-up, patient showed no sign of recurrence

evidence_events.source_span: A 46-year-old male patient presented with a gait disorder and reported having experienced poor balance for 2 years.
Neurological examination revealed horizontal nystagmus, intention tremor, and ataxic gait, and his score on the Scale for the Assessment and Rating of Ataxia (SARA) was 24/40.
Routine hemogram and biochemical tests were normal, thyroid function tests were normal, but anti-thyroid peroxidase and anti-thyroglobulin levels were elevated.
Cerebral MRI showed significant bilateral cerebellar atrophy in the superior vermis.

Electroneuromyography was normal, and other known causes of ataxia were excluded (vitamin E, vitamin B12, coenzyme q10, viral infections, genetic tests as spinocerebellar ataxia, Friedreich's ataxia and whole exome sequencing).

Malignancy screening was performed; thyroid ultrasonography revealed a solitary hypoechoic nodule of 11 × 9 mm in the left lobe isthmus junction, and PET/CT detected elevated focal F-18 fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in the left lobe of the thyroid (SUV max: 7.22; late SUV max: 6.42).

Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was examined and found to be normal, and onconeuronal antibodies (anti-Hu, anti-Yo, anti-Ri, anti-amphiphysin, anti-Tr, anti-PPCA-2, anti-Ma, anti-CV-1, and anti-ANNA-3) were negative.
A biopsy of the thyroid nodule showed that it was consistent with category V (suspected papillary carcinoma) of the Bethesda system.
A bilateral total thyroidectomy was performed, and the pathologic examination revealed papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC).

The patient was diagnosed with 'definite' paraneoplastic neurological syndrome (PNS) according to diagnostic criteria (a classical syndrome, with cancer that develops within 5 years of the diagnosis of the neurological disorder and where the presence of onconeural antibodies is not required).
The patient was treated with 0.4 g/kg intravenous immunoglobulin for 10 days, following which partial improvement of the ataxia was detected by a SARA score of 20/40.
Radioactive iodine treatment was started by nuclear medicine during follow-up, and thyroid replacement therapy was also started when permanent hypothyroidism occurred.

source_metadata.title: Rare case of plasmablastic myeloma diagnosed on lung biopsy

evidence_events.source_span: A 60-year-old man presented on 23 January 2019 with a history of chest pain, back pain, abdominal distention, leg weakness and numbness.
Chest pain had started 6 weeks earlier, was sharp and mostly on the left side and worse with breathing. Pain was present all the time and was often made worse when laying down.

He reported increasing back pain while walking and had been taking pain killers for about 6 weeks prior to admission and was complaining of constipation. In addition, he had weakness and numbness of lower limbs suggestive of spinal cord compression.

General physical examination was normal. There was no clubbing or palpable lymphadenopathy. Cardiovascular and respiratory examination was essentially normal. His abdomen was distended but without palpable hepatomegaly. Examination of lower limbs demonstrated minimal leg weakness.

On admission the patient’s blood count was normal: haemoglobin 138 g/L, white cell count 5.14×10⁹/L with a normal differential and platelets 256×10⁹/L. Chemistry was normal with no evidence of renal failure or hypercalcaemia.

A contrast MRI scan of his spine showed widespread features of skeletal metastatic disease. At least three large soft-tissue deposits in the thoracic paraspinal space were noted, the largest on the left at level T2/T3. An intervertebral deposit at level T4/T5 was seen to be causing significant compression of the adjacent thoracic cord.
A routine chest X-ray at the time showed a left upper lobe mass raising the suspicion of possible pulmonary tumour.

A contrast CT scan was done which showed a large lobular mass with chest wall invasion particularly involving the left third rib, measuring up to 75 mm in maximum diameter with adjacent chest wall muscular invasion. A mild to moderate left-sided pleural effusion was noted. CT evidence of lumbar vertebral and pelvic bony metastatic appearances was also seen.

Lung biopsy was organised, which showed features of plasmablastic myeloma. The biopsy showed infiltration by sheets of atypical plasmacytoid cells with some multinucleated forms. Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated that this population was positive for CD138 and MUM1 and weakly positive for CD56. TTF1, p63, S100, AE1/AE3, CD3, CD20 and CD79a were negative. Ki67 was remarkably high (90%). Further immunostains revealed CD38 was strongly positive, lambda light chain restriction was seen on immunostaining as well as ISH. Cyclin d1, CD45, pancytokeratin and kappa were negative. Epstein-Barr virus encoded small nuclear RNAs was negative.

Immunoglobulin studies showed a slightly low IgA level of 0.62 g/L with a normal IgM level. Protein electrophoresis demonstrated the presence of 2 g/L of paraprotein consisting of IgG lambda paraprotein and lambda light chains. Light chain studies showed a normal free kappa concentration of 6.12 mg/L and an elevated free lambda concentration of 1178.1. His kappa/lambda ratio was reduced at 0.01.
Bone marrow aspirate, trephine and immunophenotyping showed no evidence of infiltration by myeloma.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: bone marrow aspirate and trephine biopsy

evidence_events.source_span: Routine viral serology was negative for hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV 1/2.

The patient received radiotherapy to his spine and was started on chemotherapy with bortezomib (Velcade), cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin and prednisolone (VCAP). Repeat CT scans showed a reduction in size of previous spinal lesions.

Due to evidence of disease progression, the decision was made to start him on a second line chemotherapy regimen. He received dexamethasone, thalidomide, cisplatin, doxorubicin, cyclophosphamide and etoposide (DT-PACE) chemotherapy. Repeat CT scans showed good response.
He went onto an autologous stem cell transplantation on 29 January 2020 at King’s College Hospital. He successfully engrafted his neutrophils on day 12.

A follow-up CT scan was done in early May 2020 following his stem cell transplant. This showed ongoing good response to therapy at his previously identified sites of disease, healing at the anterior ends of the left fourth rib was noted. A further reduction in the previously noted paraspinal soft-tissue was seen with now only minimal residual soft-tissue in the aortocaval region just above the bifurcation of the aorta.

source_metadata.title: Metastatic Mixed Adeno-Neuroendocrine Carcinoma of the Colon to the Liver with Multiple Peritoneal Deposits: A Case Report

evidence_events.source_span: A 48-year-old man presented with a 1-month history of right upper-quadrant pain and unintentional weight loss of 18 kg. He was also complaining of constipation and fatigue for 6 days.

Physical examination revealed a palpable mass in the epigastric region; abdomen was soft, not tender or distended; rectal examination revealed an empty rectum; patient was vitally stable and afebrile.
Laboratory investigations, including tumor markers, were all within normal ranges.

Contrast-enhanced CT scan of chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed circumferential wall thickening of the proximal descending colon, 6.3 cm long, with maximum wall thickness of 1.6 cm; peri-colonic fat stranding; multifocal regional nodules and lymph nodes; multiple peritoneal deposits including a 4.9×3 cm deposit along the mesenteric margin; innumerable hypovascular ring-enhancing hepatic masses scattered in both lobes involving all liver segments, largest 8.1 cm at segment 4b; necrotic lymphadenopathy at gastrohepatic ligament; lungs clear with no suspicious pulmonary nodules.
Full colonoscopy showed circumferential wall thickening; biopsy was taken; stenting was performed over the area of thickening secondary to the tumor.

Histopathological examination of the colon biopsy demonstrated dual morphologies: predominant component of tumor cells arranged in nested, organoid, and rosette-like growth patterns with brisk mitotic activity (30 mitoses per 10 high-powered fields); second minor component (30%) exhibited intermingled malignant glandular structures consistent with adenocarcinoma.

Immunohistochemical stains showed the predominant component was diffusely positive for Pancytokeratin (AE1/AE3) and Synaptophysin and negative for Chromogranin; adenocarcinoma component was negative for neuroendocrine markers; Ki-67 proliferative index in neuroendocrine carcinoma estimated at more than 90%.
Diagnosis was metastatic poorly differentiated mixed adenoneuroendocrine carcinoma (MANEC) of the colon with liver metastasis and multiple peritoneal deposits; lesions deemed unresectable.
Patient received 9 cycles of cisplatin and etoposide chemotherapy over 8 months; CT scan showed regression of the primary tumor, liver, and bony metastasis indicating good response to chemotherapy.
Patient later developed right retinal vein thrombosis.

source_metadata.title: Primary Takotsubo Syndrome as a Complication of Bladder Cancer Treatment in a 62-Year-Old Woman

evidence_events.source_span: An obese female patient, aged 62, with a 3-day medical history of chest pain, was transferred to the Department of Invasive Cardiology by a district hospital as she was suspected to have had an acute coronary event.
She had the habit of smoking tobacco and had chronic arterial hypertension, hypothyroidism, and inflammatory arthritis.

Six months before admission, the patient had been diagnosed with a high-grade urothelial bladder cancer. After the transurethral electroresection of the tumor 5 months before admission and the following chemotherapy (gemcitabine and cisplatin), the patient had been qualified for a further cancer surgery.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: 6 months before admission; 5 months before admission

evidence_events.source_span: On admission to the clinic, she remained hemodynamically stable, with no chest pain, and had a systemic arterial pressure of 110/80 mmHg.
The ECG record demonstrated a normal sinus rhythm of 96/min with singular ventricular and supraventricular beats, as well as inverted T waves in the leads from above the anterior and lateral wall.
The patient was subject to cardiac catheterization, which demonstrated minor atherosclerotic changes in the coronary arteries.
The left ventriculography conducted at the same time presented akinesis of the apex and the apical and mid-segment of the anterior wall, and the ejection fraction was 38%.

Laboratory testing revealed decreased red blood cells with a hemoglobin level of 9.3 g/dl and a markedly elevated concentration of cardiac markers such as troponin I hs – 9552 ng/l, B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP – 175 pg/ml), and N-terminal pro-B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP – 2691 pg/ml).
The subsequent ECG records demonstrated deeply inverted T waves and numerous ventricular premature beats, with the QTc interval increased to 528 ms.

In the echocardiographic examination, apart from the normal function of all valves, an improved left ventricular contractive function with 47% ejection fraction was observed, which confirmed the diagnosis of TTS.
On the 4th day of hospitalization, the patient was discharged and referred for further surgical and oncological treatment.

source_metadata.title: Patient with respiratory distress, facial oedema and refractory hypokalaemia

evidence_events.source_span: A 56-year-old Asian man admitted with a 3-month history of worsening respiratory distress, proximal muscle weakness, hyperpigmentation, significant loss of weight (10 kg) and apathy. He had developed facial swelling in the last 1 month, which had gradually progressed to upper limbs and chest with a worsening headache.

Clinical examination revealed prominent upper body swelling including face, neck, chest and upper limbs with skin plethora and prominent neck and upper body veins. He had hyperpigmentation of the face and hands. The patient was cachectic with a low body mass index (18.1 kg/m2). He had severe hypertension (180/100 mm Hg), moderate respiratory distress and reduced proximal muscle power in all four limbs.

Initial biochemical investigations revealed severe hypokalaemia (2.1 mmol/L), hyperglycaemia (random glucose 323 mg/dL), mild hypocalcaemia (1.99 mmol/L), metabolic alkalosis (pH 7.63, bicarbonate 37.7 mmol/L), and refractory hypokalaemia despite intravenous KCl infusion.

Chest radiograph revealed a mass lesion in the right hilar region; contrast-enhanced CT scan showed a lobulated solid soft-tissue mass (11.7 × 5.7 × 4.7 cm) at the right hilar region with severely stretched proximal superior vena cava and luminal narrowing confirming superior vena cava syndrome (SVCS).
Cytological examination of bronchial brushing indicated atypical cells with nuclear atypia; histological examination of bronchial biopsy confirmed small cell lung carcinoma (SCLC).

Further investigations showed metabolic alkalosis and urinary potassium wasting. Raised 9 am serum cortisol level (1640 nmol/L) and increased ACTH level (285 pg/mL) indicated ACTH-dependent hypercortisolism.

Patient was on high-dose intravenous dexamethasone for 2 days at the time of basal cortisol measurement; unsuppressed cortisol despite exogenous glucocorticoids suggested ectopic ACTH secretion. Bilateral inferior petrosal sinus sampling was not performed due to severe comorbidities.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: at time of basal cortisol measurement

evidence_events.source_span: Immunohistochemical staining of bronchial biopsy was strongly positive for chromogranin and synaptophysin; intense staining for ACTH confirmed the source of ACTH as the SCLC tumour.

Patient was treated with chemotherapy (etoposide and cisplatin), spironolactone and intravenous KCl for hypokalaemia, ketoconazole for steroidogenesis inhibition, and prophylactic antibiotics. Serum cortisol level reduced from 1640 nmol/L to 213 nmol/L indicating good initial response.

Patient became clinically and psychologically stable with subsidence of SVCS and hypercortisolism symptoms but developed severe neutropenia after chemotherapy, progressed to severe pneumonia, and died 10 days later.

He had undergone examinations and consultation with a cardiologist, who identified arrhythmia and started medication (metoprolol 25 mg). Because of the continuation of symptoms, after 1 week, a geriatrician performed general examinations, like a hemogram, PSA, urea, creatinine, and albumin. The examinations evidenced hemoglobin 12.0 g/dL, total PSA was 130 ng/mL, and free PSA > 20 ng/mL. The patient stated that the last PSA done 2 years ago was normal. source_metadata.title: Pancytopenia as an initial manifestation of prostate cancer: a case report
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case narrative sections only, preserving source order and granularity.

evidence_events.source_span: An 86-year-old Caucasian man presented to the emergency department with a chief complaint of worsening dyspnea.
One month prior to admission, he started with progressive dyspnea on minimal effort, fatigue, and palpitations. Cardiologist identified arrhythmia and started metoprolol 25 mg.

Initial labs showed hemoglobin 12.0 g/dL, total PSA 130 ng/mL, free PSA > 20 ng/mL; prostate ultrasound showed normal prostate size (10 cm3) and no nodularity; bone scintigraphy showed probable bone metastases in L4 vertebra and right iliac crest.
One month later, labs showed hemoglobin 6.2 g/dL, platelets 51,000/μL, leukocytes 3950/μL, total PSA 84 ng/mL, free PSA > 20.0 ng/mL.

Patient developed pancytopenia with frank dyspnea; peripheral blood smear showed marked anisocytosis with macrocytosis and elliptocytes, thrombocytopenia, hypogranulation of neutrophils with segmentation failure; vitamin B12 and folic acid normal; reticulocytosis 5.2%; LDH increased at 350 IU/L.

Bone marrow aspiration showed markedly increased cellularity with cell conglomerates of non-hematological characteristics suggestive of spinal infiltration; bone marrow biopsy showed diffuse bone marrow replacement by metastatic adenocarcinoma; PSA immunostaining positive in tumor cells.
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: Bone marrow biopsy and PSA stain confirmed metastatic prostate adenocarcinoma.

evidence_events.source_span: Prostate examination revealed normal prostate without nodularity and normal consistency; kidney ultrasound showed non-obstructive nephrolithiasis and diffusely thickened bladder walls; abdominal CT showed increased density areas in L4 vertebra posterior elements suggestive of secondary neoplastic involvement; lymph node metastases in para-aortic, interaortocaval, and right iliac chains; pulmonary nodules up to 1.0 cm in middle lobe.

source_metadata.title: Malignant ascites following radical nephrectomy for cystic renal cell carcinoma

evidence_events.source_span: A 69-year-old man presented to the emergency department with a 1-week history of worsening generalised abdominal pain, abdominal distension and loss of appetite.

Clinical examination indicated the presence of ascites associated with generalised mild abdominal tenderness. He was haemodynamically stable with no evidence of systemic infection. There were no features suggestive of peritonism.
This presentation occurred 5 months following a laparoscopic left radical nephrectomy for an 80 mm contrast-enhancing, Bosniak IV left lower pole cystic renal mass.

Histopathology of the specimen showed a pT2 Nx type 1 papillary RCC, nuclear grade 2, with the greatest tumour dimension of 80 mm. Necrotic features were evident. Negative surgical margin was achieved, and all tumours were confined within the renal capsule without lymphovascular invasion. There was no evidence of rhabdoid or sarcomatoid differentiation.
The cytology from the aspirated cystic content showed no evidence of malignancy.

CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis identified a moderate-volume ascites with evidence of peritoneal nodules. Other findings included right pleural effusion and a 14 mm right apical subpleural nodule. There was no locoregional recurrence in the left renal bed.
Diagnostic paracentesis was performed with fluid biochemistry: lactate dehydrogenase 1255 U/L, total protein 53 g/L, pH 7.76 and alkaline phosphatase 51 U/L.

Fluid cytology showed neoplastic cells with moderate amount of eosinophilic cytoplasm and rare papillary-like structures. Immunochemistry staining showed PAX8-positive, CD10-positive and CK7-positive cells consistent with carcinoma of renal origin.
There was no bacterial growth from the ascitic fluid culture.
Repeat ultrasound prior to discharge showed marked interval reduction of the ascites volume.
The patient was commenced on 20 mg daily cabozantinib, a small-molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitor, with initial good improvement in abdominal pain within 1 month of therapy.
Repeat staging CT showed stable peritoneal and pulmonary nodules and resolution of ascites and pleural effusion. No other metastatic foci were identified on CT and whole-body bone scan.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: repeat staging CT and bone scan

evidence_events.source_span: Following a trial of higher dosage, the patient developed multiple symptoms including chest pain, abdominal pain, heartburn and swelling of hands and feet, prompting dose reduction.
The patient subsequently developed recurrence of malignant ascites 5 months after presentation, managed with regular paracentesis due to reaccumulation.

evidence_events.source_span: A 32-year-old man presented to the Emergency Department with a 4-h history of severe abdominal pain in the right upper quadrant. He reported having similar episodes of this pain recently, but they were milder in severity. Such episodes were precipitated by meal intake. The pain was not associated with nausea or vomiting. He also noticed a yellowish discoloration of his skin and eyes over the previous days.

Upon presentation, he was icteric and his vital signs were as follows: blood pressure 128/84 mmHg, pulse rate 60 beats/min, respiratory rate 12 breaths/min, temperature 37.1°C, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. The abdominal examination revealed tenderness in the right upper quadrant with a positive Murphy sign. The abdomen was soft, with no guarding or rigidity.

Blood analysis revealed a hemoglobin level of 14.8 g/dL, leukocyte count of 4.8×10³/μL, platelet count of 290×10³/μL, total bilirubin of 3.6 mg/dL with a direct bilirubin of 3.0 mg/dL, alkaline phosphatase level of 323 IU/L, γ-glutamyltransferase level of 1153 IU/L, alanine transaminase level of 685 IU/L, and aspartate transaminase level of 319 IU/L. Amylase, urea, and electrolytes were within normal ranges. The patient had a normal coagulation profile and a negative viral hepatitis serology.

Abdominal ultrasound examination revealed numerous echo-genic foci lining the gallbladder with posterior acoustic shadowing denoting cholelithiasis and the presence of a positive Murphy sign. The common bile duct had a normal diameter of 6 mm. No wall thickening or pericholecystic fluid was noted.

Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography was attempted but aborted due to technical difficulties caused by a mass lesion in the second part of the duodenum. Biopsy specimens were obtained by fine-needle aspiration. A stent was placed to relieve obstruction.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography with biopsy and stent placement

evidence_events.source_span: Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography demonstrated a well-defined broad-based pedunculated solid mass lesion within the lumen of the second part of the duodenum inseparable from the ampulla of Vater. Two small calculi were noted in the lower part of the common bile duct. Mild diffuse thickening of the gallbladder wall was present without pericholecystic fat stranding or free fluid collection. No dilatation of the pancreatic ducts was seen.

Histopathological examination of biopsy specimens revealed an unencapsulated submucosal lesion composed of epithelioid, spindle, and ganglion-like cells. The spindle cells showed immunohistochemical positivity for S100, synaptophysin, and chromogranin.

A staging computed tomography scan demonstrated an ampullary mass lesion measuring 2.0×2.7×3.4 cm along with multiple enlarged mesenteric lymph nodes. No abnormalities were found in the thoracic region.

During the hospital course, the patient experienced multiple spikes of fever and elevation of leucocytes up to 13.0×10³/μL. Intravenous piperacillin/tazobactam was started for suspected cholangitis, with subsequent clinical and laboratory improvement. The patient was discharged on oral antibiotic therapy.
Surgical resection of the tumor was advised. However, the patient refused the operation despite the recommendation of the oncology team.

source_metadata.title: Paraneoplastic sensorimotor neuropathy and ventral cauda equina nerve root enhancement as initial presentation of small cell lung carcinoma: a case study

evidence_events.source_span: 51-year-old man presented with asymmetric subacute sensorimotor deficits in the lower limbs, weakness throughout the right lower limb and normal strength on the left with objective numbness in a mixed dermatomal and stocking-glove distribution

Electrophysiology was consistent with axonal sensorimotor neuropathy; right peroneal motor response was absent with reduced right peroneal sensory amplitude and velocity; needle EMG showed increased insertional activity with fibrillations and positive sharp waves in right leg muscles and active denervation in L5 paraspinous muscles

Cerebrospinal fluid showed pleocytosis and elevated protein (WBC 14 × 10⁶/L and protein 1.1 g/L initially; persistently elevated protein 0.58 g/L and 1.67 g/L and pleocytosis 13 × 10⁶/L and 8 × 10⁶/L on repeat CSF)

Magnetic resonance imaging of the spine showed smooth enhancement of the ventral nerve roots of the cauda equina extending from T11-T12 to the lumbosacral thecal sac; denervation atrophy noted over right psoas and dorsal paraspinal muscles; mild STIR high signal and enlargement in extrathecal lumbosacral plexus

Flow cytometry negative twice for neurolymphomatosis; random skin and bone marrow biopsies negative; left sural nerve biopsy showed mild nonspecific changes with patchy loss of larger myelinated fibers and no vasculitis, amyloid, or neoplastic infiltrates; gastrocnemius biopsy showed mild nonspecific changes without inflammatory infiltrates
Serum protein electrophoresis revealed mild polyclonal increase in gamma globulins without monoclonal peak; porphyria screen negative; low-dose full-body CT negative
Full-dose CT chest, abdomen, and pelvis with contrast revealed vascular scarring of the left lower lobe and 7 × 6 mm soft tissue nodule in right upper lobe apex
Positron emission tomography identified fluorodeoxyglucose-avid right pretracheal, precarinal, subcarinal, and hilar lymphadenopathy with no hypermetabolism in nerve roots
Bronchoscopy-guided lymph node biopsy confirmed diagnosis of small cell lung carcinoma

Serum and CSF paraneoplastic and peripheral neurologic disease antibody panels were negative including onconeural antibodies anti-Hu, anti-Ri, anti-amphiphysin, anti-Yo, anti-Ma, anti-CV2.1, anti-recoverin, anti-SOX1, anti-titin, and antiganglioside antibodies
Patient treated with intravenous immunoglobulin, IV methylprednisolone, and chemoradiotherapy; subsequently experienced improvement in motor function and weight gain

source_metadata.title: Immune thrombocytopenic purpura secondary to SARS-CoV-2 infection in a child with acute lymphoblastic leukaemia: a case report and review of literature

evidence_events.source_span: A five-and-a-half-year-old girl was brought with complaints of reddish-purple spots on neck, shoulder, arms and legs. She was a known case of B-cell ALL, diagnosed 18 weeks ago and was started on MCP 841 protocol.

She had completed 4 weeks of induction phase with vincristine, L-asparaginase, oral prednisolone and intrathecal methotrexate, then consolidation phase for 4 weeks with vincristine, 6-mercaptopurine and intrathecal methotrexate, and was started on maintenance therapy.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: had completed 4 weeks of induction phase; then consolidation phase; started on maintenance therapy

evidence_events.source_span: Five days into her maintenance therapy, she developed high-grade fever with cold and coryza. RT-PCR of the oropharyngeal swab was positive for SARS-CoV-2. Chemotherapy was withheld and she was managed symptomatically. Symptoms subsided over 5 days. Routine blood examination was normal at that time.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: Five days into her maintenance therapy

evidence_events.source_span: On the 22nd day of recovery from SARS-CoV-2, she presented with reddish-purple spots on neck, shoulder, arms and legs. On examination, she was alert and playful with stable vitals. Several pinpoint and round to oval (>1 cm) reddish-purple, non-blanching spots suggestive of petechiae and purpura were seen on skin over neck, shoulder, arms and legs. No other bleeding manifestations. Rest of systemic exam was normal.

Routine blood examination showed normal haemoglobin (119 g/L), normal white cell count (5.85×10^9/L), but severe thrombocytopenia (3000/mm^3). Peripheral smear showed normal morphology of red blood cells and leucocytes but significantly reduced platelets. No blast cells or atypical cells were seen. Liver and kidney function tests were normal. Coagulation profile (PT, aPTT, INR) was normal. Fibrinogen slightly elevated (411 mg/dL; range 162–401 mg/dL). Serum triglyceride (55 mg/dL), serum ferritin (350 ng/mL), and pro-calcitonin levels were normal.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: Peripheral smear, coagulation profile, liver and kidney function tests

evidence_events.source_span: Bone marrow aspiration cytology showed normocellular bone marrow with increased megakaryopoiesis and no blast cells.
Antinuclear antibody (ANA) levels, thyroid function tests were normal. Anti-HCV antibody was non-reactive. Direct Coombs’ test was negative. Immunoglobulin profile (IgA, IgM, IgE, IgG) was normal.
With history of SARS-CoV-2 infection and exclusion of relapse or other causes, diagnosis of ITP secondary to SARS-CoV-2 was established.

Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg) was administered at 1 g/kg. Oral prednisolone was started at 2 mg/kg/day and later increased to 4 mg/kg/day. There was no response; platelet count remained below 10,000/mm^3 with new petechiae and oral mucosal bleeding. Platelet transfusion was given again.

Due to refractory thrombocytopenia, thrombopoietin receptor agonists were started: a single dose of romiplostim (1 mcg/kg) and eltrombopag (25 mg/day). Two weeks after initiation, platelet counts improved to 24,000/mm^3 and subsequently to 157,000/mm^3.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: two weeks after thrombopoietin receptor agonist initiation

evidence_events.source_span: Eltrombopag was stopped 2 weeks after discharge; prednisolone was tapered and stopped after 1 more week. The patient was well with normal blood counts and maintenance chemotherapy was restarted.

source_metadata.title: Rare, disseminated Kaposi sarcoma in advanced HIV with high-burden pulmonary and skeletal involvement

evidence_events.source_span: A 30-year-old heterosexual man presented with a 4-day history of dry cough and exertional dyspnoea, hypoxic on room air (SpO2 92%), afebrile, tachycardic at 117 beats/min, with severe lower limb and scrotal oedema, disseminated pigmented rash on torso, extensive non-tender cervical lymphadenopathy, marked cachexia (45 kg), and unquantified weight loss over the preceding year.
Chest radiograph showed extensive airspace opacification involving upper-mid and lower zones bilaterally, more marked in middle zone and left base.

Blood tests showed low albumin (29 g/L), elevated C reactive protein (73 mg/L), slightly raised ferritin (395 µg/L), and grossly elevated D-dimer (4.79 mg/L). Transthoracic echocardiography indicated reduced left ventricular ejection fraction of 20%–25%.

Two negative nasopharyngeal swabs for SARS-CoV-2 by RT-PCR; CT thorax showed nodular interlobular and peribronchial interstitial thickening with diffuse thickening of major fissures without cavitation; innumerable multifocal lytic bone lesions predominantly in pelvis and cervical, thoracic, and lumbar spine.

CT-guided biopsy of iliac crest bone lesion showed spindle cell proliferation strongly positive for CD34 and HHV-8 on immunohistochemistry, confirming widely disseminated HIV-associated Kaposi sarcoma.

HIV serology positive; CD4+ T-helper lymphocyte count 116 cells/µL (9%); initial viral load 87,272 copies/mL; patient denied intravenous drug use or sex with other men, presumed heterosexual acquisition.

Serum β-D-glucan and serum cryptococcal antigen were negative, helping exclude opportunistic infections such as Pneumocystis jirovecii and cryptococcosis; differential included disseminated mycobacterial infection, bacillary angiomatosis, lymphoma, bronchogenic neoplasm, Langerhans’s cell histiocytosis, and disseminated tuberculosis.

Patient received broad-spectrum anti-infective agents including intravenous trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, meropenem, ganciclovir, and combination antiretroviral therapy (bictegravir, tenofovir alafenamide, emtricitabine) while undergoing evaluation.
Cardiac MRI performed 4 weeks into admission showed normalization of left ventricular function; patient commenced weekly paclitaxel chemotherapy for symptomatic visceral Kaposi sarcoma.

Over 3 months, patient showed clinical improvement with reduced peripheral oedema, weight gain, improved oxygenation; viral load suppressed since June 2021; CD4+ count improved to 221 cells/µL (15%); recent CT showed substantial radiological response with reduced nodular interlobular septal thickening and stable skeletal lesions with increased sclerosis.

source_metadata.title: BRAF V600E-mutated combined large cell neuroendocrine carcinoma and adenocarcinoma responding to targeted therapy

evidence_events.source_span: A 57-year-old woman with a history of well-controlled bronchial asthma and smoking (25 pack-years) was referred to our hospital for headache and vomiting.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: One month prior to the consult, the patient noted the headache

evidence_events.source_span: A head MRI showed a large tumour in her brain
The whole-body CT revealed a tumour in the right pulmonary hilum and mediastinal lymphadenopathies
The tumour was resected to control the symptoms associated with the brain tumour

The pathological specimens of the cerebral tumour contained a mixture of adenocarcinoma-like area with atypical cells forming small ducts and nests and an area with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm and prominent nucleoli

Immunohistochemical analysis showed that CK AE1/3, CK7 and synaptophysin were diffusely positive in all regions; TTF-1 was diffusely positive in the adenocarcinoma-like area but focally positive in the other; chromogranin A and CD56 were focally positive; p40, Napsin A and CK20 were negative
Endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial needle aspiration on mediastinal lymph nodes showed atypical cells considered to be LCNEC without adenocarcinoma-like atypical cells
Gene analysis using the mediastinal lymph node sample detected a BRAF V600E mutation
Immunostaining of BRAF V600E with cerebellar tumours tested positive in both adenocarcinoma and LCNEC
Next-generation sequencing data showed two major somatic mutations: BRAF V600E (MAF 0.483) and TP53 H179Q (MAF 0.916)
Dabrafenib and trametinib (DT) combination therapy was started for BRAF-mutated NSCLC; fever and rash appeared on the fourth day, leading to temporary suspension and dose adjustment
evidence_events.procedural_cue: DT therapy initiation and management of adverse events

evidence_events.source_span: CT 10 weeks after start of DT revealed a decrease in size of the tumour in the right lung hilum, corresponding to a partial response
MRI showed no recurrence after surgical removal of the brain tumour for at least a year
evidence_events.temporal_cue: at least a year after surgery

source_metadata.title: Abnormal Schwannoma-like Growth of multiple, multifocal BRAF V600E-positive Glioblastoma in the Interior Acoustic Canal with Leptomeningeal Infiltration: a case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 60-year-old Caucasian male was admitted to the emergency unit upon having a seizure, with no significant medical history.
He reported a 2-month history of numbness in the left hand and intermittent dysarthria.
Physical examination showed impaired fine motor skills and hypoesthesia in the left arm.

Cranial magnetic resonance imaging (cMRI) revealed a multifocal 38 × 42 × 38 mm lesion in the right temporal lobe and a singular lesion in the left internal auditory canal (IAC) with a discreet hyperintense signal and abnormal enhancement.
Gross resection of the lesion in the right temporal lobe was performed.

Immunohistopathological analyses identified the lesion as an isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) wild-type epithelioid glioblastoma with O6-methylguanine-DNA methyltransferase (MGMT) methylation at 12% and BRAF V600E mutation.

The patient was started on adjuvant concomitant chemoradiotherapy that included temozolomide and stereotactic radiotherapy of the tumor cavity in the right temporal lobe and its marginalizing solid components.
The enhancement in the left IAC was not irradiated as the signal alteration was not interpreted as a metastasis.

A cMRI on therapy day 42 showed that the right-sided tumor cavity remained unchanged in size but with a larger perifocal edema; however, the lesion in the left IAC excluded from the irradiation field was progressive.
Within 2 weeks, the patient developed marked imbalance, new rapidly advancing left-sided facial nerve weakness, dysphagia, dysarthria, and left-sided deafness.
The Romberg test was positive, and his gait was wide and ataxic, requiring assistance to prevent falling during tandem walking trials.

Four weeks following adjuvant chemoradiotherapy, cMRI demonstrated rapid growth of the lesion in the left IAC measuring 31 × 24 × 33 mm and infiltrating adjacent cranial nerves (II, V, VII–XII), leptomeninges, and the left parotid gland.
The meninges of the Sylvian fissure showed enhanced contrast uptake breaching the left orbit and cerebellum with suspicious infiltrations into the medulla oblongata.
A lumbar puncture confirmed meningeosis glioblastoma on cytopathological analysis.
Laboratory tests showed that hematological and organ functions were not impaired.
Radiotherapy of the whole brain was initiated to control the impact of the expanding intracranial mass.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: after progression and confirmation of meningeosis glioblastoma

evidence_events.source_span: The patient died 4 months after the initial diagnosis owing to rapid tumor progression that led to paralyses of multiple cranial nerves.

source_metadata.title: Necrotizing fasciitis of the vulva due to carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae as a complication of acute myeloid leukemia treatment: a case report

evidence_events.source_span: A Caucasian 52-year-old woman was diagnosed with acute myeloid leukemia (AML) after presenting with respiratory symptoms, fever, pancytopenia, and febrile neutropenia; bone marrow aspirate showed 42% myeloblasts, immunophenotyping showed CD34+, CD117+, CD13+ myeloblasts, and cytogenetics showed normal karyotype with no recurrent mutations.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: bone marrow aspirate and core biopsy

evidence_events.source_span: On examination, the patient was fatigued with temperature 38.3°C, pale conjunctiva and oral mucosa, normal vital signs, no hepatosplenomegaly or adenopathies, and normal neurologic exam.

Laboratory hemogram showed hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL, leukocytes 1940 cells/μL with neutrophils 230 cells/μL, lymphocytes 1650 cells/μL, platelets 61,000 cells/μL; normal glucose, renal, liver, and thyroid function tests; negative serologies for HIV, syphilis, hepatitis B, C, A, E, toxoplasmosis, and herpes virus type 2; positive serologies for cytomegalovirus, Epstein–Barr virus, and herpes virus type 1 with negative viral loads; rectal swab positive for carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae colonization.

Patient received first line chemotherapy with idarubicin and cytarabine (IDAC regimen) starting 31 March 2019, with prophylaxis using oral fluconazole and acyclovir; on day +8 developed distal thrombophlebitis of right lower limb with cutaneous bacterial infection treated with intravenous vancomycin, meropenem, amikacin, and colistin, with resolution; blood cultures at that time were negative.

On day +11 after chemotherapy, patient developed fever, elevated inflammatory markers (CRP 30 mg/mL, procalcitonin 16 ng/mL), vulvar pain, swelling, pruritus, and a hard painful phlegm on right outer labia with surrounding inflammation; previous antimicrobials were suspended except colistin; empiric intravenous acyclovir, tigecycline, and daptomycin were started; lesion rapidly progressed over 48 hours to extensive cellulitis and necrosis with hematologic, neurologic, liver, and respiratory dysfunction.

Blood cultures and vulvar exudate collected at day +11 isolated carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae resistant to meropenem and amikacin but sensitive to tigecycline and colistin; antibiotic regimen was changed to intravenous ceftazidime/avibactam, meropenem, amikacin, vancomycin, oral acyclovir, and posaconazole for 13 days.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: blood cultures and vulvar exudate collected

evidence_events.source_span: Pelvic CT scan performed at day +12 showed diffuse perineal adipose tissue densification with cutaneous thickening and liquid lamination extending to anterior inferior abdominal wall and presacral area; no gas or liquid collections; mesenteric and iliac adenomegalies present.

Surgical superficial debridement of soft tissue above fascia of pubic area extending to right paragenital area was performed; patient admitted to ICU for short period due to multiorgan dysfunction; post-surgery, vulvar necrotic tissue persisted with less edema and cellulitis, granulation tissue, serous exudate, and mummified pubic wound developed.

Second surgical debridement with extensive removal of necrotic and granulation tissue was performed; carbapenemase-producing Klebsiella was isolated from removed skin; antibiotics changed to intravenous colistin, daptomycin, amphotericin B, meropenem, and amikacin; ceftazidime/avibactam and vancomycin were suspended; rapid recovery with progressive wound closure and pain control observed.

Bone marrow aspirate on day +44 after chemotherapy showed 9% blastic cells and 37% monocytoid cells, but immunophenotyping revealed 3.3% blastic population; patient considered in complete response after first induction cycle; 5-azacitidine started for maintenance.

On day 7 after second surgery, recurrence of local cellulitis at surgical borders with increased CRP prompted antibiotic change; intravenous ceftazidime/avibactam was resumed and colistin suspended; progressive local and systemic infection control observed.

Surgical wound treated with sterilization and cleansing using Dakin's solution, hydrogen peroxide, honey antimicrobial wound matrix, and negative pressure wound vacuum suction dressings, resulting in successful recovery with viable granulation tissue.
Skin graft performed 6 weeks after surgical debridement using donor skin from patient's right thigh; plastic surgery team maintained follow-up with hydration dressings and good clinical evolution.
Antimicrobial therapy was suspended after 27-day course of ceftazidime/avibactam; patient remained free from antibiotics for 2 weeks with no evidence of infection recurrence.
At 60 days after skin graft, patient was asymptomatic, undergoing motor rehabilitation with excellent tolerance and tissue healing.

evidence_events.source_section: Case presentation and investigations / Case report number 1
evidence_events.source_span: A female patient in her 60s, multiparous, ECOG-PS grade 0, without relevant personal or family history of cancer disease, presented with a vulvar mass on the left labium minus that measured approximately 20 mm.

evidence_events.source_section: Case presentation and investigations / Case report number 1
evidence_events.source_span: Pathological review reported a nodule of 32 mm, with cribriform and papillary architecture, with some solid areas, moderate cytological atypia, and mitotic index of 31 mitoses per 10 HPF; no lymphovascular or perineural invasion; tumour margins 0.3 mm deep and 0.9 mm lateral.

evidence_events.source_section: Case presentation and investigations / Case report number 1
evidence_events.source_span: Immunohistochemistry showed positivity for ER (90%-100%), CK7, CAM5.2, and GATA3; negativity for PR, GCDDP-15, SOX10, p63, and CK20; HER-2 equivocal (2+) but FISH negative for amplification.

evidence_events.source_section: Case presentation and investigations / Case report number 1
evidence_events.source_span: Clinical examination, breast ultrasound, mammography, chest CT, gastrointestinal tract study, and whole-body PET showed no evidence of primary breast tumour or additional hypermetabolic lesions besides the vulvar lesion.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: breast imaging, chest CT, GI tract study, PET

evidence_events.source_section: Case presentation and investigations / Case report number 2
evidence_events.source_span: A multiparous woman in her 70s, ECOG-PS grade 2, with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, obstructive sleep apnoea, and family history of melanoma and colon cancer, presented with a 30 mm vulvar mass on the inner side of right labium majus.

evidence_events.source_section: Case presentation and investigations / Case report number 2
evidence_events.source_span: Pathological review described a neoplasm with ductal architecture, nests and cords, infiltrative growth, moderate to high nuclear atypia, mitotic index 20 per 10 HPF, lymphovascular and perineural invasion, and tumour-positive margins.

evidence_events.source_section: Case presentation and investigations / Case report number 2
evidence_events.source_span: IHC showed positivity for CK7, SOX10, p53, and E-cadherin; negativity for ER, PR, HER-2, GCDDP-15, GATA-3, TTF1, p63, PAX-8, and CK20; HER-2 negative (0).

evidence_events.source_section: Case presentation and investigations / Case report number 2
evidence_events.source_span: Abdominal and pelvic MRI revealed a 12 mm right inguinal heterogeneous adenopathy; breast examination and imaging were negative; gastrointestinal tract study and chest CT were normal; carcinoembryonic antigen elevated at 12.2 ng/mL; CA 125, CA 15.3, and CA 19.19 normal.

evidence_events.source_section: Case presentation and investigations / Case report number 2
evidence_events.source_span: Biopsy of the right inguinal adenopathy revealed metastasis of the vulvar neoplasia.

evidence_events.source_section: Case presentation and investigations / Case report number 2
evidence_events.source_span: Gynaecological examination showed a painful scarring area adherent to the pubic bone; PET revealed hypermetabolic lesions in right inguinal and external iliac regions, likely metastases.

Radical scar tissue excision with preservation of the clitoris and left inguinal lymphadenectomy was performed; pathology showed no residual neoplasia and no lymph node metastasis in seven excised nodes; hormone therapy with aromatase inhibitor was started.

Neoadjuvant chemotherapy with four cycles of carboplatin and paclitaxel was given; PET showed tumour regression with lower FDG uptake in right inguinal metastasis and absence of uptake in right external iliac region.

Radical excision of scar tissue and right inguinal lymphadenectomy showed residual neoplasia with infiltrative borders, extensive lymphovascular invasion, positive margins, and two metastatic lymph nodes.
Postoperative vulvar surgical wound dehiscence occurred; surgery to widen margins was performed; pathology showed persistent tumour with positive margins.
New PET showed hyperuptake in right external iliac ganglion and hypermetabolic areas in right vulva; external radiotherapy with palliative intent was administered with good tolerance.

hidden_reference.final_diagnosis_verbatim: Adenocarcinoma of mammary gland type (AMGT) of the vulva, invasive ductal carcinoma, no special type, with molecular variability including ER-positive and triple-negative subtypes.
diagnostic_reasoning_verbatim_spans: Morphological aspects combined with the IHC profile support the diagnosis of AMGT of the vulva.
Clinical examination, breast ultrasound and mammography did not reveal signs of primary breast tumour.
Biopsy of the inguinal adenopathy revealed a metastasis of the vulvar neoplasia previously described.
The triple-negative immunohistochemical (IHC) profile of one of the cases represented a diagnostic challenge.
Interestingly, it presented an immunophenotypical profile similar to triple-negative breast cancers, supporting the molecular similarities between vulvar AMGT and breast carcinomas.
diagnostic_reasoning_items: Diagnosis based on histopathological patterns consistent with breast carcinoma morphology.
Exclusion of metastatic breast carcinoma by imaging and clinical evaluation.
Confirmation of metastatic spread by lymph node biopsy in case 2.
Recognition of molecular heterogeneity with ER-positive and triple-negative profiles.
Use of IHC markers such as ER, GATA3, SOX10 to support diagnosis.
hidden_reference.final_diagnosis: Primary vulvar adenocarcinoma of mammary gland type (AMGT), invasive ductal carcinoma, with molecular subtype variability including ER-positive and triple-negative forms.
hidden_reference.diagnostic_reasoning: The diagnosis was established by histopathological examination showing invasive ductal carcinoma morphology and immunohistochemical profiles consistent with mammary gland origin. Imaging and clinical studies excluded a primary breast tumor, confirming the vulvar origin. Lymph node biopsy confirmed metastasis in one case. The molecular variability, including a triple-negative subtype expressing SOX10, supports the diagnosis and illustrates diagnostic challenges.
hidden_reference.article_derived_evidence_summary: Two postmenopausal women presented with vulvar masses diagnosed as AMGT by pathology and IHC. Imaging excluded primary breast tumors. One case was ER-positive and treated surgically with hormone therapy; the other was triple-negative with lymph node metastasis, treated with chemotherapy, surgery, and palliative radiotherapy.
diagnosis_synonyms_or_variants: Invasive ductal carcinoma of vulvar mammary gland type

evidence_events.source_span: A 21-year-old sexually virgin female was referred with provisional diagnosis of epithelial ovarian malignancy based on MRI findings and raised CA125 level of 129.8 U/ml

Patient had irregular menstruation for 6 months, abdominal distension for 2 months, and lower abdominal pain for 1 month; no fever or night sweats; past history of cervical lymph node tuberculosis treated with 18 months of antitubercular therapy

Clinical examination showed fair general condition, stable vitals, normal neurological, respiratory, cardiovascular systems; mild tenderness in lower abdomen without guarding, rigidity, or free fluid; no palpable mass

MRI showed extensive smooth peritoneal thickening with moderate ascites, multiloculated cystic lesion in bilateral adnexa variably hyperintense on T2 and T1-weighted images, lesions close to ovaries but bilateral ovaries visualized normally

Routine labs including CBC, renal and liver function, chest X-ray, HIV, HBsAg, HCV were normal except raised ESR 32 mm/h; tumor markers LDH, AFP, CEA, beta-hCG were normal; interferon gamma release assay was negative

Transabdominal USG-guided aspiration of fluid was done; geneXpert negative for tuberculosis; cytology negative for malignant cells; cell block showed reactive mesothelial cells and neutrophils; bacterial culture sterile; fungal culture identified Curvularia lunata by MALDI-TOF MS

Started oral itraconazole 200 mg once daily; after 2 weeks, abdominal contrast-enhanced CECT showed bilateral adnexal masses with dilated tubular structures, thickened enhancing walls, moderate pelvic fluid collection, peritoneal thickening, calcifications, and cystic components consistent with tubo-ovarian abscess

source_metadata.title: Isolated Splenic Infarction: An Initial Manifestation of Postoperative Atrial Fibrillation

evidence_events.source_span: A 68-year-old female with a past medical history of colonic Crohn’s disease with sigmoid strictures (previously on ustekinumab, status post colectomy with Hartman’s pouch ileostomy, 3 weeks prior to presentation), hypertension, and hypothyroidism, presented to the emergency Department (ED) for persistent nausea, abdominal pain, high ostomy output, and generalized weakness.

Abdominal pain, in the mid-epigastric region, started 2 to 3 days after the procedure (colectomy with ileostomy) and was persistent with progressive worsening. She also reported decreased oral intake and reduced urine output.

On physical exam, the patient was in mild distress. Vital signs showed blood pressure at 106/48, heart rate 86 bpm, afebrile at 36.8 C, respiratory rate 18 and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Patient had regular heart rate and rhythm; no murmurs were auscultated; lungs were clear to auscultation bilaterally; abdominal examination was positive for generalized abdominal tenderness, without any palpable masses, guarding, rigidity, or rebound tenderness. The ostomy was patent, pink with an ileostomy bag filled with fluid and gas.

Laboratory tests were significant for severely elevated creatinine of 9.56 (baseline Cr 0.56), hyponatremia with a sodium of 124 and metabolic acidosis with bicarbonate level of 9 (high anion gap and non-anion gap metabolic acidosis). Complete blood count was significant for thrombocytosis with a platelet count of 493. Venous blood gas showed a pH of 7.13, pCO2 of 37, pO2 of 43, bicarbonate of 12.
Electrocardiography was normal, with regular rate and rhythm.

Computed tomography (CT) abdomen pelvis without contrast was performed. This imaging was normal except for herniation of the mesenteric fat of the abdominal wall at the ileostomy site, and multiple gallstones without any evidence of gallbladder wall thickening or pericholecystic fluid.
Imaging of abdomen was repeated with CT with contrast, which showed multiple splenic infarctions of the entire lower pole with occlusion of the branch splenic arteries.

The patient’s elevated creatinine was pre-renal in etiology (secondary to decreased intake and high ileostomy output). With repletion of intravenous fluids and avoiding nephrotoxins, acute kidney injury was resolved.
Phospholipid antibodies and JAK2 mutation testing were negative.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: phospholipid antibodies and JAK2 mutation testing

evidence_events.source_span: Echocardiogram revealed normal left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF), without any evidence of vegetation or PFO.
On telemetry, the patient had an episode of atrial fibrillation with subsequent reversion back to sinus rhythm in a day. The patient was, however, asymptomatic.
Paroxysmal atrial fibrillation was determined to be the culprit of her splenic infarct, and the patient was discharged on apixaban and metoprolol.
Her CHA2DS2-VASc score was 3 (age 65-74 years, female, and hypertension history), necessitating the continuation of anticoagulation.
At outpatient follow-up visit, the abdominal pain had subsided.

evidence_events.source_span: Initial physical exam revealed a large painless mass in the left breast exceeding 30 cm, with thin skin, small erosions, intertrigo in submammary sulcus and sternum, tortuous dilated veins, polylobate tumor with hard consistency, mobile on deep planes but adherent to skin in areas, and palpable enlarged but mobile lymph nodes in ipsilateral axilla.

Ultrasound of left breast showed multiple hypoechoic structures 5 mm to 85/61 mm, imprecisely delineated, complex echostructure, tortuous blood vessels peripherally and inside largest nodules; mammography showed multiple non-homogeneous opacities with irregular macro-bosselated outline, microcalcifications, BI-RADS score 5.
US-guided core needle biopsy with HE staining of six specimens described lesions compatible with fibroadenoma and benign/borderline phyllodes tumor but could not exclude malignancy.

Contrast-enhanced CT scan of chest, abdomen, pelvis showed tumoral enlargement of left breast with multiple tissue density formations distorting glandular and interstitial tissue, infiltration of subcutaneous tissue over 68/13 mm, left axillary and retrosternocleidomastoid lymphadenopathy, and a small peripheral lung nodule without specific features.
Left mastectomy with level I axillary lymphadenectomy performed; five enlarged lymph nodes resected; tumor resected with fascia of pectoralis major; margins evaluated at 36 points.

Microscopic examination of surgical specimen showed canalicular structures lined by cubic double-layer epithelium with rare nuclear atypia and mitoses; abundant stromal component with dense connective tissue, few fibroblast-like cells without atypia; intracanalicular stromal proliferations compressing ducts; margins clear over 1 cm; five of six axillary lymph nodes showed reactive changes.

Immunohistochemistry performed with antibodies including pan-CK MNF116, CK7, CK20, alpha-SMA, p63, CD117, EGFR, p16, p53, CD34, Ki67; ductal epithelial cells intensely positive for pan-CK MNF116 and CK7, negative for CK20; ductal and stromal cells moderately positive for alpha-SMA, p63, CD117, EGFR; negative for p16 and p53; CD34 intensely marked stromal and vascular endothelial cells but not ductal cells; Ki67 proliferation marker weak, 4-6 positive cells per medium power field, stromal Ki67 labeling index less than 1%.
At one year evaluation, patient had no signs of recurrence; reconstruction postponed due to COVID-19.

source_metadata.title: A Case of Lymphomatoid Granulomatosis in a Lymph Node with Unique Clinical and Histopathologic Features

evidence_events.source_span: A 60-year-old man with a past medical history of HIV, remote history of hepatitis C, diabetes mellitus type II, and Hodgkin’s lymphoma was admitted to the hospital for altered mental status.

On the physical exam, vitals were stable, with temperature 36.8°C, BP 104/55, pulse 84/min, respiratory rate 20/ min, and SpO2 98% on room air. A physical exam revealed that the patient had bilateral lymphadenopathy along the anterior cervical chain; a respiratory exam revealed shallow breathing with diffuse rhonchi; a cardiovascular exam revealed harsh systolic murmur grade 3; the abdomen was soft, nontender, no rebound; and a genitourinary exam he had left inguinal lymphadenopathy.
Laboratory tests revealed pancytopenia, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, acute kidney injury, with lactic acidosis.
A CT head without contrast not revealing any acute intracranial process; a chest X-ray PA showed airspace opacity of the lateral right lung base, concerning for pneumonia.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: CT head without contrast, chest X-ray PA

evidence_events.source_span: Blood cultures grew MRSA; lumbar puncture revealed glucose of 351, colorless fluid, 6 RBC, lymphocytes 30, protein 66.3, and no detection of multiple infectious agents including Enterovirus, E. coli, Haemophilus influenzae, Listeria monocytogenes, Neisseria meningitidis, Streptococcus agalactiae, Streptococcus pneumonia, CMV, HSV, HHV 6, Human Parechovirus, Varicella Zoster, or Cryptococcus neoformans.
BAL sampling was negative for acid-fast bacteria; autoimmune disease workup for antinuclear antibodies (ANA) was negative.
A TEE ruled out any vegetations despite MRSA bacteremia and cardiac murmur.

CT scan of the abdomen showed moderate splenomegaly without discrete splenic lesions, multiple prominent and enlarged lymph nodes (left cardiophrenic, retrocrural, celiac, mesenteric, portacaval, aortocaval, and iliac). The largest lymph node at right common iliac station measured 25.4 mm. Visualization of the lower thorax showed enlarged hilar, subcarinal, and periesophageal lymph nodes.

Aspiration of the largest lymph node revealed EBV-EBER-positive, CD30-positive, and CD15 rarely positive cells. LCA, BOB-1, ALK, CD79a, bcl-2, CD3, OCT 2, CD20, PAX-5, and CD68 were also positive. AE1/AE3 and HHV8 were negative. Histopathology staining showed fibrinoid necrosis and atypical lymphocytes in the background.

Special staining revealed numerous Epstein-Barr virus-encoded small RNA with quantification of more than 50 EBV particles per high-power field and necrosis present, diagnosing grade III lymphomatoid granulomatosis.
Oncology started the patient on a regimen of brentuximab/bendamustine. He was hemodynamically stable and discharged home to follow up with Oncology as an outpatient.

source_metadata.title: Metastatic thoracic and lumbar intramedullary and extramedullary Ewing’s sarcoma: a rare case report and literature review

evidence_events.source_span: A 46-year-old woman was referred to our outpatient clinic from the oncology clinic with progressive paraparesis and paresthesia for 1 week prior to presentation (August 2021).

She was diagnosed with Ewing sarcoma in December 2019, and again, with left clavicular Ewing sarcoma approximately 2 years prior to presentation. She presented with a progressively enlarging neck mass on the left side that had developed within the previous 2 months.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: 2 years prior to presentation; previous 2 months

evidence_events.source_span: Spiral computed tomography (CT) of the chest and mediastinum revealed a large mildly enhanced mass measuring approximately 60 × 80 mm in the apex of the left lung with small extension to the base of the neck on the left side, just touching the tracheal wall. No signs of bone destruction or bone erosion were seen.
The tumor was totally excised and histopathologically proven to be Ewing sarcoma of the clavicle.

She then underwent chemotherapy with vincristine sulfate, doxorubicin hydrochloride, and cyclophosphamide, followed by ifosfamide and etoposide phosphate (VAC/IE protocol) and subsequent radiotherapy.

Positron emission tomography (PET) was performed in March 2021. The findings revealed mild soft tissue thickening in the right apical hemithorax with insignificant fluordeoxyglucose (FDG) activity demonstrating post-therapy changes with no remarkable active residual focus. The PET scan findings suggested a complete metabolic response; thus, the disease was considered cured.

On physical examination at the current presentation, the patient’s muscle strength in her lower extremities was as follows: right: 3/5 and left: 1/5 (proximal/distal, respectively). There was a sensory level in the thoracic region (T6), and spastic hyperreflexia was present in the lower extremities (American Spinal Injury Association (ASIA) impairment scale C). Urinary sphincter function was intact, but the patient complained of incomplete evacuation of the bladder. A urodynamic study revealed a spastic bladder. Bilateral Babinski reflexes were upward.

Emergency whole-spine contrast-enhanced magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed a huge intramedullary thoracic lesion extending from T5 to T8 that was hyperintense in T2-weighted images, with scattered enhancement after the injection of contrast. Additionally, there was a round intradural extramedullary mass lesion at the L1 and L2 levels causing a compression effect on the conus medullaris that was isointense in T2-weighted images, with homogenous enhancement after the injection of contrast.

Surgery was performed with intraoperative neuromonitoring comprising motor evoked potentials (MEP), sensory evoked potentials (SEP), and electromyography (EMG). The dura was opened, and midline myelotomy was performed in the thoracic region. The lesion was microscopically resected as much as possible (intralesional resection and multiple biopsies of the lesion).

Histopathological examination of the thoracic lesion revealed small round cells with moderate pleomorphism, nuclear atypia, and some true rosette formations in a pauci-vascular background. Immunohistochemical staining of the tumor showed diffuse, strong immunoreactivity for cluster of differentiation (CD)99, and a high proliferative index (Ki-67: 85%–90%), with negative staining for leukocyte common antigen (LCA). The diagnosis of Ewing sarcoma was confirmed accordingly.
She received temozolomide (100 mg/m2/day orally) and irinotecan (40 mg/m2/day intravenously) in accordance with the standard protocol as adjuvant therapy for recurrent or metastatic Ewing sarcoma.
Postoperative imaging of the thoracic spine revealed appropriate decompression and showed that the lumbosacral lesion had completely resolved.

At the 10-month follow-up, the patient’s neurological status had worsened, with bilateral lower extremity muscle strength scores of 0/5 (proximal/distal, respectively; ASIA impairment scale B), with spasticity and urofecal retention. She was alive with disease at the time of this report.

source_metadata.title: Sinus Node Dysfunction Co-occurring with Immune Checkpoint Inhibitor-associated Myocarditis

evidence_events.source_span: A 71-year-old woman was diagnosed with cT4N2M1 squamous cell lung carcinoma at the Osaka International Cancer Institute through a histopathological analysis of her lung tumor and systemic imaging studies, including enhanced computed tomography, brain magnetic resonance imaging, and fluorodeoxyglucose-positron emission tomography.

The patient had been administered combination therapy of carboplatin, nab-paclitaxel, and pembrolizumab as the first line therapy; however, she experienced severe pulmonary infection. After recovery, her treatment was switched to pembrolizumab monotherapy.

After the second course of pembrolizumab monotherapy, she developed a high fever (CTCAE grade 1) and worsening kidney function (eGFR declined from 72 to 39 mL/min/1.73 m2; CTCAE grade 3), leading to hospital admission.
The following evening, frequent sinus pauses of approximately 5 s and paroxysmal atrial fibrillation were observed on electrocardiogram monitoring, diagnosed as sick sinus syndrome (CTCAE grade 3).

She had no history of cardiovascular disease or arrhythmia and was not treated with bradycardia-inducing drugs; no viral infectious symptoms or laboratory data suggested viral myocarditis; thyroid and adrenal functions were normal; hemodynamics were preserved.

Cardiac biomarkers were elevated: troponin I at 0.032 ng/mL (normal ≤0.026) and NT-proBNP at 1,724 pg/mL (normal ≤125), although no ischemic ECG changes or chest pain were observed; echocardiography showed preserved left ventricular ejection fraction (60-65%) without local asynergy, pericardial effusion, or valvular disease.

Based on fever, worsening kidney function, new arrhythmia, and elevated cardiac biomarkers, the patient was clinically diagnosed with multi-organ immune-related adverse events including myocarditis; pulse steroid therapy was started with methylprednisolone 1 g for 3 days followed by prednisolone maintenance.

From the second day of steroid therapy, eGFR increased, troponin I and NT-proBNP decreased, frequency of sinus pauses reduced, atrial fibrillation disappeared completely and did not recur; temporary pacing was still observed during sinus rhythm.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: From the second day of pulse steroid therapy

evidence_events.source_span: On the fourth day after steroid pulse therapy initiation, cardiac catheterization and coronary angiography showed no coronary artery stenosis; an endomyocardial biopsy of the right ventricular septum was performed.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: On the fourth day after steroid pulse therapy initiation
evidence_events.procedural_cue: cardiac catheterization, coronary angiography, endomyocardial biopsy

evidence_events.source_span: Endomyocardial biopsy revealed CD3-positive lymphocytes and CD163-positive macrophages infiltrating the interstitium adjacent to degenerated and necrotic myocytes, which showed localized immunopositivity for programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1); immunostaining for tenascin-C was positive in the interstitium adjacent to necrotic myocytes.

After steroid therapy, no sick sinus syndrome was observed; the temporary pacemaker was removed; no symptoms or documentation of SSS occurred thereafter; sinus node damage was considered caused by ICI-induced myocarditis and reversible by steroid therapy; no permanent pacemaker was required; no arrhythmia or cardiac failure occurred during six months follow-up.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: After steroid therapy and during six months follow-up

source_metadata.title: Paediatric inflammatory multisystem syndrome: temporally associated with SARS-CoV-2 (PIMS-TS) — A mimic of intra-abdominal malignancy

evidence_events.source_span: A school-aged boy presented to a regional district general hospital with a 2-day history of fever and central/lower abdominal pain associated with reduced appetite and vomiting.

He was initially thought to have acute appendicitis and underwent an ultrasound scan, which showed inflammatory changes between his stomach and pancreas raising the suspicion of acute pancreatitis despite a serum amylase within normal range.
He underwent a CT scan, which revealed a mass-like thickening of the transverse colon involving the mesocolon, which raised the suspicion of a lymphoma.
He was found to have a palpable epigastric fullness, his abdomen became rapidly more distended and abdominal plain radiograph showed intestinal obstruction.
An open incisional biopsy of the nodal mass was performed revealing an inflammatory nodal mass in transverse mesocolon; flexible sigmoidoscopy showed a normal appearance of the intestinal lumen.
Histopathology results of his biopsy did not show evidence of lymphoma but instead changes in both lymph nodes and mesenteric fat in keeping with a necroinflammatory process.

The patient had positive COVID-19 antibodies, elevated C-reactive protein up to 274, raised D-dimer, echocardiography findings including borderline low left ventricular function, mild mitral regurgitation and a small pericardial effusion.

Initial blood tests showed haemoglobin 112 g/L, platelet count 228 ×10⁹/L, white blood cell 4.79 ×10⁹/L, lymphocytes 0.96 ×10⁹/L, amylase 46 IU/L, C-reactive protein 130 mg/L, bilirubin 11 umol/L, alanine aminotransferase 14 iu/L, alkaline phosphatase 177 IU/L, Na 137 mmol/L, K 3.8 mmol/L, urea 4.1 mmol/L, creatinine 50 µmol/L.

PIMS-TS-specific blood tests showed prothrombin time 15 s (peak 18 s), activated partial thromboplastin time 32.5 s, fibrinogen >4.5 g/L (peak 6.1), D-dimer 1126 ng/mL, lactate dehydrogenase 236 IU/L, plasma N-terminal pro b-type natriuretic peptide 1523 ng/L, vitamin D 44 nmol/L, amylase 29 IU/L, ferritin 225 µg/L, troponin 16 ng/L.

Blood and urine tests to investigate other intra-abdominal tumours including alpha fetoprotein, beta-human chorionic gonadotropin, urinary dopamine/homovanillate/vanillylmandelic acid were within normal range.

Chest X-ray showed globular heart and prominent perihilar vasculature; abdominal ultrasound showed echogenic ill-defined thickening with round echopoor lymph node in gastrocolic mesentery/omentum ± foci of free fluid; CT abdomen showed ill-defined inflammatory mass with smoky mesentery and enlarged lymph nodes in gastrocolic mesentery and root of mesentery; spleen mildly enlarged; staging CT showed no metastatic disease; echocardiogram showed borderline low left ventricular function, mild mitral regurgitation and small pericardial effusion.

Histology of mass biopsy showed no evidence of lymphoma; extensively necrotic fibrocollagenous tissue fragment with mixed inflammation predominated by neutrophils and eosinophils and collections of macrophages; vessel injury around necrosis; prominent necrotising lymphadenitis with karyorrhectic debris and some palisading histiocytes but no true granuloma; mesenteric fat infiltrated by lymphocytes, eosinophils and abundant histiocytes without Langerhans cells; early fibroblastic proliferation and damage to mesenteric vessels noted.

Microbiology tests showed nose and throat swabs COVID-19 PCR not detected; SARS-CoV-2 antibody (IgG and IgM) positive; blood cultures negative; faecal culture insufficient; CMV/EBV/adenovirus PCR negative; CMV IgM and IgG antibodies not detected; EBV IgM and IgG antibodies not detected; varicella-zoster virus IgG antibody positive; PCR for bacterial DNA negative; DNA from Mycobacterium species and Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex negative.

initial_presentation.first_contact_summary: A 4‐year‐old boy was admitted to our hospital because of fever and convulsions, with a body temperature of 39.4°C. No specific abnormalities were found in immunochemistry, urine, or fecal analyzes, except for elevated serum neuron‐specific enolase (21.45 ng/ml, normal range: 0–16.3). Computed tomography showed what might be an enlarged frontal boundary of the right ventricle with calcified foci. On magnetic resonance imaging, this seemed to correspond to a T1 low intensity mass, measuring 2.5 × 2.0 × 2.1 cm, with a few darker strands and no enhancement (Figure 1).

source_metadata.title: A 4‑year‑old boy with a ventricular mass
source_metadata.notes: Case report of a 4-year-old boy with fever, convulsions, and a ventricular mass ultimately diagnosed as myxoid glioneuronal tumor with PDGFRA mutation.

evidence_events.source_span: A 4‑year‑old boy was admitted to our hospital because of fever and convulsions, with a body temperature of 39.4°C.
No specific abnormalities were found in immunochemistry, urine, or fecal analyzes, except for elevated serum neuron‑specific enolase (21.45 ng/ml, normal range: 0–16.3).
Computed tomography showed what might be an enlarged frontal boundary of the right ventricle with calcified foci.
On magnetic resonance imaging, this seemed to correspond to a T1 low intensity mass, measuring 2.5 × 2.0 × 2.1 cm, with a few darker strands and no enhancement.
A preliminary diagnosis of a low grade glial/glioneuronal neoplasm was made.
The tumor was completely removed, with no complications.

Histopathological examination showed a low‑grade neoplasm composed of oligodendroglial‑like tumor cells with round to ovoid nuclei and scant cytoplasm immersed in a mucus‑rich extracellular matrix. Focal microcalcifications were also observed. No mitoses, microvascular proliferation or necrosis were observed.
Immunohistochemical staining demonstrated Olig2, Sox10, GFAP, ATRX, and nestin expression.
Myxoid glioneuronal tumor (CNS WHO grade 1).
Targeted next‑generation sequencing analysis using a 599 gene panel revealed PDGFRA p.K385L (rate: 38.76%) and NSD2 p.L581H (rate: 2.02%) mutations.

initial_presentation.first_contact_summary: A 63-year-old man was admitted to a local hospital with a 29-month history of dizziness. Gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain revealed multiple small nodules with enhancement in the bilateral cerebrum, brainstem, and cerebellum. Fluid-attenuated inversion recovery imaging of the brain depicted high-intensity lesions corresponding to part of the nodules showing enhancement on gadolinium-enhanced MRI but showed no other abnormalities.
