source_metadata.title: Erdheim-Chester Disease Involving the Central Nervous System with Latent Toxoplasmosis

evidence_events.source_span: A 63-year-old man was admitted to a local hospital with a 29-month history of dizziness.
Gadolinium-enhanced T1-weighted magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain revealed multiple small nodules with enhancement in the bilateral cerebrum, brainstem, and cerebellum.

Fluid-attenuated inversion recovery imaging of the brain depicted high-intensity lesions corresponding to part of the nodules showing enhancement on gadolinium-enhanced MRI but showed no other abnormalities.
A subcortical mass in the right frontal lobe was biopsied, but no diagnosis could be confirmed.
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: Initial biopsy inconclusive

evidence_events.source_span: On admission, he presented with cerebellar ataxia of the left limbs and trunk, saccadic eye movements, and right tinnitus; physical examination findings were otherwise normal.

Blood tests were normal or negative: blood cell count, biochemical and endocrine examination, C-reactive protein, serum autoantibodies, and serum tumor markers including carcinoembryonic antigen and soluble interleukin-2 receptor (sIL-2R).
CSF examinations revealed a slight elevation of protein (68 mg/dL), but the cell count, glucose, immunoglobulin G index, and sIL-2R were normal.
Brain biopsy specimens showed infiltration of foamy cells; immunohistochemical staining revealed these cells were CD68-positive, CD163-positive, and CD1a-negative.
Biopsy specimens appeared slightly positive for B-Raf proto-oncogene (BRAF) on immunohistochemical staining and positive for the BRAF V600E mutation through DNA sequencing.
Bone scintigraphy using 99mTc-methylene diphosphonate revealed markedly increased uptake in surrounding areas of both knees.
CT of the lower limbs revealed sclerotic lesions in the same areas around both knees.
Contrast-enhanced CT of the trunk revealed soft-tissue shadows in areas surrounding the descending thoracic aorta and left kidney.
Interferon-γ release assay for Mycobacterium tuberculosis, β-D glucan, syphilis test, human immunodeficiency virus test, and bacterial and fungal cultures of CSF were all negative.

Serum Toxoplasma gondii IgM antibody was negative and IgG antibody was positive (titer, 61.6 U/mL); Toxoplasma nested PCR testing of peripheral blood was negative but positive in one of three cerebrospinal fluid samples.
Brain biopsy specimens did not reveal any Toxoplasma gondii tachyzoites or bradyzoites by immunohistochemistry, and Toxoplasma nested PCR testing of brain biopsy specimens was negative.

Administration of pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine, and folinic acid was initiated as anti-Toxoplasma treatment, but the patient showed no improvement of neurologic symptoms and brain MRI showed no marked changes.

evidence_events.source_span: A 58-years-old female was referred to the Clinic for Maxillofacial Surgery, University Clinical Center of Vojvodina in Novi Sad, complaining of a nonhealing post-extraction wound in the gingiva of the mandible on the left side.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: Three months after tooth 36 was extracted

evidence_events.source_span: Swelling and vegetation of the gingiva were observed in the mandibular region on the left side after the intraoral examination, and the OPT determined that the bone was destroyed.
An incisional biopsy of the gingival tumor was performed and the patient underwent computed tomography of the head, neck, and chest as part of the oral carcinoma TNM staging protocol.

Computed tomography showed an expansive-infiltrating tumor in the mandible body with infiltration into surrounding tissue, bone destruction with a 'sunburst' periosteal reaction, and infiltration of mylohyoid, pterygoid, and digastric muscles; expansive soft tissue changes in the left breast and infiltrating lymph nodes in the left axilla were also described.
Mammography and core biopsy of the breast tumor were done.
Osteoblastic changes were observed in the 3rd thoracic spinal vertebra.

The pathologist described metastatic mucinous adenocarcinoma based on the gingival biopsy tissue; microscopic examination revealed nests of cells floating in lakes of mucin partitioned by delicate fibrous septa containing capillary blood vessels.

Pathophysiological analysis and immunohistochemistry of the breast tumor biopsy showed estrogen receptor positivity (90% of cells, Allred score 8), progesterone receptor positivity (40% of cells, Allred score 6), Ki67 proliferative index 30%, HER2 receptors 1+, CK7+, CK20+, mammaglobin negative, and GATA-3 positive.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: IHC performed on breast tumor biopsy

evidence_events.source_span: The patient was sent to the Oncology Committee for Breast Diseases, where chemotherapy was indicated with 3 cycles per anthracycline (AC) protocol, followed by evaluation for irradiation therapy for mandible metastasis.

evidence_events.source_span: A 63-year-old woman with a negative family history of cancer was diagnosed with anorectal malignant tumor in February 2019 due to intermittent blood in the stool for 2 months
Laboratory assessment illustrated a hemoglobin (Hb) level of 108 g/L (normal range: 115–150 g/L)

Abdominal CT scan discovered that the intestinal wall of the lower rectum-anal canal area is thickened and eccentric, mainly on the left and the posterior parts, local lumen is constricted, and some of the surrounding lymph nodes are enlarged
Surgical resection was performed and histology revealed anorectal malignant melanoma
Immunohistochemical staining showed HMB-45 (+), Melan-A (+), S100 (+), Vimentin (+), PCK (−), P16 (−)
29 months later, chest CT scan showed a newly visible lump with unclear boundaries in the outer upper quadrant of the right breast, measuring 2.3 cm, considered as neoplastic lesion
Core needle biopsy of the right breast mass under ultrasound guidance revealed malignant tumor
PET/CT showed no other metastases
Modified radical mastectomy was performed and histology confirmed metastatic malignant melanoma in the breast
Immunohistochemical staining of breast tumor showed HMB-45 (+), Melan-A (+), S100 (+), Vimentin (+), CK (−), CK7 (−), CD34 (−), WT-1 (−)

evidence_events.source_span: A 63-year-old Saudi man, with no medical history and a 30-pack-year smoking history, presented to the ED with weakness involving the left upper and lower limbs as well as a headache for the previous 2 weeks.
He reported unintentional weight loss of 6 kg in the previous couple of weeks, associated with lack of appetite, and gave a history of subjective fever and night sweats.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: in the previous couple of weeks

evidence_events.source_span: He had no cough, chest pain, shortness of breath, dysphagia, or hemoptysis. He denied other neurological symptoms, including loss of consciousness, convulsions, dysarthria, dysphasia, or memory loss.

On the clinical examination, the patient was vitally stable, conscious, and coherent. He scored 15 of 15 on the Glasgow Coma Scale. The pupils were bilaterally equally reactive, at 3 mm. The cranial nerves were intact. On the hand examination, clubbed fingers were identified. The patient had left-sided weakness in the upper and lower limbs, with grades 4 of 5 and 3 of 5, respectively.
The results of his complete blood count, liver function tests, renal function tests, amylase, lipase, and serum calcium all were within the normal range.
A non-contrast computed tomography (CT) scan of the brain showed lesions with vasogenic edema in the right parietal lobe.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: non-contrast CT scan of the brain

evidence_events.source_span: A chest X-ray showed right lung opacity, suggesting a mass in the right upper lobe of the lung.
A CT scan of the chest showed a mass in the anterior segment of the right upper lobe.
CT scan of the abdomen showed multiple hypodense liver lesions, indicating metastasis.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain showed evidence of 2 ring-enhancing lesions within the right temporal and right parietal region, with extensive perifocal edema showing mild diffusion restriction and mid-line shift towards the left side.
A bronchoscopy was unremarkable.
Endobronchial ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration was done, and the biopsy was taken from the 4R lymph node; a total of 6 specimens were taken.

The slides were fixed by Spray-Cyte and sent to the Pathology Laboratory, which showed that the patient’s sample was positive for malignancy, since there were clusters of malignant epithelial cells with enlarged hyperchromatic pleomorphic nuclei with coarse chromatin.
Cell-block immunostaining showed positive reactivity of the malignant cells to CK-7, TTF-1, and focally for Napsin-A. These findings indicated primary lung adenocarcinoma.

initial_presentation.chief_complaint: severe abdominal pain
initial_presentation.first_contact_summary: A previously healthy woman in her 20s presented acutely to the surgical emergency department with a 1 day history of severe abdominal pain. The pain had started at the periumbilical area, gradually intensifying into colicky pain that radiated to the right iliac fossa and suprapubic area. This was accompanied by nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea. There was no history of constitutional symptoms or recent weight loss. Medical and surgical history was unremarkable. On admission, her vital signs were stable; temperature 37.2°C, blood pressure 110/60 mm Hg, pulse 80 beats per minute and respiratory rate 40 breaths per minute. On deep palpation, the patient was found to have abdominal tenderness localised to the right iliac fossa with a positive rebound sign, negative Rovsing’s sign and no muscular rigidity. The Alvarado score for acute appendicitis was 5 out of 10. The patient was afebrile and had no leucocytosis on total blood cell count. The overall clinical picture was atypical for acute appendicitis; therefore, an urgent CT scan of abdomen and pelvis was requested mainly to exclude gynaecological emergencies.
presenting_symptoms: colicky pain radiating to right iliac fossa and suprapubic area

source_metadata.title: Intestinal LMNA::NTRK1-fused spindle cell neoplasm with S100 and CD34 coexpression: a new case

evidence_events.source_span: A previously healthy woman in her 20s presented acutely to the surgical emergency department with a 1 day history of severe abdominal pain starting at the periumbilical area, radiating to the right iliac fossa and suprapubic area, accompanied by nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea

On admission, vital signs were stable; temperature 37.2°C, blood pressure 110/60 mm Hg, pulse 80 beats per minute and respiratory rate 40 breaths per minute; abdominal tenderness localized to right iliac fossa with positive rebound sign, negative Rovsing’s sign, no muscular rigidity; Alvarado score 5/10; afebrile and no leucocytosis

CT scan of abdomen and pelvis revealed a relatively defined mass in the terminal ileum measuring 2.7 × 2.6 × 1.8 cm, isodense on plain images and hyperenhanced postcontrast, with partial ileal dilation, fluid levels, circumferential mural thickening, mucosal hyperenhancement, submucosal oedema, prominent adjacent fat stranding, and prominent surrounding mesenteric vessels; no intussusception or bowel perforation
Surgical segmental small bowel resection performed; tumour identified 30 cm proximal to ileocecal valve
Gross pathology showed a circumscribed firm grey-white mass in the bowel wall measuring 2.0 × 1.9 × 1.0 cm

Microscopically, tumour had highly irregular borders infiltrating muscularis propria and mucosa, infiltrating mesenteric fat with honeycomb pattern, prominent vascularity with haemangiopericytoma-like vessels, perivascular keloid-like hyalinised collagen rings, band-like stromal collagen, haphazardly arranged monomorphic spindle cells with storiform pattern, bland nuclei with occasional pleomorphic multinucleated cells, low mitotic count (2/10 HPF), no necrosis, scattered lymphocytes and lymphoid aggregates

Immunohistochemistry showed tumour cells negative for GIST markers CD117 and DOG1 (confirmed on repeat), positive for CD34 and S100, negative for STAT6, SOX10, pan-cytokeratin/EMA, desmin/SMA, HMB45/Melan-A, ALK1, beta-catenin, synaptophysin/chromogranin; Ki-67 low proliferation index; H3K27me3 nuclear expression intact

Molecular testing by targeted DNA-based NGS panel showed no mutations in KIT, PDGFRA, RAS, BRAF or NF1 genes, excluding GIST; RNA-based gene fusion assay revealed LMNA (exon2)::NTRK1 (exon11) fusion on chromosome 1
evidence_events.procedural_cue: NGS panel and RNA fusion assay

evidence_events.source_span: Pan-TRK immunostaining performed externally showed strong cytoplasmic positivity
Three months postoperatively, patient was symptom-free; follow-up CT showed no recurrence or metastasis; no TRK inhibitor or adjuvant therapy given due to low histological grade and localized disease

source_metadata.title: Sinonasal teratocarcinosarcoma: a therapeutic dilemma

evidence_events.source_span: A man in his 50s sought medical attention at an emergency department due to difficulty breathing through the nose.

A CT scan and subsequent MRI revealed a sizeable soft tissue mass in the nasopharynx measuring 1.6×6.3×4.6 cm3 arising from the medial wall of the lateral wall of the nose extending into the ostiomeatal complex, the left frontal recess and the sphenoethmoidal recess with associated fullness and expansion of the pterygopalatine fossa.
The patient was in a good state of health with a history of benign goitre, hypertension and benign prostatic hyperplasia.

PET/CT scan revealed an irregular expansile hypermetabolic mass within the left nasal cavity and left maxillary sinus causing osseous erosion of the left maxillary sinus medial wall, extending slightly past the midline in the posterior nasopharynx, superiorly involving the left ethmoid sinus and inferiorly extending to the palate level.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: Once the imaging of the primary site was obtained

evidence_events.source_span: PET/CT scan also showed a thyroid nodule and a very small sclerotic lesion without fluorodeoxyglucose activity affecting the second lumbar vertebrae; biopsy of the L2 sclerotic lesion did not show evidence of malignancy.
The patient underwent resection of the tumour including ipsilateral medial maxillectomy, total ethmoidectomy, septectomy and anterior skull base resection via an endonasal approach.

Histopathology showed variable epithelial, neuroendocrine–neuroectodermal and mesenchymal differentiation; epithelial component positive for AE1/3, CK7, MNF116, P63 and CDX2; neuroendocrine component positive for synaptophysin, chromogranin, AE1/3, MNF116, CD56, calretinin and S100; mesenchymal component positive for androgen receptor and desmin, negative for SOX10 and myogenin.
Final pathology reported teratocarcinosarcoma.
Molecular analysis of the tumour revealed DNMT3 deletion exon 4–15, KDM6A G5fs*15, and SMARCA4 mutations.
The patient received adjuvant concurrent chemotherapy and radiation: 60 Gy in 30 fractions to tumour bed, 54 Gy to bilateral neck, with weekly carboplatin AUC 1 plus paclitaxel 30 mg/m2 for 6 weeks.
Fifty months after treatment, the patient is doing very well with no evidence of recurrence or metastasis; partial loss of sense of smell noted.

diagnostic_reasoning_verbatim_spans: Histopathologic pictureshowed a variable epithelial, neuroendocrine–neuroectodermal and mesenchymal differentiation pattern.
The epithelial component included both squamoid (mostly fetal type or immature) cells with clear cytoplasm. These areas were positive by immunohistochemistry for AE1/3, CK7, MNF116, P63 and CDX2.
The neuroendocrine–neuroectodermal component was synaptophysin, chromogranin, AE1/3, MNF116, CD56, calretinin and S100 positive.

The mesenchymal component consisted of hypercellular areas of spindle cells with increased mitoses without a specific type of differentiation. These areas were positive for androgen receptor and desmin, and SOX10 and myogenin were negative.
Overall, the findings were consistent with the diagnosis of SNTCS, also referred to as malignant teratoma.
Molecular analysis of the tumour revealed DNMT3 deletion exon 4–15, KDM6A G5fs*15, and SMARCA4 mutations.

Molecular genetic findings support the diagnosis and provide additional tumour characterization.
Imaging and biopsy ruled out distant metastasis.
Surgical resection provided tissue for definitive diagnosis.
Adjuvant chemoradiotherapy was administered based on tumour aggressiveness and anatomical considerations.

Imaging confirmed a large aggressive sinonasal mass without distant metastasis. Surgical resection provided diagnostic tissue, and adjuvant chemoradiotherapy was given. The patient remains disease-free at long-term follow-up.

evidence_events.source_span: A 23-year-old man was referred to our ENT-Head and Neck clinic from the Orthopedic clinic. He initially presented with a right humeral lesion around 10 cm in size.
An X-ray image confirmed a proximal right humeral osseous lesion with a pathological fracture.
His shoulder MRI scan showed an aggressive lytic lesion involving the right humerus.
His head and neck examination revealed a nasopharyngeal mass with bilateral palpable cervical lymph nodes.
A head and neck CT scan confirmed a large nasopharyngeal mass.
A Tru-Cut biopsy demonstrated that the lesion was a malignant metastatic nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC).
A nasopharyngeal biopsy further revealed his lesion to be an NPC undifferentiated type III.
The patient was diagnosed with a T3 N2b M1 stage tumor and chemotherapy was planned.
He received chemotherapy with gemcitabine and cisplatin, but he did not complete treatment and was lost to follow-up.

source_metadata.title: Primary central nervous system CD20-negative diffuse large B-cell lymphoma: a case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 54-year-old female patient was admitted to the hospital due to a headache lasting for more than 10 days and did not have any indication of fever, night sweats, weight loss, or other B symptoms.

Physical examination of the patient revealed a clear consciousness, poor speech, and a GCS score of 15. Bilateral pupils were large and round with a diameter of approximately 3 mm. The patient’s indirect light reflex was sensitive and no bleeding was observed in the bilateral external auditory canal and nasal cavity. Spinal fluid flow and movement were not limited and no tenderness was noted. The patient’s limb muscle strength was assessed to be grade 5 and limb muscle tension was normal. The patient had a normal physiological reflex and the pathological reflex was negative.

Routine blood tests prior to admission revealed a white blood cell count of 4.7 × 10⁹/L, lymphocyte count of 1.09 × 10⁹/L, 0.23% lymphocytes, 165U/L lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), and 213 mg/L albumin. Serology revealed that the patient was HIV and HHV-8 negative.

Cranial computed tomography (CT), as well as regular magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in combination with contrast-enhanced MRI, showed an irregular mass measuring 31 × 27 × 20 mm in the right temporal lobe. The contrast-enhanced scan was unevenly enhanced, and a large area of non-enhanced edema involving the basal ganglia was observed. The right lateral ventricle and third ventricle were compressed, and the midline structure was shifted to the left by approximately 9.4 mm. CT and MRI findings suggested a high probability of right temporal lobe lymphoma.

Cranial functional magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) indicated that the right temporal lobe tumor had increased Cho, a decreased Cr peak, a decreased NAA peak, and a maximum Ch/NAA ratio of 4.58, which suggests that the occupation of the right temporal lobe was malignant.

The PET-CT data indicated that, characteristic of primary brain tumors, the right temporoparietal space-occupying lesions had increased metabolism (SUVmax 25) and large surrounding edema. No obvious areas of increased metabolism were found elsewhere.

The patient underwent a craniotomy to remove the intracranial, space-occupying lesion that was located on the deep surface of the right temporal lobe. The tumor was solid, translucent jelly-like, with clear borders, no capsule, minimal vasculature, and possessed a soft texture.

Gross pathological examination revealed an area of broken gray-white tissue (2.5 × 2 × 1 cm) with partial hyperemia, no capsule, and gray-white matter on the cut surface. Under low magnification, the brain tissue was diffusely infiltrated and severely damaged by many large lymphoid cells and no lymphoid follicle structures were observed. Local tumor interstitial microvascular proliferation, tumor cell arrangement around the blood vessels, and tumor cell infiltration of the blood vessel’s intracavity were noted. Under high magnification, the tumor cells were medium to large, round or oval, possessed clear nuclear membranes, displayed different nuclear staining characteristics, were variably vacuolated or possessing of irregular mass, exhibited nucleoli, and had 1 to 3 nucleoli with central or near nuclear membranes, cytoplasmic dichromatic or basophilic cells, centroblast-like and immunoblastic-like cells, and pathological mitotic cells.

Immunohistochemical assays identified the presence of large lymphoid cells by LCA+++, CD79a+, PAX-5+, MUM1+, CD3-, and CD5- staining that, together, are indicative of B cells involvement. The tissue was CD10-, Bcl-6+, MUM1+, CyclinD1-, CD5-, SOX-11-, and Bcl-2-. EMA, GFAP, IDH1, P53, O1igo-2, S100, Syn, and CgA marks were all negative. Ki-67 expression was 90% positivity.

CD20 and CD21 staining of the tissues was negative. Upon repetition of the assay with a robust positive control, the tissue remained CD20 negative. Reactive lymphocytes in the brain tissue surrounding the tumor were CD20 positive, excluding false negatives.

Additional immune indicators were assessed: ALK, CD138, CD38, and EBER/ISH markers were all negative. Bcl-6 was positive and EMA was negative. Laboratory serology revealed HIV and HHV-8 negativity. These findings dismissed EBV-positive LBCL with plasmacytoid differentiation, primary effusion lymphoma, plasmablastoma, ALK+ LBCL, and HHV8+ DLBCL, NOS. The patient had no history of tumor or drug use including rituximab, excluding drug-induced CD20 antigen loss.

evidence_events.source_span: Next-generation sequencing (NGS) detected 11 gene mutations including BTG2, ITPKB, TET2, FAT1, PIM1, CARD11, KMT2C, NOTCH1, KMT2D, SOCS1, and BCORL1.
The patient was diagnosed with CD20-negative diffuse large B-cell lymphoma of the right temporal lobe, unclassifiable subtype.

The patient was treated with high-dose methotrexate combined with temozolomide chemotherapy. After 2 rounds of chemotherapy, the disease progressed rapidly and the patient died 4 months after the operation.

Routine blood tests prior to admission revealed a white blood cell count of 4.7 × 10⁹/L, lymphocyte count of 1.09 × 10⁹/L, 0.23% lymphocytes, 165U/L lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), and 213 mg/L albumin. Serology revealed that the patient was HIV and HHV-8 negative.

evidence_milestones.display_name: Imaging findings of right temporal lobe mass
evidence_milestones.visible_evidence: CT and MRI showed an irregular mass in the right temporal lobe with uneven enhancement and surrounding edema compressing ventricles and shifting midline. MRS indicated malignancy with increased Cho and decreased NAA. PET-CT showed increased metabolism (SUVmax 25) in the lesion with surrounding edema.
evidence_milestones.dialogue_visible_evidence: Brain imaging revealed a right temporal lobe mass with features suggestive of malignancy and significant surrounding edema. PET-CT confirmed high metabolic activity localized to the lesion.
evidence_milestones.test_visible_evidence: CT, MRI with contrast, MRS, and PET-CT imaging studies.
evidence_milestones.source_span: Cranial computed tomography (CT), as well as regular magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in combination with contrast-enhanced MRI, showed an irregular mass measuring 31 × 27 × 20 mm in the right temporal lobe. The contrast-enhanced scan was unevenly enhanced, and a large area of non-enhanced edema involving the basal ganglia was observed. The right lateral ventricle and third ventricle were compressed, and the midline structure was shifted to the left by approximately 9.4 mm. CT and MRI findings suggested a high probability of right temporal lobe lymphoma. Cranial functional magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) indicated that the right temporal lobe tumor had increased Cho, a decreased Cr peak, a decreased NAA peak, and a maximum Ch/NAA ratio of 4.58, which suggests that the occupation of the right temporal lobe was malignant. The PET-CT data indicated that, characteristic of primary brain tumors, the right temporoparietal space-occupying lesions had increased metabolism (SUVmax 25) and large surrounding edema.

evidence_milestones.grouping_reason: Surgical resection and pathological examination of the brain lesion.
evidence_milestones.display_name: Pathology and histomorphology of brain lesion
evidence_milestones.visible_evidence: The patient underwent craniotomy and tumor resection. Gross pathology showed broken gray-white tissue without capsule. Microscopy revealed diffuse infiltration of large lymphoid cells destroying brain tissue, with microvascular proliferation and tumor cells arranged around blood vessels and infiltrating vessel lumens. Tumor cells were medium to large, with clear nuclear membranes, nucleoli, vacuolation, and pathological mitoses.
evidence_milestones.dialogue_visible_evidence: Surgical pathology demonstrated diffuse infiltration of large atypical lymphoid cells with vascular involvement and brain tissue destruction, consistent with lymphoma.
evidence_milestones.test_visible_evidence: Gross and microscopic pathological examination of resected brain tumor.
evidence_milestones.source_span: The patient underwent a craniotomy to remove the intracranial, space-occupying lesion that was located on the deep surface of the right temporal lobe. The tumor was solid, translucent jelly-like, with clear borders, no capsule, minimal vasculature, and possessed a soft texture. Gross pathological examination revealed an area of broken gray-white tissue (2.5 × 2 × 1 cm) with partial hyperemia, no capsule, and gray-white matter on the cut surface. Under low magnification, the brain tissue was diffusely infiltrated and severely damaged by many large lymphoid cells and no lymphoid follicle structures were observed. Local tumor interstitial microvascular proliferation, tumor cell arrangement around the blood vessels, and tumor cell infiltration of the blood vessel’s intracavity were noted. Under high magnification, the tumor cells were medium to large, round or oval, possessed clear nuclear membranes, displayed different nuclear staining characteristics, were variably vacuolated or possessing of irregular mass, exhibited nucleoli, and had 1 to 3 nucleoli with central or near nuclear membranes, cytoplasmic dichromatic or basophilic cells, centroblast-like and immunoblastic-like cells, and pathological mitotic cells.
evidence_milestones.question: How do the pathological findings contribute to narrowing the diagnosis, and what lymphoma subtype features are suggested by the histomorphology?

hidden_reference.image_finding: Diffuse infiltration of large lymphoid cells destroying brain tissue; tumor cells arranged around blood vessels; pathological mitoses present.
hidden_reference.diagnostic_significance: Morphology consistent with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma.

evidence_milestones.grouping_reason: Immunohistochemical profiling confirming B-cell lineage and CD20 negativity.
evidence_milestones.visible_evidence: IHC showed tumor cells positive for LCA, CD79a, PAX-5, MUM1, Bcl-6, and Ki-67 (90%), and negative for CD3, CD5, CD10, CyclinD1, SOX-11, Bcl-2, EMA, GFAP, IDH1, P53, O1igo-2, S100, Syn, and CgA. CD20 and CD21 staining were negative on tumor cells but positive in reactive lymphocytes. Repeat IHC with positive controls confirmed true CD20 negativity.
evidence_milestones.dialogue_visible_evidence: Immunohistochemistry confirmed B-cell markers with high proliferation index and consistent CD20 negativity in tumor cells, excluding technical error.
evidence_milestones.test_visible_evidence: IHC panel including CD20 with repeat testing and controls.
evidence_milestones.source_span: Immunohistochemical assays identified the presence of large lymphoid cells by LCA+++, CD79a+, PAX-5+, MUM1+, CD3-, and CD5- staining that, together, are indicative of B cells involvement. The tissue was CD10-, Bcl-6+, MUM1+, CyclinD1-, CD5-, SOX-11-, and Bcl-2-. EMA, GFAP, IDH1, P53, O1igo-2, S100, Syn, and CgA marks were all negative. Ki-67 expression was 90% positivity. CD20 and CD21 staining of the tissues was negative. Upon repetition of the assay with a robust positive control, the tissue remained CD20 negative. Reactive lymphocytes in the brain tissue surrounding the tumor were CD20 positive, excluding false negatives.
evidence_milestones.question: What is the diagnostic significance of the immunohistochemical profile, especially the confirmed CD20 negativity, and how does it affect the lymphoma classification?

source_metadata.title: Diagnostic and treatment dilemma during the coronavirus disease 2019 pandemic: a primary pulmonary lymphoma presenting as a cavitary mass in a patient with coronavirus disease 2019: a case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 26-year-old previously healthy Caucasian male initially presented with three months of symptoms including a productive cough, fever, night sweats, myalgias, anorexia, and weight loss.
Initial chest X-ray showed a large right upper lobe cavitary lesion.

Computed tomography of the chest demonstrated a right upper lobe 9 × 10 × 14 cm necrotic cavitary lesion with mediastinal adenopathy and compression of the superior vena cava and azygous vein by the right paratracheal extent of the lesion and lymph node conglomerate.
Physical examination revealed normal vital signs and oxygen saturation, clear breath sounds bilaterally, no lymphadenopathy, and an otherwise unremarkable exam.
Repeat chest X-ray at 2-week follow-up showed the right upper lobe cavitary lesion had increased in size.

CT chest/abdomen/pelvis demonstrated a larger cavitary pulmonary lesion along with several new smaller cavitary lesions in the right upper lobe but no intra-abdominal masses, abdominal lymphadenopathy, or splenomegaly.

Laboratory studies showed elevated ESR 86, CRP 13.7, ferritin 835, and d-dimer 1; fungal antigen testing and bacterial cultures were negative; AFB smears and interferon gamma release assay for tuberculosis were negative; HIV test was nonreactive; autoimmune serologies including ANA, ANCA, ACE, and rheumatoid factor were negative or normal.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: awaiting serologic and microbiologic study results

evidence_events.source_span: Preprocedural testing prior to tissue biopsy revealed positive COVID-19 RT-PCR from nasopharyngeal swab.

Bronchoscopy was deferred due to high risk of viral aerosolization; CT-guided percutaneous needle biopsy was performed under mechanical ventilation with elective intubation in a negative pressure room with enhanced airborne precautions.

Histopathologic evaluation of the core needle biopsy specimen demonstrated classic Hodgkin lymphoma with mixed cellularity type showing typical Reed–Sternberg cells and immunohistochemical staining positive for CD15, CD30, and PAX-5; AFB and GMS stains were negative for mycobacteria and fungal organisms.
Patient received prophylactic subcutaneous low molecular weight heparin during hospitalization without thrombotic or hemorrhagic complications.

Treatment with combined chemotherapy and immunotherapy was delayed for 3 weeks following diagnosis to allow for viral clearance; patient eventually tested negative for COVID-19 and started treatment with six cycles of doxorubicin, dacarbazine, nivolumab, and brentuximab vedotin with favorable interim PET scan response.

evidence_events.source_span: A baby girl, delivered by spontaneous vaginal delivery at term, cried immediately and had APGAR scores of 7 and 8 at 1 and 5 min, respectively. She weighed 2.5 kg. A swelling was noted soon after delivery at the posterior aspect of the right ear which was slightly tender. The swelling was a variegated mass. It gradually increased in size and produced a foul-smelling pus-like discharge. It was not associated with fever or convulsions, and the infant was breastfeeding normally.

She was referred to our facility at the age of 15 days. Local examination revealed a mass on the right post-auricular region measuring 12 cm × 18 cm at the greatest dimensions, lobulated, cystic superiorly and firm inferiorly. The lesion was not ulcerative or tender. It was mobile with hyperpigmentation of the surrounding skin with the pinna, ear canal and tympanic membrane unaffected. There was no fever.

source_metadata.title: A Rare Case of Ruptured Malignant Ovarian Brenner Tumor
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case report section and related narrative, preserving source order and granularity.

evidence_events.source_span: A 39-year-old P0A0 woman first came to Gynecologic Outpatient Clinic with an abdominal mass, weight loss, and a 2-year history of bleeding outside of her menstrual cycle.
Gynecological transabdominal ultrasonography revealed a normal uterus with an adnexal solid mass measuring 11.86×12.50×11.24 cm and normal liver.

Around 3 months later, the patient presented to the Emergency Department with 12 h of abdominal pain and tenderness, with vital signs showing BP 150/100 mmHg, HR 110 bpm, RR 24/min, and temperature 38.3°C.
On abdominal examination, there was abdominal tenderness and muscle guarding; no ascites was found.
Laboratory tests showed anemia, high white blood cell and neutrophil counts, with other hematological panels within normal limits.
Ultrasonography performed at the Emergency Department showed no free fluid.
Chest X-ray examination revealed bilateral pleural effusions.
Perforated appendicitis was suspected and an emergency laparotomy was performed by the General Surgery Department.

Intraoperatively, a 25×20×15 cm grayish cystic mass with solid parts and irregular surface originating from the right adnexa was found, adhered to the omentum and peritoneum, with rupture on the posterior surface and approximately 300 cc of blood and blood clotting.

Complete surgical staging was performed intraoperatively after consultation with Gynecology Oncology; uterus was enlarged to 16–18 weeks gestation size; peritoneal seeding and enlarged right and left pelvic lymph nodes (2×3 cm and 2×2 cm) were found, with suspected metastasis to pelvic lymph nodes, rectum, pre-vesica, and Douglas pouch (pT2bN1bMx).

Grossly, the mass was a whitish-brown rubbery split cyst measuring 16×13×7 cm with smooth outer surface; cut surfaces showed dull solid parts (15×12×6 cm) and hollow parts (2–5 cm diameter) filled with clear liquid.

Histopathological examination confirmed right ovarian malignant Brenner tumor infiltrating corpus uteri, lymphovascular invasion, and metastasis to 2 right pelvic lymph nodes, 1 left pelvic lymph node, rectum, prevesical space, and Douglas pouch; fallopian tube, cervix, left ovary, and omentum were free of malignant cells.
Surgery achieved optimal debulking with zero residual tumor (R0); patient discharged on postoperative day 3.
Patient received adjuvant chemotherapy with paclitaxel carboplatin regimen every 21 days for 3 cycles.
At 1 month after completion of adjuvant chemotherapy, patient was recurrence-free with normal CA-125 level.

Immunohistochemistry showed the malignant cells expressed PAX5, CD20, MYC, and BCL2 (weak 30%). Ki-67 proliferation index was greater than 90%. The cells were negative for AE1/AE3, S100, CD30, and cyclin D1.

Aggressive B-cell lymphoma FISH panel was positive for rearrangement of BCL6 and MYC, with no evidence of BCL2 rearrangement; findings consistent with high-grade B-cell lymphoma/double-hit lymphoma with MYC and BCL2 and/or BCL6 rearrangements by WHO classification.

Immunohistochemistry for BCL6 and MU M1 showed positive staining in the malignant cells. CD10 was negative. The staining profile was consistent with nongerminal center B-cell-like type (non-GCB/ABC) of DLBCL.

source_metadata.title: Central Nervous System and Cardiac Abnormalities in the Setting of a De Novo Heterozygous Col4a1 Variant

evidence_events.source_span: A male infant born at 38 weeks and 4 days gestation presented to the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit with microcephaly, central nervous system (CNS) anomalies, and a hypoplastic aortic arch.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: born at 38 weeks and 4 days gestation

evidence_events.source_span: Prenatal ultrasound showed multiple fetal anomalies, including microcephaly, scattered multifocal hemorrhagic/ischemic infarcts, ex-vacuo dilatation, polymicrogyria, moderate ventricular septal defect (VSD), and a narrowed aortic arch.
Fetal MRI of the brain confirmed suspected ultrasound findings.
Fetal echocardiogram showed a dilated right cardiac chamber and mild hypoplasia of the left cardiac chambers, along with a moderate muscular VSD and narrow aortic arch.

On physical examination, the infant had a dusky appearance of the bilateral feet and cool extremities. The baby was limp at birth with no spontaneous respiratory effort, required positive pressure ventilation at birth, and was then transitioned to continuous positive airway pressure.

Postnatal echocardiography showed a fenestrated atrial septum and moderate mid-muscular VSD, mild to moderate hypoplastic left ventricle, moderately hypoplastic left aortic arch, small to moderate patent ductus arteriosus, and suprasystemic right ventricular systolic pressure.
The infant was started on intravenous prostaglandin E1 owing to suspected coarctation of the aorta and given intravenous epinephrine and dopamine drips because of hypotension.
Electroencephalogram showed frequent subclinical seizures that were difficult to control, requiring multiple agents including intravenous levetiracetam, lacosamide, and phenobarbital.
Ophthalmology evaluation showed small, hypoplastic optic nerves of both eyes concerning for septo-optic dysplasia; the left eye showed a posterior polar cataract with microspherophakia.

Postnatal MRI of the brain confirmed findings of multifocal infarcts of unknown etiology, diffuse mild polymicrogyria, dysgenesis of the corpus callosum, optic nerve hypoplasia, a defect within the intraventricular septum, and inferior vermian hypoplasia.
Genetic analysis with rapid whole exome sequencing showed a de novo heterozygous variant at c.2771 G>A of the Col4a1 gene.

Chromosomal microarray analysis revealed a normal male sex chromosome with no other clinically significant abnormalities and a nonspecific contiguous region of copy neutral absence of heterozygosity on chromosome 11.
Postnatal renal ultrasound showed mild calyceal dilatation of the left kidney.
Cytomegalovirus workup was negative.

source_metadata.title: Retinochoroiditis secondary to Rickettsia typhi infection: a case report

evidence_events.source_span: 24-year-old male soldier with no previous eye disease, who was referred due to bilateral retinochoroiditis and vitritis
7-day history of persistent paracentral scotoma in the right eye and 2-day history of scattered dark spots in the left eye
Two-week episode of fever (39 °C), headaches, night sweats, rapid weight loss of 10 kg, and a transient rash covering the body
Physical examination revealed bilateral keratic precipitates on the lower corneal periphery, 1+ anterior vitreous cells, small retinal lesions, and mild optic discs elevation

Fluorescein angiography indicated mild disc hyperfluorescence without vascular leakage; ICG scan showed no focal lesions in right eye and small hypofluorescent foci in left eye macula and nasally to disc

OCT showed inner retinal hyper-reflective lesions para-centrally with irregularities in the photoreceptor layer and choroidal thickening (>400 µm), with small hyperreflective foci in posterior vitreous

Laboratory tests showed thrombocytosis, elevated ESR (24 mm/hr), elevated liver enzymes, elevated ACE levels, mild elevation of immunoglobulins, normal complement, ANA and ANCA, negative toxoplasmosis serology, negative RPR and TPHA, and positive Rickettsia typhi serology
Rheumatology consultation ruled out autoimmune diseases; infectious disease consultation confirmed Rickettsia typhi infection
Treatment with systemic doxycycline and prednisone led to improvement of visual acuity, ocular symptoms, OCT abnormalities, and resolution of inflammation
Two months after initial presentation, further ocular improvement with stable visual acuity, few vitreous cells, unremarkable discs, dry macula, and preserved retinal structures on OCT

source_metadata.title: CMV neuroretinitis in an immunocompetent patient: a unique case report
source_metadata.notes: Case report from Romanian Journal of Ophthalmology 2024; includes clinical, serological, imaging, and treatment response evidence.

evidence_events.source_span: A 40-year-old man came with the main concern of experiencing diminished vision in his right eye, which was more pronounced than in his left eye, persisting for five months. He presented a history of trauma to RE 5 months back.
On examination, his visual acuity RE was hand movement, and LE vision was 6/60, with sluggish pupillary reaction in LE. On a slit lamp, he had traumatic cataract RE.
The RE fundus could not be examined on indirect ophthalmoscopy due to cataracts; a normal B-scan was done.
Cataract surgery was done in the RE.
Postoperative fundus examination of the RE was within normal limits.

LE Fundus examination showed one large approximately half-a-disc diameter white, fluffy lesion with overlying retinal hemorrhages and a few scattered necrotic spots along the inferotemporal arcade. Mild optic disc pallor was noted with a macular star about 2DD away from the optic disc, the rest of the fundus was normal.
A slit lamp examination showed grade 1 optic disc edema.
OCT showed hyperreflective signals at the level of the outer plexiform layer representing retinal exudate.
The patient did not report any accompanying systemic symptoms, and overall physical examination yielded no abnormalities.

All necessary laboratory tests, including CBC, ESR, ACE, FTA-ABS, PPD, VDRL, Antiphospholipid antibody, ANA, RF, chest X-ray, anti-HIV antibody, anti-HCV antibody, and anti-HbsAg antibody, were conducted, and the results were within normal ranges except TORCH profile, which showed IgG titer of Toxoplasma gondii - 36.785 IU/ml, Rubella virus - 142.690 IU/ml, Cytomegalovirus (CMV) - 1073 AU/ml, Herpes simplex virus (HSV) - 57.335 AU/ml. Immunoglobulin M (Ig M) titers were normal.
The CD4 cell count of the patient was within the normal range, measuring 950 cells/mm3.
Initially, the treatment regimen included an oral tablet of prednisolone 60 mg/day and a tablet of Septran DS twice daily. Still, the patient did not show any improvement.

He was started on valganciclovir - an oral loading dose of Valganciclovir 900 mg once daily dose for 21 days followed by a maintenance dose of 450 mg once daily for 6 weeks and oral prednisolone, which was tapered over 6 weeks.

1.5 months after the initiation of valganciclovir therapy, the patient's vision improved to 6/6 and the fundus examination showed a healing choroiditis patch with a resolving hemorrhagic patch and macular star.

Blood serology (TORCH profile) repeated after 1.5 months showed IgG titer of Toxoplasma gondii - 30.120 IU/ml, Rubella virus - 109 IU/ml, Cytomegalovirus (CMV) - 159 AU/ml, Herpes simplex virus (HSV) - 3.5 AU/ml.

source_metadata.title: Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis Discovered Because of Repeated Upper Eyelid Swelling
source_metadata.notes: Case report of a 25-year-old female with repeated eyelid swelling and PR3-ANCA positive probable GPA isolated to ocular lesion.

evidence_events.source_span: A 25-year-old Japanese female visited her local doctor complaining of left eye pain and redness for 1 month.
She was prescribed antibacterial eye drops and steroid eye drops; however, no improvement was observed for one month.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: prescribed antibacterial and steroid eye drops

evidence_events.source_span: She visited the Department of Ophthalmology, Asahi General Hospital, in February 2017, presenting with upper eyelid swelling and conjunctival and episcleral hyperemia in the left eye.
Orbital magnetic resonance imaging revealed edematous signal changes in the left eyelid and periorbital skin.
We suspected hordeum, periorbital cellulitis, and episcleritis.
The patient was treated with 1.5% levofloxacin eye drops and 0.1% betamethasone eye drops; however, the eyelid swelling worsened and improved markedly every week.

Throughout the follow-up period, there were no inflammatory findings in the anterior chamber, and the vitreous body and fundus did not show any inflammatory complications such as vitreous opacities or vasculitis.

After a blood sample was positive for PR3-ANCA, the patient was referred to the Department of Collagen Disease, where she was diagnosed with GPA (probable) with an ocular lesion alone according to the diagnostic criteria of the Health and Welfare Ministry in Japan.
Otolaryngological examination, electrocardiogram, and chest computed tomography revealed no abnormalities.

Treatment with prednisolone (PSL; 40 mg/day) was initiated 1 month after she first visited our hospital. Dramatic improvements in hyperemia and eyelid swelling were observed immediately after treatment initiation.
After PSL was reduced to 6 mg/day (7 months after the patient’s first visit to our clinic), PR3-ANCA became negative.
Thereafter, the PSL dose was gradually reduced and eventually discontinued at 4 years and 2 months. During this time, the patient remained negative for PR3-ANCA and had no recurrent ocular symptoms.

source_metadata.title: Optic Nerve Glioblastoma with Optic Chiasm Involvement: A Case Report and a Brief Literature Review

evidence_events.source_span: A 68-year-old woman presented to the hospital with painless outward protrusion of the left eye which first manifested six months earlier, accompanied by deteriorating eyesight, limited ability to look upward, and partial loss of vision in the same eye.
Ocular examination revealed exophthalmos, ptosis, optic nerve atrophy, senile macular degeneration, corpus vitreum destruction of the left eye, and limited left eye movement.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: ocular ultrasonography, optical coherence tomography (OCT), slit lamp and torch light examinations, and visual acuity assessments

evidence_events.source_span: Ocular ultrasound showed a tissue type echo signal mass, measuring about 1.3 cm × 1.4 cm, behind the left eye.

Optical coherence tomography (OCT), retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) analysis, and ganglion cell layer (GCL) measurement revealed a flattened thinner retina around the macular area in the left eye, reduced retinal nerve fiber layer in all left eye quadrants, and ganglion cell damage.
CT scan revealed a pathological mass in the intraconal space, ~1.5 cm × 2.5 cm × 1.5 cm, occupying most of the orbit with thinning and depression of the rectus muscles of the eye.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: noncontrast enhanced CT scan of the orbits

evidence_events.source_span: Contrast enhanced MRI revealed an altered optic nerve affecting retrobulbar, prechiasmal, and optic chiasm levels with a pathological, smoothly contoured mass with cystic changes measuring about 5.2 cm × 2.0 cm × 1.9 cm, with peripheral contrast accumulation extending along the optic chiasm and close to the frontal lobe's straight gyrus and A1 segment of the anterior cerebral artery.
Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) showed restricted diffusion with ADC value of 1500 × 10⁻⁶ mm²/s and high T2 signal intensity in the contrast-enhancing tumor component.
MRI report concluded a probable diagnosis of optic nerve glioma and surgical resection via pterional craniotomy was proposed and accepted.
Left-sided pterional craniotomy with partial resection of the superior orbital wall was performed; tumor tissue appeared light gray, loose, fragmented, and was aspirated with CUSA.
Tumorous tissue (1.5 cm × 0.5 cm × 0.3 cm) was extracted during surgery and sent for pathology.

Histopathology showed spherical cells with nuclear polymorphism, multinucleated tumor cells, vascular proliferation, multiple mitotic figures, positive GFAP, negative ATRX and IDH1 R132H, and KI-67 around 20–25%.

Postoperative head MRI showed partial resection of the left optic nerve with residual tumor tissue and edema extending into the left retrobulbar space, prechiasmal space, and left side of the optic chiasm.
Based on morphological, immunohistochemical, and radiological postoperative data, diagnosis of glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, with optic chiasm involvement was determined.

source_metadata.title: Alkaptonuria: a rare disease with multiorgan manifestation and a long-awaited diagnosis

evidence_events.source_span: We present a case of alkaptonuria in a Caucasian male patient diagnosed in his 70s. The patient has a monozygotic twin brother, and they have consistently exhibited similar symptoms throughout their adult lives, ultimately leading to a shared medical diagnosis.

The symptoms include early-onset arthropathy, tendinopathy, osteopenia, visible discolouration of the auricular regions and fingers, discolouration of the sclera, secondary glaucoma, proteinuria, calcification of the mitral valve and the formation of black urethral and prostate stones.
Since they were young, the two brothers’ mother noticed small black spots on their underpants and bed sheets that wouldn’t disappear even after washing.

In their early 40s, pigmentation of the sclera began to appear in both brothers, along with pigmentation of the ears and fingers. The patient was examined at an ophthalmology department, but no underlying cause for the discolouration could be concluded.

When the patient was in his late 40s, he began regular monitoring for chronic cough, during which eosinophils were detected in blood samples. The initial lung function test revealed a result of 60%, raising suspicion of eosinophilic asthma.

In his early 50s, the patient was incidentally found to have proteinuria during a routine check by his general practitioner, despite never experiencing urinary tract symptoms. This led to an extended examination of the kidneys due to differential diagnoses such as renal cancer, glomerulonephritis, diabetic kidney failure and myelomatosis.

Regarding musculoskeletal symptoms, he first sought medical attention for knee problems in his 50s. Musculoskeletal symptoms progressed from knee problems to diffuse lower back pain and eventually pain in the groin and hips.
Before diagnosis, the patient underwent multiple X-rays, six steroid blocks, MRIs, a positron emission tomography/CT and two hospital admissions due to spontaneous tendon ruptures.

In his early 70s, the patient himself suggested alkaptonuria due to similar symptoms in his twin brother. During the brother’s surgery, black discolouration of bone tissue was observed, prompting termination of the procedure and genetic investigations.

Diagnosis was established through a diagnostic triad including a urine spot test for homogentisic acid (HGA) in both brothers and genetic DNA testing of the twin brother revealing heterozygous pathogenic variants c.481G>A, p.(Gly161Arg) and c.1017G>T, p.(Met339Ile).

source_metadata.title: Simultaneous central retinal vein and cilioretinal artery occlusion in a young female patient with progestin-only oral contraceptive use: a case report
source_metadata.notes: Extraction based on case presentation and discussion sections with source order preserved.

evidence_events.source_span: A 28-year-old Pakistani female patient presented with sudden, painless vision loss in the left eye, 3 hours prior to her arrival at the ophthalmology clinic.
Visual acuity in the affected eye was limited to counting fingers at a distance of 0.5 feet, with a best-corrected visual acuity of 6/6 in the right eye.

Fundoscopic examination revealed optic disc edema, preretinal hemorrhages, venous dilation, and cotton wool spots consistent with central retinal vein occlusion, alongside ischemic changes in the foveal region suggestive of cilioretinal artery occlusion.
Optical coherence tomography revealed inner retinal hyperreflectivity.
Fluorescein fundus angiography revealed delayed dye filling of the ciliary retinal artery, with a masking effect due to preretinal hemorrhages in the left eye.

Systemic workup to rule out thrombophilia and other vascular risks was negative, including normal prothrombin time, activated partial thromboplastin time, international normalized ratio, antiphospholipid antibodies, factor V Leiden mutation, autoimmune profile, carotid Doppler ultrasonography, echocardiography, and abdominal and pelvic ultrasound.
The patient had been taking progestin-only pills for contraception for 25 days before discontinuing, starting 3.5 months after her last cesarean section delivery.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: started after last delivery 3.5 months ago

evidence_events.source_span: The patient was treated with acetazolamide, aspirin, ocular massage, and a dorzolamide-timolol combination for intraocular pressure control; panretinal photocoagulation was performed 6 weeks later to prevent neovascular complications.
At 12 weeks, the patient's vision improved to 6/36 in the affected eye with intraocular pressure of 12 mmHg.

source_metadata.title: Intracameral gnathostomiasis presenting as neuroretinitis

evidence_events.source_span: A male patient in his 40s presented with a 1 week history of periocular swelling, redness and decreased vision in his right eye.

His best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 6/60 in the right eye and 6/6 in the left eye. Intraocular pressure (IOP) was 24 mm Hg in the right eye and 14 mm Hg in the left eye. Both pupils responded normally to light, indicating no relative afferent pupillary defect.

On slit-lamp examination, the right eye showed ciliary congestion, anterior chamber cells 4+ and vitreous cells 2+. Fundus examination of the right eye revealed fibrous proliferation superior and temporal to the hyperaemic oedematous disc with peripapillary exudation superior and inferior to the disc and peripapillary haemorrhage, accompanied by macular edema that was confirmed by optical coherence tomography (OCT). The left eye examination was normal.

A presumptive diagnosis of panuveitis in the right eye was made, and the patient was initially treated with topical corticosteroids, cycloplegics and IOP-lowering medication, pending laboratory results.

One week later, a slit-lamp examination of the right eye revealed a live nematode in the anterior chamber with whitish material attached to the iris hole. Fundus examination showed a macular star, indicating improvement in macular edema.

Laboratory tests for infections, including HIV, Rapid Plasma Reagin, Venereal Disease Research Laboratory, Treponema pallidum haemagglutination antibody and QuantiFERON-TB Gold, were negative. Serological testing for toxoplasmosis was positive for IgG, and the complete blood count revealed elevated eosinophils at 8%, with an absolute eosinophil count of 6.16 x 10^8 cells/L (normal <5 x 10^8 cells/L). An immunofluorescent assay (IFA) for IgM and IgG anti-Bartonella henselae showed no evidence of B. henselae-specific antibodies. A brain CT scan showed no intraocular parasites, and oesophagogastroduodenoscopy and colonoscopy exhibited normal findings.

Following surgical removal, the nematode was sent to the Department of Microbiology and was identified as Gnathostoma spinigerum, measuring approximately 5 mm in length and 0.5 mm in width. The parasite has a typical lip and head bulb. The body was covered with cuticular spines, while the wall of the parasite contained the intestinal tract, cervical sac and oesophagus.

The surgical removal of the nematode was performed using retrobulbar anaesthesia. Initially, we administered the viscoelastic agent through anterior chamber paracentesis to facilitate the removal of the living nematode using intraocular forceps.

Following surgery, the patient received postoperative management consisting of topical prednisolone acetate 1% every 2 hours, atropine 1% two times per day and oral prednisolone at a dosage of 1 mg/kg/day, with tapering doses. By postoperative day 7, the anterior chamber reaction had subsided and become quiet, with slight improvement observed in vitreous cells. Consequently, albendazole at a dosage of 400 mg two times per day was initiated for a 21-day course.

Three weeks post-surgery, a significant improvement was noted in the vitreous reaction. Fundus examination of the right eye revealed a whitish scar in the superior and temporal regions of the optic disc, accompanied by a persistent macular star. At 6 weeks postoperation, the macula status remained similar to that observed at the third week postoperation, with a reduction in the hard exudates. BCVA in the right eye had improved to 6/9.

evidence_milestones.test_visible_evidence: Surgical removal of nematode; postoperative corticosteroids; albendazole started day 7 post-op for 21 days.
evidence_milestones.source_span: The surgical removal of the nematode was performed using retrobulbar anaesthesia. Initially, we administered the viscoelastic agent through anterior chamber paracentesis to facilitate the removal of the living nematode using intraocular forceps. Following surgery, the patient received postoperative management consisting of topical prednisolone acetate 1% every 2 hours, atropine 1% two times per day and oral prednisolone at a dosage of 1 mg/kg/day, with tapering doses. By postoperative day 7, the anterior chamber reaction had subsided and become quiet, with slight improvement observed in vitreous cells. Consequently, albendazole at a dosage of 400 mg two times per day was initiated for a 21-day course.

diagnostic_reasoning_verbatim_spans: One week later, a slit-lamp examination of the right eye revealed a live nematode in the anterior chamber with whitish material attached to the iris hole.
Following surgical removal, the nematode was sent to the Department of Microbiology and was identified as Gnathostoma spinigerum.
Laboratory tests for infections, including HIV, Rapid Plasma Reagin, Venereal Disease Research Laboratory, Treponema pallidum haemagglutination antibody and QuantiFERON-TB Gold, were negative.
Serological testing for toxoplasmosis was positive for IgG, and the complete blood count revealed elevated eosinophils at 8%.
An immunofluorescent assay (IFA) for IgM and IgG anti-Bartonella henselae showed no evidence of B. henselae-specific antibodies.
The concurrent optic disc swelling and macular star formation strongly suggest an association between intraocular gnathostomiasis and neuroretinitis.
diagnostic_reasoning_items: Initial presentation with periocular swelling, redness, and decreased vision suggested ocular inflammation.
Slit-lamp and fundus findings indicated panuveitis with macular edema.
Discovery of live nematode in anterior chamber was a major diagnostic clue.
Negative infectious labs ruled out common infectious causes such as HIV, syphilis, tuberculosis, and Bartonella henselae.
Positive toxoplasmosis IgG indicated past infection but no active disease.
Morphological identification of Gnathostoma spinigerum confirmed intraocular gnathostomiasis.
The optic disc swelling and macular star pattern linked the parasitic infection to neuroretinitis.
hidden_reference.final_diagnosis: Intracameral gnathostomiasis presenting as neuroretinitis
hidden_reference.diagnostic_reasoning: The patient presented with ocular inflammation and decreased vision. Initial workup showed panuveitis and macular edema. One week later, a live nematode was found in the anterior chamber. Infectious labs were negative except for past toxoplasmosis exposure. Surgical removal and morphological identification confirmed Gnathostoma spinigerum infection. The optic disc swelling and macular star indicated neuroretinitis caused by intraocular gnathostomiasis.
hidden_reference.article_derived_evidence_summary: The case documents a middle-aged male with right eye periocular swelling, redness, and vision loss. source_metadata.title: Bilateral idiopathic macular hole in a young female
source_metadata.notes: Case report of a young female with bilateral idiopathic full thickness macular holes, surgical treatment and follow-up.

evidence_events.source_span: A woman in her early 30s presented to the retina clinic with a progressive decrease in central vision in both eyes and metamorphopsia over 6 months.
She had no significant past medical or ocular history, and she denied any history of trauma.

On examination, the best-corrected visual acuity (OD) was 6/24, N8 (-3.50 dioptre sphere, -2.00 dioptre cylindrical, axis 10 degree) and (OS) was 4/60 (-4.00 dioptre sphere, -1.00 dioptre cylindrical, axis 180 degree).
Examination with the Amsler grid chart revealed bilateral metamorphopsia.
Anterior segment examination of both eyes was normal. She had a clear crystalline lens. The axial length was 24.02 mm (OD) and 24.15 mm (OS). The intraocular pressure was 14 mm Hg in both eyes.
Fundoscopic examination revealed full-thickness macular holes in both eyes. The right eye showed a mild temporal peripapillary atrophy. No peripheral retinal breaks were seen.
Spectral domain OCT confirmed the presence of full-thickness macular holes with cystic spaces in both eyes. The minimum inner diameter length of the macular hole was 431 µm (OD) and 512 µm (OS).
Systemic evaluation included blood tests for autoimmune markers, infectious agents and metabolic disorders, all of which were unremarkable.
The patient underwent a standard three-port 25-gauge pars plana vitrectomy in the left eye with brilliant blue green-assisted internal limiting membrane peeling and 14% C3F8 gas tamponade.
Surgery for the right eye was performed 4 weeks later with the same technique.

Postoperative visual acuity improved to 6/9 (OD) and 6/18p (OS) after 2 weeks. Fundus examination and OCT showed closure of the macular holes with type 2A closure in the right eye and type 1B closure in the left eye.
At 10 weeks, best corrected visual acuity improved further to 6/9p (OD) and 6/9 (OS). OCT still showed type 2A closure (OD) and type 1B closure (OS) of the macular holes.

source_metadata.title: A Case of Tubulointerstitial Nephritis and Uveitis Syndrome in an Elderly Patient

evidence_events.source_span: A 61-year-old man came to the hospital complaining of bilateral flank pain. Left flank pain began approximately a month earlier, followed by right flank pain 4 days later. The patient also complained of dyspnea on exertion, urinary frequency, and foamy urine.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: Left flank pain began approximately a month earlier, followed by right flank pain 4 days later

evidence_events.source_span: He was diagnosed with hypertension 15 years prior and had taken traditional Korean herbal medicines, such as acanthopanax, phellinus, licorice root, and steamed red ginseng.
One week before coming to our hospital, he visited a local ophthalmologic clinic for bilateral floater symptoms and was diagnosed with anterior uveitis and treated with systemic and topical steroids.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: One week before coming to our hospital

evidence_events.source_span: Laboratory tests conducted at the hospital showed a blood urea nitrogen of 26 mg/dL, a serum creatinine of 2.3 mg/dL, and an estimated glomerular filtration rate (GFR) of 30.9 mL/min (normal, 80 to 120 mL/min).
evidence_events.procedural_cue: Laboratory tests conducted at the hospital

evidence_events.source_span: An ultrasonography of the kidney showed elevated echogenicity of the parenchyma.
A kidney biopsy specimen revealed diffuse interstitial infiltration of lymphocytes and eosinophils and mild tubular atrophy with focal fibrosis of the interstitium.
No electron-dense deposits were seen on electron microscopy. No antibody deposits or immune complexes were apparent on immunofluorescent studies.
Systemic administration of prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day was started and slowly tapered; furosemide and carvedilol were added for blood pressure control.

An ophthalmologic examination showed visual acuity 20/20 in the right eye and 20/25 in the left eye. A slit lamp examination showed a mild degree (1+ to 2+) of inflammatory cells in the anterior chamber of both eyes; synechia of the iris was not observed. Funduscopic examination was normal, and vitreous opacity was not observed.
Based on these findings, a diagnosis of TINU syndrome was made, and the patient was treated with a topical steroid for anterior uveitis. Subsequently, the anterior uveitis was well-controlled.

source_metadata.title: Visual evoked potentials in early diagnosis of demyelinating diseases – a case report of Devic’s disease
source_metadata.notes: Case report of a 21-year-old woman with early diagnosis of Devic's disease (NMO) using visual evoked potentials.

evidence_events.source_span: A 21-year-old woman presented with non-specific ocular phenomena, referred as a subjective visual impairment and “blurry” vision for 3 weeks.
The patient’s best corrected visual acuity was 6/6 in both eyes on Snellen charts.
Colour vision testing using the Ishihara tables was normal.

Examinations of pupillary reflexes, anterior segment, the eye fundus and the visual field (full field 120, Humphrey) were normal. A fluorescein angiography and macular OCT (Cirrus, Zeiss) were also non-contributory.
A multifocal ERG was performed to assess retinal function. The mfERG results were normal.

Pattern visual evoked responses (PVER) were performed according to ISCEV standards and compared with normal values. The latencies of P100 wave was 132 ms and 127 ms in right and left eye, respectively, so they were prolonged over 20% in both eyes in comparison to normal values. The morphology of the waves was also abnormal.

The brain MRI with contrast revealed 3 lesions not meeting diagnostic criteria for multiple sclerosis. The orbital MRI with contrast revealed no lesions. A spinal cord MRI showed 1 lesion on the C3/C4 level.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: brain, orbital, and spinal cord MRI with contrast

evidence_events.source_span: Within 6 weeks after first symptoms (three weeks after ophthalmic examination) the patient presented a weakening of the lower limbs and developed clinical transverse myelitis.
The spinal cord MRI revealed lesions extending over 3 vertebral segments.
The diagnosis of Devic’s syndrome was established, which was later confirmed by NMO-IgG seropositive status.
In 4 years’ observation, the visual function remains quite good (6/9 in both eyes), but urinary incontinence and walking disorders significantly worsen the 25-year-old patient’s quality of life.

source_metadata.title: Ocular Involvement of Brucellosis

evidence_events.source_span: A 29-year-old male was referred to Infectious Disease Clinic of Hamadan Sina Hospital in summer 2008 with acute onset of fever, headache, malaise, sweating and low back pain.
On examination, the patient was conscious and his temperature was 39°C. There were no obvious systemic findings such as organomegaly on physical examination.

Laboratory test findings were: white blood cell (WBC) count of 13350 (Neutrophil: 85%), erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) 48m/h, CRP+, RF-, ANA-, Wright’s agglutination titer of 1/1280. Results of serologic testing for syphilis, hepatitis, tuberculosis and AIDS were negative.
Outcomes of a lumbar puncture were normal. Blood levels for sugar, sodium and potassium were normal. Blood cultures were negative and electrocardiogram and chest-X-ray (CXR) were normal.
The patient was diagnosed with brucellosis, and treated with rifampin 600 mg/day and doxycycline 100 mg/twice daily.
After a week, the patient was referred for an Ophthalmology consult with complaints of ocular pain and redness and visual complaints.

On ophthalmic examination, visual acuity in both eyes was 20/25. There was diffuse conjunctival injection bilaterally which was more prominent in the right eye. The conjunctional injection was a mixture of ciliary injection, episcleritis and conjunctivitis but more severe in the ciliary area. Neither eye had signs of intraocular inflammation. Pupillary light reflexes were sluggish bilaterally but no afferent pupillary defect was present. The patient was orthophoric without any muscle involvement and there was no diplopia.
On funduscopy, there was bilateral optic disc swelling along with retinal hyperemia (optic disc hyperemia and vascular tortuosity) and diffuse intraretinal hemorrhage.
Intraocular pressure (IOP) was 26 mmHg in the right eye and 24 mmHg in the left eye.

The patient was hospitalized with a probable diagnosis of ocular brucellosis and was treated with co-trimoxazole adult two tablets, three times a day (tid), rifampin 600 mg/day doxycycline 100 mg/BID and prednisolone 1 mg/kg for 2 months.
Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging studies of the brain and optic nerve were requested. Both studies were unremarkable.
A brief visual field limitation was reported on perimetry.
Fever and headache diminished within 48 hours of the treatment however, ophthalmic complaints lingered.
One week after treatment, visual acuity improved to 20/20. Conjunctival hyperemia had decreased but previous funduscopic findings remained unchanged. IOP was 19 mmHg OD and 16 mmHg OS using timolol.
Four weeks after treatment, there were no visual complaints. Optic disc swelling and hyperemia had decreased and IOP bilaterally was within normal limits.
Thirteen months after treatment, the funduscopic examination was normal.

evidence_events.source_span: A 69-year-old Caucasian male was referred to our department for purulent conjunctivitis. He had no past medical history except for an angioimmunoblastic-T-cell-lymphoma, currently treated with chemotherapy, including lenalidomide and CHOP.

Five days after his third round of chemotherapy, his Dachshund dog struck his right eye while sneezing. Four hours later, redness around his eye and inflammatory peri-orbital edema appeared, associated with fever reaching 39°C during the following night.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: Five days after chemotherapy; 33 hours after dog sneezing

evidence_events.source_span: Physical examination revealed purulent conjunctivitis with chemosis and conjunctival hyperemia of the right eye associated with inflammatory edema of both the upper and lower lids. Skin rupture and purulent encystment were observed above and below his eye respectively. Visual acuity was 3/10 in the right eye and 4/10 in the left eye.

Slit lamp examination showed bilateral corticonuclear cataract. Intraocular pressure was 10 mm Hg and fluorescein eye test was normal in the left eye but could not be performed on the right eye. There were neither relative afferent pupillary defects nor extraocular movement abnormalities.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: Slit lamp and fluorescein eye test

evidence_events.source_span: White blood-cell count was normal (4900/mm3) but differential revealed lymphopenia (300/mm3). Absolute neutrophil count was within normal range (4400/mm3).
A computerized tomography scan revealed no evidence of intra-orbital extension.
Blood cultures were negative.

Conjunctival secretions were sampled on admission for bacteriological analysis and cultured on blood agar. Direct examination showed numerous leukocytes and rare gram-negative bacilli. Regular, grey, smooth colonies grew the next day. The oxidase test was positive for the 1-3 mm diameter, non-hemolytic colonies, strongly suggesting that the isolated strain belonged to Pasteurella genus.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: Conjunctival secretion sampling, culture, gram stain, oxidase test

evidence_events.source_span: The involvement of Pasteurella multocida was strongly suggested by mannitol fermentation (API-20E Array) and confirmed by MALDI TOF mass spectrometry.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: API-20E array and MALDI TOF mass spectrometry

evidence_events.source_span: An antibiotherapy associating intravenous amoxicillin 2 g tid and amoxicillin/clavulanate 2 g tid was administered immediately after bacteriological sampling. No topical therapy was prescribed except artificial tears.

The outcome was favorable in the next three days, allowing discharge of the patient with amoxicillin (2 g tid per os) alone once full sensitivity of Pasteurella multocida strain to amoxicillin was confirmed.

source_metadata.title: An unusual case of congenital cytomegalovirus infection-related retinopathy

evidence_events.source_span: An infant boy weighing 1860 g was born at 36 weeks and three days because of fetal growth restriction (FGR) and an abnormal biophysical examination.
The mother was HIV-negative but had reported a fever at four weeks of gestation, and blood examination suggested a primary CMV infection with positive CMV-IgG and CMV-IgM titers.
During pregnancy, hepatosplenomegaly, intravertebral calcification and microcephaly were detected by ultrasonography and fetal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI).
The infant was diagnosed with severe symptomatic congenital CMV infection confirmed by positive CMV-DNA in urine and whole blood.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: CMV-DNA testing in urine and whole blood

evidence_events.source_span: Slit-lamp examination revealed no abnormalities in the cornea, iris or anterior chamber in either eye.

Ophthalmoscopic examinations revealed posterior vessel dilation and a demarcation line at the temporal peripheral zone in both eyes, and an arteriovenous anastomosis in the right eye with no signs of chorioretinitis.

On the fourth day of life, fluorescein angiography (FA) revealed a filling delay and an arterio-venous anastomosis, but no leakage from retinal vessels; a small avascular zone was found at the most peripheral retina.
Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) of aqueous humor was positive for CMV-DNA, confirming ocular CMV infection.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: after FA on fourth day of life

evidence_events.source_span: Systemic antiviral therapy with oral valgancyclovir was initiated and continued for six weeks.
Six days after starting valgancyclovir, vessel dilation regressed completely and arterio-venous anastomosis improved remarkably.
At three months of age, fluorescein angiography showed almost complete regression of arterio-venous anastomosis but revealed chorioretinal atrophy at the macula and around the optic disc.

source_metadata.title: A Rare Case of Tubulointerstitial Nephritis and Uveitis Syndrome Treated with a Multi-Specialty Approach

evidence_events.source_span: A 23-year-old female presented initially to her PCP with complaints of nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain.

A week later, she still had symptoms and a complete blood count (CBC), complete metabolic panel (CMP), and urine analysis (UA) were repeated. All were normal except for an increase in creatinine of 2.35 mg/dL and 4+ proteinuria.

She was sent to the ER, where she received IV fluids and potassium. A week later, repeat labs showed a still elevated serum creatinine of 2.17 mg/dL and she was consequently referred to nephrology for evaluation.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: ER treatment with IV fluids and potassium; repeat labs

evidence_events.source_span: Nephrologic evaluation revealed an elevated Alb/Cr ratio 130, urine β2-microglobulin 33,100 μg/L (normal <300 μg/L), ESR 81, Cr 2.2, CRP 5.3, HgA1c 5.7, and proteinuria (100 mg/dL).
Serologic studies, including ANCA, cryoglobulin, complement, anti-RNP, anti-SSA/B, anti-Smith, anti-dsDNA, C3, C4, were negative.
Renal nuclear scan was within normal limits.

Kidney biopsy showed marked interstitial infiltrate with tubulitis and focal tubular epithelial cell necrosis, as well as an admixture of eosinophils in a background of otherwise T-cells with rare admixture of B-cells within the interstitium.
One week after the biopsy, she revealed that over the past 8–9 days, she had developed progressively worsening bilateral eye redness.
Urinalysis revealed a protein of 900 mg/dL; serum creatinine was 2.5.
Ophthalmologist determined that there was anterior uveitis present in both eyes with keratic precipitates and posterior synechiae present bilaterally as seen in Figure 1.
Visual acuity declined from her pre-inflammation baseline of 20/20 with correction in both eyes to 20/30-2 in her right and 20/20-2 in her left eye.
With the diagnosis of anterior uveitis, TINU syndrome was confirmed.
She was started on 60 mg of prednisone daily for three weeks and prednisolone acetate ophthalmic one drop every two hours while awake.
Three weeks later, proteinuria improved to 100 mg/dL, serum creatinine improved to 1.8.
After tapering steroids over months, urine was negative for protein and serum creatinine was 1.1, then 1.0, and visual acuity returned to her normal baseline.
