source_metadata.title: Paraneoplastic mucous membrane pemphigoid with ocular and laryngeal involvement

evidence_events.source_span: A 73-year-old Caucasian woman presented to the ear–nose–throat clinic with a diffuse oral burning sensation and disabling pharyngodynia over the last 3 months. She reported weight loss with asthenia, cough when lying down, hoarseness and dyspnoea.

Previous treatments included topical and systemic antifungal agents because of Candida-positive oral swabs, antibiotics and antiviral therapy. Two previous oral biopsies revealed fibrin deposits with leucocytes without malignant cells.

Her past medical history was marked by two simultaneous cancers: a breast carcinoma and an endometrial adenocarcinoma treated successfully 8 years previously by right mastectomy, axillary dissection, adjuvant radiotherapy and hormonotherapy, and by adnexectomy and hysterectomy, respectively.

Clinical examination revealed bilateral conjunctival inflammation and three blister-type skin lesions on the arms and legs. Inspection of the oral cavity showed mucosal ulcerations of the ventral tongue, cheeks, soft palate, uvula and posterior oropharyngeal wall. A flexible transnasal endoscopy revealed crusts on the right middle turbinate and nasopharynx, as well as diffuse whitish pseudomembrane-covered erosions of almost all the supraglottic area and posterior hypopharyngeal wall.
Full blood tests were unremarkable.
A perilesional skin biopsy of a bullous lesion on the left leg revealed subepithelial cleavage with a rare eosinophilic infiltrate on routine histopathological haematoxylin and eosin staining.
Direct immunofluorescence analysis revealed a linear deposit of IgG and C3 at the dermo-epidermal junction. Indirect immunofluorescence analysis was negative.
Immunoblotting studies demonstrated circulating autoantibodies to bullous pemphigoid (BP)180 and laminin 5 (ELISA-BP 180 +: 26.99 U/mL; ELISA-BP 230: −).
A PET-CT scan was performed and revealed a left supraclavicular and multiple retroperitoneal adenopathies.

Ultrasound-guided and CT-guided fine-needle biopsies were compatible with metastatic adenocarcinoma of breast origin, were hormone dependent and were considered as a late metastatic recurrence of the previous breast tumour, without locoregional relapse.
The patient was treated initially with intravenous dexamethasone followed by oral prednisone and dapsone at increasing doses. Hormonal therapy with letrozole was also started.

After 2 months, a transnasal endoscopy revealed an interarytenoid synechia with a somewhat decreased laryngeal patency, while the ophthalmic examination showed bilateral moderate symblepharon without active inflammation.
Due to mild haemolysis and general ill feeling when taking dapsone, intravenous immunoglobulin was introduced every 6 weeks and prednisone and dapsone doses were slowly tapered.
At 18 months, she suffered from a laryngeal relapse, requiring the introduction of rituximab and a transitory increase of prednisone and dapsone doses, with a good clinical response.

After 3 years, the cicatricial supraglottic scar and symblepharon have remained stable under regular immunoglobulin therapy, dapsone and prednisone. The metastatic breast adenocarcinoma has stayed under control, and the patient reports an entirely satisfactory quality of life.

source_metadata.title: Agenesis of the dorsal pancreas: a rare cause of insulin-dependent diabetes without abdominal pain

evidence_events.source_span: A 23-year-old Chinese woman visited our department because of hyperglycemia that had been detected during a routine school blood test 3 days earlier. The patient denied any history of abdominal pain, chronic diarrhea, dry mouth, polydipsia, polyuria, overeating, and/or emaciation, and had no evidence of gastrointestinal disease, trauma, or history relevant to hyperglycemia.
Upon physical examination, the patient was found to have a body mass index of 20.8 kg/m2, with regular menstrual cycles and no congenital defects. No abnormal signs were observed.

Laboratory analysis showed fasting plasma glucose: 12.29 mmol/L; postprandial 2-hours plasma glucose: 22.3 mmol/L without ketosis; fasting C peptide release test at 0, 0.5, 1, 2, 3 hours: 0.621, 0.878, 0.615, 0.353, and 0.128 ng/mL, respectively (normal range: 1.1–4.4 ng/mL); fructose: 598.13 μmol/L; glycated hemoglobin/HbA1c: 13.4%; random urinary microfilming: 25.4 mg/L; uric acid: 517 μmol/L; triglycerides: 24.27 mmol/L; cholesterol: 15.47 mmol/L. Anti-insulin, anti-islet cell, and antiglutamic acid decarboxylase antibodies were negative, and amylase and lipase levels were normal. The patient was diagnosed with fatty liver, hyperlipidemia, and hyperuricemia.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed the absence of most of the neck, body, and tail of the pancreas, and these findings were further confirmed by magnetic resonance angiography (MRA) and diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI). The pancreatic head was not enlarged. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP) revealed the absence of the dorsal pancreatic duct. There was no evidence of chronic pancreatitis or other visceral malformations.
Although the patient had no symptoms of diabetes or neurological changes, she exhibited obvious and severe diabetes-related retinal changes.

Insulin replacement therapy at a daily dosage up to 45 U was administered for diabetes treatment. The patient's blood glucose levels improved after insulin therapy and were maintained with intensive insulin therapy. She was subsequently referred to the Ophthalmology Department for the treatment of diabetic retinopathy.

source_metadata.title: Sequential retinal necrosis secondary to varicella zoster in unrecognised long-standing HIV infection: patient safety report

evidence_events.source_span: A retired woman who developed left-sided herpes zoster ophthalmicus (HZO) for 18 months prior was attending the corneal clinic for keratouveitis in the left eye for 7 months.
She offered new symptoms of a 4-week reduction of right vision.
Vision; no perception of light (NPL) in both eyes.

Anterior segment examination of right eye was unremarkable. Diffuse stromal corneal scaring with long-standing pigmented keratic precipitates and 360 degrees posterior synechiae was present in left eye.

Funduscopy in the left eye was precluded by cataract. Funduscopy in the right eye was impaired by vitreous haze. Multiple areas of white retinal swelling in the posterior pole with macula involvement were apparent in the right eye. Obliterated arterioles with perivascular sheathing (Kyrieleis’ plaques) were detected.
Ultrasound showed bilateral retinal detachments.
Haemoglobin 112 g/L, white cell count 3.1 ×10⁹/L, liver function tests and urea and electrolytes were normal; C reactive protein 5.6 mg/L.
Blood cultures were negative for aerobic and anaerobic culture.
Toxoplasma and CMV serology negative, serum varicella zoster IgG positive, HIV positive, viral load was 116 912 copies/mL and CD4 T lymphocyte count was 37 cells/μL.
CMV DNA positive: 2308 IU/mL in serum.
Aqueous from anterior chamber paracentesis of right eye was positive for VZV DNA on PCR and negative for CMV and herpes simplex.

This patient was admitted to hospital and acyclovir 1.8 g daily by intravenous infusion was provided followed by oral valacyclovir 3 g per day. She received an intravitreal forscarnet injection (1.2 mg/0.05 mL).
The HIV-positive result was discussed with the patient and antiretroviral therapy (ART) commenced.

Following 1 week of ART, a repeat serum VZV DNA test was negative. Vision remains at NPL in both eyes. Bilateral retinal detachments were considered as inoperable. The patient was registered blind and has had input from social services and community occupational therapy including modifications to her home because of acquired visual loss.

HIV test was positive with a very low CD4 count.

diagnostic_reasoning_items: Detection of VZV DNA in ocular fluid confirms viral retinitis due to varicella zoster virus.
Positive HIV test with severe immunosuppression explains susceptibility to progressive outer retinal necrosis.
Negative CMV and herpes simplex PCR in eye fluid excludes other herpesviruses as cause.

Poor visual outcome despite antiviral and antiretroviral therapy due to advanced retinal damage.
hidden_reference.final_diagnosis: Varicella zoster virus-induced sequential retinal necrosis in the setting of previously unrecognised advanced HIV infection
hidden_reference.diagnostic_reasoning: The detection of VZV DNA in ocular aqueous humor by PCR combined with positive HIV serology and very low CD4 count supports the diagnosis of varicella zoster virus-induced acute retinal necrosis and progressive outer retinal necrosis in an immunocompromised host. The clinical presentation with bilateral retinal detachments and characteristic fundus findings further supports this diagnosis. Other infectious causes were excluded by negative serology and PCR. Despite antiviral and antiretroviral treatment, the retinal damage was irreversible, resulting in blindness.

source_metadata.title: Fever of unknown origin: a challenging case

evidence_events.source_span: A 31-year-old Caucasian female smoker was admitted to the hospital with a 7-week history of fever associated with night sweats, joint pains, myalgia and nasal congestion.

She had already been hospitalised 3 weeks prior to this admission, at which time she was treated with empirical antibiotics for a presumed community-acquired pneumonia as CT scan of the thorax/abdomen/pelvis had revealed subsegmental patchy consolidation of the left lower lobe of the lung.
The patient was readmitted as she continued to have fever despite completing the course of antibiotics prescribed.
She had also been experiencing drenching night sweats, joint pains and myalgias, with recent development of dizziness and hearing impairment.

On examination she was noted to have conjunctival injection secondary to episcleritis and a non-pruritic maculopapular rash over the upper limbs, as well as nodular, tender lesions over her lower limbs.
Routine blood investigations were unremarkable apart from a normocytic normochromic anaemia with a high reticulocyte count, a neutrophilic leucocytosis and raised inflammatory markers.
Blood and urine cultures, as well as an extensive viral screen which included serology for Epstein-Barr virus, Cytomegalovirus and HIV, were negative.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: blood and urine cultures, viral serology

evidence_events.source_span: Repeat autoimmune screens, which included ANA, ANCA, ASMA, rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP and complement levels, were negative.
Repeat imaging of the chest showed complete resolution of the previous pulmonary consolidation following antibiotic treatment.
Serological tests for Mycoplasma, Bartonella, Coxiella, Brucella, Borrelia burgdorferi and Chlamydia, as well as for other infective conditions including syphilis and leishmania, were negative.
An MRI of the patient’s brain was performed in view of her audiovestibular symptoms; however, this only revealed long-standing mastoid effusions.
Audiometry was performed and this confirmed bilateral sensorineural hearing loss.
Biopsies from the lower limb rash showed a perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate typical of small-sized and medium-sized vessel vasculitis.
On considering all of the patient’s symptoms and their evolution, a tentative diagnosis of Cogan’s syndrome was entertained.
After being diagnosed with Cogan’s syndrome, the patient was started on oral prednisolone therapy with subsequent addition of methotrexate and folic acid.
Within a week of starting systemic steroids, our patient became afebrile with significant improvements in both her skin rash and hearing.

She was advised to gradually tail off her steroids but returned soon after in view of flare-up of all her prior symptoms, including low-grade fever, skin lesions, hearing impairment and conjunctival suffusion. It was also noted that her inflammatory markers had started to increase again.

source_metadata.title: New headaches with normal inflammatory markers: an early atypical presentation of giant cell arteritis
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from BMJ Case Reports 2018 article, focusing on case presentation, investigations, and diagnostic trajectory.

evidence_events.source_span: An 80-year-old man with a medical history of glaucoma, hypertension and first degree heart block presented with a 3-month history of frontal headaches.
A routine CT head was requested by his general practitioner (GP). This showed no intracranial masses or bony lesions but incidentally revealed a mature lacunar infarct of the left ventral thalamus.
Alongside his headaches, the patient developed bilateral jaw pain with claudication. He independently sought advice from his dentist and returned with a diagnosis of bruxism.

Three days after the CT scan (3 months after initial presentation to healthcare), the patient visited ophthalmology for a routine glaucoma follow-up appointment. The ophthalmologist elicited episodes of diplopia, amaurosis fugax and significant weight loss in the preceding months.
Examination revealed bilateral tender, nodular and weakly pulsatile temporal arteries. There was no relative afferent pupillary defect or anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy.

In light of the ongoing headaches, jaw claudication, diplopia, amaurosis fugax and weight loss, a diagnosis of GCA was suspected. The patient was referred the same day to the rheumatology department for prompt review.
Inflammatory markers were not significantly raised: C-reactive protein (CRP) 11 mg/L (<10) and ESR 15 mm/hour (1–19).
Temporal and axillary artery ultrasound (US) demonstrated a characteristic positive halo sign in the right temporal artery.
A right temporal artery biopsy (TAB) revealed a muscular artery with focal adventitial chronic inflammation and intimal hyperplasia with mild inflammation, consistent with GCA.
Sixty milligrams of prednisolone was initiated due to the presence of jaw claudication and visual symptoms in accordance with the British Society of Rheumatology guidelines.
At 4-week follow-up, his symptoms improved significantly and inflammatory markers remained low (CRP <3, ESR 2).

source_metadata.title: Lingual liability: macroglossia and dyspnoea as the harbinger of systemic AL (light-chain) cardiac amyloidosis
source_metadata.notes: Extraction based on case presentation, investigations, and relevant clinical course narrative.

evidence_events.source_span: A 58-year-old man initially presented to his dentist with a chief complaint of tongue discomfort with unusual indentations
Otolaryngology treated him for oral thrush with counselling to avoid tongue biting
He reported a progressive dyspnoea with activity
The bilateral periorbital plaques developed with the onset of his tongue discomfort
His tongue symptoms remained stable for a year while the dyspnoea on exertion was not associated with paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, orthopnoea or angina
He was re-evaluated by otolaryngology who biopsied the tongue given his persistent symptoms

During his initial evaluation with oncology, his clinical examination revealed findings of acute heart failure syndrome, characterised by a 6-month history of worsening dyspnoea on exertion and fatigue consistent with New York Heart Association class II symptoms with pitting lower extremity oedema, jugular venous distention while sitting upright, increased abdominal distention and mild bibasilar rales
He reported history of bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome status postsurgical release 2 years prior to the onset of his symptoms

Initial laboratory assay revealed a microcytic anaemia (haemoglobin 11.7 g/dL mean corpuscle value of 78.0fL), hyperlipidemia (an elevated LDL cholesterol of 148 mg/dL), hypoalbuminemia (3.3 g/dL), proteinuria (552 mg/dL), a mild elevation in serum troponin (0.050 ng/mL), an elevated proBNP (3407.0 pg/mL), normal hepatic enzymes, normal thyrotropin and a normal serum coagulation profile
Histopathology from tongue biopsy demonstrated AL amyloid with positive Congo red stain and mass spectrometry
Immunofixation study revealed monoclonal free lambda light chain in gamma region
Free light-chain analysis was normal for kappa but markedly elevated for lambda at 2297 mg/dL
Bone marrow biopsy demonstrated 95% plasma cell myeloma with concomitant amyloidosis
Molecular cytogenetics indicated a variant FGFR3/IGH fusion resulting from the t(4:14) with deletion of one IGH gene region in 90.5% of the nuclei and monosomy 13q deletion in 93.5% of the nuclei

Transthoracic echocardiogram revealed increased ventricular wall thickness with concentric hypertrophy, enlarged atria, small pericardial effusion and mild diffuse thickening of the mitral and tricuspid valves

Two-dimensional strain using speckle-tracking echocardiography of the left ventricle demonstrated abnormal regional and average global longitudinal peak systolic strain rates with relative normal strain rates in the apex, consistent with apical sparing
Electrocardiogram was significant for low voltage in the limb leads, indeterminate axis, poor R wave progression in the precordial leads, left atrial enlargement and non-specific T wave changes

source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case narrative sections with source order preserved.

evidence_events.source_span: A 45-year-old man visited our ophthalmology department with an about a 3-year history of vertical diplopia. His best corrected visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes when looking forward that decreased to hand motion /10 CM when gazing upward.

External examination showed slight proptosis and upward displacement of the right eye. Hertel exophthalmometry revealed a 3 mm proptosis on the right side. Globe mobility was complete in the left eye, but infraduction and supraduction was compromised in the right eye. Slit lamp, fundoscopic, Humphrey visual fields and visual evoked potential examinations of both eyes were unremarkable. The intraocular pressure measured by Goldmann tonometer was 15 mm Hg in both eyes.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: Hertel exophthalmometry, slit lamp, fundoscopic, Humphrey visual fields, visual evoked potential, Goldmann tonometer

evidence_events.source_span: Orbital computed tomography (CT) scanning showed enlargement of the right inferior rectus muscle infiltrated by a muscle-density tumor which was about 11 × 17 × 7 mm3 that displaced the globe upward.

An axial magnetic resonance images (MRI) view of the orbit revealed a nodule-like tumor derived from the inferior rectus muscle, which was slightly hypo-intense to the extraocular muscles on T1W with a very low central intensity on T2W and a higher intensity along the periphery. Sagittal MRI images showed that the tumor was very close to the optic nerve with almost no gap in between. Enhanced MRI after intravenous contrast administration showed that the tumor was significantly enhanced in the periphery but only slight enhanced in the center.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: Axial and sagittal MRI with contrast

evidence_events.source_span: The tumor was surgically removed via a transconjunctival approach along inferior rectus muscle. Intraoperatively, the tumor was completely separated from muscle tissue since it was pseudoencapsular. The gross specimen exhibited a firm fibrotic nodule-like and pale-colored mass.
Subsequent histopathological analysis demonstrated that the encapsulated tumor contained large nested or cord-like cells with small nuclei and abundant eosinophilic cytoplasmic particles.
Immunohistochemistry showed that tumor cells strongly expressed CD68, S100 and vimentin, were weakly positive for Ki67, and negative for CK.
There was no significant improvement in globe mobility after surgery; however, a longer term follow-up is required.

Visual acuity was 20/20 looking forward but decreased to hand motion at 10 cm when gazing upward. External exam showed slight proptosis and upward displacement of the right eye with 3 mm proptosis on Hertel exophthalmometry. Right eye had impaired infraduction and supraduction; left eye was normal. Other eye exams including slit lamp, fundus, visual fields, and visual evoked potentials were unremarkable.
evidence_milestones.dialogue_visible_evidence: Patient has 3-year vertical diplopia with normal forward vision but severe vision loss when looking up. Right eye shows slight proptosis and limited vertical movement; other eye exams normal.
evidence_milestones.test_visible_evidence: 3-year vertical diplopia; visual acuity 20/20 forward, hand motion upward; right eye proptosis 3 mm; limited vertical eye movement; normal slit lamp, fundus, visual fields, VEP.
evidence_milestones.source_span: A 45-year-old man visited our ophthalmology department with an about a 3-year history of vertical diplopia. His best corrected visual acuity was 20/20 in both eyes when looking forward that decreased to hand motion /10 CM when gazing upward. External examination showed slight proptosis and upward displacement of the right eye. Hertel exophthalmometry revealed a 3 mm proptosis on the right side. Globe mobility was complete in the left eye, but infraduction and supraduction was compromised in the right eye. Slit lamp, fundoscopic, Humphrey visual fields and visual evoked potential examinations of both eyes were unremarkable. The intraocular pressure measured by Goldmann tonometer was 15 mm Hg in both eyes.

evidence_milestones.grouping_reason: Imaging studies revealing a tumor in the right inferior rectus muscle with characteristic features and proximity to optic nerve.
evidence_milestones.visible_evidence: Orbital CT showed enlargement of the right inferior rectus muscle infiltrated by a muscle-density tumor measuring about 11 × 17 × 7 mm3 displacing the globe upward. MRI revealed a nodule-like tumor slightly hypo-intense on T1, very low central intensity on T2, higher peripheral intensity, closely adjacent to the optic nerve with peripheral contrast enhancement and slight central enhancement.
evidence_milestones.dialogue_visible_evidence: Imaging shows a tumor in the right inferior rectus muscle displacing the globe upward and closely abutting the optic nerve, with characteristic MRI signal and contrast enhancement patterns.
evidence_milestones.test_visible_evidence: CT: enlarged inferior rectus muscle with tumor 11x17x7 mm3; MRI: T1 hypo-intense, T2 low central intensity, peripheral enhancement; tumor close to optic nerve.
evidence_milestones.source_span: Orbital computed tomography (CT) scanning showed enlargement of the right inferior rectus muscle infiltrated by a muscle-density tumor which was about 11 × 17 × 7 mm3 that displaced the globe upward. An axial magnetic resonance images (MRI) view of the orbit revealed a nodule-like tumor derived from the inferior rectus muscle, which was slightly hypo-intense to the extraocular muscles on T1W with a very low central intensity on T2W and a higher intensity along the periphery. Sagittal MRI images showed that the tumor was very close to the optic nerve with almost no gap in between. Enhanced MRI after intravenous contrast administration showed that the tumor was significantly enhanced in the periphery but only slight enhanced in the center.

evidence_events.source_span: A 17-year-old girl with an unremarkable past medical history presents with 3 weeks of right-sided headache and horizontal binocular diplopia.
She was initially diagnosed with migraines and prescribed amitriptyline without improvement in symptoms.
She was diagnosed with a right cranial nerve VI palsy.
A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain with and without gadolinium was ordered and read as "normal."
evidence_events.procedural_cue: MRI brain with and without gadolinium

evidence_events.source_span: She was prescribed a 7-day prednisone taper and fioricet for migraine; while on prednisone, her headaches improved but did not resolve; diplopia persisted; headaches worsened after taper.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: while on prednisone and after taper

evidence_events.source_span: Eleven days after the first study, a repeat MRI brain and orbits with/without gadolinium revealed a possible cavernous sinus lesion.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: repeat MRI brain and orbits with/without gadolinium

evidence_events.source_span: Physical examination revealed 20/20 vision, full color vision, full confrontation visual fields, normal pupillary responses, impaired abduction of the right eye with esotropia.
Initial workup revealed normal complete blood count, serum electrolytes, and an unremarkable chest X-ray.
Magnetic resonance angiogram and magnetic resonance venography were normal and ruled out cavernous sinus thrombosis.

Anti-nuclear antibody, IgG subclasses, anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibody, anti-double stranded DNA, serum protein electrophoresis, cryptococcal antibodies, rapid plasma reagin, Lyme disease screen, mycoplasma antibodies, HIV antigen, and West Nile polymerase chain reaction were normal.

Cerebral spinal fluid (CSF) studies showed normal cell count, normal meningitis PCR panel, no growth on culture, normal α-fetoprotein level, no malignant cells, no oligoclonal bands, and normal angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE). Serum ACE and lysozyme were also within normal limits.
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: ACE and lysozyme have poor sensitivity for sarcoid; chest CT not performed

evidence_events.source_span: Biopsy of the lesion in the right cavernous sinus was discussed but not performed due to potential complications.

Because neurological status remained stable, CSF cytology and serum protein electrophoresis were negative, the diagnosis of an idiopathic inflammatory process, or Tolosa-Hunt syndrome (THS), was concluded rather than neoplastic process.
Patient met the diagnostic criteria for THS as defined by the 2013 International Classification of Headache Disorders (Third Edition, ICHD-3 beta).
Intravenous high-dose methylprednisolone, 1 g per day, was given for 3 days; patient noted improvements in headaches and diplopia; abduction of right eye slightly improved.

source_metadata.title: Delayed Orbital Emphysema Mimicking Orbital Cellulitis: An Uncommon Complication of Dental Surgery

evidence_events.source_span: A 79-year-old man with a history of hyperlipidemia, atrial fibrillation, Parkinson's disease, hepatitis, and peripheral vascular disease awoke with acute-onset swelling around the left eye and cheek.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: replacement of loose mandibular denture-anchoring implants with a zygomatic implant

evidence_events.source_span: He had not taken the prescribed postoperative antibiotics and denied systemic symptoms, trauma, sneezing, blowing his nose, or airway device use.
On evaluation, marked periocular and facial swelling was appreciated with palpation revealing crepitus consistent with subcutaneous emphysema and 2.5-mm relative proptosis by Hertel exophthalmometry.

There was no erythema, warmth, or tenderness; visual acuity was 20/30 OU; intraocular pressure was 14 mmHg right eye and 12 mmHg left eye; pupils were symmetric and briskly reactive with no relative afferent pupillary defect; orthophoria and normal extraocular movements were noted.
Computed tomography confirmed subcutaneous air extending into the left periocular area and orbit with a defect in the left maxillary wall adjacent to the dental implant.
There were no clinical or radiographic signs to suggest infection, so the patient was observed closely.
The subcutaneous emphysema and proptosis resolved spontaneously within 2 weeks with visual function and motility remaining intact.

source_metadata.title: Simultaneous dermatophytosis and keratomycosis caused by Trichophyton interdigitale infection: a case report and literature review

evidence_events.source_span: A 67-year-old man presented with extensive erythema all over the body since 4 years ago, fungal infection of left eye for 2 years, and loss of vision in the eye

Dermatological examinations showed extensive erythematous plaques with clear borders and scales, scattered red papules with ulceration, and scabs throughout the body; onychomycosis was observed on the nails of left hand; conjunctival infection with secretion and loss of vision were noted in left eye
Direct microscopy with 10% potassium hydroxide revealed hyaline septate hyphae

Biopsy specimens from skin lesions, nail and corneal scrapings were cultured on Sabouraud dextrose agar and potato dextrose agar, producing white downy colonies with white powdery surfaces; slide culture revealed branched septate hyphae and masses of spherical-to-pyriform microconidia
Internal transcribed spacer (ITS) sequencing of PCR products showed 99% identity with Trichophyton interdigitale reference sequence
Histopathological examination of biopsy specimen revealed parakeratosis, mild acanthosis, dense dermal blood vessels, and lymphocyte and plasma cell infiltration

Laboratory tests revealed decreased IgG (4.07 g/L), IgA (0.59 g/L), CD3+CD4+ T-cells (15.6%), CD4+/CD8+ T-cells ratio (0.20), increased CD3+ T-cells (96.3%) and CD3+CD8+ T-cells (78.5%); other tests were normal or negative
Genetic analysis of CARD9 and STAT3 exons showed no disease-causing mutations
Diagnosis of dermatophytosis and keratomycosis caused by Trichophyton interdigitale with loss of vision in left eye was made
Patient was treated with luliconazole cream and itraconazole 100 mg BID PO for 1 month, with complete clinical remission after 1 month
Subsequently, the patient underwent left eye enucleation in the ophthalmology department

source_metadata.title: Rare case of hepatocellular carcinoma metastasising to the pituitary and cavernous sinus causing panhypopituitarism and bilateral ophthalmoplegia
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from BMJ Case Reports 2020 article, case report sections used for evidence events.

evidence_events.source_span: A 68-year-old man with chronic hepatitis B, HIV on highly active antiretroviral therapy and history of anal cancer in remission for 3 years initially presented with headache, generalised weakness, abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting. Physical examination was consistent with left eye ptosis with difficulty in opening his eye, while the rest of his neurological examination was unremarkable.

Initial labs were significant for haemoglobin (128 g/L), white cell count (8.5×10⁹/L) and platelet count (192×10⁹/L). HIV labs were significant for absolute CD4 count (305 cells/µL), CD4/CD8 ratio (0.78) and HIV viral load (<20), indicating an intact immune system. He also had a mild transaminitis (aspartate aminotransferase=98, alanine aminotransferase=33) and positive hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis B e-antigen. His hepatitis B viral DNA was 37 603.
A sinus X-ray showed right lateral maxillary sinus thickening.
CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed multiple hypoattenuating poorly defined clustered hepatic lesions with mild surrounding hyperenhancement with invasion of the portal vein by tumour thrombus.
MRI of the abdomen revealed a large 8.7×8.5 cm² lesion in the right posterior hepatic lobe.

His unilateral ptosis progressed rapidly to bilateral ptosis with complete ophthalmoplegia. CT of the head confirmed sphenoid sinus opacification with a mass in the pituitary invading into the cavernous sinus.
Hormonal studies revealed panhypopituitarism with low LH (<1), FSH (1), prolactin (3.64), AM cortisol (2.7), TSH (0.022) and free T4 (0.4).
Liver biopsy confirmed hepatocellular carcinoma.
Transsphenoidal biopsy of the pituitary lesion revealed moderately differentiated carcinoma with immunoprofile compatible with hepatocellular carcinoma.
He received palliative whole-brain radiation (3000 cGy) over 10 days, which did not reverse his ophthalmoplegia.
He was discharged to a subacute rehabilitation facility with plans for outpatient oncology follow-up. He died 2 weeks after discharge.

diagnostic_reasoning_items: Initial presentation with neurological symptoms and left eye ptosis suggested possible central nervous system involvement.
Laboratory and imaging studies identified hepatic lesions suspicious for malignancy in a patient with hepatitis B.
Neurological progression with bilateral ophthalmoplegia and pituitary mass on imaging localized disease to pituitary and cavernous sinus.
Hormonal studies confirmed panhypopituitarism consistent with pituitary dysfunction.
Pathology from liver and pituitary biopsies confirmed metastatic hepatocellular carcinoma.

hidden_reference.final_diagnosis: Metastatic hepatocellular carcinoma involving liver, pituitary gland, and cavernous sinus causing panhypopituitarism and bilateral ophthalmoplegia.
hidden_reference.diagnostic_reasoning: The diagnosis was established by imaging evidence of hepatic lesions and pituitary mass, hormonal evidence of panhypopituitarism, and confirmatory pathology from liver and pituitary biopsies showing hepatocellular carcinoma. The clinical progression of neurological symptoms and imaging findings localized the metastatic disease to the pituitary and cavernous sinus. Despite treatment, the aggressive nature of the disease led to rapid mortality.

evidence_events.source_span: A healthy 22-year-old woman presented with acute-onset blurring of vision and absolute inferior scotoma in the right eye for 4 days, without neurological symptoms
History of fever, sore throat, and fatigue 10 days prior; exposure to laboratory confirmed COVID-19 case 15 days prior

Optic Nerve Head-Optical Coherence Tomography showed retinal nerve fiber layer thickening in superior, inferior and nasal quadrants in right eye

Patient tested positive for COVID-19 by real-time reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR)
Patient received injection methylprednisolone 1 g three doses over 3 days after physician clearance
Resolution of disc edema in inferior margin noted post treatment; patient reported subjective resolution of inferior scotoma 3 weeks post discharge

source_metadata.title: Compressive optic neuropathy (CON) in Graves’ disease caused by hypertrophy of levator and superior rectus muscles

evidence_events.source_span: A 66-year-old woman undergoing medical treatment for hyperthyroidism with methimazole and potassium iodide for 23 years presented with right-eye upper eyelid retraction.

Initial examination showed right and left margin reflex distance-1 (MRD-1) of 3.2 mm and 2.1 mm respectively, normal exophthalmometry (13.5 mm right eye, 12.5 mm left eye), no diplopia or visual dysfunction.
Blood tests revealed free thyroxine (FT4) 1.27 ng/dl, free triiodothyronine (FT3) 6.37 pg/ml, thyroid-stimulating antibody (TSAb) 1557%, and thyroid-stimulating hormone 0.008 μU/L.
Patient had a prominent goiter measuring 188.05 cc by ultrasound but refused surgical removal.
At 3 months post initial presentation, thyroid hormone control worsened: FT4 3.88 ng/dl, FT3 24.90 pg/ml, TSAb 3185%, and right-eye upper eyelid retraction progressed to MRD-1 of 7.3 mm.

At 6 months post initial presentation, MRD-1 worsened to 7.7 mm, and right eye developed 12 prism diopters (PD) exotropia and 20 PD hypertropia with onset of compressive optic neuropathy (CON) and visual acuity reduced to 20/200.
Computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed inflammation and hypertrophy only in the superior levator and superior rectus (SL/SR) muscles in the right orbit.

Intravenous steroid pulse therapy and radiation therapy were administered, resulting in resolution of inflammation on imaging and visual acuity recovery to 20/20, but residual upper eyelid retraction (MRD-1 5.9 mm) and hypertropia (25 PD) remained.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: intravenous steroid pulse and radiation therapy

evidence_events.source_span: After 9 months of treatment, thyroid hormones improved (FT4 0.5 ng/dl, FT3 2.33 pg/ml, TSAb 1428%), and bilateral orbital decompression was performed to prevent CON recurrence and improve disfigurement.

Three months after decompression, superior levator and superior rectus muscles were recessed (5 mm and 10 mm respectively); muscles were firm and fibrotic on histopathology consistent with thyroid orbitopathy.
Postoperative improvement of MRD-1 from 5.9 mm to 3.2 mm and hypertropia from 35 PD to 10 PD was observed; exotropia remained.
Despite persistent large goiter and elevated TSAb (3000% to 4000%), no recurrence of CON was observed for more than 1.5 years postoperatively.

source_evidence_items: After 9 months of treatment, thyroid hormones improved (FT4 0.5 ng/dl, FT3 2.33 pg/ml, TSAb 1428%), and bilateral orbital decompression was performed to prevent CON recurrence and improve disfigurement.

Three months after decompression, superior levator and superior rectus muscles were recessed (5 mm and 10 mm respectively); muscles were firm and fibrotic on histopathology consistent with thyroid orbitopathy.
Postoperative improvement of MRD-1 from 5.9 mm to 3.2 mm and hypertropia from 35 PD to 10 PD was observed; exotropia remained.

source_metadata.title: Anisocoria in an intubated patient with COVID-19

evidence_events.source_span: A 74-year-old man was admitted to the hospital with a 2-week history of cough, fever and progressive shortness of breath. His initial imaging and swab test confirmed COVID-19.

The patient was placed on a trial of continuous positive airway pressure to support his deteriorating oxygen saturation. After a week of supportive therapy, he was transferred to the ICU and was supported with mechanical ventilation and proning.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: proning protocol used involves patients being proned for up to 18 hours a day

evidence_events.source_span: While in ICU, the patient’s recovery was impacted by a Klebsiella-positive pneumonia, and a subsequent CT scan showed multiple pulmonary emboli. This was treated with low molecular weight heparin.

During the second week in ICU, the patient’s critical care team identified anisocoria. They reported a left relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD) with no new neurology or squint on gross assessment.
CT scan of the head and accompanying venogram did not highlight any notable pathology and ruled out venous sinus thrombosis.

Ophthalmology review: left pupil was 6 mm and fixed with no change in light or dark. Right pupil was 3 mm in light and 4 mm in dark. Left pupillary reflex showed no direct or consensual response and an RAPD. Right pupillary reflex was normal direct response, no consensual response and no RAPD. Anterior segment was normal without inflammation. Early cataract in both eyes. IOP readings were 18 mmHg right eye and 22 mmHg left eye.

Around week 4, the patient underwent a tracheostomy and was eventually decannulated. As he was weaned off sedation, no ptosis was identified. Anisocoria did not change and patient expressed blurred vision.
MRI of the head showed scattered intracranial haemorrhages, with a particular concentration of microhaemorrhages in the midbrain.

Ophthalmology clinic: visual acuity right eye 6/6, left eye 6/30. IOP right eye 13 mmHg, left eye 44 mmHg. Ishihara scores right eye 17/17, left eye 3/17. Diluted pilocarpine or accommodation did not cause constriction of left pupil. Gonioscopy showed closed angle in right eye and 180°-270° angle closure in left eye. No optic disc cupping. Visual fields normal right eye, glaucomatous defect left eye. Diagnosis of subacute closed angle glaucoma was made.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: ophthalmology clinic examination including gonioscopy and visual fields

diagnostic_reasoning_verbatim_spans: CT venogram excluded a cavernous sinus thrombosis.
MRI of the head showed microhaemorrhages in the midbrain where the pupil reflex nuclei are located.
After the patient was stepped down from ICU, intraocular pressure (IOP) was found to be raised in that eye.
Gonioscopy showed closed angle and visual fields revealed glaucomatous defect.
Diluted pilocarpine did not cause constriction of the left pupil.

diagnostic_reasoning_items: Initial concern for thrombotic causes of anisocoria was ruled out by CT venogram.
Midbrain microhaemorrhages on MRI suggested possible vascular injury affecting pupillary reflex.
Elevated IOP and angle closure on ophthalmology exam confirmed subacute closed angle glaucoma.
Pharmacologic testing excluded Adie’s tonic pupil.
No medication-induced cause for glaucoma was identified.
Final diagnosis supported by clinical, imaging, and ophthalmologic findings.
hidden_reference.final_diagnosis: Subacute closed angle glaucoma
hidden_reference.diagnostic_reasoning: The initial differential diagnosis included thrombotic events such as cavernous sinus thrombosis, which was excluded by CT venogram. MRI showed midbrain microhaemorrhages consistent with possible vascular injury affecting pupillary reflex nuclei. However, elevated intraocular pressure and gonioscopic evidence of angle closure, along with glaucomatous visual field defects, confirmed subacute closed angle glaucoma as the cause of anisocoria and visual symptoms. Pharmacologic testing excluded Adie’s pupil, and no medication was implicated in causing increased IOP. Thus, the diagnosis was confirmed by combined clinical, imaging, and ophthalmologic evidence.

source_metadata.title: Retinitis pigmentosa and molar tooth sign caused by novel AHI1 compound heterozygote pathogenic variants

evidence_events.source_span: The patient was a 31-year-old male who presented difficulty at finding toys at the age of 2 years, night blindness from age of 5 years, intention tremor and walking imbalance from 29 years of age.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: at the age of 2 years, from age of 5 years, from 29 years of age

evidence_events.source_span: Physical examination showed tubular visual field, retina pigmentation on Fundus photograph, retinal nerve fiber layer thinning on optical coherence tomography (OCT), decreased smooth pursuit, slight nystagmus on bilateral gaze, slight intention tremor on finger–nose pointing, unstable at toe-heel walking and straight walking, with normal muscle strength and tension.
Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed a molar tooth sign (MTS) in the midbrain and cauda cerebelli hypoplasia.

Blood tests, including complete blood count, liver and kidney function, electrolytes, creatine kinase, and lactic acid, were normal. Other examinations, including electrocardiogram, electroencephalogram, abdominal and kidney ultrasound, were normal.

Whole exome sequence revealed two compound heterozygous variants at c.2105C>T (p.T702M) and c.1330A>T (p.I444F) in AHI1 gene; the c.2105C>T variant was inherited from the unaffected mother, and the c.1330A>T variant was inherited from the unaffected father.

The c.2105C>T variant has been previously reported as pathogenic in compound heterozygous patterns; the c.1330A>T mutation is novel but predicted pathogenic by Mutation Taster, SIFT, PolyPhen-2, with a CADD phred score of 28.2.

3D structure prediction showed that the T702M mutation changes the Jouberin protein structure from β-sheet to D-loop, and the I444F mutation alters the structure from α-helix to D-loop, both decreasing protein stability.

source_metadata.title: When obstetrics–gynecology specialists need to call an ophthalmologist urgently: a case report

evidence_events.source_span: A healthy 23-year-old Western-European female patient consulted the gynecological emergency service for vulvar pain and edema with small vulvar lesions, associated with febrile episodes up to 39.5 °C.
Clinical examination showed diffuse vulvar erythema and edema with several small slightly erosive papules, and one small (< 1 cm) painless inguinal lymph node.

Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) swab of the genital ulcerative lesions was performed, and the patient was discharged with antiviral treatment (valaciclovir) and nonsteroidal antiinflammatory pain medications.

One day later, she consulted the general emergency department complaining of blurred vision in both eyes, headache, persistent genital lesions, lumbar pain, and recurrent fever (39 °C). Neurological examination was normal, with the exception of bilateral decreased visual acuity.

C-reactive protein (CRP) was 204 mg/L and leukocytes 13.9 G/L. Repetitive hemocultures, white blood cell count, protein PCR and culture of cerebrospinal fluid from a lumbar puncture, PCR samples of vulvar lesions (HSV, chlamydia, and gonococcus), and serology results (Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), syphilis, Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV)) were all negative.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: lumbar puncture performed; multiple PCR and serologies performed

evidence_events.source_span: Given the suspicion of retinal lesions, the patient was advised to rapidly consult an ophthalmologist. As blurred vision can be a possible side effect of valaciclovir, the antiviral treatment was switched to acyclovir.
Four days after initial symptoms, genital lesions had progressed to multiple painful deep ulcerations with scabs, accompanied by dysuria, urinary retention, and persistent blurred vision.

source_metadata.title: Kearns–Sayre syndrome with a novel large-scale deletion: a case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 13-year-old boy presented to our hospital with progressive vision loss and difficulty with opening his eyes.

Best-corrected visual acuity was LogMAR 0.3 in the right eye (RE) and LogMAR 0.3 in the left eye (LE), cycloplegic refraction revealed + 0.50 + −1.50 × 180 (RE) and + 1.00 × 95 (LE). Intraocular pressure was approximately 18 mmHg (RE) and 17 mmHg (LE). Approximately 5° exotropia was found based on the Hirschberg test, and movements of both eyes were restricted in all gaze directions. Because of weakness in the levator palpebrae muscle, bilateral ptosis was slight and the upper eyelid always covered the upper third of the pupil when looking ahead.
Color fundus photography showed hyperpigmentation of both eyes, and binocular perimetric examination revealed a superior temporal visual field defect and centripetal reduction in both eyes.

Macular spectral-domain optical coherence tomography revealed an interruption in the ellipsoid band, and several hyperreflective deposits above the retinal pigment epithelium were remarkable. The average subfoveal choroidal thickness (Cht) in both eyes was 223 μm (LE) and 224 μm (RE).
OCTA showed that the deep retinal capillary density decreased and the choroid microvessels atrophied greatly, but foveal area zone and superficial retinal capillary changed insignificantly.

The child also complained of dizziness and fatigue, and he had missed school for a long time. From the time of birth, his height and weight had been lower than that of his peers. Currently, his body max index is 14.17 (138 cm tall and 27 kg weight), which is significantly inferior to that of healthy children. He had been diagnosed with growth retardation, and growth hormone therapy was administered.

Findings from echocardiography were unremarkable, however, 24-h ambulatory electrocardiogram revealed intermittent first-degree atrioventricular block and partial second-degree type I atrioventricular block.

Brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) indicated diffuse demyelinating lesions in the white matter of both cerebral hemispheres and the inner capsule, middle cerebral crura, pons and medulla oblongata.

Long-range polymerase chain reaction (PCR) of the blood samples revealed that the deletion started at nucleotide position 6341 and ended at 13993, indicating a deletion of 7652 bp; no abnormality was noted in the mother’s genes.
Complete evidence obtained from ocular examination and evaluation of other organs as well as from gene detection supported the final diagnosis of KSS.
The patient was given a pair of applicable glasses to wear and was followed up every 3 months. An implantable pacemaker was also installed based on the advice of the physician.

source_metadata.title: Giant cell-rich solitary fibrous tumour of the lacrimal gland with prominent angiomatoid cystic changes and an underlying NAB2ex3-STAT6ex18 fusion

evidence_events.source_span: A 47-year-old man presented with progressive painless protrusion of the right eye for several years associated with blurred vision

Physical examination showed right eye proptosis measuring 30 mm on exophthalmometry with conjunctival chemosis, corneal exposure and dryness, diffuse punctate erosions, restricted extraocular movements in all gaze directions, visual acuity 20/400 in the affected eye and 20/25 in the opposite eye, no afferent pupillary defect, and normal fundus examination bilaterally

MRI revealed an extraconical anterolateral 3.8×3.5×2.0 cm solid-cystic mass in the right orbit, showing heterogeneous intensity and marked contrast enhancement, most likely originating from the lacrimal gland, abutting the lateral aspect of the eye globe and lateral rectus muscle causing globe displacement and proptosis without ocular or muscular infiltration, and no bone erosion or marrow oedema
Previous biopsy attempted in 2015 yielded non-representative benign lacrimal tissue only

Differential diagnosis included benign/indolent neoplasm favored clinically due to longstanding history and circumscribed non-infiltrative lesion; pleomorphic adenoma, malignant epithelial lesions less likely, cavernous vascular malformation considered but atypical location, lymphoma unlikely without systemic disease, metastatic tumor not ruled out, and non-neoplastic conditions such as sarcoidosis also entertained; SFT was not considered at this point

Surgery via upper lid crease anterolateral orbitotomy was performed; procedure was challenging due to intraoperative haemorrhage and adherence of the mass to surrounding structures; hypervascularity and bleeding precluded complete removal, so subtotal resection was performed; vascular tumour/malformation was highly suspected clinically
Gross pathological examination showed a 3.5×2.0×2.0 cm mass with blood-filled cystic spaces and solid areas

source_metadata.title: Recurrent painful ophthalmoplegic neuropathy revealing oculomotor nerve schwannoma

evidence_events.source_span: A 18-year-old girl, born to first consanguineous parents, presented to our department with ten-year history of left recurrent migrainous headaches associated with ipsilateral intermittent oculomotor nerve palsy.
At the age 8, she presented with continuous left orbito frontal throbbing headache with nausea, vomiting and photophobia.
Within 10 days, when headache improved, ptosis and left monocular horizontal diplopia appeared for 45 days.
This episode relapsed three times at 13, 16 and 17 years old.
Ophthalmoplegia always resolved after roughly one month without particular treatments.
She kept an increasingly frequent and disabling headache without ophthalmoplegia lasting about 12 hours and occurring twice a week.
At 18 years old, neurological examination was normal.
Brain MRI, performed one year from the last attack, revealed an enhancing nodule on the cisternal segment of the left oculomotor nerve suggestive of schwannoma.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: one year from the last attack

evidence_events.source_span: The patient was kept on symptomatic treatment based on non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and anlagesic if headache. No surgical intervention was attempted.
On follow-up, she no longer presented additional episodes.

source_metadata.title: Spontaneously Arrested Bilateral Primary Congenital Glaucoma: A Case Report From Ethiopia

evidence_events.source_span: A 32-year-old man from North Shewa, Central part of Ethiopia, presented to Menelik II Hospital in June 2019 with chief complaint of reduction of vision of 2 year duration.
The reduction of vision had been since childhood but worsened in the past 2 years. The low vision was worse at distance and he has learned that his eyes were large since childhood.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: since childhood; worsened in past 2 years

evidence_events.source_span: Physical examination showed that best corrected visual acuity (BCVA) of counting finger at one and three meters in the right and left eyes respectively.
Average repeated IOP measured by I-care tonometer was 12 mmHg for right eye and 11 mmHg in the left eye.
Horizontal corneal diameter was 14mm in both eyes with stromal opacities and Haab's striae.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: corneal measurement and slit lamp exam

evidence_events.source_span: Anterior chambers were deep and gonioscopy revealed wide open angles in both eyes.
There was iridodonesis, phacodonesis, as well as superiorly and nasally subluxated cataract lenses in both eyes. The cataract in the right eye was denser.
Optic nerve head evaluation by 90D lens showed pink rim with vertical cup-to-disc ratio of 0.6 in both eyes with no nerve fiber layer loss.
Visual field examination was normal in both eyes (right eye examination was done after cataract surgery).
Central corneal thickness was 466um in the right eye and 467um for the left eye. Axial length was 30.3mm and 29.9mm for right and left eyes respectively.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: corneal pachymetry and axial length measurement

evidence_events.source_span: The diagnosis of subluxated cataract of both eyes, but denser on right and spontaneously arrested primary congenital glaucoma was reached.
Manual small incision cataract surgery was done for the right eye.
On 2nd post-operative week, the right eye BCVA was 6/36 and poor vision was explained by amblyopia.
After one month the IOP was normal, but intraocular lens (IOL) was dislocated and BCVA decreased to 6/60.

diagnostic_reasoning_verbatim_spans: A 32-year-old man presented with deterioration of vision and large eyes since childhood.
Physical exam showed large corneas (14 mm), stromal opacities, Haab's striae, wide open anterior chamber angles, subluxated cataract lenses.
IOP was normal and optic nerve head showed no nerve fiber layer loss with normal visual fields.
Axial length was increased bilaterally.
These findings are consistent with spontaneously arrested primary congenital glaucoma.
Diagnosis was reached clinically based on these findings.
diagnostic_reasoning_items: History of vision loss and large eyes since childhood suggests congenital eye pathology.
Large corneas, Haab's striae, and wide open angles are classic signs of congenital glaucoma.
Normal IOP and optic nerve head without damage indicate arrested disease.
Subluxated cataract lenses are known sequelae of congenital glaucoma.
Increased axial length supports globe enlargement from prior elevated IOP.
Clinical diagnosis is spontaneously arrested primary congenital glaucoma with subluxated cataract.
hidden_reference.final_diagnosis: Spontaneously arrested primary congenital glaucoma with bilateral subluxated cataract lenses.
hidden_reference.diagnostic_reasoning: The patient presented with longstanding vision loss and large eyes. source_metadata.title: Antibodies against Toxoplasma gondii positive in serum and aqueous humor to diagnose clinically suspected ocular toxoplasmosis: A case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 38-year old male patient visited our ophthalmology clinic with a chief complaint of decreased vision for about five days in his right eye.
He had no history of any systemic illness such as diabetes, hypertension, trauma or surgery. He denied exposure to animals such as cats and dogs, eating undercooked meat or drinking unfiltered water.
The best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was 18/20 in his right eye and 20/20 in his left eye, respectively. The intraocular pressure (IOP) was normal in both eyes.
A little punctate gray-white keratopigmentation was found under the cornea, positive atrial flashes, and light vitreous turbidity in his right eye.

The fundus examination of his right eye showed a round lesion with two optic disc sizes, having clear boundary and pigmentation in the inferior temporal vascular arch of the retina. Below it, there was a yellow-white round retinochoroidal lesion, about 1.5 optic disc sizes, with poorly defined borders and a small patch of pigmentation in the center.

Spectral-domain optical coherence tomography (SD-OCT) confirmed mild edema of the neuroepithelial layer in active lesions, with small-scale serous detachment, unclear interlayer structure of neuroepithelial layer in old lesions, atrophy and thinning, and slightly stronger reflex.

His BCVA dropped to 20/60, the vitreous opacity was significantly increased, and the scope of the active lesions in the right eye fundus examination was slightly enlarged, with a size of about two optic disc sizes, then, the boundary of lesions were blurred, and the milky yellow lesions deepened.
SD-OCT showed thickening of the entire neuroepithelial layer at the lesion, enhanced reflexes, and disappearance of the structure.

Aqueous humor sample analysis found Toxoplasma DNA detectable, and Toxoplasma immunoglobulin G (IgG) and immunoglobulin M (IgM) to be positive. His serum Toxoplasma IgG was also positive (10.04 IU/mL; reference range: 0–7.2 IU/mL).

evidence_events.source_span: Oral prednisone 60 mg/day and azithromycin 0.25 g/day were started. Oral antibiotic treatment for toxoplasma was continued for 4 weeks, and prednisone followed by weekly stepwise tapering in steps of 10 mg/day.

In the follow-up session after 7 days, the BCVA of the right eye was 18/20, IOP was normal in both eyes, and no cells were observed in the anterior chamber of right eye. The fundus examination of his right eye showed yellow-white round retinochoroidal lesions with the size of 1.5 optic discs, and SD-OCT showed a similar lesion as previous.

Three weeks after the medication, the patient’s BCVA was still 18/20, fundus examination revealed reduction changes of the pigmented chorioretinal scars and yellow-white retinochoroidal lesions (1 optic disc size). A repeat SD-OCT showed a reduction in retina thickness.

Three months after the medication, the patient’s BCVA increased to 20/20. His IOP was still normal. The lens and vitreous were clear. Fundus examination revealed obvious pigmented chorioretinal scars and yellow-white retinochoroidal lesions (1 optic disc size). A SD-OCT showed no edema of the neuroepithelial layer at the lesion subsided, retina atrophy and thinning.

source_metadata.title: Severe Retinal Necrosis Due to Klebsiella pneumoniae After Acute Prostatitis

evidence_events.source_span: A 72-year-old immunocompetent male presented with severe high fever and gastrointestinal and genitourinary symptoms.
He was diagnosed with acute prostatitis, hospitalized, and started on systemic antibiotic therapy.
He received gentamycin 240 mg per 24 h i.v. empirically.
From urine culture collected on admission, ampicillin-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae was isolated in numbers greater than 100,000 CFU/ml.
After 3 days, he experienced floaters in the right eye with consequent loss of vision.
Examination showed intraocular inflammation; topical therapy with cycloplegics and corticosteroid eye drops was prescribed, with little benefit.

Three days later, endogenous endophthalmitis was suspected; BCVA in the right eye was hand motion, intraocular pressure 12 mmHg, slit lamp showed marked exudation in anterior chamber, fibrin on anterior lens capsule, and opaque fundus view; right eye ultrasound showed vitreous chamber with hyper-reflective signal compatible with abscess or hemorrhage.
The patient underwent urgent and complete pars plana vitrectomy (PPV) and vitreous biopsy with intravitreal injection of vancomycin and ceftazidime in the right eye.
Intraoperatively, the retina appeared moderately ischemic, with signs of vasculitis and an area of infiltrated retina temporal to the central fovea.
Vitreous samples underwent Gram staining and microbiological cultures for bacteria and fungi, which showed growth of Klebsiella pneumoniae.
The strain of Klebsiella pneumoniae was resistant to ampicillin and sensitive to all other tested antibiotics.

Three days after complete vitrectomy, the patient received a targeted intravitreal injection of ceftazidime but developed fever and was transferred to infectious disease department for suspected sepsis.
After 9 days, due to re-deterioration of vision, ophthalmoscopy revealed vitreous opacities and retinal detachment temporal to the central fovea with moderate cataract.
The patient underwent phacoemulsification with intraocular lens implantation, posterior capsulotomy, and second PPV with silicone oil tamponade.

Intraoperative retinal examination showed vitreous cavity highly infiltrated with dense inflammatory cells and fibrin; temporal to the fovea was a large retinal necrotic area of 4×5 optic disk diameters.
Due to extensive necrotic retina, no laser photocoagulation or cryotherapy was performed; no holes identified intraoperatively; silicone oil tamponade chosen.
During postoperative followup, scar tissue developed at necrotic retina location; retina remained flat; inflammation disappeared; BCVA improved to 0.2.
After 10-month followup, silicone oil was removed; laser photocoagulation performed around retinal defect edges; visual function improved; retina remained attached.

hidden_reference.final_diagnosis_verbatim: Endogenous endophthalmitis
diagnostic_reasoning_verbatim_spans: Vitreous samples underwent Gram staining and microbiological cultures for bacteria and fungi, which showed growth of Klebsiella pneumoniae.
From urine culture collected on admission, ampicillin-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae was isolated in numbers greater than 100,000 CFU/ml.
Intraoperatively, the retina appeared moderately ischemic, with signs of vasculitis and an area of infiltrated retina temporal to the central fovea.
After 9 days, ophthalmoscopy revealed vitreous opacities and retinal detachment temporal to the central fovea with moderate cataract.

Intraoperative retinal examination showed vitreous cavity highly infiltrated with dense inflammatory cells and fibrin; temporal to the fovea was a large retinal necrotic area of 4×5 optic disk diameters.
diagnostic_reasoning_items: Initial systemic infection with Klebsiella pneumoniae prostatitis identified by urine culture.
Development of ocular symptoms with intraocular inflammation and vitreous changes suggested endogenous endophthalmitis.
Pars plana vitrectomy and vitreous biopsy confirmed Klebsiella pneumoniae infection intraocularly.
Retinal ischemia, vasculitis, and necrosis observed intraoperatively indicated severe ocular involvement.
Retinal detachment developed as a complication requiring second surgery with silicone oil tamponade.
Postoperative follow-up showed retinal attachment and partial visual recovery.
hidden_reference.final_diagnosis: Endogenous endophthalmitis due to Klebsiella pneumoniae secondary to acute prostatitis
hidden_reference.diagnostic_reasoning: The diagnosis was established by microbiological confirmation of Klebsiella pneumoniae in urine and vitreous samples, clinical presentation of ocular inflammation and vision loss following acute prostatitis, intraoperative findings of retinal ischemia and necrosis, and imaging evidence of retinal detachment. The clinical course and response to surgical and antibiotic treatment support this diagnosis.
hidden_reference.article_derived_evidence_summary: A 72-year-old man with acute prostatitis caused by ampicillin-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae developed endogenous endophthalmitis with retinal necrosis and detachment. Vitrectomy and vitreous biopsy confirmed the pathogen. Surgical interventions including two PPVs and silicone oil tamponade were performed. Postoperative follow-up showed retinal attachment and partial visual recovery.

source_metadata.title: An Infant with Bilateral Keratitis: From Infectious to Genetic Diagnosis

evidence_events.source_span: A 10-month-old previously healthy White infant was referred to Ophthalmology for acute onset of photophobia.
The mother reported a 7-day history of eye blinking and rubbing, irritability, and decreased oral intake.

Ophthalmological examination showed significant photophobia, epiphora, and difficulty maintaining his eyelids open. Dendritiform corneal lesions were seen bilaterally, raising the suspicion of herpetic keratitis.
A papular, crusted, raised lesion on the thumb was found after a few days of hospitalization, raising concerns about HSV.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: after a few days of hospitalization

evidence_events.source_span: A conjunctival swab and a papular, crusted, raised lesion on the thumb were each tested for HSV using a polymerase chain reaction (PCR) technique. Both PCRs were negative.
After 10 days of intravenous acyclovir, the corneal lesions had resolved completely.
Plasma amino acid chromatography was performed because of the presence of dentritiform corneal lesions, compatible with tyrosinemia type II (TYRII).
The diagnosis of TYRII was confirmed by finding a markedly elevated plasma tyrosine level (1262 µmol/L, reference range, 40–80 µmol/L).

Molecular analysis further confirmed the diagnosis of TYRII, revealing 2 variants in the TAT gene, 1 from each parent: c.889C>T (p.Arg297*, a known pathogenic premature stop variant) and c.227T>C (p.Leu76Pro, not previously reported, of unknown significance).
After 2 weeks on diet, the patient’s plasma tyrosine level was 152 µmol/L, which is mildly elevated. The corneal lesions had not recurred.
One year later, his developmental milestones were age-appropriate.

source_metadata.title: Unilateral Mooren’s ulcer in a patient with bilateral partial optic nerve atrophy - a case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 58-year-old Caucasian male presented to our clinic for unilateral pain, tearing, photophobia and decreased vision, affecting the right eye (OD).
evidence_events.temporal_cue: The symptomatology began 4 months prior to the presentation

evidence_events.source_span: The patient reported that the onset of the symptoms occurred 4 months earlier, following ocular trauma with a vegetal corneal foreign body. After the foreign body was removed in another Ophthalmology Service, the patient was treated with topical broad-spectrum antibiotics and lubricants in the affected eye, without any improvement.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: foreign body was removed; treated with topical antibiotics and lubricants

evidence_events.source_span: The diagnosis was reconsidered one month prior to the presentation to metaherpetic keratitis, therefore, when we first encountered the case, the patient was following a topical treatment in the right eye with antivirals and lubricants.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: topical antivirals and lubricants treatment ongoing

evidence_events.source_span: The past ocular history revealed partial optic nerve atrophy affecting both eyes (right eye - due to an episode of non-arteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy diagnosed 7 years back, left eye - due to contusive ocular trauma reported 5 years before presentation).
evidence_events.temporal_cue: 7 years back (right eye), 5 years before presentation (left eye)

evidence_events.source_span: At the clinical ocular exam, the best corrected visual acuity was 0.1 in the right eye and 0.2 in left eye, while the intraocular noncontact pressure was 20 mmHg in both eyes.

The slit lamp exam of the right eye revealed conjunctival injection, a peripheral, crescent-shaped corneal ulcer situated 2 mm from the limbus, extended on approximately 180° inferiorly and nasally (between 7:00 and 1:00 o’clock).

The defect involving the epithelium and the superficial stroma is better illustrated after fluorescein staining. Conjunctival blood vessels invading the peripheral margin of the ulcer were documented. The corneal sensitivity was normal.

Fundus examination of both eyes revealed a pale neuroretinal rim (superior two thirds in the right eye, entirely in the left eye), an absent foveal reflex, numerous macular, small, round, white-yellow subretinal deposits, located around the fovea (highly suggestive of macular hard drusen).

The RNFL exam showed decreased thickness in the superior, temporal and nasal quadrants in the right eye, while in the left eye RNFL thickness was decreased in the superior, nasal and inferior quadrants, with borderline values for the temporal quadrant. The visual field examination revealed a dense inferior altitudinal defect in the right eye and severe visual field constriction in the left eye.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: RNFL exam and visual field examination

evidence_events.source_span: An extensive laboratory evaluation was initiated. The blood investigations including complete blood count, biochemistry, coagulation tests, liver and kidney function, glycemia, electrolytes and inflammatory markers were within normal limits. Hepatitis C markers (anti-HCV antibodies, viral ARN) and syphilis screening test (RPR) were negative. Further immunological tests were also performed: rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP antibodies, antinuclear antibodies, pANCA, cANCA, anti-Ro and anti-La antibodies were within normal range. Urinary sediment analysis revealed no modifications. A superficial corneal swab was collected for several microbiological cultures and the results proved to be negative.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: extensive laboratory evaluation and corneal swab cultures

evidence_events.source_span: At the initial presentation, while waiting for the laboratory results to establish a diagnosis, the patient was kept under observation and received topical treatment for the right eye with wide-spectrum antibiotics (5 times daily) and preservative-free lubricants (5 times daily), and oral treatment with retinal and optic nerve supplements. An aggravation of the corneal lesion was noted in this period, with central migration of the ulcer, further advancement of the corneal blood vessels close to the ulceration’s edge and increased astigmatism (+2.75/-2.50/85°). The base of the lesion stained with fluorescein.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: topical antibiotics and lubricants treatment; observation

evidence_events.source_span: Noting this evolution and after eliminating all the specific causes of peripheral ulcerative keratitis (PUK), a final principal diagnosis of right unilateral Mooren’s ulcer was established, while secondary diagnosis for both eyes were: partial optic atrophy, macular drusen, simple hyperopic astigmatism and presbyopia.

Treatment with topical steroids (5 times daily) was initiated in the right eye. A topical combination of a Carbonic Anhydrase Inhibitor and a Beta-blocker was administered twice daily to avoid intraocular pressure increase under steroid treatment. Prophylactic topical antibiotics and lubricants were used until the closure of the epithelial defect. Retinal and optic nerve oral supplements were continued permanently.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: topical steroids and adjunctive treatments initiated

evidence_events.source_span: A 5 days follow-up showed an improved visual acuity (0.3 with best correction), complete regression of the corneal blood vessels and a shallow ulcer that stained with fluorescein only centrally. Also, a decreased corneal astigmatism was noted (+1.75/ -1.75/ 83°).

At the 1-month follow-up, the visual acuity in the right eye was 0.5 with best correction (the same visual acuity as before the ulcer’s onset), noncontact tonometry showed 18 mmHg intraocular pressure and corneal astigmatism was diminished (+1.25/ -1.25/ 78°). The complete closing of the epithelial defect and regression of corneal blood vessels were observed.

source_metadata.title: First Case Report of Developmental Bilateral Cataract with a Novel Mutation in the ZEB2 Gene Observed in Mowat-Wilson Syndrome

evidence_events.source_span: A 9-year-old girl, diagnosed with p.Gln694Ter mutation in ZEB2 gene and suspicion of MWS was urgently referred to the Children’s Outpatient Ophthalmology Clinic to expand the diagnosis of visual pathway conduction disorders and further evaluation.
Previous ophthalmic assessments revealed pallor of the temporal part of optic nerve discs; the patient was also diagnosed with convergent strabismus and astigmatism.

Birth history was normal with natural delivery at 39 weeks; postnatal period revealed patent ductus arteriosus and aortic valve stenosis; constipation led to diagnosis of Hirschsprung’s disease; MRI revealed callous body dysgenesis and lateral and III ventricular dilatation.
Molecular testing of the ZEB2 gene detected a novel p.Gln694Ter mutation causing premature termination of translation; mutation was de novo as parental testing was negative.

On first visit, patient had alternating convergent strabismus with Hirschberg test 15–20°, normal pupillary light responses, and cycloplegic autorefraction showed significant astigmatism in both eyes; anterior segment showed minor posterior synechiae; optic media were translucent; fundus exam showed pallor of temporal optic nerve discs and subtle inferior elevation of optic disc in right eye; ocular ultrasound showed slight increased echogenicity at optic disc consistent with optic nerve drusen.

Less than a year later, patient showed decreased interest in surroundings; right eye did not follow objects while left eye did; pupil responses normal; anterior segment exam revealed total cortical cataract in right eye and partial cortical cataract in left eye; fundus exam of right eye impossible due to cataract; left eye fundus poorly visible with optic nerve rim pallor; ultrasound of right eye showed increased echogenicity of lens and optic nerve disc; FVEP performed on right eye showed prolonged latencies and vestigial right hemisphere amplitudes.

Cataract surgery with foldable intraocular lens implantation was performed first in the right eye and then in the left eye; post-surgical fundus exam of right eye revealed optic nerve pallor with pigment regrouping at retinal periphery.
During 3-year postoperative follow-up, patient regained ability to follow objects and FVEP results normalized; no complications observed and visual acuity improved significantly.

source_metadata.title: Idiopathic Acroosteolysis: A Novel Cutaneous Sign Can Help Identify the Condition Early

evidence_events.source_span: A 5-year-old girl born to noncontagious parents, after an uneventful pregnancy, developed a transverse cutaneous “split” on the plantar aspect of the right third toe for 3 months that was associated with serous discharge.
The “split” elongated circumferentially over a period of 1 month to involve the dorsal aspect of the toe.

The mother gave a similar history of a demarcation line on the second, fourth, and fifth toes of the right foot with durations of 3 months, 1 year, and 2 years, respectively, that disappeared before she noticed a shortening of those toes.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: durations of 3 months, 1 year, and 2 years

evidence_events.source_span: The patient had no history of traveling, Raynaud phenomenon, trauma, exposure to vinyl chloride gas, skin fragility, blisters at the site of trauma, joint pain, or swelling of the extremities.

Examination of the feet revealed a distinct boundary between normal skin and affected crusted skin overlying osteolysis (“split” sign) on the third toe involving circumferentially the entire toe. It was slightly painful and associated with serous discharge but no discharge of the bony spicules. Additionally, there was a shortening of the distal phalanx of the second, fourth, and fifth toes. The sensation and peripheral pulses of the feet were normal.

X-rays of the right foot revealed complete resorption of the middle and terminal phalanx of the fifth toe, complete resorption of the terminal phalanx of the fourth toe, partial resorption of the terminal phalanx of the third toe, and partial resorption of the middle and terminal phalanx of the second toe.
Consultations with several specialists ruled out cardiac, respiratory, ophthalmologic, and otologic problems.

Laboratory investigations that included complete blood count, renal function tests, liver function tests, parathyroid hormone, anti-nuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP test, C-reactive protein, fasting blood sugar, serum calcium, inorganic phosphate, albumin, and thyroid function tests were in normal ranges.

This workup helped rule out infections, e.g., osteomyelitis, connective tissue, endocrine, and lipid storage disease. There were no clinical or radiographic findings of inflammatory/rheumatic disorders such as psoriatic arthritis.
The clinical and radiologic features and workup helped establish the diagnosis of IAO in our patient.

X-rays of the right foot revealed complete resorption of the middle and terminal phalanx of the fifth toe, complete resorption of the terminal phalanx of the fourth toe, partial resorption of the terminal phalanx of the third toe, and partial resorption of the middle and terminal phalanx of the second toe.

There were no clinical or radiographic findings of inflammatory/rheumatic disorders such as psoriatic arthritis.

evidence_events.source_span: A 22-year-old male patient reported swelling without pain on the right side of his face since childhood as the chief complaint.
The swelling had been growing gradually over the years and has now become approximately fist-sized.
The painless swelling was fluctuant, compressible, and soft in consistency on palpation with a slight rise in temperature over the surface.
Temporomandibular joint examination showed deviation towards the left side while closing the jaw without pain, crepitus, or clicking sound.
Intra-oral examination revealed bluish-red discolouration in the posterior part of the right side buccal mucosa extending up to the right side soft palatal region.

On bimanual palpation, the lesion was soft, compressible, non-tender, with a diffuse periphery and evident pulsation; manipulation exaggerated the lesion and revealed an elevated red-purplish lesion in the posterior mucosa.
Panoramic and submentovertex radiographs showed multiple concentric calcifications in the soft tissue shadow of the lesion suggestive of phleboliths.
The patient was referred to the department of interventional radiology for management after assuring the benign nature of the disease and possible definite treatment.
