evidence_events.procedural_cue: selective digital subtraction angiography and embolization

The hematoma was displacing the left kidney anteriorly and compressing the renal parenchyma, suggesting a page kidney. An ill-defined, partially exophytic, heterogeneously enhancing lesion was noted at the interpolar region of the left kidney, approximately 45 mm × 45 mm × 40 mm. Multiple prominent vessels were seen at the periphery of the lesion, raising suspicion of minimal contrast extravasation at the site of the lesion. A prominent vessel was seen adjacent to the inferior pole of the left kidney, with active IV contrast extravasation noted in the delayed study.

source_metadata.title: Intestinal tuberculosis and inflammatory bowel disease; the usual challenging differential diagnoses: A case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 37-year-old female housekeeper from Bangladesh presented to us in September 2022 suffering from 2 months of abdominal pain, which was located mainly in the right mid and lower sides of the abdomen, worsens after meals and is accompanied by diarrhea, bloating, and fatigue.
The abdominal examination was distended with palpable bowel loops and increased bowel sounds, suggesting acute intestinal obstruction; rectal examination was normal.

Laboratory tests of blood and stools confirmed positive Helicobacter pylori infection and anemia with leukocytosis (WBC:14.35×10^9/L), low MCHC (30.8 g/dL), hemoglobin 10.30 g/dL, and elevated erythrocyte-sedimentation-rate (ESR).
Chest X-ray and upper ultrasound abdomen were normal.

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) showed distended ileum with fecal matter and dilated jejunal and ileal loops, minimal free fluid adjacent to the terminal ileum, reduced caliber of caecum with prominent submucosal fat and diffuse postcontrast mucosal enhancement in the caecum and ascending colon, increasing suspicion of inflammatory bowel disease.
Endoscopic biopsy for the ileum and cecum showed granulomatous with focal chronic active disease.
Colonoscopy revealed a patulous ileocecal valve with terminal ileum ulcerations and ileal stenosis, and the cecum and ileocecal valves were deformed.
Mycobacterium tuberculosis was identified by PCR in lymph node biopsies from the mesentery sent for microbiological analysis, indicating tuberculosis.
The woman was given antituberculous medicine and was followed in an outpatient clinic with noticeable improvement in symptoms, weight gain, and strength.
The patient contracted SARS-COV2 infection (COVID-19) while on anti-TB treatment, with moderate symptoms resolving within 72 hours.

source_metadata.title: Metastatic methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus infection with infective endocarditis, pulmonary septic emboli, axillary abscess with a subacute presentation in a patient with chronic end-stage kidney disease on maintenance haemodialysis

evidence_events.source_span: A male patient in his 40s with end-stage diabetic nephropathy on maintenance haemodialysis through a cuffed tunnelled catheter presented with a history of intermittent, low to moderate-grade fever for 3 weeks associated with generalised weakness, night sweats, exertional breathlessness, mild intermittent cough, loss of appetite, and left axillary pain for 2 days

Physical examination revealed tachycardia of 120 beats per minute, blood pressure of 110/76 mm Hg, normal oxygen saturation, respiratory rate of 20/min, reduced breath sounds on the left side, focal tenderness in the left axilla without palpable mass or skin changes, and no signs of catheter site infection

Chest radiography revealed left hydropneumothorax with multiple focal pulmonary nodular opacities; chest CT with contrast showed left loculated hydropneumothorax with multiple cavitary nodules and some nodules with reverse halo signs

Laboratory investigations showed significant leucocytosis (16,000/mL) with neutrophilia (90%), anaemia (Hb 90 g/L), raised inflammatory markers including CRP 6 mg/dL and ESR 60 mm/hour, poorly controlled diabetes (HbA1c 8.5%), and elevated D-dimer (2800 ng/mL); sputum and urine cultures were negative

Repeated blood cultures from right antecubital venepuncture, cuffed tunnelled haemodialysis catheter, and haemodialysis circuit were negative for aerobes, anaerobes, and yeasts after 2 to 7 days of incubation

Ultrasonography on the fourth day of admission showed a small irregular collection (~5 cc) in the left axilla, which was aspirated under ultrasound guidance; axillary aspirate microscopy showed gram-positive bacteria
evidence_events.temporal_cue: on the fourth day of admission

evidence_events.source_span: Transthoracic and transoesophageal echocardiography revealed multiple tiny vegetations at the septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve on the atrial side with near moderate tricuspid regurgitation and a peak gradient of 15 mm Hg
Culture of the axillary aspirate grew methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) sensitive to clindamycin, vancomycin, linezolid, and ciprofloxacin

source_metadata.title: Spontaneous rectus sheath and retroperitoneal haemorrhage secondary to enoxaparin injections

evidence_events.source_span: A 79-year-old woman on the medical ward was complaining of severe abdominal pain overnight. She was admitted 1 week prior with coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) pneumonitis and was being treated with remdesivir and dexamethasone. She was on a high-dose subcutaneous enoxaparin regime (1 mg/kg BD) as per local guidelines for VTE prophylaxis. She had a background of neurofibromatosis type-1 (NF1) and osteoarthritis.

The patient described the abdominal pain starting several days prior but denied any acute injury or event as a potential trigger. The patient was pale with cold peripheries and a prolonged central capillary refill time. Her vital signs showed a hypotension of 90 systolic and a heart rate of 85 beats per minute. There were multiple visible suprapubic bruising sites indicative of enoxaparin injections. On palpation, there was a small mass posterior to the area of bruising with a separate and much larger mass in the left iliac fossa. There was no evidence of external bleeding.

Blood results are illustrated in Table 1, which compare results on assessment to 3 days prior. Significant abnormalities included an acute fall in haemoglobin to 67 g/l, an increase in the white blood cell count to 24.5 × 10^9/l and a two-fold increase in both urea and creatinine with a reduction in the estimated glomerular filtration rate indicating an acute kidney injury.

evidence_events.source_span: Suspecting internal haemorrhage, contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) of the abdomen and pelvis was arranged.
The CT images showed the presence of multiple haematomas with evidence of active bleeding (Figs 1 and 2).

After discussions between the interventional radiologist, general surgeon and haematologist, a conservative approach to management was taken. The patient’s old age, moderate frailty and comorbidities favoured conservative treatment, with an interventional approach to be considered if conservative measures were unsuccessful.

A total of 6 units of packed red blood cells were transfused over the course of 5 days. Tranexamic acid was also administered during the same time period at a regime of 1 g three times a day. Empirical antibiotic cover was also given.
As there was no coagulopathy and a significant interval since the last enoxaparin injection, no reversal agent nor coagulation factors were given.
After monitoring for 5 days, the patient’s haemoglobin normalized to 121 g/l. She was subsequently discharged following 5 further days. No routine follow-up was required.

initial_presentation.first_contact_summary: Upon admission, cognitive slowing and impaired memory function were detected by neurological examination; no abnormalities were found in other physical examinations. Relevant scales showed Mini-Mental State Examination score 27/30, Montreal Cognitive Assessment score 27/30, Barthel Index score 100. Blood and CSF tests were normal. MRI revealed multiple round lesions in the genu and splenium of the corpus callosum on T1WI, T2WI, FLAIR and DWI. EEG showed paroxysmal short-range slow waves. source_metadata.title: Not your usual neurodegenerative disease: a case report of neuronal intranuclear inclusion disease with unconventional imaging patterns
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case presentation and case description sections with imaging and genetic evidence.

evidence_events.source_span: A 39-year-old man presented with chronic headache, blurred vision, tinnitus, and numbness in the hands as initial symptoms, accompanied by cognitive slowing and decreased memory.
Neurological examination detected cognitive slowing and impaired memory function; no abnormalities were found in other physical examinations.

Blood biochemistry, routine blood panel, anti-endothelial cell antibody, anticardiolipin antibody, anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide antibody, antikeratin antibody, antiperinuclear factor, and routine and biochemical cerebrospinal fluid tests were all normal.
Brain MRI revealed multiple round hypointense lesions on T1-weighted imaging and hyperintense lesions on T2WI/FLAIR/DWI in the genu and splenium of the corpus callosum.
Contrast-enhanced MRI revealed multiple round hypointense lesions on T1WI and hyperintense lesions on T2WI in the genu and splenium of the corpus callosum; no lesion enhancements were found.
Electroencephalogram demonstrated paroxysmal short-range (5–7 Hz) slow waves in the eye-closed resting state.
Fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) demonstrated dilated macular capillary and fluorescein leakage from dilated blood vessels.
Initial diagnosis of Susac syndrome was made based on typical symptoms and characteristic radiology changes including multiple round hyperintense lesions in the corpus callosum on DWI.
Patient's neurological symptoms improved after combined pharmacotherapy with high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone, oral aspirin, and oral idebenone.
Follow-up brain MRI at 1 month and 3 months showed no significant changes in corpus callosum lesions despite clinical improvement.
Patient was readmitted with paroxysmal visual field defect, headache, hypoesthesia of right hand, cognitive slowing, and reduced tendon reflexes; other neurological exams were normal.
Brain MRI and contrast-enhanced MRI remained unchanged from initial findings at readmission.
Electroencephalogram showed paroxysmal short-range (4–7 Hz) slow waves and epileptic waves after hyperventilation.
Nerve conduction velocity revealed no peripheral nerve damage but prolonged F-wave latencies in both lower limbs; electromyography showed no neurogenic or myogenic lesions.
Genetic testing revealed 101 GGC repeats in the 5′-untranslated region of the NOTCH2NLC gene (normal <40).
Skin biopsy showed eosinophilic spherical inclusion bodies within some sweat gland epithelial cell nuclei.

evidence_events.source_span: Patient refused immunohistochemical staining (p62 and ubiquitin) for skin biopsy.
Patient was prescribed symptomatic treatment including oral analgesics and idebenone; symptoms gradually relieved over subsequent months.
Follow-up 18 months after discharge revealed no paroxysmal visual field defect or hypoesthesia and only occasional headaches.

evidence_events.source_span: 40-year-old male who presented with a medical history of hematospermia, painful ejaculation, and perineal discomfort for five years
He denied any previous medical issues and any urinary complaints such as urgency, frequency, or dysuria
He was medicated with different antibiotics and anti-inflammatory drugs, without any improvement
Urine culture was negative
General blood analysis was completely innocent
Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) was normal: 0.31 ng/mL
Urethrocystoscopy was performed and showed a normal urethra with a nonobstructive prostate and bladder mucosa with normal characteristics
Transrectal ultrasound (TRUS) showed a 30 cc prostate without any abnormality

Pelvic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) was performed, showing asymmetric seminal vesicles, due to the enlarged volume of the left one probably because of hematic content and a possible lithiasic focus in prostatoseminal angle measuring 7 mm
Robot-assisted laparoscopic excision of the left seminal vesicle was performed
The left seminal vesicle was removed en bloc
Six months after the surgery, he showed total remission of the symptoms

source_metadata.title: Multiple liver abscesses secondary to Listeria monocytogenes complicated by hepatic artery mycotic aneurysm

evidence_events.source_span: A woman in her 50s with no known prior medical history presented to the emergency department for 5 days of right upper quadrant abdominal pain, nausea and vomiting.

On presentation, the patient was afebrile with a temperature of 36.7°C, heart rate 87 bpm, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, blood pressure 139/77 mm Hg, oxygen saturation 99% on room air; abdominal exam was soft, non-tender, non-distended with no guarding.

Initial laboratory studies demonstrated a leucocytosis to 15.0×10⁹ cells/L with neutrophilic predominance of 78%; liver enzymes did not demonstrate significant transaminitis; haemoglobin A1C was 14.2%.

CT of chest, abdomen and pelvis revealed three peripherally enhancing, cystic lesions in hepatic parenchyma segments VI, VII and VIII; a large arterially enhancing vascular lesion in the porta hepatis measuring up to 3.2 cm concerning for hepatic artery aneurysm.

Given leucocytosis and peripheral enhancement of lesions on CT, the patient was presumed to have multiple liver abscesses; differential diagnosis included metastatic disease, primary liver malignancy and atypical haemangioma.
Multiphase abdominal MRI on hospital day 3 showed interval enlargement of aneurysm to 3.9×3.1 cm and three stable lesions consistent with abscesses.

CT angiography on hospital day 5 demonstrated worsening inflammatory changes in porta hepatis, new wall thickening of aneurysm, diffuse periportal oedema, near complete luminal narrowing of proper hepatic artery, and interval change in enhancement pattern of vascular lesion with minimal arterial phase filling.

Catheter angiography of proper hepatic artery on hospital day 6 demonstrated lack of opacification of aneurysm sac suggestive of thrombosis; significant narrowing of mid and proximal proper hepatic artery noted.
Drainage catheters were placed under ultrasound guidance in two right hepatic liver abscesses on hospital day 7; third abscess was unamenable to drainage.
Listeria monocytogenes grew from two hepatic abscess cultures on hospital day 12; blood cultures remained without growth.
Susceptibility testing demonstrated isolate sensitive to ampicillin, meropenem, penicillin and TMP/SMX; patient switched to intravenous ampicillin.
All abscesses decreased in size on repeat liver CTs on hospital days 13 and 20; hepatic artery aneurysm remained thrombosed.
Patient discharged on hospital day 23 on outpatient intravenous ampicillin until resolution of undrained liver abscess on imaging; repeat CT at 5 weeks showed ongoing improvement.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: outpatient intravenous antibiotics and follow-up CT

source_metadata.title: Iliopsoas Hematoma Progression to Abscess in the Setting of Diabetic Ketoacidosis

evidence_events.source_span: The patient is a 40-year-old male with a history of diabetes mellitus and ethanol use who was struck by a motor vehicle while ambulating in the street.

A physical exam at the time of presentation to the Emergency Department (ED) revealed exquisite midline and sacral spinal tenderness with no significant paraspinal tenderness. The patient had subacute bruising throughout his lower extremities, torso, back, and face, with bilateral bruising over his infraorbital region.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: at the time of presentation to the Emergency Department

evidence_events.source_span: CT spine showed a nondisplaced L2 vertebral body fracture.

Six days after the initial presentation, the patient presented to the ED again with increasing back and left lower extremity pain, confusion, auditory hallucinations, and fever for three days. He was tachycardic to 109 bpm and febrile to 101-102F (38.8C). Neuromuscular examination demonstrated 2/5 strength in bilateral lower extremities. He was unable to perform hip flexion and leg elevation. Sensation was grossly intact throughout both lower extremities.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: Six days after the initial presentation

evidence_events.source_span: He had a white blood cell count of 24,000/mcL with a lactate of 2.8 mmol/L. The patient was also found to be in diabetic ketoacidosis with a blood glucose of 588 mg/dL, an anion gap of 26, and a pH of 7.35.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: Six days after the initial presentation

evidence_events.source_span: Subsequent imaging showed L2 paraspinal soft tissue mass with multilocular low attenuation changes in the left psoas muscle, raising concern for an infected hematoma or an intramuscular abscess.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: Six days after the initial presentation

evidence_events.source_span: Interventional radiology percutaneously drained 20 mL of purulent material from the left psoas muscle, which was positive for Methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA). A JP drain was placed.
MRI showed bilateral psoas abscesses, an L2 fracture with edema throughout the vertebral body, and an L5-S1 disc protrusion approaching the S1 roots.

Repeat CT scan revealed a new fluid collection with gas in the left gluteal region. Interventional radiology performed percutaneous drainage of the left gluteal and right psoas collections, with JP drains inserted. Fluid cultures yielded negative results.

Subsequent imaging disclosed a large, peripherally enhancing fluid collection measuring 20cm x 4.5cm x 4cm in the posterior thigh. Interventional radiology performed percutaneous drainage of serosanguineous fluid from the posterior thigh and placed an additional JP drain. Fluid cultures yielded negative results.

source_metadata.title: CT diagnosis and laparoscopic treatment of hepatic abscess secondary to fish bone transmigration through the stomach wall

evidence_events.source_span: A 43-year-old male with no known past medical history arrives at the emergency department complaining of fever and headache for the past 5 days.
The patient denied chest pain, dyspnea, cough, abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, or urinary symptoms.

The patient was febrile at 38.2°C, tachycardic to 121 beats per minute, and hypertensive with systolic blood pressure of 168 and diastolic blood pressure of 101 mm Hg. Physical examination including the abdomen was unremarkable.

Laboratory assessment showed a white blood cell count of 12,600/mm3, Aspartate transferase (AST) 48 U/L, and Alanine transferase (ALT) 83 U/L. An otherwise unremarkable chest X-ray revealed mild elevation of the right hemidiaphragm.
The patient returned to the emergency department 3 days later after suffering a syncopal episode in the context of recurrent fever and new onset abdominal pain.
Initial blood culture results returned negative for bacteremia.
Now, the patient was febrile at 39.4°C, tachycardic to 104 bpm, and hypertensive at 153/82 mm Hg. Physical examination demonstrated tenderness in the right upper quadrant and epigastrium.
Labs showed an interval increase of leukocytosis to 16,500/mm3, AST 52 U/L, and ALT 105 U/L.

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed a 5.1 × 7.5 × 3.9 cm heterogeneous hypoattenuating lesion in the left hepatic lobe extending up to the lesser curvature of the stomach with and centered over gastro-hepatic recess. There was a rim of peripheral enhancement around the lesion. A hypodense ring paralleling the rim of enhancement was seen around the lesion in the liver often referred to as a double target sign, which is characteristically seen in hepatic abscess. A curvilinear dense foreign body was noted extending from the left hepatic lobe lesion into the gastro-hepatic recess.
Notably, there was no extraluminal air or significant intraperitoneal fluid that would suggest an active leak from the stomach.

The patient was admitted to the surgical service for the management of a liver abscess, presumed to be secondary to perforation of the stomach by an ingested foreign body. The patient was resuscitated and given broad-spectrum antibiotics.

During laparoscopy, the greater curvature of the stomach and the anterior surface of the liver appeared grossly normal. There were dense inflammatory adhesions between the anterior gastric wall and the undersurface of the left lobe of the liver, and careful dissection revealed a large amount of purulent fluid which was aspirated and sent for bacterial culture. A moderate amount of fibrinous material adhering the liver surface to the stomach wall was debrided and indicated the abscess had been unroofed. An approximately 3 cm white foreign body consistent with a fish bone was removed under direct visualization and sent to pathology.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: laparoscopic drainage and foreign body removal

evidence_events.source_span: The stomach was insufflated with air via a nasogastric tube which did not show any obvious leak.
Postoperatively, the patient underwent an upper gastrointestinal series which was negative for extravasation of contrast.
The abscess grew Streptococcus anginosus and Actinomyces odontolyticus on culture.

After a noneventful postoperative course, the patient was discharged with a drain in place and treated with oral Cefdinir and Metronidazole for 1 week. At the patient's follow-up visit, the patient was recovering well without adverse sequelae from treatment.

source_metadata.title: Misty mesentery, ascites, and bowel wall thickening in a child: Diagnostic clue for intestinal lymphangiectasia

evidence_events.source_span: A 6-year-old boy presented to our hospital with the presenting complaint of recurrent diarrhea for 11 months and weight loss of the same duration.
On examination, there was bilateral pitting edema of the lower limbs. Vital parameters were stable. Systemic examination was not significant.
Laboratory investigations revealed hypoalbuminemia and lymphopenia.

Axial contrast-enhanced CT abdomen showed circumferential thickening of the jejunum, islands of echogenic fat in the mesentery, enlarged oval-shaped lymph nodes in the mesentery, and minimal pelvic ascites.

An endoscopic biopsy was carried out with histopathologic examination of duodenal tissue showing intact columnar lining with blunting of villi, dilated lymphatic channels with proteinaceous fluid within the lumen, and moderate lymphoplasmacytic infiltration.
The patient was started on a high-protein diet with replacement of long-chain triglycerides by medium-chain triglycerides and showed gradual improvement in symptoms on follow-up.

source_metadata.title: Magnetic Resonance Imaging Findings in a Rare Case of a Ruptured Intracranial Dermoid Cyst

evidence_events.source_span: A 40-year-old woman came to the hospital with complaints of a decrease in left-sided vision, decreased palpebral fissures, and left-sided diplopia.
She had intense, sharp, throbbing, sporadic, burning, and shock-like pain around the eyes, lips, nose, jaw, forehead, and scalp on the left side. Attacks of sharp pain were triggered by touch.
She had a history of occasional headaches.
On examination, the eyeball was downward and outward.

Plain and contrast MRIs of the brain revealed a heterogenous lobulated lesion in the region of the left side of the interpeduncular cistern extending to the prepontine cistern measuring 3 x 2.5 x 4 cm.
The lesion was predominantly hyperintense on both the T1 weighted image (T1WI) and the T2 weighted image (T2WI), with some hypointense areas within, without significant enhancement.
Tiny T1 hyperintensities were seen diffusely scattered in subarachnoid spaces in the brain, likely to be fat.
There was a mass effect on the left mid-brain and the left pons. Anteriorly, it abutted the left internal carotid artery. Restricted diffusion was seen.
The patient underwent a craniotomy with the removal of the dermoid cyst and irrigation of subarachnoid spaces to remove ruptured contents and debris.

evidence_events.source_span: A 20-year-old gravida 2 para 2 (G2P2) Guatemalan female, with no past medical history, presented to the emergency department (ED) nine days following uncomplicated full-term pregnancy via vaginal delivery with a three-day history of multiple episodes of nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramping, profuse non-bloody dark diarrhea up to eight times per day, residual non-bloody vaginal discharge, and lower abdominal pain rated as eight out of 10.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: nine days following uncomplicated full-term pregnancy

evidence_events.source_span: Upon arrival, the patient was tachycardic with a heart rate of 124, respiratory rate of 28, blood pressure of 135/74, and temperature of 39.4 Celsius (102.9 F). Physical examination revealed a soft and tender abdomen in all four quadrants on deep palpation, with mild guarding and suprapubic tenderness. Foul-smelling material was noted in undergarments.

Complete blood count (CBC) and comprehensive metabolic panel (CMP) revealed decreases in hemoglobin, hematocrit, sodium, and potassium, with elevated platelet count, bands, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), and glucose.

Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous contrast revealed an enlarged post-gravid uterus with air in the lower uterine segment of the endometrial cavity, mild wall thickening diffusely throughout the large bowel possibly reflecting infectious or inflammatory colitis, and a large fluid collection superior to the spleen.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast

evidence_events.source_span: The patient remained persistently tachycardic and developed fever; concern was for endometritis with concurrent colitis after vaginal exam. She was admitted with continued IV antibiotics and observation.

After three days of admission without improvement, antibiotics were changed to ceftriaxone and metronidazole. Interventional radiology paracentesis was performed yielding a minty, milky drainage; fluid cultures showed no bacterial growth.
Four days later, repeat CT showed multiple fluid collections of increased size and metabolic activity with remote enhancement consistent with peritonitis.

On admission day 8, the patient underwent exploratory laparotomy with peritoneal lavage. Operative findings included diffuse fibrinous peritonitis with no obvious perforation of abdominal viscus. Postoperative cultures remained negative.
Repeat CT one week postoperatively showed a small, partially loculated fluid collection superior to the spleen with significantly decreased volume compared to prior imaging.
The patient remained hospitalized for three weeks postoperatively and was discharged after complete recovery.

source_metadata.title: Budd Chiari Syndrome: A Case Report on Classic Imaging Findings With Successful Intervention

evidence_events.source_span: A 40-year-old lady presented with complaints of pain in the abdomen for one month. She also had several episodes of vomiting, which was non-projectile. On examination, there was mild tenderness in the epigastric and right hypochondriac region. The liver was palpable below the subcostal margin, suggestive of hepatomegaly.
On grayscale ultrasound examination, heterogeneous echotexture was seen in the liver and a fibrous cord was noted replacing the middle hepatic vein along with the presence of mild ascites
On color Doppler, no color flow was noted in hepatic veins

On contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CECT) scan, no contrast opacification was noted in the middle and left hepatic veins and partial opacification was noted in the right hepatic vein suggestive of complete thrombosis of middle and left hepatic veins and partial thrombosis of the right hepatic vein associated with slit-like visualization of the hepatic part of IVC. A slight enlargement of the caudate lobe was noted. The liver shows a heterogeneous mottled appearance (nutmeg liver)
The patient underwent a diagnostic hepatic vein venography procedure, which confirmed imaging findings

Following this, hepatic vein stenting was performed successfully. The right internal jugular vein was used for gaining venous access. A balloon-expanding stent of size 8 x 37 mm was used for the procedure.

evidence_events.source_span: A 31-year-old female with a history of infertility presented to the ED with gradually worsening abdominal pain and tenderness in the right lower quadrant which began the previous night following intercourse.
The patient had recently undergone infertility treatment, including ovulation induction with clomiphene and a round of intrauterine insemination.

source_metadata.title: Large Angiomatous Nasal Polyp Presents With Epistaxis Imitating Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case presentation and clinical course sections with figure references.

evidence_events.source_span: A 16-year-old male with no significant past medical history presents with a six-month history of epistaxis and nasal obstruction.

On exam, the patient was noted to be solely mouth-breathing due to nasal obstruction. His nose was normal externally without septal deviation, with bilateral polyposis and abundant drainage noted. The oral cavity exhibited a centrally located soft palate mass which pressed the soft palate inferiorly, pointing the uvula anteriorly.

CT with contrast showed a hypervascular 3.4 x 4.7 x 6.1 cm mass that extended from the nasal cavity to the oropharynx. The left maxillary sinus demonstrated erosion of the medial wall, making it the likely site of origin. Posterior maxillary sinus bowing (Holman-Miller sign) was not noted and the pterygopalatine fossa and pterygomaxillary fissure were not widened, making JNA less likely. Left-sided cervical lymphadenopathy was also noted.

MRI of the face and neck revealed a large, heterogeneously enhancing polypoid mass that appeared to arise from the left nasal mucosa or left maxillary sinus and extend into the nasopharynx and oropharynx. Abnormal signal enhancement involved the left pterygopalatine fossa, and the mass was noted to extend into the left mastication space. The left maxillary sinus medial wall appeared eroded, which may be secondary to vascular invasion or chronic inflammatory processes. Sinonasal carcinoma or rhabdomyosarcoma was favored based on the radiological findings.

An arteriogram performed under awake orotracheal intubation revealed hyperemic nasal mucosal and a tumor blush from branches of the distal left internal maxillary artery (IMAX). The polyp was successfully embolized using polyvinylalcohol (PVA).

Nasal endoscopy showed diffuse polyposis in both nasal cavities, heavier on the left side. The nasopharynx on the right side showed a firm, brown mass. Two biopsies were obtained of the nasopharyngeal mass, which showed granulation tissue without malignancy and necrotic tissue with colonies of bacteria without malignancy.

One month later, the patient underwent endoscopic sinus surgery to debulk the polyposis and further assess the origin and features of the mass. A left maxillary antrostomy was performed and polypoid tissue within the left maxillary sinus was debulked. The necrotic nasopharyngeal mass was biopsied and sent for frozen and permanent analyses. After frozen specimens were confirmed to be benign, the stalk of the nasopharyngeal mass was cut and the mass was pulled through the mouth.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: endoscopic sinus surgery, biopsy, frozen section

evidence_events.source_span: The final pathology of the nasopharyngeal mass revealed an angiomatous inflammatory nasal polyp with no malignancy identified.
Seven weeks after surgery, the patient had recovered well and upon physical exam showed no signs of recurrence or synechia on nasal endoscopy.

source_metadata.title: Pheochromocytoma: A Troublesome Tumor

evidence_events.source_span: A 45-year-old man presented with a history of episodic headaches, palpitations, and sweating for the past six months. He also reported feeling anxious and irritable during these episodes. Physical examination was unremarkable except for an elevated blood pressure of 170/100 mmHg.

Laboratory investigations revealed elevated levels of plasma catecholamines (epinephrine: 550 pg/mL, norepinephrine: 700 pg/mL) and metanephrines (metanephrine: 1800 pg/mL, normetanephrine: 1200 pg/mL), confirming the diagnosis of pheochromocytoma.
Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and computed tomography (CT) imaging studies demonstrated a 3 cm mass in the left adrenal gland with evidence of local invasion into the surrounding tissues.
MRI of the brain was normal. Genetic testing for MEN and VHL was negative.

The patient was started on an alpha-adrenergic blocker (phenoxybenzamine) to prevent an intraoperative hypertensive crisis and underwent a laparoscopic left adrenalectomy following 10 days of phenoxybenzamine.
Intraoperative findings confirmed the presence of left pheochromocytoma with local invasion into the adjacent tissues. The tumor was removed completely, and the postoperative period was uneventful.

Histopathological examination confirmed the diagnosis of pheochromocytoma. The tumor measured 3.5 cm in diameter and showed evidence of capsular and vascular invasion. The mitotic rate was low, and the Ki-67 index was 5%. The tumor was negative for malignancy markers.

The patient was followed up in the clinic for six months postoperatively. He reported resolution of his symptoms, and his blood pressure was normal on follow-up visits. Repeat imaging did not show any evidence of tumor recurrence.

source_metadata.title: MRI Findings of Desmoplastic Infantile Ganglioglioma: A Case Report and Analysis
source_metadata.notes: Case report of a 7-year-old boy with desmoplastic infantile ganglioglioma (DIG) including clinical presentation, imaging, pathology, and outcome.

evidence_events.source_span: The patient in question is a seven-year-old boy who has been experiencing recurring headaches and vomiting in recent days. His parents did not report any previous medical issues.
During the investigation, the patient rapidly developed amaurosis, a complete loss of vision.
A CT scan, carried out at the originating facility, unveiled an expansive tumor within the CNS.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) at our institution executed pre- and post-contrast T1 sequences, T2/FLAIR, and DWI/ADC sequences discerned a substantial lesion situated in the right cerebral hemisphere, encompassing both cystic and solid constituents.
The lesion was centered in the parietal lobe, causing compression on the right lateral ventricle and midline deviation.

The cystic component appeared hypointense on T1-weighted images and hyperintense on T2-weighted and FLAIR sequences, while the solid component showed heterogeneous enhancement on post-contrast T1 and iso-intensity on ADC maps compared to normal brain parenchyma.

evidence_events.source_span: The patient underwent total resection of the tumor.
Histopathological analysis confirmed the presence of a glioneuronal tumor, leading to a diagnosis of DIG.
Over the course of the first two years, he remained asymptomatic, with no evidence of new lesions observed in the MRI scans.

source_metadata.title: Metastatic Epithelial-Myoepithelial Carcinoma in a Female Presenting with Neck Mass and Lytic Lesion in Acetabulum: A Diagnostic Challenge on Cytology

evidence_events.source_span: A 58-year-old female presented with a history of low-backache for the last month, which was moderate in intensity and continuous in nature.

On clinical examination, a single lymph node in the right lower cervical region (level III) measuring 2x2.5 cm in diameter, which was mobile, non-tender and firm in consistency was identified. The swelling was present for more than 20 years and was neither associated with pain nor an increase in size.
She had undergone surgery 35 years ago for a right-sided upper neck swelling, the medical records of which were not available.
Radiological investigations revealed a lytic lesion in the left acetabulum.

A computerised tomography (CT)-guided biopsy was obtained from the lesion. The histopathological examination of the hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) stained sections revealed occasional fragments of dead bone with a few clusters of round to polygonal tumor cells with mild cellular pleomorphism, eccentrically placed round nuclei, coarse chromatin, occasional prominent nucleoli, and a moderate amount of cytoplasm.
Immunohistochemistry revealed the tumor cells to be positive for cytokeratin-7 (CK7) and GATA3 and negative for TTF1 and p63.
Clinical examination, mammography and positron emission tomography (PET) all failed to identify any lesion in the breast or lungs.

Fine needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) from the right cervical swelling was performed. The smears were cellular and showed tumor cells predominantly dispersed singly as well as arranged in loose clusters in a background of chondromyxoid stroma.

The tumor cells were round to polygonal with mild pleomorphism, eccentrically placed round nuclei, coarse chromatin, occasional prominent nucleoli, and a moderate amount of cytoplasm with some showing cytoplasmic vacuolations. Occasional loose clusters of relatively smaller cells with scant cytoplasm were also noted.

The H&E stained section from the cell-block revealed tumor cells arranged in the form of tubules lined by a dual layer of tumor cells. The luminal cells showed a scant to moderate amount of pale to eosinophilic cytoplasm and the basally placed cells showed a moderate amount of clear to vacuolated cytoplasm. A few scattered mitotic figures and occasional lymphoid aggregates were also noted.

On performing immunohistochemistry, the luminal cells showed strong diffuse membranous positivity for CK7 (epithelial marker) and the abluminal cells showed strong nuclear positivity for p63 (myoepithelial marker). Less than 10% of tumor cells showed nuclear positivity for GATA3.
Based on the cytomorphological features on smears and cell-block and the immunocytochemistry, a final diagnosis of metastatic epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma was given.

evidence_events.source_span: Clinical examination of the left ear revealed a central wet tympanic membrane perforation with mildly congested middle ear mucosa.
Audiological assessment revealed left conductive hearing loss.
Flexible nasopharyngoscopy revealed a bulge in the left nasopharyngeal wall, but no obvious mass was observed.
Her ear infection resolved after a course of oral and topical ciprofloxacin.

Computed tomography (CT) of the temporal bone revealed a large mass of mixed density with cystic and solid components. It was ill-defined and infiltrative and had an extensively enhancing component extending to the left petrous apex and left side of the clivus. There was an inferior extension to the left infratemporal fossa and nasopharyngeal and parapharyngeal spaces, displacing the nasopharynx anteriorly with adjacent airway narrowing without mucosal invasion. The lesion extended to the left mastoid air cells and middle ear cavity. It infiltrated the left jugular bulb and inferiorly extended to the proximal jugular vein with non-opacification, invasion, and significant osseous destruction of the left petrous bone and occipital condyle. Dehiscence, left carotid canal resorption, and left jugular foramen widening were also observed.

source_metadata.title: Aorto–mesenteric compass syndrome (Wilkie’s syndrome) in the differential diagnosis of chronic abdominal pain
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case presentation, investigations, outcome, and discussion sections.

evidence_events.source_span: A woman in her 40s was admitted to our department with weight loss, asthenia, post-prandial nausea and vomiting and persistent abdominal pain, mainly located in the epigastrium.
The patient reported that the pain increased at the end of meals and she described it as colic.
She also had anxiety-depressive disorder, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease and fibrocystic mastopathy.
She reported that in adolescence she had suffered from eating disorders with anorexia and bulimia.
Deep palpation showed that the patient’s abdomen was tense with an upper part guarding and marked epigastric regional pain; no abdominal organ enlargement was found.
A tympanitic sound to percussion was found in all quadrants together with normal bowel peristalsis.
Blood chemistry did not show any changes other than a mild increase in indirect bilirubin values related to Gilbert’s syndrome.
A urine test showed a urinary tract infection which was treated with specific antibiotic therapy.

At admission, the patient’s weight was 45 kg with a body mass index (BMI) of 14.69 kg/m2. The patient reported a weight loss of 6 kg in the previous 3 months linked to the severe post-prandial epigastric pain.
Abdominal ultrasonography, influenced by considerable gastrointestinal meteorism, showed two cystic formations in the right ovary, which was previously known.
Transabdominal and transvaginal ultrasonography showed the presence of a small infiltrating endometriotic outbreak isolated at the right sacral uterine ligament level.
An x-ray of the digestive tract with Gastrografin showed significant gastric dilation compatible with Wilkie’s syndrome.

A contrast-enhanced abdominal CT scan (oral and intravenous) showed significant dilation of the stomach with progression of the contrast slowing down in the first and second portion of the duodenum and an accentuated reduction in the third portion.
Extrinsic compression of the duodenum between the superior mesenteric artery and the aorta was also seen.

The radiological images also showed a reduction in the retroperitoneal adipose pad which normally interposes between the upper margin of the duodenum and the lower surface of the superior mesenteric artery.

The angle between the aorta and the upper mesenteric artery was less than 20° (normal value 25–60°), confirming compression of the third duodenal portion between the aorta and the superior mesenteric artery.

Management of the patient was discussed in a multidisciplinary meeting involving an internist, a radiologist, a gastroenterologist and a surgeon and, after close evaluation, a conservative option was chosen with nutritional rehabilitation support.

A high-calorie semi-liquid oral diet consisting of frequent meals of liquid or blenderised food was prescribed. In addition, liquid oral nutritional supplements (total volume 600 mL, energy density 1.5 kcal/mL, protein/carbohydrate/lipid ratio 25%/55%/30%) were prescribed.

At the 1-year follow-up the patient’s weight had increased to 50 kg (BMI 19.5 kg/m2) with a consequent relief of abdominal symptoms. The epigastric pain, although persistent, had reduced and no post-prandial nausea and vomiting episodes were reported.
A CT scan showed that the dilation of the stomach was reduced.

source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case presentation and clinical course sections with figure references.

evidence_events.source_span: A 64 year-old white woman was admitted to our hospital because of an episode of seizures and transient left hemiparesis.
Her clinical history was significant for repeated episodes of epistaxis and for exertional dyspnea.

The clinical examination was remarkable for pale skin and cyanosis of the nails. Small cutaneous telangiectases on the face were at the beginning considered not significant. The oxygen saturation while breating ambient air was 82%.
Laboratory exams showed severe iron deficiency anemia (hemoglobin level 5.8 g/dl, normal values 12 to 16; serum ferritin level 4 ng/ml, normal range 11 to 307). Fecal occult blood was positive.
An echocardiogram and an electroencephalogram were unremarkable.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the head, performed after the administration of intravenous contrast material, revealed increased signal intensity on diffusion weighted imaging in the cerebellum without associated contrast enhancement, as for ischemic stroke.
Gastroduodenoscopy and colonoscopy were normal, while a capsule endoscopy documented multiple telangiectasias in the jejunum.

To investigate the hypoxia a chest and abdomen computed tomography (CT) with administration of intravenous contrast material was ordered. The exam showed a group of dilated vessels in right upper and lower pulmonary lobes. These lesions were reported as likely arteriovenous malformations (PAVM).
The CT of the abdomen was unremarkable.
The association of recurrent nasal bleeds, cutaneous telangiectasias and visceral vascular malformations allowed us to diagnose HHT.

Right heart catheterization was performed and a 8 french catheter was introduced first in the right lower lobar pulmonary artery and then in the upper one. The angiography confirmed the PAVMs and the feeding arteries were embolized through coil occlusion. The procedure led to the exclusion of the PAVMs from the pulmonary circulation.

evidence_events.source_span: After the embolization the oxygen saturation improved (90% in ambient air) and the patient was discharged with the recommendation to return to the hospital after three months for follow-up.

evidence_events.source_span: six-year-old male who presented with a dislocated left elbow after failed reduction attempts at a level-one trauma center facility
The patient underwent successful closed reduction under conscious sedation with ketamine
Post-reduction x-rays demonstrated a well-reduced elbow without apparent fracture
At the clinical follow-up five days later, the splint was removed, and x-rays demonstrated a well-reduced elbow without periosteal reaction, fracture, and stable effusion

At the one-week follow-up, the cast was removed, and X-rays again demonstrated a well-reduced elbow without apparent fracture; there was a very small rim of calcification in the medial soft tissues visualized

At six weeks post injury, x-rays continued to show only additional ossification at the location of the medial epicondyle and a small second ossification area possibly representing mild heterotopic ossification
At five years post injury, the patient presented with intermittent discomfort on the medial elbow with some popping during pushups; physical exam revealed mild tenderness and limited range of motion
X-rays obtained at this visit demonstrated a chronic nonunion of a medial condyle fracture
CT scan confirmed nonunion of the medial condyle with multiple areas of ossification of the medial condyle and epicondyle, mild incongruity of the articular surface, and loose bodies
The patient underwent open reduction and internal fixation with an autologous bone graft from the bare area on the medial condyle
X-rays through the postoperative course demonstrate the healing of nonunion sites with the maintenance of orthopedic implants
At six months post surgery, range of motion was satisfactory with improvement in sports activities

source_metadata.title: A Large Retroperitoneal Liposarcoma Mimicking an Angiomyolipoma on Pre-operative Imaging: A Case Report
source_metadata.notes: Extraction based on case presentation and clinical course narrative with figure references.

evidence_events.source_span: A 58-year-old African American male presented to the urology office with a chief complaint of abdominal distention, early satiety, abdominal and left-sided flank pain that was progressively worsening for the past year.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: progressively worsening for the past year

evidence_events.source_span: On physical exam, patient was noted to have abdominal distention with a large palpable left sided mass.

Abdominal CT with intravenous contrast found hypodensities along the lateral margin of the right kidney measuring 1.5 cm in size, thought to represent cysts; adjacent to the left kidney, a large mixed echogenic lesion measuring 22 x 13 cm with diffuse fat contribution and soft tissue elements, suspicious for a giant renal angiomyolipoma with mass effect but no definitive acute hemorrhage or enhancing blood vessels were identified.
The patient underwent selective arterial embolization by interventional radiology in an attempt to reduce the tumor size prior to seeking a urology consult.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: selective arterial embolization by interventional radiology

evidence_events.source_span: MRI of the abdomen taken eight months later reported an interval increase in the size of the left retroperitoneal fat-containing mass, now measuring 20 x 18.6 x 22.2 cm and compressing the inferior vena cava; radiology suggested that although findings were consistent with left renal angiomyolipoma, other neoplastic processes such as liposarcoma should be considered.

After reviewing clinical history and serial imaging, concern was raised that the mass could be a liposarcoma; surgical resection of the mass and radical left nephrectomy were performed with 2 cm surgical margins.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: surgical resection and radical left nephrectomy

evidence_events.source_span: The resected tan-yellow, lobulated mass measured 39 x 32 x 22 cm and weighed 14,360 g (14 kg); external surface was tan-yellow, smooth, and glistening and was resected intact.
Hematoxylin & eosin microscopic images showed well-differentiated liposarcoma on the right and kidney tissue on the left; tumor abuts but does not invade adjacent kidney tissue.

Hematoxylin & eosin microscopic imaging showed variably sized mature adipocytes with bands of fibrotic stroma containing spindle cells with enlarged, hyperchromatic nuclei, indicating a well-differentiated liposarcoma as opposed to an angiomyolipoma.
The patient's post-operative course was uncomplicated and he was discharged on day five; at follow-up one week after discharge, the patient was recovering well and pending follow-up imaging.

source_metadata.title: Tuberculosis or Gallbladder carcinoma? A confusing presentation in an endemic region

evidence_events.source_span: A 43-year-old man, operated 10 years ago for anal fistula, presented to the emergency department for acute abdominal pain in the right hypochondrium non-irradiating and without vomiting or other accompanying signs, that had persisted for 4 days.
There was no history of fever, night sweats, cough with hemoptysis, unintentional weight loss or pulmonary tuberculosis.

Abdominal examination revealed right hypochondrial tenderness, there was no scleral icterus and Murphy's sign was negative. There was no cervical lymphadenopathy. Physical examination was otherwise unremarkable.

Laboratory investigations found an elevated white blood cells count (12,000/ml), C-reactive protein concentration was at (20 mg/l) and a very high level of cancer antigen 19-9 (2016 U/ml), liver function tests, including alcaline phosphatase were normal.
Ultrasonography showed perivascular edema with thickened wall with polypoid content.
A CT scan with intravenous contrast reported a suspicious irregular thickening of the gallbladder wall (Fig. 1).
Bili-MRI also revealed an aspecific and irregular parietal thickening with a porcelain-like gallbladder wall (Fig. 2).
Intraoperatively, we found a hard gallbladder with a thickened wall and contiguous infiltration of the liver. The patient underwent radical cholecystectomy (Glenn operation).
Histological examination of the specimen showed an ulcerated mucosa surrounded by epithelioid cells mixed with rare giant Langerhans cells without caseous necrosis (Fig. 3).
Quantiferon levels were above 0.34 IU/ml.
Antitubercular therapy with isoniazid, rifampicin, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide for 6 months was started.
After the 9-month follow-up, he is doing well.

source_metadata.title: Primary Mucoepidermoid Carcinoma of the Lung Coexisting With Pulmonary Tuberculosis: A Rare Case Report

evidence_events.source_span: A 54-year-old male patient presented to the otorhinolaryngology outpatient department six months ago with chief complaints of hoarseness of voice and dysphagia.
On video-laryngoscopy, bilateral adductor cord palsy was noted.
He presented again one month ago with persistent symptoms of dysphagia, hoarseness of voice, and additional complaints of weight loss, loss of appetite, and fever.
The CT scan of the neck and thorax revealed tracheal luminal narrowing and centrilobular nodules with a tree-in-bud appearance in the right upper lobe of the lung.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: CT scan of the neck and thorax

evidence_events.source_span: MRI of the brain was suggestive of diffuse cerebral atrophy.

On endoscopy, the oesophageal lumen showed narrowing due to external compression, with an indentation on the mucosa. However, no luminal growth was observed. A biopsy was taken, which tested negative for malignancy and dysplasia.
Bronchoscopy revealed significant nodular growth in the mid-trachea, leading to circumferential luminal narrowing.
The right upper lobe bronchus displayed necrotic bands. Additionally, a broncho-alveolar lavage (BAL) was obtained from the right upper lobe and sent for both cytology and Gene-Xpert.

Histopathological examination of the oesophageal biopsy showed strips of hyperplastic and spongiotic stratified squamous epithelium with mild intraepithelial inflammation but no evidence of dysplasia or malignancy.

Histopathological examination of the endobronchial biopsy showed a malignant epithelial neoplasm with nests and trabeculae of infiltrating tumor cells, focal acinar formation with intra-luminal eosinophilic material, cribriforming, and cells with moderate pleomorphism and features suggestive of mucus cells and intermediate cells. There was no marked cytological atypia, necrosis, or heightened mitotic activity.

Immunohistochemistry showed TTF1 focal nuclear positivity in respiratory epithelium but negativity in tumor cells; p40 and p63 nuclear positivity in basal layer of glandular structures and nests of intermediate cells; CK7 positivity in mucus cells; CD117, Synaptophysin, Chromogranin, CD56, and S100 were negative in tumor cells.

Adenocarcinoma was ruled out due to negativity of TTF1 and Napsin A. Adenoid cystic carcinoma was excluded due to absence of perineural invasion and negative immunostaining for CD117 and S100. Based on these findings, a final diagnosis of low-grade mucoepidermoid carcinoma (MEC) was rendered.

Cytomorphological examination of the BAL showed neutrophils, lymphocytes, alveolar macrophages, and columnar epithelial cells on a mucus-laden dirty background with no evidence of granuloma or malignancy, but Ziehl-Neelsen stain revealed a significant number of acid-fast bacilli.
Gene-Xpert MTB detected the Mycobacterial Tuberculosis complex, confirming tuberculosis.
The patient was immediately started on an antitubercular regimen and referred to oncology for further follow-up.

evidence_events.source_span: Physical examination revealed a cachectic male in respiratory distress with low oxygen saturation (86% on room air), which improved with supplemental oxygen. On auscultation, inspiratory crackles and expiratory wheezes were heard.
An electrocardiogram showed a first-degree atrioventricular block.
Chest radiograph showed bilateral hilar adenopathy with a reticular consolidation pattern suggestive of interstitial lung disease.
High-resolution CT of the chest revealed severe traction bronchiectasis of the upper lobes with multiple cysts in a honeycomb pattern, central and peripheral nodules, and mediastinal lymphadenopathy.
Serological studies revealed eosinophilia of 7,22,000 cells/microliter, elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme (103 units/L), and IgG (2320 mg/dL) levels.
Bronchoscopy showed a large conglomeration of lymph nodes at station 7.
Pathology from a transbronchial biopsy revealed non-caseating epithelioid granulomas in the alveoli, confirming the diagnosis of pulmonary sarcoidosis.
The patient was started on steroid therapy with improvement in symptoms.

source_metadata.title: Liver abscess caused by the ingested foreign body without sign of gastrointestinal perforation: A case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 66-year-old male patient presented to the emergency department because of abdominal pain. During the past 7 days, they had dull pain in the right hypochondriac region and intermittent low-grade fever.
The patient resided in an area with a high incidence of Fasciola infection. The patient was immunocompetent and tested negative for hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and human immunodeficiency virus (HIV).

evidence_events.source_section: Physical exam and pertinent laboratory values
evidence_events.source_span: Physical examination revealed mild tenderness in the right hypochondriac region without guarding or rebound tenderness. Laboratory results showed leukocytosis (12.3 G/L) with 75.3% neutrophils, elevated C-reactive protein (79.8 mg/dL), increased fibrinogen (6.88 g/L), normal liver enzymes and bilirubin, and negative immunodiagnosis for amebiasis and fascioliasis.

Ultrasonography revealed a poorly demarcated, heterogeneous lesion in segment 4B of the liver with hypoechoic areas indicating liquefied necrosis. Abdominal CT scan showed a localized lesion spreading from segment 4B to segment 3, 38 mm in diameter, peripherally enhancing with irregular margins and centrally hypoattenuating with incomplete septal formation.

Preliminary diagnosis was parasitic hepatic abscess based on radiology findings and epidemiological factors. The patient was treated with fluid infusion, anthelmintics (triclabendazole), and antibiotics (cefixime and metronidazole) and discharged in stable condition.

Two weeks later, on follow-up, the patient reported persistent intermittent low-grade fever and mild right hypochondria tenderness. White blood cell count increased to 29.62 G/L with 94.8% neutrophils, procalcitonin elevated to 53.9 ng/mL, hemoglobin decreased to 107 g/L, and gamma-glutamyl transferase elevated to 245 U/L.

Follow-up CT scan identified an abnormal high-attenuation linear structure inside the liver lesion in segment 4B, suspected to be a foreign body. No intra- or extraperitoneal gas or fluid was observed.

Laparoscopic surgery was performed to extract the foreign body and drain the liver abscess. A 3 cm fishbone was removed from the abscess cavity. No evidence of perforation was found in the stomach, duodenum, or bowel.

Blood culture was positive for Streptococcus gordonii, and surgical abscess drainage culture was negative. Postoperatively, the patient had no fever, and inflammatory markers gradually decreased. One week later, the condition was fully resolved.

source_metadata.title: Rare Lymphoma of the Breast: A Case Report

evidence_events.source_span: A 55-year-old Hispanic woman presented with a palpable left breast mass localized to the upper outer quadrant in the axillary tail of Spence. Physical exam was remarkable for a yellow discoloration overlying a mobile, palpable two-centimeter mass with no axillary lymphadenopathy.
Mammography showed an oval mass with indistinct margins at the one o’clock position, located 13 centimeters from the nipple.

The ultrasound demonstrated an oval mass with indistinct margins measuring 16 x 11 x 15 millimeters. No axillary, infraclavicular, supraclavicular, or internal mammary chain lymphadenopathy was noted. The mass was characterized as Breast Imaging Reporting and Data System (BI-RADS) category 4C.
Ultrasound-guided biopsy showed diffuse proliferation of large, atypical cells with clear cytoplasm, irregular nuclei, vesicular chromatin, and prominent nucleoli.

Immunohistochemistry analysis demonstrated positive staining for CD-20, CD-45, BCL-6, and CD-10, negative for Her-2-neu, ER, PR, MUM-1, CD-30, ALK, and C-MYC. Ki-67 staining showed a proliferation index of 60-70%. These findings are consistent with Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma (DLBCL).

A staging 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography combined with computed tomography (FDG-PET/CT) showed diffuse osseous involvement of the appendicular and axial skeleton, a two-centimeter mass of the left breast with ipsilateral axillary lymph node involvement, bilateral pulmonary spiculated nodules with ground-glass opacities, bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, liver involvement, and abdominal lymph node involvement, consistent with diffuse metastatic disease.
The final diagnosis was determined to be stage IV, diffuse large B-cell non-Hodgkin’s lymphoma, and the patient was referred to surgery and oncology.

The patient underwent left heme port placement and completed six cycles of Rituximab, Cyclophosphamide, Hydroxydaunorubicin, Oncovin, and Prednisone (R-CHOP) chemotherapy. Currently, the patient is in remission and continues to have no recurrence, confirmed with a normal mammogram and no suspicious lesions on FDG-PET/CT scan at a two-year follow-up appointment.

source_metadata.title: Sclerosing Angiomatoid Nodular Transformation of the Spleen: A Report of Rare Case and Literature Review

evidence_events.source_span: A middle-aged woman with a medical history of diabetes mellitus underwent an abdominopelvic CT scan for an unrelated condition. The scan incidentally revealed a hypodense mass lesion in her spleen, measuring 1.7 cm in its largest dimension.
Over a span of four years, the mass grew from 1.7 cm to 3.4 cm.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: Over a span of four years

evidence_events.source_span: Her blood work showed no significant abnormalities, except for mild normocytic anemia, with a hemoglobin level of 11.4 g/dL.
The patient underwent a robotic-assisted partial splenectomy to remove the mass.

The gross examination of the specimen indicated the presence of a tan-brown, rubbery portion of the spleen, weighing 8.5 g, and measuring 3.5 cm. The outer surface appeared smooth and shiny, with no identifiable nodules. Upon making cut sections, a white-tan sclerotic mass with focal hemorrhage was observed, measuring 3.4 cm.
Microscopic examination at low power revealed the presence of multiple nodules of different sizes, encompassed by fibrosclerotic stroma.

On closer examination at higher magnification, the nodules displayed round to slit-like vascular spaces containing numerous red blood cells. The internodular stroma consisted of dense fibrous tissue with scattered plump myofibroblasts and lymphoplasmacytic inflammatory cells.
These unique and specific morphological characteristics led to the diagnosis of sclerosing angiomatoid nodular transformation (SANT) of the spleen.
At five months follow-up, there have been no recurrences of the symptoms.

source_metadata.title: Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumor Masquerading As Acute Decompensated Heart Failure: A Challenging Diagnosis

evidence_events.source_span: An 89-year-old female with a medical history of hyperlipidemia and osteopenia presented to the hospital with a five-day history of worsening lower extremity edema along with dyspnea on exertion and orthopnea.
The patient endorsed an unquantified amount of weight loss over several months which she attributed to early satiety and generalized abdominal pain.
On exam, the patient had bilateral 2+ pitting edema extending up to her pretibial region and diffuse abdominal distention with associated tenderness.
Initial laboratory analysis indicated hyponatremia, hypomagnesemia, elevated NT-proBNP of 1,324 PG/mL (reference range <450 pg/mL), and iron deficiency anemia.
The EKG demonstrated normal sinus rhythm with left ventricular hypertrophy (as per Sokolow-Lion criteria) (Figure 1).
The initial chest X-ray was concerned for mild diffuse interstitial lung prominence likely accentuated by low lung inspiration (Figure 2).
A bedside cardiac ultrasound of the cardiac chambers showed a mildly reduced ejection fraction estimated to be 40-45% based on endpoint septal separation.
Evaluation of the patient’s inferior vena cava (IVC) demonstrated a large hypodense lesion neighboring the hepatic parenchyma.

CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast demonstrated a large solid and cystic appearing intraperitoneal supra colic mass measuring 15 cm x 22 cm x 23 cm with cystic necrosis and significant mass effect on the greater curvature of the stomach, porta hepatis, and duodenum (Figures 3-5).
evidence_events.procedural_cue: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast

evidence_events.source_span: Radiology report detailed heterogeneous enhancement of the peripheral solid components of the mass.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast

evidence_events.source_span: Differential diagnoses included colon cancer, retroperitoneal/peritoneal sarcomas, lymphoma, and other malignancies such as GIST.
Interventional radiology performed a biopsy of the abdominal mass.
Tissue samples were characterized as a spindle cell tumor, suggestive of a GIST.
Radiological evidence staged the tumor as III T4N0M0 with next-generation sequencing significant for exon 11 mutation and PDGFRA-mutant negative.

The patient deferred treatment options during her hospital stay and was discharged in stable condition after receiving diuretics with improvement of her lower extremity edema, shortness of breath, and orthopnea.
Upon follow-up, the patient endorsed continued improvement of her functional status while on maintenance diuretics.
The patient decided against bulk resection of her tumor but started targeted molecular therapy with imatinib 100 mg twice daily to reduce tumor size with anticipated resection later.

evidence_events.source_span: MRI showed a predominately cystic slow growing mass centred on the distal spinal canal measuring 12 cm by 9 cm with solid components anteriorly and posteriorly, avid contrast enhancement of solid components and cyst walls, bony remodelling and scalloping of adjacent vertebral bodies, widening of spinal canal, and bilateral extradural extension into piriformis muscles without sciatic nerve involvement.
Positron emission tomography scan showed increased tracer uptake along peripheral aspects of the tumour (SUV max 13.9 g/mL) and central photopenia.
Biopsy histology confirmed a grade 1 myxopapillary ependymoma with glial fibrillar acidic protein and epithelial membrane antigen positivity suggestive of glial origin.

Surgical resection of the sacral ependymoma was ruled out due to the highly destructive nature of the tumour and its location near the cauda equina; the patient received palliative radiotherapy of 50 Gy in 28 fractions.
Postradiotherapy, the patient improved mobility using a tri-wheeler, reduced pain and opiate requirements, and follow-up CT showed reduction in tumour size.

source_metadata.title: Parosteal lipoma of rib causing widening of intercostal space in an adolescent
source_metadata.notes: Case report of adolescent female with parosteal lipoma of rib, rare pediatric presentation.

evidence_events.source_span: A female child in her adolescence presented with swelling on the left upper back over the scapular region for the past 4 years, gradually increasing in size, not associated with pain, no loss of function or neurological deficit.

On clinical examination, a single swelling measuring about 12×11 cm was observed over the left scapular region, firm, non-tender, smooth surface, immobile; distal pulse and neurological exam of left upper extremity were normal.
Plain radiograph of the right chest revealed normal study.

MRI of the left scapula revealed a hyperintense lesion (12×1.7×12 cm) on the left paravertebral region extending from D5 to D12, suppressed on STIR sequence, extending into the fifth intercostal space causing widening due to mass effect; vertebral bodies normal.
Tru-cut biopsy was performed which was suggestive of lipoma.
Based on clinical examination, lipoma, lipoblastoma and liposarcoma were considered; radiology and histopathology confirmed lipoma only.

The patient underwent complete surgical excision; the mass was densely adhered to underlying periosteum; the fifth intercostal space was widened and the mass entered into the intercostal space but pleura was not breached.
Histopathology of the excised specimen was given as lipoma; patient recovered without complication and was asymptomatic at 6 months follow-up.

source_metadata.title: Retroperitoneal Hematoma as an Atypical Presentation of Choriocarcinoma: A Case Report

evidence_events.source_span: A 38-year-old gravida 6, para 2 woman with an etonogestrel implant in place was presented to the emergency center with sudden onset abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding.
She was found to have a beta-hCG of 12,712 mUI/mL with an acute abdomen and vital signs suggestive of hypovolemia.
A focused assessment with sonography in trauma was performed and a large amount of free fluid was seen in the abdominal-pelvic cavity.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: focused assessment with sonography in trauma

evidence_events.source_span: No intrauterine pregnancy was noted on transvaginal ultrasound.
Laboratories revealed a hemoglobin of 10.9 g/dL and creatinine of 0.9 mg/dL.
On laparoscopy, she was found to have 1.5 L of hemoperitoneum along with a normal-appearing uterus and left fallopian tube and a surgically absent right fallopian tube.
A large expanding left retroperitoneal hematoma was visualized and noted to be pushing the sigmoid colon to the right pelvis.
A laparotomy was performed, and the retroperitoneum was opened without a clear source of the bleeding identified.
A computerized tomography (CT) angiogram found active bleeding from a pseudoaneurysm of the left renal artery.
She underwent emergent interventional radiology embolization with good clinical response.
Endometrial biopsy showed fragments of inactive endometrium; CA 125 was slightly elevated (71 U/mL), LDH elevated (560 U/L), CEA and AFP were normal.
CT scan of the chest revealed small non-specific lesions which were biopsied with insufficient cellularity noted.
After several weeks, beta-hCG decreased to 6,230 mUI/mL but patient was readmitted with headache, dizziness, imbalance; imaging showed 6 mm right cerebellar infarct and small left occipital lesions.
Beta-hCG had risen to 100,811 mUI/mL.
Patient developed sudden right flank pain and hemodynamic instability; imaging revealed 16-cm right perinephric hematoma; underwent emergent embolization of right renal artery.
CT chest revealed larger lesions suggestive of metastasis; diagnosed with GTN with WHO score of 14.
Patient received chemotherapy with cisplatin/etoposide induction followed by EMA-CO regimen.
After first EMA-CO cycle, patient developed hemothorax from bleeding pulmonary metastasis; chest tube placed; underwent gamma knife surgery for brain metastases.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: chest tube placement, gamma knife surgery

evidence_events.source_span: Patient received seven cycles of EMA-CO with good response; beta-hCG decreased to <5 mIU/mL; placed on surveillance.

Patient presented with headache, dizziness, blurry vision; imaging revealed acute right occipital hemorrhage concerning for new metastasis; underwent craniotomy with pathology confirming metastatic choriocarcinoma.
Beta-hCG increased to 20,832 after craniotomy; patient continues chemotherapy for brain metastases; most recent beta-hCG is 9 a year after initial presentation.

She had no major medical issues. She was a past smoker, with no occupational risk factors for urothelial malignancy. Urine culture and cytology confirmed no infection or malignant cells. Ultrasound demonstrated a hypoechoic lesion on the right anterior bladder wall, measuring 44 × 42 × 28 mm. CT showed a soft-tissue attenuation mass protruding into the bladder lumen, exhibiting equivocal mild lesional enhancement. MRI demonstrated a heterogeneous bladder tumor appearing intramural, rather than intraluminal. The mass was mobile on bimanual examination and cystoscopic evaluation visualized a large mass indenting the right bladder wall. A transurethral resection biopsy was considered but not performed for the concern of spreading a malignant process.

source_metadata.title: A rare case of parapelvic cyst: A case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 27-year-old male with a 3-year history of partial urinary retention presented with intermittent loin pain. History of fever, stone passage through urine, and hematuria was denied. His vital signs were within normal limits. Physical examinations were within normal limits.
Laboratory examinations including hematology, renal function, and urinalysis found no abnormalities.
Initial ultrasonography was performed and found pelvicalyceal dilatation and the proximal ureter was dilated, indicating pelvico ureteric junction obstruction (PUJO).
Renal ultrasound was unable to identify the source of obstruction, thus further imaging was conducted.

A renal computed tomography (CT) scan was performed and showed the normal size of the right kidney measuring 10.44 × 4.68 cm. The parenchyma structure is homogeneous, pelvocalyceal system is widened. There was a hypodense lesion in the renal pelvis, extending to the proximal ureter that was not filled with contrast measuring 5.03 × 5.36 × 5.98 cm.
The proximal right ureter was dilated. The cyst presses the right renal pelvic system and right proximal ureter causing PUJO, causing hydronephrosis grade III.

He was advised to undergo a nephrostomy for ureteral dilation followed by double J stent placement. A percutaneous approach for cyst removal was deemed very difficult in this patient, thus nephrostomy was conducted using an 8-8.9 Fr nephroscope.

To be able to remove the cyst, the cyst wall had to be very thin and well-visualized to avoid renal parenchyma injury. However, in our case, the cyst wall was too thick and poorly visualized, thus cyst removal was not conducted.

Cyst removal failed, thus we proceeded to perform ureteral dilatation. The double J stent was inserted and bleeding was checked. Four months after surgery, the cyst remained, but the patient was asymptomatic.

source_metadata.title: Pulmonary Barotrauma After Diving Without Breathing Equipment
source_metadata.notes: Case report of a 19-year-old male with pulmonary barotrauma after diving without breathing equipment.

evidence_events.source_span: A 19-year-old previously healthy male, a nonsmoker with no pulmonary history presented with voice change, face and neck swelling, chest pain, and shortness of breath after diving in a river.
The patient reported diving approximately 10 to 12 feet without using a mask or any additional diving gear, including oxygen tanks or breathing apparatuses.
Within the next two hours, he developed facial swelling along with chest pain and shortness of breath.

Emergency medical services gave him 0.3 milligrams of intramuscular epinephrine and 50 milligrams of intravenous diphenhydramine due to fear this could be anaphylaxis; however, there was minimal improvement.
Upon arrival at the emergency department, the patient was hemodynamically stable, with heart rate 66 bpm, respiratory rate 18, blood pressure 115/61, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air.

Physical exam showed swelling over the neck and shoulders with palpable crepitus, clear lungs bilaterally, edematous oropharynx extending to posterior pharynx, lip and tongue swelling, muffled voice, and no rashes or neurologic deficits.
Chest radiograph revealed large volume mediastinal and neck emphysema and concern for possible aspiration in the bilateral lower lobes.
Neck radiograph showed severe subcutaneous emphysema.
The patient was intubated using ketamine, rocuronium, and a 7.5 endotracheal tube and ventilated with lung protective settings.

Chest CT revealed fluid filling of bilateral lower lobe bronchi and diffuse interstitial emphysema throughout both lungs suggesting mediastinal and subcutaneous emphysema secondary to diffusely increased alveolar pressures.
CT of the neck showed extensive emphysema of the neck with intact esophagus, pharynx, larynx, and trachea without obvious injury or defect.
The patient was admitted to the intensive care unit for further evaluation and management for likely pulmonary barotrauma secondary to repetitive dives.
The patient was successfully extubated the following day; subcutaneous emphysema continued but was improving.
Pulmonology recommended outpatient evaluation including pulmonary function tests and instruction to avoid diving.

Within the next two hours, he developed facial swelling along with chest pain and shortness of breath.

evidence_milestones.grouping_reason: Initial emergency treatment and physical examination findings.
evidence_milestones.visible_evidence: EMS administered epinephrine and diphenhydramine for suspected anaphylaxis with minimal improvement. On arrival, patient was hemodynamically stable. Physical exam showed neck and shoulder swelling with palpable crepitus, edematous oropharynx, lip and tongue swelling, muffled voice, and clear lungs.
evidence_milestones.dialogue_visible_evidence: Patient received epinephrine and diphenhydramine with minimal effect. Exam revealed swelling with crepitus in neck and shoulders, airway edema, muffled voice, and clear lungs.
evidence_milestones.test_visible_evidence: EMS treatment and detailed physical exam findings.
evidence_milestones.source_span: Emergency medical services gave him 0.3 milligrams of intramuscular epinephrine and 50 milligrams of intravenous diphenhydramine due to fear this could be anaphylaxis; however, there was minimal improvement. Upon arrival at the emergency department, the patient was hemodynamically stable, with heart rate 66 bpm, respiratory rate 18, blood pressure 115/61, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Physical exam showed swelling over the neck and shoulders with palpable crepitus, clear lungs bilaterally, edematous oropharynx extending to posterior pharynx, lip and tongue swelling, muffled voice, and no rashes or neurologic deficits.
evidence_milestones.question: How do the physical exam findings and minimal response to anaphylaxis treatment influence the differential diagnosis, and what imaging studies would be most informative next?
