source_metadata.title: A rare and challenging case of intrapericardial hydatidosis

evidence_events.source_span: A 22-year-old man presented to our hospital with ongoing dry cough for more than 1 month prior to admission. Other symptoms included chest pain, fatigue, low grade fever, and night sweats, which have worsened in the past 2 weeks.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: more than 1 month prior to admission; worsened in past 2 weeks

evidence_events.source_span: Physical examination revealed normal respiratory and heart function.
Chest X-ray demonstrated mediastinal enlargement and left pleural effusion.

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography images showed a walled cystic mass lesion measuring up to 56 × 50 mm in close proximity to the upper left atrium, ascending aorta and pulmonary artery, potentially localized in the pericardium, with a 10 mm endoatrial filling defect, findings were compatible with hydatid cyst, left pleural effusion and peripheral pulmonary upper left lobe consolidation.

Magnetic resonance imaging and transesophageal ultrasound showed an extracardiac multicameral cystic mass adjacent to the left atrium with a mass effect in the left upper pulmonary vein and no cardiac infiltration after contrast medium.
Fine needle aspiration of the upper left lobe consolidation and thoracocentesis were performed; no malignancy was found, and biopsy confirmed pulmonary infarction.
Test of antibody titers for hydatid disease was performed and was negative.

After 7 days of premedication with albendazole, the patient underwent left anterolateral thoracotomy; a 5 cm cystic mass was found next to the left atrium and left pulmonary veins compressing them. The cyst content was completely removed after isolating the surgical area with gauze impregnated with hypertonic solution (NaCl 10%).
evidence_events.procedural_cue: left anterolateral thoracotomy and cyst removal

evidence_events.source_span: The cystic mass was an echinococcal cyst with multiple daughter cysts within it, measuring up to 10 mm, without penetration or involvement of the cardiac wall.
Wedge resection of the left upper lobe consolidation was performed; biopsy confirmed lung infarction.
Postoperatively, the patient had a good recovery and was treated with three courses of albendazole 400 mg twice daily for 28 days each.

source_metadata.title: Bronchogenic cyst at unusual location

evidence_events.source_span: A 12 years old, apparently healthy boy referred to us with the complaints of occasional mild, diffuse, dull aching, non-radiating, right-sided chest pain for a few months having a non-resolving shadow in the chest x-ray without any other associated factors.
General physical and systemic examination revealed no abnormality.
New chest x-ray showed a tubular inhomogeneous opacity in the medial part of the right lower lung field.
CECT chest revealed a well-defined, thin-walled cystic lesion about 8.5 × 3.6 × 4.5 cm within the right lower lobe with mild marginal enhancement of the lesion.
Routine blood workup was within normal limits.

Right mini-thoracotomy revealed a tubular, narrow-based pedunculated, mobile, pinkish, cystic smooth lesion arising from the mediastinum around the area of the inferior pulmonary ligament; the lesion was completely mobile and contained thick mucus.
Histopathological examination confirmed that the lesion was a bronchogenic cyst, which was lined by respiratory epithelium with a variable amount of seromucinous gland, cartilage and smooth muscle.
The post-operative event was uneventful. The patient was discharged without any complication on the 5th Post-operative day and has no recurrence after 6 month follow up.

source_metadata.notes: Extraction based on case narrative sections Patient Story and Molecular Tumor Board.

evidence_events.source_span: A 43-year-old man with no relevant medical history, who did not smoke and worked in insurance, presented to his local emergency department with cough and shortness of breath.
He had been diagnosed with a diffuse bilateral pneumonia 1 week prior and was symptomatically worsening despite cefpodoxime, azithromycin, and prednisone.
In the preceding weeks, he reported decreased appetite and oral intake, mild sinusitis, left lower extremity swelling, and purple discoloration of 2 toes.

Upon presentation to the emergency department, he was hypertensive (145/94), tachycardic (118 bpm), tachypneic (est. 20-25 breaths per minute), and hypoxic requiring supplemental oxygen (91% on 2 L, improved on 4 L).

Laboratory testing was notable for hyponatremia (125 mmol/L), hypoalbuminemia (2.9 g/L), thrombocytopenia (121 × 10⁹/L), mild leukocytosis (11.3 K/μL), and hyperglycemia (314 mg/dL). His liver function tests and creatinine were within normal limits, and viral testing, including influenza and SARS-CoV-2, was negative.
An initial chest x-ray showed worsening bilateral pneumonia and pleural effusion but could not rule out an underlying mass.

Radiologic workup (CT) revealed a 4.7 × 4.7 cm mass in the lower pole of the right kidney, along with enlarged retroperitoneal and mesenteric lymph nodes and masses in infracarinal and hilar lymph nodes, suspicious for metastases.

A biopsy of a left retroperitoneal lymph node stained with synaptophysin (weakly), CD56, CAM 5.2, MNF 116, and MITF, and no significant staining was appreciated with chromogranin, HMB-45, S-100, Sox 10, cytokeratin AE1/AE3, CD3, CD20, PAX5, CD30, neurofilament, and CD15. The staining pattern seemed most consistent with epithelioid angiomyolipoma (eAML).
Thoracentesis fluid demonstrated atypical epithelioid cells, but cytology was inconclusive.
In approximately 3 weeks, imaging demonstrated that the renal mass had grown to 6 cm, and several lymphatic metastases had enlarged.
He was admitted with worsening thrombocytopenia (85 × 10⁹/L) and hypoxia requiring high flow oxygen up to 10 L, and treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics for pulmonary infection.
On day 3 post-transfer, he suffered cardiac arrest attributed to respiratory causes, was resuscitated and intubated.
Urgent systemic anticancer therapy was started with temsirolimus, an mTOR inhibitor, as first-line therapy for presumed metastatic eAML.
On day 5 post-transfer, a 4R lymph node biopsy was performed to confirm the diagnosis and identify genomic targets via IHC and whole exome and transcriptome sequencing (WES/WTS).
evidence_events.procedural_cue: 4R lymph node biopsy and molecular testing

evidence_events.source_span: The 4R lymph node pathology report demonstrated a metastatic malignant epithelioid neoplasm with rhabdoid morphology; definitive classification was deferred to autopsy.
Molecular testing revealed pathogenic variants in BAP1 and VHL, resulting in a post-mortem diagnosis of metastatic clear cell renal cell carcinoma (mccRCC).
Post-mortem analysis confirmed renal mass and metastases with tumor cells showing clear cytoplasm, positive for EMA and CA-IX, consistent with mccRCC with rhabdoid differentiation.

evidence_events.source_span: 63-year-old Hispanic gentleman with no significant past medical history presented with left lower extremity swelling and pain ongoing for one week
Physical examination revealed erythematous left lower extremity with tenderness and edema

Lower extremity Doppler ultrasonography showed occlusive DVT in left calf extending to left femoral vein, involving superficial small saphenous and great saphenous veins; chronic occlusive DVT in right popliteal veins
Venogram confirmed popliteal vein thrombosis and need for intervention
evidence_events.temporal_cue: after initial Doppler and clinical evaluation

evidence_events.source_span: Venogram demonstrated complete thrombosis from popliteal vein to common femoral vein; diagnosis of May-Thurner syndrome confirmed by venogram
evidence_events.procedural_cue: venogram with contrast and catheter placement

evidence_events.source_span: Overnight infusion of tissue plasminogen activator (tPA) at 1 mg per hour via infusion catheter
Second venogram on hospital day one showed persistent thrombus in left superficial, common femoral, external iliac, and common iliac veins; severe 75% stenosis at left common femoral and iliac veins
Mechanical thrombectomy and balloon dilation performed at left superficial femoral, common femoral, and iliac veins; refractory stenosis persisted with >50% residual stenosis after balloon dilation
evidence_events.temporal_cue: hospital day one after second venogram

evidence_events.source_span: Deployment of 12 x 60 mm Life Star self-expanding stent within left iliac vein centered on critical stenosis
evidence_events.temporal_cue: after refractory stenosis persisted post balloon dilation

evidence_events.source_span: Subsequent balloon dilation post stent deployment showed improved flow and caliber with no significant residual thrombus
Patient reported symptomatic improvement on hospital day three and was discharged on chronic anticoagulation with rivaroxaban

source_metadata.notes: Extraction based on case presentation and discussion sections; images assigned to milestones per diagnostic role.

evidence_events.source_span: A 65-year-old Han Chinese woman who worked as a crop farmer presented to Taihe Hospital for a routine physical examination in August 2018. The patient had no respiratory symptoms and denied any other discomfort.

Chest CT showed a 2.4×2.0-cm nodule in the anterior segment of the left superior lobe, which was highly suspected to be peripheral lung cancer. A 1.3×0.9-cm nodule was detected in the posterior basal segment of the left lower lobe, which was suspected to be intrapulmonary metastasis.

The patient denied any respiratory symptoms, such as cough, sputum, fever, chest pain, wheezing or weight loss. Immune function was normal, no history of travel or exposure to pigeon feces or soil, no history of smoking or alcohol consumption within the last month, and had not been extensively treated with hormones and/or antibiotics before coming to the hospital.

Laboratory examination indicated normal leukocytes, red blood cells, hemoglobin slightly low, platelets normal, blood glucose normal, liver enzymes normal, lactate dehydrogenase slightly low, highly sensitive C-reactive protein normal. Tumor markers were normal except Cyfra21-1 was elevated at 3.75 μg/l (normal range 0-3.3 μg/l). Sputum Gram staining and bacterial culture showed no microorganisms. Acid-fast staining and sputum culture showed no acid-fast bacteria. Bronchofiberscopy showed no lesions and bacterial, cytological and pathological examinations from bronchoscope were negative.
A CT-guided percutaneous lung biopsy was performed on the nodule in the anterior segment of the left upper lobe, which was pathologically confirmed to be adenocarcinoma.

A CT-guided percutaneous lung biopsy was performed on the nodule in the posterior basal segment of the left inferior lobe 1 week later, which was confirmed by histopathology as pulmonary cryptococcosis infection. Histologically, hematoxylin & eosin staining revealed granulomatous inflammation and yeast-form fungi in multinucleated cells, and cryptococcus was identified by periodic acid Schiff (PAS), Gomori methenamine silver (GMS) and mucicarmine (MC) staining.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: CT-guided percutaneous lung biopsy; special stains PAS, GMS, MC

evidence_events.source_span: Two weeks later, the patient underwent thoracoscopic resection of the left lung cancer. Macroscopic examination revealed a 3.1×2.5×2-cm mass with gray and grayish black sections, solid, medium in texture, indistinct from surrounding boundary. Histologically, the tumor cells were moderately to poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma of the acinar and micropapillary type. No cryptococcal infection was observed in the tumor. No metastatic cancer was found in lymph nodes (0/11), bronchial margin was negative, pathological TNM stage was T2aN0Mx.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: thoracoscopic resection; macroscopic and histologic examination

evidence_events.source_span: The patient received fluconazole 200 mg/day antifungal therapy for 6 months. During 5-year follow-up, contrast-enhanced CT showed no recurrence of either lung cancer or pulmonary cryptococcosis.

evidence_events.source_span: A 42-year-old Saudi male patient presented with a two-month history of diffuse ulceration on the oral cavity involving the tongue, floor of the mouth, buccal mucosa, lips, and palate in addition to skin lesions on the dorsal surface of the hand and nasal sill
The patient was a nonsmoker with no relevant family history or known allergy; associated dysphagia, dehydration, and severe weight loss were reported

Medical history revealed lesions for approximately four months; patient was on topical corticosteroids for skin lesions and 25 mg systemic prednisolone for oral ulcers but had relapse and recurrence after two months of treatment
evidence_events.temporal_cue: four months, after two months of treatment

evidence_events.source_span: Extraoral examination showed erythema multiforme (EM)-like symptoms including crusting ulceration on the lips and nasal sill
Intraoral examination revealed desquamative gingivitis and diffuse ragged erosions on buccal mucosa, tongue, palate, and floor of the mouth
Two perilesional biopsies were taken from the buccal mucosa and sent for histopathological and direct immunofluorescence (DIF) examinations

Hematoxylin and eosin-stained sections showed nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium with acantholysis and suprabasal clefting, leaving one to two layers of basal and parabasal keratinocytes, 'row of tombstones'; superficial lamina propria infiltrated by mixed inflammatory cells
Direct immunofluorescence (DIF) showed intercellular immunoglobulin (Ig) G and C3 in a mesh-like pattern, with C3 restricted to basal and suprabasal cell layers
Initial treatment with 5 mg prednisone twice daily was started; after DIF results, systemic prednisone increased to 40 mg daily plus nystatin mouthwash, then increased to 60 mg daily
After two weeks of systemic prednisone, significant improvement was seen, followed by gradual dose reduction to 5 mg daily with healed ulcers without scarring

source_metadata.title: Glass shards masquerading as calcifications in the breast: A case report

evidence_events.source_span: Screening mammogram of a generally healthy 41-year-old female revealed calcifications in the periareolar region of the right breast
These calcifications were present on her prior baseline screening mammogram but were less conspicuous on the prior study due to mild motion artifact
Magnification views of the right anterior breast demonstrated numerous apparent round and punctate calcifications in a regional distribution in the right subareolar breast
Correlation with full field CC and ML tomosynthesis images indicated that these apparent periareolar calcifications were predominantly in the skin, with extension into the nipple
evidence_events.procedural_cue: full field CC and ML tomosynthesis images

evidence_events.source_span: Diagnostic ultrasound was not performed as there was no concern for mass or asymmetry
The patient was referred to Dermatology for a skin biopsy
A breast radiologist utilized the screening and diagnostic mammograms to localize the skin microcalcifications, thus playing a crucial role in identifying and marking the optimal site for skin biopsy
Radiograph of the biopsy specimen demonstrated numerous apparent punctate and pleomorphic calcifications

Histopathological evaluation of the biopsy specimen showed multiple small but variably-sized fragments of foreign material, some with an angulated and refractile appearance consistent with glass shards on a background of scar
Follow up discussion with the patient revealed that she sustained a motor vehicle accident several years earlier, with trauma to the chest

source_metadata.title: Hyperintense Perilesional Edema on T1-Weighted Imaging in Cavernoma: A Case Report

evidence_events.source_span: A 35-year-old female patient without a significant medical history presented to the emergency department complaining of a seven-day history of left-side weakness that began gradually from an upper limp and then involved a lower limp, with gait changes and falling suddenly due to weakness. The weakness was accompanied by nausea.

During the physical examination, the patient was aware and oriented to time, place, and person. Language and attention exams were both intact. Limbs power was 4/5 on the left side and 5/5 on the right. The patient's tone was normal, and she exhibited bilateral Hoffman's sign.

Imaging studies were crucially important for further assessment. A CT and MRI of the brain were obtained, which showed a gradient of hyperintense content of the lesion with surrounding relatively hyperintense perilesional edema.

The unenhanced CT scan of the brain showed a well-defined iso- to hyper-dense lesion with surrounding vasogenic edema within the right parietal lobe, causing mild mass effect upon the adjacent sulci and posterior horn of the right lateral ventricle. However, there was no midline shift, hydrocephalus, or brain herniation.

On the T2-weighted MRI images, the lesion exhibited a fluid-fluid level with predominantly hypointense content. On the other hand, the non-contrast T1-weighted images displayed a gradient of hyperintense content of the lesion with surrounding relatively hyperintense perilesional edema. The most inferior aspect of the lesion exhibited hyperintense content with a rim of hypointensity, featuring a popcorn appearance.
Similarly, the susceptibility-weighted images demonstrated a susceptibility effect. The post-contrast images showed a margin of thin enhancement, best seen in subtraction images.
Coronal and sagittal images of T2 and T1 weighted sequences displayed the extent of the lesion and the fluid-fluid level. The constellation of the findings were most consistent with a cavernoma.
The patient had an uneventful right parietal craniotomy to evacuate the hematoma and excise the lesion. A right parietal subacute hematoma with a mulberry-looking lesion was found intraoperatively.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: right parietal craniotomy and lesion excision

evidence_events.source_span: Post-operative CT scan showed the expected immediate post-operative changes without complications or residual lesion. Post-operative CNS findings were significant for midline shift interval change, measuring now 0.5 cm compared to 0.7 cm previously. There was no evidence of uncal or tonsillar herniation. There was no acute intra/extra-axial bleeding.
MRI was done after two months, which showed complete resection of the right parietal cavernoma with no signs of residual.

source_metadata.title: Case report - Embolic shotgun pellet to the right internal carotid artery causing hemiplegia

evidence_events.source_span: A 13-year-old boy who presented at accident and emergency service after an accidental chest injury from an air rifle. The entry wound, measuring 5 mm, was located on the lower sternum, with no exit wound.

Upon admission, the patient displayed stable vital signs, with normal breathing rates, equal air entry on both sides, and maintained oxygen saturation on air. The abdomen was soft, and the patient had a Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score of 15/15, indicating no focal neurological deficits.

Four hours after admission, the child suffered two episodes of generalized tonic-clonic convulsions, each lasting less than two minutes, accompanied by a reduction in consciousness level. Subsequent neurological examination revealed weakness in the left upper and lower limbs, along with contralateral facial weakness.

Initial evaluations, including plain chest X-ray and extended FAST scan, did not reveal the presence of a lodged pellet in the chest or any signs of pneumo- or hemothorax. However, a minimal pericardial effusion was observed in the extended FAST scan.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: plain chest X-ray and extended FAST scan

evidence_events.source_span: 2D Echocardiography showed a thin layer of pericardial effusion.

Non-contrast CT scan of the brain (NCCT brain) revealed a hyperdense pellet near the right base of the skull, adjacent to the carotid canal. Additionally, hyperdensity observed in the middle cerebral artery indicated a thrombus in the right middle cerebral artery.

Contrast-enhanced CT scan (CECT) of the head, neck, and thorax confirmed the presence of the pellet embolism in the right internal carotid artery, located within the carotid foramen at the inferior opening of the carotid canal. This imaging also indicated non-opacification of the right internal carotid artery and proximal carotid artery, suggesting a thrombus causing an acute cerebral infarction in the right cerebral territory. The CECT scan further showed minimal pericardial and pleural effusion.
Carotid duplex study revealed turbid flow within the right internal carotid artery, linked to distal obstruction by the pellet. No dissection flaps were noted.
Decompressive craniotomy was performed to alleviate the mass effect from acute cerebral edema resulting from the cerebral infarction.

Four-vessel cerebral Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA) was conducted to assess cerebral vasculature and attempt retrieval of foreign bodies. Attempts to aspirate thrombus in the proximal internal carotid artery using the penumbral clot retrieval system were unsuccessful due to the pellet being tightly lodged.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: DSA and penumbral clot retrieval system

evidence_events.source_span: No cross-circulation was observed from the left internal carotid artery during DSA, limiting alternative approaches.
Multidisciplinary team decided against open surgery due to massive cerebral infarction and risk of worsening prognosis.
After two weeks of inpatient care, the patient sustained permanent hemiplegia and was transferred to a rehabilitation center for occupational therapy.

source_metadata.title: Gastric Artery Injury Due to Blunt Abdominal Trauma

evidence_events.source_span: The patient, a 66-year-old woman with no remarkable medical history, was operating a lightweight vehicle at a speed of 50 km/h when she accidentally broadsided an oncoming vehicle. Emergency medical personnel noted she was in a state of shock, and she also complained of upper abdominal pain.

Upon arrival, her upper abdominal pain persisted, but she maintained clarity of consciousness. Vital signs revealed respiratory rate 28 breaths/min, SpO2 97% ambient air, systolic blood pressure oscillating in the 70 mmHg range, heart rate 79 beats per minute, and peripheral cold sensations. After extracellular fluid and four units of irradiated red blood cells, systolic blood pressure stabilized to approximately 100 mmHg. FAST was negative, and chest and pelvis radiographs showed no abnormalities. She complained of spontaneous pain and tenderness in the upper abdomen.

Simple and contrast-enhanced CT from head to pelvis showed left fourth to eighth rib fractures, liver injury (grade IIIa Japanese Association of Traumatology/grade II AAST), splenic injury (grade IIIa Japanese Association of Traumatology/grade II AAST), intra-abdominal hemorrhage, and extravascular leakage of contrast medium suggesting right gastric artery involvement.

Upon admission to our hospital, systolic blood pressure increased to 110 mmHg range, indicating amelioration of shock. Review of prior contrast-enhanced CT confirmed right gastric artery injury, prompting decision for arterial embolization.
Angiography of the celiac artery revealed irregularities in the diameter of the right gastric artery without signs of aneurysm or active hemorrhage.
Coil embolization of the right gastric artery was performed due to vessel irregularities and suspected structural damage despite absence of active bleeding on angiography.
No additional arterial injury was suspected due to absence of active bleeding, pseudoaneurysm, or irregular diameter in hepatic, splenic, or left gastric arteries. Conservative treatment was adopted.

Post-embolization, patient remained cardiopulmonary stable; fibrinogen decreased to 157 mg/dL requiring eight units fresh frozen plasma transfusion. Contrast-enhanced CT on day 2 showed resolution of extravascular contrast leakage, no pseudoaneurysms, and reduced hematoma volume.
On day 6, contrast-enhanced CT showed no rebleeding, pseudoaneurysm, or abscess formation. On day 7, patient was discharged without sequelae and resumed daily activities.

source_metadata.title: When Two Worlds Collide: A Rare Case of Multiple Myeloma With Extramedullary Plasmacytoma

evidence_events.source_span: A 67-year-old gentleman presented to the emergency department with a 1½-month history of bilateral lower extremity weakness, numbness, and mid-lower back pain. His symptoms had progressed to the point of impaired ambulation, and he experienced a fall due to leg weakness.

On physical examination, the patient displayed alertness, intact cranial nerve function, and symmetric motor strength (5/5) in the upper extremities but significant weakness (1/5) in the lower extremities. Sensation remained intact, with noted paraspinal tenderness upon palpation throughout the spine.

Laboratory studies revealed leukopenia, normocytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, hypercalcemia, elevated total protein, and hypoalbuminemia. Of note, an elevated protein gap was noted, along with evidence of monoclonal gammopathy.

The CT scan of the chest with IV contrast revealed widespread bony metastatic disease with numerous small lytic lesions throughout the spine and pelvis. There was a 1 cm lytic lesion with a pathologic fracture on the posterior right seventh rib, along with a sternomanubrial lesion. source_metadata.title: Unusual case of bullous emphysema with superimposed pneumonia

evidence_events.source_span: A 42-year-old woman presented to the ED with progressively worsening productive cough, fatigue, shortness of breath, and palpitations for 1 week duration.

The patient noticed initial dyspnea and fatigue while walking more than 1 block duration which is new from her baseline as she was able to carry out regular activity with no limitations prior to presentation.
She denied any chest pain, fever, nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and abdominal pain.
She reports no past medical history or smoking/tobacco use or illicit drugs use.
She has received 2 doses of the Pfizer vaccination.
Upon the physical exam, the patient was fatigued and in mild respiratory distress with increased work of breathing and had diffuse rales and rhonchi bilaterally on auscultation.
Oxygen saturation (SPO2) was 98% on room air at rest and decreased to 69% on room air after ambulation.
Chest computed tomography showed emphysematous changes bilaterally with multiple prominent pulmonary bullae bilaterally, the largest in the anterior left upper lobe and posterior right lower lobes.
There were multiple associated regions of bronchiectasis and bronchial wall thickening.
There was also dilatation of the pulmonary vasculature, which should measure <3 cm just proximal to the bifurcation of the left and right pulmonary arteries.
Alpha-1 Antitrypsin levels were within normal limits.
The patient tested negative for COVID-19 and reported no previous history of COVID-19.

Empirical treatment with ceftriaxone and azithromycin was started initially and later switched to broad-spectrum antibiotics with vancomycin, cefepime, and doxycycline as the respiratory culture was positive for gram-negative bacillus Pseudomonas aeruginosa and moderate yeast growth of Candida albicans.
Alongside antibiotics, treatment regimen included supplemental O2, methylprednisolone, and albuterol/ipratropium bronchodilators.
Spirometry results reported FEV1 of 23% and FEV1/FVC ratio of 65%.

source_metadata.title: Adamantinoma: An Uncommon Cause of Bone Pain in a Young Adolescent Male
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case presentation and imaging/pathology narrative.

evidence_events.source_span: A 17-year-old boy presented with a four-year history of pain and swelling in the right leg. The pain was insidious in onset, non-progressive, and dull aching.

There was a history of trauma to the same side of the leg two years back while playing kabaddi, following which he had a fracture of the tibia. He was managed with cast application for the same for three months and became fine after cast removal.

On physical examination of the right leg, the anterior aspect of the tibial contour was mildly deformed with mild tenderness; however, there was no obvious redness, warmth, discharge, or other inflammatory signs over the site. The range of motion of the right knee was within normal limits, distal circulation was intact, and no distal neurovascular deficit was observed. There were no signs of any systemic involvement.
His laboratory findings were unremarkable.

Anteroposterior and lateral plain radiographs of the right lower limb showed a well-defined, expansile lytic-sclerotic lesion with a partially sclerotic border and multiple septa within the lesion in the proximal tibia.
On the computed tomography (CT) scan, there was an expansile lytic lesion noted along the anterior aspect of the tibia involving the cortex and medulla.

An MRI scan showed a defined cortical-based diaphyseal lesion in the anterior aspect of the proximal tibial shaft with a narrow zone of transition, hyperintense on PD-SPAIR, isointense on T1WI, mildly hyperintense on T2WI, and vivid post-contrast enhancement. There was no evidence of periosteal reaction or soft tissue involvement. A provisional diagnosis of adamantinoma was kept.

A biopsy of the lesion was performed, and histopathological examination showed a combination of epithelial and fibrous mesenchymal cells; the nest of epithelial cells was arranged in a palisading pattern; the histopathological features confirmed the diagnosis of adamantinoma.

The patient underwent excision and curettage of the lesion, followed by filling the cavity with hydroxyapatite bone blocks and sealing with bone wax. Postoperative X-rays confirmed adequate filling with no evidence of bone breakage.
Postoperative physiotherapy was started, the patient had no postoperative complications, suture removal was done on post-op day 12, and the patient was discharged with advice for regular follow-up.

Medications included amlodipine, aspirin, atorvastatin, lisinopril, and prednisone; prior echocardiogram showed normal LV size and function with mild to moderate LVH and minimal valvular abnormalities; 24-hour Holter monitor showed sinus rhythm with no arrhythmias.

evidence_events.source_span: A 29-year-old female presented with intermittent respiratory symptoms, including a mild cough and sputum, that she has been complaining of since 2020.
During the COVID-19 outbreak, the patient developed a fever and body pains for about ten days and was diagnosed with a COVID-19 infection.
She received Panadol Extra (1 mg/day) for 5 days, and her condition recovered after 10 days of isolation, but she later developed intermittent respiratory symptoms like a mild cough and sputum.
She was treated by an internist with periodic antibiotics (amoxiclav tab, 1 gm, 1×2) and steroids for 7 days which resulted in symptomatic improvement.
On the physical examination, she had only mild respiratory symptoms as mentioned, and no other significant findings were noticed.
A blood investigation revealed elevated inflammatory markers like erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR) (25 mm/h), C-reactive protein (CRP) (>5 mg/dl), and white blood cells (WBC) (>11×10⁹/l).
A high-resolution computed tomography (HR-CT) scan of the chest was performed and revealed an irregular pulmonary opacity in the right lower lobe with central fluid attenuation.

evidence_events.source_span: It was suspected to be an abscess or, less likely, a pulmonary neoplasm.
The patient underwent an FNAC on the right hemithorax in a prone position, which suggested the presence of a hydatid cyst.
A thoracotomy was performed, and the abscess was removed.
Histopathological results confirmed the previous diagnosis.
The postoperative period was uneventful, and the patient’s symptoms improved.

source_metadata.title: A Case Report of Ibandronic Acid Induced Non-Exposed BRONJ Involving the Maxillary Sinus
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case description and results section with supporting intro and discussion.

evidence_events.source_span: A female patient, 62 years old, was referred ... complaining about pain in the first quadrant.
Her medical history revealed osteoporosis and BP administration for the past four years, ibandronate 150 mg once per month.
The clinical examination demonstrated an oral fistula with exudate upon pressure at the area of the first upper molar which could not be explained by an odontogenic cause.
The dental history revealed that the patient had an extraction of the specific tooth four months ago.
A periapical radiograph was performed showing non healed alveolar bone, and radiolucent process extending to the floor of right sinus.
The CBCT revealed a round bony sequestrum at the area of the right upper first molar and almost complete radiopacification of the maxillary sinus.
The portrayed borders of the sinus floor were discontinuous, revealing a communication between the necrotic bone and the sinus cavity.
The osteolysis extending beyond the alveolar crest of the maxilla was considered to be associated with the observed chronic sinusitis (almost complete opacification of sinus).

The clinical and radiological examination combined with patient’s medical history of oral bisphosphonate administration for the past 4 years led to stage 0 medication related osteonecrosis of jaw diagnosis affecting the sinus (classification by AAOMS).

A surgical approach was implemented to remove the bony sequestrum. After raising a full-thickness mucoperiosteal flap a piece of devitalized bone, well-separated from the surrounding vital bone, was revealed.
Following diligent curettage of the lesion, the bony defect and the sinus was irrigated with saline, and finally primary closure was achieved.
Postoperatively, the patient received amoxicillin/clavulanic acid for 7 days.

After 5 months, the patient remained free of symptoms and a second CBCT showed regeneration of new bone at the site of the defect, restoration of the sinus floor and remission of mucosal inflammation.

source_metadata.title: An Atypical Presentation of Emphysematous Pyelonephritis Complicated by Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus Bacteremia

evidence_events.source_span: A 60-year-old non-diabetic woman presented with acute-on-chronic right knee, left hip, and paraspinal lumbar back pain with increased frequency of falling for approximately one week; physical exam showed pursed-lip breathing and tenderness to right knee and left hip without dyspnea
Initial vital signs were stable with blood pressure 131/75, heart rate 96, respiratory rate 20, oxygen saturation 95% on room air, and temperature 98.2°F

Laboratory results showed leukocytosis with white blood cell count 35.1 x 10^9/L, hemoglobin 8.75 mmol/L, hematocrit 0.434, platelets 137 x 10^9/L, potassium 3.2 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 17.1 mmol/L, creatinine 123.76 umol/L, blood glucose 5.16 mmol/L
Chest X-ray was obtained; urinalysis was unsuccessful due to urinary retention

Elevated d-dimer at 4,036 ug/L DDU and mildly elevated troponin with pursed-lip breathing prompted CT chest with contrast to rule out pulmonary embolus; CT chest was negative for PE but showed extensive air in the left renal collecting system and bilateral staghorn calculi
CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast showed prominent left renal staghorn calculus with suspicious intraparenchymal gas locules, consistent with emphysematous pyelonephritis
evidence_events.procedural_cue: CT abdomen and pelvis with contrast

evidence_events.source_span: Broad-spectrum antibiotics vancomycin and Zosyn were initiated; patient became tachycardic and febrile with early signs of shock; emergent percutaneous nephrostomy tube placement was performed
Post-operatively, urinalysis and urine culture revealed large blood, positive leukocyte esterase, and Escherichia coli urinary tract infection
Patient developed acute respiratory distress syndrome requiring prolonged intubation in ICU

Blood cultures revealed methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) bacteremia, presumed secondary to staghorn calculi; antibiotic regimen escalated to ertapenem; echocardiogram negative for valvular vegetations
Patient was extubated and discharged after extended ICU course with outpatient monitoring and plans for surgical stone removal

source_metadata.title: A Rare Case of Page Kidney With Superimposed Infection

evidence_events.source_span: A 67-year-old female presented to the emergency department with lethargy, vomiting, lower back pain, flank pain, dysuria, urinary frequency, malodorous urine, and hyperglycemia.

Vital signs were notable for temporal temperature of 39.3 °C, blood pressure of 194/82 mmHg, pulse of 112 beats per minute, respiratory rate of 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation of 93% while breathing ambient air.
On examination, there was tenderness in the left lower quadrant of the abdomen on palpation without any guarding or rigidity and positive left-sided costovertebral angle tenderness.

Laboratory test results showed leukocytosis (12.07 x 10³/µL), neutrophilia (8.90 x 10³/µL), monocytosis (1.26 x 10³/µL), anemia (hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL), elevated blood urea nitrogen (25 mg/dL), elevated creatinine (1.40 mg/dL), hypoalbuminemia (2.8 g/dL), and elevated alkaline phosphatase (152 U/L).
Urinalysis revealed a small leukocyte esterase, with 21-50 white blood cells per high-power field.
Initial chest X-ray indicated a left lower lobe consolidation with pleural effusion.
EKG demonstrated sinus tachycardia.
Renal ultrasonography showed no abnormalities.
A urine culture grew Candida glabrata, and the patient’s symptoms of dysuria subsided during the hospital course.
During hospitalization, a CT of the abdomen and pelvis without contrast showed a subcapsular hematoma of the left kidney, measuring 3.8 cm x 5.4 cm x 8.3 cm.

At initial outpatient follow-up after hospitalization, the patient remained hypertensive despite a multimodal antihypertensive regimen including amlodipine and valsartan and continued to complain of left flank pain.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: at initial outpatient follow-up after hospitalization

evidence_events.source_span: An outpatient CT abdomen and pelvis without contrast revealed interval growth of the subcapsular fluid in the posterior aspect of the left kidney, now measuring approximately 13.3 cm x 10.9 cm x 8.5 cm, with the presence of gas foci.
The patient had associated fever, chills, and diaphoresis and was advised to go to the hospital for further assessment and treatment.

On hospital presentation, repeat CT abdomen and pelvis without contrast showed an increased interval size of left renal subcapsular fluid collection measuring 11.2 cm x 9.2 cm, with unchanged loculations and scattered peripheral gas foci.
Empiric intravenous piperacillin/tazobactam was started for broad-spectrum coverage.
Interventional radiology performed an ultrasound-guided aspiration of the left subcapsular fluid collection.
There was no clinical improvement after aspiration and a subsequent CT scan revealed that the size of the left subcapsular renal abscess remained unchanged.
A percutaneous drain was placed in the left renal abscess, and approximately 500 mL of pus was drained.
A post-procedure CT abdomen and pelvis without contrast, taken two days later, demonstrated near-complete resolution of the abscess.
Cultures grew Klebsiella pneumonia, and antibiotics were narrowed to ceftriaxone based on susceptibility testing.
After completing the treatment, a three-month follow-up renal ultrasound revealed the resolution of perinephric and subcapsular fluid collections.

source_metadata.title: A Case Report of a Giant Basilar Artery Aneurysm
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case presentation and clinical course narrative; imaging figure assigned to major_visual_evidence milestone.

evidence_events.source_span: A 54-year-old female, with a history of well-controlled hypertension, presented to the neurology clinic with a three-month history of persistent, severe headaches, occasionally accompanied by nausea and photophobia.

Initial vital signs were within normal limits, and a thorough neurological examination revealed no focal deficits, cognitive impairment, or signs of meningeal irritation. Fundoscopic evaluation showed no papilledema.
Laboratory investigations, including a complete blood count and a basic metabolic panel with normal electrolyte levels, were conducted to rule out other potential causes.

An MRI of the brain was performed, which revealed a saccular basilar artery aneurysm measuring 4.7 cm in the largest diameter, located in the mid part of the basilar artery. The aneurysm demonstrated a characteristic saccular morphology with an intact, yet irregular, wall. Within the aneurysm, a non-occlusive thrombus was identified. There was evidence of a significant pressure effect on the brainstem, manifesting as marked narrowing of the pons and medulla oblongata. Surrounding vascular anatomy appeared patent with normal caliber. The aneurysmal wall did not show any signs of rupture.

The patient was referred to a specialized center for further evaluation and management. The management approach involved collaboration among a multidisciplinary team comprising neurosurgeons, interventional radiologists, and neurologists.

We decided to treat the aneurysm endovascularly despite its wide neck since the patient had refused any surgical intervention. Due to the aneurysm configuration and size, endovascular treatment alone by coiling appeared dangerous. Hence, we employed a comprehensive strategy by placing a flow-diverter stent in the basilar artery to create a new and safe lumen for the parent artery. Subsequently, through the previously positioned microcatheter in the aneurysm sac, we filled the aneurysm sac with coils.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: endovascular flow-diverter stent placement and coiling

evidence_events.source_span: Before the procedure, the patient had been on clopidogrel, and during the intervention, we administered heparin to prevent thromboembolic complications. The procedure, conducted under general anesthesia, involved the placement of the flow-diverter stent and the precise deployment of coils within the aneurysm.

Following the endovascular procedure, the patient was transferred to the neurointensive care unit for close monitoring. The hospital course involved neurological assessments, including regular examinations of cranial nerve functions, motor and sensory evaluations, and the assessment of cognitive status. The patient's vital signs, including blood pressure and heart rate, were closely monitored to detect any signs of complications during the immediate post-procedural period.

During her hospital stay, the patient experienced a gradual resolution of her headaches. This positive response was accompanied by stability in neurological examinations. The absence of new neurological deficits and the alleviation of symptoms were promising signs of the success of the endovascular coiling procedure.

initial_presentation.encounter_context: sought our clinic’s assistance in November 2020 after experiencing persistent symptoms
initial_presentation.chief_complaint: left-sided pulsatile tinnitus (PT) for the past 10 months
initial_presentation.first_contact_summary: The patient had persistent left-sided PT despite multiple prior misdiagnoses including migraine and subjective tinnitus, previously seen at tertiary hospitals ENT departments. PT was slightly reduced with strong compression of the internal carotid artery but not affected by internal jugular vein compression. No ocular symptoms or abnormalities on ocular assessments and physical exam. CT and MR scans showed no temporal bone dehiscence but revealed a small hyperintense signal region in the lesser sphenoid wing and left para-cavernous sinus regions indicative of dural arteriovenous fistula. The patient declined invasive diagnostics and elected conservative follow-up.

source_metadata.title: Case report: Sphenoid wing dural arteriovenous fistula draining into ophthalmic veins inducing pulsatile tinnitus as the sole symptom and its spontaneous closure

evidence_events.source_span: A 31-year-old female patient, who had been experiencing left-sided PT for the past 10 months, sought our clinic's assistance in November 2020.
She had previously received multiple misdiagnoses, including migraine and subjective tinnitus, and had sought medical attention from at least three local tertiary hospitals in the ENT department.

Her PT persisted despite attempts at reducing it through internal jugular vein compression; PT showed a slight decrease in volume following strong compression to the internal carotid artery using a Doppler ultrasound probe.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: internal jugular vein compression; compression to the internal carotid artery using Doppler ultrasound

evidence_events.source_span: Ocular assessments, such as fundoscopy, visual field examination, and orbital ultrasound, uncovered no irregularities; physical examination did not reveal signs of conjunctival vascularity, exophthalmia, oculomotor paralysis, or visual acuity loss.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: fundoscopy, visual field examination, orbital ultrasound

evidence_events.source_span: CT showed no signs of temporal bone dehiscence at either the sigmoid plate or the jugular bulb regions.

3D time-of-flight MR angiography showed a relatively small region of hyperintense signal at the lesser sphenoid wing region and the left para-cavernous sinus region, extending to efferent outlets including the superior ophthalmic vein and inferior ophthalmic vein, and through meningeal emissary veins to the pterygoid plexus.
The patient was referred to interventional radiology/neurology but declined surgical intervention and digital subtraction angiography, opting for conservative observation without medication.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: referral to interventional radiology/neurology; declined DSA and surgery

evidence_events.source_span: The subject's pulsatile tinnitus abruptly ceased without any apparent provocation after persisting for 30 months; tinnitus handicap inventory score decreased from 32 to 0.

Follow-up 3D-TOF MR angiography at 42 months after initial PT onset showed no residual high-intensity signals within the sphenoid wing region, para-cavernous sinus, or associated efferent vessels, with no signs of PT recurrence or DAVF.

The subject's PT abruptly ceased without any apparent provocation after persisting for 30 months.
Follow-up MR angiography at 42 months showed no residual high-intensity signals or radiologic indications of DAVF.
Patient had no ocular symptoms or adverse effects after PT cessation.
Patient declined DSA and surgical intervention, opting for conservative observation.
diagnostic_reasoning_items: Initial presentation with isolated left-sided pulsatile tinnitus.
Physical exam and ocular assessments negative for other abnormalities.
CT excluded temporal bone defects, ruling out common causes of PT.
MR angiography identified a small vascular lesion consistent with sphenoid wing DAVF.
Patient refused invasive diagnostics and treatment, limiting detailed vascular assessment.
Spontaneous symptom resolution after 30 months suggests fistula closure.
Follow-up MR angiography confirmed absence of DAVF, supporting spontaneous closure diagnosis.

initial_presentation.first_contact_summary: The extent of blood loss could not be quantified by the patient; however, we suspect a massive PR bleed due to his syncopal episode following the PR bleed. On physical examination, the patient was an elderly male of lean body habitus in no apparent pain or cardiopulmonary distress. His mucus membranes were pink and moist with no scleral icterus noted. He was afebrile and acyanotic with no obvious signs of jaundice. On abdominal examination, no right upper quadrant pain was elicited. His abdomen was not distended, soft, and nontender with no palpable masses. All other examinations were unremarkable. His vitals were stable with a blood pressure of 134/82 mm Hg, pulse of 86 bpm, respiratory rate of 22 breaths/min and temperature of 36.3°C. Of note, he presented 5 weeks prior for an acute cholecystitis which responded to conservative management with a view to perform an elective cholecystectomy.

evidence_events.source_span: 83-year-old male who presented to the Adult Emergency Department for an acute PR bleed and syncope
Patient had no right upper quadrant pain, no jaundice, no scleral icterus, abdomen soft and nontender, vitals stable
History of acute cholecystitis 5 weeks prior which responded to conservative management
CBC showed initial Hb 11.9 mg/dL which decreased to 10.2 mg/dL within 24 hours; other labs unremarkable
CT Abdomen on day of admission showed a 6 mm cystic artery pseudoaneurysm, thick-walled gallbladder with surrounding inflammatory changes, gallbladder inseparable from hepatic flexure of colon
Decision to perform coil embolization of the cystic artery with plan for elective cholecystectomy later
Right hepatic artery angiogram showed cystic artery arising from right hepatic artery with pseudoaneurysm opacified at distal tip of cystic artery

source_metadata.title: A rare duo: Pulmonary arterial sling with a pig bronchus
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case presentation and imaging findings in case report.

evidence_events.source_span: A 6-week-old female presented to Banner Desert Medical Center for evaluation of respiratory distress and weight loss.
On physical exam, a significant murmur was heard that had not previously been noted on prior exams.
Initial echocardiogram revealed a left pulmonary arterial sling, prominent patent foramen ovale, and a moderate size patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) with continuous left to right shunting.
Subsequent CT angiogram confirmed a pulmonary sling, with the left pulmonary artery arising from the distal right pulmonary artery and wrapping around the distal trachea.
Left proximal mainstem bronchus obstruction, consistent with left-sided air trapping, was observed.
Moderate-sized patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) and a notable patent foramen ovale (PFO) were present.
A right upper lobe tracheal bronchus (pig bronchus) was identified.

At 7-months-old the patient underwent left pulmonary artery sling and PDA repair with re-implantation of the left pulmonary artery into the main pulmonary artery anterior to the trachea and PDA division/ligation.
She developed postoperative left pulmonary artery stenosis and underwent successful balloon angioplasty.
Due to the significant left pulmonary artery hypoplasia she developed recurrent left pulmonary artery stenosis.

source_metadata.title: Pelvic arteriovenous malformation causing per rectal haemorrhage – A case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 17 years old female presented to a rural hospital with 2 days history of per rectal (PR) bleeding totalling 4 episodes, initially associated with defecation but then occurred with passage of flatus with an episode of 500 mL of estimated blood loss

On presentation she denied rectal pain and had some mild mid abdominal discomfort prior to the onset of PR bleeding. She had a history of constipation but denied any prior use of aperients. She had no history of previous PR bleeding or anaemia and denied previous per vaginal bleeding as she had an Implanon inserted a year prior
On examination she was haemodynamically stable, her abdomen was soft with tenderness in the epigastrium and peri-umbilical region. A digital rectal examination revealed bright red blood on glove
Initial investigations demonstrated a haemoglobin of 13 g/dL, platelets of 247 and INR of 1.1

Following 3 further episodes of PR bleeding, she became tachycardic to 115 bpm with blood pressure 126/80 mmHg and haemoglobin dropped to 7 g/dL requiring transfusion with 2 units of packed red blood cells and 500 mL 0.9% sodium chloride bolus

A computed tomography mesenteric angiogram (CTMA) demonstrated prominent serpiginous vessels in the pelvis surrounding the vagina and involving the anterior aspect of the rectum with a right-sided predominance, highly suggestive of a pelvic AVM with no active gastrointestinal haemorrhage
She was transferred to a tertiary centre with interventional radiology capabilities; on arrival she was tachycardic with blood pressure 145/82 mmHg and haemoglobin 10.6 g/dL

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the pelvis demonstrated a tangle of vessels in the right adnexal/pararectal region at the level of mid to lower rectum with feeding vessels from the right internal iliac artery, inferior mesenteric and superior rectal arteries; draining veins predominantly coursed to the right internal iliac vein
Digital subtraction angiography (DSA) showed right sided AVM affecting the rectum and right sided haemorrhoids secondary to venous hypertension from outflow obstruction
The consensus recommendation was angioembolisation of the large right rectal AVM and precautionary banding of haemorrhoids that developed secondary to outflow obstruction

Embolisation was performed via left common femoral artery with microcatheterization to within 1 cm of the fistula point and embolised with 0.1 mL of N-butyl cyanoacrylate (NBCA) lipiodol; flexible sigmoidoscopy days later showed no recent haemorrhage and proctoscopy visualised a moderate sized internal haemorrhoid at 7 o'clock which was banded without complications
evidence_events.procedural_cue: embolisation and flexible sigmoidoscopy with banding

evidence_events.source_span: Repeat CT mesenteric angiogram one month later demonstrated diminished rectal AVM component compared to pre-embolisation with persistent prominent draining veins on the right side of the vagina extending superiorly to cervix and inferiorly to labia

source_metadata.title: Right ventricular lead perforation with iatrogenic injury to an intercostal artery causing haemothorax after pacemaker implant
source_metadata.notes: Extraction based on case presentation, investigations, differential diagnosis, treatment, and outcome sections.

evidence_events.source_span: A woman in her early 80s with a history of atrial fibrillation and temporarily interrupted apixaban treatment underwent dual chamber pacemaker implantation with active fixation leads for bradycardia-tachycardia syndrome at a regional hospital.

Two days after the procedure, the patient presented to the emergency department with chest pain that had started the night following the implantation. On arrival at 20:20 hours, the patient was in substantial pain, displayed rapid atrial fibrillation on ECG and had a blood pressure of 197/109 mm Hg. Physical examination revealed normal temperature and decreased breath sounds on the left side. The pacemaker site showed no signs of infection or haematoma. Initial evaluation revealed haemoglobin level of 130 g/L, C reactive protein level of 9 mg/L and troponin T at 33 ng/L.
A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the thorax identified a large left-side haemothorax and right ventricular lead perforation.

While in the radiology department, the patient’s systolic blood pressure significantly declined to 75 mm Hg. The patient exhibited symptoms of peripheral vasoconstriction—pale skin and cold extremities—but remained conscious. The patient was transferred to the intensive care unit and stabilised with intravenous fluids. Her haemoglobin level declined to 76 g/L. Intervention included administering four units of fresh frozen plasma and four units of packed red blood cells.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: while in radiology department and ICU transfer
evidence_events.procedural_cue: intravenous fluids and blood product transfusion

evidence_events.source_span: Transthoracic echocardiography did not reveal significant pericardial effusion. A left-sided thoracotomy tube was inserted, draining 1.5 L of dark blood.
The patient was transferred via helicopter to our tertiary specialist unit for cardiothoracic surgery, receiving three additional units of red blood cells during the transfer.
On arrival at our unit, the patients’ haemoglobin level was 103 g/L. Pacemaker interrogation revealed low R wave amplitude and low impedance of the right ventricular lead.

A subsequent ECG-triggered CT scan revealed a massive accumulation of blood in the left pleura, displacing the mediastinum to the right. Active extravasation was observed from the fourth left intercostal artery at the bone-cartilage junction. The tip of the right ventricular lead was located near the pericardium and directed towards the site of extravasation. However, the volume of blood within the pericardium was relatively small.

The symptoms and clinical findings suggested myocardial infarction or pulmonary embolism initially, but CT scan ruled out pulmonary embolism and showed no evidence of pneumothorax. The CT scan disclosed a significant left-sided haemothorax with active bleeding from an intercostal artery as the most plausible source.

Pacemaker interrogation showing low R wave amplitude and lead impedance strongly suggested lead perforation, consistent with clinical presentation and radiological evidence. Neither transthoracic echocardiogram nor CT scan revealed significant pericardial effusion, making tamponade less likely.

Following administration of thrombocytes, coagulation factors II and IX, and fibrinogen, the patient underwent cardiothoracic surgery via median sternotomy. The source of bleeding in the lateral intercostal space was sealed using sutures and reinforced with a topical fibrin sealant patch. The right ventricular lead was found to have perforated and extended through the pericardial wall. A new epicardial right ventricular lead was placed and the transvenous lead was removed. The right ventricle was repaired.
During surgery, the patient received transfusions of seven units of erythrocytes and seven units of plasma.

Postoperative, the patient’s haemoglobin levels stabilised, and no additional blood transfusions were necessary. The patient was discharged home after recovery and had no further complications at 2-year follow-up.

initial_presentation.first_contact_summary: Physical exam revealed diffuse right breast thickening and erythema, but no palpable masses. A diagnostic mammogram revealed a 7.5 cm retroareolar mass with associated skin and trabecular thickening. On ultrasound, a hypervascular complex cystic mass with thick, irregular walls measuring 7.5 x 6.8 x 7.1 cm was identified with a few prominent lymph nodes with concentric cortical thickening in the right axilla. Given the suspicious imaging, the lesion was categorized as BIRADS 4 and an ultrasound-guided core biopsy was recommended. The patient chose a skin punch biopsy which yielded inflammatory changes and neutrophils. Incision and drainage yielded purulent fluid and oral antibiotics were prescribed with clinical improvement.

evidence_events.source_span: A 57-year-old postmenopausal female presented to the breast surgery clinic with right breast swelling, pain, and bloody nipple discharge for three months.
Physical exam revealed diffuse right breast thickening and erythema, but no palpable masses.
A diagnostic mammogram revealed a 7.5 cm retroareolar mass with associated skin and trabecular thickening.
On diagnostic ultrasound, there was a hypervascular complex cystic mass with thick, irregular walls measuring 7.5 x 6.8 x 7.1 cm.
A few prominent lymph nodes with concentric cortical thickening were identified in the right axilla.
A skin punch biopsy of the right breast yielded inflammatory changes and neutrophils.
Incision and drainage of the right breast mass was performed, which yielded purulent fluid. The patient was prescribed oral antibiotics with clinical improvement.
The patient returned a year later with a new palpable mass in the right breast, new nipple retraction, and persistent right-sided bloody nipple discharge.
A diagnostic mammogram revealed a mass in the right central inner breast associated with new nipple retraction.
Ultrasound showed a 4.0 x 3.5 x 1.3 cm irregular hypoechoic mass with internal vascularity.
An ultrasound-guided core biopsy was performed, which yielded a benign intraductal papilloma.
Wire localized excision of the right breast mass was performed with final surgical pathology revealing a benign intraductal papilloma.

source_metadata.title: A Rare Incidence of Splenic Artery Aneurysm and Hypersplenism
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case presentation and clinical course sections with figure references.

evidence_events.source_span: 31-year-old woman with Child's B liver cirrhosis, portal hypertension, splenomegaly, and a one-month history of dull left hypochondriac abdominal pain
Physical examination revealed Hackett's Grade 2 splenomegaly; vital signs normal; no fever
Blood investigation showed low white blood cell count (1.9 x 10^9 cells/L) and low platelet count (54 x 10^9 cells/L) consistent with hypersplenism
Contrast-enhanced CT abdomen revealed a saccular splenic artery aneurysm at mid to distal splenic artery measuring 3.4 x 3.4 x 4.3 cm with thrombus and splenic infarction
Angiographic coiling of the splenic artery aneurysm was performed using fibered angiocoils and lipiodol; procedure was successful with visual confirmation of thrombosis within the aneurysm
Post-embolisation CT angiogram showed thrombosed splenic artery with no contrast flow to the spleen
Follow-up blood counts showed improvement: WBC increased from 1.9 to 5.0 x 10^9 cells/L and platelets from 54 to 209 x 10^9 cells/L
Follow-up CT abdomen demonstrated reduction in spleen size from 10.8 x 7.4 x 18.6 cm to 9.3 x 5.4 x 16.1 cm

source_metadata.title: A rare case of giant mediastinal thymolipoma in an 18-year man
source_metadata.notes: Extraction from case presentation and methods sections with figure references.

evidence_events.source_span: An 18-year-old male, previously hospitalized for meningitis at age five, admitted after a car accident with chest pain but stable vital signs and no dyspnea; oxygen saturation 98%.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: after being involved in a car accident

evidence_events.source_span: Physical examination showed limited chest movement, decreased tactile vocal fremitus, dullness on percussion, and decreased breath sounds on the right side.
Chest CT scout view showed an opacity in the right lower hemithorax without clear shifting of the heart to the left side.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: A chest CT scan was performed

evidence_events.source_span: CT scan revealed a predominantly fat-containing mass with soft tissue components measuring approximately 13 × 23 × 15 cm, originating from the anterior mediastinum and extending into the right hemithorax, causing near complete collapse of the right lower lung lobe.
The mass was entirely excised through a right thoracotomy.
Histopathological examination revealed an encapsulated lesion comprising mature adipose tissue containing islands of non-neoplastic thymic epithelial cells.
The patient experienced no postoperative complications and was discharged in excellent condition on the 11th day following surgery.

source_metadata.title: Peritoneal Carcinomatosis: When Everything Is Not What It Seems

evidence_events.source_span: A 73-year-old woman presented to the emergency department with constitutional syndrome, abdominal pain, and diarrhea.
She had a history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes, dyslipidemia, pancreatic cysts, and fibromyalgia, with no risk of exposure to pollutants.
Prior to admission, she underwent an upper and lower digestive endoscopy, and serum tumor markers were normal.
During her hospital stay, she was diagnosed with abdominal ascites and increased abdominal pain.

Computed tomography (CT) of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis revealed peritoneal effusion with signs of peritoneal carcinomatosis, especially in the lesser omentum, and edema of the adnexa, suggesting secondary involvement.
Breast ultrasound revealed only non-pathological microcalcifications and abdominal ultrasound confirmed aspects suggestive of peritoneal carcinomatosis.

18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) positron emission tomography (PET) scan revealed hypermetabolic abdominal-pelvic adenopathies and extensive diffuse hypermetabolic peritoneal densifications with peritoneal effusion, suggestive aspects of peritoneal carcinomatosis.
During the investigation, the patient’s clinical condition worsened, with increased ascites, intensification of abdominal pain, weight loss, and general malaise.
Gynecology evaluation was requested to rule out a tumor related to the patient’s age and sex, but this yielded no additional information.
After consultation with an oncologist, it was decided to biopsy a peritoneal implant with the help of radiology to obtain a histopathology report on the tumor.
The biopsy results revealed malignant peritoneal mesothelioma (MPM) of the epidermoid type.
Following the results, the patient underwent surgery with cytoreduction of the tumor and hyperthermic intraperitoneal chemotherapy (HIPEC).
Due to the overall extension of the disease, the patient was referred to palliative chemotherapy, with a partial response to treatment.

source_metadata.title: Ischial Tuberosity Avulsion Fracture Mimicking Calcified Mass on Plain Films: A Case Report

evidence_events.source_span: The patient is a 14-year-old boy with no significant past medical history who presented to the orthopedic department of a children’s hospital for evaluation of a right hip pain.
The patient reported that he fell down two months prior to the visit while playing football and heard a popping sound followed by pain in the posterior aspect of his right hip.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: two months prior to the visit

evidence_events.source_span: The patient did not seek medical care at the time of injury and continued participating in physical activities like water skiing.

Upon presentation to the orthopedic department, the patient described ongoing pain localized to the right ischial tuberosity and was associated with tingling down the posterior leg to the level of the mid-thigh. It was exacerbated by activity and improved with rest.
The physical exam was significant only for decreased strength (3/5) with resisted knee flexion.
Frontal and frog-leg radiographs of the pelvis were ordered for assessment.

Radiographs revealed components of a healing right-sided ischial tuberosity avulsion fracture and a 5.8cm cluster of well-corticated, ovoid and crescent-shaped calcifications in the soft tissues near the ischial tuberosity and adjacent to the avulsed bone fragment. The affected ischial tuberosity displayed lucency and irregular margins.

The unusual appearance of clustered, irregular calcific densities in the soft tissues in conjunction with the clinical context of persistent pain two months after injury raised concern for underlying calcified soft tissue mass.
Evaluation with Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) was warranted for further characterization.
MRI demonstrated a dark signal on both T1 and T2 weighted images suggesting calcifications.

The appearance on MRI confirmed the diagnosis of ischial tuberosity avulsion fracture, and the area of concern in the adjacent soft tissues was due to the accumulation of callous adjacent to the originally avulsed bone fragment.
The patient was expected to make a full recovery with conservative management including rest, physical therapy, and progressive return to activity.
The patient’s right ischial tuberosity avulsion fracture improved clinically over several months and he was able to make a gradual return to his usual activities and sports.

source_metadata.title: Massive appendiceal mucinous neoplasm diagnosed after abdominal trauma: Pitfalls in imaging and diagnosis

evidence_events.source_span: A 33-year-old man was referred to our surgical center with a history of lower abdominal pain and fullness. These symptoms were precipitated by an episode of abdominal trauma during a boxing training session. Upon investigation a palpable mass was felt in the right lower quadrant.

An abdominal MRI was conducted, revealing a 58 × 52 × 109 mm intraperitoneal cystic lesion in the right mid to lower abdomen. The inferior margin of the lesion was in close proximity to the caecal pole, thin walled and entirely simple. The interior of the lesion demonstrated T2 hyperintensity but minimal T1 hyperintensity on weighted imaging. The appendix was not identified separate to this lesion.

An abdominal ultrasound was performed, describing a well-circumscribed lesion in the right mid-lower abdomen, distinct from the small bowel and appendix, with no apparent communication. Additionally, a moderate amount of debris and increased echogenicity was seen within the lesion with no associated intrinsic vascularity.

Colonoscopy was performed with visualization to the terminal ileum. No abnormalities were visualized and the appendiceal opening appeared normal. Tumor markers including CEA, Ca-19-9, and Ca-125 were normal.

A laparoscopy was performed. A large inflammatory abdominal lesion with associated enlarged lymph nodes was visualized within the mesentery of the ascending colon. The appendix was not visualized. A right hemicolectomy with primary anastomosis was performed.
Histopathology revealed a completely excised low-grade appendiceal mucinous neoplasm with fifteen negative lymph nodes.
The patient had an unremarkable long term postoperative course, with full return to baseline functioning.

source_metadata.title: A Young Female With Takayasu Arteritis Involving the Coronary Arteries

evidence_events.source_span: A 37-year-old Indian female patient was referred to the cardiology outpatient with uncontrolled hypertension. A detailed history indicated that the patient had angina on exertion class 2 with malaise and fatigue.

Upon evaluation, she was afebrile and had stable vitals, had no bruit, and her cardiac examination was normal. The left arm's blood pressure was measured at 150/77 mm Hg, but the right arm's was higher at 179/95 mm Hg. Additionally, the left radial artery palpation revealed a weak and thready pulse as compared to a full and bounding pulse on the right radial artery palpation.
Electrocardiogram (ECG) showed a left ventricular hypertrophy(LVH) strain pattern with down-sloping asymmetrical ST-segment depression with an inverted asymmetric T wave.
Her white blood cells were within the normal range, whereas CRP and ESR were elevated.
Echocardiography revealed moderate concentric left ventricular hypertrophy without any wall motion abnormalities, and a normal aortic valve with an estimated ejection fraction of 55%.

Coronary angiography revealed a porcelain aorta (heavily calcified aorta), left anterior descending artery (LAD) showing 70% stenosis proximally with ectasis, left circumflex artery (LCX) showing about 90% stenosis distally, right coronary artery(RCA) showing 60% stenosis in middle segment, and a dilated and large left main coronary artery.
Peripheral angiography revealed multiple stenosis in the right subclavian artery and approximately 80% stenosis in the bilateral renal arteries; the left subclavian artery was not visualized.

MR angiography revealed complete thrombosis of the left subclavian and left common carotid arteries. There was also about 80-90% luminal narrowing of the long segmental lower thoracic and abdominal aorta.
These findings suggested the diagnosis of Takayasu Vasculitis as the 2022 ACR score was 12.
The patient subsequently underwent percutaneous angioplasty with drug-eluting stents in the LAD and LCX coronaries and was put on dual antiplatelet therapy.

source_metadata.title: It Can’t B: An Unusual Case of Streptococcus agalactiae (Group B) Empyema Necessitans

evidence_events.source_span: A 61-year-old male presented to our hospital with acute abdominal pain with hematemesis for one day.

Significant history included former tobacco smoking with cessation 30 years ago, throat cancer status post-chemo-radiation, syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion (SIADH) previously on tolvaptan, and gastroesophageal reflux disease.

He reported bloody emesis that started one night prior; associated with sharp, burning epigastric pain and nausea. He also reported one week of right shoulder pain and two days of right anterior “fullness” in his chest.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: one night prior; one week; two days

evidence_events.source_span: At presentation, his vitals included an initial blood pressure of 141/62 mmHg, and subsequently 95/69 mmHg. Heart rate was 83 beats a minute. Oxygen saturation was 97% on room air. Temperature 98.4 F. Physical exam revealed a hoarse voice and vesicular breath sounds bilaterally on lung auscultation.
Laboratory data were significant for leukocytosis (white blood cell count 17.8 with 90% neutrophils) and hyponatremia (sodium 115 mEq; baseline 125-128 mEq).
Portable chest radiographs did not show focal airspace opacities or pleural effusions.
Electrocardiogram revealed a new left bundle branch block which was thought to be the cause of the chest pain initially.
Cardiac catheterization revealed mild non-obstructive coronary artery disease and nonischemic cardiomyopathy with an ejection fraction of 35-40%.

He continued to have right-sided chest pain and shoulder pain and a right shoulder radiograph was obtained which revealed a lung mass. Mass was new when compared to the initial radiograph taken four days prior.
Further investigation with contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the chest revealed a 6.5x3.8cm complex right pleural space collection with air foci within the right pectoral muscles.
CT-guided drainage was performed by interventional radiology, 15 cc of purulent material was removed and a 12 French pigtail catheter was placed.

The abscess grew Group B streptococcus (GBS). Pathology revealed bacteria, no evidence of fungal growth, and no evidence of malignant cells. The acid-fast bacillus (AFB) smear was negative for mycobacteria. HIV testing was nonreactive.
Initially, he was started on Piperacillin-Tazobactam but was switched to Ampicillin/Sulbactam once sensitivities resulted.
The patient was discharged with a plan for six weeks of Ampicillin/Sulbactam and repeat chest imaging in four weeks.
The patient's chest radiograph six months after showed a resolution of the infection.

source_metadata.title: Closed Degloving Injury of the Foot Caused by a High Impact Force: A Case Report

evidence_events.source_span: An 18-year-old male came to our diagnostic center for an MRI of the foot. He was involved in a motorcycle accident a few weeks ago and sustained a crush injury. X-ray at the time of injury did not reveal any fracture. He had no obvious draining wound on the inspection of the site of injury. At the time of the scan, he was complaining of pain in foot motion. He also had a swelling over the plantar surface of his foot.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: MRI scan was recommended by his orthopedic surgeon

evidence_events.source_span: MRI examination showed that there was a serous fluid collection in two layers. A superficial collection (~48 cc) was seen in the subcutaneous layer, which was causing the swelling over the plantar surface. A second collection (~38 cc) was seen in the superficial fascial layer. This deeper collection extended into the recesses of the phalanxes of the fourth and fifth toes. It also overlaid a stress fracture of the two phalanxes. The vascular supply of the foot was intact, and no abnormal nerve injury was apparent.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: at the time of MRI scan

evidence_events.source_span: Additional CT imaging confirmed hypodense collection and the absence of overt fracture.
The serous collections were drained via incision and drainage with the debridement of tissue. The resultant wound was dressed aseptically. Serial dressing was done until discharge.

The patient was discharged when the dermis started showing signs of regeneration. At one-month and six-week follow-up, the patient was healthy and showed good recovery/regeneration of the skin surface. No subsequent tissue necrosis, recurrence, or wound infection was seen.

This deeper collection extended into the recesses of the phalanxes of the fourth and fifth toes. It also overlaid a stress fracture of the two phalanxes. The vascular supply of the foot was intact, and no abnormal nerve injury was apparent. Additional CT imaging confirmed hypodense collection and the absence of overt fracture.
