evidence_events.source_span: A 39-year-old Jamaican female presented to the emergency room with a chief complaint of blurry vision persisting for two days. The patient reported a preceding day of headaches, fever, and dry cough associated with shortness of breath. She denied abdominal pain but mentioned nausea and a single episode of non-bloody, nonbilious emesis. Vital signs revealed blood pressure of 130/103, heart rate of 105, respiration rate of 20, oxygen saturation of 100%, and oral temperature of 38.0°C. Physical examination revealed fever, hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, altered mental status, and skin malar rash.
Laboratory workup revealed normocytic anemia, elevated serum creatinine, hyperbilirubinemia, and thrombocytopenia.

The right upper quadrant ultrasound was unremarkable, but magnetic resonance venography (MRV) showed a venous aneurysm in the neck and showed outpouching, unclear if related to the confluence of venous structures versus a small venous aneurysm.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: right upper quadrant ultrasound; magnetic resonance venography (MRV)

evidence_events.source_span: A subsequent MRI of the orbits demonstrated abnormal signal intensity, mild edema, and enhancement of the optic nerve sheath complexes bilaterally.
The patient was found to be RSV-positive and was diagnosed with posterior scleritis.
Given the elevated ANA, RNP, anti-chromatin antibodies, and a recent episode of pericarditis, suspicion of a connective tissue disease arose and subsequently was determined to be SLE.
The patient underwent lumbar puncture and bone marrow biopsy, necessitating ICU placement due to acute respiratory failure and lethargy.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: lumbar puncture; bone marrow biopsy; ICU placement

evidence_events.source_span: Flow cytometry of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was predominantly composed of cellular debris and nonhematolymphoid elements with some lymphocytes and possibly some monocytes. No definite B-cell population was identified, and lymphocytes mostly consist of T-cells. Due to the limited specimen, T-cells could not be further characterized.

Bone marrow from the right iliac crest resulted in mildly hypercellular marrow with trilineage hematopoiesis and complete maturation, dyserythropoietic changes, some atypical megakaryocytes, increased eosinophils, and no increase in blasts with rare hemophagocytic cells identified.
Peripheral blood with mildly increased left shifted and immature granulocytes and increased schistocytes.
Positive ANA/RNP, along with skin malar rash, posterior scleritis, and fever, led to the diagnosis of SLE. The bone marrow and CSF findings overlap with MAS and HLH.

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain without contrast exhibiting lupus cerebritis with areas of increased T2/FLAIR signal in the bilateral occipital lobe subcortical white matter, bilateral parietal periventricular white matter, bilateral frontal centrum semiovale, patchy high flair signal in the pons, a small high T2 signal lesion in the right cerebellum, and subtle petechial hemorrhages in the bilateral cerebellum and right pons.

Laboratory results showed elevated glucose, elevated blood urea nitrogen (BUN), decreased sodium, elevated serum creatinine, low albumin, elevated ALT and AST, elevated total bilirubin, elevated phosphorus, reduced total iron-binding capacity (TIBC), elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), ferritin >10,000, triglycerides 373, and elevated interleukin-2 (IL-2) at 6361 pg/ml.

Complete blood count showed thrombocytopenia (platelets 24k/ul), decreased red blood cells (3.14 k/ul), low hemoglobin (8.6 g/dl), low hematocrit (26.4%), elevated white blood cells (15.7 k/ul), and increased red cell distribution width (22.6%).

Peripheral blood smear showed mild leukocytosis with left-shifted granulocytes including immature granulocytes, anisopoikilocytosis with increased schistocytes, rare target cells, few elliptocytes, few polychromatophilic cells, few nucleated red blood cells, decreased platelets with some large and rare giant platelets, and no blasts.
Chromosome analysis was abnormal: 46, XX, t(2:4) (g37; q12) [21/46, XX (18)]. Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization (FISH) studies were negative for PDGERA gene rearrangement located at 4q12.

Factor H was within the normal range, and Shiga toxin and factor H tests were negative, making complement-mediated Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP) or Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS) less likely.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: factor H testing; Shiga toxin testing

evidence_events.source_span: Serum markers showed elevated CD25 (>6000), ferritin (>10,000), triglycerides 373, bicytopenias, fevers, fibrinogen <250, abnormal liver function tests, and elevated CXCL9 at 14176. CD107/NK remained normal. Bone marrow biopsy revealed rare hemophagocytic cells.

Additional laboratory investigations for eosinophilia including MDS Fish, FGFR1, PDGERa/b, and NGS myeloid were negative. PF4 testing for autoimmune Heparin-Induced Thrombocytopenia (HIT) was negative.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: MDS Fish; FGFR1; PDGERa/b; NGS myeloid; PF4 testing

evidence_events.source_span: Rheumatology initiated SLE treatment with CellCept, and cardiac assessment revealed a negative echocardiogram for valvular pathology, eliminating its contribution to red blood cell shearing.
Left native kidney biopsy showed diffuse thrombotic microangiopathy and severe acute tubular injury/necrosis, suggesting a vascular component contributing to renal impairment.

source_metadata.title: Opalski Syndrome and Elucidation of Lateral Medullary Syndrome

evidence_events.source_span: A 61-year-old patient presented to the emergency department (ED) with left-sided paresthesias and hemiparesis of the arm and leg.

The patient reported that they awoke from sleep due to left-sided weakness with difficulty moving the left leg, diminished sensation, and ataxic gait which resulted in multiple near falls since they would repeatedly lean to the left side.
The patient also described left craniofacial pain.

The patient had a past medical history of hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, uncontrolled diabetes mellitus type two (T2DM), chronic kidney disease 3a, human immunodeficiency virus, late-stage syphilis, coronary artery disease status post coronary artery bypass graft times three, and aortic stenosis status post a mechanical aortic valve.

On examination, the patient had difficulty lifting the left arm, a left Horner’s pupil with mild ptosis and miosis, loss of temperature sensation on the right side of the body, and numbness on the left side of the face and right side of the body.
Deep tendon reflexes were absent in the lower extremities.
NIH stroke score (NIHSS) upon presentation was determined to be a three (minor severity) based on left upper extremity motor drift and sensory deficit, and blurred vision (diplopia).
Computed tomography (CT) of the head without contrast revealed no acute intracranial abnormality.
A carotid ultrasound displayed moderate stenosis of the right internal carotid artery (ICA).
A CT angiography of the head and neck showed no large vessel disease in the head or intracranial stenosis, but confirmed 50% stenosis of the right ICA.

A comparison non-contrast CT of the head was performed and revealed a subtle diffuse hypodensity throughout the right frontoparietal temporal region concerning for an evolving right middle cerebral artery (MCA) infarct; however, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) confirmed no infarct.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: non-contrast CT head and MRI brain

evidence_events.source_span: MRI of the brain without contrast revealed a 4 mm acute left lateral medullary infarct of the left posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) vascular territory.
There was also mild diffuse central and cortical atrophy with mild chronic ischemic small-vessel disease.

evidence_events.source_span: 45-year-old female, who presented to our hospital because of a mass on the right adrenal gland that was discovered incidentally during a periodic echocardiogram without any symptoms on the patient
history of excisional biopsy for a benign breast mass, a medical history of medication-controlled hypertension for 5 years, and Type 2 diabetes for 10 years but the family history was unremarkable

contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen revealed a large, well-defined, heterogeneous mass measuring 13 × 12 × 9.5 cm, located in the right adrenal gland, containing areas of high attenuation suggesting recent hemorrhage, along with fat-density areas consistent with adipose tissue
no signs of invasion into adjacent structures or lymphadenopathy
patient underwent a right open adrenalectomy; intraoperatively, a large, encapsulated mass was found in the right adrenal gland and removed without complications
gross examination showed a mass weighing 44.5 g, measuring 15 × 10.5 × 5 cm, encapsulated, rubbery to cystic consistency with areas of hemorrhage, heterogeneous yellow to black gelatinous cut surface

source_metadata.title: Atypical Manifestation of Adult Polycystic Kidney Disease in an Elderly Individual

evidence_events.source_span: A 95-year-old man with a past medical history of adult polycystic kidney disease, hypertension, prostate cancer, sinus bradycardia, and a recent admission due to an uncomplicated UTI two weeks prior was admitted with worsening mental status and multiple falls
An abdominal CT scan with intravenous contrast revealed a massive cystic replacement of the left kidney measuring 26.7 x 13.8 x 18.7 cm, crossing the midline and displacing bowel loops
The right kidney also had multiple large cortical and parapelvic cysts, although it was significantly smaller
These findings were consistent with the previous abdominal CT scan conducted 10 years ago
There was only one small 2.8 cm cyst in the liver
No cerebral traumas, hemorrhage, or aneurysms were observed on CT angiography of the head
His family denied any history of UTIs, apart from the recent one
According to the chart records, he was able to produce a normal amount of urine daily

The patient’s blood work results were as follows: hemoglobin of 10.6 g/dL, leukocytes of 2.8 x 10^9/L, platelets of 37 K/µL, creatinine of 1.07 mg/dL, blood urea nitrogen of 27 mg/dL, and an estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) of 64 mL/minute/1.73m2
Upon admission, the patient was lethargic and oriented only to himself
On physical examination, he had a normal constitution, a distended abdomen, and a large, uneven mass was palpable
The patient was repeatedly treated for the UTI during hospitalization; his mental status slowly improved and he was discharged in stable condition

source_metadata.title: A Rare Presentation of Polyarteritis Nodosa (PAN)

evidence_events.source_span: A 48-year-old male with a medical history of polysubstance use, including cocaine and methamphetamines, presented with generalized abdominal pain that was insidious in onset and gradually progressive for the past three days, throbbing type, present intermittently, associated with nausea.

Prior to transfer, he tested positive for COVID-19 on PCR and abdominal CT showed soft tissue heterogeneous masses arising from the greater curvature and antrum of stomach measuring 6.5 x 13.2 x 8.6 cm and 10.5 x 8 x 9.7 cm with diffuse thickening, fat stranding, minimal ascites, perihepatic space involvement, ground glass attenuation in both lower lung lobes, emphysematous changes in upper lobes, and minimal bilateral pleural effusion.

On arrival, he was afebrile with temperature 38.42°C, heart rate 105 bpm, respiratory rate 30 bpm, blood pressure 90/60 mmHg, oxygen saturation 98% on 2 L oxygen, requiring norepinephrine to maintain MAP goal of 65 mmHg.

Blood work showed normal white count and platelet count, hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL with normocytic normochromic anemia, acute kidney injury with creatinine 2.3 mg/dL, no coagulopathy, elevated venous lactate 6.3 with normal anion gap, mildly elevated inflammatory markers including procalcitonin 1.31 ng/mL, D-dimer 3.32 mcg/mL, ESR 24 mm/hour, and CRP 5.9 mg/dL.
Chest x-ray showed bilateral infiltrates in the lower lobes with small bilateral pleural effusions.

He had a progressive drop in hemoglobin to 6.3 g/dL requiring blood transfusions, prompting repeat abdominal CT which showed a 2 cm lobulated saccular aneurysm involving the left gastric artery or splenic artery with moderate hemoperitoneum and hematomas up to 8.6 cm abutting the gastric fundus and greater curvature, likely due to aneurysmal rupture.
Several other mesenteric vessels, notably the superior mesenteric artery, displayed some degree of fusiform dilation; celiac and splenic arteriograms demonstrated a mid-splenic artery pseudoaneurysm.
Interventional radiology-guided splenic artery embolization with coils for the pseudoaneurysm was performed, after which hemoglobin remained stable with no further bleeding.

The aneurysms were attributed to either cocaine-related aneurysms or polyarteritis nodosa with visceral artery aneurysms; tertiary syphilis was ruled out after negative VDRL and RPR tests; hepatitis panel was negative; cytoplasmic and perinuclear ANCAs were negative; complement C3 and C4 levels were normal.
He denied rashes, oral ulcers, joint pain, subcutaneous nodules, blood in urine, history of hepatitis or syphilis.

Given elevated blood urea nitrogen and creatinine, characteristic imaging findings, and overall clinical picture, diagnosis of PAN was made despite not fulfilling American College of Rheumatology classification criteria.

He was treated with high-dose IV methylprednisone after infection was ruled out and started on IV cyclophosphamide therapy 15 mg/kg every two weeks for three doses, then every three weeks for three to six months, combined with glucocorticoid prednisone taper; cyclophosphamide was given with IV hydration and mesna.

source_metadata.title: Urothelial Carcinoma With Bone Metastasis Mimicking Sciatica: A Common Neoplasm With an Uncommon Presentation

evidence_events.source_span: An 86-year-old male with a past medical history significant for hypertension, kidney stones, and hypothyroidism presented to the ED for evaluation of the sudden onset of worsening of his chronic lower back and right lower extremity pain and numbness ongoing for the last nine to 10 months.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: ongoing for the last nine to 10 months

evidence_events.source_span: The back pain was described as moderate in intensity, radiating to the right lower extremity, progressively getting worse, and associated with lower extremity tingling, numbness, and ambulatory dysfunction.
He was initially suspected to have sciatica but was not responding to treatment.
In the ED, the patient was found to be hemodynamically stable and saturating well on room air.
Lab work was significant for leukocytosis with a WBC count of 20.57, hemoglobin of 10.5, acute kidney injury with blood urea nitrogen of 44, creatinine of 1.7 (baseline 1.1), and lactate of 3.7.
Urinalysis was significant for pyuria and microscopic hematuria.

MRI spine findings were consistent with acute insufficiency fractures involving S1, S2, and left sacral ala, T1 low, and T2 bright signal mass in the L3 vertebral body suspicious for a metastatic lesion. Moderate to severe left hydroureteronephrosis, a nonspecific cystic focus in the right iliacus muscle, multilevel degenerative disc disease causing spinal canal and neural foraminal stenosis.

CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis revealed an irregular soft tissue mass at the left posterolateral bladder base, involving the ureterovesical junction and resulting in apparent obstruction of the left ureter, highly suggestive of neoplasm, along with numerous lytic bone lesions in the pelvic girdle with associated soft tissue masses, consistent with metastatic disease.
CT head showed no acute intracranial abnormality with no signs of metastasis.
The patient underwent left percutaneous nephrostomy placement for obstruction and was started on antibiotics for urinary tract infection.
The patient underwent an interventional radiology biopsy of the right iliac soft tissue mass to evaluate the lytic bony lesions.

The biopsy results revealed metastatic carcinoma, consistent with UC. The tumor cells were positive for CK7, CK20, P40, Uroplakin, and Gata-3, and showed focal positivity for CK5. The cytomorphology and immunoprofile were consistent with UC.

Hematology/oncology was consulted for UC with bone metastasis. The patient was advised to follow up as an outpatient for the initiation of therapy, either dual therapy or single therapy, with pembrolizumab given the patient's poor performance.

Because of the patient's age, underlying comorbidities, and poor performance status, hospice was recommended as his metastatic disease was not curable and the goal of any kind of treatment was palliative.

source_metadata.title: Primary Pulmonary Echinococcosis in the United States: A Case Report and Review of the Literature

evidence_events.source_span: A 34-year-old Middle Eastern female presented to the emergency department with excessive coughing, mild dyspnea, cough, and left-sided chest pain for the past month.
Initial work-up included CXR completed shortly after admission, which revealed a 10cm x 8cm opacity in the left lower lobe (Figure 1).

On hospital day 1, CT angiography (CTA) of the chest was ordered to rule out symptomatic concerns of pulmonary embolism (PE) but no significant filling defects were observed in the larger pulmonary vessels.
CTA revealed a hypodense abnormality with characteristic features of a simple pulmonary cyst.

Additional lab work included CBC, CMP, and quantitative beta-hCG; aminotransferase and alkaline phosphatase elevations were present with the remaining admission blood work and vital signs within normal limits.
On hospital day 2, Pulmonology was consulted and empiric IV Piperacillin-Tazobactam was initiated for a possible atypical, afebrile, pulmonary cystic abscess.
On hospital day 6, Thoracic Surgery was consulted and a complete left lower lobe lobectomy was performed for diagnostic evaluation due to lack of clinical and imaging improvement.
Post-surgical pathology of the clear cystic fluid was determined to be Echinococcus given the clinical history despite similar appearance hooklets seen in other members of the Taeniidae family.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: Pathology analysis of resected cystic fluid

evidence_events.source_span: Cytologic analysis of the left inferior pulmonary ligament lymph node biopsy showed mild anthracosis and benign lymphoid hyperplasia without malignancy.
Echinococcus antibody serology returned negative, raising questions about the test's diagnostic sensitivity and utility.
The patient was discharged with Albendazole and recommended serial follow-up CXR for the next 10 years.

source_metadata.title: Congenital tibial pseudarthrosis: A challenge in pediatric radiology

evidence_events.source_span: A newborn, 10-days-old and delivered via elective C-section (APGAR 8/9), has been transferred to our hospital's neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) due to severe respiratory distress that manifested a few hours after birth.

The pregnancy was uneventful, marked by normal fetal ultrasounds and negative results on the noninvasive prenatal testing (NIPT) for chromosomal aneuploidies and major microdeletions. Blood tests indicate a slight increase in C-reactive protein (CRP), while both chest X-ray and abdominal ultrasound show no abnormalities.
Echocardiography reveals a patent foramen ovale (PFO) with a mild shunt.
A diagnosis of resolved acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS) is established after approximately 48 hours of supportive therapy, including mechanical ventilation and antibiotic treatment.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: supportive therapy including mechanical ventilation and antibiotics

evidence_events.source_span: Upon transfer to the nursery, the newborn exhibits inconsolable crying and reduced mobility in the left lower limb. An X-ray identifies a mid-diaphyseal tibial fracture.
The limb is promptly casted, and the patient is returned to the NICU.
A decision is made to conduct a CT scan of the lower limb, revealing a morphostructural alteration of the left tibia, with curvature in the distal diaphyseal segment.

In the mid-diaphyseal regions of the tibia, there are evident discontinuities in the bone cortex, which also appears thickened. Multiple irregularly distributed hypodense areas are present along the tibia, extending to the bone cortex. The fibula, also curved, exhibits a small area of hypodensity in the proximal diaphyseal region, altering the cortical profile. No CT scan alterations are observed in the surrounding soft tissues.

Considering the imaging findings along with clinical and anamnestic data, there is a suggestion of an osteodysplastic condition of the leg, specifically leaning towards congenital tibial pseudarthrosis.

The imaging findings suggest the necessity for genetic counseling to rule out genetic disorders, particularly any association with NF1. The genetic counseling session indicates the absence of phenotypic anomalies and no visibly apparent café-au-lait spots.
The NGS analysis of genes linked to rasopathies, fibrous dysplasia, and osteogenesis imperfecta produces a negative result.
In accordance with a unanimous specialist consensus, neither an MRI nor a biopsy is deemed necessary. A leg brace is applied, and surgery is pending.
During the follow-up, our diagnostic hypothesis gains further support as there is the absence of osseous consolidation of a fracture, and characteristic features of CPT become evident.
The patient at age of 12 months undergoes cross-union surgery, with evidence of good healing progress.

source_metadata.title: Multiple Aneurysms or Pseudoaneurysms of the Gastroepiploic Artery: An Anecdotal Cause of Hemoperitoneum

evidence_events.source_span: An 82-year-old patient with a history of hypertension and dyslipidemia consulted the emergency department with sudden-onset and severe abdominal pain, predominantly in the mesogastrium, associated with pallor, sweating, and orthostatism.
Physical examination showed pulse of 108 beats per minute, blood pressure of 98/56 mmHg, notable mucocutaneous pallor, and abdominal tenderness without signs of peritoneal irritation.
Laboratory results revealed a hemoglobin level of 9.2 g/dL as the only abnormal finding.

Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen revealed two saccular images adjacent to the greater curvature of the stomach with peripheral calcifications measuring up to 28 x 23 mm, following a vascular trajectory.
High-density fluid was observed in the pelvis (up to 86 Hounsfield Units), suggesting associated hemoperitoneum.
Selective abdominal arteriography showed usual vascular anatomy of the celiac trunk with its three main branches: splenic artery, left gastric artery, and common hepatic artery.
Three saccular dilatations were documented in the gastroepiploic artery: the largest in the left gastroepiploic artery, one in the middle third, and the smallest in the right gastroepiploic artery.

Coil embolization was performed via microcatheter to occlude the described aneurysms, with arteriographic controls showing successful exclusion of the gastroepiploic artery and preservation of other visceral branches.
After four days of hospital surveillance, the patient was discharged without pain and with recommendations and warning signs.

source_metadata.title: Internal Hernia as a Rare Complication of Acute Appendicitis

evidence_events.source_span: The patient is a 47-year-old female, known to previously have adenomyosis, which resulted in a total hysterectomy with bilateral salpingectomy two years ago. Added to that she underwent a laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy six years ago, and she has maintained her body mass index (BMI) within the normal range (BMI 23).

She presented to our general surgery clinic with a complaint of constant cramping and right lower abdominal pain that started two weeks ago. The patient provided a history of having acute generalized abdominal pain, sudden onset two weeks ago. It was all over the abdomen then shifted to her right lower side, with a positive history of nausea, vomiting, and subjective fever.
An abdominal ultrasound found a borderline appendix diameter (0.8 cm) with free fluid in the pelvis.

On presentation two weeks later, she had nausea, a few episodes of post-prandial vomiting, mild abdominal distension, loss of appetite, and decreased frequency of bowel movements without constipation. On examination, the abdomen was soft and lax with mild tenderness upon palpation of McBurney's point.
CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis with intravenous and oral contrast showed a right adnexal enhancing mass with no conclusive features and a query whirl sign over the same area.
Blood work showed normal inflammatory markers (C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate) and no leukocytosis on complete blood count.

Diagnostic laparoscopy revealed a long, inflamed appendix attached to the posterior wall of the cecum forming a ring-like structure through which 8 to 10 cm of the terminal ileum was passing, causing an internal hernia.
Hernia reduction was performed, and the appendix was freed, mesentery controlled, divided with a stapler, and removed with an endobag.
Histopathology revealed acute and subacute appendicitis with periappendicitis and no evidence of malignancy.

source_metadata.title: Post-Traumatic Intracranial Pseudoaneurysm Presenting as Epistaxis

evidence_events.source_span: A 24-year-old female presented to the ED from a local nursing home with right-sided Epistaxis and a spontaneous episode of large volume hemorrhage prior to transport.
The patient had 2 prior episodes of Epistaxis within the preceding 30 days which were not as severe.
Past medical history significant for traumatic brain injury due to a gunshot wound to the head six months prior, with complete right-sided paralysis and left cerebral hemisphere injury.

Initial CT imaging showed left-sided extracranial cerebral herniation, subarachnoid hemorrhage, subdural hematoma, and multiple skull base fractures on the right side including sphenoid wall laterally and anteriorly, medial wall of maxillary sinus, and medial sphenoid septum.
Emergent decompression with left-sided craniectomy and subdural hematoma evacuation was performed; bullet fragments left in place in left skull base and left frontal lobe.

Ventriculo-peritoneal (VP) shunt placement a week later due to right-to-left cerebral herniation with 13mm midline shift secondary to elevated intracranial pressures with dilated ventricles and no new hemorrhage.

On arrival to the ED, patient was in shock with heart rate 135, blood pressure 74/48, tachypneic with respiratory rate 48, saturating 100%, pale and ill-appearing, unable to provide history due to tracheostomy dependence.
Physical exam showed prior left-sided craniectomy, right body paralysis, left-sided eye misalignment, no active nasal hemorrhage, but gagging expelled about 300 mL of blood from oral cavity.

After blood product administration, hemodynamics stabilized and bleeding ceased; CT head revealed a progressive, expansile heterogeneous density mass in the posterior right ethmoidal sinus measuring 4.4 cm in diameter.
Initial labs showed hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL, leukocyte count 17.7 k/uL, platelet count 529 k/uL, prothrombin time 15.3 seconds, INR 1.4.
At receiving ED, nasal endoscopy revealed a pulsating mass projecting into the nasal cavity posteriorly without active hemorrhage; absorbable Sinufoam placed in right nares.
CTA of the head showed pseudoaneurysm of the cavernous portion of the right internal carotid artery without contrast extravasation.
New labs at receiving hospital showed hemoglobin 11.7 after blood transfusion.

Review of historical images showed pseudoaneurysm penetrating from previously fractured right lateral sphenoid wall and other bony fractures; mobilization of internal carotid artery due to skull fractures led to pseudoaneurysm growth.
Cerebral angiogram revealed large pseudoaneurysm originating from cavernous portion of right internal carotid artery; a daughter sac measuring 6.5 mm was identified as rupture source.
Endovascular treatment with ONYX embolization and coiling was performed achieving Raymond-Roy Occlusion Classification grade I.
Postoperatively, patient returned to baseline mental status without acute complaints and was discharged to nursing home.
At 1 month follow-up, repeat CTA revealed persistent occlusion of the pseudoaneurysm and patency of the internal carotid artery.

source_metadata.title: Vein of Galen aneurysmal malformation associated with brain abscess: A computed tomography case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 12-year-old male admitted to the Emergency Room (ER) at Kassala Teaching Hospital, Sudan complaining of convulsions, headache, and high-grade fever

A brain CT scan requested to rule out any potential reasons for his headache and convulsions. Siemens Healthineers CT scanner with 130 peak tube voltage (kVp) and an 18.18-second exposure time used for the scanning operation at Kassala Advanced Diagnostic Center. A primary NECT scan reveals a ring ill-defined lesion with a hypodense component in the right brain hemisphere surrounded by a diffuse area of brain edema, in addition to a hyperdense lesion posterior to the third ventricle compressing the lateral ventricles

A 5.7 × 4.7 × 5.3 cm right frontal peripherally enhancing cystic lesion is present, encircled by a huge vasogenic edema that is creating a mass effect, and a 1.5 cm midline shift to the left, which is suggestive of a brain abscess

Another avidly enhancing lesion seen within the third ventricle in continuation with straight sinus surrounded by extensive vascular loops consistent with an aneurysm of the vein of Galen, causing compression of the cerebral aqueduct with upstream mild hydrocephalus with dilation of both lateral ventricles

CT shows no established major arterial territory infarction, no intracerebral or subarachnoid hemorrhage, absence of an extra-axial collection, intact posterior fossa and brain stem, and absence of a localized bone lesion or fracture
Diagnosis was confirmed by 2 consultant radiologists
No further treatment received by the patient because he passed away 2 hours after the scanning procedures

source_metadata.title: An Atypical Presentation of a Saddle Embolism in the Setting of Malignancy
source_metadata.notes: Case report of a 52-year-old male with incidental renal cell carcinoma and silent saddle pulmonary embolism.

evidence_events.source_span: A 52-year-old male presented to the emergency department for evaluation of right lower quadrant abdominal pain. The patient was afebrile, hypertensive, and exhibited tenderness in the right lower quadrant upon palpation.

Computed tomography (CT) of the abdomen and pelvis without contrast revealed a distended appendix with mild inflammation consistent with acute appendicitis and an incidental right lower renal pole solid mass measuring 8.0 x 6.9 x 7.1 cm without cystic components or calcifications.
evidence_events.procedural_cue: CT abdomen and pelvis without contrast

evidence_events.source_span: MRI of the abdomen revealed an 8.4-cm renal mass with a capsule that was hypo-enhancing, heterogeneous, interpolar, and exophytic, with faint central T2 hyperintensity without clear evidence of vascular involvement or lymphadenopathy.
An appendectomy with a total right nephrectomy was performed without complication the following morning.
Biopsy revealed renal cell carcinoma.

Shortly after surgery, the patient developed hypoxia requiring supplemental oxygen with tachypnea. On postoperative Day 1, he reported dyspnea with exertion but no cough, chest pain, or pleuritic pain. There was no significant calf or thigh swelling, erythema, edema, tenderness, or palpable cords.
A pulmonary ventilation and perfusion scan was ordered due to concern that contrast would be nephrotoxic after recent nephrectomy, which revealed findings suggestive of a pulmonary embolus.

On postoperative Day 2, the patient was started on heparin at a prophylactic dose. Chest X-ray revealed minimal left basilar atelectasis. Laboratory analysis revealed decreased platelet count and decreased renal function as expected after right total nephrectomy.
Confirmatory chest CT pulmonary angiogram on postoperative Day 5 revealed large saddle emboli with smaller thrombi extending to segmental and subsegmental branches of multiple lobes.
A thrombectomy was performed the following day; no additional complications were noted. Oxygen saturations improved and the patient was discharged on apixaban.

source_metadata.title: Pulmonary Manifestation of Granulomatosis With Polyangiitis: A Challenging Case Presentation

evidence_events.source_span: 54-year-old female patient, with no notable pathological history, admitted for etiological assessment of diffuse interstitial lung disease associated with chronic anemia and altered general condition
Patient reported exposure to poultry (canaries and parakeets) and essential oil vapors for 20 years, stage II dyspnea, and low-grade hemoptysis for one year

Physical examination revealed pale skin and mucous membranes, discolored conjunctiva, tachycardia at 120 beats/minute, and oxygen saturation at 89% on ambient air; ENT, pleuropulmonary, and cardiac examinations were normal
Frontal chest X-ray revealed an interstitial syndrome with bilateral infiltrative opacities
Biological workup showed normochromic normocytic regenerative anemia, negative C-reactive protein, normal white blood count, elevated D-dimers, negative 24-hour proteinuria, and normal blood urea
Sputum tests for mycobacteria were negative
Anti-fowl antibody test (FEIA) was positive at 6 mg/L, possibly consistent with bird breeder's lung disease or non-specific reactivity

Immunological workup revealed presence of ANCA with cytoplasmic fluorescence (c-ANCA) positive (>1/20 U), and p-ANCA was negative, strongly suggesting GPA; ANA positive weak homogeneous type (1/160), anti-DNA antibodies negative

Chest computed tomography (CT) showed diffuse bilateral ground glass opacities with septal and non-septal thickening (crazy paving appearance), more marked in upper lobes with sparing of subpleural region, suggestive of alveolar hemorrhage
Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) and Perls' staining revealed predominantly histiocytic macrophagic alveolitis with hemosiderosis

Diagnosis of GPA was based on clinical signs (hemoptysis, anemia), imaging (multifocal ground glass with crazy paving), presence of siderophages in BAL, and ACR/EULAR 2022 classification criteria including c-ANCA positivity and chest X-ray abnormalities

Patient received high-dose intravenous methylprednisolone corticosteroids (1,000 mg/day) for three days, then oral prednisone with progressive dose reduction; symptoms improved with disappearance of asthenia and cough and improved oxygen saturation

source_metadata.title: An aggressive soft-tissue sarcoma of the extremity: A myxofibrosarcoma, grade 3 (FNCLCC system)

evidence_events.source_span: A 58-year-old patient came to the Radiology Department for an ambulatory diagnostic examination after he expressed discomfort to his primary care physician.

The patient stated that for 3 months he had already been experiencing the exponential growth of an expansive formation in the posterior region of his femoral region, which caused him great discomfort and embarrassment but not pain until that moment.
The formation was round, hard to touch, and not very mobile about the underlying planes and had, according to the patient, grown exponentially very rapidly in the last 40 days.

The radiologist proceeded with a US. At US examination, the formation appears extremely inhomogeneous, with disorganized hypo-an-echogenic areas; these lesions may appear as cysts but were justified by their high-water content. At Colour-Doppler evaluation the vascular signal appears to increase in its vicinity and inside it.

The patient, especially after the US examination, complained of pain in the pressure of the probe and due to the initial suspicion of bone involvement, underwent a CT of the femur to better characterize the round and expansive formation and the tissue that surrounds it. At CT, the round formation appeared smooth, with a tiny capsule and apparently in the context of the semitendinosus muscle causing mass effect and compression. The density was inhomogeneous.

An MRI was scheduled for the next day, but without contrast medium due to the high creatinine value. At MRI the lesion appeared lobulated and with an inhomogeneous signal: isointense in T1 and hyperintense in T2, STIR, and PD. Focal central areas, with an isointense signal, represent the necrotic or cystic portion. There wasn't visible the typical, and pathognomonic 'fascia tail sign'. Different areas of high cellularity, narrowing in diffusion, confirmed the suspicion of malignancy.
After some days, the excisional biopsy of the mass was performed, and the result was a myxofibrosarcoma of high grade (Grade 3 according to the FNCLCC system).
Before the excisional surgery, the patient underwent a cycle of radiotherapy to increase local control rates; the patient also ensured chemotherapy to shrink the large masses before surgery.
The patient is now being closely monitored while waiting for the operation, despite the fact that such masses have a high incidence of local recurrence even after extensive surgery.

source_metadata.title: Subscapularis pyomyositis, a rare cause of shoulder pain, in a patient without apparent risk factors: A case report

evidence_events.source_span: A 45-year-old female presented with severe pain in her left shoulder and limited mobility, which had persisted for nearly four weeks, leading to her admission to the Orthopaedic Department.

Clinical examination revealed tenderness upon deep palpation in the left upper posterior thoracic region and restricted range of motion of the affected shoulder. The patient held her shoulder in an internally rotated position, keeping her arm close to her chest. Any movement beyond this position significantly intensified her pain.

She had a normal body temperature and blood pressure of 120/58 mmHg, accompanied by a heart rate of 110 BPM; however, previous records showed a fever of 38.9 °C, for which she had been regularly taking paracetamol.

She denied using intravenous drugs or experiencing recent trauma to her left shoulder or chest wall, and did not exhibit any other symptoms or signs suggesting alternative sources of infection. She had no previous history of diabetes, immunocompromised conditions, foreign travel, or clinical signs of malignancy.

Upon admission, her C-reactive protein (CRP) concentration was 263 mg/L (normal <0.5 mg/L), and she exhibited leukocytosis with a white blood cell (WBC) count of 32.87 × 10^3/μL and neutrophilia (28 × 10^3/μL). Blood cultures taken on presentation later revealed no growth after 5 days.
Initial diagnosis of cervical disc prolapse was established based on cervical MRI scans. Shoulder X-ray assessment did not yield definitive results.
Ultrasonography of her left shoulder revealed no collections within the shoulder joint.
MRI without contrast revealed diffuse enlargement and a T2 hyperintense signal within the subscapularis muscle, raising suspicion of an inflammatory cause and possible neoplastic involvement.

MRI with contrast revealed diffuse enlargement and extensive necrosis with peripheral contrast enhancement of the subscapularis muscle, necrotic areas with peripheral enhancement in the infraspinatus, teres major, and pectoralis minor muscles, and multiple confluent peripherally enhancing necrotic areas in the left axilla. The scapula was normal with no osteomyelitis or infiltration. Diagnosis of shoulder pyomyositis was established.

On hospital day 2, WBC count rose to 50.1 × 10^3/μL with neutrophils 43 × 10^3/μL. Surgical drainage of the subscapularis muscle was performed via deltopectoral approach, draining approximately 50 mL of pus. Fluid and muscle tissue samples were sent for microbiology culture, sensitivity, and cytology.

Broad-spectrum antibiotics (piperacillin/tazobactam and vancomycin) were initiated pending culture results. Culture from pus confirmed Staphylococcus aureus. Antibiotics were adjusted to cefazoline and clindamycin based on sensitivity.

Second surgery performed for further drainage and debridement of fat necrosis and abscess pockets. Multiple washouts with saline, povidone-iodine, hydrogen peroxide, and vancomycin powder applied. Partial closure with vacuum dressing.

Shoulder arthroscopy revealed fibrous tissue, swelling, inflammation around the biceps, and thickened anterior capsule. Subscapularis was circumcised to release it and minimize acute adhesive capsulitis.

Subsequent surgeries included removal of necrotic tissue, irrigation, vacuum dressing application, and arthroscopic release of fibrous adhesions. Drains were inserted and later removed after inflammatory markers normalized.
At 3-month follow-up, patient had fully recovered with no pain or complications and regained nearly full range of motion.

source_metadata.title: Transdiaphragmatic sarcomatoid carcinoma of the lung: A case report

evidence_events.source_span: An 82-year-old female with a lifetime non-smoking history presented with generalized fatigue, fever, night sweats, cough, and pleuritic chest pain.
Laboratory testing was significant for a leukocytosis of 13.5 white blood cells per microliter and a viral panel negative for respiratory syncytial virus, influenza, and coronavirus disease 2019.

Computed tomography and magnetic resonance imaging revealed a large heterogeneous mass extending from the right pulmonary hilum through the diaphragm. The lesion involved segments VII and VIII of the liver. There was a small pleural effusion and no evidence of distant metastases.
Initial radiology reports suggested hepatic abscess, but there remained a high suspicion for neoplasm.

Percutaneous fine needle aspiration was performed. Biopsy revealed pulmonary sarcomatoid carcinoma. The mass demonstrated a high-grade, malignant spindle cell proliferation with occasional multinucleated giant cells and inter-lesional acute and chronic inflammation. Immunostains demonstrated the tumor cells to be diffusely positive for low molecular weight cytokeratin Cam 5.2.
Positron-emission tomography revealed no additional disease.
Surgical consult was obtained, but the decision was made to defer surgery given the transdiaphragmatic invasion.
She was begun on systemic chemotherapy with a platinum-based regimen. On follow-up 3 weeks later, she was tolerating treatment without complication.

source_metadata.title: Idiopathic Parotid Gland Abscess in a Pediatric Patient
source_metadata.notes: Case report of a 4-year-old girl with parotid abscess without identifiable cause.

evidence_events.source_span: The patient was a four-year-old female who initially presented to her outpatient pediatrician after her parents noticed a lump on her right neck. She had a remote history of a scratch on the same area from falling on a dog leash and a subjective fever for one day in the previous week, but had no other upper respiratory symptoms and no exposure to disease or animals. She was afebrile and well-appearing, and her physical exam was notable for an abrasion on the right neck and right tonsillar lymphadenopathy.
She was diagnosed with lymphadenitis and began a course of amoxicillin-clavulanate.

Two days later, she presented for follow-up, and her parents reported a subjective decrease in the size of the right tonsillar swelling. She was instructed to finish the 10-day course of amoxicillin-clavulanate.

One week after her initial presentation, she returned with worsening symptoms. The swelling on her right neck increased and began to have erythema and tenderness. She did not have fevers and was otherwise at baseline activity. Physical exam showed right anterior superior cervical lymphadenopathy with overlying erythema. Amoxicillin-clavulanate was stopped, and she was switched to clindamycin to cover for possible community-acquired methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.

An ultrasound showed a 2.2x2.0x1.5 cm collection in the right submandibular region with heterogeneous echogenicity, anechoic center, isoechoic rim, and increased vascularity at the periphery, determined to represent an abscess.

Physical exam at emergency department showed a large, mostly firm swelling posterior to the angle of the right jaw with dolor and rubor. White blood cell count and C-reactive protein were within normal limits.
evidence_events.temporal_cue: At the recommendation of her pediatrician

evidence_events.source_span: A CT scan of her neck with contrast showed a right neck infection confined to the parotid gland determined to be an isolated parotid gland abscess with no evidence of ductal disease or stones. No anatomical variations were seen.

She was admitted for surgical management, started on intravenous fluids and clindamycin. An incision and drainage were performed, and 5 ml of purulent fluid was drained. Gram stain, fungal cultures, and acid-fast bacilli cultures of the fluid returned negative.
The patient was transitioned to oral clindamycin and had complete resolution of the parotid swelling with no further symptoms on follow-up.

evidence_events.source_span: A 25-year-old Moroccan man with no pertinent prior medical history presented 2 years ago with a mass on his second toe, initially diagnosed as malignant melanoma based on biopsy without immunohistochemical analysis
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: Initial misdiagnosis likely due to biopsy artifact and lack of IHC

evidence_events.source_span: At 18 months later, the lesion recurred as a painless ulcerated tumor measuring 3 cm on the right second toe with fibrin and pigmented areas and surrounding erythematous nodular lesions

Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) showed a lesion resembling a giant cell tumor affecting the tendon sheaths with loss of tissue in the first and second phalanx and filling of the first and second interphalangeal gaps
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: MRI findings suggested differential diagnoses including GCT-TS, TGCT, PVNS, synovial sarcoma, or metastatic disease

evidence_events.source_span: Excision of a nodular tumor measuring 3.5 × 3 × 1.5 cm revealed a firm, lobulated, grayish neoplasm with hemorrhagic foci; microscopic examination showed tumor proliferation infiltrating the tendon arranged in lobules with epithelioid cells, ovoid irregular nuclei, pale eosinophilic cytoplasm, fibroinflammatory stroma, and no epidermal involvement
Immunohistochemical analysis showed positive staining for Melan-A, PS100, HMB-45, and SOX9 in tumor cells
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: IHC profile consistent with melanocytic differentiation

evidence_events.source_span: Additional IHC markers including cytokeratin (CK AE1–AE3 and CK19), FLI1, INI1, desmin, and smooth muscle actin (SMA) were negative except for persistent INI1 expression, helping to rule out rhabdoid tumor
Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) analysis for t(12;22)(q13;q12) translocation was not available in the clinical setting
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: Molecular confirmation unavailable

evidence_events.source_span: Based on clinical presentation, imaging, and immunohistochemical analysis, a definitive diagnosis of clear cell sarcoma of soft tissue was established, differentiating it from malignant melanoma
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: Diagnosis established without molecular confirmation

evidence_events.source_span: Physical examination and imaging showed no evidence of metastatic spread; tumor staged as IA per AJCC 2018
Patient underwent metatarsal amputation; at 12-month follow-up, remains disease-free with no recurrence or metastasis
evidence_events.hidden_reference_note: Favorable clinical course after treatment

diagnostic_reasoning_verbatim_spans: Initially misdiagnosed as malignant melanoma due to biopsy artifact and lack of immunohistochemical analysis
Recurrence with clinical and MRI findings localized tumor to tendon sheaths and phalanges
Histopathology showed lobulated tumor with epithelioid cells and fibroinflammatory stroma without epidermal involvement
Immunohistochemistry positive for melanocytic markers Melan-A, PS100, HMB-45, and SOX9; negative for other lineage markers
Molecular testing for t(12;22)(q13;q12) translocation unavailable
Diagnosis established based on clinical, imaging, and immunohistochemical data
No metastatic spread detected; tumor staged as IA
Patient treated with metatarsal amputation and remains disease-free at 12 months
diagnostic_reasoning_items: Initial biopsy limitations led to misdiagnosis
Recurrence prompted further imaging and excision
Histology and IHC profile consistent with clear cell sarcoma
Molecular confirmation unavailable but diagnosis supported by multimodal evidence
Staging showed localized disease without metastasis
Surgical treatment effective with favorable outcome
hidden_reference.final_diagnosis: Clear cell sarcoma of soft tissue
hidden_reference.diagnostic_reasoning: The diagnosis was established by integrating clinical presentation, imaging findings, histopathology, and immunohistochemical profile despite the absence of molecular confirmation. The tumor's localization, morphology, and melanocytic marker positivity distinguished it from malignant melanoma. The absence of metastasis and favorable response to surgical treatment further support the diagnosis.
hidden_reference.article_derived_evidence_summary: A young adult male presented with a pigmented toe mass initially diagnosed as melanoma. Recurrence led to MRI and excision revealing a lobulated tumor infiltrating tendon. IHC showed melanocytic marker positivity. Molecular testing was unavailable. Diagnosis of clear cell sarcoma was made, staged IA, and treated with amputation with favorable outcome.
diagnosis_synonyms_or_variants: clear cell sarcoma of soft tissues
